chapters.title: I. Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov
chapters.section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov was the third son of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov. In his day Fyodor Pavlovitch was a landowner well known in our district, and people here still remember him for his gloomy, tragic death, which happened thirteen years ago. I will describe it in its proper place. For now I will say only this. This “landowner”—that is what we called him, though he hardly spent a day of his life on his own estate—was a strange type, yet quite a common one: a man both abject and vicious and, at the same time, senseless. Still, he was one of those senseless men who handle their worldly affairs very well and, it seems, nothing else. Take Fyodor Pavlovitch. He started with next to nothing. His estate was tiny. He ran from one man’s dinner table to another and clung to his hosts as a toady. Yet when he died, it turned out he had a hundred thousand roubles in cash. And all the while he was one of the most senseless, fantastical fellows in the whole district. I repeat, this was not stupidity. Most of these fantastical fellows are shrewd and intelligent enough. It was just senselessness, and a peculiarly national form of it.

He married twice and had three sons. The eldest, Dmitri, was by his first wife; the other two, Ivan and Alexey, by his second. His first wife, Adelaïda Ivanovna, belonged to the Miüsovs, a fairly rich and distinguished noble family who were also landowners in our district. How did an heiress, and a beauty too, one of those spirited, clever girls so common in this generation (though found in the last as well), come to marry such a worthless, puny weakling, as we all called him? I won’t try to explain it. I knew a young lady of the last, “romantic” generation. For some years she nursed a mysterious passion for a gentleman whom she could easily have married at any time. Then she invented impossible obstacles to their union. One stormy night she threw herself from a high bank, almost a cliff, into a fairly deep and swift river, and drowned. She did it purely to satisfy her own whim, and to be like Shakespeare’s Ophelia. In fact, if that cliff, her chosen and favorite spot, had been less picturesque, if there had been a dull flat bank instead, the suicide would most likely never have happened. That is a fact, and over the last two or three generations there have probably been quite a few similar cases. Adelaïda Ivanovna Miüsov’s act was no doubt likewise an echo of other people’s ideas, and came from the frustration of having no mental freedom. Perhaps she wanted to show her independence as a woman, to defy class barriers and the tyranny of her family. And her pliable imagination persuaded her, we must suppose, for one brief moment, that Fyodor Pavlovitch, parasite though he was, was one of the bold, ironical spirits of that progressive age. He was in fact an ill-natured buffoon, nothing more. What gave the marriage its spice was that an elopement came first, and this greatly took Adelaïda Ivanovna’s fancy. Fyodor Pavlovitch’s situation at the time made him especially eager for any such enterprise, since he was desperate to make a career somehow. To attach himself to a good family and win a dowry was a tempting prospect. Of mutual love there was apparently none, neither in the bride nor in him, for all Adelaïda Ivanovna’s beauty. This was perhaps the one case of its kind in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s life, since he was always of a lustful temper and ready to chase after any skirt at the slightest encouragement. She seems to have been the only woman who did not appeal particularly to his senses.

Right after the elopement, Adelaïda Ivanovna saw in a flash that she felt nothing for her husband but contempt. The marriage showed its true face with extraordinary speed. The family got over the shock fairly quickly and handed the runaway bride her dowry. Still, husband and wife settled into a thoroughly disorderly life, with scenes between them all the time. People said the young wife showed far more generosity and dignity than Fyodor Pavlovitch. It is now known that he grabbed all her money, as much as twenty-five thousand roubles, the moment she received it, and those thousands were lost to her for good. For a long time he did all he could to get the little village and the rather fine town house, which were part of her dowry, signed over to himself by some legal deed. He would probably have managed it, simply because she was worn out and wanted to be rid of him, and because his relentless, shameless pestering filled her with contempt and loathing. But luckily Adelaïda Ivanovna’s family intervened and foiled his greed. It is a known fact that the couple often fought. Rumor said, though, that it was not Fyodor Pavlovitch who beat his wife but she who beat him, for she was a hot-tempered, bold, dark-browed, impatient woman of remarkable physical strength. At last she left the house and ran off with a penniless divinity student, leaving Mitya, a child of three, with her husband. Fyodor Pavlovitch at once filled the house with what amounted to a harem and gave himself up to drunken orgies. Between bouts he would drive all over the province, weeping to anyone who would listen that Adelaïda Ivanovna had left him. He gave details about his married life that were too disgraceful for a husband to tell. What seemed to delight him most and to flatter his vanity was to play the ridiculous role of the injured husband and show off his woes, with embellishments.

“Anyone would think you’d been promoted, Fyodor Pavlovitch, you look so pleased despite your sorrow,” scoffers said to him. Many even added that he was glad to have a new comic part to play the buffoon in, and that he pretended not to see how ludicrous he looked simply to make it funnier. But who knows, it may have been plain simplicity. At last he managed to find out where his runaway wife was. The poor woman, it turned out, was in Petersburg. She had gone there with her divinity student and plunged into a life of complete emancipation. Fyodor Pavlovitch at once started bustling around, preparing to go to Petersburg, though for what purpose he could not have said himself. He might really have gone. But once he had decided to go, he felt entitled right away to brace himself for the trip with another bout of reckless drinking. And just then his wife’s family received word that she had died in Petersburg. She had died quite suddenly in a garret. According to one story it was typhus; according to another, starvation. Fyodor Pavlovitch was drunk when he heard of his wife’s death. The story goes that he ran out into the street shouting for joy and raising his hands to Heaven: “Lord, now You let Your servant depart in peace.” Others say he wept like a little child, with no restraint at all, so that people felt sorry for him, repulsive as he was. Quite possibly both versions were true: he rejoiced at being set free, and at the same time wept for the woman who had freed him. As a rule, people, even wicked ones, are far more naïve and simple-hearted than we suppose. And we ourselves are, too.

chapters.title: II. He Gets Rid Of His Eldest Son
chapters.section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: You can easily picture what sort of father such a man would make, and how he would raise his children. He behaved exactly as you would expect. He abandoned the child of his marriage to Adelaïda Ivanovna entirely. It was not malice, and not resentment over his marriage; he simply forgot him. All the time he was wearing everyone out with his tears and complaints and turning his house into a sink of debauchery, a faithful family servant, Grigory, took the three-year-old Mitya under his wing. If Grigory hadn’t looked after him, nobody would even have changed the baby’s little shirt.

As it happened, the boy’s relatives on his mother’s side forgot him too, at first. His grandfather was dead. His widow, Mitya’s grandmother, had moved to Moscow and was gravely ill. The daughters were all married. So for almost a year Mitya stayed with old Grigory and lived with him in the servant’s cottage. Even if his father had remembered him (he could hardly have been altogether unaware that the boy existed), he would have sent him back to the cottage anyway, since a child would only have got in the way of his debauchery. Then a cousin of Mitya’s mother, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, returned from Paris. He lived abroad for many years afterwards, but at that time he was quite a young man and stood out among the Miüsovs as a man of enlightened ideas and European culture, who had lived in the capitals and abroad. Late in life he became a Liberal of the kind common in the forties and fifties. Over his career he had met many of the most Liberal men of his day, in Russia and abroad. He had known Proudhon and Bakunin personally. In his old age he loved to describe the three days of the Paris Revolution of February 1848, hinting that he had very nearly fought on the barricades himself. It was one of the fondest memories of his youth. He owned an independent property of about a thousand souls, reckoning in the old way. His splendid estate lay on the edge of our little town and bordered the lands of our famous monastery. Almost as soon as he inherited it, Pyotr Alexandrovitch started an endless lawsuit against the monastery over fishing rights in the river or wood-cutting in the forest, I don’t know which. He saw it as his duty, as a citizen and a man of culture, to open an attack on the “clericals.” He heard the whole story of Adelaïda Ivanovna, whom, of course, he remembered, and in whom he had once taken an interest. When he learned that Mitya existed, he stepped in, for all his youthful indignation and contempt for Fyodor Pavlovitch. He met Fyodor Pavlovitch for the first time and told him bluntly that he wanted to take over the child’s education. Long afterwards he used to tell, as a telling detail, that when he began to speak of Mitya, Fyodor Pavlovitch stared for some time as if he didn’t understand which child was meant, and even seemed surprised to hear he had a little son in the house. The story may be exaggerated, but it must have been something like the truth.

All his life Fyodor Pavlovitch loved to act, to take on some unexpected role suddenly, sometimes for no reason at all and even to his own obvious disadvantage, as in this case. Many people have this trait, though, and some of them are very clever, unlike Fyodor Pavlovitch. Pyotr Alexandrovitch pushed the matter through energetically. He was named joint guardian of the child with Fyodor Pavlovitch. The boy had a small property, a house and land, left to him by his mother. Mitya did indeed pass into this cousin’s keeping. But the cousin had no family of his own, and as soon as he had secured the income from his estates he was in a hurry to get back to Paris. So he left the boy with one of his cousins, a lady in Moscow. Then, settled permanently in Paris, he forgot the child too, especially once the February Revolution broke out, which left an impression on him that he remembered for the rest of his life. The Moscow lady died, and Mitya went to live with one of her married daughters. I believe he changed homes a fourth time later. I won’t go into that now, because I shall have a great deal to tell later about Fyodor Pavlovitch’s firstborn. For now I must stick to the most essential facts about him, without which I could not begin my story.

To begin with, this Mitya, or rather Dmitri Fyodorovitch, was the only one of Fyodor Pavlovitch’s three sons who grew up believing he had property and would be independent when he came of age. His boyhood and youth were unsettled. He didn’t finish at the gymnasium. He got into a military school, then went to the Caucasus, was promoted, fought a duel, was reduced to the ranks, won promotion again, lived wildly and spent a good deal of money. He received no income from Fyodor Pavlovitch until he came of age, and until then he ran up debts. He saw his father and met him for the first time when he came of age. He had come to our neighborhood on purpose to settle with him over his property. He seems not to have liked his father. He stayed only a short time and hurried away. All he had got was a sum of money and an agreement for future payments from the estate. About the estate’s income and value he could not (this is worth noting) get any statement from his father on that occasion. Fyodor Pavlovitch noticed then, for the first time (this too should be noted), that Mitya had a vague and exaggerated idea of his property. Fyodor Pavlovitch was perfectly pleased with this, as it suited his own plans. He concluded only that the young man was frivolous, unruly, violent in his passions, impatient and dissipated, and that he would be content as long as he got ready money, though only for a short time, of course. So Fyodor Pavlovitch began to exploit this, sending him small handouts now and then, in installments. In the end, four years later, Mitya lost patience and came to our little town a second time to settle accounts with his father once and for all. To his amazement, he found he had nothing. Even getting an account was difficult. He had received the whole value of his property in cash from Fyodor Pavlovitch and might even be in debt to him. By various agreements that he had entered into of his own free will at various earlier dates, he had no right to expect anything more. And so on, and so on. The young man was stunned. He suspected deceit and fraud and was almost out of his mind. And this very situation led to the catastrophe, the story of which is the subject of my first introductory tale, or rather its outward side. But before I come to that tale, I must say a little about Fyodor Pavlovitch’s other two sons and where they came from.

chapters.title: III. The Second Marriage And The Second Family
chapters.section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: Soon after getting his four-year-old Mitya off his hands, Fyodor Pavlovitch married again. The marriage lasted eight years. His second wife, Sofya Ivanovna, was also a very young girl. He found her in another province, where he had gone on some small piece of business with a Jew. Fyodor Pavlovitch was a drunkard and a vicious debauchee, but he never failed to invest his capital, and he ran his business affairs very successfully, though, no doubt, without too many scruples. Sofya Ivanovna was the daughter of an obscure deacon. She had been an orphan with no relations since early childhood. She grew up in the house of a general’s widow, a wealthy old lady of good standing, who was at once her benefactress and her tormentor. I do not know the details. I have only heard that the orphan girl, a meek and gentle creature, was once cut down from a noose that she had tied to a nail in the loft. That was how badly she suffered from the whims and endless nagging of this old woman, who was apparently not bad-hearted, but had turned into an unbearable tyrant out of sheer idleness.

Fyodor Pavlovitch proposed to her. People asked about him, and he was turned down. But, just as with his first wife, he then suggested to the orphan girl that they elope. There is little doubt that she would never have married him if she had learned a little more about him in time. But she lived in another province, and besides, what could a girl of sixteen know, except that she would rather be at the bottom of the river than stay with her benefactress? So the poor child swapped a benefactress for a benefactor. Fyodor Pavlovitch got not a penny this time, because the general’s widow was furious. She gave them nothing and cursed them both. But he had never counted on a dowry. What had tempted him was the girl’s remarkable beauty, and above all her look of innocence. That look had a peculiar pull on a vicious profligate who, until then, had only admired the coarser kinds of feminine beauty.

“Those innocent eyes slit my soul up like a razor,” he used to say later, with his loathsome snigger. In so depraved a man, of course, that might mean no more than lust. Since he had got no dowry with his wife, and had, so to speak, taken her “from the noose,” he did not bother to be polite to her. He made her feel she had “wronged” him. Her extraordinary meekness and submissiveness gave him the chance to trample on the most basic decencies of married life. He brought loose women into his house and held drunken orgies in front of his wife. To show how far things went, I should mention that Grigory sided with the new mistress. He was a gloomy, stupid, stubborn, argumentative servant who had always hated his first mistress, Adelaïda Ivanovna. Now he took up the new wife’s cause. He abused Fyodor Pavlovitch in a way that hardly became a servant, and once he broke up the revels and chased all the disorderly women out of the house. In the end this unhappy young woman, who had lived in terror since childhood, fell ill with the kind of nervous disease found most often in peasant women, who are said to be “possessed by devils.” After terrible fits of hysterics she sometimes even lost her reason. Yet she bore Fyodor Pavlovitch two sons, Ivan and Alexey, the first in the first year of the marriage and the second three years later. When she died, little Alexey was in his fourth year. Strange as it sounds, I know he remembered his mother for the rest of his life, like a dream, of course. At her death, almost exactly the same thing happened to the two little boys as to their elder brother Mitya. Their father forgot them completely and abandoned them. The same Grigory looked after them, and they lived in his cottage. That is where the tyrannical old lady who had raised their mother found them. She was still alive, and in all those eight years she had never forgotten the insult done to her. All that time she had been getting exact reports on how her Sofya lived. When she heard of the girl’s illness and her hideous surroundings, she announced to her servants, two or three times, out loud:
“It serves her right. God has punished her for her ingratitude.”

Exactly three months after Sofya Ivanovna’s death, the general’s widow suddenly turned up in our town and drove straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house. She spent only half an hour in the town, but she got a great deal done. It was evening. Fyodor Pavlovitch, who hadn’t seen her in those eight years, came in to meet her drunk. The story goes that the moment she saw him, without a word of explanation, she gave him two good, resounding slaps across the face, grabbed him by a tuft of hair, and shook him up and down three times. Then, without a word, she went straight to the cottage where the two boys were. At the first glance she saw that they were unwashed and in dirty linen, and at once she boxed Grigory’s ears as well. She announced that she was taking both children away, wrapped them up just as they were in a rug, put them in her carriage, and drove off to her own town. Grigory took the blow like a devoted slave, without a word. As he showed the old lady out to her carriage, he gave her a low bow and said solemnly that “God would repay her for the orphans.” “You are a blockhead all the same,” the old lady shouted at him as she drove away.

Fyodor Pavlovitch thought it over and decided this was all for the best. He gave the general’s widow his formal consent to whatever she proposed for his children’s education. As for the slaps she had given him, he drove all over town telling the story.

As it turned out, the old lady died soon afterward, but in her will she left the boys a thousand roubles each “for their instruction, and so that all be spent on them exclusively, with the condition that it be so portioned out as to last till they are twenty-one, for it is more than adequate provision for such children. If other people think fit to throw away their money, let them.” I have not read the will myself, but I heard that there was something odd of the kind in it, very whimsically worded. The main heir was Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, the Marshal of Nobility of the province, and he proved to be an honest man. He wrote to Fyodor Pavlovitch and saw right away that there was nothing to be got out of him for the children’s education. (Fyodor Pavlovitch never actually said no, but only stalled, as he always did in such cases, and was even, at times, gushingly sentimental.) So Yefim Petrovitch took an interest in the orphans himself. He grew especially fond of the younger one, Alexey, who lived for a long time as a member of his family. I ask the reader to note this from the start. The young people owed their schooling and upbringing to Yefim Petrovitch more than to anyone else. He was a man of a generosity and humanity one rarely meets. He left the two thousand roubles that the general’s widow had left them untouched, so that by the time they came of age, the interest had doubled their shares. He paid for both their educations out of his own pocket, and he certainly spent far more than a thousand roubles on each. I will not give a detailed account of their boyhood and youth, only a few of the most important events. About the elder, Ivan, I will say only that he grew into a rather sullen, reserved boy, though far from timid. At ten he had understood that they lived not in their own home but on other people’s charity, and that their father was a man it was shameful to speak of. From very early on, almost from infancy (so they say, at least), the boy showed a brilliant and unusual talent for learning. I don’t know exactly why, but he left Yefim Petrovitch’s family when he was barely thirteen, and went to a Moscow gymnasium, where he boarded with an experienced and famous teacher who was an old friend of Yefim Petrovitch. Ivan used to say later that it was all because of Yefim Petrovitch’s “ardor for good works.” Yefim Petrovitch was carried away by the idea that a boy of genius ought to be trained by a teacher of genius. But by the time the young man finished at the gymnasium and entered the university, neither Yefim Petrovitch nor this teacher was alive. Yefim Petrovitch had made no arrangement for paying out the tyrannical old lady’s legacy, which had grown from one thousand to two. The money was held up by the red tape that is unavoidable in Russia, and for his first two years at the university the young man was hard pressed, because he had to keep himself the whole time he was studying. It should be noted that he did not even try to contact his father. Perhaps this was pride, or contempt. Perhaps it was cool common sense, which told him he would get no real help from such a father. Whatever the reason, the young man was not at all downhearted, and he found work. At first he gave sixpenny lessons, and later he placed short items about street incidents in the newspapers, signed “Eye-Witness.” These items, it was said, were so lively and spicy that the papers soon took them. This alone showed the young man’s practical and intellectual superiority over the crowds of needy, unlucky students of both sexes who haunt the offices of newspapers and journals, unable to think of anything better than endless begging for copying work and translations from the French. Once Ivan Fyodorovitch had made contact with the editors, he always kept it up. In his later years at the university he published brilliant reviews of books on various specialized subjects, and became well known in literary circles. But only in his last year did he suddenly catch the attention of a much wider readership, so that a great many people noticed him and remembered him. It was a rather curious episode. He had just left the university and was getting ready to go abroad on his two thousand roubles, when Ivan Fyodorovitch published a strange article in one of the major journals. It attracted general notice. The subject was one he could have been supposed to know nothing about, since he was a student of natural science. It dealt with a question being debated everywhere at the time: the status of the ecclesiastical courts. After going through several opinions on the matter, he went on to give his own view. What struck people most about the article was its tone and its unexpected conclusion. Many in the Church party took him without question as one of their own. Yet the secularists, and even atheists, joined them in applauding him. In the end, some shrewd people suggested that the article was nothing but an impudent satirical burlesque. I mention this episode in particular because the article made its way into the famous monastery in our neighborhood. The monks there took a special interest in the question of the ecclesiastical courts, and the article left them completely bewildered. When they learned the author’s name, they were interested to find that he was a native of our town and the son of “that Fyodor Pavlovitch.” And just then the author himself showed up among us.

Why Ivan Fyodorovitch had come to us, I remember asking myself at the time with some uneasiness. That fateful visit was the first step toward so many consequences, and I have never fully explained it to myself. It seemed strange on the face of it. Here was a young man so learned, so proud, and apparently so careful, suddenly visiting an infamous house and a father who had ignored him all his life. The father hardly knew him, never gave him a thought, and would not have given him money under any circumstances, though he was always afraid that his sons Ivan and Alexey would turn up asking for it. And now the young man was staying in the house of such a father. He had been living there for two months, and the two got on perfectly. Many others besides me were astonished by this last fact. Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, who has been mentioned already, the cousin of Fyodor Pavlovitch’s first wife, happened to be in the neighborhood again, visiting his estate. He had come from Paris, where he lived permanently. I remember that he was more surprised than anyone when he met the young man. Ivan interested him greatly. Sometimes he argued with him, and not without an inner pang he measured his own learning against Ivan’s.

“He is proud,” he used to say. “He will never be short of pennies. He has money enough to go abroad right now. What does he want here? Anyone can see he hasn’t come for money, because his father would never give him any. He has no taste for drink and dissipation, and still his father can’t do without him. They get on so well together!”

That was the truth. The young man had a clear hold over his father, who really did seem to be behaving more decently, and at times even seemed ready to do as his son said, though he was often extremely, even spitefully, contrary.

We learned only later that Ivan had come partly at the request, and in the interest, of his elder brother Dmitri. He met Dmitri for the first time on this visit, though before leaving Moscow he had corresponded with him about an important matter that mattered more to Dmitri than to himself. The reader will learn in due time exactly what that business was. Even after I knew about this particular circumstance, though, Ivan Fyodorovitch still struck me as an enigmatic figure, and his visit still seemed rather mysterious to me.
I may add that Ivan then looked like a go-between for his father and his elder brother Dmitri. Dmitri was in open quarrel with their father and was even planning to sue him.

The family, I repeat, was now together for the first time, and some of its members were meeting for the first time in their lives. The younger brother, Alexey, had already been among us a year, having been the first of the three to arrive. It is about this brother Alexey that I find it hardest to speak in this introduction. Still, I must give some preliminary account of him, if only to explain one queer fact: I have to present my hero to the reader in the cassock of a novice. Yes, he had spent the past year in our monastery, and seemed willing to be shut up there for the rest of his life.

chapters.title: IV. The Third Son, Alyosha
chapters.section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: He was only twenty. His brother Ivan was in his twenty-fourth year at the time, and their eldest brother Dmitri was twenty-seven. First I must explain that this young man, Alyosha, was no fanatic and, in my opinion at least, not even a mystic. I may as well state my whole opinion at the outset. He was simply a lover of humanity from early on. He took up the monastic life only because, at that time, it struck him as the ideal way out for his soul, which was struggling up from the darkness of worldly wickedness toward the light of love. It struck him that way because he believed he had found in the monastery an extraordinary being, our celebrated elder, Zossima, and he had attached himself to Zossima with all the warm first love of his ardent heart. I don’t deny that he was very strange even then, and had been since the cradle. I have mentioned already that he lost his mother in his fourth year, yet remembered her all his life—her face, her caresses, “as though she stood living before me.” Such memories can reach back, as everyone knows, even to the age of two. But they seldom last a whole lifetime as isolated spots of light in the darkness, like the one corner left of a huge picture that has faded and vanished everywhere else. That is how it was with him. He remembered a still summer evening and an open window, with the slanting rays of the setting sun (that he recalled most vividly of all). In a corner of the room was the holy image with a lighted lamp before it, and on her knees in front of the image was his mother, sobbing hysterically, crying and moaning. She snatched him up in both arms and squeezed him so tight it hurt, and prayed for him to the Mother of God, holding him out in both arms toward the image as if to place him under the Mother’s protection ... and suddenly a nurse runs in and snatches him away from her in terror. That was the picture! And Alyosha remembered his mother’s face at that moment. He used to say it was frenzied but beautiful, as he remembered it. He rarely wanted to speak of this memory to anyone, though. As a child and a youth he was far from outgoing, and he talked very little. That was not from shyness or a sullen dislike of company. It was from something else, a kind of inner preoccupation, wholly his own and having nothing to do with other people, yet so important to him that it made him seem to forget them. But he was fond of people. All his life he seemed to trust people completely, and still no one ever thought him a simpleton or naïve. Something about him made you feel at once (and this held true all his life) that he had no wish to sit in judgment on others—that he would never presume to criticize, and would never condemn anyone for anything. He seemed, in fact, to accept everything without the least condemnation, although he often grieved bitterly. So thoroughly was this so, that even in his earliest youth nothing could surprise or frighten him. At twenty he came to his father’s house, a perfect sink of filthy debauchery. Chaste and pure as he was, he simply withdrew in silence whenever the sight became unbearable, and he showed no sign of contempt or condemnation. His father had once lived as a dependent himself, so he was touchy and quick to take offense, and he received Alyosha at first with distrust and sullenness. “He doesn’t say much,” he would say, “and he thinks the more.” But soon—within two weeks, in fact—he was embracing and kissing Alyosha terribly often, with drunken tears and sottish sentimentality. Still, he plainly felt a real and deep affection for him, the like of which he had never been capable of feeling for anyone before.

Everyone, in fact, loved this young man wherever he went, and that had been so since his earliest childhood. When he entered the household of his patron and benefactor, Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, he won the hearts of the whole family, who came to look on him quite as their own child. Yet he went to live there at such a tender age that he could not have been calculating or scheming to win affection. The gift of making himself loved immediately and unconsciously was simply inborn in him, part of his nature, so to speak. It was the same at school, though he seemed exactly the sort of child that other children distrust, sometimes ridicule, and even dislike. He was dreamy, for example, and rather solitary. From his earliest years he loved to creep into a corner and read, and yet he was a general favorite all the time he was at school. He was seldom playful or merry, but you could see at a glance that this was not sullenness. On the contrary, he was cheerful and good-tempered. He never tried to show off among his schoolmates. Perhaps for that reason, he was afraid of no one, yet the boys realized at once that he took no pride in his fearlessness and seemed not to know he was bold and brave. He never resented an insult. An hour after being wronged, he might speak to the one who had done it, or answer his question, with a look as trusting and open as if nothing had passed between them. It was not that he seemed to have forgotten the insult, or made up his mind to forgive it. He simply did not count it as an insult, and this completely won over the boys and captivated them. He had one trait that made all his schoolmates, from the lowest class to the highest, want to mock him—not out of malice, but because it amused them. That trait was a wild, fanatical modesty and chastity. He could not stand to hear certain words and certain talk about women. Unhappily, there are “certain” words and talk that no one can stamp out in schools. Boys who are pure in mind and heart, hardly more than children, love to discuss among themselves, and even out loud, things and pictures and images that even soldiers would think twice about mentioning. More than that, much that soldiers know nothing of is familiar to quite small children of our educated and upper classes. It isn’t moral depravity, or any real inner corruption and cynicism, but it has the look of those, and among the boys it is often considered refined, subtle, daring, and worth copying. When they saw Alyosha Karamazov stick his fingers in his ears whenever they talked of “that,” they would sometimes crowd around him, pull his hands away, and shout filth into both his ears. He would struggle, slip down onto the floor, and try to hide, without saying one word of abuse, and endure their insults in silence. In the end, though, they left him alone and stopped teasing him as a “regular girl.” What’s more, they came to view it with pity, as a weakness. In class he was always among the best, but never first.

When Yefim Petrovitch died, Alyosha had two more years to go at the provincial gymnasium. The inconsolable widow left almost at once for a long stay in Italy, taking her whole family, which consisted only of women and girls. Alyosha moved into the house of two distant relations of Yefim Petrovitch, ladies he had never met. He did not know himself on what terms he lived with them. It was very typical of him, in fact, never to care whose money was paying for him. In this he was a striking contrast to his elder brother Ivan, who fought poverty through his first two years at the university, kept himself by his own efforts, and had felt bitterly, from childhood on, that he lived at his benefactor’s expense. But I don’t think we should judge this odd trait of Alyosha’s too harshly. Anyone who knew him even slightly would have seen that Alyosha was one of those young men, almost the religious-enthusiast type, who would give away a sudden large fortune to the first person who asked, whether for good works or perhaps to some clever rogue. In general he hardly seemed to know the value of money—not in the literal sense, of course. When he was given pocket money, which he never asked for, he was either terribly careless with it and spent it in a moment, or he held on to it for weeks, not knowing what to do with it.
In later years Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, a man very sensitive about money and middle-class honesty, passed the following judgment on Alyosha, once he had got to know him:

“Here is perhaps the one man in the world you could leave alone without a penny, in the middle of an unknown city of a million people, and he would come to no harm. He wouldn’t die of cold or hunger, since someone would feed and shelter him at once. And if no one did, he would find shelter himself, and it would cost him no effort or humiliation. Sheltering him would be no burden to anyone; it would more likely be seen as a pleasure.”

He did not finish his studies at the gymnasium. With a year of the course still to go, he suddenly told the ladies that he was off to see his father about a plan that had come into his head. They were sorry, and did not want to let him go. The trip was not an expensive one, but the ladies would not let him pawn his watch, a parting gift from his benefactor’s family. They gave him plenty of money, and even fitted him out with new clothes and linen. He gave half of the money back, though, saying he intended to go third class. When he reached town, he did not answer his father’s first question, why he had come before finishing school, and he seemed, so they say, unusually thoughtful. Soon it became clear that he was looking for his mother’s tomb. He more or less admitted at the time that this was the only reason for his visit. Still, it can hardly have been the whole reason. More likely he did not understand himself, and could not have said, what had suddenly stirred in his soul and drawn him irresistibly down a new road, unknown but unavoidable. Fyodor Pavlovitch could not show him where his second wife was buried. He had never visited her grave since the day he threw earth on her coffin, and over the years he had forgotten altogether where she lay.

Fyodor Pavlovitch, by the way, had been away from our town for some time before this. Three or four years after his wife died, he went off to the south of Russia and eventually turned up in Odessa, where he spent several years. At first, as he put it, he got to know “a lot of low Jews, Jewesses, and Jewkins,” and he ended up being welcomed by “Jews high and low alike.” We may suppose that it was in this period that he developed a peculiar knack for making money and hoarding it. He came back to our town for good only three years before Alyosha arrived. His old acquaintances found him terribly aged, though he was by no means an old man. He carried himself not exactly with more dignity, but with more effrontery. The old buffoon now had an insolent itch to turn other people into buffoons. His depravity with women was not merely what it had been, but even more revolting. In a short time he opened a great number of new taverns in the district. It was plain that he had perhaps a hundred thousand roubles, or not much less. Many people in the town and the district were soon in his debt, and had put up good security, naturally. Lately, too, he looked somehow bloated. He seemed more irresponsible and more erratic, and had sunk into a sort of incoherence: he would start one thing and go on with another, as though he were letting himself go altogether. He got drunk more and more often. And without that same servant Grigory, who by then had aged a good deal himself, and who sometimes looked after him almost like a tutor, Fyodor Pavlovitch might have landed in terrible scrapes. Alyosha’s arrival seemed to touch even his moral side, as though something that had long been dead in his soul had woken up in this prematurely old man.

“Do you know,” he often said, looking at Alyosha, “you’re like her, ‘the crazy woman’”—that was what he called his dead wife, Alyosha’s mother. It was Grigory who showed Alyosha the “crazy woman’s” grave. He took him to our town cemetery and pointed out, in a remote corner, a cast-iron tombstone, cheap but decently kept. It bore the name and age of the dead woman and the date of her death, with a four-line verse underneath, the sort commonly seen on old-fashioned middle-class graves. To Alyosha’s amazement, the tomb turned out to be Grigory’s doing. He had put it up over the poor “crazy woman’s” grave at his own expense, after Fyodor Pavlovitch, whom he had often pestered about the grave, left for Odessa and abandoned both the grave and all his memories. Alyosha showed no particular emotion at the sight of his mother’s grave. He just listened to Grigory’s detailed and solemn account of how the tomb was built, stood there with his head bowed, and walked away without a word. It was perhaps a year before he went to the cemetery again. But this little episode had an effect on Fyodor Pavlovitch—and a very original one. He suddenly took a thousand roubles to our monastery to pay for requiems for his wife’s soul. Not for the second wife, Alyosha’s mother, the “crazy woman,” though, but for the first, Adelaïda Ivanovna, the one who used to thrash him. That same evening he got drunk and ran down the monks to Alyosha. He was far from religious himself; he had probably never set so much as a penny candle in front of a saint’s image. Strange surges of sudden feeling and sudden thought are common in men of that type.

I have already said that he looked bloated. His face by now carried unmistakable marks of the life he had led. There were long fleshy bags under his small eyes, which were always insolent, suspicious, and ironical, and a mass of deep wrinkles in his little fat face. His Adam’s apple hung below his sharp chin like a great fleshy goiter, which gave him a peculiar, repulsive, sensual look. On top of that came a long, rapacious mouth with full lips, and between them you could see little stumps of black, rotten teeth. He slobbered whenever he began to speak. He enjoyed making jokes about his own face, though I believe he was quite pleased with it. He liked above all to point to his nose, which was not very large, but very fine and noticeably hooked. “A regular Roman nose,” he would say, “and with my goiter I look just like an ancient Roman patrician of the decadent period.” He seemed proud of it.

Soon after visiting his mother’s grave, Alyosha suddenly announced that he wanted to enter the monastery, and that the monks were ready to accept him as a novice. He explained that he wanted this very much, and that he was solemnly asking for his father’s consent. The old man knew that the elder Zossima, who lived in the monastery’s hermitage, had made a special impression on his “gentle boy.”

“Well, he’s the most honest monk of the lot, of course,” he remarked, after listening to Alyosha in thoughtful silence, and seeming hardly surprised at the request. “H’m!... So that’s where you want to be, my gentle boy?”

He was half drunk, and suddenly he broke into his slow, half-drunken grin, which had a bit of cunning and tipsy slyness in it. “H’m!... I had a feeling you’d end up in something like this. Would you believe it? You were making straight for it. Well, of course you have your own two thousand. That’s a dowry for you. And I’ll never desert you, my angel. I’ll pay whatever they need for you there, if they ask. But if they don’t ask, why should we bother them? What do you say? You know, you spend money like a canary, two grains a week. H’m!... Do you know that near one monastery there’s a place outside the town where every baby knows that nobody lives but ‘the monks’ wives,’ as they’re called? Thirty women, I believe. I’ve been there myself. You know, it’s interesting in its own way, of course, as a change. The trouble is, it’s awfully Russian. No French women there. Of course they could get them fast enough, they’ve got plenty of money. If word gets out, they’ll turn up. Well, here there’s nothing of the sort, no ‘monks’ wives,’ and two hundred monks. They’re honest. They keep the fasts. I’ll admit it.... H’m.... So you want to be a monk? And do you know, I’m sorry to lose you, Alyosha; would you believe it, I’ve really got fond of you? Well, it’s a good chance. You’ll pray for us sinners; we’ve sinned too much here. I’ve always wondered who would pray for me, and whether there’s anyone in the world who would. My dear boy, I’m awfully stupid about that. You wouldn’t believe it. Awfully. You see, stupid as I am about it, I keep thinking, I keep thinking—now and then, of course, not all the time. I can’t imagine, I think, that the devils would forget to drag me down to hell with their hooks when I die. Then I wonder—hooks? Where would they get them? What from? Iron hooks? Where do they forge them? Have they got some sort of foundry down there? The monks in the monastery probably believe there’s a ceiling in hell, for instance. Now, I’m ready to believe in hell, but without a ceiling. That makes it more refined, more enlightened, more Lutheran, that is. And after all, what difference does it make whether it has a ceiling or not? But there’s a damnable question hidden in it, you know? If there’s no ceiling, there can be no hooks, and if there are no hooks, the whole thing collapses, which is unlikely too, because then nobody would drag me down to hell, and if they don’t drag me down, where’s the justice in the world? _Il faudrait les inventer_, those hooks, on purpose for me alone, because if you only knew, Alyosha, what a blackguard I am.”
“But there are no hooks there,” Alyosha said, looking at his father gently and seriously.

“Yes, yes, only the shadows of hooks, I know, I know. That’s how a Frenchman described hell: ‘_J’ai vu l’ombre d’un cocher qui avec l’ombre d’une brosse frottait l’ombre d’une carrosse._’ How do you know there are no hooks, darling? Once you’ve lived with the monks, you’ll change your tune. But go and find out the truth there, and then come and tell me. Anyway, it’s easier to go to the other world if you know what’s there. Besides, it’ll be more fitting for you with the monks than here with me, a drunken old man, and young harlots ... though you’re like an angel, nothing touches you. I expect nothing will touch you there either. That’s why I’m letting you go, because I hope so. You’ve got all your wits about you. You’ll burn, and you’ll burn out; you’ll be healed and come back again. And I’ll wait for you. I feel you’re the only creature in the world who hasn’t condemned me. My dear boy, I feel it, you know. I can’t help feeling it.”
And he actually started blubbering. He was sentimental. He was wicked and sentimental.

chapters.title: V. Elders
chapters.section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: Some of my readers may imagine that my young man was a sickly, ecstatic, underdeveloped creature, a pale, consumptive dreamer. Quite the opposite: at this time Alyosha was a sturdy, red-cheeked, clear-eyed lad of nineteen, glowing with health. He was very handsome, too. He was graceful and moderately tall, with dark brown hair and a regular, rather long, oval face. His dark gray eyes were wide-set and shining. He was very thoughtful and seemed very serene. I will be told, perhaps, that red cheeks do not rule out fanaticism and mysticism. But I think Alyosha was more of a realist than anyone. Oh, no doubt in the monastery he fully believed in miracles, but to my mind miracles are never a stumbling block to a realist. It is not miracles that lead realists to belief. The true realist, if he is an unbeliever, will always find the strength and ability to disbelieve in the miraculous. Faced with a miracle as an undeniable fact, he would sooner doubt his own senses than accept it. And if he does accept it, he accepts it as a fact of nature that he had simply not recognized before. In the realist, faith does not spring from the miracle; the miracle springs from faith. Once a realist believes, his very realism obliges him to admit the miraculous too. The Apostle Thomas said he would not believe until he saw, but when he did see, he said, “My Lord and my God!” Was it the miracle that forced him to believe? Most likely not. He believed only because he wanted to believe, and perhaps in his secret heart he fully believed even when he said, “I do not believe till I see.”

I will be told, perhaps, that Alyosha was stupid, undeveloped, that he had not finished his studies, and so on. It is true that he did not finish his studies, but to call him stupid or dull would be a great injustice. I will simply repeat what I said above. He chose this path only because at that time it alone struck his imagination, and it offered his soul an ideal escape from darkness into light. Add to that that he was, to some extent, a young man of our last epoch. That is, he was honest by nature. He wanted the truth, sought it and believed in it, and wanted to serve it at once with all the strength of his soul. He looked for immediate action and was ready to sacrifice everything for it, even life itself. Unfortunately, these young men fail to understand that sacrificing one’s life is, in many cases, the easiest of all sacrifices, and that to sacrifice, for instance, five or six years of their seething youth to hard and tedious study, if only to multiply tenfold their power to serve the truth and the cause they have set as their goal, is a sacrifice utterly beyond the strength of many of them. The path Alyosha chose ran in the opposite direction, but he chose it with the same thirst for swift achievement. As soon as he thought seriously, he was convinced that God and immortality exist, and at once he said to himself, instinctively: “I want to live for immortality, and I will accept no compromise.” In the same way, if he had decided that God and immortality did not exist, he would at once have become an atheist and a socialist. For socialism is not merely the labor question. It is above all the atheistic question, the question of the form atheism takes today, the question of the tower of Babel built without God, not to climb from earth to heaven but to bring heaven down to earth. Alyosha would have found it strange and impossible to go on living as before. It is written: “Give all that thou hast to the poor and follow Me, if thou wouldst be perfect.”

Alyosha said to himself: “I can’t give two roubles instead of ‘all,’ and only go to mass instead of ‘following Him.’” Perhaps his childhood memories drew him to our monastery, where his mother may once have taken him to mass. Perhaps the slanting sunlight and the holy image his poor “crazy” mother had held him up to still worked on his imagination. Brooding on these things, he may have come to us only to find out whether here he could sacrifice everything, or only “two roubles.” And in the monastery he met this elder. I must digress here to explain what an “elder” is in Russian monasteries, and I am sorry to say I do not feel very competent to do so. I will try, however, to give a superficial account in a few words. Authorities on the subject assert that the institution of “elders” is recent, not more than a hundred years old in our monasteries, though in the Orthodox East, especially on Sinai and Athos, it has existed for over a thousand years. It is maintained that it existed in ancient times in Russia too. But then came the calamities that befell Russia—the Tartars, civil war, the break in relations with the East after the fall of Constantinople—and the institution fell into oblivion. It was revived among us toward the end of the last century by one of the great “ascetics,” as they called him, Païssy Velitchkovsky, and his disciples. Even today it exists in only a few monasteries, and in Russia it has sometimes been almost persecuted as an innovation. It flourished especially in the famous Kozelski Optin Monastery. When and how it was introduced into our monastery I cannot say. There had already been three such elders, and Zossima was the last of them. But he was almost dying of weakness and disease, and they had no one to take his place. For our monastery this was an important question, because until then it had not been distinguished by anything in particular. It had no relics of saints, no wonder-working ikons, no glorious traditions, no historical exploits. It had flourished and become famous all over Russia through its elders, and pilgrims had flocked from every part of the country, thousands of miles, to see and hear them.

What was such an elder? He was one who took your soul and your will into his own soul and will. When you choose an elder, you give up your own will and hand it over to him in complete submission, complete self-denial. You take on this novitiate, this terrible school of self-denial, of your own free will. You hope to conquer and master yourself, so that after a life of obedience you may reach perfect freedom, that is, freedom from self. You hope to escape the fate of those who have lived their whole lives without finding their true selves in themselves. This institution of elders is not founded on theory. It grew up in the East out of a thousand years of practice. What is owed to an elder is not the ordinary “obedience” that has always existed in our Russian monasteries. It involves confession to the elder by all who have submitted to him, and an unbreakable bond between him and them.

The story is told, for instance, that in the early days of Christianity there was a novice who failed to carry out some command his elder had given him. He left his monastery in Syria and went to Egypt. There, after great exploits, he was at last found worthy to suffer torture and a martyr’s death for the faith. The Church regarded him as a saint. As they were burying him, the deacon called out, “Depart, all you unbaptized,” and suddenly the coffin with the martyr’s body left its place and was thrown out of the church. This happened three times. Only then did they learn that this holy man had broken his vow of obedience and left his elder. So, in spite of his great deeds, he could not be forgiven without the elder’s absolution. Only after that could the funeral take place. This, of course, is only an old legend. But here is a recent instance.

A monk was suddenly ordered by his elder to leave Athos, which he loved as a sacred place and a haven of refuge. He was to go first to Jerusalem, to pay homage to the Holy Places, and then north to Siberia: “There is the place for you, and not here.” The monk, overwhelmed with sorrow, went to the Ecumenical Patriarch in Constantinople and begged to be released from his obedience. But the Patriarch replied that he could not release him. There was not, and could not be, any power on earth able to release him, except the elder who had himself laid that duty on him. In this way the elders are given, in certain cases, unlimited and inexplicable authority. That is why in many of our monasteries the institution was at first resisted almost to the point of persecution. Meanwhile the elders at once began to be highly esteemed among the people. Crowds of ignorant people, and men of distinction as well, flocked to the elders of our monastery, for instance, to confess their doubts, their sins and their sufferings, and to ask for counsel and admonition. Seeing this, the opponents of the elders declared that the sacrament of confession was being arbitrarily and frivolously degraded. Yet the monk’s or layman’s continual opening of his heart to the elder had nothing of the character of the sacrament. In the end, however, the institution of elders has been kept, and it is becoming established in Russian monasteries. It is true, perhaps, that this instrument, which had stood the test of a thousand years as a means of moral regeneration from slavery to freedom and to moral perfection, may be a two-edged weapon. It may lead some not to humility and complete self-control but to the most Satanic pride, that is, to bondage and not to freedom.

The elder Zossima was sixty-five. He came from a family of landowners and in his early youth had been in the army, serving as an officer in the Caucasus. No doubt he had impressed Alyosha by some peculiar quality of his soul. Alyosha lived in the elder’s cell. The elder was very fond of him and let him wait on him. It should be noted that Alyosha was bound by no obligation and could go where he pleased and be away for whole days. He wore the monastic dress voluntarily, so as not to be different from the others, and no doubt he liked wearing it. Possibly his youthful imagination was deeply stirred by the power and fame of his elder. It was said that over the years so many people had come to confess their sins to Father Zossima, and to beg him for words of advice and healing, that he had acquired the keenest insight. From an unfamiliar face he could tell what a newcomer wanted and what was torturing his conscience. He sometimes astounded and almost alarmed his visitors by knowing their secrets before they had spoken a word.

Alyosha saw that many people, almost all of them, entered the elder’s cell for the first time anxious and uneasy, yet left with bright, happy faces. What struck him most was that Father Zossima was not stern at all. He was nearly always cheerful. The monks used to say that he felt drawn to the more sinful, and the bigger the sinner, the more he loved him. No doubt there were some monks who hated and envied him, and they went on doing so to the end of his life. But there were few of them, and they kept quiet, though a few were men of real standing in the monastery. One was an older monk, famous for keeping strict fasts and vows of silence. Still, most of the monks were on Father Zossima’s side, and a great many loved him with all their hearts, warmly and sincerely. Some were devoted to him almost to the point of fanaticism. They said, not quite aloud, that he was a saint, that this was beyond doubt. Seeing that his end was near, they looked forward to miracles and great glory for the monastery before long, from his relics. Alyosha believed in the elder’s miraculous power without a shadow of doubt, just as he believed without a shadow of doubt in the story of the coffin that flew out of the church. He saw many people come with sick children or relatives and beg the elder to lay his hands on them and pray over them. Soon afterward, some of them the very next day, they returned and fell weeping at the elder’s feet to thank him for healing their sick.

Whether they had truly been healed or had merely got better as the illness ran its natural course was a question that did not exist for Alyosha. He had complete faith in his teacher’s spiritual power, and he rejoiced in the elder’s fame and glory as if it were his own triumph. His heart pounded, and he fairly shone all over, whenever the elder came out through the hermitage gates to the crowd of humbler pilgrims waiting there. They had come from every part of Russia for the sole purpose of seeing the elder and receiving his blessing. They threw themselves down before him, wept, kissed his feet, kissed the ground where he stood, and wailed. The women held their children up to him and brought him the sick who were “possessed with devils.” The elder spoke to them, read a short prayer over them, blessed them and sent them away. Recently he had grown so weak with his illness that sometimes he could not leave his cell, and the pilgrims would wait for days for him to appear. Alyosha did not wonder why they loved him so much, or why they fell down before him and wept with emotion at the mere sight of his face. Oh, he understood! The humble soul of the Russian peasant is worn out by grief and toil, and still more by the endless injustice and endless sin, his own and the world’s. For that soul it was the greatest need and comfort to find someone or something holy to fall down before and worship.

“Among us there is sin, injustice, and temptation. But still, somewhere on earth, there is someone holy and exalted. He has the truth; he knows the truth. So the truth is not dead upon the earth, and it will come one day to us too and rule over all the earth, as was promised.”

Alyosha knew that this was just how the people felt, and even how they reasoned. He understood it. But that the elder Zossima was this saint, this guardian of God’s truth—of that he had no more doubt than the weeping peasants and the sick women holding out their children to the elder. His conviction that the elder would bring extraordinary glory to the monastery after his death was even stronger than anyone else’s there. And lately a deep flame of inner ecstasy had been burning more and more strongly in his heart. It did not trouble him at all that this elder stood before him as a solitary example.

“No matter. He is holy. In his heart he carries the secret of renewal for everyone. He carries the power that will at last establish truth on the earth, so that all men will be holy and love one another, and there will be no more rich and poor, no high and low, but all will be like children of God, and the true Kingdom of Christ will come.” That was the dream in Alyosha’s heart.

The arrival of his two brothers, whom he had never known before, seemed to affect Alyosha deeply. He became friends with his half-brother Dmitri sooner than with his own brother Ivan, although Dmitri arrived later. Alyosha was extremely interested in Ivan. But Ivan had now been two months in the town, and though the two had met fairly often, they were still not close. Alyosha was silent by nature, and he seemed to be waiting for something and ashamed of something. Ivan, he had noticed, had at first looked at him long and with curiosity, but soon seemed to have stopped thinking about him. Alyosha noticed this with some embarrassment. At first he blamed his brother’s indifference on the gap in their ages and education. But he also wondered whether Ivan’s lack of curiosity and sympathy had some other cause altogether, one he knew nothing about. He kept fancying that Ivan was absorbed in something inward and important, that he was struggling toward some goal, perhaps a very difficult one, and that this was why he had no thought to spare for him. Alyosha wondered, too, whether the learned atheist might feel some contempt for him, a foolish novice. He knew for certain that his brother was an atheist. If there was contempt, he could not take offense at it. Yet, in an uneasy embarrassment that he did not understand himself, he waited for his brother to come nearer. Dmitri spoke of Ivan with the deepest respect and a peculiar earnestness. From Dmitri, Alyosha learned every detail of the important affair that had lately drawn the two elder brothers together in such a close and remarkable bond. Dmitri’s warm words about Ivan struck Alyosha all the more because Dmitri was, beside Ivan, almost uneducated. And the two brothers were such opposites in personality and character that it would be hard to find two men less alike.

It was at this time that the meeting, or rather the gathering, of this ill-matched family took place in the cell of the elder, who had such an extraordinary influence over Alyosha. The pretext for it was a false one. The quarrel between Dmitri and his father seemed to be at its worst just then, and relations between them had become unbearably strained. Fyodor Pavlovitch seems to have been the first to propose, apparently as a joke, that they should all meet in Father Zossima’s cell, and that, without appealing to his direct intervention, they might come to an understanding more decently under the soothing influence of the elder’s presence. Dmitri had never seen the elder. He naturally supposed that his father was trying to intimidate him. But he secretly blamed himself for losing his temper with his father several times lately, and so he accepted the challenge. It should be noted that he did not stay with his father, as Ivan did, but lived apart at the other end of the town. It happened that Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, who was staying in the district at that time, seized eagerly on the idea. He was a Liberal of the forties and fifties, a freethinker and an atheist, and he may have been driven by boredom or by the hope of some idle amusement. Suddenly he wanted to see the monastery and the holy man. His lawsuit with the monastery was still dragging on, and he made that his excuse to call on the Superior and try to settle it on friendly terms. A visitor with such praiseworthy intentions might get a warmer, more attentive reception than one who came out of simple curiosity. Pressure was put on the elder from inside the monastery. He had hardly left his cell lately, and illness had forced him to turn away even his usual visitors. In the end he agreed to see them, and the day was set.
“Who made me a judge over them?” was all he said to Alyosha, smiling.

Alyosha was deeply troubled when he heard about the planned visit. Of all that quarrelsome, bickering company, Dmitri was the only one who could treat the meeting seriously. All the others would come with frivolous motives, which might even insult the elder. Alyosha knew that very well. Ivan and Miüsov would come out of curiosity, perhaps of the coarsest kind, and his father might be planning some piece of buffoonery. Alyosha said nothing, but he understood his father through and through. The boy, I repeat, was far from being as simple as everyone took him to be. He waited for the day with a heavy heart. No doubt he was forever turning over in his mind how the family discord might be ended. But his main worry was for the elder. He trembled for him and for his glory. He dreaded any insult to him, above all the refined, polite irony of Miüsov and the supercilious half-remarks of the highly educated Ivan. He even wanted to take the risk of warning the elder and telling him something about them, but on second thought he said nothing. He only sent a message the day before, through a friend, to his brother Dmitri, saying that he loved him and expected him to keep his promise. Dmitri was puzzled, because he could not remember what he had promised. He answered by letter that he would do his utmost not to be provoked “by vileness.” But although he had a deep respect for the elder and for his brother Ivan, he was convinced that the meeting was either a trap for him or an unworthy farce.
“All the same, I would rather bite out my tongue than fail in respect to the holy man you revere so highly,” he wrote in closing. The letter did not cheer Alyosha much.

chapters.title: I. They Arrive At The Monastery
paragraphs: It was a warm, bright day at the end of August. The meeting with the elder had been set for half-past eleven, right after late mass. Our visitors did not attend the service. They arrived just as it ended. First came an elegant open carriage drawn by two valuable horses, carrying Miüsov and a distant relative of his, a young man of twenty named Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov. The young man was getting ready to enter university. He was staying with Miüsov for now, and Miüsov kept urging him to go abroad, to the university at Zurich or Jena. The young man still hadn’t decided. He was thoughtful and absent-minded. He was good-looking, strongly built, and fairly tall. At times his gaze had a strange fixity. Like all very absent-minded people, he would sometimes stare at a person without seeing him. He was silent and rather awkward. But sometimes, when he was alone with someone, he became talkative and gushing, and would laugh at anything or nothing. His liveliness vanished as quickly as it came. He was always well dressed, even elaborately so. He already had some independent money and expected much more. He was a friend of Alyosha’s.

A long way behind Miüsov’s carriage came Fyodor Pavlovitch with his son Ivan, in an ancient, jolting but roomy hired carriage drawn by a pair of old pinkish-gray horses. Dmitri was late, though he had been told the time the evening before. The visitors left their carriage at the hotel outside the monastery grounds and walked to the monastery gates. Apart from Fyodor Pavlovitch, none of them had ever seen the monastery, and Miüsov had probably not set foot in a church for thirty years. He looked around with curiosity and an air of assumed ease. But apart from the church and the service buildings, which were ordinary enough too, he found nothing of interest inside the monastery. The last of the worshippers were coming out of the church, bareheaded and crossing themselves. Among the humbler people there were a few of higher rank, two or three ladies and a very old general. They were all staying at the hotel. Beggars at once surrounded our visitors, but none of them gave anything, except young Kalganov. He took a ten-copeck piece out of his purse and, nervous and embarrassed (God knows why!), hurriedly gave it to an old woman, saying, “Divide it equally.” None of his companions said a word about it, so he had no reason to be embarrassed. But when he saw that, he felt even more flustered.

It was strange that nobody seemed to expect them, and that they were not received with any special honor. One of them had recently donated a thousand roubles, and another was a very rich, highly cultured landowner. In a sense the whole monastery depended on him, because a court ruling in the lawsuit might at any moment hand their fishing rights over to him. Yet no one in authority came out to meet them.

Miüsov looked absent-mindedly at the tombstones around the church. He was about to say that the dead buried here must have paid a pretty penny for the right to lie in this “holy place,” but he held back. His liberal irony was quickly turning almost into anger.
“Who the devil is there to ask in this idiotic place? We must find out, because time is passing,” he said suddenly, as if talking to himself.

All at once an elderly, bald man came up, with ingratiating little eyes, wearing a full summer overcoat. Lifting his hat, he introduced himself in a honeyed lisp as Maximov, a landowner from Tula. He at once took up our visitors’ problem.
“Father Zossima lives in the hermitage, on his own. It’s four hundred paces from the monastery, past the copse.”
“I know it’s on the other side of the copse,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch, “but we don’t remember the way. It’s a long time since we were last here.”
“This way, through this gate, and straight across the copse ... the copse. Come with me, won’t you? I’ll show you. I have to go.... I’m going there myself. This way, this way.”

They left by the gate and headed for the copse. Maximov was sixty, and he half ran as he went, twisting sideways to stare at each of them with an incredible, jittery curiosity. His eyes looked as if they might pop out of his head.

“You see, we’re visiting the elder on private business,” Miüsov said sternly. “That gentleman has given us an audience, so to speak. We thank you for pointing out the way, but we can’t invite you to come along.”
“Oh, I’ve been there. I’ve been already; _un chevalier parfait_!” And Maximov snapped his fingers in the air.
“Who is a _chevalier_?” asked Miüsov.
“The elder! The splendid elder, the elder! Zossima, the honor and glory of the monastery. What an elder he is!”
But his rambling was cut short by a monk who caught up with them, a very pale, worn-looking man of medium height in a monk’s cap. Fyodor Pavlovitch and Miüsov stopped.
With a deep and very courteous bow, the monk announced:
“The Father Superior asks all of you gentlemen to dine with him once you’ve finished at the hermitage. At one o’clock, not a minute later. You too,” he added, turning to Maximov.

“I’ll certainly come, without fail,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, enormously pleased at the invitation. “And believe me, we’ve all given our word to behave properly here.... And you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, will you go too?”
“Yes, of course. What did I come for, if not to study all the customs here? The only thing in my way is your company....”
“Yes, Dmitri Fyodorovitch doesn’t exist yet.”
“It would be a splendid thing if he never turned up. Do you think I enjoy any of this, and with you along, too? So, we’ll come to dinner. Thank the Father Superior,” he told the monk.
“No, it’s my duty now to take you to the elder,” answered the monk.
“Then I’ll go to the Father Superior right now—right to the Father Superior,” babbled Maximov.
“The Father Superior is occupied at the moment. But do as you wish—” the monk said, hesitating.
“Impertinent old man!” Miüsov said aloud, as Maximov ran back to the monastery.
“He’s like von Sohn,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said suddenly.
“Is that the best you can come up with?... How is he like von Sohn? Have you ever even seen von Sohn?”
“I’ve seen his portrait. It’s not the features, it’s something you can’t quite name. He’s a second von Sohn. I can always tell from the physiognomy.”

“Ah, I’m sure you’re an expert on that. But listen, Fyodor Pavlovitch. You said yourself a minute ago that we’d given our word to behave. Remember that. Keep a grip on yourself, I’m advising you. If you start playing the fool, I won’t be seen with you here.... You see the kind of man he is”—he turned to the monk—“I’m afraid to go among decent people with him.” A faint smile, with a touch of slyness in it, crossed the pale, bloodless lips of the monk. He said nothing in reply, obviously staying quiet out of a sense of his own dignity. Miüsov frowned harder than ever.
“Oh, devil take them all! A show put on for the outside, built up over centuries, and nothing but charlatanism and nonsense underneath,” flashed through Miüsov’s mind.
“There’s the hermitage. We’re here,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. “The gates are closed.”
And he crossed himself again and again before the saints painted above the gates and on either side of them.

“When in Rome, do as the Romans do. In this hermitage there are twenty-five saints working out their salvation. They gaze at each other and eat cabbage. And not a single woman passes through this gate. That’s the remarkable thing. And it’s really true. But I did hear that the elder receives ladies,” he said suddenly to the monk.

“There are peasant women here right now too, lying in the portico, waiting. For ladies of higher rank, two rooms have been built beside the portico, but outside the grounds—you can see the windows—and the elder goes out to them through an inner passage when he is well enough. They always stay outside the grounds. A lady from Harkov, Madame Hohlakov, is waiting there now with her sick daughter. He has probably promised to come out to her, though he has been so weak lately that he has barely shown himself even to the common people.”

“So there are loopholes after all, to slip out of the hermitage to the ladies. Don’t think, holy father, that I mean any harm. But do you know, on Athos not only are visits from women forbidden, but no creature of the female sex is allowed—no hens, no turkey-hens, no cows.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, I warn you, I’ll go back and leave you here. They’ll throw you out as soon as I’m gone.”
“But I’m not getting in your way, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. Look,” he cried suddenly, stepping inside the grounds, “what a valley of roses they live in!”

Though there were no roses now, there were masses of rare and beautiful autumn flowers growing wherever there was room for them, plainly tended by a skillful hand. There were flower-beds around the church and between the tombs. The one-story wooden house where the elder lived was also surrounded by flowers.
“And was it like this under the last elder, Varsonofy? He had no taste for such refinement. They say he’d leap up and thrash even ladies with a stick,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch, going up the steps.

“The elder Varsonofy did sometimes seem rather strange, but a great deal of what’s told about him is foolishness. He never beat anyone,” answered the monk. “Now, gentlemen, if you’ll wait a minute, I’ll announce you.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, for the last time, remember your promise, do you hear? Behave properly or I’ll make you pay for it!” Miüsov had time to mutter once more.

“I can’t think why you’re so worked up,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said sarcastically. “Are you uneasy about your sins? They say he can tell from a person’s eyes what he’s come about. And how much you think of their opinion, you, a Parisian, and so advanced! I’m surprised at you.”
Miüsov had no time to answer the jibe. They were called in. He went in feeling rather irritated.
“Now, I know myself. I’m annoyed, I’ll lose my temper and start quarreling—and lower myself and my ideas,” he thought.

chapters.title: II. The Old Buffoon
paragraphs: They entered the room almost at the same moment that the elder came in from his bedroom. Two monks of the hermitage were already waiting in the cell: the Father Librarian, and Father Païssy, who was said to be very learned and was in poor health, though not old. A tall young man of about twenty-two also stood in the corner, and stayed there for the whole visit. His face was broad and fresh, his narrow brown eyes clever and watchful, and his clothes were ordinary. He was a divinity student living under the monastery’s protection. His expression was one of unquestioning but self-respecting reverence. His position was dependent and beneath the guests’, so he did not bow to them.

Father Zossima was accompanied by a novice and by Alyosha. The two monks rose and greeted him with a very deep bow, touching the ground with their fingers, and then kissed his hand. The elder blessed them, then bowed to them just as low and asked for their blessing in return. The whole ceremony was carried out very seriously, with every sign of feeling, nothing like a routine rite. Miüsov, though, imagined it was all staged to impress. He was standing in front of the other visitors. He had thought it over the evening before: out of simple courtesy, since it was the custom here, he ought to step up and take the elder’s blessing, even if he skipped kissing the hand. But the moment he saw all this bowing and kissing among the monks, he changed his mind. With solemn dignity he made a rather deep, conventional bow and walked off to a chair. Fyodor Pavlovitch did the same, mimicking Miüsov like an ape. Ivan bowed with great dignity and courtesy, but he too kept his hands at his sides, while Kalganov was so confused that he did not bow at all. The elder let the hand he had raised in blessing fall, bowed to them once more, and asked them all to sit. Alyosha flushed deeply. He was ashamed. His fears were coming true.

Father Zossima sat down on a very old-fashioned mahogany sofa covered with leather. He seated his visitors in a row against the opposite wall, on four mahogany chairs upholstered in shabby black leather. The monks sat down, one by the door and one by the window. The divinity student, the novice and Alyosha remained on their feet. The cell was not large, and it looked faded. It had only the barest necessary furniture, coarse and poor. Two pots of flowers stood in the window, and there were several holy pictures in the corner. A lamp burned in front of one huge old ikon of the Virgin. Beside it hung two other holy pictures in shining frames, then carved cherubs, china eggs, an ivory Catholic cross with a Mater Dolorosa clasping it, and a few foreign engravings of great Italian artists of past centuries. Next to these expensive, artistic engravings were some very crude Russian prints of saints and martyrs, the kind sold for a few farthings at any fair. Portraits of Russian bishops, past and present, covered the other walls.

Miüsov gave all these “conventional” surroundings a brief glance, then studied the elder closely. He thought highly of his own insight. This was a forgivable weakness at fifty, an age when a clever, established man of the world can hardly avoid taking himself rather seriously. At first sight he disliked Zossima.
