And there really was something in the elder’s face that other people besides Miüsov might have disliked. He was small and bent, with very weak legs. He was only sixty-five but looked at least ten years older. His face was very thin, covered with a web of fine wrinkles, thickest around the eyes. The eyes were small, pale, quick and bright, like two points of light. A little gray hair showed at his temples. His pointed beard was small and sparse, and his thin lips, which often smiled, were no more than two threads. His nose was not long but sharp, like a bird’s beak.
“To judge by his looks, a spiteful soul, full of petty pride,” thought Miüsov. He was thoroughly unhappy with his situation.
A cheap little clock on the wall hurriedly struck twelve, and that got the conversation started.

“Right on the dot,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, “only my son Dmitri hasn’t shown up. I apologize for him, sacred elder!” (Alyosha shuddered all over at “sacred elder.”) “I’m always punctual myself, to the minute, remembering that punctuality is the courtesy of kings....”
“But you’re not a king, anyway,” Miüsov muttered, losing his self-control at once.

“Yes, that’s true. I’m not a king, and, would you believe it, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, I knew that myself. But there! I always say the wrong thing. Your reverence,” he cried, with sudden pathos, “you see before you a buffoon in earnest! I introduce myself as such. It’s an old habit, alas! And if I sometimes talk nonsense out of place, it’s with an object, the object of amusing people and making myself agreeable. One must be agreeable, mustn’t one? Seven years ago I was in a little town where I had some business, and I made friends with some merchants there. We went to the captain of police, because we had to see him about something and ask him to dine with us. He was a tall, fat, fair, sulky man, the most dangerous type in such cases. It’s their liver. I walked straight up to him, with the ease of a man of the world, you know, and said, ‘Mr. Ispravnik, be our Napravnik.’ ‘What do you mean by Napravnik?’ said he. I saw in the first half-second that it had misfired. He stood there so glum. ‘I wanted to make a joke,’ said I, ‘for everyone’s entertainment, since Mr. Napravnik is our well-known Russian orchestra conductor, and what we need for the harmony of our undertaking is someone like that.’ And I explained my comparison very reasonably, didn’t I? ‘Excuse me,’ said he, ‘I am an Ispravnik, and I don’t allow puns on my calling.’ He turned and walked away. I followed him, shouting, ‘Yes, yes, you’re an Ispravnik, not a Napravnik.’ ‘No,’ he said, ‘since you called me a Napravnik, I am one.’ And would you believe it, it ruined our business! And I’m always like that, always like that. Always hurting myself with my politeness. Once, many years ago, I said to an influential person, ‘Your wife is a ticklish lady,’ meaning it in an honorable sense, about her moral qualities, so to speak. But he asked me, ‘Why, have you tickled her?’ I thought I’d be polite, so I couldn’t help saying, ‘Yes,’ and he gave me a fine tickling on the spot. Only that happened long ago, so I’m not ashamed to tell the story. I’m always hurting myself like that.”
“You’re doing it now,” muttered Miüsov, in disgust.
Father Zossima studied the two of them in silence.

“Am I? Would you believe it, I knew that too, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, and let me tell you, I even foresaw I would, the moment I began to speak. And do you know, I foresaw too that you’d be the first to point it out. The minute I see my joke isn’t coming off, your reverence, both my cheeks feel as if they’re being dragged down to the lower jaw, and there’s almost a spasm in them. It’s been that way since I was young, when I had to make jokes for my living in noblemen’s houses. I’m an inveterate buffoon, and have been from birth, your reverence. It’s like a craze in me. I suppose it’s a devil inside me. But only a little one. A more serious one would have chosen another lodging. Though not your soul, Pyotr Alexandrovitch; you’re not a lodging worth having either. But I do believe—I believe in God, though I’ve had doubts lately. But now I sit and wait for words of wisdom. I’m like the philosopher Diderot, your reverence. Did you ever hear, most Holy Father, how Diderot went to see the Metropolitan Platon, in the time of the Empress Catherine? He walked in and said straight out, ‘There is no God.’ And the great bishop lifted his finger and answered, ‘The fool hath said in his heart there is no God.’ And Diderot fell down at his feet on the spot. ‘I believe,’ he cried, ‘and I will be christened.’ And so he was. Princess Dashkov was his godmother, and Potyomkin his godfather.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, this is unbearable! You know you’re lying, and that stupid story isn’t true. Why are you playing the fool?” cried Miüsov, his voice shaking.

“I’ve suspected all my life that it wasn’t true,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried with conviction. “But let me tell you the whole truth, gentlemen. Great elder! Forgive me, the last bit, about Diderot being christened, I just made up this minute. It never occurred to me before. I invented it to give the story some spice. I play the fool, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, to make myself agreeable. Though sometimes I honestly don’t know myself why I do it. As for Diderot, I heard the story as far as ‘the fool hath said in his heart’ twenty times from the local gentry when I was young. I heard your aunt tell it, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. To this day they all believe that the infidel Diderot came to argue about God with the Metropolitan Platon....”
Miüsov stood up, forgetting himself in his impatience. He was furious, and knew he was making himself look ridiculous.

What was happening in the cell was really incredible. For forty or fifty years, going back to the earlier elders, no visitor had come into that cell without the deepest veneration. Nearly everyone let in felt that a great favor was being done him. Many knelt through the whole visit. Many of the visitors had been men of high rank and learning, and some were even freethinkers who came out of curiosity. Yet every one of them, without exception, had shown profound reverence and tact, for here money was not in question. On one side there was only love and kindness, and on the other repentance and an eager wish to resolve some spiritual problem or crisis. So this buffoonery amazed and bewildered the onlookers, or some of them at least. The monks kept their faces unchanged and waited with earnest attention to hear what the elder would say, but looked ready to get up, like Miüsov. Alyosha stood with his head down, close to tears. Strangest of all to him was that his brother Ivan, the one person he had counted on, and the only one with enough influence over their father to stop him, now sat completely unmoved with his eyes lowered, apparently curious to see how it would end, as if it had nothing to do with him. Alyosha did not dare to look at Rakitin, the divinity student. He knew him almost intimately, and he alone in the monastery knew what Rakitin was thinking.

“Forgive me,” Miüsov began, turning to Father Zossima. “You may think I am sharing in this shameful foolery. My mistake was to assume that even a man like Fyodor Pavlovitch would know how to behave when he visits so honored a person. I never imagined I would have to apologize just for arriving in his company....”
Pyotr Alexandrovitch could say no more. Overcome with embarrassment, he was about to walk out of the room.

“Please, do not distress yourself.” The elder rose on his weak legs, took Pyotr Alexandrovitch by both hands and sat him down again. “Do not let it trouble you. I especially ask you to be my guest.” He bowed, went back to his little sofa and sat down again.
“Great elder, tell me! Does my liveliness annoy you?” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried suddenly. He gripped the arms of his chair with both hands, as if he meant to jump up if the answer was a bad one.

“I earnestly ask you, too, not to trouble yourself or feel uneasy,” the elder said impressively. “Do not worry. Make yourself entirely at home. And above all, do not be so ashamed of yourself, because that is the root of all of it.”

“Entirely at home? To be my natural self? Oh, that’s much too much, but I take it with grateful joy. You know, blessed Father, you’d better not invite me to be my natural self. Don’t risk it.... I won’t go so far myself. I’m warning you for your own good. As for the rest, it’s still lost in the mists of uncertainty, though there are people who’d be delighted to describe me to you. I mean that for you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. But you, holy being, I tell you, I’m simply overflowing with ecstasy.”

He got to his feet, flung up his hands and declaimed, “Blessed be the womb that bore you, and the paps that gave you suck—the paps especially. Just now you said, ‘Do not be so ashamed of yourself, for that is the root of it all.’ With that one remark you pierced me through and read me to the core. The truth is, whenever I meet people I feel I’m lower than any of them, and that they all take me for a buffoon. So I say, ‘Very well, let me play the buffoon in earnest. I’m not afraid of what you think, because every one of you is worse than I am.’ That’s why I’m a buffoon. It comes from shame, great elder, from shame; it’s only over-sensitiveness that makes me rowdy. If I could only be sure that everyone would take me for the kindest and wisest of men, oh, Lord, what a good man I’d be! Teacher!” Suddenly he dropped to his knees. “What must I do to gain eternal life?”
Even now it was hard to tell whether he was joking or truly moved.
Father Zossima lifted his eyes, looked at him and said with a smile:

“You have known for a long time what you must do. You have sense enough. Do not give way to drunkenness, or to loose talk, or to sensual lust, and above all, do not give way to the love of money. And close your taverns. If you cannot close them all, close at least two or three. And above all—do not lie.”
“You mean about Diderot?”

“No, not about Diderot. Above all, do not lie to yourself. A man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to a point where he cannot tell the truth in himself or around him, and so he loses all respect for himself and for others. Having no respect, he stops loving. And to keep himself occupied and distracted without love, he gives himself up to passions and coarse pleasures, and in his vices he sinks to the level of a beast. All of this comes from lying continually to other men and to himself. The man who lies to himself can be more easily offended than anyone. You know, it is sometimes very pleasant to take offense, is it not? A man may know that no one has insulted him, that he has invented the insult himself, lied and exaggerated to make it picturesque, seized on one word and made a mountain out of a molehill. He knows all this, and still he is the first to take offense. He revels in his resentment until it gives him great pleasure, and so he passes to real vindictiveness. But get up, sit down, please. All this, too, is deceitful posturing....”
“Blessed man! Give me your hand, let me kiss it.”

Fyodor Pavlovitch skipped up and planted a quick kiss on the elder’s thin hand. “It is, it is pleasant to take offense. You said that so well, I never heard it put that way before. Yes, I’ve gone through my whole life taking offense, to please myself, taking offense on esthetic grounds, because it’s not so much pleasant as distinguished sometimes to be insulted—you forgot that, great elder, it is distinguished! I’ll make a note of it. But I’ve been lying, positively lying, my whole life long, every day and every hour. Truly, I am a lie, and the father of lies. Though no, I don’t think I’m the father of lies. I’m getting my texts mixed up. Let’s say the son of lies, and that will do. Only ... my angel ... now and then I may talk about Diderot! Diderot does no harm, though a word now and then may do harm. Great elder, by the way, I was forgetting, though for two years I’ve been meaning to come here on purpose and ask you something, to find something out. Only please tell Pyotr Alexandrovitch not to interrupt me. Here is my question. Somewhere in the _Lives of the Saints_ there’s a story of a holy saint, martyred for his faith, who stood up when his head was finally cut off, picked it up, and, ‘courteously kissing it,’ walked a long way carrying it in his hands. Is that true or not, honored Father?”
“No, it is not true,” said the elder.
“Nothing of the kind appears anywhere in the lives of the saints. Which saint is the story told of, did you say?” asked the Father Librarian.

“I don’t know which saint. I don’t know, I can’t tell you. I was deceived. Someone told me the story. I heard it from him, and do you know who it was? Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov here, who got so angry just now about Diderot. He’s the one who told it.”
“I never told you that. I never speak to you at all.”

“True, you didn’t tell it to me, but you told it with me in the room. Three years ago. I mention it because that ridiculous story shook my faith, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. You had no idea, but I went home with my faith shaken, and it’s been shakier and shakier ever since. Yes, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, you caused a great fall. That was no Diderot!”
Fyodor Pavlovitch was working himself up into a pathetic state, though by now everyone could see plainly that he was acting a part again. Still, his words stung Miüsov.

“What nonsense, it’s all nonsense,” he muttered. “I may well have told it some time ... but not to you. It was told to me. I heard it in Paris, from a Frenchman. He said it was read out at our mass from the _Lives of the Saints_ ... he was a very learned man who had made a special study of Russian statistics and had lived in Russia a long time.... I haven’t read the _Lives of the Saints_ myself, and I don’t intend to ... all sorts of things get said over dinner—and we were at dinner then.”
“Yes, you were at dinner, and so I lost my faith!” Fyodor Pavlovitch mimicked him.
“What do I care about your faith?” Miüsov was on the point of shouting, but he stopped himself abruptly and said with contempt, “You defile everything you touch.”

The elder suddenly stood up. “Excuse me, gentlemen, if I leave you for a few minutes,” he said to all his guests. “There are visitors waiting for me who came before you. But do not tell lies all the same,” he added to Fyodor Pavlovitch, with a good-humored face. He left the cell, and Alyosha and the novice hurried after him to escort him down the steps. Alyosha was out of breath. He was glad to get away, but glad too that the elder was in good humor and not offended. Father Zossima was heading for the portico to bless the people waiting there. But Fyodor Pavlovitch stubbornly stopped him at the door of the cell.

“Blessed man!” he cried, with feeling. “Let me kiss your hand once more. Yes, with you I could still talk, I could still get along. Do you think I always lie and play the fool like this? Believe me, all this time I’ve been acting this way on purpose, to put you to the test. I’ve been trying you out all along, to see whether I could get along with you. Is there room for my humility beside your pride? I’m ready to give you a certificate that a man can get along with you! But now I’ll be quiet. I’ll keep quiet the whole time. I’ll sit in a chair and hold my tongue. Now it’s your turn to speak, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. You’re the main person left now—for ten minutes.”

chapters.title: III. Peasant Women Who Have Faith
paragraphs: Down by the wooden portico, which was built onto the outer wall of the precinct, a crowd of about twenty peasant women had gathered. They had heard that the elder was finally coming out, and they stood waiting for him. Two ladies, Madame Hohlakov and her daughter, had come out into the portico as well. They waited in a separate section, set aside for women of rank.

Madame Hohlakov was a rich lady, still young and attractive, and always dressed with taste. She was a little pale, with lively black eyes. She was no more than thirty-three and had been a widow for five years. Her daughter, who was fourteen, was partly paralyzed. The poor girl had not been able to walk for six months, and people wheeled her around in a long reclining chair. She had a charming little face, thin from illness but full of gaiety. Her big dark eyes, with their long lashes, had a mischievous gleam. Her mother had meant to take her abroad since spring, but business over their estate had held them up all summer. They had now been in our town for a week. They had come more on business than out of devotion, but they had already visited Father Zossima once, three days earlier. They knew the elder hardly received anyone. Even so, they had suddenly turned up again and were pleading urgently for “the happiness of looking once again on the great healer.”

The mother sat on a chair next to her daughter’s invalid carriage. Two paces from her stood an old monk. He was not from our monastery but a visitor from some obscure religious house in the far north, and he too had come for the elder’s blessing.

Father Zossima came into the portico and went first straight to the peasants, who were crowded at the bottom of the three steps up to it. He stood on the top step, put on his stole, and began blessing the women as they pressed around him. A crazy woman was brought up to him. The moment she saw the elder, she began to shriek and writhe as if in the pains of childbirth. He laid the stole on her forehead and said a short prayer over her, and at once she grew calm and quiet.

I do not know how it is now, but in my childhood I often saw and heard these “possessed” women in villages and monasteries. They were brought to mass, and there they would squeal and bark like dogs so loudly that the whole church heard them. But when the sacrament was carried in and they were led up to it, the “possession” stopped at once, and for a while the sick women were always calm. As a child I was deeply impressed and amazed by this. Then I heard from our country neighbors and from my teachers in town that the whole illness was faked to get out of work, and that it could always be cured by suitable severity. They told various stories to prove it. Later, though, medical specialists told me, to my astonishment, that nothing is faked here. It is a terrible illness that women suffer from, and it is especially widespread among us in Russia. It comes, they said, from the hard lot of peasant women. A woman goes back to exhausting work too soon after a difficult, unnatural childbirth with no help. Add hopeless misery and beatings and the like, which some women could not bear as well as others. The strange, instant cure of the frantic, struggling woman as soon as she was brought to the holy sacrament had been explained to me as malingering and the trickery of the “clericals.” In fact, it probably came about in the most natural way. The women who held her up, and the sick woman herself, were completely certain that the evil spirit inside her could not hold out once she was brought to the sacrament and made to bow down before it. So in a nervous, mentally disturbed woman, the whole body always went into a sort of convulsion, and it was bound to, at the moment of bowing down. The expectation of a miraculous cure and the unquestioning belief that it would come set it off. And it did come, though only for a moment. It was exactly the same now, as soon as the elder touched the sick woman with the stole.
The moment moved many of the women in the crowd to tears of ecstasy. Some reached out to kiss the hem of his robe, and others called out in sing-song voices.
He blessed all of them and talked with a few. He already knew the “possessed” woman. She was from a village just six versts from the monastery, and she had been brought to him before.

“But here is one who has come from far away.” He pointed at a woman who was not at all old but very thin and worn, with a face not just sunburnt but nearly black from the weather. She knelt there staring at the elder without blinking. Her eyes had something almost frenzied in them.

“From far away, Father, from far away! From two hundred miles away. From far away, Father, from far away!” the woman began in a sing-song voice, like someone chanting a dirge. She swayed her head from side to side, her cheek resting on her hand.

Among the peasantry you meet a silent, patient sorrow. It draws into itself and goes still. But there is also a grief that breaks out. From that moment it dissolves in tears and pours itself out in wailing. This is especially common in women. It is not a lighter grief than the silent kind. Lamentations bring comfort only by tearing the heart still more. Such grief does not want consolation. It feeds on its own hopelessness. Lamentations come only from a constant craving to open the wound again.
“You belong to the tradesman class?” asked Father Zossima, looking at her with curiosity.

“We’re townfolk, Father, townfolk. But we’re peasants all the same, even though we live in town. I’ve come to see you, O Father! We heard about you, Father, we heard about you. I’ve buried my little son, and I’ve come on a pilgrimage. I’ve been to three monasteries, and they said to me, ‘Go to them, Nastasya, go to them’—that means to you. So I came. I was at the service yesterday, and today I’ve come to you.”
“What are you weeping for?”

“It’s my little son I’m grieving for, Father. He was three years old—three years all but three months. I’m in anguish for my little boy, Father, for my little boy. He was the last one we had left. We had four, my Nikita and I, and now we have no children. Our dear ones are all gone. I buried the first three without grieving too much, but now that I’ve buried the last one, I can’t forget him. He seems to be standing in front of me all the time. He never leaves me. He’s withered my heart. I look at his little clothes, his little shirt, his little boots, and I wail. I lay out everything that’s left of him, all his little things. I look at them and I wail. I say to Nikita, my husband, ‘Let me go on a pilgrimage, master.’ He’s a driver. We’re not poor, Father, not poor. He drives our own horse. It’s all ours, the horse and the carriage. And what use is it all to us now? My Nikita has started drinking while I’m away. I’m sure of it. It was like that before. The minute I turn my back, he gives in to it. But now I don’t think about him. I left home three months ago. I’ve forgotten him. I’ve forgotten everything. I don’t want to remember. And what would our life together be now? I’m through with him, I’m through. I’m through with all of them. I don’t even want to look at my house and my belongings. I don’t want to see anything at all!”

“Listen, mother,” said the elder. “Once, in olden times, a holy saint saw in the Temple a mother like you. She was weeping for her little one, her only one, whom God had taken. ‘Do you not know,’ said the saint to her, ‘how bold these little ones are before the throne of God? Truly, no one in the Kingdom of Heaven is bolder than they. “You gave us life, O Lord,” they say, “and we had hardly looked at it when You took it back.” And they ask so boldly, and ask again, that God gives them the rank of angels at once. Therefore,’ said the saint, ‘you too, O mother, rejoice and weep no more, for your little son is with the Lord, in the company of the angels.’ That is what the saint said to the weeping mother of old. He was a great saint, and he could not have spoken falsely. So you too, mother, must know that your little one is surely before the throne of God. He is rejoicing, and happy, and praying to God for you. Therefore do not weep, but rejoice.”
The woman listened to him, looking down, her cheek on her hand. She sighed deeply.

“My Nikita tried to comfort me with the very same words as you. ‘You foolish woman,’ he said, ‘why are you crying? Our son is surely singing with the angels before God.’ That’s what he says to me, but he cries himself. I can see he cries just like me. ‘I know, Nikita,’ I said. ‘Where else could he be but with the Lord God? It’s only that here with us he’s not the way he used to sit beside us.’ And if only I could see him one little time, if only I could peep at him one little time, without going up to him, without saying a word, if I could hide in a corner and just see him for one little minute, hear him playing in the yard, calling in his little voice, ‘Mammy, where are you?’ If only I could hear him pattering across the room on his little feet, just once, only once. So often, so often I remember how he used to run to me, shouting and laughing. If only I could hear his little feet, I would know him! But he’s gone, Father, he’s gone, and I’ll never hear him again. Here’s his little sash, but him I’ll never see or hear now.”

She pulled her boy’s little embroidered sash out of her bosom. The moment she looked at it, she began to shake with sobs. She hid her eyes behind her fingers, and the tears came pouring through them in a sudden stream.

“This is Rachel of old,” said the elder, “weeping for her children, and she will not be comforted, because they are not. This is the lot set on earth for you mothers. Do not be comforted. Consolation is not what you need. Weep, and do not be consoled, but weep. Only, each time you weep, be sure to remember that your little son is one of the angels of God. He looks down at you from there and sees you. He rejoices at your tears and points to them for the Lord God to see. For a long while yet you will carry that great mother’s grief. But in the end it will turn into a quiet joy. Your bitter tears will become tears of tender sorrow, which purifies the heart and frees it from sin. And I will pray for the peace of your child’s soul. What was his name?”
“Alexey, Father.”
“A sweet name. Was he named for Alexey, the man of God?”
“Yes, Father.”

“What a saint he was! I will remember him in my prayers, mother, and your grief too, and I will pray for your husband’s health. It is a sin for you to leave him. Your little one will see from heaven that you have abandoned his father, and he will weep over you. Why do you disturb his happiness? He is alive, for the soul lives forever. Though he is not in the house, he is near you, unseen. How can he go into the house when you say you hate it? Where is he to go if he does not find you together, his father and mother? He comes to you in dreams now, and you grieve. But then he will send you gentle dreams. Go to your husband, mother. Go this very day.”

“I will go, Father, as you say. I will go. You’ve gone straight to my heart. My Nikita, my Nikita, you’re waiting for me,” the woman began in her sing-song voice. But the elder had already turned to a very old woman. She was dressed like someone from the town, not like a pilgrim. Her eyes showed that she had come with a purpose and had something to say. She said she was the widow of a non-commissioned officer and lived close by, in town. Her son Vasenka worked in the commissariat and had gone to Irkutsk, in Siberia. He had written twice from there, but now a year had gone by without a word. She had asked about him, but she did not know where the proper place to ask was.

“Just the other day Stepanida Ilyinishna—she’s a rich merchant’s wife—said to me, ‘Go, Prohorovna, and put your son’s name down in the church for prayers, and pray for the peace of his soul as if he were dead. His soul will be troubled,’ she said, ‘and he will write you a letter.’ And Stepanida Ilyinishna told me it was certain, that it had been tried many times. Only I’m in doubt.... Oh, you light of ours! Is it true or false, and would it be right?”

“Do not even think of it. It is shameful to ask such a question. How can anyone pray for the peace of a living soul? And his own mother, too! It is a great sin, close to sorcery. Only because you did not know better are you forgiven. Pray instead to the Queen of Heaven, our swift defense and help, for his good health, and ask her to forgive you for your mistake. And I will tell you something else, Prohorovna. Either your son will soon come back to you, or he will surely send a letter. Go, and from now on be at peace. Your son is alive, I tell you.”
“Dear Father, God reward you, our benefactor, who prays for all of us and for our sins!”

But the elder had already noticed two glowing eyes in the crowd, fixed on him. A young peasant woman, worn out and looking consumptive, was watching him in silence. Her eyes pleaded with him, but she seemed afraid to come closer.
“What is it, my child?”
“Absolve my soul, Father,” she said softly, and slowly sank to her knees and bowed down at his feet. “I have sinned, Father. I am afraid of my sin.”
The elder sat down on the lowest step. The woman crept closer to him, still on her knees.

“I have been a widow for three years,” she began in a half-whisper, with a kind of shudder. “My life with my husband was hard. He was an old man. He used to beat me cruelly. He lay sick, and I thought, looking at him, what if he got well, what if he got up again, what then? And then the thought came to me—”
“Wait!” said the elder, and he put his ear close to her lips.
The woman went on in a low whisper, so low that it was almost impossible to catch anything. She was soon done.
“Three years ago?” asked the elder.
“Three years. At first I didn’t think about it, but now I’ve started to be ill, and the thought never leaves me.”
“Have you come far?”
“Over three hundred miles.”
“Have you told it in confession?”
“I’ve confessed it. Twice I’ve confessed it.”
“Have you been allowed to take Communion?”
“Yes. I’m afraid. I’m afraid to die.”

“Fear nothing, never be afraid, and do not fret. As long as your repentance does not fail, God will forgive everything. There is no sin, and there can be no sin on all the earth, that the Lord will not forgive the truly repentant! No man can commit a sin so great that it uses up the infinite love of God. Can there be a sin that goes beyond the love of God? Think only of repentance, continual repentance, but put fear away completely. Believe that God loves you more than you can imagine, that He loves you with your sin, in your sin. It was said long ago that there is more joy in heaven over one repentant sinner than over ten righteous men. Go, and do not be afraid. Do not be bitter against people. Do not be angry if you are wronged. Forgive the dead man in your heart for whatever wrong he did you. Be truly reconciled with him. If you repent, you love. And if you love, you belong to God. Love atones for everything and saves everything. If I, a sinner like you, am tender with you and pity you, how much more will God. Love is so priceless a treasure that you can buy back the whole world with it, and make amends not only for your own sins but for the sins of others.”
He made the sign of the cross over her three times, took a little ikon from his own neck, and hung it on her. She bowed to the ground without a word.
He rose and looked cheerfully at a healthy peasant woman holding a tiny baby.
“From Vyshegorye, dear Father.”
“Five miles you have dragged yourself, with the baby. What do you want?”

“I came to look at you. I’ve been to see you before—or have you forgotten? You don’t have much of a memory if you’ve forgotten me. They told us you were ill. I thought, I’ll go and see for myself. Now I see you, and you’re not ill! You’ll live another twenty years. God bless you! There are plenty of people praying for you. How could you be ill?”
“I thank you for everything, daughter.”

“By the way, I’ve got something to ask, nothing much. Here are sixty kopecks. Give them, dear Father, to someone poorer than me. I thought on my way here, better to give it through him. He’ll know who to give it to.”
“Thank you, my dear, thank you! You are a good woman. I love you. I will certainly do it. Is that your little girl?”
“My little girl, Father, Lizaveta.”
“May the Lord bless you both, you and your baby Lizaveta! You have made my heart glad, mother. Farewell, dear children, farewell, dear ones.”
He blessed them all and bowed low to them.

chapters.title: IV. A Lady Of Little Faith
paragraphs: Another visitor, a lady, had been watching the elder talk with the peasants and bless them. She shed silent tears and dabbed them away with her handkerchief. She was a sentimental society lady, and in many respects a truly kind-hearted woman. When the elder finally came over to her, she met him with enthusiasm.

“Ah, what I felt as I watched that touching scene!...” She was too moved to go on. “Oh, I understand why the people love you so. I love the people myself. I want to love them. And who could not, our splendid Russian people, so simple in their greatness!”
“How is your daughter? You wanted to speak with me again?”

“Oh, I begged and begged for this, I prayed for it! I was ready to fall on my knees and stay there three days under your windows until you let me in. We have come, great healer, to thank you from the bottom of our hearts. You have healed my Lise, healed her completely, simply by praying over her last Thursday and laying your hands on her. We rushed here to kiss those hands, and to pour out our feelings and our reverence.”
“What do you mean, healed? She is still lying in her chair.”

“But the fevers she had at night have stopped altogether, every night since Thursday,” said the lady, nervous and hurried. “And that isn’t all. Her legs are stronger. This morning she got up feeling well, after sleeping the whole night through. Look at her rosy cheeks, her bright eyes! She used to cry constantly, and now she laughs, and she’s cheerful and happy. This morning she insisted that I let her stand, and she stood for a whole minute without anything to hold on to. She’s betting that in two weeks she’ll be dancing a quadrille. I called in Doctor Herzenstube. He shrugged and said, ‘I’m amazed; I can’t make anything of it.’ And you expect us not to come and trouble you? Not to fly here and thank you? Lise, thank him—thank him!”

Lise’s pretty, laughing little face turned suddenly serious. She lifted herself in her chair as high as she could, looked at the elder, and clasped her hands in front of him. Then she could not contain herself, and she burst out laughing.
“It’s at him,” she said, pointing at Alyosha. She was as cross with herself as a child for being unable to hold back her laughter.
If anyone had looked at Alyosha, standing a step behind the elder, he would have seen a quick blush flood his cheeks in an instant. His eyes shone, and he looked down.
“She has a message for you, Alexey Fyodorovitch. How do you do?” the mother went on, and she held out her exquisitely gloved hand to Alyosha.
The elder turned around and suddenly studied Alyosha closely. Alyosha stepped nearer to Lise and, with a strangely awkward smile, held out his hand to her as well. Lise put on a solemn air.

“Katerina Ivanovna gave me this to pass on to you.” She handed him a little note. “She very much wants you to go and see her as soon as you possibly can. She asks that you not fail her, but be sure to come.”

“She wants me to come and see her? Me? Why?” Alyosha muttered in great astonishment. His face at once turned anxious. “Oh, it all has to do with Dmitri Fyodorovitch and—what happened recently,” the mother explained in a rush. “Katerina Ivanovna has come to a decision, but she needs to see you about it.... Why, naturally, I can’t say. But she wants to see you at once. And you will go to her, of course. It’s a Christian duty.”
“I’ve only met her once,” Alyosha protested, just as bewildered as before.

“Oh, she is such a noble, matchless creature! If only for what she has suffered.... Think of what she has gone through, and what she is going through now! Think of what lies ahead of her! It’s all terrible, terrible!”
“All right, I’ll come,” Alyosha decided, after a quick look at the short, baffling note. It was an urgent plea for him to come, and it explained nothing at all.

“Oh, how sweet and generous of you!” cried Lise, suddenly lively. “I told Mamma you’d be sure not to go. I said you were saving your soul. How wonderful you are! I’ve always thought you were wonderful. How glad I am to tell you so!”
“Lise!” said her mother firmly, though she smiled as she said it.
“You have forgotten us altogether, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she said. “You never come to see us. And yet Lise has told me twice that she’s never happy except with you.”

Alyosha raised his downcast eyes, blushed again, and again smiled without knowing why. But the elder was no longer watching him. He had started talking to a monk who, as I mentioned before, had been waiting for him beside Lise’s chair. This was plainly a monk of the humblest kind, which is to say a peasant, narrow in his outlook, but a true believer and, in his own way, a stubborn one. He said that he came from the far north, from Obdorsk, from Saint Sylvester, and that he belonged to a poor monastery with only ten monks. The elder blessed him and told him to come to his cell whenever he liked.
“How can you presume to do such deeds?” the monk asked suddenly, pointing at Lise with great solemnity and meaning. He was talking about her “healing.”

“It is much too early to speak of that, of course. Relief is not the same as a complete cure, and it can have different causes. But if there has been any healing, it came from no power but God’s will. It is all from God. Come and visit me, Father,” he added to the monk. “I cannot often receive visitors. I am ill, and I know my days are numbered.”
“Oh, no, no! God won’t take you from us. You’ll live a long, long time yet,” cried the lady. “And what is wrong with you? You look so well, so cheerful and happy.”

“Today I am remarkably better. But I know it will last only a moment. I understand my illness thoroughly now. If I seem happy to you, nothing you could say would please me more. For human beings are made for happiness, and whoever is completely happy has the right to say to himself, ‘I am doing God’s will on earth.’ All the righteous, all the saints, all the holy martyrs were happy.”

“Oh, how you talk! What bold, lofty words!” cried the lady. “Your words seem to pierce right through me. And yet—happiness, happiness—where is it? Who can say of himself that he is happy? Oh, since you have been kind enough to let us see you once more today, let me tell you what I could not say last time, what I did not dare to say, everything I suffer and have suffered for so long! I am suffering! Forgive me! I am suffering!”
And in a surge of passionate feeling she clasped her hands before him.
“What is it, in particular, that you suffer from?”
“I suffer ... from lack of faith.”
“Lack of faith in God?”

“Oh, no, no! I don’t even dare to think of that. But the life to come—it’s such a riddle! And no one, no one can solve it. Listen! You are a healer, you know the human soul so deeply, and of course I can’t expect you to believe me entirely. But I give you my word of honor that I’m not speaking lightly now. The thought of the life beyond the grave drives me to anguish, to terror. And I don’t know whom to ask, and I never have dared, all my life. And now I’m bold enough to ask you. Oh, God! What will you think of me now?”
She clasped her hands.
“Do not worry about what I think of you,” said the elder. “I fully believe that your suffering is sincere.”

“Oh, how grateful I am to you! You see, I shut my eyes and ask myself: if everyone has faith, where did it come from? And then people do say it all comes from terror of the threatening forces of nature, and that none of it is real. And I say to myself, ‘What if I’ve believed all my life, and when I come to die there’s nothing but burdocks growing on my grave?’ as I read in some author. It’s dreadful! How—how can I get my faith back? But I only believed when I was a small child, mechanically, without thinking about anything. How, how is it to be proved? I’ve come now to lay my soul open to you and ask you about it. If I let this chance go by, no one will ever answer me, not in my whole life. How can I prove it? How can I convince myself? Oh, how unhappy I am! I stand and look around me and see that hardly anyone else cares. No one bothers his head about it, and I’m the only one who can’t stand it. It’s deadly—deadly!”
“No doubt. But there is no proving it, though you can be convinced of it.”
“How?”

“Through the experience of active love. Try to love your neighbor actively and without tiring. The further you go in love, the more certain you will be that God exists and that your soul is immortal. If you reach complete self-forgetfulness in loving your neighbor, then you will believe without doubt, and no doubt can enter your soul. This has been tried. This is certain.”

“In active love? Now that’s another question—and what a question! You see, I love humanity so much that—would you believe it?—I often dream of giving up everything I have, leaving Lise, and becoming a sister of mercy. I close my eyes and think and dream, and at that moment I feel strong enough to overcome any obstacle. No wounds, no festering sores could frighten me then. I would bind them up and wash them with my own hands. I would nurse the afflicted. I would be ready to kiss their wounds.”
“That is a great deal, and it is good that your mind is full of such dreams and not others. One day, without noticing, you may really do a good deed.”

“Yes. But could I stand such a life for long?” the lady went on, fervent, almost frantic. “That’s the main question—that’s the question that torments me most. I shut my eyes and ask myself, ‘Would you keep going on that path for long? And what if the patient whose wounds you were washing did not meet you with gratitude? What if he pestered you with his whims, never valued or even noticed your charity, abused you and bossed you rudely, and complained about you to the authorities (which often happens when people are in great pain)—what then? Would you keep on loving, or not?’ And do you know, I reached a horrifying conclusion. If anything could kill my love for humanity, it would be ingratitude. In short, I’m a hired servant. I expect my wages at once—that is, praise, and love paid back with love. Otherwise I can’t love anyone.”
She was in a perfect frenzy of self-punishment, and when she finished she looked at the elder with defiant resolve.

“That is just the story a doctor once told me,” observed the elder. “He was getting on in years, and undoubtedly a clever man. He spoke as frankly as you do, though in jest, in bitter jest. ‘I love humanity,’ he said, ‘but I am surprised at myself. The more I love humanity in general, the less I love people one at a time. In my dreams,’ he said, ‘I have often made rapturous plans to serve humanity, and I might even have gone to the cross for it, had that suddenly been required. And yet I cannot share a room with anyone for two days running, as I know from experience. The moment anyone is near me, his personality offends my self-importance and cramps my freedom. In twenty-four hours I begin to hate the best of men: one because he takes too long over his dinner, another because he has a cold and keeps blowing his nose. I turn hostile to people the moment they come close. But it has always happened that the more I hate people one by one, the more ardent my love for humanity becomes.’”
“But what is to be done? What can one do in such a case? Must one despair?”

“No. It is enough that it distresses you. Do what you can, and it will be counted to your credit. A great deal is already done in you, since you can know yourself so deeply and honestly. But suppose you have been talking to me so frankly only to win praise for your frankness, as you did from me just now. Then of course you will get nowhere in achieving real love. It will never go beyond dreams, and your whole life will slip away like a phantom. In that case you will naturally stop thinking about the future life too, and in the end you will calm down on your own, after a fashion.”

“You have crushed me! Only now, as you speak, do I see that I was really only angling for your praise of my sincerity when I said I couldn’t bear ingratitude. You have shown me myself. You have seen through me and explained me to myself!”

“Are you telling the truth? Well, then, after such a confession I believe that you are sincere and good at heart. If you do not find happiness, always remember that you are on the right road, and try not to leave it. Above all, avoid falsehood, every kind of falsehood, especially falseness toward yourself. Watch your own deceitfulness and examine it every hour, every minute. Avoid scorn, toward others and toward yourself. What seems bad in you will grow purer simply because you see it in yourself. Avoid fear too, though fear is only the consequence of every sort of falsehood. Never be frightened by your own faint-heartedness in pursuing love. Do not be too frightened even by your evil actions. I am sorry I can say nothing more consoling to you, for love in action is a harsh and dreadful thing compared with love in dreams. Love in dreams is greedy for immediate action, quickly done and seen by all. People will even give their lives, if only the trial does not last long but is soon over, with everyone watching and applauding as if at a play. But active love is labor and endurance, and for some people, perhaps, a whole science. But I predict that just when you see with horror that, in spite of all your efforts, you are moving farther from your goal and not closer to it—at that very moment, I predict, you will reach it. You will see clearly the miraculous power of the Lord, who has loved you all along and has been guiding you in secret. Forgive me, I cannot stay longer with you. They are waiting for me. Goodbye.”
The lady was weeping.
“Lise, Lise! Bless her—bless her!” she cried, jumping up suddenly.
“She does not deserve to be loved. I have seen her naughtiness the whole time,” the elder said teasingly. “Why were you laughing at Alexey?”

In fact Lise had spent the whole time mocking him. She had noticed earlier that Alyosha was shy and tried not to look at her, and she found this extremely funny. She waited intently to catch his eye. Alyosha could not bear her fixed stare. Suddenly, helplessly, he was pulled into glancing at her, and at once she smiled at him in triumph. Alyosha was more flustered and vexed than ever. At last he turned away from her completely and hid behind the elder’s back. A few minutes later, drawn by the same irresistible force, he turned again to see whether she was looking at him. He found Lise nearly hanging out of her chair to peep at him from the side, eagerly waiting for him to look. When she caught his eye, she laughed so much that the elder could not help saying, “Why do you make fun of him like that, you naughty girl?”
Lise suddenly, quite unexpectedly, blushed. Her eyes flashed and her face turned quite serious. She began to speak fast and nervously, in a hot, resentful voice:

“Why has he forgotten everything, then? He used to carry me around when I was little. We used to play together. He used to come and teach me to read, you know. Two years ago, when he went away, he said he would never forget me, that we were friends for ever, for ever, for ever! And now all of a sudden he’s afraid of me. Am I going to eat him? Why won’t he come near me? Why won’t he talk? Why won’t he come and visit us? It’s not that you won’t let him. We know he goes everywhere. It isn’t proper for me to invite him. He should have thought of it first, if he hasn’t forgotten me. No, now he’s saving his soul! Why did you put that long gown on him? If he runs, he’ll fall.”

And suddenly she hid her face in her hand and burst into helpless, long, nervous laughter that made no sound. The elder listened to her with a smile and blessed her tenderly. As she kissed his hand, she suddenly pressed it to her eyes and began to cry.
“Don’t be angry with me. I’m silly and good for nothing ... and maybe Alyosha is right, quite right, not to want to come and see such a ridiculous girl.”
“I will certainly send him to you,” said the elder.

chapters.title: V. So Be It! So Be It!
paragraphs: The elder had been out of his cell for about twenty-five minutes. It was already past twelve-thirty, and Dmitri, the reason they had all gathered there, still had not appeared. He seemed almost forgotten, though, and when the elder came back in, he found his guests deep in lively conversation. Ivan and the two monks were doing most of the talking. Miüsov was trying to take part too, and quite eagerly, it seemed. But he had no luck at that either. He was plainly pushed into the background, and his remarks were ignored, which only made him more irritable. He had crossed swords with Ivan before, and he could not stand a certain offhandedness Ivan showed toward him.
“Up to now, at least, I have stood in the front ranks of everything progressive in Europe, and here the new generation simply ignores us,” he thought.

Fyodor Pavlovitch, who had given his word to sit still and keep quiet, had in fact kept quiet for some time. But he was watching his neighbor Miüsov with a mocking little smile, clearly enjoying his discomfort. He had been waiting a good while to settle old scores, and he was not going to let the chance slip. Leaning over Miüsov’s shoulder, he started teasing him again in a whisper.

“Why didn’t you leave just now, after the ‘courteously kissing’? Why did you agree to stay in such improper company? Because you felt insulted and wronged, and you stayed to prove yourself by showing off your brains. Now you won’t go until you’ve shown them what a mind you have.”
“You again?... On the contrary, I’m just leaving.”
“You’ll be the last, the last of all to go!” Fyodor Pavlovitch jabbed at him once more, almost at the very moment Father Zossima came back.

The discussion died down for a moment. The elder sat down in his old place and looked around at them all as if warmly inviting them to go on. Alyosha, who knew every expression of his face, saw that he was dreadfully tired and was forcing himself. Lately he had been prone to fainting fits from exhaustion. His face had the pallor that usually came before such attacks, and his lips were white. Yet he plainly did not want to break up the gathering. He seemed to have some purpose of his own in keeping them there. What purpose? Alyosha watched him closely.

“We were discussing this gentleman’s most interesting article,” said Father Iosif, the librarian, addressing the elder and nodding toward Ivan. “He puts forward a lot that is new, but I think the argument cuts both ways. It is an article written in reply to a book by a churchman on the question of the ecclesiastical court and how far its jurisdiction extends.”
“I’m sorry to say I haven’t read your article, though I’ve heard about it,” said the elder, giving Ivan a keen, steady look.
“He takes a most interesting position,” the Father Librarian went on. “As far as Church jurisdiction goes, he is apparently entirely opposed to the separation of Church and State.”
“That’s interesting. But in what sense?” Father Zossima asked Ivan.
At last Ivan answered him—not condescendingly, as Alyosha had feared, but modestly and with reserve, with obvious goodwill and, it seemed, without the slightest _arrière-pensée_.

“I start from the premise that this confusion of elements—that is, of the essential principles of Church and State—will of course go on forever, although it is impossible for them to mix, and although this confusion can lead to no consistent or even normal results, because there is falsehood at the very foundation of it. A compromise between the Church and the State on questions like jurisdiction is, I think, impossible in any real sense. My clerical opponent maintains that the Church holds a precise, defined position within the State. I maintain, on the contrary, that the Church ought to include the whole State and not merely occupy a corner of it. And if that is for some reason impossible at present, then it ought to be set up as the direct and chief aim of the future development of Christian society!”
“Quite right,” Father Païssy, the silent, learned monk, agreed firmly and warmly.
“Pure Ultramontanism!” Miüsov cried impatiently, crossing his legs one way and then the other.

“Oh, well, we have no mountains,” cried Father Iosif, and turning to the elder he went on: “Look at how he answers these ‘fundamental and essential’ propositions of his opponent, who is, mind you, a churchman. First: ‘No social organization can or ought to take it upon itself to dispose of the civic and political rights of its members.’ Second: ‘Criminal and civil jurisdiction ought not to belong to the Church, and does not fit its nature, either as a divine institution or as an organization of men for religious ends.’ And third and last: ‘The Church is a kingdom not of this world.’”

“What an unworthy play on words, and from a churchman!” Father Païssy could not stop himself from breaking in again. “I have read the book you answered,” he said to Ivan, “and I was astounded by the words ‘the Church is a kingdom not of this world.’ If it is not of this world, it cannot exist on earth at all. In the Gospel, the words ‘not of this world’ do not mean that. It is indefensible to play with words like this. Our Lord Jesus Christ came to establish the Church on earth. The Kingdom of Heaven, of course, is not of this world but in Heaven. Yet it can be entered only through the Church, which He founded and set up on earth. So a frivolous play on words here is unpardonable and improper. The Church is truly a kingdom, ordained to rule, and in the end it must surely become the kingdom that rules over all the earth. We have God’s promise of that.”
He stopped speaking suddenly, as if checking himself. After listening attentively and respectfully, Ivan went on, addressing the elder with perfect composure and the same ready cordiality as before:

“The whole point of my article is that during the first three centuries Christianity existed on earth only in the Church and was nothing but the Church. When the pagan Roman Empire wanted to become Christian, it inevitably happened that, in becoming Christian, it took in the Church but remained a pagan State in very many of its departments. In reality this was bound to happen. But Rome as a State kept too much of pagan civilization and culture—for example, in the very aims and fundamental principles of the State. The Christian Church, entering into the State, could of course give up no part of its fundamental principles—the rock on which it stands—and could pursue no aims other than those ordained and revealed by God Himself. Among them was that of drawing the whole world, and therefore the ancient pagan State itself, into the Church. In that way (that is, looking to the future), it is not the Church that should seek a definite position in the State, like ‘every social organization,’ or as ‘an organization of men for religious purposes’ (as my opponent calls the Church). On the contrary, every earthly State should in the end be completely transformed into the Church and become nothing but a Church, rejecting every purpose out of keeping with the aims of the Church. None of this will degrade it in any way, or take from its honor and glory as a great State, or from the glory of its rulers. It only turns it from a false, still pagan and mistaken path onto the true and rightful path, which alone leads to the eternal goal. That is why the author of the book _On the Foundations of Church Jurisdiction_ would have judged correctly if, in seeking and laying down those foundations, he had regarded them as a temporary compromise, unavoidable in our sinful and imperfect days. But as soon as the author ventures to declare that the foundations he now proposes, some of which Father Iosif just listed, are permanent, essential and eternal, he goes directly against the Church and its sacred and eternal vocation. That is the gist of my article.”

“In short,” Father Païssy began again, stressing each word, “certain theories, all too clearly formulated in the nineteenth century, say that the Church ought to turn into the State, as though that were progress from a lower form to a higher one. She would vanish into it and make room for science, for the spirit of the age, and for civilization. And if the Church resists and refuses, a corner will be set aside for her in the State, and even that under supervision. This is how it will be everywhere in modern Europe. But Russian hopes and ideas demand something else. They do not want the Church to pass into the State as from a lower type to a higher. They want the State to end by becoming worthy of being only the Church and nothing else. So be it! So be it!”

“Well, I must say you’ve reassured me somewhat,” Miüsov said with a smile, crossing his legs again. “So as I understand it, the realization of such an ideal is infinitely remote, at the second coming of Christ. That’s up to you. It’s a beautiful Utopian dream of the abolition of war, diplomacy, banks, and so on—something like socialism, in fact. But I imagined it was all meant seriously, and that the Church might be going to try criminals _now_, and sentence them to beatings, prison, and even death.”

“But if there were nothing but the ecclesiastical court, the Church would not sentence a criminal to prison or to death even now. Crime and the way it is viewed would inevitably change—not all at once, of course, but fairly soon,” Ivan replied calmly, without flinching.
“Are you serious?” Miüsov gave him a sharp look.

“If everything became the Church, the Church would exclude all the criminal and disobedient, and would not cut off their heads,” Ivan went on. “I ask you, what would become of the excluded man? He would then be cut off not only from men, as now, but from Christ. By his crime he would have sinned not only against men but against the Church of Christ. Strictly speaking, this is so even now, but it is not clearly stated, and very, very often the criminal of today comes to terms with his conscience: ‘I steal,’ he says, ‘but I don’t go against the Church. I’m not an enemy of Christ.’ That is what the criminal of today keeps telling himself. But when the Church takes the place of the State, it will be hard for him, standing against the Church all over the world, to say: ‘All men are mistaken, all in error, all mankind is the false Church. I, a thief and murderer, am the only true Christian Church.’ It will be very hard to say this to himself. It takes a rare combination of unusual circumstances. Now consider the other side, the Church’s own view of crime. Is it not bound to give up its present, almost pagan attitude? Is it not bound to change from the mechanical cutting off of its tainted member to protect society, as now, into wholly and honestly adopting the idea of the regeneration of the man, of his reformation and salvation?”

“What are you saying? I’m lost again,” Miüsov broke in. “Another sort of dream. Something shapeless, even impossible to grasp. What is this excommunication? What kind of exclusion? I suspect you’re just amusing yourself, Ivan Fyodorovitch.”

“Yes, but you know, in reality it is so even now,” said the elder suddenly, and all turned to him at once. “Without the Church of Christ, nothing would hold the criminal back from doing evil, and there would be no real punishment for it afterward. I mean no punishment but the mechanical kind spoken of just now, which in most cases only embitters the heart. I mean not the real punishment, the only effective one, the only one that deters and softens, which lies in the conscience’s own recognition of sin.”
“How is that, may I ask?” Miüsov asked, with lively curiosity.

“Why,” began the elder, “all these sentences of exile with hard labor, and in the past with flogging too, reform no one. What is more, they hardly deter a single criminal, and crimes do not grow fewer but keep on increasing. You must admit that. So society is not made safe. The harmful member is cut off mechanically and sent far away, out of sight. But another criminal at once comes to take his place, and often two. If anything protects society, even in our time, and does regenerate and transform the criminal, it is only the law of Christ speaking in his conscience. Only when he sees his wrongdoing as a son of a Christian society—that is, of the Church—does he see his sin against society—that is, against the Church. So the criminal of today can recognize that he has sinned only against the Church, not against the State. If society, as a Church, held jurisdiction, it would know when to call a man back from exclusion and join him to itself again. But the Church has no real jurisdiction, only the power of moral condemnation, and so she of her own accord refrains from punishing the criminal in practice. She does not excommunicate him. She simply goes on exhorting him as a mother would. More than that, the Church tries to keep up full Christian fellowship with him. She lets him attend church services and receive the holy sacrament, she gives him alms, and she treats him more as a captive than as a convict. And what would become of the criminal, O Lord, if even Christian society—that is, the Church—rejected him, as the civil law rejects him and cuts him off? What would become of him if the Church punished him with excommunication as the direct consequence of the secular law? There could be no more terrible despair, at least for a Russian criminal, for Russian criminals still have faith. Yet who knows? Perhaps something fearful would happen then. Perhaps the criminal’s despairing heart would lose its faith, and then what would become of him? But the Church, like a tender, loving mother, keeps back from active punishment herself, because the sinner is already punished too severely by the civil law, and someone at least must have pity on him. Above all, the Church keeps back because her judgment alone holds the truth. So it cannot be joined, in practice or in morals, to any other judgment, even as a temporary compromise. She can make no bargain over that. The foreign criminal, they say, rarely repents, since the very doctrines of today persuade him that his crime is no crime, only a reaction against an unjustly oppressive force. Society cuts him off completely, by a force that overpowers him mechanically. (So at least they say of themselves in Europe.) It accompanies this exclusion with hatred, forgetfulness, and the deepest indifference to the final fate of the erring brother. So it all happens without the compassionate intervention of the Church, for in many places there are no churches at all. Churchmen and splendid church buildings remain, but the churches themselves long ago strove to pass from Church into State and disappear into it entirely. So it seems, at least, in Lutheran countries. As for Rome, it was proclaimed a State instead of a Church a thousand years ago. And so the criminal no longer feels himself a member of the Church, and sinks into despair. If he returns to society, he often does so with such hatred that society itself instinctively cuts him off. You can judge for yourself how it must end. In many cases it might seem to be the same with us. But the difference is that, besides the established law courts, we have the Church too, which always keeps up its bond with the criminal as a dear and still precious son. And there is something more. The judgment of the Church is still preserved, though only in thought. It no longer exists in practice, but it lives on as a dream for the future, and the criminal, no doubt, recognizes it instinctively in his soul. What was said here just now is also true: if the jurisdiction of the Church were brought into practice in its full force—if the whole of society were changed into the Church—then the Church’s judgment would influence the reformation of the criminal as it never does now. Possibly, too, crimes themselves would become incredibly fewer. And there can be no doubt that the Church would regard the criminal, and the crime of the future, quite differently in many cases. She would succeed in restoring the excluded, in restraining those who plan evil, and in raising up the fallen. It is true,” said Father Zossima, with a smile, “Christian society is not ready now and rests only on some seven righteous men. But since they are never lacking, it will stand unshaken, awaiting its complete transformation from a society almost heathen in character into a single, universal and all-powerful Church. So be it, so be it! Even if it comes at the end of the ages, for it is ordained to come to pass! And there is no need to be troubled about times and seasons, for the secret of the times and seasons lies in the wisdom of God, in His foresight and His love. What seems still far off by human reckoning may, by Divine ordinance, be close at hand, on the eve of its appearing. And so be it, so be it!”
“So be it, so be it!” Father Païssy repeated sternly and reverently.
“Strange, extremely strange!” Miüsov declared, not so much with heat as with suppressed indignation.
“What strikes you as so strange?” Father Iosif asked cautiously.

“Why, it’s out of all bounds!” cried Miüsov, suddenly bursting out. “The State is abolished and the Church is raised to the rank of the State. It’s not just Ultramontanism, it’s arch-Ultramontanism! Pope Gregory the Seventh never dreamed of such a thing!”

“You have got it completely wrong,” said Father Païssy sternly. “Understand this: the Church is not to be turned into the State. That is Rome and its dream. That is the devil’s third temptation. It is the other way around. The State is turned into the Church. It will rise and become a Church over the whole world. That is the exact opposite of Ultramontanism and Rome, and of your reading of it. It is simply the glorious destiny ordained for the Orthodox Church. This star will rise in the east!”

Miüsov said nothing, and the silence was pointed. Everything about him spoke of extraordinary personal dignity. A superior, patronizing smile played on his lips. Alyosha watched it all, his heart pounding. The whole conversation had shaken him deeply. In passing, he glanced at Rakitin, who stood rooted to his spot by the door, listening and watching closely, though his eyes were lowered. Alyosha guessed from the color in his cheeks that Rakitin was probably just as excited, and he knew what excited him.

“Allow me to tell you a little anecdote, gentlemen,” Miüsov said impressively, with a peculiarly majestic air. “Some years ago, soon after the _coup d’état_ of December, I happened to be calling in Paris on an extremely influential figure in the Government, and at his house I met a very interesting man. He was not exactly a detective, but a sort of superintendent over a whole regiment of political detectives—a rather powerful position in its own way. Curiosity prompted me to seize the chance to talk with him. He had not come as a visitor but as a subordinate bringing a special report, and he saw the reception his chief gave me. So he condescended to speak with some openness—to a certain extent only, of course. He was more courteous than open, as Frenchmen know how to be courteous, especially to a foreigner. But I understood him perfectly. The subject was the socialist revolutionaries, who were being persecuted at that time. I will quote only one most curious remark this man let drop. ‘We are not particularly afraid,’ he said, ‘of all these socialists, anarchists, infidels and revolutionists. We keep watch on them and know all their doings. But there are a few peculiar men among them who believe in God and are Christians, yet are socialists all the same. Those are the people we fear most. They are dreadful people! The socialist who is a Christian is more to be dreaded than a socialist who is an atheist.’ The words struck me at the time, and now they have suddenly come back to me here, gentlemen.”
“You apply them to us, and take us for socialists?” Father Païssy asked bluntly, without beating about the bush.

But before Pyotr Alexandrovitch could think what to answer, the door opened and the long-awaited guest, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, came in. They had in fact given up expecting him, and his sudden appearance caused a moment of surprise.

chapters.title: VI. Why Is Such A Man Alive?
paragraphs: Dmitri Fyodorovitch was twenty-eight, a man of medium height and pleasant looks, though he seemed older than he was. He was muscular, and clearly very strong. Yet his face did not look healthy. It was rather thin, the cheeks were hollow, and their color was an unwholesome yellow. His large, dark, prominent eyes were firm and determined, and yet there was something vague in them as well. Even when he was worked up and talking angrily, his eyes somehow did not follow his mood. They gave away something else, at times quite at odds with what was happening. “You can’t tell what he’s thinking,” people who spoke with him would sometimes say. Those who read something brooding and sullen in his eyes were startled when he suddenly laughed, since the laugh showed that cheerful, light-hearted thoughts were in his mind just when his eyes looked so gloomy. The strained look on his face just now was easy to understand. Everyone knew, or had heard, what a wild and dissolute life he had been leading lately, and how violently angry he had become in his quarrels with his father. Several stories about it were going around town. It is true that he was hot-tempered by nature, “of an unstable and unbalanced mind,” as our justice of the peace, Katchalnikov, aptly put it.

He was dressed stylishly and impeccably, in a frock-coat buttoned up with care. He wore black gloves and carried a top hat. He had only recently left the army, so he still wore a mustache and no beard. His dark brown hair was cropped short and combed forward over his temples. He strode in the long, determined way of a soldier. He paused for a moment on the threshold and looked over the whole company. Then he guessed that the elder was their host, went straight to him, bowed low and asked for his blessing. Father Zossima rose in his chair and blessed him. Dmitri kissed his hand respectfully and said, with deep feeling, almost with anger:

“Please be generous enough to forgive me for keeping you waiting so long. Smerdyakov, the servant my father sent me, told me twice, when I asked him, that the appointment was for one o’clock. And now I suddenly find out—”
“Don’t upset yourself,” the elder interrupted. “It’s nothing. You are a little late, that’s all. It makes no difference....”
“I’m very grateful to you. I expected no less from your kindness.”

With that, Dmitri bowed again. Then he turned abruptly to his father and gave him a bow just as low and respectful. He had plainly planned it beforehand, and he made this bow in all seriousness, feeling it was his duty to show respect and good intentions.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was taken by surprise, but he rose to the occasion. He jumped up from his chair and answered Dmitri’s bow with an equally deep one. His face turned suddenly solemn and impressive, which made him look positively spiteful. Dmitri bowed once to everyone present. Then, without a word, he crossed to the window with his long, resolute stride and sat on the one empty chair, next to Father Païssy. He leaned forward, ready to listen to the conversation he had broken off.
Dmitri’s entrance had taken no more than two minutes, and the talk picked up again. But this time Miüsov did not think it worth answering Father Païssy’s insistent and almost irritable question.

“Please let me step out of this discussion,” he said, with a touch of well-bred indifference. “It’s a subtle question anyway. Look, Ivan Fyodorovitch is smiling at us. He must have something interesting to say on it too. Ask him.”

“Nothing special, only one small remark,” Ivan answered at once. “European Liberals in general, and even our own liberal amateurs, often mix up the end results of socialism with those of Christianity. This wild idea is, of course, typical of them. But it isn’t only Liberals and amateurs who mix up socialism and Christianity. In many cases, it seems, the police do it too—the foreign police, naturally. Your Paris anecdote fits rather well, Pyotr Alexandrovitch.”

“Let me ask your permission to drop this subject altogether,” Miüsov repeated. “Instead, gentlemen, I’ll tell you another interesting and fairly typical story about Ivan Fyodorovitch himself. Just five days ago, at a gathering here, mostly of ladies, he solemnly declared in the middle of an argument that nothing in the whole world makes people love their neighbors. He said there is no natural law that man should love mankind. If there has been any love on earth up to now, he said, it was not because of a natural law but only because men have believed in immortality. Ivan Fyodorovitch added in passing that the whole of natural law rests on that belief. Destroy mankind’s faith in immortality, he said, and not only love but every living force that keeps the world going would dry up at once. Moreover, nothing would be immoral then, and everything would be lawful, even cannibalism. And that’s not all. He finished by claiming that for every individual like ourselves, who believes neither in God nor in immortality, the natural moral law must at once turn into the exact opposite of the old religious law. Egoism, even to the point of crime, would become not merely lawful but recognized as the inevitable, the most rational, even the most honorable outcome of his situation. From this one paradox, gentlemen, you can judge the rest of the theories of our eccentric and paradoxical friend Ivan Fyodorovitch.”
“Excuse me,” Dmitri suddenly cried out, “did I hear right? Crime must not only be allowed but recognized as the inevitable and most rational outcome, for every unbeliever! Is that it, or not?”
“Exactly,” said Father Païssy.
“I’ll remember that.”
With these words Dmitri fell silent, as abruptly as he had spoken up. Everyone looked at him curiously.
“Do you really hold that conviction about what follows if faith in immortality disappears?” the elder suddenly asked Ivan.
“Yes, that was my argument. There is no virtue without immortality.”
“Blessed are you if you believe that. Or else you are most unhappy.”
“Why unhappy?” Ivan asked with a smile.
“Because most likely you do not believe in the immortality of your own soul, nor in what you wrote yourself in your article on Church jurisdiction.”
“Maybe you’re right! ... But I wasn’t entirely joking,” Ivan said suddenly, strangely, and flushed quickly as he did.

“You were not entirely joking. That is true. The question still gnaws at your heart, and you have not answered it. But a man in torment sometimes likes to play with his despair, as if despair itself had driven him to it. In your despair you play with it too, with magazine articles and talk in society. You do not believe your own arguments, and with an aching heart you laugh at them inwardly.... That question you have not answered, and it is your great grief, for it demands an answer.”
“But can I answer it? Can it be answered in the affirmative?” Ivan went on asking in the same strange way, still looking at the elder with the same unexplained smile.

“If it cannot be settled in the affirmative, it will never be settled in the negative. You know that this is the peculiarity of your heart, and all its suffering comes from that. But thank the Creator, who gave you a lofty heart, able to suffer so, able to think and to seek higher things, for our dwelling is in the heavens. May God grant that your heart finds the answer while you are still on earth, and may God bless your path.”

The elder raised his hand, meaning to make the sign of the cross over Ivan from where he stood. But Ivan got up from his seat, went to him, took his blessing, kissed his hand, and returned to his place without a word. His face was firm and earnest. This gesture, and the whole conversation before it, so surprising coming from Ivan, struck everyone as strange and somehow solemn. They all stayed silent for a moment, and Alyosha’s face showed something close to alarm. But Miüsov suddenly shrugged. And at that same moment Fyodor Pavlovitch sprang up from his seat.

“Most pious and holy elder,” he cried, pointing at Ivan, “that is my son, flesh of my flesh, the dearest of my flesh! He is my most dutiful Karl Moor, so to speak. This other son, who has just come in, Dmitri, the one I’m asking you to give me justice against, is the undutiful Franz Moor. They’re both out of Schiller’s _Robbers_, and that makes me the reigning Count von Moor! Judge us and save us! We need not only your prayers but your prophecies!”
“Speak without buffoonery, and don’t begin by insulting your own family,” answered the elder, in a weak, worn-out voice. He was plainly growing more and more tired, and his strength was failing.

“A disgraceful farce, and I knew it would come to this when I came here!” cried Dmitri indignantly. He too jumped to his feet. “Forgive it, reverend Father,” he added, turning to the elder. “I’m not a cultured man and I don’t even know how to address you properly. But you’ve been deceived, and you were too kind-hearted to let us meet here. All my father wants is a scandal. Why he wants it, only he can say. He always has his reasons. But I think I know why—”

“They all blame me, all of them!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch in his turn. “Pyotr Alexandrovitch here blames me too. You’ve been blaming me, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, you have!” he said, rounding suddenly on Miüsov, who had no thought of interrupting him. “They all accuse me of hiding the children’s money in my boots and cheating them. But isn’t there a court of law? There they’ll add it all up for you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, from your notes, your letters and your agreements: how much money you had, how much you’ve spent, how much you’ve got left. Why does Pyotr Alexandrovitch refuse to give judgment? Dmitri is no stranger to him. Because they’re all against me, that’s why, while Dmitri Fyodorovitch owes me money, and not a little, but some thousands, and I have the papers to prove it. The whole town is echoing with his debauchery. And at his old post, more than once he spent a thousand or two on seducing some respectable girl. We know all about that, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, down to the most secret details. I’ll prove it.... Would you believe it, holy Father, he has captured the heart of the most honorable of young ladies, from a good family, with money of her own, the daughter of a gallant colonel who had once been his superior officer, a man who had won many honors and wore the Anna Order on his chest. He compromised the girl with a promise to marry her. Now she’s an orphan, and she’s here, and she’s engaged to him. And yet right in front of her he’s dancing attendance on a certain enchantress. And although this enchantress has lived, so to speak, in a civil marriage with a respectable man, still she has an independent character and is an unapproachable fortress to everyone, just like a lawful wife—for she is virtuous, yes, holy Fathers, she is virtuous. Dmitri Fyodorovitch wants to open this fortress with a golden key. That’s why he’s so insolent to me now and tries to squeeze money out of me, though he’s already thrown away thousands on this enchantress. He’s forever borrowing for the purpose. From whom, do you think? Shall I say, Mitya?”

“Be silent!” cried Dmitri. “Wait until I’ve left. Don’t you dare, in my presence, to smear the good name of an honorable girl! That you should say a single word about her is an outrage, and I won’t allow it!”
