He was gasping for breath.
“Mitya! Mitya!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch in a hysterical voice, squeezing out a tear. “Does your father’s blessing mean nothing to you? What if I curse you?”
“Shameless hypocrite!” Dmitri shouted furiously.

“That’s how he talks to his father! His own father! Think how he treats other people! Gentlemen, just imagine. There’s a poor but honorable man living here, loaded down with a big family, a captain who got into trouble and was discharged from the army, though not in public, not by court-martial, and with no stain on his honor. Three weeks ago Dmitri grabbed him by the beard in a tavern, dragged him out into the street and beat him there in front of everyone. And all because the man is my agent in a little business of mine.”

“It’s all a lie! The outside is true, but the inside is a lie!” Dmitri was shaking with rage. “Father, I don’t defend what I did. Yes, I say it openly: I treated that captain like a brute. I’m sorry for it now, and I’m sick at myself for my brutal rage. But this captain, this agent of yours, went to that lady you call an enchantress. He suggested to her, from you, that she take my I.O.U.’s that you’re holding and sue me for the money, to get me thrown into prison with them, if I kept demanding an account of my property from you. And now you blame me for having a weakness for that lady, when you yourself pushed her to captivate me! She told me so to my face.... She told me the whole story and laughed at you.... You wanted to put me in prison because you’re jealous of me over her, because you’d started pressing your attentions on her. I know all about that too. She laughed at you for that as well—do you hear?—she laughed at you as she described it. And here he is, this man, this father, who reproaches his dissolute son! Gentlemen, forgive my anger, but I foresaw that this cunning old man would bring you together only to make a scandal. I had come ready to forgive him, if he held out his hand. To forgive him, and to ask his forgiveness! But he has just insulted not only me but an honorable young lady, whom I revere so much that I dare not speak her name carelessly. So I’ve decided to expose his game, though he is my father....”

He could not go on. His eyes glittered and he could hardly breathe. But everyone in the cell was shaken. All of them except Father Zossima rose from their seats, uneasy. The monks looked stern, but they waited for a lead from the elder. He sat still. He was pale, not from excitement but from the weakness of his illness. An imploring smile lit his face. From time to time he lifted his hand as if to calm the storm, and of course one gesture from him would have been enough to end the scene. But he seemed to be waiting for something, and he watched them closely, as though trying to make out something that was not entirely clear to him. At last Miüsov felt utterly humiliated and disgraced.

“We are all to blame for this scandalous scene,” he said heatedly. “But I did not foresee it when I came, though I knew who I was dealing with. This must be stopped at once! Believe me, your reverence, I had no exact knowledge of the details that have just come out. I did not want to believe them, and I am hearing them for the first time.... A father jealous over his son’s dealings with a woman of loose behavior, and plotting with the creature to get his son jailed! This is the company I’ve been made to sit in! I was deceived. I tell you all, I was deceived as much as anyone.”

“Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Fyodor Pavlovitch suddenly yelled, in an unnatural voice, “if you weren’t my son, I’d challenge you right now to a duel ... with pistols, at three paces ... across a handkerchief,” he ended, stamping both feet.

Old liars who have spent their whole lives acting have moments when they slip so completely into the part that they shake or weep real tears, even though at that very moment, or a second later, they can whisper to themselves, “You know you’re lying, you shameless old sinner! You’re acting now, for all your ‘holy’ anger.”
Dmitri frowned painfully and looked at his father with indescribable contempt.

“I thought ... I thought,” he said, in a soft, almost controlled voice, “that I was coming home with the angel of my heart, my betrothed, to cherish his old age. And all I find is a depraved libertine and a despicable clown!”

“A duel!” the old wretch yelled again, gasping and spluttering on every syllable. “And you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, I’ll have you know that in all your family there has never been a loftier, or more honest—you hear?—more honest woman than this ‘creature,’ as you’ve dared to call her! And you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, you’ve dropped your betrothed for that ‘creature,’ so you must have thought yourself that your betrothed couldn’t hold a candle to her. That’s the woman you call a ‘creature’!”
“Shameful!” broke from Father Iosif.
“Shameful and disgraceful!” Kalganov cried out in a boyish voice. He had said nothing until then, and now he flushed crimson and shook with feeling.

“Why is such a man alive?” Dmitri growled in a hollow voice, beside himself with rage, his shoulders hunched up so high that he looked almost deformed. “Tell me, can he be allowed to go on defiling the earth?” He looked around at them all and pointed at the old man. He spoke evenly and deliberately.

“Listen, listen, monks, to the parricide!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, rushing at Father Iosif. “There’s your answer to ‘shameful!’ What is shameful? That ‘creature,’ that ‘woman of loose behavior,’ may be holier than you are, you monks who are out to save your souls! She fell, perhaps, in her youth, ruined by the world around her. But she loved much, and Christ himself forgave the woman ‘who loved much.’”
“It was not for that kind of love that Christ forgave her,” the gentle Father Iosif broke in impatiently.
“Yes, it was, monks, it was for that kind! You save your souls here eating cabbage, and think you’re the righteous. You eat a gudgeon a day, and you think you can bribe God with a gudgeon.”
“This is intolerable!” was heard from all sides of the cell.

But this shameful scene was ended in the most unexpected way. Father Zossima suddenly rose from his seat. Alyosha was nearly frantic with worry for the elder and for everyone else, but he managed to hold him up by the arm. Father Zossima walked toward Dmitri, and when he reached him he sank to his knees. Alyosha thought he had fallen from weakness, but he had not. The elder bowed down at Dmitri’s feet, clearly and deliberately, until his forehead touched the floor. Alyosha was so astonished that he did not help him up again. There was a faint smile on the elder’s lips.
“Good-by! Forgive me, all of you!” he said, bowing to his guests on every side.

Dmitri stood for a few moments, amazed. Bowing down to him—what did it mean? Suddenly he cried out, “Oh, God!” He covered his face with his hands and ran from the room. The guests all streamed out after him, so confused that they did not say good-by or bow to their host. Only the monks went up to him again for a blessing.

“What did it mean, falling at his feet like that? Was it a symbol, or what?” said Fyodor Pavlovitch. He had suddenly gone quiet, and he tried to start the conversation again without daring to address anyone in particular. They were all just then leaving the grounds of the hermitage.
“I can’t answer for a madhouse and for madmen,” Miüsov answered at once, in a sour mood, “but I’ll spare myself your company, Fyodor Pavlovitch, and, believe me, for good. Where’s that monk?”

“That monk” was the one who had invited them to dine with the Superior, and he did not make them look for him. He met them the moment they came down the steps from the elder’s cell, as if he had been waiting for them all along.

“Reverend Father, would you do me a favor? Please give my deepest respects to the Father Superior, and apologize for me, Miüsov, in person to his reverence. Tell him I very much regret that, because of unforeseen circumstances, I can’t have the honor of sitting at his table, much as I would wish to,” Miüsov said to the monk, irritably.

“And that unforeseen circumstance, of course, is me,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cut in immediately. “Do you hear, Father? This gentleman doesn’t want to stay in my company, or he’d go right away. And you’ll go, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, please go to the Father Superior, and enjoy your meal. I’ll be the one to decline, not you. Home, home, I’ll eat at home. I don’t feel up to it here, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, my amiable relative.”
“I am not your relative and never have been, you contemptible man!”

“I said it on purpose, to drive you mad. You always deny we’re related, but you are, whatever your wriggling. I’ll prove it from the church calendar. Ivan, you stay if you like, and I’ll send the horses back for you later. Pyotr Alexandrovitch, it’s only proper for you to go to the Father Superior and apologize for all the disturbance we’ve been making....”
“Is it true you’re going home? You’re not lying?”

“Pyotr Alexandrovitch! How could I dare, after what’s happened! Forgive me, gentlemen, I got carried away! And upset, too! And honestly, I’m ashamed. Gentlemen, one man has the heart of Alexander of Macedon and another has the heart of the little dog Fido. Mine is the heart of the little dog Fido. I’m ashamed! After such an escapade, how can I go to dinner and gobble up the monastery’s sauces? I’m ashamed, I can’t. You must excuse me!”

“The devil only knows, what if he’s tricking us?” thought Miüsov. He hesitated, watching the retreating buffoon with suspicious eyes. The buffoon turned around, saw that Miüsov was watching him, and blew him a kiss.
“Well, are you coming to the Superior’s?” Miüsov asked Ivan sharply.
“Why not? I was specially invited yesterday.”

“Unfortunately I feel forced to go to this blasted dinner,” said Miüsov, with the same irritability, not caring that the monk was listening. “We ought at least to apologize for the disturbance, and explain that it wasn’t our doing. What do you think?”
“Yes, we should explain that it wasn’t our doing. Besides, father won’t be there,” Ivan said.
“Well, I should hope not! Blast this dinner!”

They all walked on, though. The monk listened in silence. On the path through the copse he made just one remark: the Father Superior had been waiting for a long time, and they were more than half an hour late. He got no reply. Miüsov looked at Ivan with hatred.
“Look at him, off to the dinner as if nothing had happened,” he thought. “A brazen face, and the conscience of a Karamazov!”

chapters.title: VII. A Young Man Bent On A Career
paragraphs: Alyosha led Father Zossima to his bedroom and settled him on the bed. The room was small and held only the bare necessities: a narrow iron bedstead with a strip of felt for a mattress, and in the corner, under the ikons, a reading-desk with a cross and the Gospel lying on it. The elder sank onto the bed, worn out. His eyes shone and his breath came hard. He gazed at Alyosha closely, as if turning something over in his mind.
“Go, dear boy, go. Porfiry is all I need. Be quick, they need you over there. Go and wait on the Father Superior’s table.”
“Let me stay with you,” Alyosha pleaded.

“You are of more use over there. There is no peace in that place. You will wait at table and make yourself useful. If evil spirits rise up, say a prayer. And remember this, my son”—the elder liked to call him that—“you do not belong here in the time to come. When God wills to call me, leave the monastery. Leave it for good.”
Alyosha gave a start.

“Why do you look so? This is not your place for now. I bless you for great service out in the world. Yours will be a long pilgrimage. You will have to take a wife as well. You must bear _all_ of it before you return. There will be much to do. But I have no doubt of you, and that is why I send you forth. Christ is with you. Do not abandon Him, and He will not abandon you. You will see great sorrow, and in that sorrow you will be happy. This is my last word to you: seek happiness in sorrow. Work, and work without rest. Remember my words. I will speak with you again, but not only my days, even my hours, are numbered.”
Again strong emotion showed in Alyosha’s face. His lips quivered at the corners.

“What is it this time?” Father Zossima asked with a gentle smile. “Worldly people may follow their dead weeping, but here we rejoice for a father who is leaving us. We rejoice and we pray for him. Now leave me, for I must pray. Go, and be quick. Stay near your brothers—and not near one of them only, but near both.”

Father Zossima lifted his hand to bless him. Alyosha could raise no objection, though he badly wanted to stay. He also wanted to ask what the elder’s bow to Dmitri meant. The question was on the tip of his tongue, yet he did not dare. He knew the elder would have explained it without being asked, had he thought it right. Evidently it was not his will. That act had left a terrible impression on Alyosha, who believed blindly that it had a mysterious meaning. Mysterious, and perhaps dreadful.

As he hurried out of the hermitage grounds, to reach the monastery in time to serve at the Father Superior’s dinner, a sudden pang struck his heart and he stopped short. He seemed to hear Father Zossima’s words once more, foretelling his end. What the elder had foretold so exactly was bound to happen. Alyosha believed that without any doubt. But how was he to be left without him? How could he live without seeing and hearing him? Where was he to go? The elder had told him not to weep, and to leave the monastery. Good God! He had not known such anguish for a long time. He hurried through the copse between the hermitage and the monastery. He could not bear the burden of his thoughts, and he fixed his eyes on the old pines beside the path. He had not far to go, about five hundred paces. He expected to meet nobody at that hour, but at the first bend in the path he saw Rakitin, who was waiting for someone.
“Are you waiting for me?” Alyosha asked as he caught up.

“Yes,” Rakitin said with a grin. “You’re hurrying to the Father Superior’s, I know; he’s laid on a banquet. There hasn’t been one like it since he entertained the Bishop and General Pahatov. Remember? I won’t be there, but you go and pass the sauces. Tell me one thing, Alexey. What does that vision mean? That’s what I want to ask.”
“What vision?”
“That bowing to your brother Dmitri. And didn’t he tap the ground with his forehead, too!”
“You’re speaking of Father Zossima?”
“Yes, Father Zossima.”
“Tapped the ground?”
“Ah, that’s disrespectful, is it? So what? Anyway, what does the vision mean?”
“I don’t know what it means, Misha.”

“I knew he wouldn’t explain it to you! Of course there’s nothing marvelous in it, only the usual holy mummery. But the show had a point. Every pious soul in town will talk about it and spread the tale around the province, asking what it meant. In my opinion the old man does have a keen nose. He smelled a crime. Your house reeks of it.”
“What crime?”
Rakitin clearly had something he was dying to say.

“It’ll come in your family, this crime. Between your brothers and your rich old father. That’s why Father Zossima flopped down, to be ready for whatever turns up. If something does happen later, they’ll say: ‘Ah, the holy man saw it coming, he prophesied it!’ A poor sort of prophecy, though, just flopping down. ‘Ah, but it was symbolic,’ they’ll say, ‘an allegory,’ and the devil knows what else! They’ll remember it to his glory: ‘He foretold the crime and marked out the criminal!’ It’s always the way with these crazy fanatics. They cross themselves at the tavern and throw stones at the temple. Your elder’s the same: he takes a stick to a just man and falls at the feet of a murderer.”
“What crime? What murderer? What are you saying?”
Alyosha halted. Rakitin halted, too.

“What murderer? As if you didn’t know! I’d bet you’ve thought of it already. That’s interesting, by the way. Listen, Alyosha. You always speak the truth, though you always sit between two stools. Have you thought of it or not? Answer me.”
“I have,” Alyosha answered quietly. Even Rakitin was startled.
“What? You really have?” he cried.
“I ... I haven’t quite thought it,” Alyosha mumbled, “but as soon as you began to talk so oddly, it seemed to me I had thought of it myself.”
“There, you see? (And how neatly you said it!) You looked at your father and your brother Mitya today and thought of a crime. So I’m right?”
“But wait, wait a moment,” Alyosha cut in uneasily. “What makes you see all this? Why does it matter to you? That’s my first question.”

“Two questions, separate but natural enough. I’ll answer one at a time. What made me see it? I’d never have seen it if I hadn’t suddenly understood your brother Dmitri, looked straight into the heart of him in a flash. I got the whole man from one trait. These very honest but passionate people have a line they must not cross. If he crossed it, he’d run at your father with a knife. And your father’s a drunken, shameless old sinner who has never been able to hold back at any line. If both of them let go, they’ll both end badly.”
“No, Misha, no. If that’s all, you’ve set my mind at rest. It won’t come to that.”

“Then why are you shaking? Listen. Our Mitya may be honest (stupid, but honest), but he’s a sensualist. That’s the definition of him, the very core. It’s your father who passed his low sensuality on to him. Do you know, Alyosha, I honestly marvel at how you’ve kept yourself pure. You’re a Karamazov, too, remember! In your family sensuality is a disease. And now these three sensualists are watching each other with knives in their belts. The three of them have their heads knocking together, and you may be the fourth.”
“You’re mistaken about that woman. Dmitri—despises her,” Alyosha said, with something like a shudder.

“Grushenka? No, brother, he doesn’t despise her. He openly threw over his betrothed for her; he can’t despise her. There’s something here you don’t yet understand, my dear boy. A man falls in love with a beauty, with a woman’s body, or even just a part of a woman’s body (a sensualist will understand that), and for her he’ll give up his own children, sell his father and mother, and his country, Russia, too. If he’s honest, he’ll steal for her; if he’s humane, he’ll murder; if he’s faithful, he’ll deceive. Pushkin, the poet of women’s feet, sang of their feet in his verse. Others don’t sing about them, yet they can’t look at a woman’s feet without a thrill—and it’s not only the feet. Contempt doesn’t help here, brother, even if he did despise Grushenka. He does, but he can’t tear himself away.”
“I understand that,” Alyosha suddenly blurted.

“Do you really? Well, I suppose you do, since you blurt it out at the very first word,” said Rakitin with spite. “It slipped out of you without your noticing, and that makes the confession all the more precious. So it’s a familiar subject, you’ve already thought about it, about sensuality, I mean! Oh, you virgin soul! You’re the quiet type, Alyosha, a saint, I know, but the devil alone knows what you’ve thought about and what you already know! You’re pure, but you’ve been down into the depths.... I’ve been watching you for a long time. You’re a Karamazov yourself, a thorough Karamazov. No doubt birth and selection have something to answer for. From your father you get the sensualist, from your mother the crazy saint. Why are you shaking? Is it true, then? And do you know, Grushenka has been begging me to bring you along. ‘I’ll pull off his cassock,’ she says. You can’t think how she keeps begging me to bring you. I wondered why she was so interested in you. Do you know, she’s an extraordinary woman, too!”
“Thank her, and tell her I’m not coming,” Alyosha said with a forced smile. “Finish what you were saying, Misha. I’ll tell you my own idea afterward.”

“There’s nothing to finish. It’s all clear; it’s the same old tune, brother. If even you are a sensualist at heart, what about your brother Ivan? He’s a Karamazov, too. The root of the whole lot of you Karamazovs is that you’re sensual, grasping and crazy! Your brother Ivan writes theological articles for a joke, with some idiotic private motive of his own, though he’s an atheist and admits himself that it’s a fraud. That’s your brother Ivan. He’s trying to win Mitya’s betrothed for himself, and I think he’ll manage it. And what’s more, he’ll have Mitya’s consent. Mitya will hand his betrothed over to be rid of her, and run off to Grushenka. He’s ready to do that in spite of all his nobility and unselfishness. Mark that. Those are the deadliest people! Who the devil can figure you out? He sees his own vileness and carries on with it! And I’ll tell you something else: the old man, your father, is standing in Mitya’s way now. He has suddenly gone mad over Grushenka. His mouth waters when he sees her. It’s purely on her account that he made that scene in the cell just now, because Miüsov called her an ‘abandoned creature.’ He’s worse than a tom-cat in love. At first she only worked for him, on his taverns and some other shady business. Now he has suddenly realized what she is, and he’s wild about her. He keeps pestering her with offers, not honorable ones, naturally. And on that road they’ll crash into each other, the precious father and son! But Grushenka favors neither. She’s still playing with them, teasing them both and calculating which will get her more. She could filch a lot of money from the papa, but he wouldn’t marry her, and in the end he may turn stingy and keep his purse shut. That’s where Mitya’s worth comes in. He has no money, but he’s ready to marry her. Yes, ready to marry her! To drop his betrothed, a rare beauty, Katerina Ivanovna, rich and a colonel’s daughter, and marry Grushenka, who has been the mistress of that dissolute old merchant Samsonov, a coarse, uneducated provincial mayor. A murderous clash may very well come out of all this, and that’s exactly what your brother Ivan is waiting for. It would suit him down to the ground. He’ll carry off Katerina Ivanovna, whom he’s pining for, and pocket her dowry of sixty thousand. That’s a great temptation to begin with, for a man of no account and a beggar. And note this: he won’t be wronging Mitya, he’ll be doing him the greatest favor. I know for a fact that only last week Mitya got drunk in a tavern with some gypsy girls and shouted out that he was unworthy of his betrothed, Katya, but that his brother Ivan was the man who deserved her. And Katerina Ivanovna won’t refuse in the end a man as fascinating as Ivan. She’s wavering between the two already. And how has that Ivan won all of you, so that you all worship him? He’s laughing at you, enjoying himself at your expense.”
“How can you know that? How can you talk so sure of yourself?” Alyosha asked sharply, with a frown.
“Why do you ask, and why does my answer scare you? It shows you know I’m telling the truth.”
“You don’t like Ivan. Ivan wouldn’t be tempted by money.”
“Wouldn’t he? And what about Katerina Ivanovna’s beauty? It isn’t only the money, though sixty thousand is an attraction.”
“Ivan is above that. He wouldn’t court anyone for thousands. Money isn’t what Ivan is after, nor comfort. Perhaps what he’s after is suffering.”
“What wild dream is that? Oh, you—aristocrats!”
“Ah, Misha, his spirit is stormy. His mind is held in bondage. A great unsolved doubt haunts him. He is one of those who don’t want millions, but an answer to their questions.”

“That’s plagiarism, Alyosha. You’re quoting your elder’s phrases. Ah, so Ivan has set you a problem!” cried Rakitin, with open malice. His face changed and his lips twitched. “And a stupid problem it is. It’s no use guessing at it. Rack your brains and you’ll understand it. His article is absurd and ridiculous. And did you hear his stupid theory just now? If there’s no immortality of the soul, there’s no virtue, and everything is lawful. (And by the way, remember how your brother Mitya cried out: ‘I will remember!’) A charming theory for scoundrels!—(I’m being abusive, which is stupid.) Not for scoundrels, but for pedantic _poseurs_, ‘haunted by profound, unsolved doubts.’ He’s showing off, and it all boils down to ‘on the one hand we cannot but admit’ and ‘on the other it must be confessed!’ His whole theory is a fraud! Humanity will find the power to live for virtue within itself, even without believing in immortality. It will find it in love of freedom, of equality, of fraternity.”
Rakitin could hardly contain himself in his heat, but all at once, as if he had remembered something, he broke off.
“Well, that’s enough,” he said, with a smile twisted still further. “What are you laughing at? Do you take me for a vulgar fool?”

“No, it never crossed my mind to take you for a vulgar fool. You’re clever, but ... never mind, it was silly of me to smile. I understand why you get so hot about it, Misha. From your warmth I guess you’re not indifferent to Katerina Ivanovna yourself. I’ve suspected it for a long time, brother, and that’s why you dislike my brother Ivan. Are you jealous of him?”
“Jealous of her money, too? Won’t you add that?”
“I won’t say a word about money. I’m not going to insult you.”

“I believe you, since you say so, but the devil take you, and your brother Ivan with you. Can’t you see a man might dislike him quite apart from Katerina Ivanovna? And why the devil should I like him? He condescends to abuse me, you know. Why shouldn’t I abuse him?”
“I’ve never heard him say anything about you, good or bad. He doesn’t mention you at all.”

“Well, I heard that the day before yesterday, at Katerina Ivanovna’s, he abused me for all he was worth. That shows what an interest he takes in your humble servant. And which of us is the jealous one after that, brother, I can’t say. He was so kind as to give his opinion that if I don’t take up the career of an archimandrite in the near future and become a monk, I’m sure to go to Petersburg and get on some solid magazine as a reviewer. I’ll write for it ten years, he says, and in the end become the owner of the magazine and publish it on the liberal and atheistic side, with a socialistic tinge, a tiny gloss of socialism, but keeping a sharp lookout all the while, that is, keeping in with both sides and fooling the fools. By your brother’s account, the tinge of socialism won’t prevent me from putting the profits aside and investing them under the guidance of some Jew, until at the end of my career I build a great house in Petersburg, move my publishing offices into it, and rent the upper floors to lodgers. He has even picked the spot, near the new stone bridge over the Neva, which they say is going to be built in Petersburg.”
“Ah, Misha, that’s exactly what will happen, every word of it,” cried Alyosha, who could not hold back a good-humored smile.
“So you’re pleased to be sarcastic, too, Alexey Fyodorovitch.”

“No, no, I’m joking, forgive me. I’m thinking of something quite different. But excuse me, who can have told you all this? You can’t have been at Katerina Ivanovna’s yourself when he was talking about you?”

“I wasn’t there, but Dmitri Fyodorovitch was, and I heard him tell it with my own ears. If you must know, he didn’t tell me. I overheard him, without meaning to, of course, because I was sitting in Grushenka’s bedroom and couldn’t get away, with Dmitri Fyodorovitch in the next room.”
“Oh, yes, I forgot that she’s a relation of yours.”
“A relation! Grushenka, a relation of mine!” cried Rakitin, turning crimson. “Have you gone mad? You’re out of your mind!”
“Why, isn’t she a relation of yours? So I was told.”

“Where on earth did you hear that? You Karamazovs brag about being an ancient, noble family, though your father used to run around playing the buffoon at other men’s tables and was let into the kitchen only as a favor. I may be only a priest’s son, and dirt in the eyes of noblemen like you, but don’t insult me so lightly and so wantonly. I have a sense of honor, too, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I couldn’t be a relation of Grushenka, a common harlot. Kindly get that into your head!”
Rakitin was thoroughly irritated.

“Forgive me, for heaven’s sake, I had no idea ... besides ... how can you call her a harlot? Is she ... that kind of woman?” Alyosha suddenly flushed. “I tell you again, I heard she was a relation of yours. You go to see her often, and you told me yourself that you’re not her lover. I never dreamed that you, of all people, felt such contempt for her! Does she really deserve it?”

“I may have my own reasons for visiting her. That’s none of your business. As for relationship, your brother, or even your father, is more likely to make her your relation than mine. Well, here we are. You’d better go to the kitchen. Hello! What’s the matter, what is it? Are we late? They can’t have finished dinner so soon! Have the Karamazovs been making trouble again? Of course they have. Here’s your father, and your brother Ivan after him. They’ve burst out of the Father Superior’s. And look, Father Isidor is shouting something after them from the steps. Your father’s shouting back and waving his arms. Cursing, I expect. Bah, and there goes Miüsov, driving off in his carriage. You see, he’s leaving. And old Maximov is running!—there must have been a row. There can’t have been any dinner. Surely they haven’t beaten the Father Superior! Or were they beaten themselves, maybe? It would serve them right!”
Rakitin’s cries had good cause. A scandalous, unheard-of scene had taken place. It had all sprung from the impulse of a moment.

chapters.title: VIII. The Scandalous Scene
paragraphs: Miüsov was a man of breeding and delicacy, and as he arrived at the Father Superior’s with Ivan, he couldn’t help feeling a little uneasy inside. He was ashamed that he had lost his temper. A man like him, he thought, ought to have held that despicable wretch Fyodor Pavlovitch in too much contempt to be rattled by him in Father Zossima’s cell, and so to forget himself. “The monks weren’t to blame, anyway,” he told himself on the steps. “And if they’re decent people here (the Father Superior, I hear, is a nobleman), why shouldn’t I be friendly and polite to them? I won’t argue. I’ll agree to everything. I’ll win them over with good manners, and ... and ... make it clear that I have nothing to do with that Æsop, that buffoon, that Pierrot, and was simply fooled into this business, as they were.”

He made up his mind to end his lawsuit with the monastery and give up, then and there, his claims to the timber and fishing rights. He was all the more willing because those rights had lost much of their value, and he had only the haziest notion where the woods and river in question lay.

These good intentions only grew when he walked into the Father Superior’s dining room. Strictly speaking, it wasn’t a dining room at all, because the Father Superior had just two rooms, though they were far bigger and more comfortable than Father Zossima’s. There was no great luxury in them either. The furniture was old-fashioned mahogany covered in leather, in the style of 1820. The floor wasn’t even painted, but everything was spotless, and there were lots of fine flowers in the windows. The richest thing in the room just then was, naturally, the handsomely set table. The tablecloth was clean and the tableware sparkled. There were three kinds of well-baked bread, two bottles of wine, two of excellent mead, and a big glass jug of kvas. The mead and kvas were both made at the monastery and well known throughout the district. There was no vodka. Rakitin said afterwards that there were five courses: sterlet soup with little fish pies; then boiled fish prepared in a special way; then salmon cutlets, ice pudding and compote; and last, blanc-mange. Rakitin knew all about these delicacies because he couldn’t resist peeking into the kitchen, where he already had his foot in the door. He had his foot in the door everywhere and picked up news about everything. He had a restless, envious nature. He knew very well how talented he was, and in his vanity he anxiously overestimated it. He was sure he would play some prominent role. Alyosha, who was fond of him, was grieved to see that Rakitin was dishonorable without realizing it himself. Rakitin thought just the opposite: because he wouldn’t steal money left lying on a table, he was a man of the highest integrity. Neither Alyosha nor anyone else could have talked him out of that.

Rakitin, of course, was far too minor a figure to be asked to the dinner. Of the monks, only Father Iosif, Father Païssy and one other had been invited. They were already waiting when Miüsov, Kalganov and Ivan came in. The other guest, Maximov, stood slightly apart, waiting as well. The Father Superior came forward to the middle of the room to greet his guests. He was a tall, thin but still vigorous old man, his black hair streaked with gray, his face long, grave and ascetic. He bowed to his guests without a word. This time they went up to ask his blessing. Miüsov even tried to kiss his hand, but the Father Superior pulled it back in time to avoid the kiss. Ivan and Kalganov, however, carried out the ritual wholeheartedly and in full, kissing his hand the way peasants do.

“We must humbly apologize, your reverence,” Miüsov began, with an affable simper and in a dignified, respectful tone. “Please forgive us for arriving without the gentleman you invited, Fyodor Pavlovitch. He felt he had to decline the honor of your hospitality, and with good reason. In the reverend Father Zossima’s cell he got carried away by the unfortunate quarrel with his son and said some things that were quite out of place ... indeed, quite improper ... as”—he glanced at the monks—“your reverence no doubt knows already. So, seeing that he was at fault, he felt real regret and shame, and asked me and his son Ivan Fyodorovitch to bring you his apologies and regrets. In short, he hopes and means to make amends later. He asks for your blessing and begs you to forget what happened.”
With the last word of his tirade, Miüsov was entirely pleased with himself again, and no trace was left of his earlier irritation. He loved humanity once more, fully and sincerely.
The Father Superior heard him out with dignity and, bowing his head slightly, answered:
“I truly regret that he is not here. Perhaps at our table he would have come to like us, and we him. Do sit down, gentlemen.”
He stood in front of the holy icon and began to say grace aloud. All bowed their heads respectfully, and Maximov clasped his hands before him with unusual fervor.

At this moment Fyodor Pavlovitch played his final prank. It should be said that he really had intended to go home. After his disgraceful behavior in the elder’s cell, he truly felt that he couldn’t go to dine with the Father Superior as if nothing had happened. It wasn’t that he was very ashamed of himself—perhaps quite the opposite. But he still felt it would be improper to go to dinner. And yet his creaking carriage had barely been brought round to the hotel steps, and he had barely climbed in, when he suddenly stopped. He remembered what he had said at the elder’s: “Whenever I meet people, I feel that I’m lower than all of them and that they all take me for a buffoon. So I say, let me play the buffoon, because every one of you is stupider and lower than I am.” He wanted to get his revenge on everyone for his own improper behavior. He suddenly remembered that someone had once asked him, “Why do you hate so-and-so so much?” And with his shameless impudence he had answered, “I’ll tell you. He has never done me any harm. But I played a dirty trick on him, and I’ve hated him ever since.”

As he remembered this, he smiled, quietly and spitefully, and hesitated a moment. His eyes glittered and his lips actually trembled. “Well, I’ve started, so I may as well finish,” he decided. What he mainly felt at that moment might be put like this: “There’s no restoring my reputation now. So I’ll shame them for all I’m worth. I’ll show them I don’t care what they think—and that’s that!”

He told the coachman to wait and went back to the monastery with quick steps, straight to the Father Superior’s. He had no clear idea what he would do. But he knew he could not control himself, and that the slightest push might drive him to the furthest limits of obscenity—though only obscenity, nothing criminal, nothing the law could punish him for. When it came to it, he could always hold himself back, and at times he had actually marveled at himself for that. He appeared in the Father Superior’s dining room at the moment the prayer ended and everyone was heading for the table. He stood in the doorway and surveyed the company. Then, with his long, impudent, spiteful chuckle, he looked them all boldly in the face. “They thought I’d gone, and here I am again!” he cried to the whole room.

For a moment everyone stared at him in silence, and everyone sensed at once that something revolting, grotesque, downright scandalous was about to happen. Miüsov swung from the kindest mood to the most savage. Every feeling that had calmed and died in his heart came back to life at once.
“No! I can’t stand this!” he cried. “I absolutely can’t! And ... I certainly can’t!”
The blood rushed to his head. He actually stammered, but he was beyond caring about style, and he grabbed his hat.
“What is it he can’t?” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. “What is it he absolutely can’t and certainly can’t? Your reverence, may I come in or not? Will you take me in as your guest?”

“You are welcome with all my heart,” answered the Superior. “Gentlemen!” he added, “I dare to beg you most earnestly to put aside your quarrels and be joined in love and family harmony—with prayer to the Lord at our humble table.”
“No, no, it’s impossible!” cried Miüsov, beside himself.

“Well, if it’s impossible for Pyotr Alexandrovitch, it’s impossible for me, and I’m not staying. That’s what I came for. From now on I’m sticking with Pyotr Alexandrovitch wherever he goes. If you leave, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, I’ll leave too. If you stay, I’ll stay. Father Superior, you stung him with that talk of family harmony—he won’t admit he’s any relation of mine. That’s right, isn’t it, von Sohn? Here’s von Sohn. How do you do, von Sohn?”
“Do you mean me?” muttered Maximov, puzzled.
“Of course I mean you,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. “Who else? The Father Superior can’t be von Sohn.”
“But I’m not von Sohn, either. I am Maximov.”

“No, you are von Sohn. Your reverence, do you know who von Sohn was? It was a famous murder case. They killed him in a house of harlotry—I believe that’s what such places are called among you—killed him and robbed him. Old as he was, they nailed him into a box and shipped him from Petersburg to Moscow in the baggage car. While they nailed him up, the harlots sang songs and played the harp—that is, the piano. And here he is, the very same von Sohn. He’s risen from the dead, hasn’t he, von Sohn?”
“What’s happening? What is this?” voices said in the knot of monks.
“Let’s go,” Miüsov called to Kalganov.

“No, excuse me,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cut in shrilly, stepping further into the room. “Let me finish. In the cell you scolded me for behaving disrespectfully, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, just because I talked about eating gudgeon. My relation Miüsov likes his words to have _plus de noblesse que de sincérité_, but I like mine to have _plus de sincérité que de noblesse_—and damn the _noblesse_! That’s right, isn’t it, von Sohn? Father Superior, allow me. I may be a buffoon and play the buffoon, but I’m the soul of honor, and I mean to speak my mind. Yes, I’m the soul of honor, while Pyotr Alexandrovitch has nothing in him but wounded vanity. Maybe I came here to look around and speak my mind. My son Alexey is here, working out his salvation. I’m his father. His welfare matters to me, and it’s my duty to care. All the time I’ve been playing the fool, I’ve been listening and looking on the sly. And now I want to give you the last act of the show. You know how it is with us? Whatever falls stays where it fell. Once something has fallen, it has to lie there for ever. Well, not a bit of it! I want to get up again. Holy Father, I’m angry with you. Confession is a great sacrament, and I’m ready to bow down before it in reverence. But in that cell they all kneel and confess out loud. Is it right to confess out loud? The holy Fathers decreed that confession should be in secret. Only then is it a mystery, and that’s how it was in the old days. But how can I explain to him in front of everyone that I did this and that ... well, you know what I mean—sometimes it wouldn’t even be decent to speak of it—so it really is a scandal! No, Fathers, at this rate a man could be dragged along with you into the Flagellants, I suppose ... at the first chance I’ll write to the Synod, and I’ll take my son Alexey home.”

We should note here that Fyodor Pavlovitch knew just where to find the sore spot. Some time earlier, malicious rumors had gone around, and had even reached the Archbishop (not only about our monastery but about others that had elders), saying that the elders were shown too much respect, even at the expense of the Superior’s authority, that the elders misused the sacrament of confession, and so on and so on. They were absurd charges, and everywhere they had faded away on their own. But the spirit of folly that had seized Fyodor Pavlovitch, and was sweeping him along on the current of his own nerves into ever deeper shame, suggested this old slander to him. Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t understand a word of it. He couldn’t even state it sensibly, since this time no one had knelt and confessed aloud in the elder’s cell, and so he couldn’t have seen anything of the kind. He was only speaking from a muddled memory of old slanders. But the moment his foolish tirade was out, he felt he had been talking absurd nonsense. At once he longed to prove to his audience, and above all to himself, that it had not been nonsense. And although he knew perfectly well that every word would add more absurdity, he couldn’t stop himself, and charged blindly on.
“How disgraceful!” cried Pyotr Alexandrovitch.

“Forgive me!” said the Father Superior. “It was said long ago, ‘Many have begun to speak against me and have said evil things about me. And hearing it I said to myself: it is the correction of the Lord, and He has sent it to heal my vain soul.’ And so we thank you humbly, honored guest!” And he bowed low to Fyodor Pavlovitch.

“Tut—tut—tut—sanctimonious talk and stock phrases! Old phrases and old gestures. The same old lies and ceremonial kowtowing. We know all about it. A kiss on the lips and a dagger in the heart, like in Schiller’s _Robbers_. I don’t like falsehood, Fathers. I want the truth. But the truth isn’t found in eating gudgeon, and I say so out loud! Father monks, why do you fast? Why do you expect a reward in heaven for it? For a reward like that, I’ll come and fast myself! No, saintly monk, you try being virtuous out in the world. Do some good for society, without locking yourself in a monastery at other people’s expense and without hoping for a reward up above—you’ll find that a bit harder. I can talk sense too, Father Superior. What have they got here?” He went up to the table. “Old port wine, and mead brewed by the Eliseyev Brothers. Fie, fie, Fathers! That’s a long way past gudgeon. Look at the bottles the fathers have set out, he he he! And who paid for all this? The Russian peasant, the working man, brings the farthing he earned with his horny hand, wrung from his family and the tax collector! You bleed the people, you know, holy fathers.”
“This is too disgraceful!” said Father Iosif.
Father Païssy stubbornly said nothing. Miüsov rushed out of the room, and Kalganov hurried after him.

“Well, Father, I’m going after Pyotr Alexandrovitch! I won’t be coming to see you again. Beg me on your knees, and I still won’t come. I sent you a thousand roubles, and now you’ve begun watching me. He he he! No, I’ll say no more. I’m taking revenge for my youth, for all the humiliation I went through.” In a fit of pretended feeling, he banged his fist on the table. “This monastery has played a great part in my life! It’s cost me many bitter tears. You used to turn my wife against me—the crazy one. You cursed me with bell and book. You spread tales about me everywhere. Enough, fathers! This is the age of Liberalism, the age of steamers and railways. You won’t get a thousand roubles out of me, nor a hundred, no, nor a hundred farthings!”

We should note again that the monastery had never played any great part in his life, and he had never shed a bitter tear on its account. But he was so swept up in his pretended emotion that for a moment he almost believed it himself. He was so moved that he nearly wept. But in that very instant he sensed it was time to back off.
At this malicious lie the Father Superior bowed his head, and again he spoke with great weight:
“It is written again, ‘Bear with care and gladness the dishonor that comes upon you through no act of your own. Do not be confounded, and do not hate the one who has dishonored you.’ And so will we.”

“Tut, tut, tut! Thinking it over, and all the rest of the rigmarole. You think it over, Fathers. I’m off. But I’m taking my son Alexey away from here for good, on my authority as his father. Ivan Fyodorovitch, my most dutiful son, allow me to order you to follow me. Von Sohn, what are you staying for? Come to my place in town now. It’s fun there. It’s only a short verst away. Instead of lenten oil, I’ll give you roast suckling pig and kasha. We’ll have dinner with brandy and liqueur on the side.... I’ve got cloudberry wine. Hey, von Sohn, don’t miss your chance.” He went out, shouting and waving his arms.
That was the moment when Rakitin saw him and pointed him out to Alyosha.
“Alexey!” his father shouted from a distance when he caught sight of him. “You’re coming home with me today, for good. Bring your pillow and mattress, and don’t leave a trace behind.”

Alyosha stood frozen to the spot, watching the scene in silence. Meanwhile Fyodor Pavlovitch had climbed into the carriage, and Ivan was about to get in after him, grimly silent, without even turning to say goodbye to Alyosha. But now another scene of grotesque buffoonery, almost unbelievable, put the finishing touch on the whole episode. Maximov suddenly turned up at the side of the carriage. He had come running, panting, afraid of being too late. Rakitin and Alyosha saw him run. He was in such a rush that, in his impatience, he planted his foot on the step where Ivan’s left foot still rested, and gripping the carriage, he kept trying to jump in. “I’m coming with you!” he kept shouting, with a thin, merry laugh and a look of reckless glee on his face. “Take me too.”

“Look at that!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, delighted. “Didn’t I tell you he was von Sohn? It’s von Sohn himself, risen from the dead. Well, how did you tear yourself away? What did you _vonsohn_ there? And how did you get out of the dinner? You must have a brass face! I have one myself, but you surprise me, brother! Jump in, jump in! Make room, Ivan. It’ll be fun. He can lie somewhere at our feet. Will you lie at our feet, von Sohn? Or sit up on the box with the coachman. Hop up on the box, von Sohn!”
But Ivan, who had already taken his seat, said nothing and punched Maximov hard in the chest, sending him flying. It was pure luck that he didn’t fall.
“Drive on!” Ivan shouted angrily to the coachman.
“Why, what are you doing? What’s the matter with you? Why did you do that?” Fyodor Pavlovitch protested.
But the carriage had already pulled away. Ivan gave no answer.
“Well, you’re quite a fellow,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said again.

After a two-minute pause, with a sidelong look at his son, he said, “It was you who cooked up this whole monastery business, wasn’t it? You pushed for it, you approved of it. So why are you angry now?”
“You’ve talked enough rubbish. Give it a rest now,” Ivan snapped sullenly.
Fyodor Pavlovitch fell silent again for two minutes.
“A drop of brandy would be nice now,” he observed, as if uttering a great truth, but Ivan made no response.
“You’ll have some too, when we get home.”
Ivan was still silent.
Fyodor Pavlovitch waited another two minutes.
“But I’ll take Alyosha away from the monastery all the same, however much it annoys you, most honored Karl von Moor.”
Ivan shrugged contemptuously, turned away, and stared at the road. They didn’t speak again all the way home.

chapters.title: I. In The Servants’ Quarters
paragraphs: The Karamazovs’ house stood a good way from the center of town, though not quite on the outskirts. It was a pleasant old house of two stories, painted gray, with a red iron roof. Roomy and snug, it had many years of life left in it. It was full of unexpected little cupboards, closets and staircases. It also had rats, but Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t altogether mind them. “You don’t feel so lonely when you’re left by yourself in the evening,” he used to say. His habit was to send the servants off to the lodge for the night and lock himself in alone. The lodge was a big, solid building in the yard. Fyodor Pavlovitch had his cooking done there, although the house had a kitchen of its own. He couldn’t stand the smell of cooking, so winter and summer the dishes were carried across the courtyard. The house had been built for a large family, with room for five times as many people, servants included. But at the time of our story the only people living in it were Fyodor Pavlovitch and his son Ivan. The lodge held just three servants: old Grigory, his old wife Marfa, and a young man called Smerdyakov. These three deserve a few words. Of old Grigory I have already said something. He was firm and determined. Once something had convinced him, whatever the reasons (and they were often very illogical ones), that a thing was unalterably right, he went after it blindly and stubbornly. He was honest and incorruptible. His wife, Marfa Ignatyevna, had obeyed his will without question all her life. Yet after the emancipation of the serfs she had pestered him terribly. She was set on leaving Fyodor Pavlovitch and opening a little shop in Moscow with their small savings. Grigory settled the matter then, once and for all. “The woman is talking nonsense,” he said, “for every woman is dishonest.” They must not leave their old master, whatever he might be, because “that was their duty now.”
“Do you know what duty is?” he asked Marfa Ignatyevna.
“I know what the word means, Grigory Vassilyevitch. But why it’s our duty to stay here, that I’ll never understand,” Marfa answered firmly.
“Well, then, don’t understand. That’s how it’s going to be. And hold your tongue.”

And so it was. They stayed, and Fyodor Pavlovitch promised them a small wage and paid it on time. Grigory also knew that he had an undeniable hold over his master. It was true, and he was well aware of it. Fyodor Pavlovitch was a stubborn, cunning buffoon. His will was strong enough “in some of the affairs of life,” as he put it, yet in certain other emergencies he found himself, to his own surprise, extremely feeble. He knew his weaknesses and was afraid of them. In some situations a man has to keep a sharp lookout, and that’s hard without someone he can trust. Grigory was a thoroughly trustworthy man. More than once in his life Fyodor Pavlovitch had narrowly escaped a good thrashing because Grigory stepped in, and each time the old servant gave him a thorough lecture afterwards. But it wasn’t only thrashings Fyodor Pavlovitch feared. There were graver occasions, subtle and complicated ones, when a craving for someone faithful and devoted would come over him all at once, for no reason he could have explained. It was almost a sickness. In his lust he was corrupt and often cruel, like some poisonous insect. Yet when he was drunk he was sometimes overcome by a superstitious terror, a moral convulsion that almost took physical form. “My soul’s simply quaking in my throat at those times,” he used to say. In such moments he liked to feel that a strong, faithful man was close by, in the lodge if not in the room. He wanted a man who was virtuous and unlike himself, who had seen all his debauchery and knew all his secrets, and yet in his devotion was ready to overlook it all. This man was not to oppose him, and above all not to reproach him or threaten him with anything, in this world or the next. And in case of need, he was to defend him—from whom? From somebody unknown, but terrible and dangerous. What Fyodor Pavlovitch needed was to feel that there was _another_ man, an old and tried friend. In his sick moments he could call for him merely to look at his face, or perhaps to exchange a few quite irrelevant words. If the old servant wasn’t angry, Fyodor Pavlovitch felt comforted. If he was angry, he felt worse. Now and then (though very rarely) he even went to the lodge at night, woke Grigory and fetched him over for a moment. When the old man arrived, Fyodor Pavlovitch would start in on the most trivial matters, and soon send him away again, sometimes even with a joke. After Grigory had gone, Fyodor Pavlovitch would get into bed with a curse and sleep the sleep of the just. Something of the same kind had happened to him when Alyosha arrived. Alyosha “pierced his heart” by “living with him, seeing everything and blaming nothing.” More than that, Alyosha brought something his father had never known: no contempt for him at all, an unfailing kindness, and a perfectly natural, unaffected devotion to an old man who deserved it so little. All of this took the old profligate completely by surprise, since he had thrown off every family tie. It was a new and astonishing experience for a man who until then had loved nothing but “evil.” After Alyosha had left, he admitted to himself that he had learned something he hadn’t been willing to learn before.

I have already mentioned that Grigory detested Adelaïda Ivanovna, the first wife of Fyodor Pavlovitch and mother of Dmitri. Sofya Ivanovna, the poor “crazy woman,” he had protected, against his master and against anyone who happened to speak ill or lightly of her. His sympathy for the unhappy wife had become something sacred to him. Even now, twenty years later, he couldn’t stand to hear a slighting word about her from anyone, and he would stop the offender at once. Outwardly Grigory was cold, dignified and silent. He weighed his words and never spoke frivolously. At first sight you couldn’t tell whether he loved his meek, obedient wife, but he really did, and she knew it.

Marfa Ignatyevna was by no means foolish. She was probably cleverer than her husband, or at least shrewder than he in worldly matters. Even so, she had given way to him in everything, without question or complaint, from the day they married, and she respected him for his spiritual superiority. It was remarkable how little they spoke to each other in all their years together, and then only about the barest daily necessities. The grave and dignified Grigory thought over all his cares and duties alone, and Marfa Ignatyevna had long ago grown used to the fact that he didn’t need her advice. She felt that he respected her silence and took it as a sign of good sense. He had beaten her only once, and only lightly. It was in the year after Fyodor Pavlovitch’s marriage to Adelaïda Ivanovna. The village girls and women, who were serfs then, had been called together in front of the house to sing and dance. They had just started “In the Green Meadows” when Marfa, a young woman at the time, skipped out and danced “the Russian Dance.” She didn’t dance it the village way. She danced it as she had learned to when she was a servant in the rich Miüsov household, in their private theater, where a dancing master from Moscow taught the actors to dance. Grigory saw how his wife was dancing. An hour later, at home in their cottage, he gave her a lesson, pulling her hair a little. And that was all: it was never repeated, and Marfa Ignatyevna gave up dancing.

God had not blessed them with children. One child was born, but it died. Grigory was fond of children and wasn’t ashamed to show it. When Adelaïda Ivanovna ran away, Grigory took the three-year-old Dmitri, combed his hair, washed him in a tub with his own hands, and looked after him for almost a year. Later he looked after Ivan and Alyosha, for which the general’s widow rewarded him with a slap in the face; but I have already told all that. The only happiness his own child ever gave him was in the waiting for its birth. When it was born, grief and horror overwhelmed him. The baby had six fingers. Grigory was so crushed that he said nothing until the day of the christening, and kept out in the garden. It was spring, and he spent three days digging the kitchen garden. The third day was the day set for the christening. By then Grigory had come to a conclusion. The clergy had gathered in the cottage and the guests had arrived, among them Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was to be godfather. Grigory walked in and suddenly announced that the baby “ought not to be christened at all.” He said it quietly and briefly, forcing the words out, with a dull, fixed stare at the priest.
“Why not?” asked the priest, good-humoredly surprised.
“Because it’s a dragon,” muttered Grigory.
“A dragon? What dragon?”
For some time Grigory didn’t answer. “It’s a confusion of nature,” he muttered, vaguely but firmly, plainly unwilling to say more.

They laughed and, naturally, christened the poor baby. Grigory prayed earnestly at the font, but he didn’t change his opinion of the newborn child. Still, he didn’t interfere. As long as the sickly infant lived, he hardly looked at it. In fact he tried not to notice it, and mostly stayed out of the cottage. But after a fortnight the baby died of thrush. Then he laid the child in its little coffin himself and gazed at it in deep grief. When they were filling in the shallow little grave, he fell on his knees and bowed to the ground. For years he never mentioned his child, and Marfa never spoke of the baby in front of him. Even when Grigory wasn’t there, she never spoke of it above a whisper. Marfa noticed that from the day of the burial he gave himself up to “religion.” He took to reading the _Lives of the Saints_, mostly alone and in silence, always putting on his big, round, silver-rimmed spectacles. He rarely read aloud, perhaps only in Lent. He was fond of the Book of Job. Somehow he had got hold of a copy of the sayings and sermons of “the God-fearing Father Isaac the Syrian,” and for years he read it doggedly. He understood very little of it, but perhaps prized and loved it all the more for that. Recently he had started listening to the teachings of the Flagellant sect that had settled in the neighborhood. They plainly shook him, but he thought it improper to go over to the new faith. His habit of theological reading gave him a look of still greater gravity.

He may have been inclined to mysticism from the start. And the birth of his deformed child and its death were followed, as though by special design, by another strange and marvelous event. As he said later, it left a “stamp” on his soul. On the very night after the burial of his child, Marfa was woken by the wail of a newborn baby. She was frightened and woke her husband. He listened, and said it sounded more like someone groaning, “it might be a woman.” He got up and dressed. It was a rather warm night in May. As he went down the steps, he heard groans clearly, coming from the garden. But the gate from the yard into the garden was locked at night, and there was no other way in, since a strong, high fence ran all the way around. Grigory went back into the house, lit a lantern and took the garden key. His wife was hysterical, still convinced she heard a child crying, and that it was her own baby crying and calling for her. He paid no attention and went into the garden in silence. There he realized at once that the groans were coming from the bath-house near the garden gate, and that they were a woman’s groans. He opened the door of the bath-house and saw a sight that turned him to stone. An idiot girl who wandered the streets, known to the whole town by the nickname Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya (Stinking Lizaveta), had got into the bath-house and had just given birth. She lay dying, with the baby beside her. She said nothing, for she had never been able to speak. But her story needs a chapter to itself.

chapters.title: II. Lizaveta
paragraphs: Something about this affair struck Grigory in particular, and it confirmed a very ugly, revolting suspicion. Lizaveta was a dwarfish creature, “not five foot, within a wee bit,” as many of the pious old women said of her with pity after her death. She had a broad, healthy, red face with a look of blank idiocy. Her eyes had a meek expression, but their fixed stare was unpleasant. She wandered about summer and winter alike, barefoot, wearing nothing but a hempen smock. Her hair was coarse, almost black, and curled like lamb’s wool, so that it made a sort of huge cap on her head. It was always caked with mud, with leaves, bits of stick and wood shavings stuck in it, because she always slept on the ground, in the dirt. Her father, Ilya, was a homeless, sickly drunkard who had lost everything and for many years had worked for some well-to-do tradespeople. Her mother had died long before. Ilya was spiteful and diseased, and whenever Lizaveta came back to him he beat her inhumanly. She seldom did, though, because everyone in town was ready to look after her. She was an idiot, and so especially dear to God. Ilya’s employers, and many others in the town, mostly tradespeople, tried to dress her better. For the winter they always fitted her out with high boots and a sheepskin coat. But although she let them dress her up without a struggle, she would usually walk off, preferably to the cathedral porch. There she took off everything they had given her—kerchief, sheepskin, skirt or boots—left it all lying, and walked away barefoot in her smock as before. Once a new governor of the province came through our town on a tour of inspection and saw Lizaveta. His tenderest feelings were wounded. He was told she was an idiot, but he ruled that a young woman of twenty wandering about in nothing but a smock was an offense against decency, and that it must not happen again. But the governor went on his way, and Lizaveta stayed as she was. At last her father died. As an orphan she became even more acceptable to the religious people of the town. In fact, everyone seemed to like her. Even the boys didn’t tease her, and the boys of our town, the schoolboys especially, are a mischievous lot. She would walk into strangers’ houses, and no one drove her out. Everyone was kind to her and gave her something. If she was given a copper, she took it and dropped it straight into the alms-jug at the church or the prison. If she was given a roll or a bun in the market, she handed it to the first child she met. Sometimes she would stop one of the richest ladies in town and give it to her, and the lady would be glad to accept it. She herself tasted nothing but black bread and water. When she went into an expensive shop, where costly goods or money lay about, no one watched her. They knew that even if she saw thousands of roubles left unguarded, she wouldn’t touch a farthing. She hardly ever went to church. She slept either in the church porch or in a kitchen garden, climbing over a hurdle to get in (to this day our town has many hurdles where other places have fences). At least once a week she turned up “at home,” meaning the house of her father’s old employers. In winter she went there every night and slept in the passage or the cowhouse. People were amazed that she could bear such a life, but she was used to it, and tiny as she was, she was robust. Some townspeople said she did all this out of pride, but that is hardly believable. She could scarcely speak, and only now and then gave an inarticulate grunt. How could she have been proud?

It happened on a clear, warm, moonlit night in September, many years ago. Five or six drunken revelers were walking home from the club, at what we in the provinces thought a very late hour. They took the “back-way,” which ran between the back gardens of the houses, with hurdles on both sides. It leads out onto the bridge over the long, stinking pool we were used to calling a river. Among the nettles and burdocks under the hurdle, the revelers noticed Lizaveta, asleep. They stopped to look at her, laughing, and started joking with no restraint at all and no decency. One young gentleman took it into his head to ask, as a whimsical question, whether anyone could possibly regard such an animal as a woman, and so on.... They all declared, with lofty disgust, that it was impossible. But Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was one of them, sprang forward and declared that it was by no means impossible, that there was in fact a certain piquancy in it, and so on.... It’s true that he was overplaying the buffoon at that time. He liked to push himself forward and entertain the company, ostensibly on equal terms, of course, though really he stood to them in the position of a servant. It was just after he had received the news in Petersburg of his first wife’s death. He was drinking, with crape on his hat, and behaving so shamelessly that even the most reckless among us were shocked to see him. The revelers laughed, naturally, at this unexpected opinion. One of them even began to dare him to act on it. The others rejected the idea still more emphatically, though still in the highest spirits, and at last they all went on their way. Later Fyodor Pavlovitch swore that he had gone off with them, and perhaps he had. No one knows for certain, and no one ever knew. But five or six months afterwards, the whole town was talking, with intense and sincere indignation, about Lizaveta’s condition, and trying to discover which scoundrel had wronged her. Then suddenly a terrible rumor spread across town that the scoundrel was none other than Fyodor Pavlovitch. Who started that rumor? Of the drunken band, five had left town. The one still among us was an elderly and much respected civil councilor, the father of grown-up daughters, who could hardly have spread the tale even if there had been anything in it. But rumor pointed straight at Fyodor Pavlovitch, and went on pointing at him. Of course he didn’t take it much to heart. He wouldn’t have bothered to contradict a set of tradespeople. In those days he was proud, and he talked only with his own circle of officials and nobles, whom he entertained so well.

At the time, Grigory defended his master vigorously. He picked quarrels and arguments on his behalf and managed to bring some people over to his side. “It’s the wench’s own fault,” he insisted. The culprit, he said, was Karp, a dangerous convict who had escaped from prison and whose name was well known to us, since he had been hiding in our town. The guess sounded plausible, because people remembered that Karp had been in the neighborhood that very autumn and had robbed three people. But all this talk didn’t turn popular sympathy away from the poor idiot. She was looked after better than ever. A well-to-do merchant’s widow named Kondratyev arranged to take her into her house at the end of April, meaning to keep her indoors until after the confinement. They watched her constantly, but despite their care she escaped on the very last day and made her way into Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden. How she managed, in her state, to climb the high, strong fence stayed a mystery. Some held that someone must have lifted her over it. Others hinted at something more uncanny. The likeliest explanation is that it came about naturally: Lizaveta was used to clambering over hurdles to sleep in gardens, and somehow she had got up this fence, in spite of her condition, and then jumped down and hurt herself.

Grigory rushed to Marfa and sent her to Lizaveta, while he ran off to fetch an old midwife who lived nearby. They saved the baby, but Lizaveta died at dawn. Grigory took the baby, brought it home, sat his wife down and put it in her lap. “A child of God—an orphan is kin to everyone,” he said, “and to us more than to others. Our little lost one has sent us this child, who has come from the devil’s son and a holy innocent. Nurse him, and weep no more.”

So Marfa raised the child. He was christened Pavel, and people were quick to add Fyodorovitch (son of Fyodor). Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t object to any of this. He thought it amusing, though he kept strongly denying that he was responsible. The townspeople were pleased that he had taken in the foundling. Later Fyodor Pavlovitch made up a surname for the boy and called him Smerdyakov, after his mother’s nickname.

So this Smerdyakov became Fyodor Pavlovitch’s second servant, and when our story begins he was living in the lodge with Grigory and Marfa. He worked as the cook. I ought to say more about this Smerdyakov, but I am ashamed to hold my readers’ attention for so long with these common menials. I will return to my story, hoping to say more about Smerdyakov as it goes on.

chapters.title: III. The Confession Of A Passionate Heart—In Verse
paragraphs: After hearing the order his father shouted from the carriage, Alyosha stood undecided for a while. But for all his uneasiness, he did not stay standing there. That was not his way. He went straight to the kitchen to find out what his father had been up to upstairs. Then he set off, trusting that somewhere on the road he would find an answer to the doubt that troubled him. I should add right away that his father’s shouts, telling him to come home “with his mattress and pillow,” did not frighten him in the least. He understood perfectly well that those domineering shouts were only “a flourish,” put on for effect. There was a tradesman in our town who did much the same thing. He was celebrating his name-day with a party of friends, and when they refused him more vodka, he got angry. He smashed his own crockery and furniture, tore his own clothes and his wife’s, and finally broke his own windows, all for effect. Next day, of course, once he was sober, he was sorry about the broken cups and saucers. Alyosha knew that his father would let him go back to the monastery the next day, maybe even that evening. Besides, he was completely sure that his father might hurt anyone else, but would never hurt him. Alyosha was certain that nobody in the whole world would ever want to hurt him. More than that, he knew that nobody could. For him this was an axiom, taken for granted once and for all, and he went on his way without hesitation, relying on it.

But now a different kind of anxiety was bothering him, and it worried him all the more because he could not put it into words. He was afraid of a woman, Katerina Ivanovna. In the note that Madame Hohlakov had handed him, she had urgently begged him to come and see her about something. The request, and the need to go, had stirred an uneasy feeling in his heart straight away. All morning that feeling had been growing more painful, in spite of the scenes at the hermitage and at the Father Superior’s. It was not that he was uneasy about what she would talk of, or what he ought to answer. Nor was he afraid of her simply because she was a woman. He knew little of women, but he had lived among women all his life, from early childhood until he entered the monastery. No, he was afraid of that particular woman, Katerina Ivanovna. He had been afraid of her since the first time he saw her. He had seen her only two or three times, and had happened to say only a few words to her. To him she was a beautiful, proud, commanding girl. It was not her beauty that troubled him, but something else. And because his dread was so vague, it only grew worse. He knew her aims were of the noblest. She was trying to save his brother Dmitri, out of pure generosity, even though Dmitri had already treated her badly. Alyosha saw all these fine and generous feelings, and gave them full credit. Still, a shiver began running down his back as soon as he got near her house.

He thought that he would not find Ivan there with her, though Ivan was such a close friend of hers, because Ivan was surely with their father by now. He was even more certain that Dmitri would not be there, and he had a foreboding of why. So he would be talking to her alone. He badly wanted to run and see his brother Dmitri before that fateful meeting. He could talk to Dmitri about it without showing him the letter. But Dmitri lived a long way off, and was bound to be out as well. Alyosha stood still for a minute and made his final decision. He crossed himself with a quick, habitual gesture, smiled at once, and turned resolutely toward his terrible lady.

He knew her house. Going by the High Street and then across the market-place was a long way round. Our town is small, but it is spread out, and the houses are far apart. Meanwhile his father was waiting for him, and might not yet have forgotten his order. He could be unreasonable, so Alyosha needed to hurry to get there and back. He decided, therefore, on a short cut through the back ways, since he knew every inch of the ground. That meant skirting fences, climbing over hurdles, and crossing other people’s back-yards, where everyone he met knew him and greeted him. By this route he could reach the High Street in half the time.

On the way he had to pass the garden next to his father’s. It belonged to a little tumbledown house with four windows. As Alyosha knew, the house belonged to a bedridden old woman who lived with her daughter. The daughter had been a genteel maid-servant in generals’ households in Petersburg, and had now been home for a year, nursing her sick mother. She always dressed up in fine clothes, although she and her old mother had fallen into such poverty that they went to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s kitchen every day for soup and bread, which Marfa gave them readily. And yet, for all that she came up for soup, the young woman had never sold any of her dresses. One of them even had a long train. Alyosha had learned this from Rakitin, who always knew everything that went on in town. He had forgotten it the moment he heard it. But now, as he reached the garden, he remembered the dress with the train. He lifted his head, which had been bowed in thought, and met with something quite unexpected.

Dmitri was standing on something behind the hurdle in the garden, leaning forward, waving his arms wildly and beckoning to him. He was clearly afraid to say a word in case he was overheard. Alyosha ran up to the hurdle.
“Good thing you looked up! I was almost shouting to you,” Mitya said in a happy, hurried whisper. “Climb in here, quick! How wonderful that you’ve come! I was just thinking of you!”

Alyosha was delighted too, but he did not know how to get over the hurdle. Mitya put his powerful hand under his elbow to help him jump. Alyosha tucked up his cassock and vaulted the hurdle as nimbly as a barefoot street boy.
“Well done! Now come along,” said Mitya in an excited whisper.
“Where to?” whispered Alyosha, looking around him. He was in a deserted garden with nobody near but the two of them. The garden was small, but the house was at least fifty paces away.
“There’s no one here. Why are you whispering?” asked Alyosha.

“Why am I whispering? Deuce take it!” cried Dmitri at the top of his voice. “You see what silly tricks nature plays on a man. I’m here in secret, on the watch. I’ll explain later. But since I know it’s a secret, I started whispering like a fool, when there’s no need. Let’s go. Over there. Till then, not a word. I want to kiss you.
Glory to God in the world, Glory to God in me ...
I was just saying that over, sitting here, before you came.”

The garden was about three acres, with trees planted only along the fence on all four sides: apple-trees, maples, limes and birches. The middle was an empty stretch of grass, which gave several hundredweight of hay in the summer. The owners rented the garden out for a few roubles for the summer. There were also patches of raspberries, currants and gooseberries along the sides, and a kitchen garden had recently been planted near the house.

Dmitri led his brother to the most secluded corner of the garden. In a thicket of lime-trees and old bushes of black currant, elder, snowball-tree and lilac stood a tumble-down green summer-house, blackened with age. Its walls were lattice-work, but it still had a roof that kept off the rain. God knows when it was built. The story was that a retired colonel named von Schmidt, who owned the house back then, had put it up some fifty years before. It was all falling to pieces. The floor was rotting, the planks were loose, and the woodwork smelled musty. Inside stood a green wooden table fixed in the ground, with green benches around it that were still safe to sit on. Alyosha had noticed his brother’s exhilarated state right away, and when he entered the arbor he saw half a bottle of brandy and a wineglass on the table.
“That’s brandy,” Mitya laughed. “I can see what you’re thinking: ‘He’s drinking again!’ Don’t trust appearances.
Don’t trust the worthless, lying crowd, And put your doubts aside.

I’m not drinking, I’m just ‘indulging,’ as that pig Rakitin of yours says. He’ll be a civil councilor one day, but he’ll still be talking about ‘indulging.’ Sit down. Alyosha, I could take you in my arms and press you to my chest until I crush you, because in the whole world—in reality—in re-al-i-ty—(can you take that in?) I love no one but you!”
He said the last words in a kind of exaltation.

“No one but you, and one ‘jade’ I’ve fallen in love with, to my ruin. But being in love isn’t the same as loving. You can be in love with a woman and hate her all the same. Remember that! I can still talk about it cheerfully. Sit down here at the table. I’ll sit beside you and look at you, and keep on talking. You keep quiet and I’ll talk, because the time has come. But on second thought, you know, I’d better keep my voice down, because here—here—you can never tell who’s listening. I’ll explain everything; as they say, ‘to be continued.’ Why have I been longing for you? Why have I been thirsting for you all these days, and just now? (It’s five days since I dropped anchor here.) Because you’re the only one I can tell everything to. Because I must, because I need you, because tomorrow I’ll tumble down from the clouds, because tomorrow life ends and begins. Have you ever felt, have you ever dreamed, that you were falling down a precipice into a pit? That’s exactly how I’m falling, only it isn’t a dream. And I’m not afraid, and you shouldn’t be afraid either. Well, I am afraid, but I enjoy it. Not enjoyment, though, but ecstasy. Damn it all, whatever it is! A strong spirit, a weak spirit, a womanish spirit—whatever it is! Let’s praise nature. Look at the sunshine, how clear the sky is, the leaves all green, still summer. Four o’clock in the afternoon, and such stillness! Where were you going?”
“I was going to Father’s, but I meant to stop at Katerina Ivanovna’s first.”

“To her, and to Father! Ha! What a coincidence! Why was I waiting for you? Why was I hungering and thirsting for you in every corner of my soul, even in my ribs? To send you to Father and to her, to Katerina Ivanovna, so that I’d be done with her and done with Father. To send an angel. I could have sent anyone, but I wanted to send an angel. And here you are, already on your way to see Father and her.”
“Did you really mean to send me?” cried Alyosha, looking distressed.
