“Hold on! You knew it! And I can see you understand everything at once. But be quiet, be quiet for a bit. Don’t be sorry, and don’t cry.”
Dmitri stood up, thought for a moment, and put his finger to his forehead.
“So she asked you to come? Wrote you a letter or something, and that’s the only reason you’re going to her? You wouldn’t go otherwise?”
“Here’s her note.” Alyosha took it out of his pocket. Mitya skimmed through it.

“And you were going the back way! Oh, gods, I thank you for sending him by the back way, and he came to me like the golden fish to the silly old fisherman in the fable! Listen, Alyosha, listen, brother! Now I’m going to tell you everything, because I have to tell someone. I’ve told an angel in heaven already, but I want to tell an angel on earth. You are an angel on earth. You’ll hear me out, and judge me, and forgive me. That’s what I need, for someone above me to forgive. Listen! Say two people break away from everything on earth and fly off into the unknown, or at least one of them does. And before flying off, or going to ruin, he comes to somebody else and says, ‘Do this for me’—some favor never asked before, that could only be asked on one’s deathbed. Would the other refuse, if he were a friend or a brother?”
“I’ll do it. But tell me what it is, and be quick,” said Alyosha.

“Be quick! Hm!... Don’t rush, Alyosha, you’re always rushing and fretting. There’s no need to hurry now. The world has taken a new turn. Ah, Alyosha, what a shame you can’t understand ecstasy. But listen to me, saying that to him! As if you didn’t understand it. What an ass I am! What am I saying? ‘Be noble, O man!’—who says that?”
Alyosha made up his mind to wait. He felt that perhaps his task really was here. Mitya sank into thought for a moment, his elbow on the table and his head in his hand. Neither of them spoke.

“Alyosha,” said Mitya, “you’re the only one who won’t laugh. I’d like to start—my confession—with Schiller’s _Hymn to Joy_, _An die Freude_! I don’t know German, I only know that’s what it’s called. Don’t think I’m talking nonsense because I’m drunk. I’m not the least bit drunk. Brandy’s all very well, but it takes two bottles to get me drunk:
Silenus with his rosy face, Riding his stumbling ass.

But I haven’t drunk even a quarter of a bottle, and I’m not Silenus. I’m not Silenus, though I am strong,[1] because I’ve made a decision once and for all. Forgive the pun; today you’ll have to forgive me a lot more than puns. Don’t worry. I’m not spinning this out. I’m making sense, and I’ll get to the point in a minute. I won’t keep you in suspense. Wait, how does it go?”
He lifted his head, thought for a minute, and began with feeling:

“Wild and fearful in his cavern Hid the naked cave-dweller, And the homeless nomad wandered, Laying waste the fertile plain. With spear and arrow threatening, The hunter roamed the woods.... Woe to all poor wretches stranded On those cruel and hostile shores!

“Down from lofty Mount Olympus Mother Ceres made her way, Searching through those savage countries For her lost child Proserpine. But the Goddess found no shelter, Met with no kind welcome there, And no temple stood to witness That the gods were worshipped here.

“From the fields and from the vineyards No fruits came to deck the feasts, Only the flesh of bloodstained victims Smoldered on the altar-fires, And wherever the grieving goddess Turned her melancholy gaze, Sunk in the vilest degradation Man displayed his loathsomeness.”
Mitya burst into sobs and grabbed Alyosha’s hand.

“My dear, my dear, in degradation, in degradation now, too. Man has a terrible amount to suffer on earth, a terrible amount of trouble. Don’t imagine I’m only a brute in an officer’s uniform, wallowing in dirt and drink. Hardly a thought goes through my head except of that degraded man—if only I’m not lying. May God grant I’m not lying and showing off. I think about that man because I am that man myself.
If he would cleanse his soul of vileness And reach for light and worth, He must turn and cling forever To his ancient Mother Earth.

But the trouble is, how am I to cling forever to Mother Earth? I don’t kiss her. I don’t lie on her breast. Should I become a peasant or a shepherd? I go on and on, and I don’t know whether I’m heading for shame or for light and joy. That’s the trouble, because everything in the world is a riddle! And whenever I’ve happened to sink into the lowest degradation (and it happens all the time), I always read that poem about Ceres and man. Has it reformed me? Never! Because I’m a Karamazov. When I leap into the pit, I go in headfirst with my heels in the air, and I’m glad to be falling in that shameful position, and proud of it. And in the very depths of the degradation I start a hymn of praise. Let me be cursed. Let me be vile and base, only let me kiss the hem of the veil that wraps my God. Even if I’m following the devil, I am Your son, O Lord, and I love You, and I feel the joy without which the world cannot stand.

Joy everlasting feeds the soul Of all that was created; Her secret ferment sets aflame The cup of life. At her command the grass Turned every blade to the light, And solar systems rose from chaos And from the dark of night, Filling the realms of boundless space Beyond the sage’s sight. At bountiful Nature’s kindly breast All things that breathe drink Joy, And birds and beasts and creeping things All follow where she leads. Her gifts to man are friends in need, The wreath, the foaming must; To angels, a vision of God’s throne; To insects, sensual lust.

But enough poetry! I’m in tears, so let me cry. It may be a piece of foolishness that anyone else would laugh at. But you won’t laugh. Your eyes are shining, too. Enough poetry. Now I want to talk to you about those insects, the ones God gave “sensual lust.”
To insects, sensual lust.

I am that insect, brother, and it was said about me in particular. All of us Karamazovs are such insects, and, angel though you are, that insect lives in you, too, and will stir up a storm in your blood. Storms, because sensual lust is a storm—worse than a storm! Beauty is a terrible, awful thing! It is terrible because it can’t be fathomed and never can be, since God gives us nothing but riddles. Here the boundaries meet and all contradictions lie side by side. I’m not an educated man, brother, but I’ve thought a lot about this. The mysteries there are—it’s terrible! Too many riddles weigh men down on earth. We have to solve them as best we can, and try to come out of the water dry. Beauty! I can’t bear the thought that a man of lofty mind and heart starts with the ideal of the Madonna and ends with the ideal of Sodom. What’s still more awful is that a man with the ideal of Sodom in his soul doesn’t give up the ideal of the Madonna, and his heart may burn with that ideal, truly burn, just as it did in his innocent youth. Yes, man is broad, too broad, in fact. I’d make him narrower. The devil only knows what to make of it! What the mind finds shameful, the heart finds beautiful, and nothing else. Is there beauty in Sodom? Believe me, for the vast mass of mankind, beauty is found in Sodom. Did you know that secret? The awful thing is that beauty is mysterious as well as terrible. God and the devil are fighting there, and the battlefield is the human heart. But a man always talks about his own ache. Listen, now, let’s get to the facts.”

chapters.title: IV. The Confession Of A Passionate Heart—In Anecdote
paragraphs: “I was living wildly in those days. Father said just now that I spent several thousand roubles on seducing young girls. That’s a filthy invention. Nothing of the sort happened. And if it did, I didn’t need money for _that_. For me, money is a trimming, the overflow of my heart, the frame. One day she’d be my lady; the next, some girl from the street would be in her place. I entertained them both. I tossed money away by the fistful on music, wild parties and gypsies. Sometimes I handed it to the ladies too, since they grab it eagerly, I have to admit, and are pleased and thankful for it. Ladies were fond of me. Not every one, but it happened, it happened. Still, I always preferred the side-paths, the little dark back-alleys off the main road. That’s where the adventures are, and the surprises, and the precious metal in the dirt. I’m talking figuratively, brother. The town I lived in had no back-alleys like that in the literal sense, but morally it had plenty. If you were like me, you’d know what I mean. I loved vice. I loved the disgrace of vice. I loved cruelty. Am I not a bug, a noxious insect? A Karamazov, in a word! Once a whole crowd of us drove out on a picnic, in seven sledges. It was winter and dark, and I began squeezing a girl’s hand and forced her to kiss me. She was the daughter of an official, a sweet, gentle, yielding creature. She let me, she let me do a great deal in the dark. She thought, poor thing, that I’d come the next day and propose. (I was thought a good catch, too.) But for five months I didn’t say one word to her. At dances (we had dances all the time) I would see her in a corner with her eyes on me. I saw them glow with a fire, a fire of gentle indignation. This game just tickled the insect lust I kept in my soul. Five months later she married an official and left town, still angry, and still, perhaps, in love with me. Now they’re happy together. Note that I told nobody. I didn’t brag about it. I’m full of low desires and I love what’s low, but I’m not dishonorable. You’re blushing; your eyes flashed. That’s enough of this filth with you. And all that was nothing much, wayside blossoms _à la_ Paul de Kock, though the cruel insect had already grown strong in my soul. I’ve a whole album of memories, brother. God bless them, the darlings. I always tried to part without a quarrel. And I never gave them away. I never bragged about even one. But enough of that. You can’t think I brought you here only to talk such nonsense. No. What I’m going to tell you is more curious. And don’t be surprised that I’m glad to tell it, instead of being ashamed.”
“You’re saying that because I blushed,” Alyosha said suddenly. “I didn’t blush at what you were telling me or at what you’ve done. I blushed because I’m just like you.”
“You? Oh, come on. That’s going a bit too far!”

“It isn’t too far,” said Alyosha warmly (plainly he had thought this before). “It’s the same ladder. I’m on the bottom step and you’re up above, around the thirteenth. That’s how I see it. But it comes to the same thing. It’s exactly the same kind of thing. Whoever is on the bottom step is bound to climb to the top one.”
“Then you shouldn’t step on the ladder at all.”
“Anyone who can avoid it had better not.”
“But can you?”
“I don’t think so.”

“Hush, Alyosha, hush, my dear! You touch me so much I could kiss your hand. That rogue Grushenka knows men. She told me once that she’d eat you up some day. There, there, I won’t go on! Let’s leave this field of rot, all over flies, and go on to my tragedy, which is also all over flies, meaning every kind of baseness. The old man lied when he said I seduced innocence. But my tragedy did have something like that in it, though it happened only once, and even then it didn’t come off. The old man who accuses me of what never happened doesn’t even know about this. I never told anybody. You’re the first, apart from Ivan, of course. Ivan knows everything. He knew it long before you did. But Ivan is a tomb.”
“Ivan is a tomb?”
“Yes.”
Alyosha listened with great attention.

“I was a lieutenant in a line regiment, but I was still watched, like a sort of convict. Even so, the little town received me awfully well. I spent money left and right. People took me for rich, and so did I. But I must have charmed them in other ways too. They shook their heads over me, yet they liked me. My colonel, an old man, suddenly took against me. He was forever picking on me. But I had powerful friends, and the whole town besides was on my side, so he couldn’t do me much harm. It was my own fault, for I wouldn’t show him proper respect. I was proud. This stubborn old fellow was really a very decent sort, kind-hearted and hospitable. He’d had two wives, and both were dead. His first wife, from a humble family, left a daughter as unpretentious as herself. When I was there she was a young woman of twenty-four. She lived with her father and an aunt, her mother’s sister. The aunt was simple and had no schooling; the niece was simple too, but lively. I like saying nice things about people. I never knew a woman with a more charming nature than Agafya. Imagine, her name was Agafya Ivanovna! And she wasn’t bad-looking either, in the Russian way: tall, stout, with a full figure and beautiful eyes, though her face was rather coarse. She’d never married, though two men had asked her. She said no to both and stayed as cheerful as ever. We were close, though not in ‘that’ way. It was pure friendship. I’ve often been friends with women quite innocently. I talked to her with shocking frankness, and she only laughed. Many women enjoy such freedom, and since she was a girl as well, it was very amusing. And another thing: you could never think of her as a young lady. She and her aunt lived in her father’s house with a kind of chosen humility, never setting themselves up as equal to other people. Everyone liked her and she was useful to all, being a clever dressmaker. She had a talent for it. She gave her work freely, asking for nothing, but if someone offered to pay, she didn’t say no. The colonel, of course, was another matter altogether. He was one of the leading figures of the district. He kept open house and entertained the whole town, with suppers and dances. When I arrived and joined the battalion, the whole town was talking about the colonel’s second daughter, a great beauty, who was expected home any day. She had just left a fashionable school in the capital. This second daughter is Katerina Ivanovna. She was the child of the second wife, who came from the family of a distinguished general. Though, as I learned on good authority, she too brought the colonel no money. She had connections, and that was all. There may have been expectations, but they had come to nothing.

“Still, when the young lady came home from boarding-school for a visit, the whole town woke up. Our most distinguished ladies took her up at once—two ‘Excellencies’ and a colonel’s wife—and everyone else followed their lead and gave parties in her honor. She was the belle of the balls and picnics, and they staged _tableaux vivants_ to help poor governesses. I paid no attention and went on as wildly as before. In fact, one of my exploits just then set the whole town talking. One evening at the battery commander’s I saw her eyes taking my measure. I didn’t go over to her, as if I scorned to know her. Soon after, at an evening party, I did go over and speak to her. She barely looked at me and pursed her lips in scorn. ‘Just wait. I’ll get even,’ I thought. I played the awful fool many times back then, and I knew it myself. What made it worse was that I could tell ‘Katenka’ was no innocent boarding-school miss but a person of character, proud and truly principled. Above all she had education and intellect, and I had neither. You think I meant to propose? No. I only wanted revenge, because I was such a hero and she didn’t seem to feel it.

“Meanwhile I passed my time in drink and riot, until the lieutenant-colonel put me under arrest for three days. Right then Father sent me six thousand roubles. In return I’d sent him a deed giving up all claims on him—settling our accounts, so to speak, and saying I’d expect nothing more. I didn’t understand a word of it then. Until I came here, Alyosha, until the last few days really, and maybe even now, I haven’t been able to make head or tail of my money affairs with Father. But never mind that. We’ll talk about it later.

“The moment I got the money, a letter came from a friend, telling me something that interested me enormously. The authorities, I learned, were unhappy with our lieutenant-colonel. He was suspected of irregularities. In fact, his enemies were preparing a surprise for him. Then the commander of the division arrived and kicked up the devil of a row. Soon afterwards the colonel was ordered to retire. I won’t tell you how it all happened. He certainly had enemies. All at once the town went markedly cold on him and his whole family. His friends all turned their backs. That was when I took my first step. I met Agafya Ivanovna, whom I’d always been friendly with, and said, ‘Do you know that 4,500 roubles of government money is missing from your father’s accounts?’
“‘What do you mean? Why do you say that? The general was here not long ago and everything was all right.’
“‘It was then. It isn’t now.’
“She was terribly frightened.
“‘Don’t scare me!’ she said. ‘Who told you that?’

“‘Don’t be alarmed,’ I said. ‘I won’t tell a soul. You know I’m silent as the grave. I only wanted to add, in case of “possibilities,” that when they demand the 4,500 roubles from your father and he can’t produce it, he’ll be tried and made to serve as a common soldier in his old age. Unless you’d like to send your young lady to me, secretly. I’ve just been paid some money. I’ll give her four thousand, if you like, and keep the secret religiously.’
“‘Oh, you scoundrel!’—those were her words. ‘You wicked scoundrel! How dare you!’

“She stormed off, furiously indignant, while I shouted after her once more that the secret would be kept sacred. I may as well say right away that those two simple creatures, Agafya and her aunt, behaved like perfect angels through this whole affair. They truly adored their ‘Katya.’ They thought her far above themselves and waited on her hand and foot. But Agafya told her about our conversation. I found that out later. She didn’t hold anything back, and of course that was all I wanted.

“Suddenly the new major arrived to take over the battalion. The old lieutenant-colonel fell ill at once. For two days he couldn’t leave his room, and he didn’t hand over the government money. Dr. Kravchenko declared he really was ill. But I knew for a fact, and had known for a long time, that for the past four years the money had never been in his hands except when the Commander came on inspection. He used to lend it to a man he could trust, a merchant of our town named Trifonov, an old widower with a big beard and gold-rimmed spectacles. Trifonov would go to the fair, make a profitable business out of the money, and return the whole sum to the colonel, along with a present from the fair and interest on the loan. This time, though (I heard all about it by pure chance from Trifonov’s son and heir, a slobbering youth and one of the most vicious in the world)—this time, I say, Trifonov brought nothing back from the fair. The lieutenant-colonel flew at him. ‘I’ve never had any money from you, and couldn’t possibly have had any.’ That was the only answer he got. So now our lieutenant-colonel sits shut up at home with a towel round his head, and all three of them are busy putting ice on it. Suddenly an orderly appears with the book and the order to ‘hand over the battalion money at once, within two hours.’ He signed the book (I saw the signature in it afterwards) and got up, saying he would put on his uniform. He ran to his bedroom, loaded his double-barreled gun with a service bullet, pulled the boot off his right foot, set the gun against his chest, and began feeling for the trigger with his toe. But Agafya, remembering what I’d told her, was suspicious. She crept up and looked into the room just in time. She rushed in, threw herself on him from behind and wrapped her arms round him. The gun went off, hit the ceiling and hurt no one. The others ran in, took the gun away and held him by the arms. I heard all this afterwards. I was at home. It was getting dark, and I was about to go out. I had dressed, brushed my hair, scented my handkerchief and picked up my cap, when suddenly the door opened, and in front of me in the room stood Katerina Ivanovna.

“Strange how things turn out sometimes. Nobody had seen her in the street, so nobody in the town knew. I lodged with two decrepit old ladies who looked after me. They were the most obliging old things and would do anything for me, and when I asked, they kept as quiet afterwards as two cast-iron posts. Of course I understood the situation at once. She came in and looked me straight in the face, her dark eyes determined, even defiant, but on her lips and around her mouth I saw uncertainty.
“‘My sister has told me,’ she began, ‘that you’ll give me 4,500 roubles if I come and ask you for it myself. I’ve come ... give me the money!’
“She couldn’t keep it up. She was out of breath and frightened, her voice gave out, and the corners of her mouth and the lines around it trembled. Alyosha, are you listening, or are you asleep?”
“Mitya, I know you’ll tell the whole truth,” said Alyosha, agitated.

“I am telling it. If I tell the whole truth just as it happened, I won’t spare myself. My first thought was a—Karamazov one. A centipede bit me once, brother, and I lay in bed with fever for a fortnight. Well, that’s how it felt then: a centipede biting at my heart—a noxious insect, you understand? I looked her over from head to foot. You’ve seen her? She’s a beauty. But she was beautiful in a different way then. At that moment she was beautiful because she was noble and I was a scoundrel. She stood there in all the grandeur of her generosity, sacrificing herself for her father, and I—a bug! Scoundrel that I was, she was entirely in my power, body and soul. She was cornered. I tell you frankly, that thought, that venomous thought, took such hold of my heart that it nearly fainted with suspense. It seemed there was no resisting it. I felt I would act like a bug, like a venomous spider, without a spark of pity. I could scarcely breathe. Understand me: I would have gone the next day to ask for her hand, so it might all end honorably, so to speak, and nobody would or could know. Because I may be a man of base desires, but I’m honest. And that very second some voice seemed to whisper in my ear, ‘But when you come tomorrow to propose, that girl won’t even see you. She’ll tell her coachman to throw you out of the yard. “Shout it all over town,” she’ll say. “I’m not afraid of you.”’ I looked at the young lady, and my voice hadn’t deceived me. That was exactly how it would be, no doubt of it. I could tell from her face that I’d be thrown out of the house. My spite was aroused. I wanted to play her the nastiest, most swinish cad’s trick there is: to look at her with a sneer, and right there where she stood in front of me, to stun her with a tone of voice only a shopman could use.

“‘Four thousand! What are you talking about? I was joking. You’ve counted your chickens too soon, madam. Two hundred, if you like, with all my heart. But four thousand is no sum to throw away on a frivolity like that. You’ve put yourself out for nothing.’

“Of course I’d have lost the game. She would have run away. But it would have been an infernal revenge, and worth everything. I’d have howled with regret the rest of my life, only for having played that trick. Would you believe it, with no other woman, not one, has it ever happened to me that I looked at her with hatred at such a moment. But I swear on my oath, for three seconds, or maybe five, I looked at her with a fearful hatred—the kind of hate that is only a hair’s-breadth from love, from the maddest love!

“I went to the window and pressed my forehead against the frozen pane, and I remember the ice burned my forehead like fire. I didn’t keep her long, don’t be afraid. I turned round, went to the table, opened the drawer and took out a banknote for five thousand roubles (it was lying in a French dictionary). I showed it to her without a word, folded it and handed it to her. I opened the door into the passage, stepped back and made her a deep bow, a most respectful, most impressive bow, believe me! She shuddered all over and stared at me for a second. She turned horribly pale, white as a sheet in fact, and then all at once, not impetuously but softly and gently, she bowed down to my feet. It wasn’t a boarding-school curtsey but a Russian bow, forehead to the floor. Then she jumped up and ran off. I was wearing my sword. I drew it and nearly stabbed myself with it on the spot. Why, I don’t know. It would have been frightfully stupid, of course. I suppose it was out of delight. Can you understand killing yourself out of delight? But I didn’t stab myself. I only kissed my sword and put it back in its scabbard—which I needn’t have told you, by the way. And I imagine that in telling you about my inner struggle I’ve laid it on rather thick, to glorify myself. But let it go, and to hell with everyone who pries into the human heart! Well, so much for that ‘adventure’ with Katerina Ivanovna. So now Ivan knows about it, and you—no one else.”

Dmitri stood up and took a step or two in his excitement. He pulled out his handkerchief and wiped his forehead, then sat down again, not where he’d sat before but on the opposite side, so that Alyosha had to turn all the way round to face him.

chapters.title: V. The Confession Of A Passionate Heart—“Heels Up”
paragraphs: “Now I get the first half,” said Alyosha.
“The first half, yes. That part was a drama, and it was played out over there. The second part is a tragedy, and it’s being acted out right here.”
“And that second part I don’t understand at all, so far,” said Alyosha.
“And me? Do you think I understand it?”
“Hold on, Dmitri. There’s one important question. Tell me, you were engaged, and you’re still engaged?”

“We didn’t get engaged right away. It was three months after that adventure. The next day I told myself the affair was closed, finished, and there’d be no sequel. Making her an offer seemed caddish to me. And she gave no sign of life herself in the six weeks she stayed on in town, apart from one thing. The day after her visit, her maid slipped round with an envelope addressed to me. I tore it open, and inside was the change from the banknote. Only four thousand five hundred roubles had been needed, but changing the note cost a discount of about two hundred. So all she sent me was about two hundred and sixty. I don’t remember exactly. But there wasn’t a note, not a word of explanation. I went over the packet looking for a pencil mark—n-nothing! So I spent what was left on such an orgy that the new major had to give me a reprimand.

“Then the lieutenant-colonel came up with the battalion money, and everyone was astonished, because nobody believed he still had it untouched. He had barely paid it back when he fell ill and took to his bed. Three weeks later he had softening of the brain, and five days after that he was dead. They buried him with military honors, because he hadn’t had time to get his discharge. Ten days after the funeral Katerina Ivanovna left for Moscow with her aunt and her sister. And on the very day they left (I hadn’t seen them, I didn’t see them off or say goodbye) I got a tiny note, a sheet of thin blue paper, with a single line in pencil: ‘I will write to you. Wait. K.’ That was all.

“I’ll tell you the rest in two words. In Moscow their luck turned as fast as lightning, as unexpectedly as in an Arabian fairy tale. That general’s widow, their nearest relative, suddenly lost the two nieces who were her heiresses and next of kin. Both died of smallpox in the same week. The old lady was crushed with grief. She took Katya in as a daughter, as her one remaining hope, held on to her, and rewrote her will in Katya’s favor. That was for the future, though. For now, she handed her eighty thousand roubles as a marriage portion, to do with as she pleased. She was a hysterical woman. I saw something of her in Moscow, later.

“Then, out of nowhere, four thousand five hundred roubles arrived for me in the post. You can imagine I was speechless. Three days after that came the letter she’d promised. I’ve got it on me now. You must read it. She offers to be my wife. She offers herself to me. ‘I love you madly,’ she writes, ‘even if you don’t love me, never mind. Be my husband. Don’t be afraid. I won’t hamper you in any way. I will be your chattel. I will be the carpet under your feet. I want to love you forever. I want to save you from yourself.’ Alyosha, I’m not fit to repeat those lines in my vulgar words and my vulgar tone, the everlastingly vulgar tone I can never cure myself of. That letter stabs me even now. Do you think I don’t mind? That I don’t mind still? I answered her at once, since I couldn’t possibly go to Moscow. I wrote it in tears. There’s one thing I’ll be ashamed of forever. I brought up her being rich and having a dowry, while I was nothing but a stuck-up beggar! I mentioned money! I should have kept quiet about it, but it slipped out of my pen. Right after that I wrote to Ivan and told him everything I could in a letter of six pages, and I sent him to her. Why are you looking like that? Why are you staring at me? Yes, Ivan fell in love with her. He’s in love with her still. I know it. In the world’s opinion it was a stupid thing to do, but maybe that one stupid thing is what will save all of us now. Oo! Can’t you see how much she thinks of Ivan, how she respects him? When she compares the two of us, do you think she can love a man like me—especially after everything that’s happened here?”
“But I’m sure she loves a man like you, not a man like him.”

“She loves her own _virtue_, not me.” The words burst out of Dmitri, unplanned and almost spiteful. He laughed, but a minute later his eyes flashed, his face went crimson, and he slammed his fist on the table.

“I swear to you, Alyosha,” he cried, in real and bitter anger at himself, “you may not believe me, but as God is holy and Christ is God, I swear it: I smiled at her lofty feelings just now, but I know my soul is a million times baser than hers, and those lofty feelings of hers are as sincere as a heavenly angel’s. That’s the tragedy—I know that for certain. So what if someone shows off a little? Don’t I do it myself? And still I’m sincere, I’m sincere. As for Ivan, I can see how he must be cursing nature now, a man with a mind like his! He sees the preference go to—whom? To what? To a monster who is engaged, with every eye on him, and still can’t hold back his debauchery—and right in front of his fiancée, too! A man like me is the one preferred, and he’s the one turned away. And why? Because a girl wants to throw away her life and her future out of gratitude. It’s ridiculous! I’ve never said a word of this to Ivan, and of course Ivan has never hinted at it to me. But fate will work itself out. The better man will keep his place, and the unworthy one will disappear for ever into his back-alley, his filthy back-alley, his beloved back-alley, where he feels at home and will sink in filth and stink of his own free will and enjoy it. I’ve been talking nonsense. I’m out of words. I’m using them at random, but it will be just as I’ve said. I’ll drown in the back-alley, and she’ll marry Ivan.”

“Stop, Dmitri,” Alyosha broke in again, very worried. “There’s one thing you still haven’t explained: you’re engaged all the same, aren’t you? How can you break it off if she, your fiancée, doesn’t want to?”

“Yes, formally and solemnly engaged. It was settled as soon as I got to Moscow, with great ceremony, with ikons, everything done in style. The general’s widow gave us her blessing and—can you believe it?—congratulated Katya. ‘You’ve chosen well,’ she told her. ‘I can see right through him.’ And—can you believe this too?—she didn’t care for Ivan and barely said hello to him. In Moscow I talked with Katya at length. I told her about myself, sincerely and honorably. She listened to everything.
There was sweet confusion, there were tender words.
Though there were proud words too. She wrung a mighty promise from me to reform. I gave my promise, and now here—”
“What?”
“Why, I called you and dragged you out here today, this very day—remember that!—so I could send you, again today, to Katerina Ivanovna, and—”
“What?”
“To tell her I will never come to see her again. Say, ‘He sends you his compliments.’”
“But is that possible?”
“That’s exactly why I’m sending you in my place: because it can’t be done. How could I say it to her myself?”
“And where will you go?”
“To the back-alley.”
“To Grushenka, then!” Alyosha exclaimed sadly, clasping his hands. “Can Rakitin really have told the truth? I thought you’d only called on her, and that was all.”

“Is a man who’s engaged allowed to make such calls? Is it even possible, with a fiancée like mine, and under the eyes of the whole world? Damn it, I have some honor! The moment I started going to Grushenka, I stopped being engaged, and I stopped being an honest man. I understand that. Why are you looking at me like that? Listen, I went to her first of all to beat her. I’d heard—and now I know for a fact—that the captain, father’s agent, had handed Grushenka an I.O.U. of mine so she could sue me for payment and finish me off. They meant to scare me. So I went to beat her. I’d seen her once in passing before. She doesn’t strike you at first sight. I knew about her old merchant, who’s lying paralyzed and ill now, though he’s leaving her a decent little sum. I knew, too, that she loves money, that she hoards it, that she lends at a wicked rate of interest, that she’s a merciless cheat and swindler. I went to beat her, and I stayed. The storm broke, and it knocked me flat like the plague. I’m plague-stricken still, and I know everything is over, that nothing more will ever come to me. The cycle of the ages is complete. That’s where I stand. And though I’m a beggar, as fate would have it, I happened to have three thousand in my pocket. I drove with Grushenka to Mokroe, twenty-five versts from here. I hired gypsies there, and got champagne, and made all the peasants drunk on it, and all the women and girls. I sent thousands flying. In three days I was stripped bare, but a hero. Do you think the hero got what he was after? Not a sign of it from her. I tell you, that rogue Grushenka has a supple curve running all through her body. You can see it in her little foot, even in her little toe. I saw it, and I kissed it, but that was all, I swear! ‘I’ll marry you if you like,’ she said, ‘but you’re a beggar, you know. Say you won’t beat me and that you’ll let me do whatever I choose, and maybe I’ll marry you.’ She laughed, and she’s laughing still!”
Dmitri sprang to his feet in a kind of fury. All at once he looked drunk. His eyes had suddenly turned bloodshot.
“And do you really mean to marry her?”

“This minute, if she’ll have me. And if she won’t, I’ll hang around anyway. I’ll be the porter at her gate. Alyosha!” he cried. He halted in front of him, took him by the shoulders and shook him hard. “Do you know, you innocent boy, that this is all delirium, senseless delirium? Because there’s a tragedy in it. I’ll tell you something, Alexey. I may be a low man, with low and degraded passions, but Dmitri Karamazov can never be a thief or a pickpocket. Well, then, here it is: I am a thief and a pickpocket. That very morning, just before I went to beat Grushenka, Katerina Ivanovna sent for me. She told me in strict secrecy (why, I don’t know; I suppose she had her reasons) to go to the chief town of the province and mail three thousand roubles to Agafya Ivanovna in Moscow, so that no one here in town would know of it. So I had that three thousand roubles in my pocket when I went to see Grushenka, and that was the money we spent at Mokroe. Later I pretended I’d been to the town, but I never showed her the post office receipt. I said I’d sent the money and would bring her the receipt, and I still haven’t. I forgot it. Now, what do you think you’re going to say to her today? ‘He sends his compliments,’ and she’ll ask you, ‘And the money?’ You could still have told her, ‘He’s a degraded sensualist, a low creature with no control over his passions. He didn’t send your money then. He wasted it, because, like a low brute, he couldn’t restrain himself.’ But you could have added, ‘Still, he isn’t a thief. Here are your three thousand; he sends them back. Send them to Agafya Ivanovna yourself. But he told me to say “he sends his compliments.”’ But as things stand, she’ll ask, ‘But where is the money?’”
“Mitya, you are unhappy, yes! But not as unhappy as you think. Don’t torment yourself to death with despair.”

“What, you think I’ll shoot myself because I can’t find three thousand to pay back? That’s the whole point. I won’t shoot myself. I don’t have the strength for it now. Later, perhaps. For now I’m going to Grushenka. What happens after that, I don’t care.”
“And then what?”
“I’ll be her husband, if she condescends to have me, and when her lovers come I’ll step into the next room. I’ll clean her friends’ galoshes, fan their samovar, run their errands.”

“Katerina Ivanovna will understand all of it,” Alyosha said gravely. “She’ll see how deep this trouble goes, and she’ll forgive you. She has a lofty mind, and she’ll see for herself that no one could be more unhappy than you.”
“She won’t forgive all of it,” said Dmitri with a grin. “There’s something here, brother, that no woman could forgive. Do you know what would be best?”
“What?”
“Paying back the three thousand.”
“But where would we get it? Look, I have two thousand. Ivan will give you another thousand, and that makes three. Take it and pay her back.”

“And when will you have your three thousand in hand? Besides, you’re under age. And you have to—you absolutely have to—carry my farewell to her today, with the money or without it. I can’t drag this out any longer; it’s come to that. Tomorrow will be too late. I’m going to send you to father.”
“To father?”
“Yes, to father first. Ask him for three thousand.”
“But, Mitya, he won’t give it.”
“Of course he won’t! I know that. Alexey, do you know what despair is?”
“Yes.”

“Listen, then. By law he owes me nothing. I’ve had everything from him; I know that. But morally he owes me something, doesn’t he? He started out with twenty-eight thousand of my mother’s money and turned it into a hundred thousand. If he gives me back only three of those twenty-eight thousand, he’ll pull my soul out of hell, and it will make up for a great many of his sins. For that three thousand I give you my solemn word that I’ll put an end to everything, and he’ll never hear of me again. It’s the last time I’ll offer him the chance to be a father. Tell him that God Himself sends him this chance.”
“Mitya, he won’t give it, whatever you say.”

“I know he won’t. I know it perfectly well, and now more than ever. And that’s not all. I know something else. Only a few days ago, perhaps just yesterday, he understood for the first time _in earnest_ (underline _in earnest_) that Grushenka may not be joking after all, and really means to marry me. He knows what she’s like; he knows the cat. So do you imagine he’ll give me money to help that along, when he’s mad about her himself? And that isn’t all, either. I can tell you more than that. I know that for the past five days he’s had three thousand drawn from the bank, changed into notes of a hundred roubles, packed into a big envelope, sealed with five seals and tied crosswise with red tape. You see how well informed I am! On the envelope he’s written: ‘To my angel Grushenka, when she chooses to come to me.’ He scrawled it himself, silently and in secret, and nobody knows the money is there except the valet Smerdyakov, whom he trusts as he trusts himself. So for three or four days now he’s been expecting Grushenka. He hopes she’ll come for the money. He’s sent word to her about it, and she’s sent word back that perhaps she’ll come. And if she does go to the old man, can I marry her afterwards? Now you see why I’m here in secret, and what I’m keeping watch for.”
“For her?”

“Yes, for her. Foma rents a room in the house of these sluts. Foma is from our part of the country; he was a soldier in our regiment. He does odd jobs for them. He’s their watchman at night, and in the daytime he goes shooting grouse. That’s how he makes his living. I’ve moved into his room. Neither he nor the women of the house know the secret, I mean that I’m on watch here.”
“So nobody but Smerdyakov knows?”
“Nobody else. He’ll let me know if she goes to the old man.”
“It was he who told you about the money, then?”

“Yes. It’s a dead secret. Even Ivan knows nothing of the money, or of anything. The old man is sending Ivan to Tchermashnya, a journey of two or three days. A buyer has turned up for the copse, who’ll give eight thousand for the timber. So the old man keeps pressing Ivan to help him out by going to arrange it. It will take him two or three days. That’s what the old man wants, so that Grushenka can come while Ivan is away.”
“So he’s expecting Grushenka today?”

“No, she won’t come today. There are signs. She’s sure not to come,” Mitya suddenly cried. “Smerdyakov thinks so too. Father’s drinking right now. He’s sitting at the table with Ivan. Go to him, Alyosha, and ask for the three thousand.”
“Mitya, dear, what’s wrong with you?” cried Alyosha, leaping up from his seat and staring hard at his brother’s frenzied face. For a moment the thought struck him that Dmitri had gone mad.
“What’s the matter? I’m not insane,” said Dmitri, looking at him intently and earnestly. “Don’t worry. I’m sending you to father, and I know what I’m saying. I believe in miracles.”
“In miracles?”
“In a miracle of Divine Providence. God knows what is in my heart. He sees my despair. He sees the whole picture, and surely He won’t let something awful happen. Alyosha, I believe in miracles. Go!”
“I’m going. Tell me, will you wait here for me?”

“Yes. I know it’ll take a while. You can’t go at him head on. He’s drunk now. I’ll wait three hours—four, five, six, seven. Only remember that you have to go to Katerina Ivanovna today, even at midnight, _with the money or without the money_, and say, ‘He sends his compliments to you.’ I want you to say that very line to her: ‘He sends his compliments to you.’”
“Mitya! And what if Grushenka comes today—or if not today, tomorrow or the day after?”
“Grushenka? I’ll see her. I’ll burst out and stop it.”
“And if—”
“If there’s an if, there will be murder. I couldn’t bear it.”
“Who will be murdered?”
“The old man. I won’t kill her.”
“Brother, what are you saying?”

“Oh, I don’t know.... I don’t know. Maybe I won’t kill him, and maybe I will. I’m afraid that at that moment his face will suddenly become so loathsome to me. I hate his ugly throat, his nose, his eyes, his shameless snigger. I feel a physical disgust. That’s what I’m afraid of. That’s what might be too much for me.”
“I’ll go, Mitya. I believe God will order things for the best, and nothing awful will happen.”
“And I’ll sit here and wait for the miracle. And if it doesn’t happen—”
Alyosha walked off, deep in thought, toward his father’s house.

chapters.title: VI. Smerdyakov
paragraphs: Sure enough, he found his father still at the table. The house had a dining room, but as always the meal was laid in the drawing room, which was the biggest room and was furnished in a showy, old-fashioned way. Everything in it was white and very old, upholstered in worn red silky cloth. Mirrors with elaborate, old-style carved frames of white and gold hung between the windows. The walls were covered in white paper, torn in many places, and two large portraits hung on them. One showed some prince who had been governor of the district thirty years before. The other showed some bishop, also long dead. In the corner opposite the door stood several ikons, with a lamp burning in front of them from nightfall ... more to light the room than out of devotion. Fyodor Pavlovitch went to bed very late, at three or four in the morning. Until then he would pace the room in the night, or sit in an armchair and think. It had become a habit. Often he slept in the house entirely alone, having sent his servants off to the lodge. Usually, though, Smerdyakov stayed and slept on a bench in the hall.

By the time Alyosha came in, dinner was over, but coffee and preserves had been brought out. After dinner Fyodor Pavlovitch liked something sweet with his brandy. Ivan was still at the table, sipping coffee. The servants, Grigory and Smerdyakov, stood by. Masters and servants alike seemed to be in unusually high spirits. Fyodor Pavlovitch was roaring with laughter. Alyosha heard that shrill laugh, which he knew so well, before he even reached the room. By the sound of it he could tell that his father had got only as far as the good-humored stage and was nowhere near properly drunk.

“Here he is! Here he is!” yelled Fyodor Pavlovitch, delighted to see Alyosha. “Come and join us. Sit down. Coffee’s a lenten dish, but it’s hot and it’s good. I won’t offer you brandy, you’re keeping the fast. But would you like some? No, I’d better give you a little of our famous liqueur. Smerdyakov, go to the cupboard, second shelf on the right. Here are the keys. Quick, now!”
Alyosha began to turn the liqueur down.
“Never mind. If you won’t, we will,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch, beaming. “But hold on—have you eaten?”
“Yes,” answered Alyosha, who had in fact had only a piece of bread and a glass of kvas in the Father Superior’s kitchen. “I would like some hot coffee, though.”

“Bravo, my darling! He’ll take coffee. Does it need heating up? No, it’s boiling. Excellent coffee, too: Smerdyakov made it. My Smerdyakov’s an artist at coffee, and at fish patties, and at fish soup as well. You must come some day for the fish soup. Tell me ahead of time.... But wait a minute; didn’t I tell you this morning to come home with your mattress and pillow and everything? Did you bring your mattress? He he he!”
“No, I didn’t,” said Alyosha, smiling too.

“Ah, but you were scared, you were scared this morning, weren’t you? There, my darling, I could never do anything to hurt you. Do you know, Ivan, I can’t stand up to the way he looks you straight in the face and laughs? It sets me laughing all over. I’m so fond of him. Alyosha, let me give you my blessing—a father’s blessing.”
Alyosha got up, but Fyodor Pavlovitch had already changed his mind.

“No, no,” he said. “I’ll just make the sign of the cross over you for now. Sit still. We’ve got a treat for you, and in your own line, too. It’ll make you laugh. Balaam’s ass has started talking to us—and how he talks! How he talks!”

Balaam’s ass, it turned out, was the valet Smerdyakov. He was a young man of about twenty-four, remarkably unsociable and silent. This was not shyness or bashfulness. Quite the reverse: he was conceited and seemed to look down on everybody.

I have to stop here and say a few words about him. Grigory and Marfa had raised him, but the boy grew up “with no gratitude in him,” as Grigory put it. He was an unfriendly child who seemed to eye the world with suspicion. When he was little, he loved to hang cats and then bury them with great ceremony. He would put a sheet on as if it were a priest’s vestment, chant, and swing something over the dead cat as if it were a censer. He did all of this on the sly, in absolute secrecy. Grigory caught him at it once and gave him a good thrashing. The boy crept into a corner and sulked there for a week. “He doesn’t care about you or me, the little monster,” Grigory used to tell Marfa, “and he doesn’t care about anybody. Are you even a human being?” he said, addressing the boy himself. “You’re no human being. You grew out of the mildew in the bath-house.[2] That’s what you are.” Smerdyakov, as we learned later, never forgave him those words. Grigory taught him to read and write, and when the boy turned twelve he started on the Scriptures. But nothing came of it. At the second or third lesson the boy suddenly gave a grin.
“What are you smirking at?” asked Grigory, glaring at him over his spectacles.
“Nothing. God made light on the first day, and the sun and moon and stars on the fourth. So where did the light come from on the first day?”

Grigory was stunned. The boy looked at his teacher mockingly, with something almost patronizing in his face. Grigory lost his temper. “I’ll show you where!” he shouted, and gave the boy a hard slap across the cheek. The boy took it without a word, and went back to his corner for a few days. A week later he had his first fit of the illness that stayed with him for the rest of his life—epilepsy. When Fyodor Pavlovitch heard about it, his attitude to the boy changed at once. Before that, he had paid him no attention. He never scolded him, and whenever they met he gave him a kopeck. Sometimes, in a good mood, he would send the boy a sweet from his table. But the moment he learned of the illness, he took a lively interest in him. He called in a doctor and tried various cures, but the disease proved incurable. On average the fits came once a month, though the gaps between them varied. Their severity varied too, some light and some very bad. Fyodor Pavlovitch strictly forbade Grigory to beat the boy, and began letting him come upstairs. For a while he also forbade anyone to teach him anything at all. One day, when the boy was about fifteen, Fyodor Pavlovitch saw him hanging around the bookcase, reading the titles through the glass. Fyodor Pavlovitch owned quite a few books—over a hundred—but nobody had ever seen him read one. He handed Smerdyakov the bookcase key on the spot. “Go on, read. You can be my librarian. It’s better for you to sit and read than to loaf around the yard. Here, read this,” and Fyodor Pavlovitch gave him _Evenings in a Cottage near Dikanka_.
He read a little but didn’t like it. Not once did he smile, and in the end he frowned.
“What’s wrong? Isn’t it funny?” asked Fyodor Pavlovitch.
Smerdyakov said nothing.
“Answer me, you fool!”
“It’s all lies,” the boy mumbled, with a grin.
“Then go to the devil! You’ve got the soul of a lackey. Wait, here’s Smaragdov’s _Universal History_. That’s all true. Read that.”
But Smerdyakov did not get past ten pages of Smaragdov. He found it boring. So the bookcase was locked up again.

Not long after, Marfa and Grigory told Fyodor Pavlovitch that Smerdyakov was slowly turning extraordinarily fussy. He would sit down to his soup, pick up the spoon, and peer into the soup. He would bend over it, inspect it, scoop up a spoonful and hold it to the light.
“What is it? A beetle?” Grigory would ask.
“Maybe a fly,” Marfa remarked.

The finicky youth never answered, but he did the same with his bread, his meat, and everything else he ate. He would lift a piece on his fork to the light, examine it as if under a microscope, and only after long thought decide to put it in his mouth.
“Ach! Look at the airs of a fine gentleman!” Grigory muttered as he watched him.

When Fyodor Pavlovitch heard how Smerdyakov was turning out, he made up his mind to have him as his cook, and sent him to Moscow to train. He stayed there some years and came back strikingly changed in looks. He seemed extraordinarily old for his age. His face had gone wrinkled and yellow, and strangely unmanly. In character he seemed almost exactly as he had been before leaving. He was as unsociable as ever and showed not the slightest wish for company. In Moscow, too, as we heard afterwards, he had always kept silent. Moscow itself had little interest for him; he saw very little of it and noticed hardly anything. He went to the theater once, and came back quiet and put out by it. On the other hand, he returned to us from Moscow well dressed, in a clean coat and clean linen. Every day, without fail, he brushed his clothes with great care twice, and he loved cleaning his smart calf boots with a special English polish until they shone like mirrors. He turned out to be a first-rate cook. Fyodor Pavlovitch paid him a salary, and Smerdyakov spent nearly all of it on clothes, pomade, perfume and the like. But he seemed to hold women in just as much contempt as men. With them he was discreet, almost unapproachable. Fyodor Pavlovitch began to see him a little differently. The fits were coming more often, and on the days when he was ill Marfa cooked, which did not suit Fyodor Pavlovitch at all.
“Why are your fits getting worse?” asked Fyodor Pavlovitch, eyeing his new cook sideways. “Do you want to get married? Shall I find you a wife?”

But Smerdyakov went pale with anger and gave no answer. Fyodor Pavlovitch walked away from him with an impatient wave of the hand. What mattered most was that he trusted Smerdyakov’s honesty absolutely. Once, when Fyodor Pavlovitch was drunk, he dropped three hundred-rouble notes, which he had only just been paid, in the muddy courtyard. He didn’t notice they were gone until the next day, and was hurrying to turn out his pockets when he saw the notes lying on the table. How had they got there? Smerdyakov had picked them up and brought them in the day before.

“Well, my lad, I’ve never come across anyone like you,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said gruffly, and gave him ten roubles. I should add that he not only believed in his honesty but, for some reason, actually liked him, though the young man looked at him as sourly as at everyone else and never said a word. He rarely spoke at all. If anyone at that time had asked what interested the young man, or what went on in his head, you could not have told by looking at him. And yet he would sometimes stop short in the house, or even out in the yard or the street, and stand there for ten minutes, deep in thought. Anyone who studied faces would have said that his held no thought, no reflection, only a kind of contemplation. There is a remarkable painting by Kramskoy called “Contemplation.” It shows a forest in winter and, on a road through the forest, in total solitude, a peasant in a ragged kaftan and bark shoes. He seems lost in thought. But he is not thinking; he is “contemplating.” If someone touched him, he would give a start and look at them like a man waking up, bewildered. True, he would come to himself at once; but if you asked what he had been thinking about, he would remember nothing. Yet he most likely carries within him, hidden away, the impression that held him in those moments. Those impressions are precious to him, and no doubt he stores them up without noticing, even without knowing it. How and why, naturally, he doesn’t know either. After storing up impressions for many years, he may suddenly drop everything and go on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem to save his soul, or perhaps he will suddenly burn down his own village, or perhaps do both. There are a good many “contemplatives” among the peasantry. Well, Smerdyakov was probably one of them, and he was probably greedily storing up his impressions, hardly knowing why.

chapters.title: VII. The Controversy
paragraphs: But Balaam’s ass had suddenly found its voice. The topic was an odd one. Grigory had gone out that morning to do some shopping. The shopkeeper Lukyanov had told him about a Russian soldier whose story was in that day’s newspaper. The soldier had been captured somewhere in a remote corner of Asia. His captors threatened him with a sudden, agonizing death unless he gave up Christianity and became a Muslim. He would not deny his faith. They tortured him and flayed him alive, and he died praising and glorifying Christ. Grigory had told this story at the table. Fyodor Pavlovitch always enjoyed laughing and chatting over dessert after dinner, even if it was only with Grigory. This afternoon he was in an especially cheerful, talkative mood. He sipped his brandy and listened to the story, and then he remarked that a soldier like that ought to be made a saint, and his skin sent to some monastery. “The people would flock to see it, and the money would roll in.”

Grigory frowned. He could see that Fyodor Pavlovitch was not moved at all, and was beginning, as usual, to sneer. At that moment Smerdyakov, who was standing by the door, smiled. Smerdyakov often waited at table toward the end of dinner. Since Ivan had arrived in our town, he had done it every day.
“What are you grinning at?” asked Fyodor Pavlovitch. He had caught the smile instantly and knew it was aimed at Grigory.

“Well, my opinion is,” Smerdyakov began suddenly, in a loud voice nobody was expecting, “that if that praiseworthy soldier’s feat was so very great, then in my view there would have been no sin in it if, in such an emergency, he had renounced, so to speak, the name of Christ and his own christening. By that means he would have saved his life, and could use it for good deeds, and over the years make up for his cowardice.”
“How can that not be a sin? You’re talking rubbish. You’ll go straight to hell for that, and be roasted like a leg of mutton,” Fyodor Pavlovitch put in.
At this point Alyosha came in, and Fyodor Pavlovitch, as we have seen, was thrilled to see him.
“We’re on your subject, your subject!” he chuckled gleefully, and sat Alyosha down to listen.
“As for mutton, that’s not how it is. There will be nothing like that waiting for him for this, and there shouldn’t be, if things are done according to justice,” Smerdyakov insisted stoutly.
“What do you mean, ‘according to justice’?” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried, even merrier, and he jabbed Alyosha with his knee.
“He’s a scoundrel, that’s what he is!” Grigory burst out. He glared at Smerdyakov.

“As for being a scoundrel, just wait a little, Grigory Vassilyevitch,” Smerdyakov answered, perfectly composed. “Kindly think about it yourself. Say I am taken prisoner by the enemies of the Christian race, and they demand that I curse the name of God and give up my holy christening. I am fully entitled to decide by my own reason, because there would be no sin in it.”
“But you’ve said all that already. Don’t waste words. Prove it,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch.
“Soup-maker!” Grigory muttered scornfully.

“As for being a soup-maker, wait a bit with that as well, Grigory Vassilyevitch, and think it over for yourself, instead of abusing me. For the moment I say to those enemies, ‘No, I am not a Christian, and I curse my true God,’ then at once, by God’s high judgment, I become, immediately and specially, anathema accursed. I am cut off from the Holy Church exactly as if I were a heathen. So at that very instant, not only when I say it aloud but when I merely think of saying it, before even a quarter of a second has gone by, I am cut off. Is that so or not, Grigory Vassilyevitch?”
He spoke to Grigory with open satisfaction. In fact he was answering Fyodor Pavlovitch’s questions, and he knew it perfectly well, and he was deliberately pretending that Grigory had put them.
“Ivan,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried suddenly, “lean down, let me whisper. He’s staged all this for your benefit. He wants you to praise him. Go on, praise him.”
Ivan listened to his father’s excited whisper with complete seriousness.
“Hold on, Smerdyakov, quiet for a minute,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch again. “Ivan, give me your ear once more.”
Ivan bent down again, with a perfectly solemn face.
“I love you like I love Alyosha. Don’t think I don’t love you. Have some brandy?”
“Yes.—But you’re a bit drunk yourself,” thought Ivan, studying his father.
He was watching Smerdyakov with keen curiosity.
“You’re anathema accursed as it is,” Grigory suddenly burst out, “so how dare you argue, you scoundrel, after that, when—”
“Don’t scold him, Grigory, don’t scold him,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cut in.

“You ought to wait, Grigory Vassilyevitch, even for a short while, and listen, because I have not finished what I had to say. At the very moment I become accursed, at that same supreme moment, I am exactly like a heathen. My christening is taken from me and counts for nothing. Is that not so?”
“Get on and finish, my boy,” Fyodor Pavlovitch urged him, savoring a sip from his wine-glass.

“Now, if I have ceased to be a Christian, then I told the enemy no lie when they asked whether I was a Christian or not. God Himself had already relieved me of my Christianity, on account of the thought alone, before I had time to say a word to the enemy. And if I have already been discharged, then in what manner, and by what sort of justice, can I be held answerable as a Christian in the next world for denying Christ? Through the thought alone, before I denied Him, I had been relieved of my christening. If I am no longer a Christian, I cannot renounce Christ, for I have nothing left to renounce. Who will hold an unclean Tatar to account, Grigory Vassilyevitch, even in heaven, for not being born a Christian? And who would punish him for that, seeing that you can’t take two skins off one ox? Even if God Almighty did hold the Tatar to account, then when the Tatar dies, I imagine, God would give him the smallest punishment there is (since punished he must be). He would judge that the Tatar is not to blame for coming into the world an unclean heathen, the child of heathen parents. Surely the Lord God can’t take a Tatar and declare that he was a Christian? That would mean the Almighty was telling a real untruth. And can the Lord of Heaven and earth tell a lie, even in a single word?”

Grigory was thunderstruck. He stared at the orator, his eyes nearly popping out of his head. He did not clearly follow what had been said, but he had caught something in all this rigmarole, and he stood there like a man who has just banged his head against a wall. Fyodor Pavlovitch drained his glass and broke into his shrill laugh.

“Alyosha! Alyosha! What do you say to that! Ah, you casuist! He must have been with the Jesuits somewhere, Ivan. Oh, you stinking Jesuit, who taught you? But you’re talking nonsense, you casuist, nonsense, nonsense, nonsense. Don’t cry, Grigory, we’ll reduce him to smoke and ashes in a moment. Answer me this, you ass. Before your enemies you may be in the right, but in your own heart you renounced your faith all the same, and you say yourself that in that very hour you became anathema accursed. And once you’re anathema, they won’t give you a pat on the head for it in hell. What do you say to that, my fine Jesuit?”
“There is no doubt that I renounced it in my own heart, but there was no special sin in that. Or if there was a sin, it was a most ordinary one.”
“What do you mean, most ordinary?”
“You’re lying, you accursed man!” Grigory hissed.

“Think it over for yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch,” Smerdyakov went on, sedate and unruffled. He was aware of his triumph, yet, as it were, generous toward the beaten foe. “Think it over for yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch. The Scripture says that if you have faith as small as a mustard seed and tell a mountain to move into the sea, it will move at your word without the slightest delay. Very well, Grigory Vassilyevitch. I am without faith, and you have so great a faith that you swear at me constantly. So you try it. Tell this mountain to move, not into the sea, which is a long way off, but just into our stinking little river at the bottom of the garden. You will see for yourself that it will not budge. It will stay exactly where it is, however much you shout at it. That shows, Grigory Vassilyevitch, that you do not have faith in the proper manner, and only abuse other people about it. Consider this as well. In our day nobody, not only you but actually nobody, from the highest person to the lowest peasant, can push mountains into the sea—except perhaps one man in the whole world, or two at the most, and they are very likely saving their souls in secret somewhere in the Egyptian desert, so you would never find them. Now, if that is the case, and all the rest have no faith, will God curse all the rest? That is, the population of the entire earth, except for about two hermits in the desert? And in His well-known mercy, will He not forgive even one of them? And so I am convinced that although I may once have doubted, I shall be forgiven if I shed tears of repentance.”
“Wait!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, in a rapture of delight. “So you really suppose there are two who can move mountains? Ivan, make a note of it, write it down. That’s the Russian all over!”
“You are quite right that it is typical of the people’s faith,” Ivan agreed, with an approving smile.
“You agree! Then it must be so, if you agree. It’s true, isn’t it, Alyosha? That’s the Russian faith all over, isn’t it?”
“No, Smerdyakov doesn’t have the Russian faith at all,” said Alyosha, firmly and gravely.
“I’m not talking about his faith. I mean those two in the desert, only that notion. Surely that’s Russian?”
“Yes, that is purely Russian,” said Alyosha with a smile.

“Those words of yours are worth a gold piece, you ass, and I’ll hand it over to you today. But as for the rest, you talk nonsense, nonsense, nonsense. Let me tell you, you fool, that all of us here have little faith, but only through carelessness, because we haven’t the time. We’re overwhelmed with things to do. And second, the Lord God has given us so little time, only twenty-four hours in a day, that a man can’t even get enough sleep, let alone repent of his sins. Whereas you denied your faith to your enemies when you had nothing else on your mind but showing your faith! So I hold, brother, that it amounts to a sin.”

“It may amount to a sin, but kindly consider, Grigory Vassilyevitch, that if it does, it only makes the sin lighter. Suppose I had believed in very truth then, as I ought to have believed. Then it really would have been sinful if I had not endured torture for my faith and had gone over to the pagan Mohammedan religion. But of course it would not have come to torture, because I would only have had to say to the mountain at that moment, ‘Move and crush the tormentor,’ and it would have moved and crushed him that very instant like a black-beetle. I would have walked away as if nothing had happened, praising and glorifying God. But suppose I had tried all that at that very moment and cried to the mountain, ‘Crush these tormentors,’ and it had not crushed them. How could I have kept from doubting, I ask you, at such a time, in such a dreadful hour of mortal terror? And besides, I would know already that I could not reach the fullness of the Kingdom of Heaven (since the mountain had not moved at my word, they could not think much of my faith up above, and no very great reward could be waiting for me in the world to come). So why should I let them flay the skin off me as well, and to no good purpose? Even if they had skinned me half off my back, the mountain would still not have moved at my word or at my cry. And at such a moment not only might doubt come over a man, but he might lose his reason from fear and be unable to think at all. So how could I be especially to blame if, seeing no advantage or reward either there or here, I at least saved my skin? And so, trusting fully in the grace of the Lord, I would cherish the hope that I might be forgiven altogether.”

chapters.title: VIII. Over The Brandy
paragraphs: The argument was over. But oddly enough, Fyodor Pavlovitch, who had been in such good spirits, suddenly started to scowl. He scowled and gulped brandy, and that glass was already one too many.

“Clear out, you Jesuits!” he shouted at the servants. “Go away, Smerdyakov. I’ll send you that gold piece I promised you today, but get out! Don’t cry, Grigory. Go to Marfa. She’ll comfort you and put you to bed. These rascals won’t even leave us in peace after dinner,” he snapped peevishly, while the servants hurried out at his word.
“Smerdyakov always shoves his way in now, after dinner. It’s you he’s so keen on. What have you done to charm him?” he added, to Ivan.
“Nothing at all,” answered Ivan. “He likes to think highly of me. He’s a lackey and a mean soul. But he’s raw material for a revolution, when the time comes.”
“A revolution?”
“There will be others, and better ones. But there’ll be some like him as well. His sort will come first, and the better ones after.”
“And when will that time come?”
“The rocket may go up and just fizzle out. So far the peasants don’t much like listening to these soup-makers.”
“Ah, brother, but a Balaam’s ass like that thinks and thinks, and the devil only knows where he ends up.”
“He’s storing up ideas,” said Ivan, with a smile.

“Look, I know he can’t bear me, or anybody else, even you, though you imagine he thinks highly of you. With Alyosha it’s worse: he despises Alyosha. But he doesn’t steal, I’ll say that for him, and he’s no gossip. He keeps quiet and doesn’t air our dirty linen in public. And he makes first-rate fish pasties. But damn him, is he worth all this talk?”
“Of course he isn’t.”

“And as for whatever ideas he’s hatching, the Russian peasant, generally speaking, needs a good thrashing. I’ve always said so. Our peasants are swindlers, they don’t deserve any pity, and it’s a good thing they still get flogged now and then. Russia is rich in birches. If they cut down the forests, Russia would be ruined. I stand up for the clever people. We’ve given up thrashing the peasants, we’ve got so clever, but they keep right on thrashing themselves. And a good thing too. ‘For with what measure ye mete it shall be measured to you again,’ or how does it go? Anyway, it will be measured out. But Russia is all swinishness. My dear boy, if you only knew how I hate Russia.... That is, not Russia, but all this vice! But maybe I do mean Russia. _Tout cela c’est de la cochonnerie_.... Do you know what I like? I like wit.”
“You’ve had another glass. That’s enough.”

“Hold on a minute. I’ll have one more, then another, and then I’ll stop. No, wait, you cut me off. At Mokroe I got talking to an old man, and he said to me: ‘What we like best of all is sentencing the girls to a thrashing, and we always hand the job to the lads. Then the girl he thrashes today, the young fellow asks to marry tomorrow. So the girls are quite happy with it too,’ he said. A fine set of de Sades, eh? But it’s clever, all the same. Shall we drive over and take a look, eh? Alyosha, are you blushing? Don’t be shy, child. What a pity I didn’t stay for dinner at the Superior’s and tell the monks about the girls at Mokroe. Alyosha, don’t be angry that I insulted your Superior this morning. I lost my temper. If there is a God, if He exists, then of course I’m to blame, and I’ll have to answer for it. But if there’s no God at all, what do they deserve, those fathers of yours? Cutting off their heads wouldn’t be enough, since they hold back progress. Will you believe, Ivan, that it lacerates my feelings? No, you won’t, I can see it in your eyes. You believe what people say, that I’m nothing but a buffoon. Alyosha, do you believe I’m nothing but a buffoon?”
“No, I don’t believe that.”

“And I believe you don’t, and that you’re telling the truth. You look honest and you speak honestly. Not Ivan, though. Ivan is stuck-up.... All the same, I’d finish off your monks. I’d take all that mystic stuff and stamp it out, once and for all, across the whole of Russia, to bring every fool to his senses. And think of all the gold and silver that would pour into the mint!”
“But why stamp it out?” asked Ivan.
“So that Truth can win. That’s why.”
“Well, if Truth did win, you know, you’d be the first one to be robbed and stamped out.”

“Ah! You may well be right. Ah, what an ass I am!” burst out Fyodor Pavlovitch, giving his forehead a light slap. “Very well, then, your monastery can stay, Alyosha, if that’s how it is. And we clever people will sit comfortable and enjoy our brandy. You know, Ivan, the Almighty Himself must have arranged it that way. Ivan, tell me, is there a God or not? No, wait, tell the truth, tell it seriously. Why are you laughing again?”
“I’m laughing at the clever remark you made just now, about Smerdyakov believing in those two saints who could move mountains.”
“What, am I like him now?”
“Very much so.”

“Well, that proves I’m a Russian too, with a Russian trait. And you can be caught the same way, philosopher or not. Shall I catch you? What do you bet I’ll catch you tomorrow? Tell me anyway, is there a God or not? Only be serious. I want you serious now.”
“No, there is no God.”
“Alyosha, is there a God?”
“There is.”
“Ivan, and is there some kind of immortality, just a little, just a tiny bit?”
“There’s no immortality either.”
“None at all?”
“None at all.”
“Then it’s absolute nothingness. But maybe there’s just something? Anything is better than nothing!”
“Absolute nothingness.”
“Alyosha, is there immortality?”
“There is.”
“God and immortality?”
“God and immortality. Immortality is in God.”

“H’m! Ivan is probably right. Good Lord! Think of all the faith, all the strength of every kind, that man has poured into that dream for nothing, and for so many thousands of years. Who is it that laughs at man? Ivan! One last time, once and for all, is there a God or not? I’m asking for the last time!”
“And for the last time, there is not.”
“Then who is laughing at mankind, Ivan?”
“It must be the devil,” said Ivan, with a smile.
“And the devil? Is there one?”
“No, there’s no devil either.”
“What a shame. Damn it all, what I wouldn’t do to the man who first thought up God! Hanging from a bitter aspen would be too good for him.”
“There’d have been no civilization if they hadn’t thought up God.”
“There wouldn’t? Without God?”
“No. And no brandy either. Still, I’m going to take your brandy away from you.”
“Stop, stop, stop, my dear boy, just one more little glass. I’ve hurt Alyosha’s feelings. You’re not angry with me, Alyosha? My dear little Alexey!”
“No, I’m not angry. I know how you think. Your heart is better than your head.”
“My heart is better than my head, is it? Oh, Lord! And coming from you. Ivan, do you love Alyosha?”
“Yes.”

“You must love him” (Fyodor Pavlovitch was by now very drunk). “Listen, Alyosha, I was rude to your elder this morning. But I was all stirred up. Still, that elder has some wit, don’t you think, Ivan?”
“Quite possibly.”

“He has, he has. _Il y a du Piron là-dedans._ He’s a Jesuit, a Russian one, that is. He’s an honorable man, so there’s a hidden indignation seething in him at having to put on an act and play the holy man.”
“But surely he does believe in God.”

“Not a bit. Didn’t you know? Why, he says so himself, to everyone. That is, not everyone, but all the clever people who go to see him. He told Governor Schultz to his face, not long ago: ‘_Credo_, but I don’t know in what.’”
“Really?”

“He really did. But I respect him. There’s something of Mephistopheles in him, or rather of ‘The Hero of Our Time’ ... Arbenin, or whatever his name is?... You see, he’s a sensualist. He’s such a sensualist that I’d fear for my daughter or my wife if she went to confess to him. You know, when he starts telling stories.... The year before last he asked us to tea, tea with liqueur (the ladies send him liqueur), and began telling us about the old days until we nearly split our sides.... Especially how he once cured a paralyzed woman. ‘If my legs weren’t bad, I know a dance I could show you,’ he said. What do you make of that? ‘I’ve played plenty of tricks in my day,’ said he. He swindled Dernidov, the merchant, out of sixty thousand.”
“What, he stole it?”

“The merchant brought him the money, as to a man he could trust, and said, ‘Keep it for me, friend, the police are searching my place tomorrow.’ And he kept it. ‘You gave it to the Church,’ he declared. I said to him: ‘You’re a scoundrel,’ I said. ‘No,’ said he, ‘I’m not a scoundrel, I’m broad-minded.’ But that wasn’t him, that was somebody else. I’ve mixed him up with somebody else ... and never noticed. Come on, one more glass and that’s all. Take the bottle away, Ivan. I’ve been telling lies. Why didn’t you stop me, Ivan, and tell me I was lying?”
“I knew you’d stop on your own.”
“That’s a lie. You did it out of spite, plain spite against me. You despise me. You came into my house and despised me under my own roof.”
“Well, I’m leaving. You’ve had too much brandy.”
“I begged you, for Christ’s sake, to go to Tchermashnya for a day or two, and you won’t go.”
“I’ll go tomorrow, if you’re so set on it.”
“You won’t go. You want to keep an eye on me. That’s what you’re after, you spiteful fellow. That’s why you won’t go.”
The old man would not let it drop. He had reached the stage of drunkenness where a drunkard who has been quiet until then starts picking a quarrel and trying to throw his weight around.

“What are you staring at me for? Why do you look like that? Your eyes look at me and say, ‘You ugly drunk!’ Your eyes don’t trust me. They’re full of contempt.... You’ve come here with some plan in mind. Now Alyosha looks at me and his eyes shine. Alyosha doesn’t despise me. Alexey, you mustn’t love Ivan.”
“Don’t be nasty to my brother. Stop going after him,” Alyosha said firmly.
“Oh, all right. Ugh, my head aches. Take the brandy away, Ivan. That’s the third time I’m telling you.”
He brooded for a moment, and then a slow, sly grin crept over his face.

“Don’t be angry with a feeble old man, Ivan. I know you don’t love me, but don’t be angry anyway. You’ve got nothing to love me for. You go to Tchermashnya. I’ll come out to you myself and bring you a present. I’ll show you a little wench there. I’ve had my eye on her for a long time. She still runs around barefoot. Don’t be scared of barefoot wenches—don’t despise them—they’re pearls!”
And he kissed his hand with a smack.

“To my mind,” he came to life at once, seeming to sober up the moment he touched on his favorite subject. “To my mind ... Ah, you boys! You children, you little sucking-pigs, to my mind ... I have never in my life found a woman ugly—that’s been my rule! Can you grasp that? How could you grasp it? There’s milk in your veins, not blood. You haven’t crawled out of your shells yet. My rule has always been that in every woman you can find something devilishly interesting that you won’t find in any other. You just have to know how to find it, that’s the point! That’s a talent! To my mind there are no ugly women. The mere fact that she’s a woman is half the battle ... but how could you grasp that? Even in _vieilles filles_, even in them you can find something that makes you wonder how men could be such fools as to let them grow old without noticing them. Barefoot girls and plain ones, you have to take by surprise. Didn’t you know that? You have to astonish them until they’re enchanted, thrown, ashamed that a gentleman like you should fall in love with a little slut like them. It’s a jolly good thing that there always are, and always will be, masters and slaves in the world. So there will always be a little maid-of-all-work and her master, and you know, that’s all anyone needs for happiness. Wait ... listen, Alyosha, I always used to surprise your mother too, but in a different way. I paid her no attention at all, and then all at once, when the moment came, I’d be devotion itself, crawling on my knees, kissing her feet, and I always, always—I remember it as if it were today—brought her to that tinkling, quiet, nervous, queer little laugh. It was hers alone. I knew her attacks always began that way. The next day she’d start shrieking in hysterics, and this little laugh was no sign of delight, though it made a very good fake. That’s the great thing, knowing how to handle each person. Once Belyavsky—a handsome fellow, and rich—used to like coming here and hanging around her—suddenly gave me a slap in the face in front of her. And she—such a mild sheep—why, I thought she’d knock me down for that blow. How she went for me! ‘You’re beaten, beaten now,’ she said. ‘You took a blow from him.
