You’ve been trying to sell me to him,’ she said.... ‘And how dared he hit you in front of me! Don’t you ever come near me again, never, never! Run at once, challenge him to a duel!’... So then I took her to the monastery to bring her to her senses. The holy Fathers prayed her back to reason. But I swear by God, Alyosha, I never insulted the poor crazy girl! Only once, maybe, in the first year; she was very fond of praying then. She kept the feasts of Our Lady above all, and on those days she’d throw me out of her room. I’ll knock that mysticism out of her, I thought! ‘Look,’ I said, ‘here’s your holy image. Here it is. See, I’m taking it down. You believe it works miracles, but watch, I’ll spit on it this minute and nothing will happen to me for it!’... When she saw that, good Lord! I thought she’d kill me. But all she did was jump up and wring her hands, then suddenly cover her face with them, start trembling all over, and drop to the floor ... dropped all in a heap. Alyosha, Alyosha, what’s the matter?”

The old man leaped up in alarm. From the time he began talking about Alyosha’s mother, a change had been coming over Alyosha’s face little by little. He had flushed crimson, his eyes glowed, his lips trembled. The old sot had gone spluttering on without noticing anything, until something very strange happened to Alyosha. Exactly what he was describing in the crazy woman was suddenly happening again in Alyosha. He sprang up from his seat just as his mother was said to have done, wrung his hands, hid his face in them, and fell back into his chair, shaking all over in a hysterical fit of sudden, violent, silent weeping. His extraordinary likeness to his mother struck the old man especially.

“Ivan, Ivan! Water, quick! It’s just like her, exactly how she used to be then, his mother. Spit some water over him from your mouth, that’s what I used to do with her. He’s upset about his mother, his mother,” he muttered to Ivan.

“But she was my mother too, I believe, his mother. Wasn’t she?” said Ivan, in uncontrolled anger and contempt. The old man cringed before his blazing eyes. But something very strange had happened, though only for a second: it really seemed to have slipped the old man’s mind that Alyosha’s mother was in fact Ivan’s mother as well.

“Your mother?” he muttered, not understanding. “What do you mean? What mother are you talking about? Was she?... Why, damn it! Of course she was yours too! Damn it! My mind has never been so clouded before. Forgive me, why, I was thinking, Ivan.... He he he!” He broke off. A broad, drunken, half-witless grin spread across his face.
At that moment a dreadful din and uproar broke out in the hall. There were violent shouts, the door was flung open, and Dmitri burst into the room. The old man ran to Ivan in terror.
“He’ll kill me! He’ll kill me! Don’t let him get at me!” he screamed, clutching the tail of Ivan’s coat.

chapters.title: IX. The Sensualists
paragraphs: Grigory and Smerdyakov came running into the room after Dmitri. They had been struggling with him in the passage and trying to keep him out, on orders Fyodor Pavlovitch had given them some days before. Dmitri stopped for a moment inside the door to look around. Grigory took the chance to run around the table and shut the double doors on the far side of the room, the ones that led to the inner rooms. Then he stood in front of them with his arms stretched wide, ready to defend the way in, so to speak, to his last drop of blood. When Dmitri saw this, he let out a scream rather than a shout and rushed at Grigory.
“So she’s there! She’s hidden in there! Out of my way, you scoundrel!”

He tried to drag Grigory aside, but the old servant pushed him back. Dmitri, beside himself with fury, lashed out and hit Grigory with all his strength. The old man dropped like a log, and Dmitri leaped over him and broke down the door. Smerdyakov stayed at the other end of the room, pale and trembling, pressed up against Fyodor Pavlovitch.
“She’s here!” Dmitri shouted. “I saw her turn toward the house a minute ago, but I couldn’t catch her. Where is she? Where?”
That shout, “She’s here!”, had an extraordinary effect on Fyodor Pavlovitch. All his terror left him at once.

“Hold him! Hold him!” he cried, and dashed after Dmitri. Meanwhile Grigory had got up from the floor, though he still seemed dazed. Ivan and Alyosha ran after their father. In the third room something fell to the floor with a ringing crash. It was a large glass vase, not an expensive one, on a marble pedestal, and Dmitri had knocked it over as he ran past.
“Get him!” shouted the old man. “Help!”
Ivan and Alyosha caught hold of the old man and began forcing him back.
“Why are you running after him? He’ll murder you,” Ivan cried angrily to his father.
“Ivan! Alyosha! She has to be here. Grushenka’s here. Mitya said he saw her himself, running.”
He was choking. He hadn’t been expecting Grushenka that evening, and the sudden news that she was here drove him out of his mind. He was shaking all over. He seemed frantic.
“But you’ve seen for yourself that she hasn’t come,” cried Ivan.
“But she may have come in by that other entrance.”
“You know that entrance is locked, and you have the key.”

Dmitri suddenly appeared again in the drawing-room. He had found the other entrance locked, of course, and the key was in fact in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s pocket. The windows of all the rooms were shut too, so Grushenka could not have come in anywhere or run out anywhere.

“Hold him!” shrieked Fyodor Pavlovitch the moment he saw him again. “He’s been stealing money from my bedroom.” And he tore himself away from Ivan and rushed at Dmitri again. But Dmitri threw up both hands and suddenly grabbed the old man by the two tufts of hair that were left on his temples. He tugged at them and flung him to the floor with a crash. Then he kicked him two or three times in the face with his heel. The old man let out a shrill moan. Ivan was not as strong as Dmitri, but he threw his arms around him and pulled him away with all his might. Alyosha helped with what slender strength he had, holding Dmitri from the front.
“Madman! You’ve killed him!” cried Ivan.
“Serves him right!” shouted Dmitri, out of breath. “If I haven’t killed him, I’ll come back and kill him. You can’t protect him!”
“Dmitri! Go away at once!” cried Alyosha in a commanding voice.
“Alexey! You tell me. You’re the only one I can believe. Was she here just now, or not? I saw her myself, creeping this way along the fence from the lane. I shouted, and she ran away.”
“I swear she hasn’t been here, and no one was expecting her.”

“But I saw her.... So she must have ... I’ll find out right now where she is.... Goodbye, Alexey! Don’t say a word to Æsop about the money now. But go to Katerina Ivanovna straight away and be sure to tell her, ‘He sends you his compliments!’ Compliments, his compliments! Only compliments and farewell! Describe the scene to her.”

Meanwhile Ivan and Grigory had picked the old man up and sat him in an armchair. His face was smeared with blood, but he was conscious, and he listened eagerly to Dmitri’s shouts. He still believed that Grushenka really was somewhere in the house. Dmitri glared at him with hatred as he left.
“I’m not sorry I shed your blood!” he cried. “Watch out, old man, watch out for your dream, because I have a dream of my own. I curse you, and I disown you for good.”
He ran out of the room.
“She’s here. She must be here. Smerdyakov! Smerdyakov!” the old man wheezed, barely audible, beckoning to him with one finger.
“No, she’s not here, you old lunatic!” Ivan shouted at him furiously. “Look, he’s passing out! Water! A towel! Quick, Smerdyakov!”

Smerdyakov ran to fetch water. At last they got the old man undressed and into bed, and wrapped a wet towel around his head. The brandy, the violent excitement and the beating had worn him out. He closed his eyes and was asleep the moment his head touched the pillow. Ivan and Alyosha went back to the drawing-room. Smerdyakov swept up the pieces of the broken vase, while Grigory stood by the table staring gloomily at the floor.
“Why don’t you put a wet cloth on your head and go to bed too?” Alyosha said to him. “We’ll look after him. My brother hit you terribly hard, on the head.”
“He’s insulted me!” Grigory said gloomily, slowly and distinctly.
“He’s ‘insulted’ his father, not just you,” remarked Ivan with a forced smile.
“I used to wash him in his tub. He’s insulted me,” Grigory repeated.
“Damn it all, if I hadn’t pulled him away, he might have murdered him. It wouldn’t take much to finish off Æsop, would it?” Ivan whispered to Alyosha.
“God forbid!” cried Alyosha.
“Why should He?” Ivan went on in the same whisper, with a spiteful grimace. “One reptile will eat the other. And they both deserve it.”
Alyosha shuddered.
“Of course I won’t let him be murdered, just as I didn’t just now. Stay here, Alyosha. I’ll go out and walk around the yard. My head’s starting to ache.”

Alyosha went to his father’s bedroom and sat by his bed, behind the screen, for about an hour. Suddenly the old man opened his eyes and looked at Alyosha for a long time, plainly remembering and thinking. All at once his face showed extraordinary excitement.
“Alyosha,” he whispered anxiously, “where’s Ivan?”
“In the yard. He has a headache. He’s keeping watch.”
“Give me that looking-glass. It’s over there. Give it to me.”

Alyosha gave him a small round folding mirror that stood on the chest of drawers. The old man looked at himself in it. His nose was badly swollen, and on the left side of his forehead there was a fairly large crimson bruise.
“What does Ivan say? Alyosha, my dear, my only son, I’m afraid of Ivan. I’m more afraid of him than of the other one. You’re the only one I’m not afraid of....”
“Don’t be afraid of Ivan either. He’s angry, but he’ll defend you.”
“And Alyosha, what about the other one? He’s run off to Grushenka. My angel, tell me honestly, was she here just now or wasn’t she?”
“No one has seen her. It was a mistake. She hasn’t been here.”
“You know Mitya wants to marry her, to marry her.”
“She won’t marry him.”
“She won’t. She won’t. She won’t. She won’t, not for anything!”

The old man positively fluttered with joy, as if nothing more comforting could have been said to him. In his delight he seized Alyosha’s hand and pressed it warmly to his heart. There were actually tears glittering in his eyes.

“That icon of the Mother of God I mentioned earlier,” he said. “Take it home and keep it. And I’ll let you go back to the monastery.... I was joking this morning, so don’t be angry with me. My head hurts, Alyosha.... Alyosha, comfort my heart. Be an angel and tell me the truth!”
“You’re still asking whether she’s been here?” Alyosha said sadly.
“No, no, no. I believe you. I’ll tell you what: you go to Grushenka yourself, or see her somehow. Hurry up and ask her. See for yourself which one she means to choose, him or me. Eh? What? Can you?”
“If I see her, I’ll ask her,” Alyosha muttered, embarrassed.
“No, she won’t tell you,” the old man cut in. “She’s a rogue. She’ll kiss you and say it’s you she wants. She’s a sly, shameless hussy. You mustn’t go to her, you mustn’t!”
“No, father, and it wouldn’t be suitable. It wouldn’t be right at all.”
“Where was he sending you just now? He shouted ‘Go’ as he ran away.”
“To Katerina Ivanovna.”
“For money? To ask her for money?”
“No. Not for money.”

“He’s got no money, not a farthing. I’ll settle down for the night and think things over, and you can go. Maybe you’ll meet her.... Only be sure to come to me tomorrow morning. Be sure to. I have something to say to you tomorrow. Will you come?”
“Yes.”
“When you come, pretend you’ve come on your own to ask how I am. Don’t tell anyone I told you to. Don’t say a word to Ivan.”
“Very well.”
“Goodbye, my angel. You stood up for me just now. I’ll never forget it. There’s something I want to tell you tomorrow, but I have to think it over first.”
“And how do you feel now?”
“I’ll get up tomorrow and go out, perfectly well, perfectly well!”

As Alyosha crossed the yard, he found Ivan sitting on the bench by the gateway. He was writing something in pencil in his notebook. Alyosha told Ivan that their father had woken up, was conscious, and had let him go back to the monastery for the night.
“Alyosha, I’d be very glad to see you tomorrow morning,” said Ivan warmly, standing up. His warmth was a complete surprise to Alyosha.
“I’ll be at the Hohlakovs’ tomorrow,” answered Alyosha. “I may be at Katerina Ivanovna’s too, if I don’t find her now.”
“But you’re going to her now, aren’t you? To deliver that ‘compliments and farewell’?” said Ivan with a smile. Alyosha was thrown off balance.
“I think I understand his shouting just now, and part of what came before it. Dmitri asked you to go to her and tell her that he—well, in short—takes his leave of her?”
“Brother, how will all this horror between father and Dmitri end?” exclaimed Alyosha.
“No one can say for sure. Maybe nothing will come of it, and it will all fizzle out. That woman is a beast. In any case, we have to keep the old man indoors and keep Dmitri out of the house.”
“Brother, let me ask one thing more. Does any man have the right to look at other men and decide which of them is worthy to live?”
“Why bring worth into it? Most often the matter is decided in men’s hearts on other grounds, much more natural ones. And as for rights, who doesn’t have the right to wish?”
“Not for another man’s death?”

“What if it is for another man’s death? Why lie to oneself, since all men live that way, and perhaps can’t help living that way? Are you referring to what I said just now, that one reptile will devour the other? In that case, let me ask you: do you think I’m like Dmitri, capable of shedding Æsop’s blood, of murdering him, eh?”
“What are you saying, Ivan? That never even occurred to me. And I don’t think Dmitri is capable of it either.”

“Thank you, if only for that,” smiled Ivan. “Believe me, I’d always defend him. But in my wishes I keep complete freedom for myself here. Goodbye until tomorrow. Don’t condemn me, and don’t think of me as a villain,” he added with a smile.
They shook hands warmly, as they never had before. Alyosha felt that his brother had taken the first step toward him, and that he had surely done it for some definite reason.

chapters.title: X. Both Together
paragraphs: Alyosha left his father’s house more worn out and downhearted than when he had gone in. His mind felt shattered, knocked off balance. He was afraid to gather up the broken pieces and make one picture out of all the painful, clashing things this day had brought him. What he felt came close to despair, which he had never known before. Over everything else, like a mountain, loomed the fatal question that had no answer: how would it end between his father and his brother Dmitri, with this terrible woman standing between them? Now he had seen it with his own eyes. He had been present and watched the two of them face to face. And yet only his brother Dmitri could be made unhappy, terribly, completely unhappy. Trouble was waiting for him. Other people, it seemed, were involved too, and much more deeply than Alyosha could have guessed before. There was something downright mysterious in it as well. Ivan had taken a step toward him, which Alyosha had wished for a long time. Yet now, for some reason, it frightened him. And then there were the women. Strange to say, that morning he had set out for Katerina Ivanovna’s in the deepest embarrassment. Now he felt none of that. On the contrary, he was hurrying there as though he expected her to show him what to do. Yet the message he had for her was plainly harder to deliver than before. The business of the three thousand was settled beyond recall, and Dmitri, feeling dishonored and with his last hope gone, might stoop to anything. He had also told Alyosha to describe to Katerina Ivanovna the scene that had just taken place with his father.

By now it was seven o’clock and growing dark when Alyosha reached Katerina Ivanovna’s house on the High Street, a very roomy, comfortable house. He knew that she lived there with two aunts. One of them, a woman with little education, was the aunt of her half-sister Agafya Ivanovna, and had looked after Katerina Ivanovna in her father’s house when she came home from boarding school. The other aunt was a Moscow lady of style and consequence, though badly off. People said that both of them gave in to Katerina Ivanovna in everything, and that she kept them around only as chaperons. Katerina Ivanovna herself gave in to no one but her benefactress, the general’s widow. Illness had kept the widow in Moscow, and Katerina Ivanovna had to write to her twice a week, giving a full account of everything she did.

Alyosha stepped into the hall and asked the maid who opened the door to take up his name. It was obvious that they already knew he was there. Perhaps someone had seen him from the window. At any rate, Alyosha heard a commotion, the patter of hurrying feet and the rustle of skirts. Two or three women, it seemed, had dashed out of the room.

Alyosha found it odd that his arrival should set off such a flurry. All the same, he was shown straight into the drawing room. It was a big room, elegantly and lavishly furnished, nothing like the usual provincial style. There were sofas, lounges and settees in plenty, and tables large and small. There were pictures on the walls, vases and lamps on the tables, masses of flowers, and even an aquarium in the window. It was twilight, and rather dark. Alyosha made out a silk mantle thrown down on the sofa, where people had clearly just been sitting. On the table in front of the sofa stood two half-finished cups of chocolate, some cakes, a glass saucer of blue raisins and another of sweets. Alyosha saw that he had interrupted guests, and frowned. But just then the portière was raised, and Katerina Ivanovna came in with quick, hurrying steps, holding out both hands to him, her face radiant with delight. At the same moment a servant brought in two lighted candles and put them on the table.
“Thank God! You’ve come at last, too! I’ve been praying for you all day! Sit down.”

Alyosha had been struck by Katerina Ivanovna’s beauty three weeks earlier, when Dmitri first took him to meet her, at her own particular request. They hadn’t had any real conversation on that occasion. Taking Alyosha for very shy, Katerina Ivanovna had talked to Dmitri the whole time, to spare him. Alyosha had kept quiet, but he had seen a great deal, and seen it clearly. He had been struck by the commanding manner, the proud ease and the self-assurance of this haughty girl. All of that was certain, and Alyosha felt he wasn’t exaggerating. He thought her big, glowing black eyes very fine, especially in her pale, even rather sallow, longish face. But in those eyes, and in the lines of her exquisite lips, there was something his brother might well love passionately, but which perhaps couldn’t be loved for long. He had said almost exactly that to Dmitri after the visit, when his brother begged and insisted that he not hide what he thought of his betrothed.
“You’ll be happy with her, but perhaps not peacefully happy.”
“Just so, brother. People like that never change. They don’t bow to fate. So you think I won’t love her forever.”
“No, perhaps you’ll love her forever. But perhaps you won’t always be happy with her.”

Alyosha had said all this at the time blushing, and furious with himself for giving in to his brother’s pleading and putting such “foolish” ideas into words. The moment he had spoken, his opinion had struck him as awfully foolish. He was ashamed, too, to have spoken so confidently about a woman. That made it all the more astonishing to him now, at the first sight of Katerina Ivanovna running in to meet him, to feel that he might have been entirely wrong. This time her face shone with unforced, good-natured kindness and a direct, warm-hearted honesty. The “pride and haughtiness” that had struck him so much before now showed only as a frank, generous energy and a bright, strong faith in herself. Alyosha understood at the first glance, at the first word, that the whole tragedy of her position, in her relation to the man she loved so dearly, was no secret to her. She perhaps already knew everything, absolutely everything. And yet her face was bright, and her faith in the future was so strong. Alyosha felt at once that in his thoughts he had done her a grave injustice. He was conquered and captivated on the spot. On top of all this, he noticed from her very first words that she was in great excitement, an excitement perhaps quite out of the ordinary and close to ecstasy.
“I was so eager to see you because I can learn the whole truth from you, and from nobody else.”
“I’ve come,” muttered Alyosha, confused, “I—he sent me.”

“Ah, he sent you! I knew he would. Now I know everything, everything!” cried Katerina Ivanovna, her eyes flashing. “Wait a moment, Alexey Fyodorovitch, and I’ll tell you why I’ve wanted so badly to see you. You see, I probably know far more than you do yourself, so you don’t need to tell me anything. What I want from you is this. I want to know your own last impression of him. I want you to tell me, as directly and plainly as you can, even coarsely (oh, as coarsely as you like!), what you thought of him just now, and of his position, after meeting him today. That may be better than if I talked to him myself, since he doesn’t want to come to me. Do you see what I’m asking of you? Now tell me simply, tell me every word of the message he sent you with (I knew he would send you).”
“He told me to bring you his compliments—and to say he will never come again—but to bring you his compliments.”
“His compliments? Is that what he said—his own word for it?”
“Yes.”
“He might have used the wrong word by chance? Might he not have meant a different word?”
“No. He told me to repeat that very word. He begged me two or three times not to forget it.”
Katerina Ivanovna turned hotly red.

“Help me now, Alexey Fyodorovitch. Now I truly need your help. I’ll tell you what I think, and you must just say whether I’m right or wrong. Listen! If he had sent me his compliments offhand, without insisting that you repeat those words, without any stress on them, that would be the end of everything! But if he insisted on those words, if he made a point of telling you not to forget to give them to me, then perhaps he was in a fever, beside himself. He had made up his mind, and he was scared by it. He wasn’t walking away from me with a firm step. He was leaping headlong. The stress on that phrase may have been just bravado.”
“Yes, yes!” cried Alyosha warmly. “I think you’re right.”
“And if so, he’s not altogether lost. I can still save him. Wait! Did he say anything to you about money—about three thousand roubles?”

“He did speak of it, and that’s what is crushing him more than anything. He said he had lost his honor and nothing matters now,” Alyosha answered eagerly, feeling hope rush into his heart and believing that there really might be a way out, a rescue, for his brother. “But do you know about the money?” he added, and broke off suddenly.

“I’ve known about it for a long time. I telegraphed to Moscow to inquire, and heard long ago that the money had not come. He hadn’t sent it, but I said nothing. Last week I found out that he was still short of money. All I wanted in all this was for him to know whom to turn to, and who was his true friend. No, he won’t admit that I am his truest friend. He won’t know me. He looks on me only as a woman. I’ve been tormented all week, trying to think how to keep him from being ashamed to face me because he spent that three thousand. Let him be ashamed of himself, let him be ashamed of other people knowing, but not of my knowing. He can tell God everything without shame. Why is it that he still doesn’t understand how much I’m ready to bear for his sake? Why, why doesn’t he know me? How dare he not know me, after all that has happened? I want to save him forever. Let him forget me as his betrothed. And here he fears that he’s dishonored in my eyes. Why, he wasn’t afraid to be open with you, Alexey Fyodorovitch. Why do I not deserve the same?”
She said the last words in tears. Tears poured from her eyes.
“I must tell you,” Alyosha began, his voice shaking too, “what has just happened between him and my father.”

And he told her the whole scene: how Dmitri had sent him to get the money, how Dmitri had burst in and knocked his father down, and how after that Dmitri had again, specially and emphatically, begged Alyosha to carry her his compliments and his farewell. “He has gone to that woman,” Alyosha added softly.

“And you think I can’t put up with that woman? Does he think I can’t? But he won’t marry her,” she laughed suddenly, in a nervous way. “Can a Karamazov’s passion last forever? It’s passion, not love. He won’t marry her, because she won’t marry him.” Again Katerina Ivanovna laughed oddly.
“He may marry her,” said Alyosha sadly, looking down.

“He won’t marry her, I tell you. That girl is an angel. Do you know that? Do you know that?” Katerina Ivanovna burst out with extraordinary warmth. “She is one of the most fantastic of fantastic creatures. I know how bewitching she is, but I also know she is kind, firm and noble. Why are you looking at me like that, Alexey Fyodorovitch? Maybe my words surprise you, maybe you don’t believe me? Agrafena Alexandrovna, my angel!” she called suddenly to someone, peeping into the next room, “come in here. This is a friend. This is Alyosha. He knows all about our affairs. Show yourself to him.”
“All I was doing was waiting behind the curtain until you called me,” said a soft, you might even say sugary, woman’s voice.

The portière was lifted, and Grushenka herself came up to the table, smiling and beaming. A violent revulsion went through Alyosha. He fixed his eyes on her and couldn’t take them off. Here she was, that awful woman, the “beast,” as Ivan had called her half an hour earlier. And yet the creature standing before him seemed the simplest, most ordinary woman, good-natured and kind, handsome certainly, but so like other handsome ordinary women! It was true that she was very, very good-looking, with that Russian beauty which so many men love so passionately. She was fairly tall, though a little shorter than Katerina Ivanovna, who was exceptionally tall. She had a full figure and soft, almost noiseless movements, softened to a peculiar over-sweetness, like her voice. She didn’t walk as Katerina Ivanovna did, with a vigorous, bold stride, but without a sound. Her feet made absolutely no noise on the floor. She sank softly into a low chair, softly rustling her sumptuous black silk dress and delicately nestling her milk-white neck and broad shoulders in a costly cashmere shawl. She was twenty-two, and her face looked exactly that age. Her face was very white, with a pale pink tint on the cheeks. The cast of her face might be called too broad, and the lower jaw was set a little forward. Her upper lip was thin, but the lower one, slightly prominent, was at least twice as full and looked pouting. But her magnificent, abundant dark brown hair, her sable-colored eyebrows and her charming gray-blue eyes with their long lashes would have made even the most indifferent person, meeting her by chance in a crowd on the street, stop at the sight of her face and remember it long afterward. What struck Alyosha most in that face was its look of childlike good nature. Her eyes had a childlike look, a look of childish delight. She came up to the table beaming with delight, and seemed to be expecting something, with the impatient, trusting curiosity of a child. The light in her eyes gladdened the soul—Alyosha felt that. There was something else in her which he couldn’t understand, or couldn’t have defined, and which yet perhaps affected him without his knowing it. It was the softness, the voluptuousness of her bodily movements, that catlike silence. Yet it was a strong, ample body. Under the shawl you could see full, broad shoulders and a high bosom, still quite girlish. Her figure suggested the lines of the Venus of Milo, though already in somewhat exaggerated proportions. You could guess that. Connoisseurs of Russian beauty could have said with certainty that this fresh, still youthful beauty would lose its harmony by the time she was thirty, that it would “spread”; that her face would get puffy, that wrinkles would soon appear on her forehead and around her eyes, and that her complexion might turn coarse and red. In short, it was the beauty of the moment, the fleeting beauty so often found in Russian women. Alyosha, of course, wasn’t thinking of this. But though he was fascinated, he wondered, with an unpleasant feeling and something like regret, why she drawled like that and couldn’t speak naturally. She did it evidently because she felt there was a charm in the exaggerated, honeyed lilt of the syllables. It was, of course, only a bad, low-bred habit that showed poor schooling and a false idea of good manners. And yet this tone and manner of speaking seemed to Alyosha almost incredibly out of keeping with the childishly simple and happy expression of her face, the soft, babyish joy in her eyes. Katerina Ivanovna at once sat her down in an armchair facing Alyosha, and kissed her rapturously several times on her smiling lips. She seemed quite in love with her.

“This is the first time we’ve met, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she said rapturously. “I wanted to know her, to see her. I wanted to go to her, but I had barely said so when she came to me herself. I knew we would settle everything together—everything. My heart told me so. People begged me not to take this step, but I foresaw it would get us out of our difficulty, and I wasn’t wrong. Grushenka has explained everything to me and told me all she intends to do. She flew here like an angel of goodness and brought us peace and joy.”
“You didn’t look down on me, sweet, excellent young lady,” Grushenka drawled in her sing-song voice, still with the same charming, delighted smile.

“Don’t you dare talk to me like that, you sorceress, you witch! Look down on you! Here, I must kiss your lower lip once more. It looks swollen already, and now it will swell more, and more, and more. Look how she laughs, Alexey Fyodorovitch! It does your heart good to see the angel.”
Alyosha flushed, and faint shivers, hardly noticeable, kept running through him.
“You think so highly of me, dear young lady, and maybe I don’t deserve your kindness at all.”

“Not worthy! She’s not worthy of it!” Katerina Ivanovna cried again with the same warmth. “You know, Alexey Fyodorovitch, we’re fanciful, we’re self-willed, but in our little heart we’re the proudest of the proud. We’re noble, we’re generous, Alexey Fyodorovitch, let me tell you. We have only been unfortunate. We were too ready to give up everything for a man who was perhaps unworthy, or just fickle. There was one man—only one, an officer too. We loved him and sacrificed everything for him. That was long ago, five years ago, and he forgot us. He married. Now he is a widower. He has written that he is coming here. And, do you know, we’ve loved him, only him, all this time, and we’ve loved him all our life! He will come, and Grushenka will be happy again. For five years now she has been wretched. But who can reproach her? Who can boast of her favor? Only that bedridden old merchant, and he is more like her father, her friend, her protector. He found her then in despair and agony, abandoned by the man she loved. She was ready to drown herself, but the old merchant saved her—saved her!”
“You’re defending me so kindly, dear young lady. You’re in such a hurry about everything,” Grushenka drawled again.

“Defend you! Is it my place to defend you? Would I dare? Grushenka, angel, give me your hand. Look at that charming soft little hand, Alexey Fyodorovitch! Look at it! It has brought me happiness and lifted me up, and I’m going to kiss it, on both sides, here, here, here!”

And three times, in a kind of rapture, she kissed Grushenka’s hand, which was certainly charming, though rather fat. Grushenka held out her hand with a charming, musical, nervous little laugh. She watched the “sweet young lady” and clearly liked having her hand kissed.
“There may be a little too much rapture here,” thought Alyosha. He blushed. All the while he felt a strange unease in his heart.
“You won’t make me blush, dear young lady, by kissing my hand like this in front of Alexey Fyodorovitch.”
“Is that what you think, that I meant to make you blush?” said Katerina Ivanovna, a little surprised. “Oh, my dear, how little you understand me!”

“Yes, and maybe you misunderstand me completely too, dear young lady. Maybe I’m not as good as I seem to you. I have a bad heart. I will have my own way. I charmed poor Dmitri Fyodorovitch that day just for fun.”
“But now you’ll save him. You gave me your word. You’ll explain it all to him. You’ll break it to him that you have loved another man for a long time, and that he is now offering you his hand.”
“Oh, no! I never gave you my word to do that. You’re the one who kept talking about it. I didn’t give you my word.”
“Then I didn’t understand you quite right,” said Katerina Ivanovna slowly, turning a little pale. “You promised—”

“Oh, no, angel lady, I haven’t promised a thing,” Grushenka interrupted softly and evenly, with the same gay, simple look. “You can see right away, dear young lady, what a willful wretch I am next to you. If I want to do something, I do it. I may have made you some sort of promise a minute ago. But now I’m thinking again: I might go back to Mitya. I liked him very much once—liked him for almost a whole hour. Now maybe I’ll go and tell him to stay with me from today on. You see, I’m so changeable.”
“Just now you said—something completely different,” Katerina Ivanovna whispered faintly.
“Ah, just now! But, you know, I’m such a soft-hearted, silly creature. Just think what he’s been through on my account! What if I get home and feel sorry for him? What then?”
“I never expected—”

“Ah, young lady, how good and generous you are next to me! Maybe now you won’t want anything to do with a silly creature like me, now that you know my character. Give me your sweet little hand, angelic lady,” she said tenderly, and with something like reverence she took Katerina Ivanovna’s hand.

“Here, dear young lady, I’ll take your hand and kiss it the way you kissed mine. You kissed mine three times, but I ought to kiss yours three hundred times to be even with you. Well, never mind that. After that it will be as God wills. Maybe I’ll be your slave completely and want to do whatever you tell me, like a slave. Let it be as God wills, without any agreements or promises. What a sweet hand—what a sweet hand you have! You sweet young lady, you incredible beauty!”
She slowly raised the hands to her lips, with the odd purpose, in fact, of “being even” with her in kisses.

Katerina Ivanovna did not pull her hand away. She listened to those last words with timid hope, though Grushenka’s promise to do her bidding like a slave was put very strangely. She looked intently into Grushenka’s eyes. She still saw in them the same simple-hearted, trusting look, the same bright gaiety.
“She may be too naïve,” thought Katerina Ivanovna, with a gleam of hope.
Meanwhile Grushenka seemed delighted with the “sweet hand.” She raised it slowly to her lips. But she held it near her lips for two or three minutes, as though reconsidering something.
“Do you know, angel lady,” she suddenly drawled in an even softer, sugarier voice, “do you know, I think I won’t kiss your hand after all?” And she gave a merry little laugh.
“As you like. What’s the matter with you?” said Katerina Ivanovna, with a sudden start.
“So that you’re left remembering that you kissed my hand and I didn’t kiss yours.”
Her eyes suddenly flashed. She looked at Katerina Ivanovna with terrible intensity.
“Insolent creature!” cried Katerina Ivanovna, as if she had suddenly understood. She flushed all over and jumped to her feet.
Grushenka got up too, but without hurrying.
“So I’ll tell Mitya how you kissed my hand and I didn’t kiss yours at all. How he’ll laugh!”
“Vile slut! Go away!”
“Oh, shame on you, young lady! Oh, shame! A word like that is beneath you, dear young lady.”
“Go away! You’re a creature for sale!” screamed Katerina Ivanovna. Every feature of her utterly distorted face was working.
“For sale, indeed! You used to go to gentlemen at dusk for money once. You brought your beauty to sell. You see, I know.”
Katerina Ivanovna shrieked and would have thrown herself at her, but Alyosha held her back with all his strength.
“Not a step, not a word! Don’t speak, don’t answer her. She’ll go away—she’ll go this minute.”
At that moment Katerina Ivanovna’s two aunts ran in at her cry, and a maid with them. They all hurried to her.
“I’ll go,” said Grushenka, picking up her mantle from the sofa. “Alyosha, darling, walk me home!”
“Go away—go away, hurry!” cried Alyosha, clasping his hands imploringly.
“Dear little Alyosha, walk me home! I’ve got a pretty little story to tell you on the way. I staged this scene for your benefit, Alyosha. Walk me home, dear, you’ll be glad you did afterwards.”
Alyosha turned away, wringing his hands. Grushenka ran out of the house with a musical laugh.
Katerina Ivanovna went into hysterics. She sobbed and shook with convulsions. Everyone fussed around her.

“I warned you,” said the elder of her aunts. “I tried to keep you from doing this. You’re too impulsive. How could you do such a thing? You don’t know women like that, and they say she’s worse than any of them. You’re too headstrong.”
“She’s a tigress!” yelled Katerina Ivanovna. “Why did you hold me, Alexey Fyodorovitch? I would have beaten her—beaten her!”
She couldn’t control herself in front of Alyosha. Perhaps, in fact, she didn’t care to.
“She should be flogged in public, on a scaffold!”
Alyosha backed toward the door.

“But, my God!” cried Katerina Ivanovna, clasping her hands. “He! He! How could he be so dishonorable, so inhuman! Why, he told that creature what happened on that fatal, accursed day! ‘You brought your beauty to sell, dear young lady.’ She knows! Your brother is a scoundrel, Alexey Fyodorovitch.”
Alyosha wanted to say something, but he couldn’t find the words. His heart was aching.
“Go away, Alexey Fyodorovitch! It’s shameful, it’s awful for me! Tomorrow—I beg you on my knees—come tomorrow. Don’t condemn me. Forgive me. I don’t know what I’ll do with myself now!”
Alyosha walked out into the street, reeling. He could have wept as she did. Suddenly the maid caught up with him.
“The young lady forgot to give you this letter from Madame Hohlakov. It’s been with us since dinnertime.”
Alyosha took the little pink envelope mechanically and, almost without realizing it, put it in his pocket.

chapters.title: XI. Another Reputation Ruined
paragraphs: The monastery lay barely three-quarters of a mile outside the town. Alyosha set off along the road at a brisk walk. Nobody else was on it at that hour. Night was nearly down, and it was too dark to make out anything clearly thirty paces ahead. Halfway there the road crossed another. Under a lone willow at the crossing, a figure came into view. The moment Alyosha reached the spot, the figure leapt out and ran at him, yelling savagely:
“Your money or your life!”
“Mitya, it’s you!” cried Alyosha, surprised, though he had been badly frightened.

“Ha ha ha! You weren’t expecting me? I couldn’t decide where to wait for you. Outside her house? Three roads lead away from it, and I might have missed you. So finally I thought, I’ll wait here. You have to pass this spot, there’s no other way to the monastery. Come on, tell me the truth. Crush me like a beetle. But what’s wrong?”

“Nothing, brother—you just scared me. Oh, Dmitri! Father’s blood, only a little while ago.” (Alyosha started to cry. He had been on the edge of tears for a long time, and now something in his soul seemed to snap.) “You nearly killed him—you cursed him—and now, here, you’re joking—‘Your money or your life!’”
“Well, so what? It’s not proper—is that what you mean? Doesn’t suit a man in my position?”
“No—it’s only that—”

“Hold on. Look at the night. See how dark it is, the clouds, the wind that’s picked up. I was hiding under that willow, waiting for you. And I swear by God above, I suddenly thought: why drag on in misery any longer? What is there left to wait for? Here’s a willow, here’s a handkerchief, here’s a shirt. In a minute I can twist them into a rope, and I have my suspenders too. Why go on weighing down the earth and shaming it with my filthy presence? And then I heard you coming—heavens, it was as if something had suddenly flown down to me. So there is someone I love after all! Here he is, my dear little brother, the one I love more than anyone in the world, the only one I love in the world. And at that moment I loved you so much, so much, that I thought, ‘I’ll throw myself on his neck this instant.’ Then a stupid notion came over me: play a joke on you, give you a scare. So I shouted that idiotic ‘Your money!’ Forgive the clowning—it was nonsense, and there’s nothing improper in my soul.... Damn it all, tell me what happened. What did she say? Hit me, crush me, show me no mercy! Was she furious?”
“No, not that.... Nothing like that happened, Mitya. It was—I found the two of them there together.”
“The two of them? Who?”
“Grushenka was at Katerina Ivanovna’s.”
Dmitri was struck speechless.
“Impossible!” he cried. “You’re raving! Grushenka with her?”

Alyosha told him everything that had happened, starting from the moment he walked into Katerina Ivanovna’s. The telling took ten minutes. It couldn’t be called a smooth or orderly account, but he seemed to get it across. He left out no word or deed that mattered, and he often described his own feelings vividly in a single word. Dmitri listened without a sound, fixing him with a terrible stare. Still, Alyosha could see that he understood everything and had caught every point. But as the story went on, his face turned from gloomy to menacing. He scowled and ground his teeth, and his stare grew more rigid, more intense, more terrible. Then, suddenly, and with astonishing speed, that angry, savage face changed. His tight lips came apart, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch burst out laughing, helplessly and without any plan to. He positively shook with it. For a long while he could not say a word.

“So she wouldn’t kiss her hand! She didn’t kiss it—she ran off!” he kept crying out in hysterical glee. It might have been called insolent glee, if it hadn’t burst out so naturally. “And the other one called her a tigress! A tigress she is! So she should be flogged on a scaffold? Yes, yes, she should. That’s exactly my opinion. She should have been long ago. Here’s how it is, brother: let her be punished, but first I have to get well. I know the queen of impudence. That’s her all over! You saw the whole of her in that hand-kissing, the she-devil! In her own line she’s magnificent! So she ran home? I’ll go—ah—I’ll run to her! Alyosha, don’t blame me. I agree, hanging’s too good for her.”
“But what about Katerina Ivanovna!” cried Alyosha sadly.

“I see through her too! I see her as I never have before! It’s a real discovery, like the four continents of the world, I mean the five! What a thing to do! That’s Katya for you, who wasn’t afraid to face a rude, coarse officer and risk a deadly insult, all on a generous impulse to save her father! But the pride, the recklessness, the defiance of fate, the boundless defiance! You say the aunt tried to stop her? That aunt is domineering herself, you know. She’s the sister of the general’s widow in Moscow, and she’s even more high and mighty than the widow. But her husband was caught stealing government funds. He lost everything, his estate and all, and the proud wife had to haul down her flag, and she hasn’t flown it since. So she tried to hold Katya back, and Katya wouldn’t hear of it! She thinks she can overcome anything, and that everything will give way before her. She thought she could bewitch Grushenka whenever she liked, and she believed it herself. She acts a part for her own benefit, and whose fault is that? Do you think she kissed Grushenka’s hand first on purpose, with some motive? No, she really was taken with Grushenka. That is, not with Grushenka, but with her own dream, her own delusion—because it was _her_ dream, _her_ delusion! Alyosha, my darling, how did you ever get away from them, those women? Did you hitch up your cassock and run? Ha ha ha!”

“Brother, you don’t seem to have noticed how badly you insulted Katerina Ivanovna by telling Grushenka about that day. And Grushenka threw it in her face just now: that she had gone to gentlemen in secret to sell her beauty! Brother, what insult could be worse than that?”
What troubled Alyosha most was that his brother seemed pleased at Katerina Ivanovna’s humiliation, incredible as that was.
“Bah!” Dmitri scowled fiercely and slapped his forehead. Only now did it sink in, though Alyosha had just told him about the insult and about Katerina Ivanovna’s cry: “Your brother is a scoundrel!”

“Yes, maybe I did tell Grushenka about that ‘fatal day,’ as Katya calls it. Yes, I told her, I remember it now! It was at Mokroe. I was drunk, the gypsies were singing.... But I was sobbing. I was sobbing then, on my knees, praying to Katya’s image, and Grushenka understood. She understood everything then. I remember, she cried herself.... Damn it all! But it’s bound to be like that now.... Then she cried, and now it’s ‘the dagger in the heart’! That’s women for you.”
He lowered his eyes and fell to thinking.

“Yes, I am a scoundrel, an out-and-out scoundrel!” he said suddenly, in a dark voice. “Whether I cried or not makes no difference, I’m a scoundrel! Tell her I accept the name, if that comforts her. There, enough. Good-by. No use talking! It’s no fun. You go your way and I’ll go mine. And I don’t want to see you again, except as a last resort. Good-by, Alexey!”
He gripped Alyosha’s hand warmly. Then, eyes still on the ground and head down, as if wrenching himself away, he strode quickly off toward the town.
Alyosha watched him go. He could not believe that Dmitri would leave so suddenly.

“Wait, Alexey, one more confession, for you alone!” cried Dmitri, wheeling around. “Look at me. Look at me carefully. You see, here, right here—a terrible disgrace is waiting for me.” (As he said “here,” Dmitri pounded his chest with his fist in a strange way, as though the dishonor sat exactly on his chest, at some spot, in a pocket perhaps, or hung from his neck.) “You know me by now, a scoundrel, a confessed scoundrel. But let me tell you this: nothing I’ve ever done, or ever will do, comes near the baseness of the dishonor I carry this very minute on my breast, here, here. It’s going to happen, though I’m perfectly free to stop it. I can stop it or I can see it through, mark that. Well, I’ll tell you: I’m going to see it through. I won’t stop it. I told you everything just now, but not this, because even I hadn’t the brass for it. I can still pull back. If I do, I can give back half of my lost honor tomorrow, the full half. But I won’t pull back. I’ll carry out my base plan, and you can bear witness that I told you beforehand. Darkness and ruin! No need to explain. You’ll learn it in good time. The filthy back alley, and the she-devil. Good-by. Don’t pray for me, I’m not worth it. And there’s no need, no need at all.... I don’t want it! Go!”
And he abruptly turned away, and this time he was gone for good. Alyosha continued toward the monastery.
“What? I’ll never see him again! What is he saying?” he wondered wildly. “But I’ll certainly see him tomorrow. I’ll hunt him up. I’ll make a point of it. What does he mean?”

He skirted the monastery wall and cut through the pine wood to the hermitage. The door was opened for him, although no one was let in at that hour. His heart trembled as he entered Father Zossima’s cell.

“Why, oh why had he left? Why had the elder sent him out into the world? Here there was peace. Here there was holiness. Out there was confusion and darkness, where a man lost his way and went astray at once....”

In the cell he found the novice Porfiry and Father Païssy, who looked in every hour to ask after Father Zossima. Alyosha heard with alarm that the elder was getting worse and worse. Even his usual talk with the brothers could not be held that day. Normally, every evening after the service, the monks crowded into Father Zossima’s cell. There each one confessed aloud the sins of his day, his sinful thoughts and temptations, and even his quarrels, if he had had any. Some confessed on their knees. The elder absolved them, reconciled them, exhorted them, gave penances, blessed them and sent them away. The opponents of “elders” protested against exactly this general “confession.” They claimed it profaned the sacrament of confession and was almost a sacrilege, though in fact it was something quite different. They even told the diocesan authorities that these confessions did no good, and in great part actually led to sin and temptation. Many of the brothers disliked going to the elder. They went against their will, because everyone else went and because they feared being accused of pride and rebellious ideas. People said some of the monks agreed in advance, “I’ll confess that I lost my temper with you this morning, and you back me up,” just to have something to say. Alyosha knew this really did happen at times. He knew, too, that some of the monks bitterly resented the custom of bringing letters from relatives to the elder first, so that he opened and read them before the people they were meant for.

All this was supposed, of course, to be done freely and in good faith, as voluntary submission and healthy guidance. In fact, though, there was sometimes a good deal of insincerity in the practice, and much that was false and forced. Still, the older and more experienced monks stood by their view. They argued: “For those who have come within these walls in sincere search of salvation, such obedience and sacrifice will surely be healthy and of great benefit. Those who find it irksome and grumble are no true monks and were mistaken to enter the monastery—their place is in the world. Even in the temple a man is not safe from sin and the devil. So it was no use paying too much attention to it.”

“He is weaker. A drowsiness has come over him,” Father Païssy whispered to Alyosha, giving him his blessing. “It’s hard to wake him, and he must not be woken. He was awake for five minutes. He sent his blessing to the brothers and asked for their prayers for him tonight. He means to take the sacrament again in the morning. He remembered you, Alexey. He asked if you had gone away, and was told you were in the town. ‘I blessed him for that work,’ he said. ‘His place is there, not here, for a while.’ Those were his words about you. He remembered you with love and with concern. Do you understand what an honor he paid you? But why has he decided that you should spend some time in the world? He must have foreseen something in your destiny! Understand this, Alexey: if you go back into the world, it must be to do the duty your elder has laid on you, and not for vain frivolity and worldly pleasures.”

Father Païssy left. Alyosha had no doubt that Father Zossima was dying, though he might last another day or two. Alyosha made a firm and fervent resolution. Despite his promises to his father, to the Hohlakovs and to Katerina Ivanovna, he would not leave the monastery the next day. He would stay with his elder to the end. His heart glowed with love. He bitterly blamed himself for having forgotten, even for one instant, the man he had left dying in the monastery, the man he honored above anyone in the world. He went into Father Zossima’s bedroom, knelt, and bowed to the ground before the elder. The elder slept calmly and did not stir. His breathing was even and barely audible, and his face was peaceful.

Alyosha went back to the other room, where Father Zossima had received his guests that morning. He took off his boots and lay down on the hard, narrow leather sofa, which he had used as a bed for a long time, bringing only a pillow. As for the mattress his father had shouted about that morning, he had long since forgotten to sleep on it. He took off his cassock and spread it over himself as a cover. But before going to bed he dropped to his knees and prayed for a long time. In his fervent prayer he did not ask God to lighten his darkness. He only thirsted for the joyful feeling that always came to his soul after the praise and worship that made up his evening prayer. That joy always brought him light, untroubled sleep. As he prayed, he suddenly felt in his pocket the little pink note the servant had handed him as he left Katerina Ivanovna’s. He was disturbed, but he finished his prayer. Then, after some hesitation, he opened the envelope. Inside was a letter to him, signed by Lise, the young daughter of Madame Hohlakov, who had laughed at him that morning in front of the elder.

“Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she wrote, “I’m writing to you behind everyone’s back, even mamma’s, and I know how wrong that is. But I can’t go on living without telling you what I feel, because something has sprung up in my heart, and for now nobody but the two of us must know. But how can I say what I so much want to tell you? They say paper doesn’t blush. I assure you that isn’t true. It’s blushing just the way I am now, all over. Dear Alyosha, I love you. I’ve loved you since I was a child, since our days in Moscow, when you were very different from what you are now, and I’ll love you all my life. My heart has chosen you, so that we can join our lives and spend them together until we’re old. On condition, of course, that you leave the monastery. As for our age, we’ll wait until the age the law sets. By then I’ll certainly be quite strong, walking and dancing. There can’t be any doubt of that.

“You see, I’ve thought of everything. There’s just one thing I can’t picture: what you’ll think of me when you read this. I’m always laughing and getting into mischief. This morning I made you angry, but I assure you that before I took up my pen I prayed in front of the Image of the Mother of God, and now I’m praying, and nearly crying.

“My secret is in your hands. When you come tomorrow, I don’t know how I’ll be able to look at you. Ah, Alexey Fyodorovitch, what if I can’t hold myself in, and laugh like a silly when I look at you, the way I did today? You’ll think I’m a nasty girl who’s making fun of you, and you won’t believe my letter. So I beg you, dear one, if you have any pity for me, when you come tomorrow don’t look me straight in the face. If I meet your eyes, I’m sure to burst out laughing, especially with you in that long gown. I go cold all over thinking of it. So when you come, don’t look at me at all for a while. Look at mamma, or out the window....

“Here I’ve written you a love letter. Oh dear, what have I done? Alyosha, don’t despise me. And if I’ve done something horrid and hurt you, forgive me. Now the secret of my reputation, ruined perhaps for ever, is in your hands.
“I’m certainly going to cry today. Good-by until we meet, our _awful_ meeting.—LISE.
“P.S.—Alyosha! You must, must, must come!—LISE.”

Alyosha read the note in amazement. He read it through twice, thought for a moment, and suddenly gave a soft, sweet laugh. He started. The laugh seemed sinful to him. But a minute later he laughed again, just as softly and happily. Slowly he put the note back in its envelope, crossed himself and lay down. The turmoil in his heart was gone at once. “God, have mercy on all of them. Keep all these unhappy, restless souls in Your care and set them on the right path. All ways are Yours. Save them according to Your wisdom. You are love. You will send joy to all!” Alyosha murmured, crossing himself, and fell into a peaceful sleep.
PART II

chapters.title: I. Father Ferapont
paragraphs: Alyosha was woken early, before daybreak. Father Zossima had woken feeling very weak, yet he wanted to get out of bed and sit in a chair. His mind was perfectly clear. His face looked worn out, but it was bright and almost joyful, full of gaiety, kindness and warmth. “Perhaps I will not live through the coming day,” he told Alyosha. Then he asked to confess and take communion at once. He always confessed to Father Païssy. After communion came the service of extreme unction. The monks gathered, and little by little the cell filled with the residents of the hermitage. By now it was daylight. People began to arrive from the monastery. When the service was over, the elder wanted to kiss every one of them and say goodbye. The cell was so small that the first visitors left to make room for the next. Alyosha stood beside the elder, who was seated in his armchair again. He talked as much as he could. His voice was weak, but fairly steady.

“I have been teaching you for so many years, and so I have been talking aloud for so many years, that talking has become a habit. It is almost harder for me to keep quiet than to speak, even now, weak as I am, dear Fathers and brothers,” he joked, looking with emotion at the group around him.

Alyosha remembered some of what he said, afterwards. The elder spoke out clearly and his voice was fairly steady, but what he said hung together rather loosely. He spoke of many things. He seemed anxious, before the moment of death, to say everything he had not said in his life. It was not only to instruct them. He seemed thirsty to share his joy and ecstasy with all men and all creation, and to open his whole heart once more in his life.

“Love one another, Fathers,” said Father Zossima, as far as Alyosha could remember afterwards. “Love God’s people. We have come here and shut ourselves up within these walls, but we are no holier than those outside. On the contrary, by the very act of coming here, each of us has admitted to himself that he is worse than others, worse than all men on earth.... And the longer a monk lives in seclusion, the more keenly he must see this. Otherwise he would have had no reason to come. When he understands that he is not only worse than others, but that he is responsible to all men for all and everything, for all human sins, national and individual, only then is the aim of our seclusion reached. For know, dear ones, that every one of us is undoubtedly responsible for all men and everything on earth. This is not merely because creation as a whole is sinful. Each one of us is personally responsible for all mankind and for every single man. This knowledge is the crown of life for the monk and for every man. For monks are not a special sort of men, but only what all men ought to be. Only through that knowledge does our heart grow soft with infinite, universal, inexhaustible love. Then each of you will have the power to win over the whole world by love and to wash away the sins of the world with your tears.... Each of you, keep watch over your heart and confess your sins to yourself without ceasing. Do not be afraid of your sins, even when you see them, so long as there is penitence. But do not make conditions with God. Again I say, do not be proud. Do not be proud before the little or before the great. Do not hate those who reject you, who insult you, who abuse and slander you. Do not hate the atheists, the teachers of evil, the materialists—and I mean not only the good ones—for there are many good ones among them, especially in our day—do not hate even the wicked ones. Remember them in your prayers in this way: Save, O Lord, all those who have no one to pray for them, save also all those who will not pray. And add: it is not in pride that I make this prayer, O Lord, for I am lower than all men.... Love God’s people. Do not let strangers draw away the flock, for if you sleep in your slothfulness and disdainful pride, or worse still, in covetousness, they will come from every side and draw your flock away. Expound the Gospel to the people unceasingly ... do not be extortionate.... Do not love gold and silver, do not hoard them.... Have faith. Cling to the banner and raise it on high.”

But the elder actually spoke more disconnectedly than Alyosha made it seem when he reported the words afterwards. Now and then he stopped altogether, as if to draw breath and gather strength, yet he was in a kind of ecstasy. They listened with emotion, though many were puzzled by his words and found them obscure.... Afterwards everyone remembered them.

Alyosha stepped out of the cell for a moment and was struck by the excitement and suspense of the monks crowding around it. In some, this expectation took the form of anxiety; in others, of devout solemnity. All of them expected some marvel to happen right after the elder’s death. Seen from one side, their suspense was almost frivolous, yet even the strictest of the monks were caught up in it. Father Païssy’s face was the gravest of all.

A monk called Alyosha aside, secretly, to see Rakitin. Rakitin had come from town with a singular letter for him from Madame Hohlakov. In it she described a strange and very timely incident. Among the women who had come the day before to receive Father Zossima’s blessing, it seemed, was an old woman from the town, a sergeant’s widow named Prohorovna. She had asked whether she might pray for the repose of the soul of her son Vassenka, who had gone to Irkutsk and had sent her no word for over a year. Father Zossima had answered her sternly and forbidden it. Praying for the living as though they were dead, he said, was a kind of sorcery. Later he forgave her, because she was ignorant, and added some words of comfort, “as though reading the book of the future” (this was Madame Hohlakov’s expression): “that her son Vassya was certainly alive and would either come himself very soon or send a letter, and that she should go home and expect him.” And then Madame Hohlakov exclaimed enthusiastically, “Would you believe it? The prophecy has come true to the letter, and more besides.” The old woman had barely got home when they handed her a letter from Siberia that had been waiting for her. But that was not all. In the letter, written on the road from Ekaterinenburg, Vassya told his mother that he was coming back to Russia with an official, and that three weeks after she got the letter he hoped “to embrace his mother.”

Madame Hohlakov warmly begged Alyosha to tell the Superior and the whole brotherhood about this new “miracle of prediction.” “All, all, ought to know of it!” she finished. The letter had been written in a hurry, and the writer’s excitement showed in every line. But Alyosha did not need to tell the monks, because they all knew already. Rakitin had told the monk who carried his message “to inform most respectfully his reverence Father Païssy that he, Rakitin, has a matter to speak of with him, so grave that he dare not put it off a moment, and humbly begs forgiveness for his presumption.” That monk had delivered the message to Father Païssy before delivering Alyosha’s. So when Alyosha had read the letter, he found nothing left to do but hand it to Father Païssy as confirmation of the story.
Even that austere and cautious man frowned as he read the news of the “miracle,” yet he could not entirely hide some inner emotion. His eyes gleamed, and a grave, solemn smile came to his lips.
“We shall see greater things!” broke from him.
“We shall see greater things, greater things yet!” the monks around him echoed.

But Father Païssy frowned again and asked them all, for a time at least, not to speak of the matter “until it is more fully confirmed, since there is so much credulity among those of this world, and besides, this may well have come about naturally.” He added this prudently, as if to ease his conscience, though he hardly believed his own disclaimer. His listeners saw that perfectly well.

Within the hour, of course, the whole monastery knew of the “miracle,” and so did many visitors who had come for the mass. No one seemed more struck by it than the monk who had come the day before from St. Sylvester, from the little monastery of Obdorsk in the far North. He had stood near Madame Hohlakov the previous day and had earnestly asked Father Zossima, referring to the “healing” of the lady’s daughter, “How can you presume to do such things?”

Now he was rather puzzled and did not know whom to believe. The evening before, he had visited Father Ferapont in his separate cell behind the apiary, and the visit had left him deeply impressed and awed. This Father Ferapont was the aged monk, devoted to fasting and silence, who has been mentioned already as opposed to Father Zossima and to the whole institution of “elders,” which he held to be a harmful and frivolous novelty. He was a formidable opponent, although his practice of silence meant he hardly spoke to anyone. He was formidable because a number of monks shared his feelings entirely, and many visitors saw him as a great saint and ascetic, even though they had no doubt he was crazy. Yet it was precisely his craziness that drew them.

Father Ferapont never went to see the elder. He lived in the hermitage, but nobody bothered him to follow its rules, and this too was because he acted as if he were crazy. He was seventy-five or older. His home was in a corner beyond the apiary, an old, decaying wooden cell built long ago for another great ascetic, Father Iona, who had lived to a hundred and five. Many curious stories about his saintly deeds were still told in the monastery and the neighborhood.

Seven years earlier, Father Ferapont had succeeded in getting himself settled in that same lonely cell. It was just a peasant’s hut, though it looked like a chapel, because it held an extraordinary number of ikons with lamps burning before them without a break—ikons that people had brought to the monastery as offerings to God. Father Ferapont had been appointed to look after them and keep the lamps lit. It was said (and it was true) that he ate only two pounds of bread in three days. The beekeeper, who lived close to the apiary, brought him the bread every three days, and even to this man who served him, Father Ferapont seldom spoke a word. These four pounds of bread, plus the sacrament bread that the Father Superior regularly sent him on Sundays after the late mass, made up his weekly food. The water in his jug was changed every day. He seldom showed himself at mass. Visitors who came to pay him homage sometimes found him kneeling in prayer all day without once looking around. When he did speak to them, he was brief, abrupt, odd, and nearly always rude. Very rarely, though, he would talk with visitors. Mostly he would come out with a single strange saying that was a complete riddle, and no pleading could make him say a word to explain it. He was not a priest, but a simple monk. There was a strange belief, mainly among the most ignorant, that Father Ferapont communicated with heavenly spirits and spoke only with them, which was why he was silent with men.

The beekeeper, who was also a very silent and surly monk, had pointed the monk from Obdorsk toward the apiary, and he made his way to the corner where Father Ferapont’s cell stood. “Maybe he will speak, since you are a stranger, and maybe you will get nothing out of him,” the beekeeper had warned. The monk said afterwards that he approached in utter dread. It was rather late in the evening. Father Ferapont was sitting at the door of his cell on a low bench. A huge old elm rustled gently overhead. There was a freshness in the evening air. The monk from Obdorsk bowed low before the saint and asked for his blessing.
“Do you want me to bow down to you, monk?” said Father Ferapont. “Get up!”
The monk got to his feet.
“Blessing, be blessed! Sit down next to me. Where have you come from?”

What startled the poor monk most was that Father Ferapont, for all his strict fasting and his great age, still looked like a vigorous old man. He was tall and stood perfectly straight. His face was thin, yet fresh and healthy. He plainly still had a good deal of strength, and his build was that of an athlete. He was very old, but his hair was thick and his beard full, and neither was even fully gray. Both had once been black. His eyes were large, gray and bright, though they stood out strikingly from his face. He had a broad country accent. He wore a peasant’s long reddish coat made of coarse convict cloth (as it used to be called), tied round the waist with a stout rope. His throat and chest were bare. Under the coat, his shirt of the coarsest linen was almost black with dirt, for it had not been changed in months. People said he wore thirty pounds of iron chains beneath the coat. On his bare feet were old slippers that were nearly falling apart.
“From the little Obdorsk monastery, from St. Sylvester,” the monk answered humbly. All the while his keen, curious, slightly frightened little eyes were watching the hermit.
“I’ve been to your Sylvester’s. I used to stay there. Is Sylvester well?”
The monk hesitated.
“What a senseless lot you are! How do you keep the fasts?”

“We eat according to the ancient rules of the monastery. In Lent no meals are provided on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. On Tuesday and Thursday we are given white bread, stewed fruit with honey, wild berries or salted cabbage, and porridge of coarse meal. On Saturday there is white cabbage soup, noodles with peas, and kasha, all of it made with hemp oil. On weekdays we get dried fish and kasha along with the cabbage soup. In Holy Week, from Monday to Saturday evening, six whole days, nothing at all is cooked. We have only bread and water, and little of that, and if possible we do not eat every day, as is ordered for the first week of Lent. On Good Friday we eat nothing. On the Saturday, too, we must fast until three o’clock, and then we take a little bread and water and drink one cup of wine. On Holy Thursday we drink wine and have something cooked without oil, or nothing cooked at all, because the council of Laodicea says of Holy Thursday: ‘It is unseemly to relax the fast on Holy Thursday and so dishonor the whole of Lent!’ That is how we keep the fast. But what is that beside you, holy Father,” added the monk, growing more confident, “who take nothing but bread and water all year round, even at Easter? What we eat in two days lasts you a full seven. Your great abstinence is truly marvelous.”
“And mushrooms?” Father Ferapont asked suddenly.
“Mushrooms?” the monk repeated, taken aback.

“Yes. I can do without their bread. I don’t need it at all. I can go off into the forest and live on mushrooms or berries. But they can’t do without their bread here, and that’s why they’re in bondage to the devil. These days the unclean say there’s no need for such fasting. Proud and unclean is their judgment.”
“Och, true,” sighed the monk.
“And have you seen devils among them?” Ferapont asked.
“Among them? Among whom?” the monk asked timidly.

“Last year on Trinity Sunday I went to see the Father Superior, and I haven’t been back since. I saw a devil sitting on one man’s chest, hiding under his cassock, only his horns sticking out. Another had one peeping out of his pocket, with sharp eyes, and it was afraid of me. Another had settled in somebody’s unclean belly. Another was hanging round a man’s neck, and the man was carrying him about without seeing him.”
“You—you can see spirits?” the monk asked.

“I tell you, I can see. I see right through them. When I came out from the Superior’s, I saw one hiding from me behind the door. A big one, a yard and a half high or more, with a thick long gray tail. The tip of the tail was in the crack of the door, and I was quick. I slammed the door and pinched his tail in it. He squealed and began to struggle. I made the sign of the cross over him three times, and he died on the spot, like a crushed spider. He must be rotting there in the corner and stinking by now, but they don’t see it, they don’t smell it. It’s a year since I was there. I’m telling you this because you’re a stranger.”

“Your words are terrible! But, holy and blessed Father,” said the monk, who was getting bolder and bolder, “is it true what people say about you, even in far-off lands, that you are in constant communication with the Holy Ghost?”
“He does fly down sometimes.”
“How does he fly down? In what form?”
“As a bird.”
“The Holy Ghost as a dove?”
“There’s the Holy Ghost, and there’s the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit can appear as other birds. Sometimes as a swallow, sometimes as a goldfinch, sometimes as a blue-tit.”
“How can you tell him from an ordinary tit?”
“He talks.”
“How does he talk? In what language?”
“Human language.”
“And what does he say to you?”
“Why, today he told me a fool would come to see me and ask me improper questions. You want to know too much, monk.”
“Your words are terrible, most holy and blessed Father,” the monk said, shaking his head. Yet there was doubt in his frightened little eyes.
“See this tree?” Father Ferapont asked, after a pause.
“I see it, blessed Father.”
“You think it’s an elm. To me it’s a different shape.”
“What shape?” asked the monk, after waiting in vain for him to go on.
“It happens at night. Do you see those two branches? At night it is Christ stretching out His arms to me, searching for me with those arms. I see it plainly, and I tremble. It’s terrible, terrible!”
“What’s terrible about it, if it is Christ Himself?”
“Why, He’ll seize me and carry me off.”
“Alive?”
“In the spirit and glory of Elijah, haven’t you heard? He’ll take me up in His arms and carry me away.”

The monk went back to the cell he was sharing with one of the brothers, and he was greatly perplexed. Even so, in his heart he revered Father Ferapont more than Father Zossima. He was all in favor of fasting, so it did not seem strange to him that a man who kept such a rigid fast as Father Ferapont should “see marvels.” His words certainly sounded queer, but only God could say what lay hidden in them. And were worse words and deeds not commonly seen in people who have given up their minds for the glory of God? The tale of the devil’s tail caught in the door he was ready and eager to believe, and not only as a figure of speech. Besides, before coming to the monastery he had been strongly prejudiced against the institution of “elders.” He knew it only from hearsay and thought it a harmful novelty. He had not been at the monastery long before he noticed the secret grumbling of some shallow brothers who disliked it. He was, besides, a meddlesome, curious man who poked his nose into everything. That was why the news of the fresh “miracle” performed by Father Zossima left him so deeply perplexed. Alyosha remembered afterwards how their inquisitive guest from Obdorsk kept flitting from one group to another, listening and asking questions among the monks crowded inside and outside the elder’s cell. At the time, though, he paid him little attention, and only recalled it later.

In fact, he had no thought to spare for it. Father Zossima had grown tired again and gone back to bed. As he was closing his eyes, he thought of Alyosha and sent for him. Alyosha ran to him at once. No one else was in the cell except Father Païssy, Father Iosif and the novice Porfiry. The elder opened his weary eyes, looked hard at Alyosha, and suddenly asked him:
“Are your people expecting you, my son?”
Alyosha hesitated.
“Do they not need you? Did you not promise someone yesterday that you would visit them today?”
“I did promise—my father—my brothers—others too.”

“You see, you must go. Do not grieve. Be sure that I will not die without your being here to hear my last word. I will say that word to you, my son. It will be my last gift to you. To you, dear son, because you love me. But now go and keep your promise.”

Alyosha obeyed at once, though it was hard to leave. But the promise that he would hear the elder’s last word on earth, and that it would be his own last gift to him, filled Alyosha’s soul with a thrill of rapture. He hurried so that he could finish what he had to do in the town and come back quickly. Father Païssy, as they left the cell together, also spoke some words of exhortation that moved and greatly surprised him.

“Remember always, young man,” Father Païssy began, without any preface, “that the science of this world has grown into a great power. In the last century especially, it has analyzed everything divine that has come down to us in the holy books. After that cruel analysis, the learned men of this world have nothing left of all that was once sacred. But they have analyzed only the parts and missed the whole, and their blindness is truly marvelous. The whole still stands firm before their eyes, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Has it not lasted nineteen centuries? Is it not still a living, moving power in the soul of the individual and in the masses of the people? It is just as strong and alive even in the souls of atheists, who have destroyed everything! Even those who have renounced Christianity and attack it still follow the Christian ideal in their inmost being. Until now neither their cleverness nor the ardor of their hearts has been able to create a higher ideal of man and of virtue than the one Christ gave long ago. When they have tried, the result has been only grotesque. Remember this above all, young man, because your dying elder is sending you out into the world. Perhaps, when you remember this great day, you will not forget my words. They come from my heart, for your guidance, since you are young, and the temptations of the world are great, beyond your strength to bear. Well, now go, my orphan.”

With these words Father Païssy blessed him. As Alyosha left the monastery and turned them over in his mind, he suddenly saw that he had found a new and unexpected friend, a warmly loving teacher, in this austere monk who until now had been stern with him. It was as if Father Zossima had left him to Father Païssy at his death. “Perhaps that is exactly what passed between them,” Alyosha thought suddenly. The philosophical reflections he had just heard so unexpectedly showed how warm Father Païssy’s heart was. He was in a hurry to arm the boy’s mind for the struggle with temptation, and to protect the young soul left in his care with the strongest defense he could think of.

chapters.title: II. At His Father’s
paragraphs: Alyosha went to his father first. On the way he remembered that his father had insisted the day before that he must come without his brother Ivan seeing him. “Why?” Alyosha suddenly wondered. “Even if Father has something to say to me alone, why should I go in unseen? Most likely he meant to say something else yesterday, he was so worked up,” he decided. Still, he was very glad when Marfa Ignatyevna opened the garden gate for him (Grigory, it turned out, was ill in bed in the lodge) and, in answer to his question, told him that Ivan Fyodorovitch had gone out two hours earlier.
“And my father?”
“He’s up, having his coffee,” Marfa answered, a little curtly.

Alyosha went in. The old man was sitting alone at the table in slippers and a shabby little overcoat. He was passing the time looking over some accounts, though without much attention. He was entirely alone in the house, since Smerdyakov had gone out to the market too. He had risen early and was trying to put a bold face on things, but he looked tired and weak.
