A red handkerchief was bound round his forehead, where huge purple bruises had come out overnight. His nose had swollen terribly in the night as well, and smaller bruises were spread over it in patches. All this gave his face a peculiarly spiteful, irritable look. The old man knew it, and as Alyosha came in he gave him a hostile glare.
“The coffee’s gone cold,” he cried harshly. “I won’t offer you any. Today I’ve ordered nothing but a Lenten fish soup, and I’m not asking anyone to share it. Why are you here?”
“To see how you are,” said Alyosha.
“Yes. And I did tell you to come yesterday. It’s of no importance. You needn’t have gone to the trouble. But I knew you’d come poking your nose in right away.”

He said this with something close to hostility. At the same moment he got up and anxiously checked his nose in the looking-glass (perhaps for the fortieth time that morning). He also started tying the red handkerchief round his forehead more becomingly.
“Red is better. A white one makes me look like I’m in the hospital,” he pronounced pompously. “Well, how are things over there? How’s your elder?”
“He is very ill. He may die today,” Alyosha answered. But his father hadn’t listened, and had forgotten his own question at once.

“Ivan’s gone out,” he said suddenly. “He’s trying his hardest to take Mitya’s betrothed away from him. That’s what he’s staying here for,” he added spitefully, and gave Alyosha a sidelong look with his mouth twisted.
“Surely he never told you that?” asked Alyosha.
“He did, a long time ago. Believe it or not, he told me three weeks back. You don’t imagine he came here to murder me as well, do you? He must have come for some reason.”
“What do you mean? Why do you say such things?” said Alyosha, upset.

“He doesn’t ask for money, it’s true, but he’ll not get a farthing out of me all the same. I mean to live as long as I can, you may as well know, my dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, and so I need every farthing, and the longer I live, the more I’ll need,” he went on, pacing from one corner of the room to the other, his hands in the pockets of his loose, greasy overcoat of yellow cotton. “I can still pass for a man of fifty-five, but I want to go on passing for one another twenty years. The older I get, you know, the less pretty I’ll be. The wenches won’t come to me of their own accord, so I’ll need my money. That’s why I’m saving up more and more, just for myself, my dear son Alexey Fyodorovitch. You may as well know that. Because I mean to go on sinning to the end, let me tell you. Sin is sweet. Everybody curses it, and everybody lives in it, only the others do it on the sly and I do it in the open. And that’s why all the other sinners jump on me, for being so simple. And your paradise, Alexey Fyodorovitch, isn’t to my taste, let me tell you. It’s no place for a gentleman, your paradise, even if there is such a thing. I believe I fall asleep and never wake up, and that’s the end of it. You can pray for my soul if you like. If you don’t want to, then don’t, damn you! That’s my philosophy. Ivan spoke well here yesterday, though we were all drunk. Ivan is a conceited coxcomb, but he has no great learning ... no education either. He sits there silent, smiling at you and saying nothing—that’s what gets him by.”
Alyosha listened to him in silence.

“Why won’t he talk to me? When he does speak, he puts on airs. Your Ivan is a scoundrel! And if I want to, I’ll marry Grushenka in a minute. If you’ve got money, Alexey Fyodorovitch, you only have to want something and you can have it. That’s what Ivan is afraid of. He’s watching to stop me from marrying, and that’s why he’s egging Mitya on to marry Grushenka himself. He hopes that will keep me away from Grushenka (as if I’d leave him my money if I don’t marry her!). And if Mitya marries Grushenka, Ivan can carry off his rich betrothed. That’s what he’s counting on! He’s a scoundrel, your Ivan!”
“How cross you are! It’s because of yesterday. You had better lie down,” said Alyosha.

“There! You say that,” the old man remarked suddenly, as if it had only now occurred to him, “and I’m not angry with you. If Ivan said it, I’d be angry with him. It’s only with you that I have my good moments. Otherwise, you know, I’m an ill-natured man.”
“You’re not ill-natured. You’re warped,” said Alyosha, smiling.

“Listen. This morning I meant to have that ruffian Mitya locked up, and now I don’t know what I’ll decide. Of course, nowadays, with all this fashion, fathers and mothers count as a prejudice. But even now the law doesn’t let a son drag his old father around by the hair, kick him in the face in his own house, and boast that he’ll murder him outright—and all of it with witnesses present. If I wanted, I could crush him and have him locked up straight away for what he did yesterday.”
“Then you don’t intend to bring charges?”
“Ivan talked me out of it. I wouldn’t care what Ivan thinks, but there’s something else.”
And bending toward Alyosha, he went on in a confidential half-whisper.

“If I put the ruffian in prison, she’ll hear of it and run to see him at once. But if she hears that he beat me, a weak old man, to within an inch of my life, she might give him up and come to me.... That’s how she is, everything by contraries. I know her through and through! Won’t you have a drop of brandy? Have some cold coffee and I’ll pour a quarter of a glass of brandy into it. It’s delicious, my boy.”

“No, thank you. I’ll take that roll along, if I may,” said Alyosha. He took a halfpenny French roll and put it in the pocket of his cassock. “And you shouldn’t have brandy either,” he suggested nervously, looking into the old man’s face.
“You’re right, it only upsets my nerves instead of calming them. Just one little glass. I’ll get it out of the cupboard.”
He unlocked the cupboard, poured a glass and drank it, then locked the cupboard again and put the key back in his pocket.
“That’s enough. One glass won’t kill me.”
“You see, you’re in a better mood now,” said Alyosha with a smile.

“Hm! I love you even without the brandy, but with scoundrels I’m a scoundrel. Ivan’s not going to Tchermashnya—why is that? He wants to spy and find out how much I give Grushenka if she comes. They’re all scoundrels! I don’t recognize Ivan, I don’t know him at all. Where does he come from? He’s not one of us in his soul. As if I’d leave him anything! I won’t leave a will at all, you may as well know. And I’ll crush Mitya like a beetle. I squash black-beetles at night with my slipper, they squelch when you step on them. And your Mitya will squelch too. _Your_ Mitya, because you love him. Yes, you love him, and I’m not afraid of you loving him. But if Ivan loved him, I’d be afraid, for myself, of his loving him. But Ivan loves nobody. Ivan is not one of us. People like Ivan aren’t our kind, my boy. They’re like a cloud of dust. The wind blows, and the dust is gone.... I had a silly idea in my head when I told you to come today. I wanted to find out from you about Mitya. Suppose I handed him a thousand now, or maybe two. Would the beggarly wretch agree to clear off altogether for five years or, better still, thirty-five, and without Grushenka, and give her up once and for all, eh?”
“I—I’ll ask him,” Alyosha muttered. “If you would give him three thousand, perhaps he—”

“That’s nonsense! No need to ask him now, no need! I’ve changed my mind. It was a nonsensical idea. I’ll give him nothing, not a penny, I want my money for myself,” cried the old man, waving his hand. “I’ll crush him like a beetle without it. Don’t say a word to him, or he’ll start hoping. There’s nothing for you to do here, you needn’t stay. That betrothed of his, Katerina Ivanovna, whom he’s kept so carefully hidden from me all this time, is she going to marry him or not? You went to see her yesterday, I believe?”
“Nothing will make her give him up.”

“There, you see how dearly these fine young ladies love a rake and a scoundrel. They’re poor creatures, I tell you, those pale young ladies, very different from—Ah, if I had his youth and the looks I had then (because at twenty-eight I was better-looking than he is), I’d have been a conquering hero just as he is. He’s a low cad! But he won’t have Grushenka, anyway, he won’t! I’ll crush him!”
His anger had flared up again with those last words.
“Go on, you can go. There’s nothing for you to do here today,” he snapped harshly.
Alyosha went up to say good-by to him, and kissed him on the shoulder.
“What’s that for?” The old man was a little surprised. “We’ll see each other again, or do you think we won’t?”
“Not at all, I didn’t mean anything.”

“Neither did I, I didn’t mean anything,” said the old man, looking at him. “Listen, listen,” he shouted after him, “come back soon and I’ll have a fish soup for you, a fine one, not like today’s. Be sure to come! Come tomorrow, do you hear, tomorrow!”
And as soon as Alyosha had gone out of the door, he went to the cupboard again and poured another half-glass.

“I won’t have any more!” he muttered, clearing his throat. Again he locked the cupboard and put the key in his pocket. Then he went into his bedroom and lay down on the bed, worn out, and in a minute he was asleep.

chapters.title: III. A Meeting With The Schoolboys
paragraphs: “Thank goodness he didn’t ask me about Grushenka,” thought Alyosha as he left his father’s house and headed for Madame Hohlakov’s. “Otherwise I might have had to tell him I met Grushenka yesterday.”

Alyosha felt painfully that since yesterday both of the rivals had found new strength, and their hearts had hardened again. “Father is spiteful and angry. He’s made some plan and he’ll stick to it. And what about Dmitri? He’ll be harder than he was yesterday too. He must be spiteful and angry as well, and no doubt he’s made a plan of his own. Oh, I must find him today, whatever happens.”

But Alyosha didn’t have long to brood. Something happened on the road that seemed trivial, yet it made a deep impression on him. He had just crossed the square and turned the corner into Mihailovsky Street, which is cut off from the High Street by a small ditch (our whole town is crisscrossed with ditches). At the bridge he saw a group of schoolboys between nine and twelve years old. They were on their way home from school. Some had their bags on their shoulders, others had leather satchels slung across their chests. Some wore short jackets, others little overcoats. A few even had those high boots, creased around the ankles, that little boys spoiled by rich fathers love to wear. The whole group was talking eagerly about something, apparently holding a council. Ever since his Moscow days Alyosha had never been able to walk past children without noticing them. He was fondest of children around three, but he liked schoolboys of ten and eleven too. So, anxious as he was today, he wanted to turn aside at once and talk to them. He looked into their excited, rosy faces and saw right away that every boy had a stone in his hand. On the other side of the ditch, about thirty paces off, another schoolboy was standing by a fence. He also had a satchel at his side. He was about ten years old, pale and delicate-looking, with sparkling black eyes. He was watching the other six closely and anxiously. They were clearly his schoolmates, he had just come out of school with them, but he had obviously had a quarrel with them.
Alyosha went up to a fair, curly-headed, rosy boy in a black jacket and remarked:
“When I used to carry a satchel like yours, I always wore it on my left side, so that my right hand would be free. You’ve got yours on the right. It’ll be awkward for you to get at it.”

Alyosha had no craft or calculation in opening with this practical remark. But it is the only way for a grown-up to win a child’s confidence at once, and even more so a group of children. You have to begin in a serious, businesslike way, so that you stand on a perfectly equal footing. Alyosha understood this by instinct.
“But he’s left-handed,” answered another boy at once, a fine, healthy-looking boy of eleven. All the others stared at Alyosha.
“He even throws stones with his left hand,” said a third.
At that moment a stone flew into the group. It only just grazed the left-handed boy, though it had been thrown well and hard by the boy on the other side of the ditch.

“Give it to him, hit him back, Smurov!” they all shouted. But Smurov, the left-handed boy, needed no urging. He got his revenge at once and threw a stone, but it missed the boy and hit the ground. The boy on the other side of the ditch, whose coat pocket was plainly bulging with stones, flung another at the group. This time it flew straight at Alyosha and hit him painfully on the shoulder.

“He aimed it at you, he meant it for you. You’re Karamazov, Karamazov!” the boys shouted, laughing. “Come on, all throw at him at once!” Six stones flew at the boy. One hit him on the head and he fell down, but he leapt up again at once and began to fire back furiously. Both sides threw stones without stopping. Many in the group had their pockets full too.
“What are you doing! Aren’t you ashamed? Six against one! Why, you’ll kill him,” cried Alyosha.
He ran forward and stood in the way of the flying stones to shield the lone boy. Three or four of them stopped throwing for a minute.

“He started it!” cried a boy in a red shirt, in an angry childish voice. “He’s a beast. The other day in class he stabbed Krassotkin with a penknife. It bled. Krassotkin wouldn’t tell on him, but he has to be thrashed.”
“But what for? I suppose you tease him.”

“There, he sent a stone into your back again, he knows who you are,” cried the children. “It’s you he’s throwing at now, not us. Come on, all of you, at him again, don’t miss, Smurov!” And again a hail of stones began, a vicious one. The boy on the other side of the ditch was hit in the chest. He screamed, started to cry and ran away uphill toward Mihailovsky Street. They all shouted: “Aha, he’s scared, he’s running away. Wisp of tow!”
“You don’t know what a beast he is, Karamazov. Killing is too good for him,” said the boy in the jacket, his eyes flashing. He seemed to be the eldest.
“What’s wrong with him?” asked Alyosha. “Is he a tattletale or what?”
The boys looked at one another as though in mockery.
“Are you going that way, to Mihailovsky?” the same boy went on. “Catch up with him.... You see, he’s stopped again. He’s waiting and looking at you.”
“He’s looking at you,” the other boys chimed in.
“Ask him whether he likes a disheveled wisp of tow. Do you hear? Ask him that!”
They all burst out laughing. Alyosha looked at them, and they looked back at him.
“Don’t go near him, he’ll hurt you,” Smurov cried in a warning voice.
“I won’t ask him about the wisp of tow, because I expect you tease him with that question somehow. But I’ll find out from him why you hate him so much.”
“Go on and find out, then,” cried the boys, laughing.
Alyosha crossed the bridge and walked uphill along the fence, straight toward the boy.
“You’d better watch out,” the boys called after him. “He’s not afraid of you. He’ll stab you in a minute, on the sly, the way he did Krassotkin.”

The boy waited for him without moving. As Alyosha came up, he saw a child of about nine standing in front of him. He was small and weak, with a thin, pale face and large dark eyes that stared at him with spite. He was wearing a shabby old overcoat that he had grown out of far too much. His bare arms stuck out past the sleeves. There was a big patch on the right knee of his trousers, and in his right boot, right at the toe, there was a big hole in the leather, carefully blackened with ink. Both pockets of his coat were weighed down with stones. Alyosha stopped two steps in front of him and looked at him questioningly. The boy saw at once from Alyosha’s eyes that he wasn’t going to hit him. He grew less defiant and spoke first.
“I’m alone, and there are six of them. I’ll beat them all, alone!” he said suddenly, his eyes flashing.
“I think one of the stones must have hurt you badly,” remarked Alyosha.
“But I hit Smurov on the head!” cried the boy.
“They told me you know me, and that you threw a stone at me on purpose,” said Alyosha.
The boy looked at him darkly.
“I don’t know you. Do you know me?” Alyosha went on.
“Leave me alone!” the boy cried irritably. But he didn’t move, as if he were waiting for something, and again there was a spiteful light in his eyes.
“All right, I’m going,” said Alyosha. “Only I don’t know you, and I don’t tease you. They told me how they tease you, but I don’t want to tease you. Good-by!”

“Monk in silk trousers!” cried the boy, following Alyosha with the same spiteful, defiant look. He threw himself into a defensive stance, sure that Alyosha would now fall on him. But Alyosha turned, looked at him and walked away. He hadn’t gone three steps before the biggest stone the boy had in his pocket hit him painfully in the back.

“So you’ll hit a man from behind! They’re telling the truth, then, when they say you attack on the sly,” said Alyosha, turning around again. This time the boy hurled a stone savagely straight at Alyosha’s face. But Alyosha had just enough time to guard himself, and the stone struck him on the elbow.
“Aren’t you ashamed? What have I done to you?” he cried.

The boy waited in silent defiance, certain that Alyosha would attack him now. Seeing that even now he wouldn’t, he flew into a rage like a little wild beast’s. He rushed at Alyosha himself, and before Alyosha had time to move, the spiteful child had seized his left hand in both of his and bitten his middle finger. He sank his teeth into it and it was ten seconds before he let go. Alyosha cried out with pain and pulled his finger away with all his might. At last the child let go and backed off to his former distance. Alyosha’s finger had been bitten badly, to the bone, close to the nail, and it began to bleed. Alyosha took out his handkerchief and bound it tightly around his injured hand. It took him a full minute to bandage it. The boy stood waiting the whole time. At last Alyosha raised his gentle eyes and looked at him.
“All right,” he said, “you can see how badly you’ve bitten me. That’s enough, isn’t it? Now tell me, what have I done to you?”
The boy stared in amazement.

“I don’t know you, and it’s the first time I’ve seen you,” Alyosha went on, with the same calm, “but I must have done something to you. You wouldn’t have hurt me like this for nothing. So what have I done? How have I wronged you? Tell me.”

Instead of answering, the boy burst into a loud, tearful wail and ran away. Alyosha walked slowly after him toward Mihailovsky Street. For a long time he could see the child in the distance, still running as fast as ever, without turning his head, and no doubt still wailing in tears. Alyosha made up his mind to find him as soon as he had time and to solve this mystery. Just now he had no time.

chapters.title: IV. At The Hohlakovs’
paragraphs: Alyosha soon got to Madame Hohlakov’s house, a handsome two-story stone building, one of the finest in our town. Madame Hohlakov spent most of her time in another province, where she had an estate, or in Moscow, where she owned a house. Even so, she had a house in our town too, passed down from her ancestors. Her estate in our district was the biggest of her three, and yet until now she had spent very little time in our province. She came running out to Alyosha in the hall.
“Did you get my letter about the new miracle?” She spoke fast and nervously.
“Yes.”
“Did you show it to everyone? He gave a son back to his mother!”
“He is dying today,” said Alyosha.

“I’ve heard, I know, oh, how I long to talk to you about all this, to you or to somebody. No, to you, to you! And how sorry I am that I can’t see him! The whole town is stirred up, everyone is in suspense. But now—do you know Katerina Ivanovna is here at this very moment?”
“Ah, that’s lucky,” cried Alyosha. “Then I can see her here. She told me yesterday that I must come and see her today without fail.”

“I know, I know everything. I’ve heard exactly what happened yesterday—and the atrocious way that—creature behaved. _C’est tragique_, and if I’d been in her place I have no idea what I’d have done. And your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch, what do you make of him?—my goodness! Alexey Fyodorovitch, I’m forgetting, just imagine it; your brother is in there with her, not that dreadful brother who was so shocking yesterday, but the other one, Ivan Fyodorovitch. He’s sitting with her, talking; they’re having a serious conversation. If you could only imagine what’s passing between them now—it’s awful, I tell you it’s lacerating, it’s like some incredible tale of horror. They’re ruining their lives for no reason that anyone can see. They both know it, and they revel in it. I’ve been watching for you! I’ve been thirsting for you! It’s too much for me, that’s the worst of it. I’ll tell you all about it in a minute, but right now I have to speak about something else, the most important thing—I’d completely forgotten what matters most. Tell me, why has Lise been in hysterics? The moment she heard you were here, she started having hysterics!”

“_Maman_, it’s you who are hysterical now, not me,” Lise’s voice rang out through a tiny crack in the side door. She sounded as if she wanted to laugh and was trying her hardest to hold it back. Alyosha noticed the crack at once, and no doubt Lise was peeping through it, but he couldn’t see her.

“And no wonder, Lise, no wonder ... your whims will make me hysterical too. But she is so ill, Alexey Fyodorovitch, she’s been so ill all night, feverish and moaning! I could hardly wait for morning and for Herzenstube to arrive. He says he can make nothing of it, that we have to wait. Herzenstube always comes and says he can make nothing of it. The minute you came near the house, she screamed, went into hysterics, and insisted that we wheel her back into this room.”
“Mamma, I didn’t know he’d come. I didn’t want to be wheeled into this room because of him.”
“That’s not true, Lise. Yulia ran to tell you that Alexey Fyodorovitch was coming. She was watching out for you.”

“My darling mamma, that wasn’t at all clever of you. But if you want to make up for it by saying something very clever, dear mamma, then tell our honored guest, Alexey Fyodorovitch, that he has shown how witless he is by daring to come to us after what happened yesterday, when everyone is laughing at him.”

“Lise, you’re going too far. I swear I’ll have to be stern with you. Who is laughing at him? I’m so glad he’s come, I need him, I can’t do without him. Oh, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I am dreadfully unhappy!”
“But what’s wrong with you, mamma, darling?”

“Ah, your whims, Lise, your restlessness, your illness, that awful night of fever, that awful, everlasting Herzenstube, everlasting, everlasting, that’s the worst of it! Everything, in fact, everything.... Even that miracle, too! Oh, how it has upset me, how it has shattered me, that miracle, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch! And that tragedy in the drawing room, it’s more than I can bear, I warn you. I can’t bear it. A comedy, maybe, not a tragedy. Tell me, will Father Zossima live till tomorrow, will he? Oh, my God! What is happening to me? Every minute I close my eyes and see that it’s all nonsense, all nonsense.”
“I’d be very grateful,” Alyosha broke in suddenly, “if you could give me a clean rag to bandage my finger. I’ve hurt it, and it’s very painful.”
Alyosha undid the handkerchief around his bitten finger. It was soaked with blood. Madame Hohlakov screamed and shut her eyes.
“Good heavens, what a wound, how awful!”
But the moment Lise saw Alyosha’s finger through the crack, she threw the door wide open.

“Come in, come in here,” she cried, in a commanding voice. “No more nonsense! Good heavens, why did you just stand there all this time and say nothing about it? He could have bled to death, mamma! How did you do it? Water, water! First of all you must wash it, just hold it in cold water to stop the pain, and keep it there, keep it there.... Hurry, mamma, bring some water in a slop basin. But do hurry,” she finished nervously. The sight of Alyosha’s wound had given her a real fright.
“Shouldn’t we send for Herzenstube?” cried Madame Hohlakov.

“Mamma, you’ll be the death of me. Your Herzenstube will come and say he can make nothing of it! Water, water! Mamma, for goodness’ sake go yourself and hurry Yulia, she’s such a slowpoke, she never can come fast! Hurry, mamma, or I’ll die.”
“Really, it’s nothing much,” cried Alyosha, frightened by this alarm.
Yulia ran in with water, and Alyosha put his finger into it.

“Some lint, mamma, for mercy’s sake, bring some lint and that muddy, caustic lotion for wounds, what’s it called? We have some. You know where the bottle is, mamma; it’s in your bedroom, in the right-hand cupboard, there’s a big bottle of it there with the lint.”
“I’ll bring everything in a minute, Lise, only don’t scream and don’t make a fuss. You see how bravely Alexey Fyodorovitch bears it. Where did you get such a dreadful wound, Alexey Fyodorovitch?”
Madame Hohlakov hurried off. This was just what Lise had been waiting for.
“First of all, answer my question: where did you get hurt like this?” she asked Alyosha quickly. “And then I’ll talk to you about something quite different. Well?”

Alyosha sensed that the time while her mother was out of the room was precious to her. So he hurried to tell her, in as few words as possible, about his puzzling encounter with the schoolboys. Lise clasped her hands as she listened.

“How can you mix with schoolboys, and dressed like that, too?” she cried angrily, as though she had a right to tell him what to do. “If you can do that, you’re nothing but a boy yourself, a perfect boy! But you must find out about that horrid boy for me and tell me everything, because there’s some mystery in it. Now for the second thing, but first a question: does the pain stop you from talking about utterly unimportant things, but talking sensibly?”
“Of course not, and it doesn’t hurt much now.”

“That’s only because your finger is in the water. We’ll have to change it right away, because it will get warm in a minute. Yulia, bring some ice from the cellar and another basin of water. Now that she’s gone I can speak; will you give me the letter I sent you yesterday, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch—be quick, because mamma will be back any minute and I don’t want—”
“I don’t have the letter.”
“That’s not true, you do. I knew you’d say that. It’s in that pocket. I’ve been sorry about that joke all night. Give me the letter back this minute, give it to me.”
“I left it at home.”

“But you can’t treat me like a child, a little girl, after that silly joke! I’m sorry for being so silly, but you must bring me the letter, if you really haven’t got it with you—bring it today, you must, you must.”
“I can’t possibly today, because I’m going back to the monastery, and I won’t be able to come and see you for the next two days—three or four, maybe—because Father Zossima—”
“Four days, what nonsense! Listen. Did you laugh at me a lot?”
“I didn’t laugh at all.”
“Why not?”
“Because I believed everything you said.”
“You’re insulting me!”

“Not at all. As soon as I read it, I thought all of it would come true, because as soon as Father Zossima dies, I have to leave the monastery. Then I’ll go back to my studies and finish them, and when you come of age we’ll be married. I’ll love you. I haven’t had time to think about it, but I don’t believe I could find a better wife than you, and Father Zossima tells me I must marry.”
“But I’m a cripple, wheeled about in a chair,” laughed Lise, her face flushing crimson.
“I’ll wheel you around myself, but I’m sure you’ll be well by then.”

“But you’re mad,” said Lise nervously, “to make all this nonsense out of a joke! And here’s mamma, perhaps just in time, _à propos_. Mamma, you’re always so slow, how can you be so long! And here’s Yulia with the ice!”

“Oh, Lise, don’t scream, above all, don’t scream. That screaming drives me ... What am I supposed to do when you put the lint somewhere else? I’ve been hunting and hunting—I do believe you did it on purpose.”
“But how could I know he’d turn up with a bad finger? Otherwise perhaps I really would have done it on purpose. My darling mamma, you’re starting to say truly witty things.”

“Never mind whether I’m witty, but I must say you’re showing a lovely feeling for Alexey Fyodorovitch’s suffering! Oh, my dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, what’s killing me isn’t any single thing, not Herzenstube, but everything all together, that’s what’s too much for me.”

“That’s enough, mamma, enough about Herzenstube,” Lise laughed merrily. “Hurry up with the lint and the lotion, mamma. That’s only Goulard’s water, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I’ve remembered the name now, but it’s a splendid lotion. Would you believe it, mamma, on his way here he got into a fight with some boys in the street, and one of them bit his finger. Isn’t he a child, a child himself? Is he fit to marry after that? Because just imagine, mamma, he wants to be married. Just think of him married, wouldn’t it be funny, wouldn’t it be awful?”
And Lise kept on laughing her thin, hysterical giggle, glancing slyly at Alyosha.
“But why married, Lise? What makes you talk about such a thing? It’s quite out of place—and perhaps that boy was rabid.”
“Oh, mamma! As if there were rabid boys!”

“Why not, Lise, as though I’d said something stupid! Your boy might have been bitten by a mad dog, and then he’d go mad and bite anyone near him. How well she has bandaged it, Alexey Fyodorovitch! I couldn’t have done it. Does it still hurt?”
“It’s nothing much now.”
“You aren’t afraid of water?” asked Lise.

“Come now, that’s enough, Lise, perhaps I really was a little too quick to talk about the boy being rabid, and you jumped on it right away. Katerina Ivanovna has only just heard that you’re here, Alexey Fyodorovitch, she simply rushed at me, she’s dying to see you, dying!”
“Ach, mamma, go to them yourself. He can’t go just now, he’s in too much pain.”
“Not at all, I can go perfectly well,” said Alyosha.
“What! You’re going away? Is that what you’re saying?”

“Well, once I’ve seen them, I’ll come back here and we can talk as much as you like. But I’d like to see Katerina Ivanovna right now, because I’m very anxious to get back to the monastery as soon as I can.”
“Mamma, take him away quickly. Alexey Fyodorovitch, don’t bother coming to see me afterwards, just go straight back to your monastery, and good riddance. I want to sleep, I didn’t sleep all night.”
“Ah, Lise, you’re only teasing, but how I wish you would sleep!” cried Madame Hohlakov.
“I don’t know what I’ve done.... I’ll stay another three minutes, or five if you like,” muttered Alyosha.
“Even five! Do take him away quickly, mamma, he’s a monster.”

“Lise, you’re out of your mind. Let’s go, Alexey Fyodorovitch, she’s too capricious today. I’m afraid to cross her. Oh, the trouble you have with nervous girls! Perhaps she really will be able to sleep after seeing you. How quickly you’ve made her sleepy, and how lucky that is!”
“Ah, mamma, how sweetly you talk! I must kiss you for that, mamma.”

“And I kiss you too, Lise. Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” Madame Hohlakov began, mysteriously and importantly, in a quick whisper. “I don’t want to hint at anything, I don’t want to lift the veil, you’ll see for yourself what’s going on. It’s appalling. It’s the most fantastic farce. She loves your brother Ivan, and she’s doing everything she can to convince herself that she loves your brother Dmitri. It’s appalling! I’ll go in with you, and if they don’t throw me out, I’ll stay to the end.”

chapters.title: V. A Laceration In The Drawing-Room
paragraphs: But in the drawing-room the talk was already over. Katerina Ivanovna was very worked up, though she looked determined. Just as Alyosha and Madame Hohlakov walked in, Ivan Fyodorovitch got up to say goodbye. His face was a little pale, and Alyosha watched him anxiously. This moment would settle a doubt that had been nagging at him, a riddle that had haunted him for some time. Over the past month, people had hinted to him more than once that his brother Ivan was in love with Katerina Ivanovna. Worse, they said he meant “to carry her off” from Dmitri. Until very recently the idea had struck Alyosha as monstrous, though it troubled him badly. He loved both his brothers, and he dreaded a rivalry between them. And only the day before, Dmitri had said straight out that he was glad Ivan was his rival, and that it was a great help to him, Dmitri. How was it a help? Toward marrying Grushenka? But Alyosha thought that the worst thing that could happen. There was more. Until the evening before, Alyosha had taken it for granted that Katerina Ivanovna loved Dmitri with a steady, passionate love. But he had believed it only until the evening before. He had also supposed that she could never love a man like Ivan, that she loved Dmitri, and loved him exactly as he was, however strange such a passion might be.

But during yesterday’s scene with Grushenka another thought had struck him. The word “lacerating,” which Madame Hohlakov had just used, nearly made him start. Half awake toward dawn that night, he had cried out “Laceration, laceration,” most likely about his dream. He had dreamed all night about the previous day’s scene at Katerina Ivanovna’s. Now Madame Hohlakov’s blunt, insistent claim impressed him: Katerina Ivanovna was in love with Ivan, and was only fooling herself with a pose, out of “self-laceration.” She tormented herself with a pretended love for Dmitri, out of some imagined duty of gratitude. “Yes,” he thought, “perhaps the whole truth is in those words.” But if so, where did that leave Ivan? Alyosha sensed that a character like Katerina Ivanovna’s had to rule, and that she could rule only a man like Dmitri, never a man like Ivan. Dmitri might in the end give in to her rule “to his own happiness” (which was just what Alyosha wished for). But Ivan—no, Ivan could not give in to her, and giving in would not make him happy. Alyosha could not help believing that about Ivan. All these doubts and reflections flitted through his mind as he came into the drawing-room. And another thought pressed itself on him: “What if she loved neither of them—neither Ivan nor Dmitri?”

It should be said that Alyosha felt almost ashamed of these thoughts, and blamed himself whenever they kept coming back during the past month. “What do I know about love and women, and how can I settle such questions?” he would think reproachfully, after such doubts and guesses. And yet he could not help thinking about it. He sensed that this rivalry mattered enormously in his brothers’ lives and that a great deal hung on it.

“One reptile will devour the other,” Ivan had said the day before, speaking angrily of their father and Dmitri. So Ivan saw Dmitri as a reptile, and perhaps had for a long time. Perhaps ever since he had known Katerina Ivanovna? Of course, the phrase had slipped out of Ivan yesterday without his meaning it, but that only made it more important. If he felt that way, what hope was there of peace? Were there not, rather, fresh grounds for hatred and hostility in their family? And whose side was Alyosha to take? And what was he to wish for each of them? He loved them both. But what could he wish for either one, with their interests clashing like this? He could lose his way completely in this maze, and Alyosha’s heart could not stand uncertainty, because his love was always active. He could not love passively. When he loved someone, he set to work at once to help him. To do that, he had to know what he was aiming at. He had to know for certain what was best for each of them, and once he knew, it came naturally to him to help them both. But instead of a clear aim, he found only uncertainty and confusion on every side. “It was lacerating,” as had just been said. But what could he make of even this “laceration”? He could not understand the first word of this baffling maze.

When she saw Alyosha, Katerina Ivanovna said quickly and happily to Ivan, who was already on his feet to leave, “One minute! Stay just one more minute! I want to hear what this person here thinks. I trust him completely. Don’t go,” she added, to Madame Hohlakov. She made Alyosha sit down beside her, while Madame Hohlakov sat across from them, next to Ivan.

“You are all my friends here, all I have in the world, my dear friends,” she began warmly, her voice trembling with real tears of suffering. Alyosha’s heart went out to her at once. “Alexey Fyodorovitch, you saw that abominable scene yesterday, and you saw what I did. You didn’t see it, Ivan Fyodorovitch, but he did. What he thought of me yesterday, I don’t know. I know only this: if it happened again today, this very minute, I would show the same feelings as yesterday—the same feelings, the same words, the same actions. You remember what I did, Alexey Fyodorovitch. You held me back from one thing” ... (as she said that, she flushed and her eyes shone). “I have to tell you, I can’t get over it. Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I don’t even know whether I still love _him_. I feel _pity_ for him, and that is a poor sign of love. If I loved him, if I still loved him, maybe I wouldn’t pity him now. I would hate him.”
Her voice trembled, and tears glittered on her lashes. Alyosha shuddered inside. “This girl is honest and sincere,” he thought, “and she doesn’t love Dmitri any more.”
“That’s true, that’s true,” cried Madame Hohlakov.

“Wait, dear. I haven’t yet told you the main thing, the final decision I reached during the night. I feel that my decision may be a terrible one—for me. But I can see that nothing will make me change it—nothing. It will be so all my life. My dear, kind, ever-faithful, generous adviser, the one friend I have in the world, Ivan Fyodorovitch, who sees so deep into the heart, approves my decision and praises it. He knows what it is.”
“Yes, I approve of it,” Ivan agreed, in a quiet but firm voice.

“But I would like Alyosha, too, to tell me (Ah! Alexey Fyodorovitch, forgive me for calling you just Alyosha), I would like Alexey Fyodorovitch, too, to tell me in front of my two friends whether I am right. I feel instinctively that you, Alyosha, my dear brother (for you are a dear brother to me),” she said again, in a rapture, taking his cold hand in her hot one, “I can see that your verdict, your approval, will give me peace in spite of all my suffering. After your words, I will be calm and I will submit—I feel it.”

“I don’t know what you’re asking of me,” said Alyosha, blushing. “All I know is that I love you, and right now I want your happiness more than my own!... But I know nothing about such things,” something made him add in a rush.

“In such things, Alexey Fyodorovitch, in such things, what counts most is honor and duty and something higher—I don’t know what—maybe even higher than duty. I feel this irresistible feeling in my heart, and it drives me on irresistibly. But it can all be said in two words. I have already decided. Even if he marries that—creature,” she began solemnly, “whom I never, never can forgive, _even then I will not abandon him_. From now on I will never, never abandon him!” she cried, breaking into a kind of pale, hysterical ecstasy. “Not that I would chase after him all the time, or get in his way and plague him. Oh, no! I will go away to another town—wherever you like—but I will watch over him all my life—I will watch over him all my life, without ever stopping. When he becomes unhappy with that woman, and that is bound to happen very soon, let him come to me. He will find a friend, a sister.... Only a sister, of course, and so for ever. But at least he will learn that this sister really is his sister, who loves him and has given up her whole life for him. I will get my way. I will make him know me and trust me completely, holding nothing back,” she cried, in a kind of frenzy. “I will be a god for him to pray to—and that, at least, he owes me, for his treachery and for what I suffered yesterday because of him. And let him see that all my life I will be true to him and to the promise I made him, even though he was untrue and betrayed me. I will—I will turn myself into nothing but a means to his happiness, or—how can I put it?—an instrument, a machine for his happiness, and that for my whole life, my whole life, and let him see that all his life! That is my decision. Ivan Fyodorovitch fully approves.”

She was out of breath. Perhaps she had meant to put her idea with more dignity, more art and more naturalness, but her speech came out too hurried and crude. It was full of youthful impulse. It showed that she was still smarting from yesterday’s insult, and that her pride wanted satisfaction. She felt this herself. Her face suddenly darkened, and an ugly look came into her eyes. Alyosha saw it at once and felt a pang of sympathy. His brother Ivan made things worse by adding:

“I have only given my own view,” he said. “From anyone else this would seem put on and overwrought. From you it does not. Any other woman would be wrong, but you are right. I can’t explain it, but I see that you are completely genuine, and therefore you are right.”
“But that’s only for the moment. And what is this moment worth? Nothing but yesterday’s insult.” Madame Hohlakov plainly had not meant to meddle, but she could not hold back this very fair remark.

“Quite so, quite so,” cried Ivan, with odd eagerness, clearly annoyed at the interruption. “In anyone else this moment would come only from yesterday’s impression and would be only a moment. But with Katerina Ivanovna’s character, that moment will last her whole life. What would be a mere promise for anyone else is for her a lifelong duty. It is heavy, perhaps grim, but it will never let up. And she will be held up by the feeling that she is fulfilling it. Katerina Ivanovna, from now on your life will be spent in painful brooding over your own feelings, your own heroism, your own suffering. But in the end that suffering will soften, and turn into a sweet contemplation of a bold and proud design carried out. Yes, proud it certainly is, and desperate in any case, but a triumph for you. And knowing that will at last be a source of complete satisfaction, and will make you resigned to everything else.”
This was said unmistakably with some malice, and clearly on purpose. Perhaps he did not even want to hide that he was being ironical and meant it so.
“Oh dear, it’s all so mistaken!” Madame Hohlakov cried again.
“Alexey Fyodorovitch, you speak. I am dying to know what you will say!” cried Katerina Ivanovna, and burst into tears. Alyosha got up from the sofa.

“It’s nothing, nothing!” she went on through her tears. “I’m upset, I didn’t sleep last night. But with two such friends beside me as you and your brother, I still feel strong—for I know—you two will never desert me.”
“Unfortunately I have to go back to Moscow—maybe tomorrow—and leave you for a long time—And unfortunately, there is no avoiding it,” Ivan said suddenly.

“Tomorrow—to Moscow!” Her face twisted suddenly. “But—but, good heavens, how lucky!” she cried, in a voice that had suddenly changed. In an instant there was no trace of her tears. She was transformed in a moment, and it astonished Alyosha. Instead of a poor, insulted girl, weeping in a kind of “laceration,” he saw a woman fully in command of herself, and even extremely pleased, as if something delightful had just happened.

“Oh, not lucky that I’m losing you, of course not,” she corrected herself suddenly, with a charming society smile. “A friend like you could never think that. I am only too unhappy to lose you.” She rushed impulsively up to Ivan, seized both his hands and pressed them warmly. “What is lucky is that in Moscow you will be able to see auntie and Agafya and tell them all the horror of my situation now. You can speak with complete openness to Agafya, but go easy on dear auntie. You will know how. You can’t think how miserable I was yesterday and this morning, wondering how I could write them that dreadful letter—for one can never tell such things in a letter.... Now it will be easy for me to write, because you will see them and explain everything. Oh, how glad I am! But I am glad only of that, believe me. Of course, no one can take your place.... I will run and write the letter right now,” she finished suddenly, and took a step as though to leave the room.
“And Alyosha? What about his opinion, the one you were so desperate to hear?” cried Madame Hohlakov. Her voice was sarcastic and angry.

“I haven’t forgotten it,” cried Katerina Ivanovna, stopping short. “Why must you be so hostile at a moment like this?” she added, with warm and bitter reproach. “What I said, I say again. I have to have his opinion. More than that, I have to have his decision! Whatever he says is what will be done. You can see how I long to hear you, Alexey Fyodorovitch.... But what’s the matter?”
“I wouldn’t have believed it. I just don’t understand it!” Alyosha cried suddenly, in distress.
“What? What?”

“He’s going to Moscow, and you cry out that you’re glad. You said it on purpose! Then you start explaining that you’re not glad about that, only sorry—sorry to be losing a friend. But that was acting too—you were playing a part—as if you were on a stage!”
“On a stage? What? What are you saying?” exclaimed Katerina Ivanovna, deeply astonished, flushing crimson and frowning.
“You tell him you’re sorry to lose a friend, and yet you keep telling him to his face how lucky it is that he’s leaving,” said Alyosha breathlessly. He was standing at the table and had not sat down.
“What are you talking about? I don’t understand.”

“I don’t understand it myself.... It was as if I saw something in a flash ... I know I’m not saying it right, but I’ll say it anyway,” Alyosha went on in the same shaking, broken voice. “What I see is that maybe you don’t love Dmitri at all ... and never have, right from the start.... And Dmitri has never loved you either ... he only respects you.... I truly don’t know how I dare say all this, but somebody has to tell the truth ... because nobody here will.”
“What truth?” cried Katerina Ivanovna, with a hysterical edge in her voice.

“I’ll tell you,” Alyosha went on, in desperate haste, as if he were leaping off a rooftop. “Call Dmitri; I’ll go and get him—let him come here, take your hand, take Ivan’s, and join your hands together. Because you’re torturing Ivan, simply because you love him—and you torture him because you love Dmitri out of ‘self-laceration’—with an unreal love—because you’ve talked yourself into it.”
Alyosha stopped short and said nothing more.
“You ... you ... you’re a little religious idiot—that’s what you are!” Katerina Ivanovna snapped. Her face had gone white, and her lips shook with anger.
Ivan suddenly laughed and got to his feet. His hat was in his hand.

“You’re wrong, my good Alyosha,” he said, with a look on his face that Alyosha had never seen there—a look of youthful sincerity and strong, openly frank feeling. “Katerina Ivanovna has never cared for me! All along she has known that I cared for her—though I never said one word to her about my love—she knew, but she didn’t care for me. And I was never her friend either, not for a moment; she’s too proud to need my friendship. She kept me beside her as a means of revenge. Through me, and against me, she paid back every insult she has had from Dmitri since the day they met. Even that first meeting has festered in her heart as an insult—that’s the kind of heart she has! She has talked to me about nothing but her love for him. I’m going now; but believe me, Katerina Ivanovna, you really do love him. And the more he insults you, the more you love him—that’s your ‘laceration.’ You love him as he is; you love him for insulting you. If he reformed, you’d drop him at once and stop loving him. But you need him, so that you can go on admiring your own heroic faithfulness and reproaching him for his unfaithfulness. And all of it comes from pride. Oh, there’s plenty of humiliation and self-abasement in it, but it all comes from pride.... I’m too young, and I’ve loved you too much. I know I shouldn’t say this; it would be more dignified of me just to leave, and less insulting to you. But I’m going far away, and I’ll never come back.... It’s for ever. I don’t want to sit beside a ‘laceration.’... But I don’t know how to speak now. I’ve said everything.... Good-by, Katerina Ivanovna; you can’t be angry with me, since I’m punished a hundred times worse than you, if only because I’ll never see you again. Good-by! I don’t want your hand. You’ve tortured me too deliberately for me to forgive you at this moment. I’ll forgive you later, but right now I don’t want your hand. ‘Den Dank, Dame, begehr ich nicht,’” he added, with a forced smile, showing, however, that he could read Schiller, and had read him till he knew him by heart—which Alyosha would never have believed. He walked out without saying good-by even to his hostess, Madame Hohlakov. Alyosha clasped his hands.

“Ivan!” he cried desperately after him. “Come back, Ivan! No, nothing will bring him back now!” he cried again, realizing it with regret. “But it’s my fault, my fault! I started it! Ivan spoke in anger, and he was wrong. Unfair, and angry. He has to come back, he has to come back here,” Alyosha kept exclaiming, beside himself.
Katerina Ivanovna suddenly went off into the next room.
“You haven’t done any harm. You were wonderful, like an angel,” Madame Hohlakov whispered quickly and ecstatically to Alyosha. “I’ll do all I can to keep Ivan Fyodorovitch from leaving.”
Her face was shining with delight, which distressed Alyosha greatly, but Katerina Ivanovna suddenly came back. She had two hundred-rouble notes in her hand.

“I have a great favor to ask you, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she began, speaking to Alyosha in a voice that sounded calm and even, as though nothing had happened. “A week ago—yes, I think it was a week—Dmitri Fyodorovitch did something hasty and unjust—something very ugly. There’s a low tavern here, and in it he came across that discharged officer, that captain, whom your father used to employ in some business. Dmitri Fyodorovitch lost his temper with this captain over something, grabbed him by the beard and dragged him out into the street, and for some distance along it, in that insulting way. And I’m told that the captain’s son, a boy, hardly more than a child, who goes to school here, saw it and ran along beside them crying and begging for his father, appealing to everyone to defend him, while everyone laughed. You must forgive me, Alexey Fyodorovitch, but I can’t think of that disgraceful act of _his_ without indignation ... one of those acts only Dmitri Fyodorovitch could commit in his anger ... and in his passions! I can’t even describe it.... I can’t find the words. I’ve asked about his victim, and I find he’s a very poor man. His name is Snegiryov. He did something wrong in the army and was discharged. I can’t tell you what. Now he has sunk into terrible poverty, with his family—an unhappy family of sick children and, I believe, an insane wife. He has lived here a long time; he used to work as a copying clerk, but now he gets no work at all. I thought that if you ... that is, I thought ... I don’t know. I’m so muddled. You see, I wanted to ask you, my dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, to go to him, to find some excuse to call on them—I mean on that captain—oh, goodness, how badly I explain it!—and gently, carefully, the way only you can” (Alyosha blushed), “to manage to give him this help, these two hundred roubles. He’ll be sure to take it.... I mean, persuade him to take it.... Or rather, what do I mean? You see, it’s not meant as payment to stop him from going to law (because I believe he meant to), but simply as a sign of sympathy, a wish to help him, from me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch’s betrothed, not from himself.... But you understand.... I’d go myself, but you’ll do it so much better. He lives in Lake Street, in the house of a woman called Kalmikov.... For God’s sake, Alexey Fyodorovitch, do this for me, and now ... now I’m rather ... tired. Good-by!”

She turned and vanished behind the portière so fast that Alyosha had no time to say a word, though he wanted to. He longed to beg her pardon, to blame himself, to say something, for his heart was full and he couldn’t bear to leave the room without saying it. But Madame Hohlakov took him by the hand and led him away with her. In the hall she stopped him again, as before.

“She’s proud, she’s fighting with herself; but she’s kind, charming, generous,” she exclaimed in a half-whisper. “Oh, how I love her, especially at times, and how glad I am about everything again! Dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, you didn’t know, but I must tell you, that all of us, all—her two aunts, I, everyone, even Lise—have for the last month been hoping and praying for one thing only: that she would give up your favorite Dmitri, who pays her no attention and doesn’t care for her, and marry Ivan Fyodorovitch—such an excellent, cultivated young man, who loves her more than anything in the world. We’re in a regular plot to bring it about, and I’m even staying on here, maybe, for that very reason.”
“But she was crying—she’s been hurt again,” cried Alyosha.
“Don’t ever trust a woman’s tears, Alexey Fyodorovitch. In cases like this I’m never for the women. I’m always on the men’s side.”
“Mamma, you’re spoiling him,” Lise’s little voice called from behind the door.
“No, it was all my fault. I’m horribly to blame,” Alyosha repeated, inconsolable, hiding his face in his hands in an agony of remorse for his thoughtlessness.
“Not at all, quite the reverse; you were an angel, an angel. I’m ready to say so a thousand times over.”
“Mamma, how was he an angel?” Lise’s voice was heard again.
“I got the idea all at once,” Alyosha went on, as though he hadn’t heard Lise, “that she loved Ivan, and so I said that stupid thing.... What will happen now?”
“To who, to who?” cried Lise. “Mamma, you really want to kill me. I’m asking you and you won’t answer.”
Just then the maid ran in.
“Katerina Ivanovna is ill.... She’s crying, struggling ... hysterics.”
“What is it?” cried Lise, in a tone of real alarm. “Mamma, I’ll be the one having hysterics, not her!”

“Lise, for mercy’s sake, don’t scream, don’t hound me. At your age you can’t know everything grown-up people know. I’ll come and tell you whatever you ought to know. Oh, mercy on us! I’m coming, I’m coming.... Hysterics is a good sign, Alexey Fyodorovitch; it’s excellent that she’s hysterical. That’s exactly as it should be. In cases like this I’m always against the woman, against all these feminine tears and hysterics. Run and tell her, Yulia, that I’ll fly to her. As for Ivan Fyodorovitch leaving like that, it’s her own fault. But he won’t leave. Lise, for mercy’s sake, don’t scream! Oh, yes; you’re not screaming. It’s I who am screaming. Forgive your mamma; but I’m delighted, delighted, delighted! Did you notice, Alexey Fyodorovitch, how young, how young Ivan Fyodorovitch looked just now when he went out, when he said all that and went out? I thought he was so learned, such a _savant_, and all of a sudden he was so warm, so open and youthful, with such youthful inexperience, and it was all so fine, just like you.... And the way he recited that German verse, it was exactly like you! But I must fly, I must fly! Alexey Fyodorovitch, hurry and do what she asked, and then hurry back. Lise, do you want anything now? For mercy’s sake, don’t keep Alexey Fyodorovitch even a minute. He’ll come straight back to you.”
Madame Hohlakov finally ran off. Before leaving, Alyosha was about to open the door to see Lise.
“Don’t you dare,” cried Lise. “Not now, not on any account. Talk through the door. How did you come to be an angel? That’s the one thing I want to know.”
“For a terrible piece of stupidity, Lise! Good-by!”
“Don’t you dare leave like that!” Lise began.
“Lise, I have a real sorrow! I’ll be back in a moment, but I have a great, great sorrow!”
And he ran out of the room.

chapters.title: VI. A Laceration In The Cottage
paragraphs: He was truly distressed, as he seldom had been before. He had rushed in like a fool, and meddled in what? A love affair. “But what do I know about it? What can I tell about such things?” he said to himself for the hundredth time, flushing crimson. “Oh, feeling ashamed would be nothing; shame is only the punishment I deserve. The trouble is that I’ve surely caused more unhappiness.... And Father Zossima sent me to reconcile them and bring them together. Is this how you bring them together?” Then he suddenly remembered how he had tried to join their hands, and felt dreadfully ashamed all over again. “I acted quite sincerely, but I’ll have to be more sensible from now on,” he concluded suddenly, and he didn’t even smile at his own conclusion.

Katerina Ivanovna’s errand took him to Lake Street, and his brother Dmitri lived close by, in a side street off it. Alyosha decided to go to Dmitri in any case before seeing the captain, though he felt sure he wouldn’t find him. He suspected that Dmitri would purposely avoid him now, but he had to find him anyhow. Time was passing. Ever since he left the monastery, the thought of his dying elder had not left him for a single minute.

One thing about Katerina Ivanovna’s errand interested him especially. When she spoke of the captain’s son, the little schoolboy who had run beside his father crying, Alyosha had at once been struck by the idea that this must be the schoolboy who had bitten his finger when he, Alyosha, asked what he had done to hurt him. Now Alyosha felt almost sure of it, though he couldn’t have said why. Turning his mind to something else was a relief, and he resolved to stop dwelling on the “mischief” he had done and not to torture himself with remorse, but to do what he had to do, whatever came of it. That thought comforted him completely. Turning into the street where Dmitri lodged, he felt hungry, so he took the roll he had brought from his father’s out of his pocket and ate it. It made him feel stronger.

Dmitri was not at home. The people of the house, an old cabinet-maker, his son and his old wife, eyed Alyosha with downright suspicion. “He hasn’t slept here these last three nights. He may have gone away,” the old man said, in answer to Alyosha’s repeated questions. Alyosha could tell that he was answering on orders. When he asked whether Dmitri might be at Grushenka’s, or hiding at Foma’s (Alyosha spoke so openly on purpose), all three looked at him in alarm. “They’re fond of him, they’re doing their best for him,” thought Alyosha. “That’s good.”

At last he found the house in Lake Street. It was a rickety little house, sagging on one side, with three windows facing the street and a muddy yard, where a lone cow stood in the middle. He crossed the yard and found the door that led into the passage. To the left of the passage lived the old woman of the house and her old daughter. Both seemed to be deaf. He asked for the captain over and over, until one of them finally grasped that he wanted their lodgers, and pointed to a door across the passage. The captain’s lodging turned out to be a plain peasant’s room. Alyosha had his hand on the iron latch when the strange silence inside struck him. Yet he knew from Katerina Ivanovna’s words that the man had a family. “Either they’re all asleep, or maybe they heard me coming and are waiting for me to open the door. I’d better knock first,” he thought, and knocked. An answer came, but not right away, after a gap of perhaps ten seconds.
“Who is it?” somebody shouted, in a loud and very angry voice.

Then Alyosha opened the door and stepped over the threshold. He found himself in a regular peasant’s room. It was large, but it was crammed with household belongings of every kind, and there were several people in it. On the left stood a big Russian stove. A string ran from the stove across the room to the window on the left, with rags hanging on it. Against the wall on each side, right and left, stood a bedstead covered with knitted quilts. On the left-hand one was a pyramid of four print-covered pillows, each smaller than the one below it. On the other there was just one very small pillow. The corner opposite was screened off by a curtain, or a sheet hung on a string. Behind the curtain you could see a bed made up on a bench, and a chair. The rough square table of plain wood had been pushed up to the middle window. The three windows, each made of four tiny greenish, mildewed panes, gave little light and were shut tight, so the room was rather dark and stuffy. On the table stood a frying pan with the remains of some fried eggs, a half-eaten piece of bread, and a small bottle with a few drops of vodka.

A genteel-looking woman in a cotton gown sat on a chair by the bed on the left. Her face was thin and yellow, and her sunken cheeks told you at first glance that she was ill. But what struck Alyosha most was the look in the poor woman’s eyes—a look of surprised inquiry and yet of haughty pride. And all the while he was talking to her husband, her big brown eyes moved from one speaker to the other with the same haughty, questioning look. Beside her at the window stood a young girl, rather plain, with thin reddish hair, poorly but very neatly dressed. She gave Alyosha a disdainful look as he came in. By the other bed sat another female figure. She was a very sad sight, a girl of about twenty, hunchbacked and crippled, “with withered legs,” as Alyosha was told afterwards. Her crutches stood in the corner close by. This poor girl’s strikingly beautiful, gentle eyes rested on Alyosha with mild serenity. At the table sat a man of forty-five, finishing the fried eggs. He was lean, small and weakly built. He had reddish hair and a thin, light-colored beard, very like a wisp of tow (this comparison and the phrase “a wisp of tow” flashed into Alyosha’s mind at once, for some reason, and he remembered it afterwards). Clearly this was the gentleman who had shouted, since there was no other man in the room. But when Alyosha came in, he jumped up from the bench he was sitting on and, hastily wiping his mouth with a ragged napkin, darted over to Alyosha.
“It’s a monk come begging for the monastery. A fine place to come to!” said the girl standing in the left corner, loudly. The man spun round to her at once and answered in an excited, cracking voice:
“No, Varvara, you’re mistaken. Allow me to ask,” he turned to Alyosha again, “what brings you to—our retreat?”

Alyosha studied him closely. It was the first time he had seen him. There was something angular, flustered and touchy about him. He had clearly been drinking, but he was not drunk. His look was extraordinarily impudent, and yet, strange to say, frightened at the same time. He looked like a man who had been kept down for a long time and had put up with it, and who had now suddenly turned and was trying to stand up for himself. Or, better still, like a man who badly wants to hit you but is terribly afraid you’ll hit him. His words and the tone of his shrill voice had a kind of crazy humor, now spiteful and now cringing, and always shifting from one note to the other. He had asked his question about “our retreat” trembling all over, rolling his eyes, and hopping up so close to Alyosha that Alyosha instinctively stepped back. He wore a very shabby dark cotton coat, patched and stained. His checked trousers were of an extremely pale color, long out of fashion, and made of very thin cloth. They were so crumpled and so short that he looked like a boy who had outgrown them.
“I’m Alexey Karamazov,” Alyosha began, in reply.
“I know that perfectly well, sir,” the gentleman snapped out at once, to make clear that he already knew who he was. “I am Captain Snegiryov, sir, but I still want to know exactly what has led you—”
“Oh, I’ve come about nothing in particular. I wanted a word with you—if you’ll let me.”

“In that case, here’s a chair, sir; kindly be seated. That’s what they used to say in the old comedies, ‘kindly be seated,’” and with a quick motion he grabbed an empty chair (a rough wooden one, not upholstered) and put it for him almost in the middle of the room. Then he took another just like it for himself and sat down facing Alyosha, so close that their knees nearly touched.

“Nikolay Ilyitch Snegiryov, sir, formerly a captain in the Russian infantry, disgraced by his vices, but still a captain. Though I may not be one anymore, going by the way I talk. For the second half of my life I’ve been learning to say ‘sir.’ It’s a word you use once you’ve come down in the world.”
“That’s very true,” smiled Alyosha. “But does it slip out on its own, or do you use it on purpose?”

“As God’s my witness, it just comes out! I never used to say it. All my life I said ‘sir’ to nobody. Then the moment I sank into low water, I started saying ‘sir.’ Some higher power did that. I can see you’re interested in the questions of the day. But how could I possibly have roused your curiosity, living as I do where there’s no room for hospitality at all?”
“I’ve come—about that business.”
“What business?” the captain cut in impatiently.
“About what happened between you and my brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Alyosha blurted out clumsily.

“What happened, sir? Surely not that? Is it my ‘wisp of tow’ you mean?” He leaned in so close that his knees actually knocked against Alyosha’s. His lips were pressed into a strange, thin line, like a thread.
“What wisp of tow?” Alyosha muttered.

“He’s come to complain about me, Father!” cried a voice Alyosha knew, the schoolboy’s, from behind the curtain. “I bit his finger just now.” The curtain was pulled back, and Alyosha saw the boy who had attacked him, lying on a little bed made up from the bench and a chair in the corner under the ikons. He lay under his coat and an old quilted blanket. He was clearly ill, and from the glitter in his eyes he had a fever. He looked at Alyosha without any fear, as if he knew he was at home and nobody could touch him.
“What! He bit your finger?” The captain leaped from his chair. “It was your finger he bit?”

“Yes. He was throwing stones with some other schoolboys, six of them against him alone. I walked up to him, and he threw a stone at me, then another one at my head. I asked him what I’d ever done to him. Then he rushed me and bit my finger badly. I don’t know why.”
“I’ll thrash him, sir, this very minute!” The captain sprang up again.
“But I’m not complaining at all, I’m only telling you ... I don’t want him thrashed. Besides, he looks ill.”

“And you think I’d thrash him? That I’d take my Ilusha and thrash him right in front of you, to give you satisfaction? Would you like it done now, sir?” said the captain, suddenly rounding on Alyosha as if he meant to fly at him. “I’m sorry about your finger, sir. But instead of thrashing Ilusha, would you rather I chopped off my own four fingers with this knife, here, before your eyes, to satisfy your just anger? Four fingers, I’d think, should be enough to slake your thirst for revenge. You won’t be asking for the fifth as well?” He broke off, his voice catching in his throat. Every feature of his face was twitching and working, and he looked wildly defiant. He was in a kind of frenzy.

“I think I see it all now,” said Alyosha, gently and sadly, still sitting where he was. “So your boy is a good boy. He loves his father, and he went for me because I’m the brother of the man who wronged you.... Now I see,” he repeated thoughtfully. “My brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch is sorry for what he did, I know that. If he can possibly come to you—or better still, meet you at the very same place—he’ll ask your forgiveness in front of everyone, if you want him to.”
“After he’s pulled out my beard, you mean, he’ll ask my forgiveness? And he thinks that will wrap it up nicely, does he?”
“Oh, no! Quite the opposite. He’ll do whatever you like, and however you like.”
“So if I were to ask his highness to go down on his knees before me in that very tavern—‘The Metropolis,’ it’s called—or in the marketplace, he’d do it?”
“Yes, he would even go down on his knees.”

“You’ve pierced me to the heart, sir. You’ve brought me to tears, and pierced me to the heart! I’m only too well aware of your brother’s generosity. Let me introduce my family: my two daughters and my son—my litter. If I die, who’ll look after them? And as long as I live, who but them will care about a wretch like me? That’s a great thing the Lord has arranged for every man of my sort, sir. Because there has to be someone who can love even a man like me.”
“Ah, that’s perfectly true!” exclaimed Alyosha.
“Oh, stop playing the fool! Some idiot walks in, and you put us to shame!” cried the girl by the window, suddenly turning to her father with a scornful, contemptuous look.
“Wait a bit, Varvara!” her father cried sharply, though he looked at her quite approvingly. “That’s her character,” he told Alyosha again.
“And in all nature there was naught That could find favor in his eyes—

or rather, to put it in the feminine, that could find favor in her eyes. But now let me present you to my wife, Arina Petrovna. She’s a cripple, forty-three years old; she can move, but only a very little. She comes of humble people. Arina Petrovna, compose your face. This is Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov. Get up, Alexey Fyodorovitch.” He took him by the hand and, with surprising strength, hauled him to his feet. “You have to stand to be introduced to a lady. This isn’t the Karamazov, mamma, who ... h’m ... et cetera, but his brother, radiant with modest virtues. Come now, Arina Petrovna, come, mamma, first, your hand to be kissed.”

And he kissed his wife’s hand with respect, even tenderness. The girl at the window turned her back on it all in disgust. Over the proud, questioning face of the woman came a look of extraordinary warmth.
“Good morning! Sit down, Mr. Tchernomazov,” she said.
“Karamazov, mamma, Karamazov. We come of humble people,” he whispered again.

“Well, Karamazov, or whatever it is, I always think of Tchernomazov.... Sit down. Why did he haul you up? He calls me a cripple, but I’m not. It’s just that my legs are swollen like barrels, and the rest of me has shriveled up. I used to be so fat, and now it’s as if I’d swallowed a needle.”
“We come of humble people,” the captain muttered again.
“Oh, Father, Father!” said the hunchback girl, who until then had sat silent on her chair, and she hid her eyes in her handkerchief.
“Buffoon!” the girl at the window burst out.

“Have you heard our news?” said the mother, pointing at her daughters. “It’s like clouds rolling in; the clouds pass and we have music again. When we were with the army, we had plenty of guests like this. I’m not comparing anyone, mind; each to their own taste. The deacon’s wife used to come then and say, ‘Alexandr Alexandrovitch is a man with the noblest heart, but Nastasya Petrovna,’ she’d say, ‘is a child of hell.’ ‘Well,’ I said, ‘that’s a matter of taste, but you’re a little spitfire.’ ‘And you need putting in your place,’ says she. ‘You black sword,’ said I, ‘who asked you to teach me?’ ‘But my breath,’ says she, ‘is clean, and yours is foul.’ ‘Go and ask all the officers if my breath is foul.’ And I’ve had it on my mind ever since. Just the other day I was sitting here, just as I am now, when I saw that same general walk in, the one who came here at Easter, and I asked him: ‘Your Excellency,’ said I, ‘can a lady’s breath be unpleasant?’ ‘Yes,’ he answered; ‘you ought to open a window-pane or the door, because the air in here isn’t fresh.’ That’s how they all carry on! And what is my breath to them? The dead smell worse! ‘I won’t spoil the air,’ said I, ‘I’ll order some slippers and be off.’ My darlings, don’t blame your own mother! Nikolay Ilyitch, why can’t I please you? Only Ilusha comes home from school and loves me. Yesterday he brought me an apple. Forgive your own mother—forgive a poor lonely creature! Why has my breath become so unpleasant to you?”
And the poor mad woman broke down in sobs, with tears running down her cheeks. The captain ran over to her.

“Mamma, mamma, my dear, don’t, don’t! You’re not lonely. Everyone loves you, everyone adores you.” He began kissing both her hands again and tenderly stroking her face. Then he took the dinner napkin and started wiping away her tears. Alyosha thought there were tears in his eyes too. “There, you see? You hear?” he said, wheeling on Alyosha in a sort of fury and pointing at the poor imbecile.
“I see and I hear,” muttered Alyosha.
“Father, Father, how can you—with him! Leave him be!” cried the boy, sitting up in bed and staring at his father with blazing eyes.
“Enough of this clowning! Enough of your silly antics that never come to anything!” shouted Varvara, stamping her foot in a passion.

“This time your anger is perfectly just, Varvara, and I’ll hurry to satisfy you. Come, Alexey Fyodorovitch, put on your cap, and I’ll put on mine. We’ll go out. I have something serious to say to you, but not inside these walls. This girl sitting here is my daughter Nina. I forgot to introduce her. She is a heavenly angel incarnate ... who has flown down among us mortals,... if you can understand.”
“Look at him, shaking all over, as though he were in convulsions!” Varvara went on indignantly.

“And she there, stamping her foot at me and calling me a fool a minute ago, she too is a heavenly angel incarnate, and she has good reason to call me one. Come along, Alexey Fyodorovitch, we have to put an end to this.”
And, seizing Alyosha’s hand, he led him out of the room and into the street.

chapters.title: VII. And In The Open Air
paragraphs: “The air out here is fresh, but in my apartment it isn’t, not in any sense of the word. Let’s take it slowly, sir. I’d be glad of your kind interest.”
“There’s something important I want to tell you too,” said Alyosha. “I just don’t know how to start.”

“Naturally you have business with me. You’d never have dropped in on me without a reason. Unless you came only to complain about the boy, and that’s hardly likely. And speaking of the boy, I couldn’t explain in there, but out here I’ll tell you how that scene went. A week ago my tow was thicker—I mean my beard. That’s the nickname they have for my beard, the schoolboys most of all. Well, your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch had me by the beard and was pulling. I’d done nothing. He was in a towering rage and I just happened to cross his path. He dragged me out of the tavern into the market-place, and right then the boys were coming out of school, Ilusha among them. The moment he saw me in that state, he ran to me. ‘Father,’ he cried, ‘father!’ He grabbed me, hugged me, tried to pull me free, and shouted at the man who was attacking me, ‘Let go, let go, it’s my father, forgive him!’—yes, he really did cry ‘forgive him.’ He seized that hand, that very hand, in his little hands and kissed it.... I remember his little face at that moment. I haven’t forgotten it and I never will!”

“I swear,” cried Alyosha, “my brother will tell you how deeply and sincerely he regrets it, even if he has to get down on his knees in that same market-place.... I’ll make him, or he’s no brother of mine!”

“Aha, so it’s only an idea of yours! It doesn’t come from him at all, just from the generosity of your own warm heart. You should have said so. Well, in that case let me tell you about your brother’s highly chivalrous, soldierly generosity, because he did show some at the time. He stopped dragging me by the beard and let me go. ‘You’re an officer,’ he said, ‘and I’m an officer. If you can find a decent man to act as your second, send me your challenge. I’ll give you satisfaction, even though you’re a scoundrel.’ That’s what he said. A chivalrous spirit indeed! I went off with Ilusha, and that scene is now a family record, printed forever on Ilusha’s soul. No, noblemen’s privileges are not for the likes of us. Judge for yourself. You’ve just been in our mansion. What did you see? Three ladies. One is a cripple and weak in the head, another is a cripple and a hunchback, and the third isn’t crippled but is far too clever. She’s a student, dying to get back to Petersburg and work for the emancipation of the Russian woman on the banks of the Neva. I won’t mention Ilusha; he’s only nine. I’m alone in the world, and if I die, what becomes of them all? That’s all I ask you. And suppose I challenge him and he kills me on the spot. Then what? What becomes of them? Or worse, suppose he doesn’t kill me but only maims me. I couldn’t work, yet I’d still be a mouth to feed. Who would feed me, and who would feed them all? Should I take Ilusha out of school and send him begging in the streets? That’s what it means for me to challenge him to a duel. It’s silly talk, nothing more.”
“He will beg your forgiveness. He will bow down at your feet in the middle of the market-place,” cried Alyosha again, his eyes glowing.

“I did think of taking him to court,” the captain went on, “but look in our legal code. Could I get much compensation for a personal injury? And then Agrafena Alexandrovna[3] sent for me and screamed at me, ‘Don’t even dream of it! If you go after him, I’ll announce to the whole world that he beat you because you were dishonest, and then you’ll be the one prosecuted.’ I call God to witness whose dishonesty it was, and on whose orders I acted. Wasn’t it on her own and Fyodor Pavlovitch’s? ‘And what’s more,’ she went on, ‘I’ll dismiss you for good, and you’ll never earn another penny from me. I’ll talk to my merchant too’ (that’s what she calls her old man) ‘and he’ll dismiss you!’ And if he dismisses me, who else will pay me anything? Those two are all I have to look to. Your Fyodor Pavlovitch has not only stopped giving me work, for a different reason, but he means to use some papers I signed to sue me. So I kept quiet, and you’ve seen what our retreat looks like. But now let me ask you something. Did Ilusha hurt your finger badly? I didn’t like to bring it up in our mansion, with him there.”

“Yes, badly, and he was in a great fury. He was avenging you on me, as a Karamazov. I see that now. But if only you’d seen how he was hurling stones at his schoolmates! It’s very dangerous. They could kill him. They’re children, and stupid. A stone gets thrown and somebody’s head is broken.”
“That’s just what has happened. A stone hit him today. Not on the head but on the chest, right over the heart. He came home crying and groaning, and now he’s ill.”
“And you know, he goes after them first. He holds a grudge against them on your account. They say he stuck a penknife into a boy named Krassotkin not long ago.”
“I’ve heard about that too. It’s dangerous. Krassotkin is an official here, so we may hear more about it.”
“I’d advise you,” Alyosha went on warmly, “not to send him to school at all for a while, until he’s calmer ... and his anger has passed.”

“Anger!” the captain repeated. “That’s exactly what it is. He’s a little creature, but it’s a mighty anger. You don’t know the whole of it, sir. Let me tell you more. Ever since that day all the boys have been teasing him about the ‘wisp of tow.’ Schoolboys are a merciless race. One at a time they’re angels, but together, and especially at school, they’re often merciless. Their teasing roused a gallant spirit in Ilusha. An ordinary boy, a weak son, would have given in and felt ashamed of his father, sir. He stood up for his father against all of them. For his father, and for truth and justice. What he suffered when he kissed your brother’s hand and cried to him ‘Forgive father, forgive him’—only God knows that, and I, his father.
