Because our children—not your children, but ours, the children of poor gentlemen that everybody looks down on—know what justice means, sir, even at nine years old. How should the rich know? They never go down into such depths in their whole lives. But in the square, at the moment he kissed that hand, my Ilusha understood all that justice means. That truth went into him and crushed him for good, sir,” the captain said hotly again, in a sort of frenzy, striking his right fist against his left palm as if to show how “the truth” had crushed Ilusha. “That same day, sir, he came down with a fever and was delirious all night. All day he hardly said a word to me, but I noticed he kept watching me from his corner, though he turned to the window and pretended to be studying his lessons. I could see his mind wasn’t on them. The next day I got drunk to forget my troubles, sinful man that I am, and I don’t remember much. Mamma started crying too—I’m very fond of mamma—well, I spent my last penny drowning my troubles. Don’t despise me for it, sir. In Russia the men who drink are the best. The best men among us are the biggest drunkards. I lay down, and I remember nothing about Ilusha, though all that day the boys were jeering at him at school. ‘Wisp of tow!’ they shouted. ‘Your father got dragged out of the tavern by his wisp of tow, and you ran along and begged forgiveness.’”

“On the third day, when he came back from school, I saw he looked pale and miserable. ‘What is it?’ I asked. He wouldn’t answer. Well, there’s no talking in our mansion without mamma and the girls joining in. Besides, the girls had heard about it on the very first day. Varvara had started snarling: ‘You fools and buffoons, can you ever do anything sensible?’ ‘Quite so,’ I said, ‘can we ever do anything sensible?’ That was how I turned it aside for the moment. So in the evening I took the boy out for a walk. You should know that we walk every evening, always the same way, the way we’re going now, from our gate to that big stone lying by itself in the road under the hurdle, where the town pasture begins. A beautiful, lonely spot, sir. Ilusha and I walked along hand in hand as usual. He has a little hand, his fingers are thin and cold—he suffers with his chest, you know. ‘Father,’ he said, ‘father!’ ‘Well?’ said I. I saw his eyes flashing. ‘Father, the way he treated you!’ ‘It can’t be helped, Ilusha,’ I said. ‘Don’t forgive him, father, don’t forgive him! At school they say he paid you ten roubles for it.’ ‘No, Ilusha,’ said I, ‘I wouldn’t take money from him for anything.’ Then he started trembling all over, took my hand in both of his and kissed it again. ‘Father,’ he said, ‘father, challenge him to a duel. At school they say you’re a coward and won’t challenge him, and that you’ll take ten roubles from him.’ ‘I can’t challenge him to a duel, Ilusha,’ I answered. And I told him in a few words what I’ve just told you. He listened. ‘Father,’ he said, ‘all the same, don’t forgive it. When I’m grown up I’ll call him out myself and kill him.’ His eyes shone and blazed. And of course I’m his father, so I had to put in a word. ‘It’s a sin to kill,’ I said, ‘even in a duel.’ ‘Father,’ he said, ‘when I’m grown up I’ll knock him down, knock the sword out of his hand, fall on him, wave my sword over him and say: “I could kill you, but I forgive you, so there!”’ You see what his little mind has been working on these two days. He must have been planning that revenge all day long, and raving about it at night.

“But then he started coming home from school badly beaten. I found out about it the day before yesterday, and you’re right, I won’t send him to that school any more. I heard that he was standing up to the whole class on his own and defying them all, that his heart was full of resentment and bitterness. I was frightened for him. We went for another walk. ‘Father,’ he asked, ‘are the rich stronger than anybody else on earth?’ ‘Yes, Ilusha,’ I said, ‘nobody on earth is stronger than the rich.’ ‘Father,’ he said, ‘I’ll get rich, I’ll become an officer and conquer everybody. The Tsar will reward me, I’ll come back here, and then no one will dare—’ Then he fell silent, though his lips kept trembling. ‘Father,’ he said, ‘what a horrid town this is.’ ‘Yes, Ilusha,’ I said, ‘it’s not a very nice town.’ ‘Father, let’s move to another town, a nice one,’ he said, ‘where people don’t know about us.’ ‘We’ll move, we will, Ilusha,’ said I, ‘only I have to save up first.’ I was glad I could turn his mind from painful thoughts, and we started dreaming about how we’d move to another town, and how we’d buy a horse and cart. ‘We’ll put mamma and your sisters inside, cover them up, and we’ll go on foot. You’ll get a ride now and then, and I’ll walk beside you, because we have to look after our horse. We can’t all ride. That’s how we’ll travel.’ He was delighted, most of all by the idea of having a horse and driving it. Of course, a Russian boy is born among horses. We chattered for a long time. Thank God, I thought, I’ve distracted him and comforted him.

“That was the day before yesterday, in the evening, but last night everything changed. He’d gone to school in the morning and came home low, terribly low. In the evening I took him by the hand and we went for our walk, but he wouldn’t talk. A wind was blowing, there was no sun, it felt like autumn, and twilight was coming on. We walked along, both of us low in spirits. ‘Well, my boy,’ said I, ‘what about setting off on our travels?’ I thought I might lead him back to our talk of the day before. He didn’t answer, but I felt his fingers trembling in my hand. Ah, I thought, this is bad; something new has happened. We’d reached the stone where we are now. I sat down on the stone. And in the sky there were lots of kites flapping and spinning. As many as thirty were in sight. Of course, it’s just the season for kites. ‘Look, Ilusha,’ said I, ‘it’s time we got out last year’s kite again. I’ll mend it. Where did you put it away?’ My boy made no answer. He looked off to one side and turned away from me. And then a gust of wind blew up the sand. He suddenly fell on me, threw both his little arms around my neck and held on tight. You know how it is with children who are silent and proud and fight back their tears in great trouble: when they finally break down, the tears come in streams. With those warm streams of tears he suddenly wet my face. He sobbed and shook as if in convulsions, and pressed himself against me where I sat on the stone. ‘Father,’ he kept crying, ‘dear father, how he insulted you!’ And I sobbed too. We sat there shaking in each other’s arms. ‘Ilusha,’ I said to him, ‘Ilusha darling.’ No one saw us then. God alone saw us. I hope He will count it in my favor. You must thank your brother, Alexey Fyodorovitch. No, sir, I will not thrash my boy to please you.”

The captain had slid back into his old tone of bitter clowning. Still, Alyosha sensed that the man trusted him. Had anyone else been standing there in Alyosha’s place, he thought, the captain would never have spoken so openly or told what he had just told. That gave Alyosha courage, though his heart was close to tears.
“Oh, I would so love to be friends with your boy!” he cried. “If you could arrange it—”
“Of course, sir,” the captain muttered.

“But now hear something quite different!” Alyosha went on. “I have a message for you. My brother Dmitri has wronged his fiancée too. She is a noble-hearted girl, and you have probably heard of her. I have every right to tell you how she was wronged. In fact I ought to, because the moment she heard of the insult to you, and of your unfortunate situation, she sent me to bring you this help. That was just now. It comes from her alone. It does not come from Dmitri, who has abandoned her, or from me, his brother, or from anyone else. It is from her, only from her! She begs you to accept it.... The same man has insulted you both. She thought of you just after he had done something similar to her, similar in its cruelty, I mean. She comes as a sister to help a brother in trouble.... She told me to persuade you to take these two hundred roubles from her, as from a sister, because she knows how badly you need them. Nobody will know about it, and no one can start any unjust gossip. Here are the two hundred roubles. I swear you must take them, unless—unless all men on earth are meant to be enemies! But there are brothers even on earth.... Your heart is generous ... you must see that, you must,” and Alyosha held out two new hundred-rouble notes, the rainbow-colored kind.

The two of them stood by the great stone near the fence, and nobody was close by. The notes seemed to hit the captain with tremendous force. He started, but at first only out of astonishment. He had never imagined their talk would end like this. Help from anyone was the furthest thing from his dreams, let alone a sum like that!
He took the notes. For a minute he could hardly answer, and a completely new look came over his face.
“That’s for me? All that money, two hundred roubles! Good heavens! Why, I haven’t laid eyes on so much money for four years! Mercy on us! And she says she’s a sister.... Is that really true?”
“I swear that all I’ve told you is true,” cried Alyosha.
The captain went red in the face.

“Listen, my dear, listen. If I take it, I’m not behaving like a scoundrel? To you, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I won’t seem a scoundrel? No, Alexey Fyodorovitch, listen, listen,” he hurried on, plucking at Alyosha with both hands. “You’re talking me into taking it, saying it comes from a sister, but deep down in your heart, won’t you despise me if I take it, eh?”
“No, no! I swear on my salvation I won’t! And nobody will ever know except me, you, her, and one other lady, her great friend.”

“Forget the lady! Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch, at a moment like this you have to listen, because you can’t understand what these two hundred roubles mean to me now.” The poor man was working himself up, little by little, into a rambling, almost wild excitement. He had lost his balance, and he talked very fast, as if afraid he would be cut off before he could say everything.

“Besides its being honestly come by, from a ‘sister’ I respect and revere so highly, do you know, I can now look after mamma and Nina, my hunchback angel of a daughter? Doctor Herzenstube came to see us, out of the goodness of his heart, and spent a whole hour examining the two of them. ‘I can’t make anything of it,’ he said. But he prescribed a mineral water, sold at the chemist’s here. He said it would surely do her good, and he ordered baths as well, with some medicine in the water. The mineral water costs thirty kopecks a bottle, and she might need forty of them. So I took the prescription, put it on the shelf under the ikons, and there it lies. And for Nina he ordered hot baths, with something dissolved in them, morning and evening. But how are we to manage a cure like that in our mansion? We have no servants, no help, no bath, not even any water! Nina has rheumatism all over, I don’t think I mentioned that. At night her whole right side aches. She’s in agony, and would you believe it, the angel suffers without a groan, so as not to wake us. We eat whatever we can find, and she will take only the scraps, what you’d hardly throw to a dog. ‘I don’t deserve it, I’m taking it from you, I’m a burden to you,’ that’s what her angel eyes are trying to say. We wait on her, but she hates it. ‘I’m a useless cripple, good for nothing.’ As if she didn’t deserve it, when she is what saves all of us, with her angelic sweetness! Without her, without her gentle word, it would be hell among us! She softens even Varvara. And don’t judge Varvara harshly either. She’s an angel too, and she’s been wronged too. She came to us for the summer with sixteen roubles she had saved from giving lessons, meant for her trip back to Petersburg in September, which is now. But we took her money and lived on it, so now she has nothing to go back with. Not that she could go back anyway, since she has to slave for us here. She’s like an overworked horse with all of us riding on her back. She waits on everyone, mends, washes, sweeps the floor, puts mamma to bed. And mamma is capricious and tearful and out of her mind! But now, with this money, I can hire a servant, you understand, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I can buy medicines for the dear creatures. I can send my student to Petersburg. I can buy beef and feed them properly. Good Lord, it’s a dream!”
Alyosha was overjoyed that he had given the man such happiness, and that the poor fellow had let himself be made happy.

“Wait, Alexey Fyodorovitch, wait,” the captain broke in, talking with frenzied speed, swept off by a fresh daydream. “Do you know, Ilusha and I may actually carry out our dream. We’ll buy a horse and cart, a black horse, he insists on black, and we’ll set off just as we pretended the other day. I have an old friend, a lawyer in K. province. A man I trust told me that if I came, this friend would give me a place as a clerk in his office. Who knows, maybe he would! So I’d simply put mamma and Nina in the cart, Ilusha would drive, and I’d walk, I’d walk.... Why, if I could just collect one debt that’s owed me, I might even have enough for that!”

“You would have enough!” cried Alyosha. “Katerina Ivanovna will send you as much more as you need. And I have money too, you know. Take what you want, as from a brother, from a friend, and pay it back later.... (You’ll get rich, you’ll get rich!) And you couldn’t have a better idea than moving to another province! It would save you, and especially your boy. You ought to go soon, before winter, before the cold sets in. Write to us when you get there, and we will always be brothers.... No, it’s not a dream!”

Alyosha was so happy he could have hugged him. But he glanced at the man and stopped short. The captain stood with his neck stretched out and his lips thrust forward, his face pale and frenzied. His lips kept moving, as if he were trying to get something out. No sound came, yet they went on moving. It was eerie.
“What is it?” asked Alyosha, startled.

“Alexey Fyodorovitch ... I ... you,” the captain muttered, stumbling, staring at him with a strange, wild, fixed gaze and a look of desperate resolve. At the same time something like a grin played on his lips. “I ... you, sir ... would you like me to show you a little trick I know?” he murmured suddenly, in a firm, quick whisper, his voice no longer stumbling.
“What trick?”
“A pretty one,” the captain whispered. His mouth was twisted to the left, and his left eye was squeezed shut. He kept staring at Alyosha.
“What’s the matter? What trick?” cried Alyosha, now truly alarmed.

“Why, look!” the captain suddenly squealed. All through the conversation he had been holding the two notes by one corner between thumb and forefinger. Now he showed them to Alyosha, then crushed them savagely into a ball in his right fist. “Do you see? Do you see?” he shrieked, white and furious. And suddenly he flung up his hand and hurled the crumpled notes onto the sand. “Do you see?” he shrieked again, pointing at them. “Look at that!”
And in a wild rage he started stamping on them with his heel, panting and shouting as he did it:
“There’s your money for you! There’s your money for you! There’s your money for you! There’s your money for you!”
Then he leaped back and drew himself up in front of Alyosha, and his whole figure spoke of unspeakable pride.

“Tell the people who sent you that the wisp of tow does not sell his honor,” he cried, raising his arm in the air. Then he whirled around and began to run. But he had not gone five steps when he turned all the way back and blew a kiss to Alyosha. He ran five paces more and turned for the last time. This time his face was not twisted with laughter. It was quivering with tears. In a tearful, broken, sobbing voice he cried:
“What could I say to my boy if I took money from you to pay for our shame?”

And then he ran on without looking back. Alyosha watched him go, grieved beyond words. Oh, he saw that until the very last moment the man had not known he would crush the notes and throw them away. The captain did not turn back, and Alyosha knew he would not. He would not follow or call him back, and he knew why. When the man was out of sight, Alyosha picked up the two notes. They were badly crumpled and had been ground into the sand, but they were not torn. They even rustled like new ones when Alyosha unfolded and smoothed them out. Once he had smoothed them, he folded them, put them in his pocket, and went to Katerina Ivanovna to report on the success of her errand.

chapters.title: I. The Engagement
paragraphs: Once again Madame Hohlakov was the one who met Alyosha first. She was in a flutter, because something important had happened. Katerina Ivanovna’s hysterics had ended in a faint, and after that “a terrible, awful weakness had come over her. She lay there with her eyes rolled back, raving. Now she had a fever. They’d sent for Herzenstube and for the aunts. The aunts had already arrived, but there was no sign of Herzenstube yet. They were all sitting in her room, waiting. She was unconscious at the moment, and what if it turned into brain fever!”

Madame Hohlakov looked truly frightened. “This is serious, serious,” she kept repeating, every few words, as if nothing that had ever happened to her before had been serious. Alyosha listened unhappily and started to tell her what he had been through, but she cut him off after the first few words. She had no time to listen. She begged him to go and sit with Lise and wait there for her.

“Lise,” she whispered, almost into his ear, “Lise has given me a real surprise just now, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch. She touched me, too, so my heart forgives her everything. Imagine, the moment you were gone she began to be honestly sorry that she’d laughed at you today and yesterday. She wasn’t laughing at you, mind, only joking. But she was seriously sorry, close to tears, and I was amazed. She has never been really sorry for laughing at me; she only turns it into a joke. And you know she laughs at me every minute of the day. But this time she meant it. She values your opinion very much, Alexey Fyodorovitch, so please don’t be offended or hurt by her, if you can help it. I’m never hard on her, because she’s such a clever little thing. Would you believe it? She said just now that you were a friend from her childhood, ‘the greatest friend of her childhood’—think of it—‘greatest friend’—and what am I, then? She has very strong feelings and memories, and what’s more, she has these phrases, these most unexpected words, that burst out suddenly when you least expect them. Lately she was talking about a pine tree, for instance. There used to be a pine tree in our garden when she was tiny. Very likely it’s still standing there, so there’s no need to use the past tense. Pine trees aren’t like people, Alexey Fyodorovitch; they don’t change quickly. ‘Mamma,’ she said, ‘I remember this pine tree as in a dream,’ only she put it in some way so original that I can’t repeat it. Anyway, I’ve forgotten it. Well, good-by! I’m so worried I feel I’ll lose my mind. Ah! Alexey Fyodorovitch, I’ve lost my mind twice in my life. Go to Lise and cheer her up, the way you always can, so charmingly. Lise,” she cried, going to her door, “I’ve brought you Alexey Fyodorovitch, the one you insulted so. He isn’t angry in the least, I assure you; on the contrary, he’s astonished that you could think so.”
“_Merci, maman._ Come in, Alexey Fyodorovitch.”

Alyosha went in. Lise looked a little embarrassed and instantly turned crimson. She was clearly ashamed of something. And as people always do when that happens, she launched at once into talk about other matters, as though they absorbed her entirely at that moment.

“Mamma has just told me everything about the two hundred roubles, Alexey Fyodorovitch, and how you took them to that poor officer ... and she told me the whole dreadful story of how he’d been insulted ... and you know, mamma gets things muddled ... she’s always jumping from one thing to another ... but I cried when I heard it. So, did you give him the money, and how is that poor man?”

“The fact is, I didn’t give it to him, and it’s a long story,” Alyosha answered, as if he, too, could think of nothing but how sorry he was to have failed. But Lise saw perfectly well that he was looking away, too, and that he, too, was trying to turn the talk to something else.

Alyosha sat down at the table and began his story. At the very first words, though, his embarrassment left him, and he had Lise’s full attention as well. He spoke with deep feeling, still under the force of what he had just seen, and he managed to tell it well and with all the details. Back in Moscow he had loved to come to Lise and tell her whatever had just happened to him, or what he’d been reading, or something he remembered from his childhood. Sometimes the two of them had dreamed up stories together, whole romances, usually cheerful and amusing ones. Now both of them felt themselves suddenly carried back to those days in Moscow, two years ago. Lise was deeply touched by his story. Alyosha described Ilusha warmly. When he got to the part where the unlucky man trampled on the money, Lise couldn’t help clasping her hands and crying out:
“So you didn’t give him the money! You let him run off! Oh dear, you should have gone after him!”
“No, Lise, it’s better that I didn’t go after him,” said Alyosha. He got up from his chair and walked across the room, deep in thought.
“How is that? How can it be better? Now they’ve got nothing to eat, and there’s no hope for them?”

“There is hope, because the two hundred roubles will still get to them. He’ll take the money tomorrow. He’s sure to take it tomorrow,” said Alyosha, pacing up and down, thinking it over. “You see, Lise,” he went on, stopping suddenly in front of her, “I made one blunder, but even that has turned out for the best.”
“What blunder? And why for the best?”

“I’ll tell you. He’s a weak, timid sort of man; he’s suffered so much, and he’s very kindhearted. I keep asking myself why he took offense so suddenly. Because I assure you, right up to the last minute he had no idea he was going to trample on those notes. And now I think there was a great deal to offend him ... and in his position it couldn’t have gone any other way.... For one thing, he was sore that he had been so glad of the money in front of me, and hadn’t hidden it. If he’d been pleased, but not so very pleased; if he hadn’t shown it; if he’d started making a show of scruples and difficulties, the way other people do when they take money, then he might have managed to bear taking it. But he was too honestly delighted, and that was humiliating. Ah, Lise, he’s a good, truthful man, and that’s the worst of the whole business. All the time he was talking his voice was so weak, so broken. He talked so fast, so fast, and he kept laughing such a laugh, or maybe he was crying—yes, I’m sure he was crying, he was so delighted—and he talked about his daughters, and about the post he could get in another town.... And when he’d poured out his heart, he felt ashamed of letting me see right into his soul like that. So all at once he began to hate me. He’s one of those dreadfully touchy poor people. What shamed him most, you see, was that he’d given in too soon and taken me for a friend. At first he almost flew at me and tried to scare me off, but the moment he saw the money he began hugging me; he kept putting his hands on me. That’s probably how he came to feel it was all so degrading. And then I made that blunder, a very serious one. I suddenly said that if he didn’t have enough money to move to another town, we’d give it to him, and in fact I’d give him as much as he wanted from my own pocket. That hit him all at once. Why, he thought, was I shoving myself forward to help him? You know, Lise, it’s terribly hard on a man who’s been wronged when other people look at him as if they were his benefactors.... I’ve heard that; Father Zossima told me. I don’t know how to put it, but I’ve often seen it myself. And I feel it myself, too. And the worst of it was that although he didn’t know, up to the very last minute, that he would trample on the notes, he had a sort of presentiment of it, I’m sure of that. That’s exactly what made him so ecstatic, having that presentiment.... And dreadful as it is, it’s all for the best. In fact, I believe nothing better could have happened.”
“Why, why couldn’t anything better have happened?” cried Lise, staring at Alyosha in great surprise.

“Because if he’d taken the money, an hour after getting home he’d be weeping with mortification. That’s exactly what would have happened. And most likely he’d have come to me first thing tomorrow and maybe thrown the notes at me and trampled on them, as he did just now. But now he’s gone home terribly proud and triumphant, even though he knows he’s ‘ruined himself.’ So now nothing could be easier than getting him to accept the two hundred roubles by tomorrow, because he’s already proved his honor, tossed the money away and stamped on it.... He couldn’t know, when he did it, that I’d bring it to him again tomorrow, and yet he’s in terrible need of that money. Proud as he is of himself now, even today he’ll be thinking what a help he has lost. At night he’ll think about it more than ever and dream about it, and by tomorrow morning he may be ready to run to me and beg my forgiveness. And that’s just when I’ll turn up. ‘Look, you’re a proud man,’ I’ll say. ‘You’ve shown it; but now take the money and forgive us!’ And then he’ll take it!”
Alyosha was swept away with joy as he said those last words, “And then he’ll take it!” Lise clapped her hands.
“Ah, that’s true! Now I understand it perfectly. Ah, Alyosha, how do you know all this? So young, and he knows what’s in people’s hearts.... I’d never have worked it out.”

“The main thing now is to convince him that he’s on an equal footing with us, even though he takes money from us,” Alyosha went on in his excitement, “and not only an equal one, but even a higher one.”
“‘On a higher footing’ is charming, Alexey Fyodorovitch; but go on, go on!”
“You mean there’s no such expression as ‘on a higher footing’; but that doesn’t matter, because—”

“Oh, no, of course it doesn’t matter. Forgive me, dear Alyosha.... You know, until now I hardly respected you—that is, I did respect you, but only on an equal footing; now I’ll begin to respect you on a higher footing. Don’t be angry with me for joking, dear,” she put in at once, with strong feeling. “I’m silly and small, but you, you! Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch. Isn’t there contempt in all this analysis of ours—I mean yours ... no, let’s call it ours—aren’t we looking down on him, on that poor man, by picking his soul apart like this, from above, as it were, eh? By deciding so surely that he will take the money?”

“No, Lise, it isn’t contempt,” Alyosha answered, as though he’d prepared for the question. “I was thinking about that on my way here. How can it be contempt, when we’re all like him, when we’re all exactly the same as he is? Because we are the same, you know, no better. And if we were better, we’d have done just as he did in his place.... I can’t speak for you, Lise, but I think my own soul is mean in many ways, and his isn’t mean; on the contrary, it’s full of fine feeling.... No, Lise, I don’t despise him. Do you know, Lise, my elder once told me to look after most people the way one looks after children, and some of them the way one looks after the sick in hospitals.”
“Ah, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, let’s look after people the way we would the sick!”
“Let’s, Lise; I’m ready. Though I’m not altogether ready in myself. Sometimes I’m very impatient, and other times I just don’t see things. It’s different with you.”
“Ah, I don’t believe that! Alexey Fyodorovitch, how happy I am!”
“I’m so glad to hear you say it, Lise.”

“Alexey Fyodorovitch, you’re wonderfully good, but sometimes you’re sort of stiff.... And yet you’re really not stiff at all. Go to the door, open it quietly, and see if mamma is listening,” said Lise, in a nervous, hurried whisper.
Alyosha went, opened the door, and reported that nobody was listening.

“Come here, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” Lise went on, turning redder and redder. “Give me your hand—that’s right. I have a great confession to make. Yesterday I didn’t write to you as a joke, but seriously,” and she covered her eyes with her hand. It was plain that she was deeply ashamed of confessing it.
All of a sudden she seized his hand and, on impulse, kissed it three times.
“Oh, Lise, how wonderful!” cried Alyosha happily. “You know, I was absolutely certain you meant it.”
“Certain? Well, really!” She pushed his hand away but kept hold of it, blushing hotly and giving a happy little laugh. “I kiss his hand, and he says, ‘How wonderful!’”
But the reproach wasn’t fair. Alyosha was thoroughly flustered himself.
“I’d like to please you always, Lise, but I don’t know how to,” he mumbled, blushing as well.

“Alyosha, dear, you’re cold and rude. Do you see that? He’s picked me for his wife and he’s completely settled about it. He was sure I meant it. What a thing to say! That’s impertinence, that’s what it is.”
“Why, was it wrong to be sure?” Alyosha asked, suddenly laughing.
“Oh, Alyosha, no, it was wonderfully right,” cried Lise, gazing at him with tenderness and joy.
Alyosha stood still, her hand in his. Then he suddenly bent down and kissed her on the lips.
“Oh, what are you doing?” cried Lise. Alyosha was horribly embarrassed.
“Oh, forgive me if I shouldn’t have.... Maybe I’m terribly stupid.... You said I was cold, so I kissed you.... But I see it was stupid.”
Lise laughed and hid her face in her hands. “And in this dress!” she blurted out in the middle of her laughing. Then she stopped abruptly and became serious, almost stern.

“Alyosha, we’ll have to put off kissing. We’re not ready for it yet, and we’ll be waiting a long time,” she finished suddenly. “Tell me instead: you’re so clever, so intellectual, so observant. Why do you pick a little idiot, an invalid like me? Oh, Alyosha, I’m awfully happy, because I don’t deserve you one bit.”

“You do, Lise. I’m leaving the monastery for good in a few days. Once I go out into the world, I have to marry. I know that. _He_ told me to marry, too. Who could I marry better than you? And who would have me but you? I’ve thought it over. For one thing, you’ve known me since we were children, and you have many good qualities that I don’t. You’re lighter-hearted than I am, and above all you’re more innocent. I’ve already been brought up against so many things.... Ah, you don’t know it, but I, too, am a Karamazov. What does it matter if you laugh and make jokes, even at my expense? Go on laughing. I’m so glad when you do. You laugh like a little child, but you think like a martyr.”
“Like a martyr? What do you mean?”

“Yes, Lise. Your question a moment ago, whether we weren’t showing contempt for that poor man by taking his soul apart—that was the question of someone who suffers.... You see, I can’t put it well, but anyone who thinks about such questions is able to suffer. Sitting in your invalid chair, you must have thought over many things already.”

“Alyosha, give me your hand. Why are you pulling it away?” murmured Lise in a failing voice, faint with happiness. “Listen, Alyosha. What will you wear when you leave the monastery? What kind of suit? Don’t laugh, don’t be angry. It’s very, very important to me.”
“I haven’t thought about the suit, Lise, but I’ll wear whatever you like.”
“I’d like you to have a dark blue velvet coat, a white piqué waistcoat and a soft gray felt hat.... Tell me, when I said I hadn’t meant what I wrote, did you believe I didn’t care for you?”
“No, I didn’t believe it.”
“Oh, you impossible person, there’s no cure for you.”
“You see, I knew you—seemed to care for me, but I pretended to believe you didn’t, to make things—easier for you.”

“That’s worse! Worse, and better than anything! Alyosha, I’m awfully fond of you. Just before you came this morning, I tried my luck. I decided I’d ask you for my letter. If you took it out calmly and handed it over (just what you’d be expected to do), that would mean you didn’t love me at all, that you felt nothing and were only a stupid boy, good for nothing, and that I was ruined. But you’d left the letter at home, and that cheered me up. You left it behind on purpose, so you wouldn’t have to give it back, because you knew I’d ask for it? That’s how it was, isn’t it?”
“Oh, Lise, it wasn’t like that at all. I have the letter with me now, and I had it this morning too, in this pocket. Here it is.”
Alyosha pulled the letter out, laughing, and held it up for her to see from where he stood.
“But I’m not giving it to you. Look at it from there.”
“Why, so you told a lie? You, a monk, told a lie!”

“I lied, if you like,” Alyosha laughed too. “I lied so I wouldn’t have to give you back the letter. It’s very precious to me,” he added suddenly, with deep feeling, and he flushed again. “It always will be, and I won’t give it up to anyone!”
Lise looked at him with delight. “Alyosha,” she murmured again, “look at the door. Isn’t mamma listening?”
“All right, Lise, I’ll look. But wouldn’t it be better not to? Why suspect your mother of something so low?”

“What’s low about it? A mother spying on her daughter, that’s her right, it’s not low!” cried Lise, flaring up. “You can be certain, Alexey Fyodorovitch, that when I’m a mother, if I have a daughter like me, I’ll spy on her for sure!”
“Really, Lise? That’s not right.”

“Oh, my goodness! What has being low got to do with it? If she were listening in on some ordinary social conversation, it would be low. But when her own daughter is shut in with a young man.... Listen, Alyosha, I’ll have you know I’ll spy on you the minute we’re married. And I’ll tell you something more: I’ll open all your letters and read them. So you may as well be prepared.”
“Yes, of course, if that’s how it is—” muttered Alyosha, “only it’s not right.”

“Ah, how disdainful! Alyosha, dear, let’s not quarrel on the very first day. I’d better tell you the whole truth. Of course it’s very wrong to spy on people. Of course I’m wrong and you’re right. But I’ll spy on you all the same.”
“Go ahead, then. You won’t find out anything,” laughed Alyosha.
“And, Alyosha, will you give way to me? We have to settle that as well.”
“I’d be glad to, Lise, and I certainly will—only not in the most important things. Even if you disagree with me there, I’ll do my duty in the most important things.”

“That’s as it should be. But I’ll tell you, I’m ready to give way to you not only in the most important matters but in everything. And I’m ready to swear it right now—in everything, for the rest of my life!” cried Lise fervently. “And I’ll do it gladly, gladly! More than that, I swear I’ll never spy on you, not once, and never read a single one of your letters. For you’re right and I’m not. And though I’ll be terribly tempted to spy, I know I won’t, since you think it’s dishonorable. You’re my conscience now.... Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch, why have you been so sad lately, both yesterday and today? I know you have a lot of worries and troubles. But I can see you have some special grief on top of that, a secret one, perhaps?”
“Yes, Lise, I have a secret one too,” answered Alyosha mournfully. “I can see you love me, since you guessed it.”
“What grief? What is it about? Can you tell me?” asked Lise, timidly pleading.
“I’ll tell you later, Lise—afterwards,” said Alyosha in confusion. “Right now you might not understand it—and maybe I couldn’t explain it.”
“I know your brothers and your father are worrying you too.”
“Yes, my brothers too,” murmured Alyosha, lost in thought.
“I don’t like your brother Ivan, Alyosha,” said Lise suddenly.
He took note of this with some surprise, but didn’t answer.

“My brothers are destroying themselves,” he went on, “and my father too. And they’re destroying others along with them. It’s ‘the primitive force of the Karamazovs,’ as Father Païssy put it the other day: a crude, unbridled, earthly force. Does the spirit of God move over that force? Even that I don’t know. I only know that I, too, am a Karamazov.... Me a monk, a monk! Am I a monk, Lise? You said a moment ago that I was.”
“Yes, I did.”
“And perhaps I don’t even believe in God.”

“You don’t believe? What’s the matter?” said Lise, quietly and gently. But Alyosha didn’t answer. These last words of his held something too mysterious and too much his own, perhaps unclear even to himself, and yet it tormented him.

“And now, on top of everything, my friend, the best man in the world, is going, is leaving the earth! If you knew, Lise, how closely my soul is bound to him! And then I’ll be left alone.... I’ll come to you, Lise.... From now on we’ll be together.”
“Yes, together, together! From now on we’ll always be together, all our lives! Listen, kiss me, I give you leave.”
Alyosha kissed her.

“Now go. Christ be with you!” and she made the sign of the cross over him. “Hurry back to _him_ while he’s still alive. I see I’ve been cruel to keep you so long. I’ll pray today for him and for you. Alyosha, we’ll be happy! Will we be happy? Will we?”
“I believe we will, Lise.”

Alyosha decided it was better not to go in to Madame Hohlakov, and he was leaving the house without saying good-by to her. But the moment he opened the door, there stood Madame Hohlakov right in front of him. From her very first word he guessed she had been waiting there deliberately to catch him.
“Alexey Fyodorovitch, this is dreadful. It’s all childish nonsense, and ridiculous. I trust you won’t imagine—It’s folly, nothing but folly!” she said, falling on him at once.
“Just don’t tell her that,” said Alyosha, “or she’ll get upset, and that’s bad for her right now.”
“Sensible advice from a sensible young man. Am I to take it that you only agreed with her out of pity for her being an invalid, because you didn’t want to upset her by contradicting her?”
“Oh, no, not at all. I was quite serious about what I said,” Alyosha declared firmly.
“To be serious about it is impossible, unthinkable. First of all, I shall never receive you here again, and I shall take her away, you may be certain of that.”
“But why?” asked Alyosha. “It’s all so far in the future. We may have to wait another year and a half.”

“Ah, Alexey Fyodorovitch, that’s true, of course. You’ll have time to quarrel and part a thousand times in a year and a half. But I’m so unhappy! It’s such nonsense, yet it’s a terrible blow to me. I feel like Famusov in the last scene of _Sorrow from Wit_. You’re Tchatsky and she’s Sofya, and, just think, I ran down to meet you on the stairs, and in the play the fatal scene takes place on the staircase. I heard everything; I nearly collapsed. So that’s the explanation of her dreadful night and her hysterics lately! It means love for the daughter but death for the mother. I may as well lie in my grave right now. And something more serious still: what is this letter she’s written? Show it to me at once, at once!”
“No, there’s no need. Tell me, how is Katerina Ivanovna now? I have to know.”

“She’s still lying in delirium; she hasn’t come to. Her aunts are here, but all they do is sigh and put on airs. Herzenstube came, and he was so alarmed that I didn’t know what to do for him. I almost sent for a doctor to see to him. My carriage took him home. And on top of everything, you and this letter! It’s true that nothing can happen for a year and a half. In the name of all that’s holy, in the name of your dying elder, show me that letter, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I’m her mother. Hold it in your hand, if you like, and I’ll read it that way.”
“No, I won’t show it to you. Even if she allowed it, I wouldn’t. I’ll come tomorrow, and if you like, we can talk about many things. But now, good-by!”
And Alyosha ran down the stairs and out into the street.

chapters.title: II. Smerdyakov With A Guitar
paragraphs: He really had no time to lose. Even while he was saying good-bye to Lise, it had occurred to him that he would need some trick to catch his brother Dmitri, who was obviously avoiding him. It was getting late, nearly three o’clock. Alyosha’s whole soul pulled him toward the monastery and his dying saint, but the need to see Dmitri outweighed everything. With each hour that passed he grew surer that some great, unavoidable disaster was about to strike. What that disaster was, and what he would say to his brother when it came, he could probably not have said clearly. “Even if my benefactor has to die without me, at least I won’t have to reproach myself for the rest of my life. I won’t have to think that I might have saved something and didn’t, that I walked past and hurried home. If I do what I mean to do, I will be following his great teaching.”

His plan was to take his brother Dmitri by surprise. He would climb the fence as he had the day before, slip into the garden and sit in the summer-house. If Dmitri wasn’t there, Alyosha thought, he would not announce himself to Foma or the women of the house. He would stay hidden in the summer-house, even if that meant waiting until evening. If Dmitri was lying in wait for Grushenka again, as before, he would very likely come to the summer-house. Alyosha did not dwell on the details of the plan, though. He simply decided to carry it out, even at the cost of not getting back to the monastery that day.

Everything went smoothly. He climbed over the hurdle at almost the same spot as the day before and got into the summer-house without being seen. He did not want to be noticed. The woman of the house, and Foma too if he was around, might be loyal to his brother and follow his orders. They might refuse to let Alyosha into the garden, or they might warn Dmitri that somebody was looking for him and asking questions.

The summer-house was empty. Alyosha sat down and began to wait. He looked around, and the place struck him as much older than before. The day was as fine as yesterday’s, yet this time the summer-house looked wretched. A ring was left on the table, no doubt from the glass of brandy spilled the day before. Foolish, pointless thoughts drifted through his head, as they always do during a dull wait. He wondered, for instance, why he had sat in exactly the same spot as before, and not on the other seat. At last he felt very low, worn down by suspense and uncertainty. But he had not been sitting there even a quarter of an hour when he suddenly heard a guitar being strummed very close by. Somewhere in the bushes, not twenty paces off, some people were sitting, or had only just sat down. Alyosha suddenly remembered that when he left the summer-house the day before, he had glimpsed an old, low green garden-seat among the bushes on the left, by the fence. That must be where they were sitting now. Who were they?
A man’s voice suddenly broke into song, in a sugary falsetto, with the guitar to accompany it:
A force I cannot fight has bound me to my dear. O Lord, have mercy on her and on me! On her and on me! On her and on me!
The voice stopped. It was a lackey’s tenor and a lackey’s song. Then a woman’s voice asked, in a coaxing and bashful tone, though with a mincing affectation:
“Why haven’t you come to see us for such a long time, Pavel Fyodorovitch? Why do you always look down on us?”

“Not at all,” a man’s voice answered, politely but with pointed dignity. It was clear that the man had the upper hand and that the woman was making advances. “That must be Smerdyakov,” thought Alyosha, “judging by the voice. And the lady must be the daughter of the house, who has come back from Moscow. The one in the dress with a train, who goes to Marfa for soup.”
“I’m awfully fond of verses of any kind, so long as they rhyme,” the woman’s voice went on. “Why don’t you sing more?”
The man began to sing again:
What do I care for a king’s riches If only my dear one keeps well? Lord, have mercy On her and on me! On her and on me! On her and on me!
“Last time it was even better,” the woman’s voice remarked. “You sang ‘If my darling keeps well,’ and it sounded more tender. I suppose you’ve forgotten it today.”
“Poetry is rubbish!” Smerdyakov said curtly.
“Oh, no! I love poetry.”

“Insofar as it is poetry, it is rubbish through and through. Just think about it: who ever talks in rhyme? And suppose we were all made to talk in rhyme, even by government decree. We wouldn’t say much, would we? Poetry is no use, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“How clever you are! How did you come to go so deep into everything?” The woman’s voice grew more and more coaxing.

“I could have gone further than this. I could have known more, if my fate hadn’t been against me from childhood. I would have shot a man in a duel for calling me names because I come from a filthy beggar and have no father. In Moscow they used to throw that in my teeth. The story had reached them from here, thanks to Grigory Vassilyevitch. Grigory Vassilyevitch accuses me of rebelling against my birth, but I would have agreed to their killing me before I was born, so that I would never have come into the world at all. In the market they used to say it, and your mamma too, with a great lack of delicacy, began telling me that her hair was like a mat on her head and that she was short of five foot by a wee bit. Why say a wee bit when she might have said ‘a little bit,’ like everybody else? She wanted to make it touching, a proper peasant feeling. Can a Russian peasant be said to feel anything, next to an educated man? In his ignorance he can’t be said to have any feeling at all. Since I was a child, whenever I hear ‘a wee bit,’ I nearly burst with rage. I hate all Russia, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“If you’d been an army cadet, or a young hussar, you wouldn’t talk that way. You’d have drawn your saber to defend all Russia.”
“I don’t want to be a hussar, Marya Kondratyevna. What’s more, I’d like to do away with all soldiers.”
“And when an enemy comes, who’s going to defend us?”

“There’s no need for defense. In 1812 Napoleon, first Emperor of the French and father of the present one, made a great invasion of Russia. It would have been a good thing if they had conquered us. A clever nation would have conquered a very stupid one and swallowed it up. We would have ended up with quite different institutions.”

“Are things really so much better in their country than in ours? I wouldn’t trade one dandy I know for three young Englishmen,” said Marya Kondratyevna tenderly, no doubt shooting him a most languishing glance as she said it.
“That depends on what one prefers.”
“But you’re exactly like a foreigner, like a most gentlemanly foreigner. I’m telling you so, though it makes me bashful.”

“If you want to know, the people over there and the people here are alike in their vices. They’re all swindlers. The only difference is that over there the scoundrel wears polished boots, and here he grovels in filth and sees nothing wrong with it. The Russian people need a good thrashing, as Fyodor Pavlovitch said very truly yesterday, mad as he is, and all his children.”
“But you told me yourself you had such respect for Ivan Fyodorovitch.”

“Yet he called me a stinking lackey. He thinks I might turn unruly. There he’s mistaken. If I had a certain sum in my pocket, I’d have left here long ago. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is lower than any lackey in how he behaves, how he thinks and how poor he is. He can’t do anything, and still everyone respects him. I may be only a soup-maker, but with a bit of luck I could open a café restaurant in Petrovka, in Moscow, because my cooking is something special, and in Moscow nobody’s cooking is special except the foreigners’. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is a beggar, but if he challenged the son of the first count in the land, he’d fight him. And yet how is he better than I am? He’s ever so much stupider than I am. Look at all the money he’s thrown away for no reason!”
“A duel must be lovely,” Marya Kondratyevna suddenly remarked.
“How so?”

“It must be so frightening and so brave, especially when young officers with pistols in their hands pop away at each other over some lady. A perfect picture! Ah, if only girls were allowed to watch, I’d give anything to see one!”
“It’s all very well while you’re the one doing the shooting. But when the other fellow is aiming right at your mug, you must feel pretty silly. You’d be glad to run, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“You don’t mean that you would run?” But Smerdyakov did not stoop to reply. After a moment of silence the guitar tinkled again, and in the same falsetto he sang once more:
Say what you like, I’m going far away. Life will be bright and gay In the city far away. I won’t grieve, I won’t grieve at all, I don’t intend to grieve at all.

Then something unexpected happened. Alyosha sneezed. The two fell silent. Alyosha got up and walked over to them. He found Smerdyakov all dressed up, in polished boots, his hair pomaded and perhaps curled. The guitar lay on the garden-seat. His companion was the daughter of the house, in a light-blue dress with a train two yards long. She was young and would not have been bad-looking, except that her face was so round and so terribly freckled.
“Will my brother Dmitri be back soon?” Alyosha asked, as calmly as he could.
Smerdyakov got up slowly, and Marya Kondratyevna rose as well.
“How should I know about Dmitri Fyodorovitch? It isn’t as if I were his keeper,” Smerdyakov answered, quietly, distinctly and with an air of superiority.
“I only asked whether you happen to know,” Alyosha explained.
“I know nothing of where he is, and I don’t wish to.”
“But my brother told me you keep him informed of everything that goes on in the house. He said you’d promised to tell him when Agrafena Alexandrovna comes.”
Smerdyakov turned a slow, unmoved gaze on him.
“And how did you get in this time, when the gate was bolted an hour ago?” he asked, with his eyes on Alyosha.
“I came through the back-alley and over the fence, and went straight to the summer-house. I hope you’ll forgive me,” he added, turning to Marya Kondratyevna. “I was in a hurry to find my brother.”

“Ach, as if we could take offense at you!” drawled Marya Kondratyevna, flattered by Alyosha’s apology. “Dmitri Fyodorovitch often comes into the summer-house that way. We don’t know he’s here, and there he is, sitting in the summer-house.”
“I’m very anxious to find him, or to hear from you where he is now. Believe me, it concerns something very important to him.”
“He never tells us anything,” lisped Marya Kondratyevna.

“I used to come here as a friend,” Smerdyakov began again, “but even here Dmitri Fyodorovitch has hounded me without mercy with his endless questions about the master. ‘What news?’ he’ll ask. ‘What’s going on in there now? Who comes and goes?’ And can’t I tell him something more? Twice already he’s threatened me with death.”
“With death?” Alyosha exclaimed in surprise.

“Do you suppose he’d think twice about it, with his temper, which you had a chance to see for yourself yesterday? He says that if I let Agrafena Alexandrovna in and she spends the night there, I’ll be the first to pay for it. I’m terribly afraid of him. If I weren’t even more afraid of doing it, I ought to tell the police. God only knows what he might do!”
“Just the other day his honor told him, ‘I’ll pound you in a mortar!’” added Marya Kondratyevna.
“Oh, if it’s pounding in a mortar, it may be only talk,” said Alyosha. “If I could meet him, I might talk to him about that too.”

“Well, here is the one thing I can tell you,” said Smerdyakov, as if on second thought. “I’m here as an old friend and neighbor, and it would be strange if I didn’t come. On the other hand, Ivan Fyodorovitch sent me first thing this morning to your brother’s lodging in Lake Street. I had no letter, only a message asking Dmitri Fyodorovitch to dine with him at the restaurant here, in the market-place. I went, but I didn’t find Dmitri Fyodorovitch at home, though it was eight o’clock. ‘He was here, but he’s long gone,’ those were the landlady’s very words. It’s as though the two of them had an understanding. Perhaps at this moment he’s in the restaurant with Ivan Fyodorovitch. Ivan Fyodorovitch hasn’t come home to dinner, you see, and Fyodor Pavlovitch dined alone an hour ago and has gone to lie down. But I beg you most particularly not to say anything about me or what I’ve told you, because he’d kill me for nothing at all.”
“Brother Ivan has invited Dmitri to the restaurant today?” Alyosha repeated quickly.
“Yes, that’s right.”
“The Metropolis tavern, in the market-place?”
“The very one.”
“That’s quite likely,” cried Alyosha, very excited. “Thank you, Smerdyakov. That’s important. I’ll go there at once.”
“Don’t give me away,” Smerdyakov called after him.
“Oh, no. I’ll go into the tavern as if by chance. Don’t worry.”
“But wait a minute, I’ll open the gate for you,” cried Marya Kondratyevna.
“No, it’s a short cut. I’ll go over the fence again.”

What he had heard threw Alyosha into great agitation. He ran to the tavern. He could not go inside in his monastic dress, but he could ask at the entrance for his brothers and call them down. But just as he reached the tavern, a window was thrown open and his brother Ivan called to him from above.
“Alyosha, can’t you come up here? I’d be awfully grateful.”
“Of course I can, only I’m not sure about going in this dress—”
“But I’m in a room by myself. Come up the steps, and I’ll run down to meet you.”
A minute later Alyosha was sitting beside his brother. Ivan was dining alone.

chapters.title: III. The Brothers Make Friends
paragraphs: Ivan wasn’t in a separate room after all. He was sitting in a corner closed off by a screen, where the other people in the room couldn’t see him. This was the first room inside the entrance, with a buffet along one wall, and waiters were constantly darting through it. The only customer was an old retired military man drinking tea in a corner. In the rest of the tavern, though, the usual racket went on: people shouting for waiters, corks popping, billiard balls clicking, the organ droning. Alyosha knew that Ivan didn’t normally come to this tavern and didn’t like taverns anyway. So, he reflected, Ivan must have come only to meet Dmitri, as they had agreed. But Dmitri wasn’t there.
“Shall I order you fish, or soup, or something? You can’t live on tea alone, I suppose,” cried Ivan, obviously delighted to have snapped up Alyosha. He had already finished dinner and was having tea.
“I’ll have soup, and tea afterwards. I’m hungry,” said Alyosha cheerfully.
“And cherry jam? They have it here. Remember how you adored cherry jam when you were small?”
“You remember that? Yes, I’ll have jam too. I like it still.”
Ivan signaled the waiter and ordered soup, jam and tea.

“I remember everything, Alyosha. I remember you up to the age of eleven, when I was nearly fifteen. Fifteen and eleven are so far apart that brothers can’t be companions at those ages. I’m not even sure I was fond of you. For my first few years away in Moscow I never thought of you at all. Then you came to Moscow yourself, and I think we met just once somewhere. Now I’ve been here over three months, and so far we’ve barely exchanged a word. I’m leaving tomorrow. I was sitting here just now, wondering how I could catch you to say good-by, and at that very moment you went by.”
“Did you want so much to see me, then?”

“Very much. I want to get to know you once and for all, and I want you to know me. Then I can say good-by. I believe it’s always best to get to know people right before you leave them. I’ve seen the way you’ve been watching me these three months. Your eyes have had a steady look of expectation, and I can’t bear that. That’s why I’ve kept my distance. But in the end I’ve come to respect you. The little man holds his ground, I thought. I’m laughing, but I mean it. You do hold your ground, don’t you? I like people who are firm like that, whatever it is they’re standing on, even small fry like you. Your expectant eyes stopped irritating me. I grew fond of them in the end, those expectant eyes. You seem to love me, for some reason, Alyosha?”

“I do love you, Ivan. Dmitri says of you—Ivan is a tomb! I say of you, Ivan is a riddle. You’re a riddle to me even now. But I’ve understood one thing about you, and I didn’t understand it until this morning.”
“What’s that?” laughed Ivan.
“You won’t be angry?” Alyosha laughed too.
“Well?”
“It’s that you’re exactly as young as other young men of twenty-three—a young, fresh, nice boy, green, in fact! There. Have I insulted you terribly?”

“On the contrary, it’s a coincidence that startles me,” cried Ivan, warmly and good-humoredly. “Believe it or not, ever since that scene with her I’ve been thinking of nothing but my youthful greenness, and then you start in on exactly that, as if you’d guessed. Do you know what I’ve been telling myself, sitting here? Say I didn’t believe in life. Say I’d lost faith in the woman I love and in the order of things, and was convinced that it’s all a disorderly, damnable, maybe devil-ridden chaos. Say I’d been hit by every horror of human disillusionment. I would still want to live. Once I’d tasted the cup, I wouldn’t turn away until I’d drained it! At thirty, though, I’m sure to put the cup down, even if I haven’t emptied it, and turn away—to where, I don’t know. But until thirty I know my youth will win out over everything, every disillusionment, every disgust with life. Many times I’ve asked myself whether any despair exists that could beat this frantic and perhaps unseemly thirst for life in me. I’ve decided that none does—until I’m thirty, that is; after that it will leave me by itself, I imagine. Some driveling, consumptive moralists, poets especially, often call that thirst for life low. It is a Karamazov trait, true enough, this thirst for life whatever happens. You have it too, no doubt. But why is it low? The centripetal force on our planet is still fearfully strong, Alyosha. I long for life, and I keep on living in spite of logic. I may not believe in the order of the universe, yet I love the sticky little leaves when they open in spring. I love the blue sky. I love certain people, whom one loves, you know, sometimes without knowing why. I love certain great deeds done by men, though I lost faith in them long ago, perhaps; but from old habit the heart still treasures them. Here, they’ve brought your soup. Eat it, it’ll do you good. It’s first-rate soup, they know how to make it here. I want to travel in Europe, Alyosha, and I’ll leave from here. And yet I know I’m going only to a graveyard—but what a precious graveyard! The dead who lie there are precious. Every stone over them tells of such burning life in the past, such passionate faith in their work, their truth, their struggle, their science, that I know I’ll fall to the ground, kiss those stones and weep over them. Though I’m convinced in my heart that it’s long been nothing but a graveyard. And I won’t weep out of despair. I’ll weep simply because my tears will make me happy; I’ll soak my soul in the feeling. I love the sticky leaves in spring, the blue sky—that’s all there is to it. It has nothing to do with intellect or logic. It’s loving with your insides, with your stomach. You love the first strength of your youth. Do you understand any of my tirade, Alyosha?” Ivan laughed suddenly.

“I understand only too well, Ivan. To love with your insides, with your stomach—that’s exactly what one longs for. You put it so well, and I’m awfully glad you have such a longing for life,” cried Alyosha. “I think everyone ought to love life above everything else in the world.”
“Love life more than the meaning of it?”

“Of course, love it regardless of logic, as you say. It has to be regardless of logic, and only then will you understand its meaning. I’ve thought so for a long time. Half your work is done, Ivan—you love life. Now you just have to try for the second half, and you’re saved.”
“You’re out to save me, but maybe I’m not lost! And what is your second half?”
“Why, that you have to raise your dead, who perhaps haven’t died after all. Come, let me have my tea. I’m so glad we’ve had this talk, Ivan.”
“You’re inspired, I see. I’m awfully fond of such _professions de foi_ from such—novices. You’re a steadfast person, Alexey. Is it true you mean to leave the monastery?”
“Yes. My elder is sending me out into the world.”

“Then we’ll meet again in the world. We’ll see each other before I’m thirty, when I start turning from the cup. Father doesn’t mean to turn from his cup until he’s seventy; he even dreams of clinging on to eighty, so he says. He means it only too seriously, buffoon though he is. He too stands on a firm rock: his sensuality—though after thirty, admittedly, there may be nothing else to stand on.... But clinging on to seventy is vile. Better to stop at thirty; one could keep ‘a shadow of nobility’ by fooling oneself. Have you seen Dmitri today?”
“No, but I saw Smerdyakov,” and Alyosha gave a quick but detailed account of meeting Smerdyakov. Ivan listened anxiously and asked him questions.
“But he begged me not to tell Dmitri that he’d told me about him,” Alyosha added. Ivan frowned and thought it over.
“Is it on Smerdyakov’s account that you’re frowning?” asked Alyosha.
“Yes, it’s because of him. Damn him, I really did want to see Dmitri, but now there’s no point,” Ivan said reluctantly.
“But are you really leaving so soon, brother?”
“Yes.”
“And Dmitri and father? How is it going to end?” Alyosha asked anxiously.

“You keep harping on that! What’s it got to do with me? Am I my brother Dmitri’s keeper?” Ivan snapped irritably, then suddenly smiled bitterly. “That was Cain’s answer about his murdered brother, wasn’t it? Maybe that’s just what you’re thinking? Well, damn it all, I can’t stay on here as their keeper, can I? I’ve done what I had to do, and I’m going. Do you think I’m jealous of Dmitri, that for three months I’ve been trying to steal his beautiful Katerina Ivanovna? Nonsense. I had business of my own. I’ve finished it. I’m going. I finished it just now, and you were there to see.”
“At Katerina Ivanovna’s?”

“Yes, and I’ve freed myself once and for all. And anyway, what has Dmitri got to do with me? He doesn’t come into it. I had my own business to settle with Katerina Ivanovna. You know, in fact, that Dmitri acted as though we had some understanding. I didn’t ask him to. He solemnly handed her over to me and gave us his blessing. It’s all too funny. Ah, Alyosha, if you knew how light my heart is now! Believe it or not, I sat here over my dinner and almost ordered champagne to celebrate my first hour of freedom. Tfoo! It dragged on for nearly six months, and all of a sudden I’ve shaken it off. Even yesterday I couldn’t have imagined how easy it would be to end it, if I chose.”
“It’s your love you’re speaking of, Ivan?”

“Call it my love, if you like. I fell in love with the young lady. I tormented myself over her, and she tormented me. I sat keeping watch over her ... and suddenly it’s all collapsed! This morning I spoke with inspiration, and then I went off and roared with laughter. Can you believe it? Yes, it’s the literal truth.”
“You seem very cheerful about it now,” Alyosha remarked, looking at his face, which had suddenly turned brighter.

“But how was I to know I didn’t care for her at all! Ha ha! Apparently I didn’t. And yet how she drew me! How attractive she was just now, when I made my speech! And do you know, she draws me terribly even now, and still it’s so easy to leave her. Do you think I’m boasting?”
“No. It’s only that perhaps it wasn’t love.”

“Alyosha,” laughed Ivan, “don’t philosophize about love; it doesn’t suit you. The way you plunged into the argument this morning! I forgot to kiss you for it.... But how she tormented me! It really was like sitting next to a ‘laceration.’ Ah, she knew how I loved her! She loved me, not Dmitri,” Ivan insisted gayly. “Her feeling for Dmitri was just self-laceration. Everything I told her just now was perfectly true. The worst of it is that it may take her fifteen or twenty years to see that she doesn’t care for Dmitri and loves me, the one she torments. She may never see it at all, in spite of today’s lesson. Well, it’s better so; I can simply leave for good. By the way, how is she now? What happened after I walked out?”
Alyosha told him she had been hysterical, and that now, he’d heard, she lay unconscious and delirious.
“Isn’t Madame Hohlakov laying it on?”
“I don’t think so.”
“I’ll find out. Nobody dies of hysterics, anyway. They’re nothing. God gave women hysterics as a relief. I won’t go to her at all. Why shove myself forward again?”
“But you told her she never cared for you.”
“I did it deliberately. Alyosha, shall I send for champagne? Let’s drink to my freedom. Ah, if you only knew how glad I am!”
“No, brother, we’d better not drink,” said Alyosha suddenly. “Besides, I feel somehow low.”
“Yes, you’ve been low for a long time; I’ve noticed.”
“So you’ve made up your mind to go tomorrow morning?”

“Morning? I never said morning.... Though it may turn out to be the morning. Believe it or not, I came to dine here today only so as not to dine with the old man, I loathe him so. As far as he’s concerned, I’d have gone long ago. But why does my leaving worry you so? We have plenty of time before I go—an eternity!”
“If you’re leaving tomorrow, how can you talk of an eternity?”

“What difference does it make to us?” Ivan laughed. “We have time enough for our talk, for what brought us here. Why do you look so surprised? Tell me: why did we meet here? To talk of my love for Katerina Ivanovna? Of the old man and Dmitri? Of travel abroad? Of the fatal position of Russia? Of the Emperor Napoleon? Is that it?”
“No.”

“Then you know what for. Other people may differ, but we, in our green youth, have to settle the eternal questions before anything else. That’s what we care about. Young Russia talks of nothing but the eternal questions right now, just when the old folks are all taken up with practical ones. Why have you been watching me expectantly for the past three months? To ask me, ‘What do you believe, or don’t you believe anything at all?’ That’s what your eyes have been saying all this time, isn’t it?”
“Maybe,” Alyosha smiled. “You’re not laughing at me now, are you, Ivan?”

“Me, laughing! I don’t want to hurt my little brother, who’s watched me so expectantly for three months. Alyosha, look me straight in the face! Of course I’m just the same sort of little boy you are, only not a novice. And what have Russian boys been up to until now—some of them, I mean? Take this stinking tavern, for instance. They meet here and settle in a corner. They’ve never met before in their lives, and when they walk out of the tavern they won’t meet again for forty years. And what do they talk about in that brief stop at the tavern? About the eternal questions: whether God exists, and immortality. And those who don’t believe in God talk about socialism or anarchism, about remaking all humanity on a new pattern, which comes to the same thing, since they’re the same questions turned inside out. And masses, masses of the most original Russian boys do nothing but talk about the eternal questions! Isn’t it so?”

“Yes. For real Russians the questions of whether God exists and of immortality—or, as you say, the same questions turned inside out—naturally come first and foremost, and so they should,” said Alyosha, still watching his brother with the same gentle, inquiring smile.

“Well, Alyosha, it’s sometimes very unwise to be a Russian at all, but you can hardly imagine anything stupider than how Russian boys spend their time. Still, there’s one Russian boy named Alyosha that I’m awfully fond of.”
“How nicely you slipped that in!” Alyosha suddenly laughed.
“Well, tell me where to start; give your orders. The existence of God, eh?”
“Start wherever you like. Yesterday at father’s you declared there was no God.” Alyosha searched his brother’s face.

“I said so at dinner yesterday on purpose, to tease you, and I saw your eyes light up. But now I have no objection to discussing it with you, and I say that in all seriousness. I want to be friends with you, Alyosha, since I have no friends and want to try it. Well, just imagine, perhaps I accept God too,” Ivan laughed; “that surprises you, doesn’t it?”
“Yes, of course, if you’re not joking.”

“Joking? Yesterday at the elder’s they told me I was joking. You know, dear boy, in the eighteenth century there was an old sinner who declared that if there were no God, He would have to be invented. _S’il n’existait pas Dieu, il faudrait l’inventer._ And man really has invented God. What is strange, what would be marvelous, is not that God actually exists. The marvel is that the idea of the necessity of God could get into the head of a creature as savage and vicious as man. It is so holy, so touching, so wise, and it does such credit to man. As for me, I made up my mind long ago not to ask whether man created God or God created man. I will not run through all the axioms Russian boys have laid down on that subject, every one of them derived from European hypotheses. What is a hypothesis there is an axiom to the Russian boy—and not just to the boys but to their teachers as well, since our Russian professors are often the same boys themselves. So I skip all the hypotheses. What are we after now? I am trying to explain, as quickly as I can, my essential nature: what sort of man I am, what I believe in, and what I hope for. That is it, isn’t it? And so I tell you that I simply accept God. But note this: if God exists, and if He really created the world, then, as we all know, He created it according to the geometry of Euclid, and He made the human mind able to conceive only three dimensions of space. Yet there have been, and still are, geometers and philosophers, some of them among the most distinguished, who doubt whether the whole universe—or, to put it more broadly, the whole of being—was created only according to Euclid’s geometry. They even dare to dream that two parallel lines, which by Euclid can never meet on earth, may meet somewhere in infinity. I have concluded that if I cannot understand even that, I cannot expect to understand anything about God. I admit humbly that I have no faculty for settling such questions. My mind is Euclidian and earthly, so how could I solve problems that are not of this world? And I advise you, my dear Alyosha, never to think about them either, above all about God, whether He exists or not. Such questions are wholly unsuited to a mind created with the idea of only three dimensions. So I accept God, and gladly. More than that, I accept His wisdom and His purpose, which are utterly beyond our understanding. I believe in the underlying order and the meaning of life. I believe in the eternal harmony into which, they say, we will one day be blended. I believe in the Word toward Which the universe is striving, Which Itself was ‘with God,’ and Which Itself is God, and so on and so on, to infinity. There are all sorts of phrases for it. I seem to be on the right road, don’t I? And yet, believe it or not, in the end I do not accept this world of God’s. Though I know it exists, I do not accept it at all. You must understand, it is not that I do not accept God; it is the world He created that I do not and cannot accept. Let me put it plainly. Like a child, I believe that suffering will be healed and made good, that the whole humiliating absurdity of human contradictions will vanish like a pitiful mirage, like the despicable invention of the feeble, infinitely small Euclidian mind of man. I believe that in the world’s finale, at the moment of eternal harmony, something so precious will happen that it will be enough for every heart, to comfort every resentment, to atone for all the crimes of humanity and for all the blood they have shed. I believe it will make it possible not only to forgive but to justify everything that has happened to men. But even if all that comes to pass, I do not accept it. I will not accept it. Even if parallel lines do meet and I see it with my own eyes, I will see it and say that they have met, and still I will not accept it. That is the root of me, Alyosha; that is my creed. I mean what I say. I began our talk as stupidly as I could, deliberately, but I have led up to my confession, because that is all you want. You did not want to hear about God; you only wanted to know what the brother you love lives by. And so I have told you.”
Ivan finished his long tirade with striking and unexpected feeling.
“And why did you start ‘as stupidly as you could’?” asked Alyosha, regarding him with a dreamy look.

“First, to be Russian about it. Russian conversations on such subjects are always conducted unbelievably stupidly. And second, the stupider you are, the nearer you are to reality. The stupider you are, the clearer you are. Stupidity is short and plain, while intelligence squirms and hides. Intelligence is a rogue, but stupidity is honest and direct. I’ve steered the conversation toward my despair, and the more stupidly I’ve put it, the better for me.”
“And will you explain why you won’t accept the world?” said Alyosha.

“Of course I will, it’s no secret; that’s what I’ve been leading up to. Dear little brother, I don’t want to corrupt you or shove you out of your stronghold. Perhaps I want you to heal me.” Ivan suddenly smiled just like a gentle little child. Alyosha had never seen such a smile on his face.

chapters.title: IV. Rebellion
paragraphs: “I have one confession to make,” Ivan began. “I never could understand how anyone can love his neighbors. To my mind, it’s precisely the people close to us that we can’t love. People far away, maybe. I read somewhere about John the Merciful, a saint. A hungry, frozen beggar came to him. The saint took him into his own bed, held him in his arms, and breathed into his mouth, which was putrid and loathsome with some dreadful disease. I’m convinced he did it out of ‘self-laceration,’ the self-laceration of falsity. He did it for the sake of a charity that duty imposed, as a penance laid on him. If you’re to love a man, he has to stay hidden. The moment he shows his face, love is gone.”

“Father Zossima has talked about that more than once,” said Alyosha. “He also said that a man’s face often stands in the way of people who haven’t practiced love. They can’t love him because of it. But there is still a great deal of love among men, almost Christ-like love. I know that myself, Ivan.”

“Well, I don’t know it yet, and I can’t understand it, and the vast mass of mankind is with me on that. The question is whether this comes from men’s bad qualities or from their nature. In my view, Christ-like love for human beings is a miracle that can’t happen on earth. He was God. We are not gods. Say I’m suffering terribly. Nobody else can ever know how much, because he is someone else and not me. And what’s more, people are rarely willing to admit that another person is suffering (as if it were some kind of distinction). Why won’t they, do you think? Because I smell bad, because I have a stupid face, because I once stepped on his foot. And besides, there’s suffering and suffering. The degrading, humiliating kind that brings me low—hunger, for instance—my benefactor may grant me. But when it comes to a higher suffering, for an idea, say, he will very seldom admit it. Maybe my face doesn’t look to him anything like the face he thinks a man should have who suffers for an idea. So he takes back his favor on the spot, and not out of any badness of heart. Beggars, especially genteel beggars, should never show themselves. They should ask for charity through the newspapers. In the abstract, or from a distance, one can love one’s neighbors. Close up, it’s almost impossible. It would be different if it were like the stage, in the ballet, where beggars appear in silk rags and tattered lace and ask for alms while dancing gracefully. Then one might like looking at them. Even so, we wouldn’t love them. But enough of this. I only wanted to give you my point of view. I meant to talk about human suffering in general, but we’d do better to stick to the suffering of children. That shrinks my argument to a tenth of what it could be. Still, let’s keep to the children, although it weakens my case. For one thing, you can love children even close up, even when they’re dirty, even when they’re ugly (though I suspect children are never ugly). My second reason for leaving grown-ups out is this. Besides being disgusting and unworthy of love, they have a compensation. They’ve eaten the apple and know good and evil, and they’ve become ‘like gods.’ They’re still eating it. The children haven’t eaten anything, and so far they’re innocent. Are you fond of children, Alyosha? I know you are, and you’ll see why I prefer to talk about them. If they, too, suffer horribly on earth, then it must be for their fathers’ sins. They must be punished for their fathers, who ate the apple. But that argument belongs to another world, and the human heart here on earth can’t make sense of it. The innocent must not suffer for someone else’s sins, and above all such innocents! It may surprise you, Alyosha, but I’m terribly fond of children, too. And note that cruel people, violent and greedy people, the Karamazovs, are sometimes very fond of children. While children are little, up to seven, say, they’re so far removed from grown-ups. They’re like different creatures, almost another species. I knew a convict in prison who had murdered whole families in his career as a burglar, children among them. Yet in prison he had a strange fondness for children. He spent all his time at his window, watching them play in the prison yard. He taught one little boy to come up to his window and became great friends with him.... You don’t know why I’m telling you all this, Alyosha? My head aches, and I’m sad.”
“You’re talking in a strange way,” Alyosha said uneasily, “as if you weren’t quite yourself.”

“Oh, by the way,” Ivan went on, as though he hadn’t heard his brother, “I met a Bulgarian in Moscow recently. He told me about the atrocities the Turks and Circassians are committing all over Bulgaria. They’re afraid of a general uprising of the Slavs. They burn villages, kill, rape women and children. They nail prisoners to fences by the ears and leave them there until morning, and in the morning they hang them. All sorts of things you can’t imagine. We sometimes speak of bestial cruelty, but that’s a great injustice and an insult to the beasts. No beast can ever be as cruel as a man, so artistically cruel. A tiger only tears and gnaws. That’s all he can do. It would never occur to him to nail people up by the ears, even if he could. These Turks enjoyed torturing children, too. They cut unborn babies out of their mothers’ wombs. They tossed infants into the air and caught them on their bayonets in front of their mothers. Doing it in front of the mothers was what gave the sport its zest. Here is another scene I found very interesting. Picture a trembling mother holding her baby, with a ring of invading Turks around her. They’ve thought up an entertainment. They fuss over the baby and laugh to make it laugh. It works, and the baby laughs. At that moment a Turk aims a pistol four inches from the baby’s face. The baby laughs with delight and reaches out its little hands for the pistol. And he pulls the trigger in the baby’s face and blows out its brains. Artistic, isn’t it? Turks are especially fond of sweets, they say, by the way.”
