“How could I help getting mixed up in it? Though truly, if you want the plain truth, I haven’t got mixed up in it at all. I kept quiet from the very start, not daring to answer him. But he picked me out to be his servant. Since then he has had one thing only to say: ‘I’ll kill you, you scoundrel, if you miss her.’ I’m certain, sir, that I’ll have a long fit tomorrow.”
“What do you mean, ‘a long fit’?”

“A long fit, one that goes on for a long time—several hours, or maybe a day or two. Once it lasted three days. I fell from the garret that time. The convulsions stopped and then started again, and for three days I couldn’t come to my senses. Fyodor Pavlovitch sent for Herzenstube, the doctor here, and he put ice on my head and tried one other remedy too.... I might have died.”
“But they say you can’t tell in advance, with epilepsy, when a fit is coming. So why do you say you’ll have one tomorrow?” Ivan asked, with a strange, irritable curiosity.
“Exactly so. You can’t tell in advance.”
“And anyway, you fell from the garret that time.”
“I climb up to the garret every day. I could fall from the garret again tomorrow. And if not, I could fall down the cellar steps. I have to go down to the cellar every day, too.”
Ivan gave him a long look.
“I can see you’re talking nonsense, and I don’t quite follow you,” he said softly, but with a kind of menace. “Are you saying you’ll pretend to be ill for three days tomorrow, eh?”
Smerdyakov had gone back to staring at the ground and fiddling with the toe of his right foot. Now he put that foot down, moved the left one forward, and said with a grin:

“If I could play a trick like that—that is, fake a fit, which wouldn’t be hard for a man who’s used to them—I would have every right to use such a means to save myself from death. Because even if Agrafena Alexandrovna comes to see his father while I’m lying ill, his honor can’t blame a sick man for not telling him. He’d be ashamed to.”

“Blast it all!” Ivan cried, his face working with anger. “Why are you always so scared for your life? Dmitri’s threats are only things he says in a temper. They mean nothing. He won’t kill you—you’re not the one he’ll kill!”
“Me first of all. He’d squash me like a fly. But what I’m even more afraid of is being taken for his accomplice when he does something mad to his father.”
“Why would anyone take you for an accomplice?”
“They’ll think I’m an accomplice, because I told him the signals as a great secret.”
“What signals? Who did you give them to? Confound you, say it plainly.”

“I have to admit,” Smerdyakov drawled with pedantic composure, “that Fyodor Pavlovitch and I share a secret in this matter. You know yourself (if you do know it) that for some days now he has been locking himself in the moment night falls, or even the evening. Lately you’ve gone up to your room early each evening, and yesterday you never came down at all. So perhaps you don’t know how carefully he now locks himself in. Even when Grigory Vassilyevitch comes to the door, he won’t open until he hears his voice. But Grigory Vassilyevitch doesn’t come, because I’m now the only one who attends him in his room. That’s how he arranged it himself, from the time this business with Agrafena Alexandrovna started. At night, though, on his orders, I go off to the lodge. So I can’t sleep before midnight. I stay on watch instead, getting up and walking around the yard, waiting for Agrafena Alexandrovna to arrive. These last few days he has been simply frantic waiting for her. His argument is that she is afraid of Dmitri Fyodorovitch (Mitya, as he calls him), ‘and so,’ says he, ‘she’ll come to me by the back way, late at night. You watch out for her,’ says he, ‘until midnight and after. If she does come, run up and knock on my door, or on the window from the garden. Knock twice to begin with, fairly gently, then three more times, quicker. Then,’ says he, ‘I’ll know at once that she’s here, and I’ll open the door to you quietly.’ He gave me a second signal in case something unexpected happens. First two knocks, then a pause, then another, much louder. Then he’ll understand that something has suddenly come up and that I need to see him, and he’ll open up so I can go in and talk to him. That’s for the case where Agrafena Alexandrovna can’t come herself but sends word. Dmitri Fyodorovitch might come as well, you see, so I have to tell him he’s near. His honor is dreadfully afraid of Dmitri Fyodorovitch. So even if Agrafena Alexandrovna had come and were shut in with him, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch turned up anywhere nearby, I’d be obliged to warn him at once by knocking three times. So the first signal, five knocks, means Agrafena Alexandrovna has come, and the second, three knocks, means ‘something important to tell you.’ His honor has shown them to me several times and explained them. Since nobody in the whole world knows these signals except me and his honor, he would open the door without the slightest hesitation and without calling out (he’s dreadfully afraid of calling out loud). Well, Dmitri Fyodorovitch knows those signals now too.”
“How does he know them? Did you tell him? How did you dare?”

“Fear made me do it. How could I dare hold it back from him? Every day Dmitri Fyodorovitch kept at me: ‘You’re deceiving me, you’re hiding something from me! I’ll break both your legs.’ So I told him the secret signals, to show him my slavish devotion and to satisfy him that I wasn’t deceiving him and was telling him everything I could.”
“If you think he’ll use those signals and try to get in, then don’t let him in.”
“But if I’m down with a fit, how am I supposed to stop him then? And even if I weren’t, would I dare, knowing how desperate he is?”
“Blast it! What makes you so certain you’re going to have a fit, confound you? Are you laughing at me?”
“How would I dare laugh at you? I’m not in the mood for laughing, with this fear on me. I feel a fit coming. I have a foreboding of it. The fright alone will bring it on.”
“Confound it! If you’re laid up, Grigory will be keeping watch. Tell Grigory ahead of time, and he’ll certainly keep him out.”

“I would never dare tell Grigory Vassilyevitch about the signals unless my master ordered it. As for Grigory Vassilyevitch hearing him and refusing to let him in, he has been unwell since yesterday, and Marfa Ignatyevna plans to give him a remedy tomorrow. They’ve only just agreed on it. It’s a very odd remedy of hers. Marfa Ignatyevna knows of a preparation and keeps it by her always. It’s a strong brew made from some herb. The secret of it is hers, and she gives it to Grigory Vassilyevitch three times a year, whenever his lumbago is so bad that he can hardly move. Then she takes a towel, soaks it in the stuff, and rubs his whole back for half an hour until it is quite red and swollen. Whatever is left in the bottle she gives him to drink, with a special prayer. Not every drop, though, because on those occasions she keeps some back and drinks it herself. And since neither of them ever touches strong drink, I assure you they both fall asleep at once and sleep soundly for a very long time. When Grigory Vassilyevitch wakes, he’s perfectly well, but Marfa Ignatyevna always has a headache from it. So if Marfa Ignatyevna carries out her plan tomorrow, they’ll hear nothing and won’t get in Dmitri Fyodorovitch’s way. They’ll be asleep.”

“What a rigmarole! And it all falls together at once, as if it were planned. You’ll have your fit and the two of them will be out cold,” cried Ivan. “Aren’t you arranging it that way?” he burst out suddenly, frowning menacingly.
“How could I?... And why would I, when everything depends on Dmitri Fyodorovitch and what he plans?... If he means to do something, he’ll do it. If not, I’m not the one pushing him at his father.”

“And why would he go to father at all, least of all sneaking in, if Agrafena Alexandrovna isn’t coming, as you say yourself?” Ivan went on, going white with anger. “You say so yourself, and the whole time I’ve been here I’ve been sure it was all the old man’s notion and that the creature won’t come to him. Why would Dmitri burst in on him if she doesn’t come? Speak up, I want to know what you’re thinking!”

“You know yourself why he’ll come. What does it matter what I think? His honor will come simply because he’s in a rage, or perhaps because my illness makes him suspicious. He’ll rush in, as he did yesterday, too impatient to wait, to search the rooms and see whether she’s slipped past him in secret. He also knows perfectly well that Fyodor Pavlovitch keeps a big envelope with three thousand roubles in it, tied with ribbon and sealed with three seals. In his own hand it says, ‘To my angel Grushenka, if she will come,’ and three days later he added, ‘for my little chicken.’ Who knows what that might lead to?”

“Nonsense!” cried Ivan, nearly beside himself. “Dmitri won’t come to steal money and kill my father to get it. He might have killed him yesterday over Grushenka, the frantic, savage fool, but he won’t steal.”

“He needs money very badly now—more badly than ever, Ivan Fyodorovitch. You don’t know how badly,” Smerdyakov explained, with perfect composure and remarkable distinctness. “He counts that three thousand as his own, too. He told me so himself. ‘My father still owes me exactly three thousand,’ he said. And there’s something else, Ivan Fyodorovitch, which is perfectly true, so consider it. It’s nearly certain, so to speak, that Agrafena Alexandrovna could make him marry her, if she cared to—the master himself, I mean, Fyodor Pavlovitch—and of course she may care to. All I’ve said is that she won’t come, but maybe she’s aiming higher, I mean to be mistress here. I know myself that Samsonov, her merchant, laughed about it with her and told her quite openly it wouldn’t be a stupid thing at all. And she has plenty of sense. She wouldn’t marry a beggar like Dmitri Fyodorovitch. So, taking that into account, Ivan Fyodorovitch, think what follows: neither Dmitri Fyodorovitch, nor you, nor your brother Alexey Fyodorovitch would get anything after the master’s death, not one rouble, because Agrafena Alexandrovna would marry him just to get her hands on all of it, every bit of the money. But if your father were to die now, there would certainly be some forty thousand, even for Dmitri Fyodorovitch, whom he hates so, because he has left no will.... Dmitri Fyodorovitch knows all that very well.”
Ivan’s face shuddered for a moment, and he flushed all at once.
“Then why on earth,” he cut in suddenly, “are you advising me to go to Tchermashnya? What did you mean by it? If I go away, you can see what will happen here.” Ivan could hardly get his breath.
“Precisely so,” said Smerdyakov, quietly and sensibly, but keeping his eyes on Ivan.
“What do you mean, ‘precisely so’?” Ivan asked, a menacing light in his eyes, holding himself in with difficulty.

“I spoke out of pity for you. In your place I’d simply drop the whole thing ... before I’d stay on in a position like this,” Smerdyakov answered, meeting Ivan’s blazing eyes with the most open look. Neither said anything.

“You’re a complete idiot, it seems, and what’s more ... a downright scoundrel.” Ivan stood up abruptly from the bench. He was about to walk straight out the gate, but stopped short and turned back to Smerdyakov. Then something strange happened. In a sudden fit, Ivan bit his lip and clenched his fists, and a moment more would have thrown himself at Smerdyakov. Smerdyakov saw it in the same instant, flinched and shrank back. But the moment went by without harm to him, and Ivan turned silently toward the gate, seemingly bewildered.
“I’m going to Moscow tomorrow, if you want to know—early tomorrow morning. That’s all!” he said suddenly, aloud and angrily. Later he himself wondered why he had needed to say it to Smerdyakov then.
“That’s the very best thing you can do,” he responded, as if he had been expecting to hear it; “only you can always be sent for by telegram from Moscow, if anything happens here.”

Ivan stopped again and turned sharply back to Smerdyakov. But a change had taken place in him too. All his easy familiarity and carelessness had vanished. His face showed attention and expectancy, eager yet timid and cringing.
“Haven’t you something more to say—something to add?” you could read in the intent look he fixed on Ivan.
“And couldn’t I be sent for from Tchermashnya as well—if something happened?” Ivan suddenly shouted, raising his voice for no reason he knew.
“From Tchermashnya as well ... yes, you could be sent for,” Smerdyakov muttered, almost whispering, looking thrown off balance but staring hard into Ivan’s eyes.
“Only Moscow is farther and Tchermashnya is closer. Do you insist on Tchermashnya to save me the cost of the fare, or to save me going so far out of my way?”

“Precisely so ...” Smerdyakov muttered, his voice breaking. He looked at Ivan with a revolting smile and prepared once more to draw back. But to his astonishment Ivan burst out laughing and went through the gate still laughing. Anyone who saw his face then would have known he wasn’t laughing from a light heart; nor could he himself have said what he felt at that moment. His movements and his walk were those of a man in a nervous frenzy.

chapters.title: VII. “It’s Always Worth While Speaking To A Clever Man”
paragraphs: And it was in the same nervous frenzy that he spoke. Meeting Fyodor Pavlovitch in the drawing-room just as he came in, he shouted to him, waving his arms, “I’m going upstairs to my room, not in to you. Good-by!” and brushed past, trying not even to look at his father. It may well be that the old man was simply too hateful to him just then. But so blunt a show of hostility surprised even Fyodor Pavlovitch. The old man obviously wanted to tell him something right away and had come out to the drawing-room on purpose to meet him. Given this friendly greeting, he stood silent and, with an ironical look, watched his son go up the stairs until he was out of sight.
“What’s got into him?” he asked Smerdyakov at once; Smerdyakov had followed Ivan in.
“He’s angry about something. Who knows?” the valet muttered evasively.
“Damn him! Let him be angry, then. Bring in the samovar and be off with you. Quick about it! Any news?”

Then came a string of questions, the sort Smerdyakov had just been complaining about to Ivan, all concerning his expected visitor. We will leave these questions out. Half an hour later the house was locked up, and the crazy old man was wandering from room to room in feverish expectation of hearing the agreed five knocks at any moment. Now and then he peered out into the darkness, and saw nothing.

It was very late, but Ivan was still awake and thinking. He stayed up that night until two. We will not set down his thoughts, though; this is not the place to look into that soul—its turn will come. Even if one tried, it would be hard to report them, because there were no thoughts in his head, only something very vague and, above all, intense agitation. He felt himself that he had lost his bearings. All sorts of strange, almost startling desires fretted him, too. After midnight, for instance, he was gripped by an intense, irresistible urge to go downstairs, open the door, go out to the lodge and beat Smerdyakov. Asked why, he could have given no exact reason, except perhaps that he loathed the valet as the man who had insulted him more seriously than anyone in the world. At other times that night he was overcome, more than once, by a sort of inexplicable, humiliating terror, which he felt was simply paralyzing his strength. His head ached and he was dizzy. A feeling of hatred rankled in his heart, as if he meant to take revenge on someone. He even hated Alyosha, remembering the talk he had just had with him. At moments he hated himself fiercely. He almost forgot to think about Katerina Ivanovna, and was greatly surprised at this afterwards, all the more because he remembered perfectly that when he had so valiantly declared to Katerina Ivanovna that he would leave for Moscow next day, something in his heart had whispered, “That’s nonsense, you’re not going, and tearing yourself away won’t be as easy as you’re boasting now.”

Years afterwards, remembering that night, Ivan recalled with peculiar disgust how he had suddenly got up from the sofa and, quietly, as if afraid someone would see him, opened the door, gone out on the staircase and listened to Fyodor Pavlovitch moving about below. He had listened for a long time—some five minutes—with a strange kind of curiosity, holding his breath, his heart pounding. Why he did all this, why he listened, he could not have said. All his life afterwards he called that “action” “infamous,” and deep in his heart he considered it the vilest action of his life. Toward Fyodor Pavlovitch himself he felt no hatred at that moment. He was simply intensely curious how the old man was walking about down there and what he might be doing. He wondered, and pictured him peeping out of the dark windows and halting in the middle of the room, listening, listening—for someone to knock. Ivan went out on the stairs to listen like this twice.

Around two o’clock, when all was quiet and even Fyodor Pavlovitch had gone to bed, Ivan lay down, firmly resolved to fall asleep at once, for he felt terribly exhausted. And fall asleep at once he did, and slept soundly without dreams, but woke early, at seven, in full daylight. Opening his eyes, he was surprised to find himself extraordinarily full of energy. He jumped up, dressed quickly, then hauled out his trunk and started packing straight away. His linen had come back from the laundress the morning before. Ivan actually smiled to think that everything was helping his sudden departure. And it was certainly sudden. The day before he had said (to Katerina Ivanovna, Alyosha and Smerdyakov) that he would leave next day. Yet he remembered that when he went to bed he had not been thinking of leaving at all, or at least had never dreamed that the first thing he would do in the morning was pack his trunk. At last his trunk and bag were ready. About nine o’clock Marfa Ignatyevna came in with her usual question, “Where will your honor take your tea, in your own room or downstairs?” He looked almost cheerful, but there was something hurried and scattered in him, in his words and gestures. He greeted his father warmly, even inquired particularly after his health, though he did not wait to hear the reply through. Then he announced that he was setting off in an hour to go back to Moscow for good, and asked him to send for the horses. His father took this news without any sign of surprise, and was ill-mannered enough to forget to show regret at losing him. Instead, he fell into a great flutter, remembering some important business of his own.

“What a fellow you are! Not telling me yesterday! Never mind, we’ll manage it all the same. Do me a big favor, my dear boy. Stop at Tchermashnya on your way. You just turn left at the Volovya station, another twelve versts and there’s Tchermashnya.”
“I’m sorry, I can’t. It’s eighty versts to the railway, and the Moscow train leaves at seven tonight. I’ll only just make it.”

“You’ll make it tomorrow or the day after. Today, turn off to Tchermashnya. Humoring your father won’t put you out much! If I weren’t tied up here, I’d have run over there myself long ago, because I have urgent business there. But here I ... this is no time for me to go.... You see, I own two pieces of woodland there. The Maslovs, an old merchant and his son, will give eight thousand for the timber. But last year I only just missed a buyer who’d have given twelve. You can’t get anyone around here to buy it. The Maslovs have everything their own way. You have to take what they offer, because no one here dares bid against them. Last Thursday the priest at Ilyinskoe wrote me that a merchant called Gorstkin, a man I know, had turned up. What makes him valuable is that he’s not from these parts, so he’s not afraid of the Maslovs. He says he’ll give me eleven thousand for the copse. Do you hear? But the priest writes that he’ll be here for a week only, so you must go at once and strike a bargain with him.”
“Well, write to the priest and he’ll strike it.”

“He can’t. He’s got no head for business. He’s an absolute treasure—I’d hand him twenty thousand to keep for me without a receipt—but he has no head for business. He’s a perfect child, a crow could fool him. And yet he’s a learned man, can you believe it? This Gorstkin looks like a peasant, he wears a blue kaftan, but he’s a regular rogue. That’s the common complaint. He’s a liar. Sometimes he lies so that you wonder why he bothers. The year before last he told me his wife was dead and he’d married another, and would you believe it, not a word of it was true? His wife never died at all, she’s alive today and thrashes him twice a week. So what you must find out is whether he’s lying or telling the truth when he says he wants to buy and would give eleven thousand.”
“I’d be no use in a business like that. I’ve no head for it either.”

“Hold on, wait! You will be of use, because I’ll tell you the signs by which you can size Gorstkin up. I’ve dealt with him for a long time. See, you have to watch his beard. He has a nasty, thin, red beard. If his beard shakes when he talks and he gets cross, that’s fine: he means what he says, he wants to do business. But if he strokes his beard with his left hand and grins, he’s trying to cheat you. Don’t watch his eyes, you’ll learn nothing from them, he’s a deep one, a rogue—watch the beard! I’ll give you a note and you show it to him. He’s called Gorstkin, though his real name is Lyagavy;[4] but don’t call him that, he’d be offended. If you come to terms with him and it looks all right, write me right away. All you need write is: ‘He’s not lying.’ Hold out for eleven thousand; you can knock off one thousand, but no more. Just think! There’s a world of difference between eight thousand and eleven. It’s as good as finding three thousand. Buyers aren’t easy to find, and I’m in desperate need of money. Just let me know it’s serious and I’ll run over and settle it. I’ll find the time somehow. But what’s the use of my galloping over there if it’s all just some idea of the priest’s? Well, will you go?”
“Oh, I can’t spare the time. Please excuse me.”

“Come on, you could do your father a favor. I won’t forget it. None of you has any heart—that’s the trouble, isn’t it? What’s a day or two to you? Where are you off to now—Venice? Your Venice will keep another two days. I would have sent Alyosha, but what use is Alyosha in a thing like that? I’m sending you just because you’re a clever fellow. Do you think I don’t see that? You know nothing about timber, but you’ve got an eye. All that’s needed is to see whether the man is in earnest. I tell you, watch his beard—if his beard shakes, you know he’s in earnest.”
“So you’re making me go to that damned Tchermashnya, are you?” cried Ivan, with a malignant smile.
Fyodor Pavlovitch did not notice the malice, or did not want to notice it, but he noticed the smile.
“Then you’ll go? You’ll go? I’ll scribble the note for you right now.”
“I don’t know if I’ll go. I don’t know. I’ll decide on the way.”

“Nonsense! Make up your mind now. My dear fellow, decide! If you get it settled, jot me a line and hand it to the priest, and he’ll forward it to me right away. That’s all I’ll ask of you. Then off to Venice with you. The priest will give you horses to take you back to Volovya station.”

The old man was absolutely delighted. He wrote the note and sent for the horses. A light lunch was brought in, with brandy. When Fyodor Pavlovitch was pleased, he usually became expansive, but today he seemed to hold himself back. He did not say a word about Dmitri, for instance. The parting left him quite unmoved, and he actually seemed at a loss for something to say. Ivan noticed this particularly. “He must be tired of me,” he thought. Only when he went out with his son onto the steps did the old man start to fuss. He would have kissed him, but Ivan hurried to hold out his hand, plainly avoiding the kiss. His father saw it at once and immediately pulled himself up.
“Well, good luck to you, good luck!” he repeated from the steps. “You’ll come again sometime, won’t you? Be sure you do. I’ll always be glad to see you. Well, Christ be with you!”
Ivan got into the carriage.
“Good-by, Ivan! Don’t be too hard on me!” the father called out one last time.
Everyone in the house came out to see him off—Smerdyakov, Marfa and Grigory. Ivan gave each of them ten roubles. Once he was seated in the carriage, Smerdyakov jumped up to straighten the rug.

“You see ... I am going to Tchermashnya,” Ivan blurted out suddenly. Once more, as the day before, the words seemed to fall from his lips on their own, and he gave a strange, nervous laugh. He remembered it long afterward.
“So the saying is true, that ‘it’s always worth while speaking to a clever man,’” Smerdyakov replied firmly, with a significant look at Ivan.

The carriage rolled off. Nothing was clear in Ivan’s soul, but he gazed eagerly at the fields, the hills, the trees, and a flock of geese flying high in the bright sky. All at once he felt very happy. He tried talking to the driver and found the peasant’s answer intensely interesting. A minute later he realized that he was not taking in a word, and that he had not really understood the answer at all. He fell silent, and even so it was pleasant. The air was fresh, pure and cool, and the sky was bright. The images of Alyosha and Katerina Ivanovna drifted into his mind. But he smiled gently and blew gently on the friendly ghosts, and they flew away. “There’s plenty of time for them,” he thought. They reached the station quickly, changed horses, and galloped on toward Volovya. “Why is it worth while speaking to a clever man? What did he mean by that?” The thought seemed suddenly to take his breath away. “And why did I tell him I was going to Tchermashnya?” They arrived at Volovya station. Ivan climbed out of the carriage, and the drivers crowded around him, haggling over the trip of twelve versts to Tchermashnya. He told them to harness the horses. He went into the station house, looked around, glanced at the overseer’s wife, and suddenly went straight back out to the entrance.
“I’m not going to Tchermashnya. Can I still get to the railway by seven, brothers?”
“We’ll just make it. Shall we bring the carriage out?”
“Right away. Is any one of you going to town tomorrow?”
“Sure. Mitri here is.”
“Can you do me a favor, Mitri? Go to my father’s, to Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, and tell him I haven’t gone to Tchermashnya. Can you?”
“Sure I can. I’ve known Fyodor Pavlovitch for ages.”
“And here’s something for you, since I imagine he won’t give you anything,” said Ivan, laughing gaily.
“You can count on it, he won’t.” Mitya laughed too. “Thank you, sir. I’ll be sure to do it.”

At seven o’clock Ivan boarded the train and set off for Moscow. “Away with the past. I’ve done with the old world for ever, and may I have no news, no echo, from it. To a new life, new places and no looking back!” But instead of delight, his soul was filled with a gloom, and his heart ached with an anguish, such as he had never known in his life. He spent the whole night thinking. The train flew on, and only at daybreak, as it neared Moscow, did he suddenly shake himself out of his brooding.
“I am a scoundrel,” he whispered to himself.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was well pleased to have seen his son off. For two hours afterward he felt almost happy and sat drinking brandy. Then something happened that was very annoying and unpleasant for everyone in the house, and it wrecked Fyodor Pavlovitch’s peace of mind at once. Smerdyakov went down to the cellar for something and fell from the top of the steps. Luckily, Marfa Ignatyevna was in the yard and heard him in time. She did not see the fall, but she heard his scream—the strange, peculiar scream she had known for years, the scream of an epileptic going down in a fit. No one could tell whether the fit had struck him as he was descending the steps, so that he must have fallen unconscious, or whether the fall and the shock had set off the fit in Smerdyakov, who was known to suffer from them. They found him at the bottom of the cellar steps, writhing in convulsions and foaming at the mouth. At first they feared he had broken something—an arm or a leg—and hurt himself badly, but “God had preserved him,” as Marfa Ignatyevna put it—nothing of the kind had happened. Getting him out of the cellar was hard, though. They called in the neighbors and managed it somehow. Fyodor Pavlovitch himself was present through the whole operation. He lent a hand, obviously alarmed and upset. The sick man did not come to; the convulsions stopped for a while and then started again, and everyone concluded that it would go the same way as a year before, when he had fallen from the garret by accident. They remembered that ice had been put on his head then. There was still ice in the cellar, and Marfa Ignatyevna had some brought up. In the evening Fyodor Pavlovitch sent for Doctor Herzenstube, who arrived at once. He was a most estimable old man, the most careful and conscientious doctor in the province. After a thorough examination, he concluded that the fit was a very violent one and might have serious consequences. For the time being, he said, he, Herzenstube, did not fully understand it, but if the present remedies failed, he would venture to try something else by tomorrow morning. The invalid was moved to the lodge, into a room next to Grigory’s and Marfa Ignatyevna’s.

After that, Fyodor Pavlovitch had one misfortune after another to endure that day. Marfa Ignatyevna cooked the dinner, and next to Smerdyakov’s, the soup was “no better than dish-water,” and the fowl was so dried up it could not be chewed. To her master’s bitter, though deserved, reproaches, Marfa Ignatyevna answered that the fowl had been a very old one to begin with, and that she had never been trained as a cook. In the evening there was fresh trouble for Fyodor Pavlovitch: he was told that Grigory, who had been unwell for the past three days, was now completely laid up with his lumbago. Fyodor Pavlovitch finished his tea as soon as he could and shut himself up alone in the house. He was in terrible excitement and suspense. That evening he reckoned on Grushenka’s coming as nearly certain. That morning Smerdyakov had assured him “that she had promised to come without fail.” The old reprobate’s heart pounded with excitement; he paced his empty rooms, listening. He had to stay alert. Dmitri might be lying in wait for her somewhere, and when she knocked on the window (Smerdyakov had told him two days before that he had shown her where and how to knock), the door must be opened at once. She must not stand a second in the passage, for fear—God forbid!—that she might be frightened and run away. Fyodor Pavlovitch had a great deal on his mind, but never had his heart been so steeped in voluptuous hopes. This time he could say almost for certain that she would come!

chapters.title: I. Father Zossima And His Visitors
paragraphs: Alyosha entered his elder’s cell with an anxious, aching heart, and he stopped in the doorway, almost astonished. He had been afraid of finding a sick man at his last gasp, perhaps unconscious. Instead the elder was sitting up in his chair. He was weak and worn out, yet his face was bright and cheerful. Visitors were gathered around him, and they were talking together quietly and happily. In fact he had left his bed only a quarter of an hour before Alyosha came. The visitors had assembled in his cell earlier and sat waiting for him to wake. Father Païssy had assured them with great confidence that “the teacher would get up and, as he had promised that morning, talk once more with those dear to his heart.” Father Païssy trusted this promise completely, as he trusted every word the dying elder spoke. Suppose he had found him unconscious, or even seen him breathe his last, and still held his promise that he would rise and say good-bye. Perhaps even then he would not have believed in death. He would have gone on expecting the dead man to revive and keep his word. That morning, as he lay down to sleep, Father Zossima had told him flatly: “I shall not die without the joy of one more conversation with you, beloved of my heart. I shall look once more on your dear face and pour out my heart to you again.” The monks who had gathered for this probably last talk with Father Zossima had been his devoted friends for many years. There were four of them. The first two were Father Iosif and Father Païssy. The third was Father Mihaïl, warden of the hermitage, a man not very old and far from learned. He came of humble people, and he had a strong will and a steadfast faith. He looked austere, but he was deeply tender, though he clearly kept this hidden, as if almost ashamed of it. The fourth, Father Anfim, was a very old, humble little monk from the poorest peasant class. He was nearly illiterate and very quiet, and he hardly spoke to anyone. He was the humblest of the humble, and he looked as if something vast and terrible, beyond his understanding, had frightened him. Father Zossima was deeply fond of this timid man and always treated him with marked respect. Yet perhaps he had said less to him than to anyone he had ever known, although he had spent years wandering with him over holy Russia. That was long ago, forty years back, when Father Zossima was just beginning his monastic life in a poor little monastery at Kostroma. Soon afterward he had gone with Father Anfim on a journey to collect alms for that poor monastery.

They were all in the bedroom, which, as we said before, was very small. There was hardly room for the four of them to sit round Father Zossima on chairs brought in from the sitting room (Porfiry the novice stood). Darkness was already coming on. The room was lit by lamps and by the candles in front of the ikons.
Seeing Alyosha standing embarrassed in the doorway, Father Zossima smiled at him joyfully and held out his hand.
“Welcome, my quiet one. Welcome, my dear, you are here too. I knew you would come.”
Alyosha went to him and bowed to the ground before him, and he wept. Something rose up from deep in his heart. His soul was shaking, and he wanted to sob aloud.

“Come now, do not weep over me yet,” said Father Zossima with a smile, laying his right hand on Alyosha’s head. “You see, I am sitting up and talking. Maybe I shall live another twenty years, as that good dear woman from Vishegorye wished me yesterday, with her little Lizaveta in her arms. God bless the mother and the little girl Lizaveta.” He crossed himself. “Porfiry, did you take her offering where I told you?”

He meant the sixty copecks that the cheerful woman had brought him the day before, to be passed on “to someone poorer than me.” Gifts like this are always made from money earned by one’s own labor, and they are offered as a penance freely chosen. The previous evening the elder had sent Porfiry to a widow whose house had recently burned down, and who had been going about begging with her children since the fire. Porfiry quickly replied that he had handed over the money as instructed, “from an unknown benefactress.”

“Get up, my dear boy,” the elder went on, speaking to Alyosha. “I want to look at you. Have you been home? Did you see your brother?” Alyosha thought it strange that he asked so confidently and so exactly about just one of his brothers. But which one? Perhaps he had sent Alyosha out yesterday and again today for that brother’s sake.
“I have seen one of my brothers,” answered Alyosha.
“I mean the elder one, the one I bowed down to.”
“I only saw him yesterday. I could not find him today,” said Alyosha.

“Hurry and find him. Go again tomorrow, and hurry. Drop everything and hurry. You may still be in time to prevent something terrible. Yesterday I bowed down before the great suffering that awaits him.”

He fell silent all at once and seemed lost in thought. His words were strange. Father Iosif, who had seen the scene the day before, exchanged a look with Father Païssy. Alyosha could not keep himself from asking:
“Father and teacher,” he began, deeply moved, “your words are too obscure.... What is this suffering that awaits him?”

“Do not ask. Yesterday I seemed to see something terrible ... as if his whole future were written in his eyes. There came a look into his eyes—and I was struck with horror at once, at what that man is preparing for himself. Once or twice in my life I have seen that look on a man’s face ... showing, as it were, the fate in store for him, and that fate, alas, came to pass. I sent you to him, Alexey, because I thought your brotherly face would help him. But everything, and all our fates, come from the Lord. ‘Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone; but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.’ Remember that. As for you, Alexey, many times I have blessed you silently because of your face. Know that,” added the elder, with a gentle smile. “This is what I think of you. You will leave these walls, but you will live in the world like a monk. You will have many enemies, yet even your enemies will love you. Life will bring you many misfortunes, but in them you will find your happiness, and you will bless life and make others bless it, which is what matters most. Well, that is your character. Fathers and teachers,” he said to his friends with a tender smile, “until today I have never told even him why this young man’s face is so dear to me. Now I will tell you. His face has been for me a remembrance and a prophecy together. When I was a child, at the dawn of my life, I had an elder brother who died before my eyes at the age of seventeen. As my life went on, I gradually came to believe that this brother was meant as a guide and a sign from above for me. Had he not entered my life, I should never have become a monk and set foot on this precious path, or so I think. He appeared to me first in my childhood, and now, at the end of my pilgrimage, it seems he has come to me a second time. It is marvelous, fathers and teachers. Alexey bears some resemblance to him in face, though not a great one. But in spirit he seems to me so like him that many times I have taken him for that young man, my brother, come back to me mysteriously at the end of my journey to remind and inspire me. I was truly amazed at so strange a fancy in myself. Do you hear this, Porfiry?” He turned to the novice who attended him. “Many times I have seen a look of mortification in your face, because I love Alexey more than you. Now you know the reason. But I love you too, know that, and many times I was grieved by your mortification. Dear friends, I want to tell you about that youth, my brother, for no one who has been in my life was more precious, more full of meaning, or more touching. My heart is full of tenderness, and at this moment I look at my whole life as though I were living it over again.”

Here I must point out that this last conversation of Father Zossima with the friends who visited him on the last day of his life has been partly preserved in writing. Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov put it down from memory, some time after his elder’s death. Whether it was only the talk of that evening, or whether he also wove in notes from earlier conversations with his teacher, I cannot say. In his account Father Zossima speaks on without a break, as if he were telling his life to his friends as a story. Yet other accounts leave no doubt that the talk that evening was shared by all. The guests did not interrupt Father Zossima often, but they did talk, and perhaps they even told some stories of their own. Besides, Father Zossima could not have gone on without pause. He sometimes gasped for breath and lost his voice, and he even lay down on his bed to rest, though he did not sleep, and his visitors stayed in their seats. Once or twice Father Païssy broke in to read from the Gospel. It is also worth noting that not one of them thought he would die that night. In the evening, after his deep sleep during the day, he seemed to have suddenly found fresh strength, and it carried him through this long conversation. It was like a last effort of love, and it gave him marvelous energy. It lasted only a short time, however, for his life was cut short at once.... But of that later. For now I will add only that I have chosen to keep to the account written by Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov. It will be shorter and less wearying, though, as I must say again, Alyosha took much from earlier conversations and added it here.
Notes on the Life of the late Priest and Monk, the Elder Zossima, taken down from his own words by Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov.
BIOGRAPHICAL NOTES
_(a)_ _Father Zossima’s Brother_

Beloved fathers and teachers, I was born in a remote northern province, in the town of V. My father was a gentleman by birth, but he had no great standing or rank. He died when I was two years old, and I have no memory of him at all. He left my mother a small house built of wood and a modest fortune, but enough to keep her and her children comfortably. There were two of us, my elder brother Markel and I. He was eight years older than I was. He had a hasty, irritable temper, but he was kind-hearted and never ironic. He was remarkably silent, especially at home, with me, with his mother and with the servants. He did well at school but could not get along with his schoolmates, though he never quarreled with them, or so my mother has told me. Six months before his death, when he was seventeen, he became friends with a political exile. This man had been sent from Moscow to our town for freethinking, and he lived there alone. He was a fine scholar who had distinguished himself in philosophy at the university. Something drew him to Markel, and he often asked him to visit. That winter the young man spent whole evenings with him, until the exile was called to Petersburg to take up his post again, at his own request, since he had powerful friends.

It was the start of Lent, and Markel would not fast. He was rude and laughed at it. “It is all silly nonsense, and there is no God,” he said, to the horror of my mother, the servants, and me as well. Though I was only nine, I was appalled at hearing such words. We had four servants, all serfs. I remember my mother selling one of them, the cook Afimya, a lame elderly woman, for sixty paper roubles, and hiring a free servant in her place.

In the sixth week of Lent my brother fell ill. He had never been strong and was prone to consumption. He was tall but thin and frail-looking, with a very pleasing face. I suppose he had caught cold. In any case, the doctor who came soon whispered to my mother that it was galloping consumption and that he would not live out the spring. My mother began to weep. She was careful not to alarm my brother, but she begged him to go to church, to confess and to receive the sacrament, since he could still get about. This angered him, and he said something profane about the church. Still, he grew thoughtful. He guessed at once that he was gravely ill, and that this was why his mother was pleading with him to confess and take the sacrament. In fact he had known for a long time that he was far from well. A year earlier he had remarked coolly at dinner, to our mother and me, “I will not be long among you. I may not live another year.” Now those words seemed like a prophecy.

Three days went by, and Holy Week arrived. On Tuesday morning my brother began going to church. “I am doing this only for you, mother, to please and comfort you,” he said. My mother wept for joy and for grief. “His end must be near,” she thought, “if he has changed so much.” But he could not go to church for long. He took to his bed, and so he had to confess and receive the sacrament at home.

Easter came late that year, and the days were bright and fine and full of fragrance. I remember that he coughed all night and slept badly, but in the morning he dressed and tried to sit in an armchair. That is how I remember him, sitting there sweet and gentle, smiling, his face bright and joyful in spite of his illness. A marvelous change had come over him, and his spirit seemed transformed. The old nurse would come in and say, “Let me light the lamp before the holy image, my dear.” Earlier he would not have let her, and would have blown it out.
“Light it, light it, dear. I was a wretch to stop you before. You are praying when you light the lamp, and I am praying when I rejoice to see you. So we are praying to the same God.”

We thought those words strange, and mother would go to her room and weep. But when she went in to him she dried her eyes and looked cheerful. “Mother, do not weep, my darling,” he would say. “I have a long life ahead of me, a long time to rejoice with you, and life is glad and joyful.”
“Oh, my dear boy, how can you speak of joy when you lie feverish all night, coughing as if you would tear yourself apart?”
“Do not cry, mother,” he would answer. “Life is paradise, and we are all in paradise, but we refuse to see it. If we wanted to, heaven would be on earth by tomorrow.”

Everyone marveled at what he said, so strange and sure was his way of speaking. We were all moved, and we wept. Friends came to see us. “Dear ones,” he would say to them, “what have I done to deserve your love? How can you love someone like me? And how was it that I never knew, and never valued it before?”

Whenever the servants came in, he would keep saying, “Dear, kind people, why do you do so much for me? Do I deserve to be waited on? If it were God’s will that I should live, I would wait on you, for we should all wait on one another.”
Mother shook her head as she listened. “My darling, it is your illness that makes you talk like this.”

“Mother, darling,” he would say, “there have to be servants and masters. But if so, I will be the servant of my servants, just as they are to me. And there is something else, mother. Each one of us has sinned against all men, and I more than any.”

Mother actually smiled at this, smiled through her tears. “How could you have sinned against all men, and more than all? Robbers and murderers have done that. But what sin have you committed yet, that you hold yourself more guilty than everyone?”

“Mother, little heart of mine,” he said (he had begun to use such strange, tender words then), “little heart of mine, my joy, believe me, each of us is truly responsible to all men, for all men and for everything. I cannot explain it to you, but I feel that it is so, even painfully. And how could we go on living as we did, getting angry and not knowing?”
So he rose each day, more sweet and joyful and loving than the day before. Then the doctor would come, an old German named Eisenschmidt:
“Well, doctor, do I have another day in this world?” he would ask, joking.
“You will have many days yet,” the doctor would answer, “and months and years too.”

“Months and years!” he would cry. “Why reckon in days? One day is enough for a man to know all happiness. My dear ones, why do we quarrel, and try to outdo each other, and nurse grudges? Let us go straight out to the garden and walk and play there, and love and value and kiss one another, and glorify life.”
“Your son cannot last long,” the doctor told my mother, as she went with him to the door. “The illness is reaching his brain.”

The windows of his room opened onto the garden. It was a shady garden with old trees, which were just coming into bud. The first birds of spring were fluttering in the branches and chirping and singing at his windows. As he watched them and admired them, he suddenly began to beg their forgiveness as well: “Birds of heaven, happy birds, forgive me, for I have sinned against you too.” None of us could understand that then, but he wept tears of joy. “Yes,” he said, “God’s glory was all around me, in birds, trees, meadows and sky. Only I lived in shame, dishonoring it all, and I never noticed the beauty and the glory.”
“You are taking too many sins on yourself,” Mother would say, weeping.

“Mother, darling, I am crying for joy, not for grief. I cannot explain it to you, but I like to humble myself before them, because I do not know how to love them enough. If I have sinned against everyone, yet everyone forgives me too, and that is heaven. Am I not in heaven now?”

And he said a great deal more that I do not remember. I do remember going into his room once when nobody else was there. It was a bright evening, the sun was going down, and the whole room was full of light. He beckoned to me and I went over to him. He put his hands on my shoulders and looked into my face, tenderly and lovingly. He said nothing for a minute. He only looked at me like that.
“Well,” he said, “go and play now. Enjoy life for me too.”

So I went out and ran off to play. And many times in my life afterwards I remembered, even with tears, how he told me to enjoy life for him too. He had many other wonderful and beautiful sayings, though we did not understand them at the time. He died in the third week after Easter. He was fully conscious, though he could no longer speak, and he did not change up to his last hour. He looked happy. His eyes shone and searched for us, and he smiled at us and beckoned us. People talked a great deal about his death, even in the town. All this made an impression on me at the time, but not too deep a one, though I cried a good deal at his funeral. I was young then, only a child. Yet a lasting impression, a hidden feeling about it all, stayed in my heart, ready to rise up and answer when its time came. And so indeed it happened.
_(b) Of the Holy Scriptures in the Life of Father Zossima_

I was left alone with my mother. Her friends began to advise her to send me to Petersburg, as other parents did. “You have only one son now,” they said, “and a fair income. If you keep him here, you may be robbing him of a brilliant career.” They suggested that I be sent to Petersburg, to the Cadet Corps, so that I could afterwards enter the Imperial Guard. My mother hesitated for a long time, because it was dreadful to part with her only child. But at last she made up her mind, though not without many tears, believing that she was acting for my happiness. She brought me to Petersburg and placed me in the Cadet Corps, and I never saw her again. For she too died, three years later. She spent those three years mourning and grieving for both of us.

From the house of my childhood I have brought away nothing but precious memories. No memories are more precious than those of early childhood in one’s first home, and that is almost always so, as long as there is any love and harmony in the family at all. Even a bad home can leave precious memories, if only the heart knows how to find what is precious in it. Among my memories of home I count my memories of the Bible, which I was very eager to read as a child. I had a book of Scripture history then, with excellent pictures, called _A Hundred and Four Stories from the Old and New Testament_. I learned to read from it. It lies on my shelf now, and I keep it as a precious relic of the past. But even before I could read, I was moved to devotion for the first time, at eight years old. I remember it well. My mother took me alone to the service on the Monday before Easter. (I do not remember where my brother was.) The day was fine. I remember it today as though I saw it now: the incense rose from the censer and floated softly upwards, and up in the cupola it mingled, in rising waves, with the sunlight streaming through the little window. The sight stirred me, and for the first time in my life I consciously received the seed of God’s word in my heart. A youth came out into the middle of the church carrying a big book. It was so large that I thought he could scarcely carry it. He laid it on the reading desk and opened it and began to read, and suddenly, for the first time, I understood something that was read in the church of God. In the land of Uz there lived a man, righteous and God-fearing, who had great wealth: so many camels, so many sheep and asses. His children feasted, and he loved them dearly and prayed for them. “It may be that my sons have sinned in their feasting.” Then the devil came before the Lord, together with the sons of God, and told the Lord that he had gone up and down the earth and under the earth. “And have you considered my servant Job?” God asked him. God boasted to the devil of His great and holy servant, and the devil laughed at God’s words. “Give him over to me, and You will see that Your servant will murmur against You and curse Your name.” So God gave up the just man He loved so much into the devil’s hands. And the devil struck down his children and his cattle and scattered his wealth, all at once, like a thunderbolt from heaven. Job tore his mantle and fell to the ground and cried aloud, “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return into the earth. The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away. Blessed be the name of the Lord for ever and ever.”

Fathers and teachers, forgive my tears, for all my childhood rises up before me again. I breathe as I breathed then, with the breast of a little child of eight, and I feel what I felt then: awe and wonder and gladness. The camels caught my imagination. So did Satan, who spoke with God like that, and God, who gave His servant up to ruin, and His servant crying out, “Blessed be Your name although You punish me.” Then there was the soft, sweet singing in the church, “Let my prayer rise up before You,” and again the incense from the priest’s censer, and the kneeling and the prayer. Ever since then (only yesterday I read it once more) I have not been able to read that sacred tale without tears. How much there is in it that is great, mysterious and unfathomable! Later I heard words of mockery and blame, proud words. “How could God hand over the most loved of His saints to amuse the devil? How could He take away his children, strike him with sore boils so that he scraped the matter from his sores with a piece of broken pot, and all for nothing, only to boast to the devil? ‘See what My saint can suffer for My sake.’” But the greatness of it lies just in its being a mystery. In it the passing show of this earth and the eternal truth are brought together. In the face of the earthly truth, the eternal truth is accomplished. On the first days of creation the Creator ended each day with praise: “It is good, what I have made.” So now He looks at Job and praises His creation again. And Job, in praising the Lord, serves not only Him but all His creation, for generations and generations and for ever and ever, since he was ordained for that. Good heavens, what a book it is, and what lessons are in it! What a book the Bible is, what a miracle, and what strength it gives to man! It is like a mold cast of the world, of man and of human nature. Everything is there, and a law for everything, for all the ages. And what mysteries are solved and revealed in it! God raises Job up again and gives him wealth again. Many years pass, and Job has other children and loves them. But how could he love those new ones, when the first children are gone, when he has lost them? Remembering them, how could he be fully happy with the new ones, however dear they might be? But he could, he could. This is the great mystery of human life: old grief passes gradually into quiet, tender joy. The mild serenity of old age takes the place of the riotous blood of youth. Each day I bless the rising sun, and my heart still sings to meet it, as before. But now I love its setting even more, with its long slanting rays, and the soft, tender, gentle memories that come with them, the dear images from my whole long, happy life. And over all of it the Divine Truth, softening, reconciling, forgiving! My life is ending, I know that well. But every day that is left to me, I feel how my earthly life touches a new life, infinite and unknown, a life that is drawing near. Its nearness sets my soul quivering with rapture, my mind glowing and my heart weeping with joy.

Friends and teachers, I have heard more than once, and lately one hears it more often, that priests, and above all village priests, complain on every side of their miserable income and their humiliating lot. They state plainly, even in print (I have read it myself), that because of their small means they are unable to teach the Scriptures to the people. And if Lutherans and heretics come and lead the flock astray, they say, they let them do it, because they have so little to live on. May the Lord increase the sustenance that is so precious to them, for their complaint is just. But truly I tell you, if anyone is to blame in this matter, half the fault is ours. The priest may be short of time. He may say truly that he is crushed all the while with work and services. Yet it is not all his time. Even he has one hour a week to remember God. And he does not work the whole year round. Let him gather people around him once a week, for an hour in the evening, if only the children at first. The fathers will hear of it, and they too will begin to come. There is no need to build halls for this. Let him take them into his own cottage. They will not spoil his cottage, because they will only be there for an hour. Let him open that book and begin to read it. Let him do it without grand words or superciliousness, without condescension, but gently and kindly, glad that he is reading to them and that they are listening attentively, loving the words himself, and stopping only now and then to explain a word the peasants do not understand. Do not be anxious. They will understand everything. The Orthodox heart will understand all! Let him read them about Abraham and Sarah, about Isaac and Rebecca, about how Jacob went to Laban and wrestled with the Lord in his dream and said, “This place is holy.” He will make an impression on the devout mind of the peasant. Let him read, especially to the children, how the brothers sold Joseph into bondage, the tender boy, the dreamer and prophet. Let him read how they told their father that a wild beast had devoured him, and showed him his blood-stained clothes. Let him read how the brothers afterwards journeyed into Egypt for corn. Joseph, by then a great ruler, was not recognized by them, and he tormented them, accused them and kept back his brother Benjamin, and all through love: “I love you, and loving you I torment you.” For all his life he remembered how they had sold him to the merchants in the burning desert, by the well, and how he had wrung his hands and wept and begged his brothers not to sell him as a slave in a strange land. And now, seeing them again after many years, he loved them beyond measure, but out of love he harassed and tormented them. In the end he left them, unable to bear the suffering of his heart, flung himself on his bed and wept. Then he wiped away his tears and went out to them joyful, and told them, “Brothers, I am your brother Joseph!” Let him read them further how happy old Jacob was to learn that his darling boy was still alive. Let him read how Jacob left his own country and went to Egypt, and died in a foreign land. He left behind his great prophecy, which had lain mysteriously hidden all his life in his meek and timid heart: that from his offspring, from Judah, would come the great hope of the world, the Messiah and Saviour.

Fathers and teachers, forgive me, and do not be angry that I have been babbling like a little child about what you have long known, and can teach me a hundred times more skillfully. I speak only out of rapture, and forgive my tears, for I love the Bible. Let him weep too, the priest of God, and let him be sure that the hearts of his listeners will throb in answer. Only a tiny little seed is needed. Drop it into the heart of the peasant and it will not die. It will live in his soul all his life, hidden amid his darkness and sin like a bright spot, like a great reminder. And there is no need of much teaching or explaining. He will understand it all simply. Do you suppose the peasants do not understand? Try reading them the touching story of the fair Esther and the haughty Vashti, or the miraculous story of Jonah in the whale. Do not forget the parables of Our Lord either. Choose especially from the Gospel of St. Luke (that is what I did). Then take from the Acts of the Apostles the conversion of St. Paul, which you must not leave out on any account. And from the _Lives of the Saints_ take, for instance, the life of Alexey, the man of God, and the greatest of all, the happy martyr and seer of God, Mary of Egypt. With these simple tales you will pierce their hearts. Give one hour a week to it in spite of your poverty, only one little hour. And you will see for yourselves that our people are gracious and grateful, and will repay you a hundredfold. They will remember the kindness of their priest and the moving words they heard from him. Of their own accord they will help him in his fields and in his house, and will treat him with more respect than before, so that his worldly well-being will even increase. The thing is so simple that sometimes one is afraid to say it, for fear of being laughed at. And yet how true it is! One who does not believe in God will not believe in God’s people. One who believes in God’s people will see His Holiness too, even if he had not believed in it until then. Only the people, and their spiritual power in the future, will convert our atheists, who have torn themselves away from their native soil.
And what use are Christ’s words unless we set an example? The people are lost without the Word of God, for their souls thirst for the Word and for all that is good.

In my youth, long ago, nearly forty years ago, I traveled all over Russia with Father Anfim, collecting funds for our monastery. One night we stayed with some fishermen on the bank of a great navigable river. A good-looking peasant lad of about eighteen joined us. He had to hurry back the next morning to tow a merchant’s barge along the bank. I noticed that he looked straight ahead with clear and tender eyes. It was a bright, warm, still night in July. A cool mist rose from the broad river. We could hear a fish splash, the birds were quiet, and everything was hushed and beautiful, everything praying to God. Only we two were awake, the lad and I, and we talked about the beauty of this world of God’s and the great mystery of it. Every blade of grass, every insect, ant and golden bee, knows its path so marvelously, though it has no intelligence. They bear witness to the mystery of God and keep accomplishing it themselves. I saw that the dear lad’s heart was moved. He told me that he loved the forest and the forest birds. He was a bird-catcher. He knew the call of each bird and could summon any of them. “I know nothing better than being in the forest,” said he, “though all things are good.”

“Truly,” I answered him, “all things are good and fair, because all is truth. Look,” said I, “at the horse, that great beast so close to man. Or look at the lowly, thoughtful ox, which feeds him and works for him. Look at their faces: what meekness, what devotion to man, who often beats them without mercy. What gentleness, what trust and what beauty! It is touching to know that there is no sin in them, for all, all except man, is sinless, and Christ was with them before us.”
“Why,” asked the boy, “is Christ with them too?”

“It cannot but be so,” said I, “since the Word is for all. All creation and all creatures, every leaf, strive toward the Word. They sing glory to God and weep to Christ, accomplishing this without knowing it, through the mystery of their sinless life. Over there,” said I, “in the forest, the dreadful bear roams, fierce and menacing, and yet innocent in it.” And I told him how a bear once came to a great saint who had taken refuge in a tiny cell in the wood. The saint pitied him. He went up to him without fear and gave him a piece of bread. “Go along,” said he, “Christ be with you,” and the savage beast went away meekly and obediently, doing no harm. The lad was delighted that the bear had gone away without hurting the saint, and that Christ was with him too. “Ah,” said he, “how good that is, how good and beautiful is all God’s work!” He sat musing, quietly and sweetly. I saw that he understood. And he slept beside me, a light and sinless sleep. May God bless youth! And I prayed for him as I went to sleep. Lord, send peace and light to Your people!

chapters.title: II. The Duel
paragraphs: _(c) Recollections of Father Zossima’s Youth before he became a Monk. The Duel_

I spent a long time at the military cadet school in Petersburg, almost eight years. Everything there was new to me, and many of my childhood impressions grew fainter, though I forgot nothing. I picked up so many new habits and opinions that I turned into a cruel, absurd, almost savage creature. I did acquire a surface polish of courtesy and social manners, along with the French language.

But all of us, myself included, looked on the soldiers who served us as cattle. I was perhaps worse than the rest in this, because I was so much more impressionable than my companions. By the time we left the school as officers, we were ready to die for the honor of the regiment. Yet not one of us had any idea what honor really meant, and if anyone had known, he would have been the first to laugh at it. Drunkenness, debauchery and devilry were almost what we prided ourselves on. I do not say we were bad by nature. All these young men were good fellows, but they behaved badly, and I behaved worst of all. What made it worse for me was that I had come into my own money. So I threw myself into a life of pleasure and plunged headlong into all the recklessness of youth.

I was fond of reading, yet, strange to say, the Bible was the one book I never opened in those days. I always carried it with me and was never parted from it. In very truth I was keeping that book “for the day and the hour, for the month and the year,” though I did not know it.

After four years of this life, I happened to be in the town of K., where our regiment was stationed at the time. We found the townspeople hospitable, rich and fond of entertainment. I was welcomed warmly everywhere, because I had a lively temperament and was known to be well off, which always counts for a great deal in the world. And then something happened that was the beginning of it all.

I became attached to a beautiful and intelligent young girl, of noble and lofty character, the daughter of highly respected people. They were well-to-do, with influence and position, and they always received me warmly and kindly. I imagined that the young lady looked on me with favor, and my heart was on fire at the thought. Later I saw and fully understood that perhaps I was not so passionately in love with her at all. I only recognized the elevation of her mind and character, which I could hardly have failed to do. But my selfishness kept me from proposing at that time. I was reluctant to give up the pleasures of my free and licentious bachelor life, in the prime of my youth and with my pockets full of money. I did drop some hint of my feelings, but I put off any decisive step for a while. Then, all of a sudden, we were ordered away to another district for two months.

When I came back two months later, I found the young lady already married to a rich landowner of the neighborhood. He was a very amiable man, still young though older than I was, connected with the best Petersburg society, which I was not, and well educated, which I also was not. I was so overwhelmed by this unexpected blow that my mind was positively clouded. The worst of it was that, as I learned then, the young landowner had been engaged to her for a long time. I had met him many times in her house, but blinded by my conceit I had noticed nothing. And this mortified me most of all: almost everybody had known about it, while I knew nothing. I was filled with sudden, uncontrollable fury. My face burned as I recalled how often I had been on the point of declaring my love to her. She had not tried to stop me or warn me, so I concluded that she must have been laughing at me all the time. Later, of course, I thought it over and remembered that she had been very far from laughing at me. On the contrary, she used to turn aside any love-making of mine with a joke and start talking about other things. But at that moment I could not reflect, and I was all eagerness for revenge. I am surprised, remembering it, that my rage and vengefulness were so extremely repugnant to my own nature. I was easygoing and found it hard to stay angry with anyone for long. So I had to work myself up artificially, and I ended by becoming revolting and absurd.

I waited for an opportunity and managed to insult my “rival” in front of a large company. I insulted him over a perfectly unrelated matter, jeering at his opinion about an important public event—it was in the year 1826[5]—and my jeer was, so people said, clever and effective. Then I forced him to demand an explanation, and I behaved so rudely that he accepted my challenge, despite the great gap between us. I was younger, a nobody, and of lower rank. I learned afterwards, for a fact, that he accepted out of jealousy too. He had been rather jealous of me on his wife’s account before they married. Now he imagined that if he swallowed my insult and refused my challenge, and if she heard of it, she might begin to despise him, and her love for him might waver. I soon found a second in a comrade, an ensign of our regiment. In those days duels were severely punished, yet dueling was a kind of fashion among the officers—so strong and deeply rooted can a brutal prejudice sometimes be.

It was the end of June, and our meeting was set for seven o’clock the next day on the edge of town. And then something happened that was truly the turning point of my life. That evening I came home in a savage and brutal mood and flew into a rage with my orderly Afanasy. I hit him twice in the face with all my strength, so that it was covered with blood. He had not been long in my service, and I had struck him before, but never with such ferocious cruelty. And believe me, though it was forty years ago, I remember it now with shame and pain. I went to bed and slept for about three hours. When I woke, day was breaking. I got up—I did not want to sleep any more—I went to the window and opened it. It looked out on the garden. I saw the sun rising. It was warm and beautiful, and the birds were singing.

“What does this mean?” I thought. “Something in my heart feels vile and shameful. Is it because I am about to shed blood? No,” I thought, “that is not what it is. Can it be that I am afraid of death, afraid of being killed? No, not that, not that at all.”... And all at once I knew what it was: I had beaten Afanasy the evening before! It all rose up in my mind, it all happened again before my eyes. He stood in front of me while I beat him straight in the face. He held his arms stiffly at his sides, his head erect, his eyes fixed on me as though he were on parade. He staggered at every blow and did not even dare to raise a hand to protect himself. That is what a man had been brought to, and it was one man beating another! What a crime! It felt as if a sharp dagger had gone right through me. I stood as though struck dumb, while the sun shone, the leaves rejoiced and the birds trilled their praise of God.... I hid my face in my hands, fell on my bed and broke into a storm of tears. And then I remembered my brother Markel and what he said on his deathbed to his servants: “My dear ones, why do you wait on me, why do you love me, am I worth your waiting on me?”

“Yes, am I worth it?” the thought flashed through me. “What am I really worth, that another man, a fellow creature, made in the likeness and image of God, should serve me?” For the first time in my life this question forced itself on me. Markel had said, “Mother, my little heart, in truth we are each responsible to all for all. It is only that men do not know this. If they knew it, the world would be a paradise at once.”

“God, can that be false too?” I thought as I wept. “In truth, perhaps I am more responsible than anyone for everything, a greater sinner than any man in the world.” And all at once the whole truth stood before me in its full light. What was I about to do? I was about to kill a good, clever, noble man who had done me no wrong. By taking away his wife’s happiness for the rest of her life, I would be torturing and killing her too. I lay there on my bed with my face in the pillow, not noticing how the time was passing. Suddenly my second, the ensign, came in with the pistols to fetch me.
“Ah,” said he, “good, you’re up already. It’s time we left. Come on!”
I did not know what to do, and I hurried back and forth, unable to decide. Still, we went out to the carriage.
“Wait here a minute,” I told him. “I’ll be right back. I forgot my purse.”
And I ran back alone to Afanasy’s little room.
“Afanasy,” I said, “yesterday I hit you twice in the face. Forgive me.”

He gave a start, as if he were frightened, and stared at me. And I saw that this was not enough. Right there, in my full officer’s uniform, I dropped at his feet and touched my forehead to the ground.
“Forgive me,” I said.
Then he was utterly aghast.
“Your honor ... sir, what are you doing? Am I worth it?”
And he burst into tears, as I had done a little while before. He hid his face in his hands, turned to the window and shook all over with sobs. I flew out to my comrade and jumped into the carriage.
“Ready,” I cried. “Ever seen a conqueror?” I asked him. “Well, here’s one for you.”
I was in ecstasy, laughing and chattering all the way. I do not remember about what.
He looked me over. “Well, brother, you’re a plucky fellow. You’ll keep up the honor of the uniform, I can see.”

So we arrived and found the others already waiting for us. We were placed twelve paces apart, and he had the first shot. I stood there cheerfully and looked him full in the face. I did not so much as blink. I looked at him with love, for I knew what I was going to do. His bullet just grazed my cheek and ear.
“Thank God,” I cried, “nobody’s dead!” Then I seized my pistol, turned around and hurled it far into the wood. “That’s where you belong,” I cried.
I turned to my adversary.

“Forgive me, sir, for being a young fool,” I said. “I insulted you for no reason, and I made you fire at me. I am ten times worse than you, and more, maybe. Tell that to the person you hold dearest in the world.”
No sooner had I said this than all three of them started shouting at me.
“Good heavens,” cried my adversary, irritated, “if you didn’t want to fight, why couldn’t you have left me in peace?”
“Yesterday I was a fool. Today I’m wiser,” I answered him cheerfully.
“About yesterday I believe you, but about today I find it hard to agree,” said he.
“Bravo,” I cried, and clapped my hands. “I agree with you there as well. I deserved that!”
“Will you shoot, sir, or won’t you?”
“No, I won’t,” I said. “If you like, fire at me again, but you would do better not to.”
The seconds were shouting too, mine most of all: “Can you disgrace the regiment like this, facing your opponent and begging his pardon! If I had only known!”
I stood facing them all, no longer laughing.
“Gentlemen,” I said, “is it really so remarkable these days to meet a man who can repent of his stupidity and openly admit he was wrong?”
“Not in a duel!” my second cried again.

“That is just what is so strange,” I said. “I should have owned up the moment I arrived, before he fired a shot, before I led him into a great and deadly sin. But we have made our life so grotesque that behaving like that was almost impossible. My words could mean something to him only after I had stood his fire at twelve paces. If I had spoken earlier, he would have said, ‘He’s a coward, the sight of the pistols has scared him, it’s no use listening to him.’ Gentlemen,” I cried suddenly, speaking straight from my heart, “look around you at the gifts of God: the clear sky, the pure air, the tender grass, the birds. Nature is beautiful and sinless, and we, only we, are sinful and foolish. We do not understand that life is heaven. We have only to understand that, and heaven will at once be fulfilled in all its beauty. We shall embrace each other and weep.”
I would have said more, but I could not. My voice broke with the sweetness and youthful joy of it, and my heart was filled with a bliss I had never known before in my life.
“All very rational and edifying,” said my antagonist, “and you are certainly an original.”
“Laugh if you like,” I said, laughing too, “but later you will approve of me.”
“Oh, I can approve of you right now,” said he. “Will you shake hands? I believe you are perfectly sincere.”
“No,” I said, “not yet. Wait until I have become a better man and earned your respect. Then shake my hand, and you will do well.”
We went home, my second berating me the whole way while I kept kissing him. All my comrades heard of the affair at once, and that same day they gathered to sit in judgment on me.
“He has disgraced the uniform,” they said. “He should resign his commission.”
Some defended me: “He stood the shot,” they said.
“Yes, but he was afraid of the second one and begged for pardon.”

“If he had been afraid of getting shot, he would have fired his own pistol before asking pardon, rather than throwing it loaded into the forest. No, there is something else behind this, something original.”

I enjoyed listening to them and looking at them. “My dear friends and comrades,” said I, “do not trouble yourselves about my resigning, because I have already done it. I sent in my papers this morning, and as soon as I get my discharge I will enter a monastery. That is why I am leaving the regiment.”
As soon as I had said this, every one of them burst out laughing.
“You ought to have told us that first. That explains everything. We can’t judge a monk.”

They laughed and could not stop, and not scornfully but kindly and merrily. All at once they felt friendly toward me, even the ones who had condemned me most sternly. For the whole month until my discharge came, they made a great fuss of me. “Ah, you monk,” they would say. Everyone said something kind to me. They began trying to talk me out of it, even to pity me: “What are you doing to yourself?”
“No,” they would say, “he is a brave fellow. He stood fire, and he could have fired his own pistol too. But the night before, he dreamed he would become a monk, and that’s why he did it.”

It was the same with the society of the town. Until then I had been received kindly but had attracted no special attention. Now everyone got to know me at once, and everyone invited me. They laughed at me, but they loved me. I should mention that although everybody talked openly about our duel, the authorities paid it no mind. My antagonist was a close relation of our general, and since no blood had been shed and nothing serious had come of it, and since I had resigned my commission, they treated it as a joke. And from then on I began to speak out loud and without fear, regardless of their laughter, for their laughter was always kindly and never spiteful. These conversations mostly took place in the evenings, in the company of ladies. Women especially liked to hear me, and they made the men listen.
