“But how can I possibly be responsible for everyone?” they would laugh in my face. “Am I, for instance, responsible for you?”

“It is no wonder you do not know it,” I would answer, “since the whole world has long been going a different way. We take the plainest lies for truth, and we demand the same lies from others. Here, for once in my life, I have acted sincerely, and, well, you all take me for a madman. You are friendly to me, but still, you see, you all laugh at me.”

“But how could we not be friendly to you?” said my hostess with a laugh. The room was full of people. Suddenly the young lady stood up, the one the duel had been fought over, the one I had lately meant to marry. I had not seen her come in. She rose, walked over to me and held out her hand.
“I want you to know,” she said, “that I am the first who does not laugh at you. I thank you with tears, and I respect you for what you did that day.”

Her husband came over too, and then they all gathered round me and very nearly kissed me. My heart was full of joy. But one man in particular caught my eye, a man of middle age who had come up with the rest. I knew his name already, yet I had never met him or spoken a word to him before that evening.
_(d) The Mysterious Visitor_

He had held office in our town for many years. His position was a prominent one, everyone respected him, he was rich, and he was known for his kindness. He gave large sums to the almshouse and the orphanage, and he was generous in secret as well, which only came out after he died. He was about fifty, almost stern in appearance, and he did not talk much. He had been married some ten years, and his wife, who was still young, had borne him three children. Well, the next evening I was sitting alone in my room when the door suddenly opened and in walked this gentleman.

I should say, by the way, that I no longer lived in my old lodgings. As soon as I left the army, I rented rooms from an old lady, the widow of a government clerk. Her servant waited on me. The reason I had moved into her house at all was that, coming back from the duel, I had sent Afanasy back to the regiment. After my last talk with him I was ashamed to look him in the face. That is how quick a worldly man is to feel shame at a righteous deed.

“For the last few days,” said my visitor, “I have listened to you with great interest as you spoke in various houses. At last I wanted to meet you in person, so that we might talk more freely. Would you grant me that favor, dear sir?”

“Gladly, with the greatest pleasure. I shall count it an honor.” I said it, though I felt almost dismayed, so deeply did this man impress me from the first moment. Others had listened to me with interest and attention, but nobody had ever come to me looking so serious, so stern and so intent. And now he had come to my own rooms. He sat down.
“I see that you have great strength of character,” he said. “You have dared to serve the truth, even at the risk of everyone’s contempt.”
“You may be praising me too highly,” I replied.

“No, not too highly,” he answered. “Believe me, what you did is much harder than you think. That is what struck me, and that is the only reason I have come to you,” he went on. “Tell me, please, if my curiosity, which may be improper, does not annoy you, what exactly did you feel, if you can remember, at the moment you decided to ask forgiveness at the duel? Do not take my question for an idle one. I have a private reason for asking, which I may explain later, if God wills that we come to know each other better.”
The whole time he spoke, I looked him straight in the face. All at once I felt complete trust in him, and I was very curious too, for I sensed that his soul held some strange secret.

“You ask what exactly I felt when I asked my opponent’s forgiveness,” I answered. “But I had better begin at the beginning, with something I have told no one yet.” And I told him everything that had passed between Afanasy and me, and how I had bowed down at his feet to the ground. “So you can see for yourself,” I concluded, “that at the duel it was easier for me. I had made a start already at home. Once I was on that road, going further along it was not hard at all. It became a source of joy and happiness.”
I liked the way he looked at me while he listened. “All of this,” he said, “is most interesting. I shall come and see you again and again.”

From then on he came to see me almost every evening. We could have become closer friends, if only he had ever spoken of himself. But of himself he said hardly a word, while he never stopped asking about me. Still, I grew very fond of him and talked to him quite openly about all I felt. “For why,” I thought, “should I need to know his secrets, when I can see without them that he is a good man? And grave as he is, and older than I, he still comes to see a youngster like me and treats me as an equal.” I learned a great deal of value from him, for he had a lofty mind.

“That life is heaven,” he said to me suddenly, “is a thought I have turned over for a long time.” Then he added all at once, “In fact, I think of nothing else.” He looked at me and smiled. “I am more sure of it than you are. I will tell you later why.”
I listened and thought that he clearly wanted to tell me something.
“Heaven,” he went on, “lies hidden in every one of us. It lies hidden in me now. If I choose, it will be revealed to me tomorrow and for all time.”
I looked at him. He spoke with deep feeling, and he gazed at me mysteriously, as if he were putting a question to me.

“As for our being all responsible to all and for all, over and above our own sins, you were quite right to think so. It is wonderful that you grasped its whole meaning at once. And truly, once men understand this, the Kingdom of Heaven will be no dream for them but a living reality.”
“And when?” I cried out bitterly. “When will that happen? Will it ever happen? Or is it only a dream of ours?”

“So you do not believe it?” he said. “You preach it and do not believe it yourself. Believe me, this dream, as you call it, will certainly come true. It will come, but not yet, for every process has its law. This is a spiritual, a psychological process. If the world is to be changed and made new, men must first turn to another path in their minds. Until you have truly, in actual fact, become a brother to everyone, brotherhood will not come. No scientific teaching, no common interest, will ever teach men to share property and privilege with the same fairness to all. Everyone will think his share too small. They will always be envying one another, complaining and attacking. You ask when it will come. It will come, but first we must pass through a time of isolation.”
“What do you mean by isolation?” I asked him.

“Why, the isolation that rules everywhere, most of all in our age. It is not yet fully grown. It has not yet reached its limit. Each man strives to hold his individuality as far apart as he can. Each wants the fullest possible life for himself. But all his efforts end not in a fuller life but in self-destruction, because instead of finding himself he ends in utter solitude. In our age all mankind has broken up into separate units. They all keep apart, each in his own rut. Each stands aloof, hiding himself and what he owns from the rest, and he ends by being pushed away by others and pushing them away. He piles up riches alone and thinks, ‘How strong I am now, how safe!’ In his madness he does not see that the more he piles up, the further he sinks into helplessness that destroys him. For he is used to trusting himself alone and to cutting himself off from the whole. He has trained himself not to believe in help from others, from men or from humanity, and he trembles only lest he lose his money and the privileges he has won. In these days, men in their mockery have stopped seeing, everywhere, that real safety lies in standing together with others, not in each one’s lonely effort. But this terrible individualism must come to an end, and suddenly all will see how unnaturally they have been parted from one another. It will be the spirit of the time, and people will be amazed that they sat so long in darkness without seeing the light. And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the heavens.... Until then, though, we must keep the banner flying. Sometimes, even if he must do it alone and even if he seems to be acting like a madman, a man has to set an example. He must draw other souls out of their loneliness and rouse them to some act of brotherly love, so that the great idea does not die.”

So our evenings went by, one after another, in this stirring and passionate talk. I gave up society and called on my neighbors far less often. My vogue, besides, was somewhat past. I do not say this to complain, for they still loved me and treated me kindly, but there is no denying that fashion is a mighty power in society. I came to look on my mysterious visitor with admiration. I enjoyed his intelligence, and I also began to see that he was brooding over some plan in his heart and perhaps preparing for a great deed. Perhaps he was pleased that I showed no curiosity about his secret and made no attempt to learn it, by direct question or by hints. But in the end I saw that he seemed to be showing signs of wanting to tell me something. About a month after his first visit this had become quite plain.
“Do you know,” he said to me once, “that the people in town are very inquisitive about us? They wonder why I visit you so often. Let them wonder, for _soon all will be explained_.”

At times a strange agitation would seize him, and nearly always he would then get up and leave. At times he would fix a long, piercing gaze on me, and I would think, “Now he is going to say something.” But he would abruptly start talking about some ordinary, familiar matter. He often complained of headaches too.
One day, with no warning at all, after he had been talking with great fervor for a long time, I saw him turn pale. His face twitched, and he stared hard at me.
“What is it?” I said. “Are you ill?” He had just been complaining of a headache.
“I ... you know ... I murdered someone.”
He said this and smiled, his face white as chalk. “Why is he smiling?” That thought flashed through my mind before I took in anything else. I turned pale too.
“What are you saying?” I cried.
“You see,” he said, with a pale smile, “what it has cost me to say the first word. Now it is said, I feel I have taken the first step, and I shall go on.”

For a long time I could not believe him. I did not believe him then, but only after he had come to me three days running and told me all of it. I thought he was mad, but I ended by being convinced, to my great grief and amazement. His crime was great and terrible.

Fourteen years earlier he had murdered a landowner’s widow, a rich and beautiful young woman who owned a house in our town. He fell passionately in love with her, told her so, and tried to persuade her to marry him. But she had already given her heart to another man, an officer of noble birth and high rank, who was away at the front at that time, though she expected him back soon. She refused his proposal and begged him to stop calling on her. After he had stopped, he used what he knew of the house to slip in one night through the garden and over the roof, at great risk of being caught. But, as often happens, a crime carried out with extraordinary boldness is more likely to succeed than others.

He climbed in through the skylight into the attic and went down the ladder. He knew the door at the foot of it was sometimes left unlocked, because the servants were careless. He hoped to find it so, and he did. In the dark he made his way to her bedroom, where a lamp was burning. As if on purpose, both her maids had gone off, without asking leave, to a birthday party in the same street. The other servants slept in their quarters or in the kitchen on the ground floor. The sight of her asleep set his passion blazing, and then spiteful, jealous rage seized his heart. Like a drunken man, out of his mind, he drove a knife into her heart, so that she did not even cry out. Then, with devilish and criminal cunning, he made sure that suspicion would fall on the servants. He was vile enough to take her purse, to open her chest with keys from under her pillow and take things out of it, doing all this the way some ignorant servant would, leaving valuable papers and taking only money. He took some of the larger gold objects but left smaller things worth ten times as much. He also took a few things for himself as keepsakes, but of that later. When he had done this dreadful deed, he went back the way he had come.

Neither the next day, when the alarm was raised, nor at any time later in his life, did anyone dream of suspecting him. Nobody even knew of his love for her, for he was always reserved and silent and had no friend to whom he would have opened his heart. People saw him merely as an acquaintance of the dead woman, and not a close one, since for the past two weeks he had not even called on her. Suspicion fell at once on one of her serfs, a man called Pyotr, and every circumstance bore it out. The man knew, and his mistress had not hidden it, that she had to send one of her serfs as a recruit and had decided on him, because he had no family and his behavior was poor. People had heard him threaten angrily, drunk in a tavern, to kill her. Two days before her death he had run away and was staying nobody knew where in the town. The day after the murder he was found on the road out of town, dead drunk, with a knife in his pocket, and by chance his right hand was stained with blood. He declared that he had had a nosebleed, but no one believed him. The maids admitted that they had gone to the party and that the street door had stood open until they got back. And a number of similar details came to light, all throwing suspicion on the innocent servant.

They arrested him and he was tried for the murder. But a week after his arrest the prisoner came down with a fever and died, unconscious, in the hospital. There the matter ended. The judges, the authorities and everyone in the town stayed convinced that the crime was the work of the servant who had died in the hospital, and no one else. And after that the punishment began.

My mysterious visitor, now my friend, told me that at first he felt no pangs of conscience whatever. He was wretched for a long time, but not for that reason. He only regretted that he had killed the woman he loved, that she was gone, that by killing her he had killed his love while the fire of passion was still in his veins. Of the innocent blood he had shed, of the murder of a fellow creature, he hardly thought. He could not bear the thought that she might have become another man’s wife, and so for a long time his conscience told him he could not have acted otherwise.

At first the servant’s arrest worried him, but the man’s illness and death soon set his mind at rest. As he reasoned at the time, the man had evidently died not of the arrest or the fright but of a chill caught on the day he ran away, when he lay all night on the damp ground, dead drunk. The theft of the money and other things troubled him little, for he argued that it had been done not for gain but to throw off suspicion. The sum was small, and soon afterwards he donated all of it, and much more, to the fund for keeping up an almshouse in the town. He did this deliberately, to quiet his conscience about the theft, and it is a remarkable fact that for a long time he really was at peace. He told me so himself. Then he threw himself into a career of great activity in the service. He volunteered for a hard and laborious duty that took up two years, and being a man of strong will, he almost forgot the past. Whenever it came back to him, he tried not to think of it at all. He became active in philanthropy as well. He founded and helped support many institutions in the town, did a good deal in the two capitals, and was elected a member of philanthropic societies in both Moscow and Petersburg.

In the end, though, he started brooding over the past, and the strain was more than he could bear. Then a fine, intelligent girl took his fancy, and soon afterward he married her. He hoped that marriage would lift his lonely gloom. He thought that if he began a new life and conscientiously did right by his wife and children, he would leave the old memories behind for good. The very opposite happened. Within the first month of the marriage he was being fretted all the time by one thought: “My wife loves me—but what if she knew?” When she first told him she would soon bear him a child, he was troubled. “I am giving life, but I have taken life.” Children came. “How dare I love them, teach and educate them? How can I talk to them of virtue? I have shed blood.” They were splendid children, and he longed to caress them. “But I can’t look at their innocent, candid faces. I am unworthy.”

Finally the blood of his murdered victim began to haunt him, bitterly and ominously: the young life he had destroyed, the blood that cried out for vengeance. He began to have awful dreams. But he was a man of fortitude, and for a long time he endured his suffering, thinking: “I shall expiate everything by this secret agony.” That hope too was in vain. The longer it went on, the worse his suffering grew.

Society respected him for his active benevolence, though his stern and gloomy character awed everyone. But the more he was respected, the less he could bear it. He confessed to me that he had thought of killing himself. Yet another idea began to haunt him, one he had at first dismissed as impossible and unthinkable, though in the end it gripped his heart so hard that he could not shake it off. He dreamed of standing up, going out and confessing before everyone that he had committed murder. For three years this dream had pursued him, taking different forms. At last he came to believe with his whole heart that if he confessed his crime, his soul would be healed and he would be at peace forever. But this belief filled him with terror, for how could he ever carry it out? And then came what happened at my duel.
“Looking at you, I have made up my mind.”
I looked at him.
“Is it possible,” I cried, clasping my hands, “that such a small thing could bring you to such a decision?”

“My decision has been growing for three years now,” he answered, “and what you told me only put the finishing touch on it. Looking at you, I blamed myself, and I envied you.” He said this almost sullenly.
“But no one will believe you,” I pointed out. “It was fourteen years ago.”
“I have proof, solid proof. I will show it.”
Then I wept and kissed him.

“Tell me one thing, just one thing,” he said, as though everything hung on me. “My wife, my children! My wife may die of grief. My children won’t lose their rank or property, but they’ll be a convict’s children, and forever! And what a memory, what a memory of me I shall leave in their hearts!”
I said nothing.
“And to be torn away from them, to leave them forever? It’s forever, you know, forever!”
I sat still and prayed silently. At last I got up, afraid.
“Well?” He looked at me.
“Go,” I said, “and confess. Everything passes; only the truth remains. When your children are grown, they will understand how noble your decision was.”

That time he left me looking like a man who had made up his mind. Yet for more than two weeks afterward he came to me every evening, still getting ready, still unable to bring himself to do it. He made my heart ache. One day he would arrive full of resolve and say with fervor:

“I know it will be heaven for me, heaven, the moment I confess. For fourteen years I’ve been in hell. I want to suffer. I will take my punishment and begin to live. You can go through the world doing wrong, but there’s no way back. Now I don’t dare love my neighbor, or even my own children. Good God, perhaps my children will understand what my punishment has cost me, and they won’t condemn me! God is not in strength but in truth.”
“Everyone will understand your sacrifice,” I told him. “If not at once, then later. For you have served truth, the higher truth, which is not of this earth.”
He would go away looking comforted. But the next day he would be back, bitter, pale and sarcastic.

“Every time I come, you look at me so inquisitively, as if to say, ‘He still hasn’t confessed!’ Wait a bit, and don’t despise me too much. It’s not as easy as you think. Maybe I won’t do it at all. You won’t go and inform on me, will you?”
Far from watching him with prying curiosity, I was afraid even to look at him. I was sick with anxiety, and my heart was full of tears. At night I could not sleep.

“I’ve just come from my wife,” he went on. “Do you know what the word ‘wife’ means? When I went out, the children called after me, ‘Good-by, father, hurry back and read _The Children’s Magazine_ with us.’ No, you can’t understand that! No one learns wisdom from another man’s woe.”
His eyes glittered and his lips twitched. Suddenly he brought his fist down on the table so hard that everything on it jumped. He had never done such a thing before; he was such a gentle man.

“But do I have to?” he cried. “Must I? No one has been condemned, no one has been sent to Siberia in my place. The man died of a fever. And I’ve been punished for the blood I shed by what I’ve suffered. Besides, I won’t be believed. They won’t believe my proofs. Do I need to confess? Do I? I’m ready to keep on suffering for the rest of my life for the blood I shed, if only my wife and children can be spared. Would it be just to drag them down with me? Aren’t we making a mistake? What is right in this case? And will people see it, will they appreciate it, will they respect it?”

“Good Lord!” I thought. “At a moment like this he is thinking of other people’s respect!” I felt so sorry for him that I believe I would have shared his fate if that could have comforted him. I saw he was beside himself. I was horrified, for I understood with my heart as well as my mind what such a decision meant.
“Decide my fate!” he cried again.

“Go and confess,” I whispered. My voice failed me, but I said it firmly. I picked up the New Testament from the table, the Russian translation, and showed him the Gospel of St. John, chapter 12, verse 24:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.”
I had been reading that very verse when he came in. He read it too.

“That’s true,” he said, but he smiled bitterly. “The things you find in those books are terrible,” he said after a pause. “It’s easy enough to push them at a person. And who wrote them? Can men really have written them?”
“The Holy Spirit wrote them,” I said.
“It’s easy for you to prattle on,” he said, smiling again, this time almost with hatred.
I took the book again, opened it somewhere else and showed him the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 10, verse 31. He read:
“It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”
He read it and simply threw the book down. He was shaking all over.

“A dreadful text,” he said. “I’ll admit you’ve picked fitting ones.” He got up from his chair. “Well!” he said. “Good-by. Perhaps I won’t come again ... we’ll meet in heaven. So for fourteen years I have been ‘in the hands of the living God.’ That is how one must think of those fourteen years. Tomorrow I will beg those hands to let me go.”
I wanted to take him in my arms and kiss him, but I did not dare. His face was twisted and dark. He left.

“Good God,” I thought, “what has he gone off to face!” I dropped to my knees before the ikon and wept for him before the Holy Mother of God, our swift defender and helper. I spent half an hour praying in tears. It was late, nearly midnight. Suddenly the door opened and he came in again. I was surprised.
“Where have you been?” I asked him.
“I think,” he said, “I’ve forgotten something ... my handkerchief, I think.... Well, even if I haven’t forgotten anything, let me stay a little.”
He sat down. I stood over him.
“You sit down too,” he said.
I sat. For two minutes we sat in silence. He looked at me intently and suddenly smiled (I remembered that), then stood up, embraced me warmly and kissed me.
“Remember how I came to you a second time,” he said. “Do you hear? Remember it!”
And he went out.
“Tomorrow,” I thought.

And so it was. I did not know that evening that the next day was his birthday. I had stayed in for the last few days, so I had had no chance to hear of it from anyone. Every year on that day he held a great gathering, and everyone in town came. This time was no different. After dinner he walked into the middle of the room holding a paper—a formal declaration addressed to the chief of his department, who was there. He read it aloud to the whole company. It gave a full account of the crime, in every detail.
“I cut myself off from men as a monster. God has visited me,” he said in conclusion. “I want to suffer for my sin!”

Then he took out all the things he had kept for fourteen years, which he thought would prove his crime, and laid them on the table. There were the murdered woman’s jewels, which he had stolen to turn suspicion away. There was a cross and a locket taken from her neck, with a portrait of her betrothed inside. There was her notebook, and two letters: one from her betrothed, telling her he would soon be with her, and her unfinished reply, left on the table to be sent next day. He had carried off those two letters—what for? Why had he kept them for fourteen years afterward, instead of destroying them as evidence against him?

And this is what happened. Everyone was amazed and horrified. No one would believe it, and they thought he had lost his wits, though they all listened with intense curiosity. A few days later every house had settled and agreed that the poor man was mad. The authorities could not refuse to take up the case, but they too let it drop. The trinkets and letters gave them pause, but they decided that even if these proved genuine, no charge could rest on them alone. Besides, she might have given him those things as a friend, or asked him to look after them for her. I heard afterward, though, that the murdered woman’s friends and relatives had proved the things were hers, and that there was no doubt about it. Yet nothing, in the end, was fated to come of it.

Five days later, everyone had heard that he was ill and in danger of dying. I cannot explain what his illness was; they said it was something with his heart. But word got out that his wife had talked the doctors into examining his state of mind as well, and that they had concluded he was insane. I gave nothing away, though people hurried to question me. And when I wanted to visit him, I was kept away for a long time, above all by his wife.

“You are the one who made him ill,” she told me. “He was always gloomy, but this past year people noticed he was strangely excited and did odd things. And now you have destroyed him. Your preaching has brought him to this. For the last month he was always with you.”

Indeed, not only his wife but the whole town was against me and blamed me. “It’s all your doing,” they said. I kept silent, and in fact I rejoiced in my heart, for I plainly saw God’s mercy toward a man who had turned on himself and punished himself. I could not believe he was insane.

At last they let me see him, since he insisted on saying good-by to me. I went in and saw at once that not only his days but his hours were numbered. He was weak and yellow, his hands shook, and he gasped for breath, but his face was full of tender, happy feeling.
“It is done!” he said. “I’ve been longing to see you for so long. Why didn’t you come?”
I did not tell him that they had refused to let me in.

“God has had pity on me and is calling me to Himself. I know I am dying, but for the first time in so many years I feel joy and peace. There was heaven in my heart from the moment I did what I had to do. Now I dare to love my children and kiss them. Neither my wife, nor the judges, nor anyone else has believed it. My children will never believe it either. I see God’s mercy to them in that. I shall die, and my name will be spotless for them. And now I feel God near. My heart rejoices as in Heaven ... I have done my duty.”
He could not go on. He gasped for breath and pressed my hand warmly, gazing at me with fervor. We did not talk for long, because his wife kept peeping in at us. But he had time to whisper to me:
“Do you remember how I came back to you that second time, at midnight? I told you to remember it. Do you know what I came back for? I came to kill you!”
I gave a start.

“When I left you, I went out into the darkness and wandered the streets, fighting with myself. And suddenly I hated you so much I could hardly stand it. He is all that binds me now, I thought, and he is my judge. I can’t refuse to face my punishment tomorrow, because he knows everything. It wasn’t that I was afraid you would betray me (I never even thought of that). I thought, ‘How can I look him in the face if I don’t confess?’ And if you had been at the other end of the earth, but alive, it would have made no difference. I could not bear the thought that you were alive, knowing everything and condemning me. I hated you as if you were the cause, as if you were to blame for it all. I came back to you then, remembering that there was a dagger lying on your table. I sat down and asked you to sit, and for a whole minute I turned it over in my mind. If I had killed you, that murder would have ruined me even if I had never confessed the other. But I didn’t think about that at all, and at that moment I didn’t want to. I only hated you and longed to take my revenge on you for everything. The Lord defeated the devil in my heart. But I tell you, you were never nearer death.”

A week later he died. The whole town followed him to the grave. The chief priest gave a speech full of feeling. Everyone mourned the terrible illness that had cut his life short. But after the funeral the whole town turned against me, and people even refused to see me. Some, at first a few and then more, did begin to believe his story. They came to me and questioned me with great interest and eagerness, for man loves to see the righteous brought down and disgraced. But I held my tongue, and very soon afterward I left the town. Five months later, by God’s grace, I set out on the safe and blessed path, praising the unseen finger that had guided me to it so clearly. And to this day I remember in my prayers the servant of God, Mihail, who suffered so greatly.

chapters.title: III. Conversations And Exhortations Of Father Zossima
paragraphs: _(e) The Russian Monk and his possible Significance_

Fathers and teachers, what is a monk? In the educated world these days, some people say the word with a sneer and others use it as a curse, and this contempt for monks keeps growing. It is true, sadly true, that many monks are sluggards, gluttons, libertines and insolent beggars. Educated people point at these and say: “You are idlers, useless to society. You live off other people’s labor. You are shameless beggars.” Yet there are so many gentle, humble monks who long for solitude and for fervent prayer in peace! People notice them less, or say nothing about them. And how surprised people would be if I told them that the salvation of Russia may come once more from these gentle monks who long to pray alone! For in peace and quiet they are truly being made ready “for the day and the hour, the month and the year.” In the meantime, in their solitude, they keep the image of Christ fair and undefiled, in the purity of God’s truth, just as it came down to them from the Fathers of old, the Apostles and the martyrs. When the time comes, they will show it to the tottering creeds of the world. That is a great thought. That star will rise out of the East.

That is how I see the monk. Is my view false? Is it too proud? Look at the worldly, at everyone who sets himself above the people of God. Has God’s image, and His truth, not been distorted in them? They have science, but science holds nothing except what the senses can grasp. The spiritual world, the higher part of man’s being, they reject entirely. They dismiss it with a kind of triumph, even with hatred. The world has proclaimed the reign of freedom, especially in recent times. But what do we see in this freedom of theirs? Nothing but slavery and self-destruction! For this is what the world says:

“You have desires, so satisfy them, for you have the same rights as the richest and most powerful. Do not be afraid to satisfy them. Multiply your desires, even.” That is the world’s modern doctrine, and in it they see freedom. And what comes of this right to multiply desires? Among the rich, isolation and spiritual suicide. Among the poor, envy and murder. For the poor have been handed rights, but nobody has shown them how to satisfy their wants. The world’s people insist that it is growing more and more united, more and more tied together in brotherly community, now that it has overcome distance and can send thoughts flying through the air.

Alas, put no faith in a union of that kind. Men understand freedom as the multiplying and quick satisfying of desires, and so they warp their own nature. They breed in themselves many senseless, foolish desires and habits and absurd fancies. They live only for mutual envy, for luxury and show. Having dinners, visits, carriages, rank and slaves to wait on you is thought a necessity. For it they sacrifice life, honor and human feeling, and some even kill themselves when they cannot have it. We see the same among those who are not rich, while the poor drown their unsatisfied need and their envy in drink. But soon they will drink blood in place of wine. They are being led toward it. I ask you, is such a man free? I knew a “champion of freedom” who told me himself that when he was denied tobacco in prison, he suffered so badly from the lack of it that he nearly betrayed his cause to get tobacco again! Yet a man like that says, “I am fighting for the cause of humanity.”

How can such a man fight? What use is he? He may be good for some action that is quickly over, but he cannot last. It is no wonder that instead of winning freedom they have sunk into slavery. Instead of serving brotherly love and the union of mankind, they have fallen, on the contrary, into quarrels and isolation. My mysterious visitor and teacher told me so when I was young. And so the idea of serving humanity, of brotherly love and the solidarity of mankind, is fading more and more from the world. Sometimes it is even met with derision. For how can a man shake off his habits? What can become of him when he is so enslaved to satisfying the countless desires he has made for himself? He is isolated. What does the rest of humanity matter to him? They have managed to pile up a bigger heap of things, but there is less joy in the world.

The monastic way is very different. People laugh at obedience, fasting and prayer, yet only through them lies the road to real, true freedom. I cut away my superfluous, unnecessary desires. I subdue my proud and wanton will and chastise it with obedience. With God’s help I reach freedom of spirit, and with it spiritual joy. Who is better able to conceive a great idea and serve it, the rich man in his isolation, or the man who has freed himself from the tyranny of material things and habits? People reproach the monk for his solitude: “You have shut yourself away behind monastery walls to save your own soul, and forgotten the brotherly service of humanity!” But we shall see who proves the more zealous for brotherly love. For it is not we who are isolated but they, though they cannot see it. In the old days the leaders of the people came from among us, and why not again? The same gentle, humble ascetics will rise up and go out to work for the great cause. The salvation of Russia comes from the people, and the Russian monk has always stood with the people. We are isolated only if the people are isolated. The people believe as we do. A reformer who does not believe will never accomplish anything in Russia, however sincere his heart and however great his genius. Remember that! The people will meet the atheist and overcome him, and Russia will be one and Orthodox. Take care of the peasant and guard his heart. Go on educating him quietly. That is your duty as monks, for the peasant has God in his heart.
(_f_) _Of Masters and Servants, and of whether it is possible for them to be Brothers in the Spirit_

Of course I do not deny that the peasants have their sin too. The fire of corruption is spreading before our eyes, hour by hour, working its way down from above. The spirit of isolation is coming upon the people as well. Moneylenders and devourers of the commune are rising up. The merchant is already hungrier and hungrier for rank. He tries to look cultured without a trace of culture in him, and to that end he meanly despises his old traditions and is even ashamed of the faith of his fathers. He calls on princes, though he is only a peasant gone bad. The peasants are rotting in drunkenness and cannot break the habit. And the cruelty to their wives, even to their children! All from drunkenness! In the factories I have seen children of nine, frail, rickety, stooped and already depraved. The stuffy workshop, the din of the machines, work all day long, the foul language and the drink, the drink. Is that what a little child’s heart needs? He needs sunshine, children’s games, good examples all around him, and at least a little love. This must stop, monks. No more torturing of children. Rise up and preach against it. Hurry, hurry!

But God will save Russia. The peasants are corrupted and cannot give up their filthy sin, yet they know that God curses it and that they do wrong when they sin. So our people still believe in righteousness, still have faith in God and still weep tears of devotion.

The upper classes are another matter. They follow science and want to build justice on reason alone, without Christ as before, and they have already proclaimed that there is no crime and no sin. That is consistent, for if you have no God, what does crime mean? In Europe the people are already rising against the rich with violence, and their leaders everywhere are leading them to bloodshed and teaching them that their wrath is righteous. But their “wrath is accursed, for it is cruel.” God will save Russia, as He has saved her many times. Salvation will come from the people, from their faith and their meekness.

Fathers and teachers, watch over the people’s faith, and this will not be a dream. All my life our great people have struck me with their dignity, a true and seemly dignity. I have seen it myself, I can bear witness to it, I have seen it and marveled at it, I have seen it in spite of the degrading sins and the poverty-stricken look of our peasants. They are not servile. Even after two centuries of serfdom they are free in manner and bearing, without insolence, and neither revengeful nor envious. “You are rich and noble, you are clever and talented. Well, be so, God bless you. I respect you, but I know that I too am a man. By respecting you without envy, I prove my dignity as a man.”

In truth, if they do not say this (they do not yet know how to say it), they act it. I have seen it myself and known it myself. And, would you believe it, the poorer the Russian peasant is, the plainer this serene goodness shows. The rich among them are mostly corrupted already, and much of that comes from our own carelessness and indifference. But God will save His people, for Russia is great in her humility. I dream of seeing our future, and I seem already to see it clearly. It will come to pass that even the most corrupt of our rich men will end up ashamed of his riches before the poor. The poor, seeing his humility, will understand and give way to him, and will answer his honorable shame with joy and kindness. Believe me, it will end like that. Things are moving that way. Equality is found only in the spiritual dignity of man, and only among us will that be understood. If we were brothers, there would be fraternity. Before that, they will never agree on dividing wealth. We keep the image of Christ, and it will shine out to the whole world like a precious diamond. So may it be, so may it be!

Fathers and teachers, something touching once happened to me. On my wanderings I met my old orderly, Afanasy, in the town of K. Eight years had passed since I parted from him. He happened to see me in the marketplace, knew me, ran up to me, and how delighted he was! He simply pounced on me: “Master dear, is it you? Is it really you I see?” He took me home with him.

He was out of the army now. He was married and already had two little children. He and his wife made their living as peddlers in the marketplace. His room was poor, but bright and clean. He sat me down, put on the samovar and sent for his wife, as if my visit were a feast day for them. He brought me his children: “Bless them, Father.”

“Is it for me to bless them? I am only a humble monk. I will pray for them. And for you, Afanasy Pavlovitch, I have prayed every day since that day, for it all came from you,” I said. And I explained that to him as well as I could. And what do you think? The man kept staring at me and could not believe that I, his former master and an officer, stood before him in such clothes and such a position. It made him weep.
“Why are you crying?” I said. “Be glad for me instead, dear friend, whom I can never forget, for my path is a glad and joyful one.”
He did not say much. He just kept sighing and shaking his head over me, tenderly.
“What happened to your fortune?” he asked.
“I gave it to the monastery,” I answered. “We live in common.”

After tea I began to say good-by. Suddenly he brought out half a rouble as a gift for the monastery, and I saw him hurriedly press another half-rouble into my hand: “That is for you on your wanderings. It may come in useful, Father.”

I took his half-rouble, bowed to him and his wife, and went out rejoicing. As I walked I thought: “Here we both are, he at home and I on the road, sighing and shaking our heads, no doubt, and yet smiling in the joy of our hearts as we remember how God brought us together.”

I have never seen him again since. I had been his master and he my servant, but when we exchanged a loving kiss with softened hearts, a great human bond was between us. I have thought about this a great deal, and this is what I think now: is it so unthinkable that this grand, simple-hearted unity might in time become universal among the Russian people? I believe that it will come to pass, and that the time is near.

About servants I will add this. In the old days, when I was young, I often lost my temper with servants: “the cook had served something too hot, the orderly had not brushed my clothes.” What taught me better then was a thought of my dear brother’s, which I had heard from him in childhood: “Am I worth it, that another should serve me and be ordered about by me in his poverty and ignorance?” And I wondered at the time that such simple, self-evident ideas are so slow to come to our minds.

There cannot fail to be servants in the world, but act so that your servant is freer in spirit than he would be if he were no servant. Why can I not be a servant to my servant and even let him see it, with no pride on my side and no mistrust on his? Why should my servant not be like my own kin, so that I take him into my family and am glad to do so? This can be done even now, and it will lead to the grand unity of men in the future. Then a man will not look for servants for himself, nor wish to turn his fellow creatures into servants as he does now. He will long, on the contrary, with his whole heart, to be the servant of all, as the Gospel teaches.

And can it be a dream that in the end man will find his joy only in deeds of light and mercy, and not, as now, in cruel pleasures: in gluttony, fornication, ostentation, boasting and the envious rivalry of one man with another? I firmly believe it is not a dream, and that the time is near. People laugh and ask: “When will that time come? Does it look like coming?” I believe that with Christ’s help we shall achieve this great thing. And think how many ideas in the history of mankind were unthinkable ten years before they appeared! Yet when their appointed hour came, they came forth and spread over the whole earth. So it will be with us. Our people will shine out in the world, and all men will say: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the corner-stone of the building.”

And we may put a question to the scornful themselves: if our hope is a dream, when will you build your edifice and order things justly by your intellect alone, without Christ? If they declare that they are the ones advancing toward unity, only the simplest-hearted among them believe it. One can truly marvel at such simplicity. In truth, their dreams are more fantastic than ours. They aim at justice, but they deny Christ, and they will end by flooding the earth with blood, for blood cries out for blood, and he that taketh up the sword shall perish by the sword. Without Christ’s covenant they would slaughter one another down to the last two men on earth. Those last two men would not be able to restrain each other in their pride, and one would kill the other and then himself. That would come to pass, were it not for Christ’s promise that for the sake of the humble and meek the days shall be shortened.

When I was still in an officer’s uniform, soon after my duel, I spoke about servants in company, and I remember that everyone was amazed at me. “What!” they asked. “Are we to sit our servants down on the sofa and offer them tea?” And I answered: “Why not, sometimes at least?” Everyone laughed. Their question was frivolous and my answer was not clear, but the thought in it was to some extent right.
(_g_) _Of Prayer, of Love, and of Contact with other Worlds_

Young man, never forget prayer. Whenever you pray sincerely, there will be new feeling and new meaning in it, which will give you fresh courage, and you will understand that prayer is an education. Remember also, every day and whenever you can, to say to yourself, “Lord, have mercy on all who appear before You today.” For every hour and every moment, thousands of men leave life on this earth, and their souls appear before God. And how many of them go in solitude, unknown, sad and dejected, because no one grieves for them or even knows whether they ever lived! And behold, from the other end of the earth perhaps, your prayer for their rest will rise to God, though you did not know them and they did not know you. How touching it must be for a soul that stands in dread before the Lord to feel, at that moment, that someone is praying for him too, that a fellow creature is left on earth who loves him too! And God will look more graciously on you both. For if you have felt so much pity for him, how much more pity will He feel, Who is infinitely more loving and merciful than you! And He will forgive him for your sake.

Brothers, do not be afraid of men’s sin. Love a person even in his sin, for that is the likeness of God’s own love, and the highest love there is on earth. Love everything God has made, the whole of it and each grain of sand. Love every leaf and every ray of God’s light. Love the animals, love the plants, love everything. If you love everything, you will see the divine mystery in all things. Once you have seen it, you will understand it a little more each day. In the end you will love the whole world with a love that holds everything in it. Love the animals. God gave them the beginnings of thought and a joy that nothing disturbs. Do not disturb it. Do not torment them, do not rob them of their happiness, do not work against God’s purpose. Man, do not boast that you are above the animals. They are without sin, while you, for all your greatness, foul the earth by your very presence on it and leave the mark of your filth behind you. Alas, this is true of nearly every one of us! Love children most of all, for they too are sinless, like angels. They are here to soften and purify our hearts, and in some way to lead us. Woe to anyone who offends a child! It was Father Anfim who taught me to love children. That kind, quiet man would often spend on sweets and cakes for the children the farthings people gave us as we wandered. He could not walk past a child without being touched. That was the sort of man he was.

There are thoughts that leave a man at a loss, above all when he looks at the sin of others. He wonders whether he should use force or humble love. Always settle on humble love. If you settle on that once and for all, you can conquer the whole world. Loving humility is wonderfully strong. It is the strongest thing there is, and nothing else compares with it.

Every day, every hour, every minute, go around yourself and look at yourself, and make sure the picture you give is a decent one. Say you pass a little child. You pass him spiteful, with ugly words, with an angry heart. You may not even have noticed the child, but he has seen you, and your ugly, ignoble image may stay in his defenseless heart. You do not know it, but you may have planted an evil seed in him, and it may grow. And all because you were not careful in front of the child, because you had not trained yourself in a watchful, actively kind love. Brothers, love is a teacher, but one has to know how to get it. It is hard to get, it costs a great deal, and it is won slowly, by long labor. For we must love not only now and then, for a moment, but always. Anyone can love now and then. Even the wicked can.

My brother asked the birds to forgive him. That sounds senseless, but it is right, because everything is like an ocean. Everything flows and runs together, and a touch in one place sets something moving at the other end of the earth. It may be senseless to ask the birds for forgiveness. But the birds would be happier near you, a little happier at least, and so would children and every animal, if you were a nobler person than you are now. It is all like an ocean, I tell you. Then you would pray to the birds too. You would be consumed by a love that takes in everything, in a kind of transport, and you would ask them to forgive your sin as well. Treasure this ecstasy, however senseless it may look to men.

My friends, pray to God for gladness. Be glad like children, like the birds of heaven. And do not let men’s sin trouble you in your work. Do not fear that it will wear your work away and keep it from being finished. Do not say, “Sin is mighty, wickedness is mighty, our evil surroundings are mighty, and we are alone and helpless. Our evil surroundings are wearing us away and keeping our good work from being done.” Flee from that gloom, children! There is only one way to be saved. Take the blame on yourself and make yourself answerable for the sins of all men. That is the truth, you know, friends. As soon as you sincerely make yourself answerable for everything and for everyone, you will see at once that it really is so, and that you are to blame for every person and every thing. But if you push your own laziness and weakness onto others, you will end by sharing the pride of Satan and complaining against God.

About the pride of Satan, this is what I think. It is hard for us on earth to grasp it, and so it is easy to fall into error and share in it, even to imagine that we are doing something grand and fine. Many of the strongest feelings and impulses in our nature, in fact, we cannot grasp on earth. Do not let that trip you up, and do not think it can excuse you for anything. For the Eternal Judge asks of you what you can grasp, not what you cannot. You will know that yourself later, for then you will see all things as they are and will not argue with them. Here on earth we are, so to speak, wandering off course. If we did not have the precious image of Christ before us, we would be undone and altogether lost, like the human race before the flood. A great deal on earth is hidden from us. But to make up for that, we have been given a precious, mysterious sense of our living bond with the other world, the higher world of heaven. The roots of our thoughts and feelings are not here, but in other worlds. That is why philosophers say that we cannot take in the reality of things on earth.

God took seeds from other worlds and sowed them on this earth. His garden grew, and everything came up that could come up. But whatever grows is alive only through its sense of touching other, mysterious worlds. If that feeling grows weak in you, or is destroyed, the heavenly growth in you will die. Then you will be indifferent to life, and even come to hate it. That is what I think.
_(h) Can a Man judge his Fellow Creatures? Faith to the End_

Above all, remember that you cannot be anyone’s judge. For no one can judge a criminal until he recognizes that he is just such a criminal as the man standing in front of him, and that he may be more to blame than anyone for that very crime. When he understands that, he will be able to judge. That sounds absurd, but it is true. If I had been righteous myself, perhaps there would be no criminal standing before me. If you can take upon yourself the crime of the criminal your heart is judging, take it at once. Suffer for him yourself, and let him go without a word of blame. And even if the law makes you his judge, act in the same spirit as far as you can, for he will go away and condemn himself more bitterly than you have done. Suppose that after your kiss he goes away unmoved and mocking you. Do not let that trip you up. It shows only that his time has not yet come. It will come in its own time. And if it never comes, no matter. If not he, then another will take his place, and will understand and suffer, and will judge and condemn himself, and the truth will be fulfilled. Believe that. Believe it without doubt, for in that lies all the hope and faith of the saints.

Work without stopping. Suppose you remember at night, as you go to sleep, “I have not done what I should have done.” Get up at once and do it. Suppose the people around you are spiteful and callous and will not listen to you. Fall down before them and ask their forgiveness, for in truth you are to blame that they do not want to listen. And if you cannot speak to them in their bitterness, serve them in silence and humility, and never lose hope. If all men abandon you and even drive you out by force, then, when you are left alone, fall on the ground and kiss it. Water it with your tears, and it will bear fruit, even though no one saw or heard you in your solitude. Believe to the end, even if all men went astray and you were the only one left faithful. Make your offering even then, and praise God in your loneliness. And if two of you are gathered together, then there is a whole world, a world of living love. Embrace each other tenderly and praise God, because His truth has been fulfilled, if only in the two of you.

If you sin yourself, and grieve to the point of death over your sins, or over a sudden sin, then be glad for others. Be glad for the righteous man. Be glad that if you have sinned, he is righteous and has not sinned.

If the evil that men do stirs you to anger and crushing distress, even to a wish for revenge on the evil-doers, avoid that feeling above all others. Go at once and look for suffering for yourself, as if you yourself were guilty of that wrong. Take that suffering and bear it, and your heart will be comforted. You will understand that you too are guilty, because you could have been a light to the evil-doers, like the one sinless man, and you were not a light to them. If you had been a light, you would have lit the way for others too, and the evil-doer might have been saved from his sin by your light. And suppose your light was shining and you see that men were not saved by it. Hold firm, and do not doubt the power of the heavenly light. Believe that if they were not saved, they will be saved later. And if they are not saved later, their sons will be, for your light will not die even when you are dead. The righteous man departs, but his light stays. Men are always saved after the death of the one who saves them. Men reject their prophets and kill them, but they love their martyrs and honor the very people they have killed. You are working for the whole, you are acting for the future. Seek no reward, for your reward on this earth is great: the spiritual joy that is given only to the righteous man. Do not fear the great or the mighty, but be wise and always calm. Know the measure, know the times, and study that. When you are left alone, pray. Love to throw yourself on the ground and kiss it. Kiss the earth and love it with an unceasing, consuming love. Love all men, love everything. Seek that rapture and ecstasy. Water the earth with the tears of your joy, and love those tears. Do not be ashamed of that ecstasy. Prize it, for it is a gift of God, and a great one. It is not given to many, only to the chosen.
_(i) Of Hell and Hell Fire, a Mystic Reflection_

Fathers and teachers, I ask myself, “What is hell?” My answer is that it is the suffering of being unable to love. Once, in an existence without end, beyond measure in time and space, a spiritual creature was given a power when he came to earth. He could say, “I am and I love.” Once, only once, he was given a moment of active, _living_ love. For that, earthly life was given to him, and with it times and seasons. And that happy creature turned the priceless gift away. He did not value it or love it. He scorned it and stayed hard. Such a one, after leaving the earth, sees Abraham’s bosom and speaks with Abraham, as the parable of the rich man and Lazarus tells us. He sees heaven and can go up to the Lord. But that is exactly his torment: to go up to the Lord without ever having loved, to be brought near to those who have loved, when he despised their love. For he sees clearly, and says to himself, “Now I understand. Though I thirst to love now, my love will have nothing great in it, no sacrifice, because my earthly life is over. Abraham will not come, even with one drop of living water (that is the gift of earthly, active life) to cool the burning thirst for spiritual love that is in me now, though I despised it on earth. There is no more life for me, and there will be no more time! Though I would gladly give my life for others, it can never be, for the life that could be sacrificed for love has passed, and now a gulf is fixed between that life and this existence.”

People speak of hell fire in a material sense. I do not go into that mystery, and I avoid it. But I think that if there were fire in the material sense, they would be glad of it. I imagine that in bodily pain their far greater spiritual pain would be forgotten for a moment. Besides, that spiritual pain cannot be taken from them, because the suffering is not outside them but inside. And if it could be taken from them, I think it would be even bitterer for those unhappy creatures. Even if the righteous in Paradise forgave them, seeing their torments, and called them up to heaven in their boundless love, that would only multiply their torments. It would wake in them a still keener, flaming thirst for a love that answers, a love that is active and grateful, and that is now impossible. Yet in the timidity of my heart I imagine that the very recognition of this impossibility would in the end console them. By accepting the love of the righteous along with the impossibility of repaying it, by this submission and the work of this humility, they will reach at last a certain likeness of the active love they scorned in life, something like its outward form.... I am sorry, friends and brothers, that I cannot put this clearly. But woe to those who have killed themselves on earth, woe to the suicides! I believe no one can be more wretched than they. They tell us it is a sin to pray for them, and outwardly the Church, so to speak, disowns them. But in my secret heart I believe that we may pray even for them. Love can never be an offense to Christ. For such as these I have prayed inwardly all my life, I admit it, fathers and teachers, and even now I pray for them every day.

Oh, there are some who stay proud and fierce even in hell, though they know the absolute truth for certain and see it plainly. There are some terrible ones who have given themselves over completely to Satan and his proud spirit. For these, hell is voluntary and consumes them forever. They are tortured by their own choice. They have cursed themselves, cursing God and life. They live on their vengeful pride like a starving man in the desert who sucks the blood out of his own body. But they are never satisfied. They refuse forgiveness, and they curse God who calls them. They cannot look on the living God without hatred, and they cry out that the God of life should be destroyed, that God should destroy Himself and everything He has made. And they will burn in the fire of their own rage forever, and long for death and annihilation. But they will not reach death....

Here the manuscript of Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov ends. I repeat that it is incomplete and in pieces. The biographical details, for instance, cover only the earliest youth of Father Zossima. As for his teaching and opinions, what we find is a collection of sayings that were plainly spoken on very different occasions. What he said in his last few hours has not been set apart from the rest, but its general character can be seen from what we have in Alexey Fyodorovitch’s manuscript.

In the end the elder’s death came quite unexpectedly. The people gathered around him that last evening knew that his death was near. Still, it was hard to imagine it would come so suddenly. On the contrary, as I said before, his friends saw him that night apparently so cheerful and talkative that they were convinced his condition had changed for the better, at least for a time. Even five minutes before he died, they said afterwards in amazement, there was no way of foreseeing it. He seemed suddenly to feel a sharp pain in his chest. He went pale and pressed his hands to his heart. Everyone got up from their seats and hurried to him. But though he was in pain, he still looked at them with a smile. He slid slowly from his chair to his knees, then bowed his face to the ground, stretched out his arms, and, as if in joyful ecstasy, praying and kissing the ground, he quietly and joyfully gave up his soul to God.

News of his death spread at once through the hermitage and reached the monastery. His closest friends, and those whose office made it their duty, began to lay out the body according to the ancient ritual, and all the monks gathered in the church. Before dawn the news reached the town. By morning the whole town was talking about it, and crowds were pouring out of town toward the monastery. But this will be told in the next book. I will only add here that before a day was over, something happened that was so unexpected, so strange, so upsetting and bewildering in its effect on the monks and the townspeople, that even after all these years that day of general suspense is still vividly remembered in the town.
PART III

chapters.title: I. The Breath Of Corruption
paragraphs: The body of Father Zossima was prepared for burial according to the established ritual. As is well known, the bodies of dead monks and hermits are not washed. The Church Ritual says: “If any one of the monks departs in the Lord, the monk designated (that is, the one whose office it is) shall wipe the body with warm water. First he shall make the sign of the cross with a sponge on the forehead of the deceased, on the breast, on the hands and feet and on the knees, and that is enough.” Father Païssy did all this himself. Then he dressed the deceased in his monastic garb and wrapped him in his cloak. By custom the cloak was slit a little, so that it could be folded around him in the form of a cross. On his head he put a hood with an eight-cornered cross. The hood was left open, and the dead man’s face was covered with black gauze. An icon of the Saviour was put in his hands. Toward morning he was laid in the coffin, which had been made ready long before. It was decided to leave the coffin in the cell all day, in the larger room where the elder used to receive his visitors and fellow monks. The deceased had been a priest and a monk of the strictest rule, so the Gospel, not the Psalter, had to be read over his body, by monks in holy orders. Father Iosif began the reading right after the requiem service. Father Païssy wanted to go on reading the Gospel over his dead friend all day and all night afterward. For the present, though, he and the Father Superintendent of the Hermitage were both very busy and occupied. Something extraordinary had begun to show among the monks, the visitors from the monastery hostels and the crowds flocking from the town: an unheard-of, even “unseemly” excitement and impatient expectation. As time went on, it became more and more marked. The Superintendent and Father Païssy did their utmost to calm the general bustle and agitation.

When it was fully daylight, some people began bringing their sick from the town, mostly children. It was as though they had been waiting for exactly this moment. They were plainly convinced that the dead elder’s remains had the power to heal, and that this would show itself at once, in keeping with their faith. Only then did it become clear how completely everyone in our town had accepted Father Zossima as a great saint while he lived. And those who came were far from all being of the humbler classes.

Father Païssy found this intense expectation among the believers unseemly, displayed as it was with such haste and openness, even with impatience and almost insistence. He had long foreseen something of the sort, but the actual show of feeling went beyond anything he had expected. Whenever he came across monks who showed this excitement, he began to reprove them. “Expecting something extraordinary so immediately,” he said, “shows a levity that is possible in worldly people but unseemly in us.”

But little attention was paid to him, and Father Païssy noticed it uneasily. Yet he himself (if the whole truth must be told) secretly cherished, at the bottom of his heart, almost the same hopes, and could not help knowing it. He was indignant at the too impatient expectation around him, and saw in it light-mindedness and vanity. Even so, it was particularly unpleasant to him to meet certain persons whose presence filled him with serious misgivings. In the crowd in the dead man’s cell he noticed, with an inward aversion (for which he at once reproached himself), Rakitin and the monk from Obdorsk, who was still staying in the monastery. Of both of them Father Païssy felt suddenly suspicious for some reason—though, indeed, he might well have felt the same about others.

Of everyone in that excited crowd, the monk from Obdorsk fussed the most. You met him wherever you turned. He asked questions here and listened there, and all around he whispered with a strange, secretive manner. Impatience was written all over his face, and even a kind of irritation.

As for Rakitin, as came out later, he had come to the hermitage so early at the special request of Madame Hohlakov. She was a good-hearted but weak-minded woman, and she could not have been admitted to the hermitage herself. As soon as she woke and heard of Father Zossima’s death, such intense curiosity seized her that she sent Rakitin off at once. He was to keep a careful lookout and report to her by letter every half-hour or so “_everything that takes place_.” She regarded Rakitin as a most religious and devout young man. He was particularly clever at getting around people and taking on whatever part he thought most to their taste, whenever he saw the slightest advantage in it for himself.

The day was bright and clear, and many of the visitors were crowding among the tombs. There were especially many of these around the church, and more were scattered about the hermitage. Walking around the grounds, Father Païssy thought of Alyosha. He had not seen him for some time, in fact not since the night. The moment he thought of him, he spotted him in the farthest corner of the hermitage garden. Alyosha was sitting on the tombstone of a monk who had been famous long ago for his saintliness. His back was to the hermitage and his face to the wall, and he seemed to be hiding behind the stone. Father Païssy went up and saw that he was weeping quietly but bitterly, with his face in his hands, and that sobs were shaking his whole body. Father Païssy stood over him for a little.

“Enough, dear son, enough, dear,” he said at last, with feeling. “Why are you weeping? Rejoice, do not weep. Don’t you know this is the greatest of his days? Just think where he is now, at this very moment!”
Alyosha glanced at him and uncovered his face, which was swollen with crying like a child’s. But he turned away at once without a word and hid his face in his hands again.
“Maybe it is well,” said Father Païssy thoughtfully. “Weep if you must. Christ has sent you those tears.”

“Your touching tears are only a relief to your spirit, and they will help to gladden your dear heart,” he added to himself as he walked away from Alyosha, thinking of him lovingly. He moved away quickly, though, because he felt that he too might weep, looking at him.

Meanwhile time was passing. The monastery services and the requiems for the dead followed in their due course. Father Païssy again took Father Iosif’s place by the coffin and began reading the Gospel. But before three o’clock in the afternoon, the thing took place that I alluded to at the end of the last book. It was so unexpected by all of us and so contrary to the general hope that, I repeat, this trivial incident is remembered in minute detail to this day in our town and all the surrounding neighborhood. I may add, for myself personally, that I find it almost repulsive to recall that event. It caused such frivolous agitation and was a stumbling block to so many, though in reality it was the most natural and trivial matter. I should of course have left it out of my story altogether, if it had not had a very strong influence on the heart and soul of the chief, though future, hero of my story, Alyosha. It formed a crisis and turning point in his spiritual development. It gave a shock to his intellect, which in the end strengthened it for the rest of his life and gave it a definite aim.

And so, to return to our story. Before dawn, when they laid Father Zossima’s body in the coffin and brought it into the front room, the people around the coffin raised the question of opening the windows. But this suggestion, made casually by someone, got no answer and was almost unnoticed. Some of those present may perhaps have noticed it inwardly, only to think that expecting decay and corruption from the body of such a saint was an actual absurdity. It called for pity (if not a smile) for the lack of faith and the frivolity it implied. For they expected something quite different.

And, behold, soon after midday there were signs of something. At first they were observed only in silence by those who came in and out, each evidently afraid to share the thought in his mind. But by three o’clock the signs had become so clear and unmistakable that the news quickly reached all the monks and visitors in the hermitage. It soon made its way to the monastery and threw all the monks into amazement. Finally, in the shortest possible time, it spread to the town and excited everyone in it, believers and unbelievers alike. The unbelievers rejoiced. As for the believers, some of them rejoiced even more than the unbelievers, for “men love the downfall and disgrace of the righteous,” as the deceased elder had said in one of his exhortations.

The fact is that a smell of decomposition began to come from the coffin. It grew gradually stronger, and by three o’clock it was quite unmistakable. In all the past history of our monastery no such scandal could be recalled. And in no other circumstances could such a scandal have been possible as the one that showed itself, in unseemly disorder, among the very monks themselves immediately after this discovery. Afterward, even many years afterward, some sensible monks were amazed and horrified when they recalled that day, that the scandal could have reached such proportions. For in the past, monks of very holy life had died, God-fearing old men whose saintliness was acknowledged by all. Yet from their humble coffins too the breath of corruption had come, naturally, as from all dead bodies, and that had caused no scandal or even the slightest excitement. Of course there had been saints in the monastery in former times whose memory was carefully preserved and whose relics, according to tradition, showed no signs of corruption. The monks regarded this fact as touching and mysterious. They cherished the tradition of it as something blessed and miraculous, and as a promise, by God’s grace, of still greater glory from those tombs in the future.

One of these, whose memory was especially cherished, was an old monk named Job, who had died seventy years before at the age of a hundred and five. He had been a celebrated ascetic, strict in fasting and silence. His tomb was pointed out to every visitor on arrival with peculiar respect and mysterious hints of great hopes connected with it. (That was the very tomb on which Father Païssy had found Alyosha sitting that morning.) Another memory cherished in the monastery was that of the famous Father Varsonofy, who had died only recently and had preceded Father Zossima as elder. During his lifetime all the pilgrims to the monastery had revered him as a crazy saint. There was a tradition that both of these men had lain in their coffins as though alive, that they had shown no signs of decomposition when they were buried, and that a holy light had shone in their faces. Some people even insisted that a sweet fragrance had come from their bodies.

Yet in spite of these edifying memories, it would be hard to explain the frivolity, absurdity and malice that showed themselves beside Father Zossima’s coffin. In my private opinion, several different causes were at work at the same time. One was a deep-rooted hostility to the institution of elders as a pernicious innovation, an antipathy hidden deep in the hearts of many of the monks. Even more powerful was jealousy of the dead man’s saintliness, which had been so firmly established during his lifetime that it was almost forbidden to question it. The late elder had won many hearts, more by love than by miracles, and had gathered around him a mass of loving followers. None the less, or rather all the more on that account, he had awakened jealousy and so had come to have bitter enemies, secret and open, not only in the monastery but in the world outside it. He did no one any harm, but “Why do they think him so saintly?” That question alone, repeated again and again, gave rise at last to an intense, insatiable hatred of him. That, I believe, was why many people were extremely delighted at the smell of decomposition that came so quickly, when not a day had passed since his death. At the same time, some of those who had until then been reverently devoted to the elder were almost mortified and personally affronted by this incident. This was how it happened.

Once the signs of decomposition had begun to appear, the monks’ faces gave away their secret reasons for going into the cell. They went in, stayed a little while, and hurried out to confirm the news to the other monks crowded outside. Some of these shook their heads sadly. Others did not even try to hide the delight that gleamed plainly in their malignant eyes. And no one reproached them for it now, or spoke up in protest. This was strange, since most of the monks had been devoted to the dead elder. But it seemed that God had, this time, let the minority have the upper hand for a while.

Visitors from outside, particularly those of the educated class, soon went into the cell too, with the same spying intent. Few of the peasantry went in, though there were crowds of them at the gates of the hermitage. After three o’clock the rush of worldly visitors increased greatly, no doubt because of the shocking news. People came who would not otherwise have come that day and had not meant to, and among them were some personages of high standing. But outward decorum was still kept up. Father Païssy, with a stern face, went on reading the Gospel aloud, firmly and distinctly. He seemed not to notice what was going on around him, though in fact he had observed something unusual long before. But at last the murmurs, at first subdued and then gradually louder and more confident, reached even him. “It shows God’s judgment is not as man’s,” Father Païssy suddenly heard. The first to say it was a layman, an elderly official from the town, known as a man of great piety. But he only said aloud what the monks had been whispering for some time. They had reached this damning conclusion long before, and the worst of it was that a kind of triumphant satisfaction in it showed more plainly every moment. Soon they began to lay aside even outward decorum, and almost seemed to feel they had a sort of right to do so.
“Why should _this_ have happened?” some of the monks said, at first with a show of regret. “He had a small frame, and his flesh was dried up on his bones. What was there to decay?”

“It must be a sign from heaven,” others rushed to add, and nobody objected; that view was taken up at once. People also pointed out that natural decay, as in any dead sinner, would have shown later, after twenty-four hours at least. This early rotting “was in excess of nature,” so the finger of God was plain. It was a sign. The argument seemed beyond answering.

Gentle Father Iosif, the librarian, one of the dead man’s great favorites, tried to answer some of the spiteful talkers. “This is not held everywhere alike,” he told them. Bodies of the just staying free of decay was no dogma of the Orthodox Church, he said, merely an opinion. Even in the most Orthodox lands, on Athos for instance, the smell of decay did not greatly disturb people. There the chief mark of a saved soul’s glorification was not an incorrupt body but the color of the bones, once the body had lain in the earth for many years and rotted away. “And if the bones are yellow as wax, that is the great sign that the Lord has glorified the dead saint. If they are black instead of yellow, it shows God did not think him worthy of such glory. That is what they believe on Athos, a great place, where Orthodox doctrine has been kept from ancient times, unbroken and in its purest form,” Father Iosif concluded.

But the meek Father’s words did little good and even brought a sneering answer. “That’s all pedantry and innovation, no point listening to it,” the monks decided. “We hold to the old teaching. Nowadays there are innovations of every kind. Do we have to follow them all?” others said.

“We’ve had as many holy fathers as they have. Look at them there among the Turks, they’ve forgotten everything. Their doctrine has been unclean for ages, and they haven’t even got bells,” the most sneering of them put in.
