He also remembered afterwards that at that moment he had noticed, on Grushenka’s face, a certain involuntary proud contempt for this message from Siberia. Grushenka told him nothing of what had passed later between her and this rival. So little by little he had completely forgotten the officer’s existence.

Whatever came later, and however things turned out, he felt that his final showdown with Fyodor Pavlovitch was near and had to be settled first. Every moment, with a sinking heart, he waited for Grushenka to decide. He always believed the decision would come suddenly, on a whim of the moment. Out of the blue she would say to him: “Take me, I’m yours for ever,” and that would be the end of it. He would seize her and sweep her off to the ends of the earth. Oh, then he would take her away at once, as far, far away as he could. To the farthest corner of Russia, if not of the earth. There he would marry her and settle down with her incognito, so that nobody would know anything about them, there, here, or anywhere. Then, oh, then, a new life would begin at once!

He dreamed feverishly at every moment of this different, reformed and “virtuous” life (“it must, it must be virtuous”). He thirsted for that reform and renewal. The filthy swamp where he had sunk of his own free will was too revolting to him. Like very many men in such cases, he put his faith above all in a change of place. If only it were not for these people, if only it were not for these circumstances, if only he could fly away from this accursed place—he would be completely regenerated and would start on a new path. That was what he believed in, and what he was yearning for.

But all of this depended on the first outcome, the _happy_ one. There was another possibility, a different and dreadful ending. Suddenly she might say to him: “Go away. I have just come to terms with Fyodor Pavlovitch. I am going to marry him and I don’t want you”—and then ... but then.... Mitya did not know what would happen then. He didn’t know it up to the last hour, and that must be said in his favor. He had no definite plans and had worked out no crime. He only watched and spied in agony, getting himself ready for the first, happy outcome of his fate. In fact, he pushed every other thought away. But even for that happy ending a quite different worry came up, a new and incidental difficulty, yet fatal and impossible to solve.

If she were to say to him: “I’m yours; take me away,” how could he take her away? Where did he have the means, the money to do it? It was just at this time that every source of income from Fyodor Pavlovitch dried up, the allowances that had gone on without a break for so many years. Grushenka had money, of course, but about this Mitya suddenly showed extraordinary pride. He wanted to carry her off and begin the new life with her himself, at his own expense, not hers. He could not imagine taking her money, and the very idea gave him a pang of intense revulsion. I won’t enlarge on this fact or analyze it here. I will only remark that this was his attitude at the moment. All this may have arisen indirectly and unconsciously from the secret stings of conscience over the money of Katerina Ivanovna, which he had dishonestly taken. “I’ve been a scoundrel to one of them, and I’ll soon be a scoundrel again to the other,” was what he felt then, as he explained afterwards, “and when Grushenka knows, she won’t care for such a scoundrel.”
So where was he to find the means? Where could he get this fateful money? Without it everything was lost and nothing could be done, “and all because I didn’t have the money. Oh, the shame of it!”

To get ahead of the story: he did, perhaps, know where to get the money, and perhaps he knew where it lay at that very moment. I will say no more about it here, since it will all become clear later. But his chief trouble, which I must explain however obscurely, was this. To have the sum he knew of, to _have the right_ to take it, he first had to pay back Katerina Ivanovna’s three thousand. If not, “I’m a common pickpocket, I’m a scoundrel, and I don’t want to begin a new life as a scoundrel,” Mitya decided. And so he made up his mind to move heaven and earth to return that three thousand to Katerina Ivanovna, and to do it _first of all_. He had reached the final stage of this decision, so to say, only in the last few hours. That was after his last meeting with Alyosha, two days before, on the high-road, on the evening when Grushenka had insulted Katerina Ivanovna. Mitya had heard Alyosha’s account of it and admitted that he was a scoundrel, and told Alyosha to tell Katerina Ivanovna so, if it could be any comfort to her. After parting from his brother that night, he had felt in his frenzy that it would be better “to murder and rob someone than fail to pay my debt to Katya. I’d rather everyone thought me a robber and a murderer, I’d rather go to Siberia than let Katya have the right to say that I deceived her and stole her money, and used her money to run away with Grushenka and begin a new life! That I can’t do!” So Mitya decided, grinding his teeth, and at times he might well imagine that his brain would give way. But meanwhile he went on struggling....

Oddly enough, you would have thought despair was all he had left. What chance did he have of raising such a sum, with nothing in the world? Yet right to the end he kept hoping he would get that three thousand, and that the money would somehow arrive of its own accord, as if it might fall from heaven. That is exactly how it is with people like Dmitri. The only dealings they have ever had with money have been squandering what came to them by inheritance, with no effort on their part, and they have no idea how money is earned. As soon as he parted from Alyosha two days earlier, a whirl of the most fantastic notions seized his brain and tangled his thoughts in confusion. That is why he fixed first on a perfectly wild undertaking. And perhaps for men of that kind in such circumstances, the most impossible and fantastic schemes are the first to occur to them, and look the most practical.

He suddenly decided to go to Samsonov, the merchant who was Grushenka’s protector, and propose a “scheme” to him. By means of it he would get from him at once the whole sum he needed. He had no doubt, not the slightest, of the commercial value of his scheme. He was only unsure how Samsonov would look on his freak, if he were to consider it from any but the commercial point of view. Mitya knew the merchant by sight, but he was not acquainted with him and had never spoken a word to him. For some unknown reason, though, he had long held the conviction that the old reprobate, who was lying at death’s door, would perhaps not object at all now to Grushenka’s securing a respectable position and marrying a man “to be depended upon.” And he believed not only that the old man would not object, but that this was what he wanted, and that he would be ready to help if the opportunity arose. From some rumor, or perhaps from some stray word of Grushenka’s, he had gathered besides that the old man would perhaps prefer him to Fyodor Pavlovitch for Grushenka.

Possibly many readers of my novel will feel that Dmitri showed great coarseness and lack of delicacy in reckoning on such help, and in being ready to take his bride, so to speak, from the hands of her protector. I will only observe that Mitya looked on Grushenka’s past as something completely over. He looked on that past with infinite pity. He resolved, with all the fervor of his passion, that once Grushenka told him she loved him and would marry him, it would mean the beginning of a new Grushenka and a new Dmitri, free from every vice. They would forgive one another and begin their lives afresh. As for Kuzma Samsonov, Dmitri saw him as a man who had had a fateful influence in that remote past of Grushenka’s, though she had never loved him. Now the old man was himself a thing of the past, completely done with and, so to say, non-existent. Besides, Mitya hardly looked on him as a man at all. It was known to everyone in the town that he was only a shattered wreck, and that his relations with Grushenka had changed their character and were now simply fatherly, and had been so for a long time.

Whatever one thinks of it, there was a great deal of simplicity in all this on Mitya’s part, for with all his vices he was a thoroughly simple-hearted man. Here is an example. Mitya seriously believed that old Kuzma, standing on the brink of the next world, must sincerely repent of his past relations with Grushenka. He believed that she had no more devoted friend and protector anywhere than this now harmless old man.

After his talk with Alyosha at the cross-roads he hardly slept all night. At ten o’clock the next morning he was at Samsonov’s house, telling the servant to announce him. It was a very large and gloomy old house of two stories, with a lodge and outhouses. On the lower floor lived Samsonov’s two married sons with their families, his old sister, and his unmarried daughter. In the lodge lived two of his clerks, one of whom also had a large family. Both the lodge and the lower floor were overcrowded, but the old man kept the upper floor to himself. He would not even let his daughter live there with him, though she waited on him. In spite of her asthma she had to run upstairs from below at certain fixed hours, and at any time he might call her.

The upper floor had a number of large rooms that were kept purely for show and furnished in the old-fashioned merchant style. Dull, long rows of clumsy mahogany chairs stood against the walls, glass chandeliers hung under covers, and gloomy mirrors hung on the walls. None of these rooms were ever used. The old man lived in one small, remote bedroom, where an old servant woman with a kerchief on her head looked after him, along with a lad who sat on the chest out in the passage. His legs were so swollen that he could barely walk. Only now and then was he lifted out of his leather armchair, and then the old woman held him up and walked him once or twice up and down the room. He was sullen and silent even with her.

When he was told that the “captain” had come, he refused flatly to see him. Mitya would not give up and sent up his name a second time. Samsonov questioned the lad closely. What did the man look like? Was he drunk? Would he make a scene? The answer was that he was sober, but he would not leave. The old man refused again. Mitya had expected this and had brought pencil and paper on purpose. He now wrote in a clear hand, “On most important business closely concerning Agrafena Alexandrovna,” and sent the note up.

Samsonov thought it over for a little. Then he told the lad to show the visitor into the drawing-room, and sent the old woman downstairs to tell his younger son to come up at once. This son was over six feet tall and uncommonly strong. He was clean-shaven and dressed in the European fashion, though his father still wore a kaftan and a beard. He came immediately and said nothing. The whole family trembled before the father. The old man had called for this giant, not because he was afraid of the “captain” (he was not at all a timid man), but to have a witness if anything went wrong. Leaning on his son and the servant lad, he waddled at last into the drawing-room. We may suppose he was very curious. The room where Mitya waited was vast and dreary, and it pressed down on the spirits. It had a double row of windows, a gallery, marbled walls, and three huge chandeliers hung with glass drops and covered with shades.

Mitya sat on a little chair near the entrance, waiting for his fate in nervous impatience. When the old man came in at the far door, seventy feet away, Mitya sprang up and went to meet him with his long, military stride. He was well dressed, in a buttoned-up frock-coat, with a round hat and black gloves in his hands. It was just how he had looked three days before at the elder’s, at the family meeting with his father and brothers. The old man stood waiting for him, dignified and unbending, and Mitya felt at once that the old man had looked him through and through as he came forward. He was also struck by Samsonov’s monstrously swollen face. The lower lip, always thick, now hung down like a bun. The old man bowed to his guest in dignified silence and waved him to a low chair by the sofa. Then, leaning on his son’s arm, he started to lower himself onto the sofa opposite, groaning with pain. Watching his struggle, Mitya at once felt remorse. He felt, too, how small he was in the presence of this dignified man he had dared to disturb.
“What do you want from me, sir?” said the old man, slowly, distinctly, sternly, but with courtesy, once he was finally seated.

Mitya jumped, leapt to his feet, then sat down again. Straight away he began to speak, loudly, in nervous haste, waving his arms, in a real frenzy. Anyone could see he was a man cornered, on the edge of ruin, clutching at his last straw and ready to go under if it failed him. Old Samsonov probably understood all this in an instant, though his face stayed as cold and still as a statue’s.

“Most honored sir, Kuzma Kuzmitch, you have surely heard more than once of my quarrels with my father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, who robbed me of my inheritance from my mother ... seeing the whole town is gossiping about it ... for here everyone gossips about things they shouldn’t ... and besides, it might have reached you through Grushenka ... Sorry, through Agrafena Alexandrovna ... Agrafena Alexandrovna, the lady I hold in the highest respect and esteem ...”

So Mitya began, and he broke down at the very first sentence. We will not give his speech word for word, only the gist. Three months ago, he said, he had gone to a lawyer in the chief town of the province, “of express intention” (Mitya deliberately used these words in place of “intentionally”). “A distinguished lawyer, Kuzma Kuzmitch, Pavel Pavlovitch Korneplodov. Perhaps you’ve heard of him? A man of vast intellect, the mind of a statesman ... he knows you, too ... spoke of you in the highest terms ...” Mitya broke down again. But these breakdowns never stopped him. He took a leap across each gap and struggled on and on.

This Korneplodov had questioned him closely and looked over the documents he could bring (Mitya referred to these documents rather vaguely and hurried past the subject). He had then reported that they could certainly bring a suit over the village of Tchermashnya, which should have come to him, Mitya, from his mother, and so checkmate the old villain, his father ... “because not every door was shut, and justice might still find a loophole.” In short, he could count on another six or even seven thousand roubles from Fyodor Pavlovitch, because Tchermashnya was worth at least twenty-five thousand, he might say twenty-eight thousand, in fact “thirty, thirty, Kuzma Kuzmitch, and would you believe it, I didn’t get even seventeen out of that heartless man!” So he, Mitya, had dropped the matter for the moment, since he knew nothing about the law. But when he came here, a counter-claim against him left him dumbstruck (here Mitya lost his way again and again took a flying leap ahead). “So won’t you, excellent and honored Kuzma Kuzmitch, agree to take over all my claims against that unnatural monster, and pay me a lump sum of only three thousand?... You see, there’s no way you can lose by it. On my honor, my honor, I swear it. Quite the opposite, you could make six or seven thousand instead of three.” Above all he wanted it settled that very day.

“I’ll do the business with you at a notary’s, or wherever it’s done ... in fact, I’m ready to do anything.... I’ll hand over all the deeds ... whatever you want, I’ll sign anything ... and we could draw up the agreement right now ... and if it were possible, if it were only possible, this very morning.... You could pay me that three thousand, for there isn’t a capitalist in this town to compare with you, and so you would save me from ... save me, in fact ... for a good, I might say an honorable deed.... For I have the most honorable feelings for a certain person you know well, and look after like a father. I wouldn’t have come at all, if it weren’t as a father. And really, it’s a struggle of three in this business, for it’s fate—that’s a fearful thing, Kuzma Kuzmitch! A tragedy, Kuzma Kuzmitch, a tragedy! And since you dropped out long ago, it’s a tug-of-war between two. I’m putting it awkwardly, perhaps, but I’m not a literary man. You see, I’m on one side, and that monster on the other. So you must choose. It’s either me or the monster. It all lies in your hands—the fate of three lives, and the happiness of two.... Forgive me, I’m making a mess of it, but you understand ... I can see from your venerable eyes that you understand ... and if you don’t understand, I’m done for ... so you see!”

With that “so you see!” Mitya cut short his clumsy speech. He jumped up from his seat and waited for an answer to his foolish proposal. At that last phrase, he had suddenly realized, with despair, that it had all fallen flat, and above all that he had been talking utter nonsense.

“How strange! On the way here it seemed all right, and now it’s nothing but nonsense.” The thought dawned on his despairing mind all at once. The whole time he had been speaking, the old man had sat without moving, watching him with an icy look in his eyes. He kept Mitya in suspense for a moment. Then Kuzma Kuzmitch said, in the flattest and most chilling tone:
“Excuse me, we don’t take on such business.”
Mitya suddenly felt his legs going weak under him.
“What am I to do now, Kuzma Kuzmitch?” he muttered, with a pale smile. “It’s all up with me, I suppose—what do you think?”
“Excuse me....”
Mitya stayed on his feet, staring, unable to move. Then he noticed a stir in the old man’s face. He started.
“You see, sir, business of that kind isn’t in our line,” said the old man slowly. “There’s the court, and the lawyers—it’s pure misery. But if you like, there’s a man here you could go to.”
“Good heavens! Who is it? You’re my salvation, Kuzma Kuzmitch,” faltered Mitya.

“He doesn’t live here, and he isn’t here at the moment. He’s a peasant, and he deals in timber. His name is Lyagavy. For the past year he’s been haggling with Fyodor Pavlovitch over your copse at Tchermashnya. They can’t settle on a price, maybe you’ve heard? He’s back again now, and he’s staying with the priest at Ilyinskoe, about twelve versts from the Volovya station. He wrote to me about the copse as well, and asked my advice. Fyodor Pavlovitch means to go and see him himself. So if you got there before Fyodor Pavlovitch and made Lyagavy the offer you’ve made me, he might possibly—”

“A brilliant idea!” Mitya broke in, ecstatic. “He’s just the man, it would suit him perfectly. He’s haggling over it, they’re asking him too much, and here he’d be getting all the papers that give him title to the property itself. Ha ha ha!”
And Mitya suddenly let out his short, wooden laugh, which made Samsonov start.
“How can I thank you, Kuzma Kuzmitch?” cried Mitya, gushing.
“Don’t mention it,” said Samsonov, with a nod of his head.
“But you don’t know, you’ve saved me. Oh, it was a true presentiment that brought me to you.... So now, off to this priest!”
“There’s no need to thank me.”
“I’ll make haste and fly there. I’m afraid I’ve worn out your strength. I’ll never forget this. A Russian is telling you that, Kuzma Kuzmitch, a R-r-russian!”
“Of course!”
Mitya reached out and seized his hand to shake it, but a spiteful gleam showed in the old man’s eye. Mitya drew back his hand, then at once scolded himself for his distrust.
“It’s because he’s tired,” he thought.

“For her sake! For her sake, Kuzma Kuzmitch! You understand that it’s for her,” he cried, and his voice rang through the room. He bowed, spun around, and with the same long stride went to the door without looking back. He was trembling with joy.

“Everything was on the edge of ruin, and my guardian angel has saved me,” he thought. If a businessman like Samsonov (a most worthy old man, and what dignity!) had suggested this way out, then ... then success was certain. He would fly off at once. “I’ll be back before night, I’ll be back tonight and it will be done. Could the old man have been laughing at me?” cried Mitya, as he strode toward his lodging. He could think of nothing else, of course, except that this was practical advice, “from such a businessman,” who knew the business and who knew this Lyagavy (curious name!). Or else the old man was laughing at him.

Alas! It was the second. Long afterward, when the catastrophe had happened, old Samsonov himself admitted, with a laugh, that he had made a fool of the “captain.” He was a cold, spiteful, sarcastic man, with a streak of violent dislikes. Maybe it was the “captain’s” excited face. Maybe it was the foolish certainty of this “rake and spendthrift” that Samsonov could be taken in by a cock-and-bull story like his scheme. Maybe it was jealousy over Grushenka, in whose name the “scapegrace” had burst in on him with such a tale, to get money. Something worked on the old man, but I can’t say what. But at the moment when Mitya stood before him, feeling his legs go weak and crying wildly that he was ruined, the old man looked at him with intense spite and made up his mind to turn him into a laughing-stock. When Mitya had gone, Kuzma Kuzmitch, white with rage, turned to his son and ordered him to see that the beggar was never seen again, and never let into the yard, or else he’d—

He did not say what he would do. But even his son, who often saw him in a rage, shook with fear. For a whole hour afterward the old man trembled with anger, and by evening he was worse and sent for the doctor.

chapters.title: II. Lyagavy
paragraphs: So he had to travel fast, and he had no money for horses. All he had was forty kopecks, all that was left after so many years of prosperity! But at home he had an old silver watch that had stopped working long ago. He grabbed it and took it to a Jewish watchmaker with a shop in the market-place. The man gave him six roubles for it.

“And I never expected that!” cried Mitya, ecstatic. (He was still in a state of ecstasy.) He seized his six roubles and ran home. There he borrowed three roubles from the people of the house. They were so fond of him that they handed it over gladly, though it was all they had. In his excitement Mitya told them right then that his fate would be decided that day. In desperate haste he described the whole scheme he had put to Samsonov, how Samsonov had decided, what he himself hoped for the future, and so on. These people had been told many of their lodger’s secrets before, so they saw him as a gentleman with no pride at all, almost one of themselves. Now that he had nine roubles, Mitya sent for posting-horses to take him to the Volovya station. This is how it came to be remembered and put on record that “at midday, on the day before the event, Mitya had not a farthing, and that he had sold his watch to get money and had borrowed three roubles from his landlord, all in the presence of witnesses.”
I note this fact now. Later it will be clear why I do.

He was radiant with joyful hope that at last he would solve all his difficulties. Yet as he came near Volovya station, he shook at the thought of what Grushenka might be doing while he was gone. What if she decided today to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch? That was why he had left without telling her, and why he had ordered his landlady not to say where he had gone if anyone came asking for him.

“I must get back tonight, I must,” he kept saying as the cart jolted along. “And I expect I’ll have to bring this Lyagavy back here with me ... to draw up the deed.” So Mitya mused, his heart pounding. But alas! His dreams were not fated to come true.

First, he was late. He took a short cut from Volovya station, and it turned out to be eighteen versts instead of twelve. Second, the priest was not at home in Ilyinskoe. He had gone off to a neighboring village. As Mitya set out there with the same worn-out horses and looked for him, it was almost dark.

The priest was a shy, pleasant-looking little man. He told Mitya right away that Lyagavy had stayed with him at first but was now at Suhoy Possyolok, spending the night in the forester’s cottage, because he was buying timber there too. Mitya begged him urgently to take him to Lyagavy at once and so “save him, so to speak.” After some hesitation the priest agreed to guide him to Suhoy Possyolok. His curiosity was plainly aroused. But unluckily he proposed going on foot, since it was not “much over” a verst. Mitya agreed, naturally, and set off with his yard-long strides, so that the poor priest nearly had to run to keep up. He was a very cautious man, though not old.

Mitya started talking to him about his plans too. Nervous and excited, he asked for advice about Lyagavy and talked the whole way. The priest listened closely but gave little advice. He fended off Mitya’s questions with: “I don’t know. Ah, I can’t say. How can I tell?” and so on. When Mitya began to speak about his quarrel with his father over the inheritance, the priest was truly alarmed, because he depended on Fyodor Pavlovitch in some way. He did ask, in surprise, why Mitya called the peasant-trader Gorstkin by the name Lyagavy. Then he explained, helpfully, that the man’s name really was Lyagavy, but nobody called him that, since the name would badly offend him. Mitya must be sure to call him Gorstkin, “or you’ll do nothing with him; he won’t even listen to you,” the priest finished.

For a moment Mitya was a little taken aback. He said that Samsonov had called him that. When he heard this, the priest let the subject drop. He would have done well to say aloud what he doubted: if Samsonov had sent Mitya to that peasant and called him Lyagavy, was there something wrong in it? Was Samsonov making a fool of him? But Mitya had no time to stop over trifles like that. He hurried on, striding. Only when he reached Suhoy Possyolok did he see that they had come not one verst, or one and a half, but at least three. That annoyed him, but he kept himself under control.

They went into the hut. The forester lived in one half, and Gorstkin was staying in the other half, the better room, on the far side of the passage. They went into that room and lit a tallow candle. The hut was stiflingly hot. On the table stood a samovar that had gone cold, a tray of cups, an empty rum bottle, a half-full bottle of vodka, and some half-eaten crusts of wheaten bread. The visitor himself lay at full length on the bench, with his coat bunched up under his head for a pillow, snoring heavily. Mitya stood there at a loss.

“Of course I have to wake him. My business is too important. I came in such a hurry. I need to get back today,” he said, very agitated. But the priest and the forester stood silent and offered no opinion. Mitya went over and tried to wake the man himself. He tried hard, but the sleeper did not wake.

“He’s drunk,” Mitya decided. “Good Lord! What do I do? What do I do?” Terribly impatient, he started tugging him by the arms and the legs, shaking his head, hauling him up and sitting him on the bench. But after long effort, all he got out of the drunken man was silly grunts and violent, slurred oaths.
“No, you’d better wait a while,” the priest said at last. “He’s obviously in no state for it.”
“He’s been drinking all day,” the forester put in.
“Good heavens!” cried Mitya. “If only you knew how much this matters to me, and how desperate I am!”
“No, you’d better wait till morning,” the priest said again.
“Till morning? Mercy! That’s impossible!”
And in his despair he was about to go at the sleeping man again, but he stopped at once, seeing how useless it was. The priest said nothing, and the sleepy forester looked sullen.

“What terrible tragedies real life cooks up for people,” said Mitya, in utter despair. Sweat was pouring down his face. The priest used the moment to point out, quite sensibly, that even if Mitya did manage to wake the man, he would still be drunk and unable to talk. “And your business is important,” he said, “so you’d certainly do better to put it off till morning.” With a hopeless gesture, Mitya gave in.

“Father, I will stay here with a light, and seize the favorable moment. The minute he wakes I’ll begin. I’ll pay you for the light,” he said to the forester, “and for the night’s lodging too. You’ll remember Dmitri Karamazov. Only, Father, I don’t know what we’ll do with you. Where will you sleep?”
“No, I’m going home. I’ll take his horse and ride home,” he said, pointing to the forester. “And now I’ll say good-bye. I wish you every success.”

So that was settled. The priest rode off on the forester’s horse, glad to get away. Still, he shook his head uneasily, wondering if he ought to tell his benefactor Fyodor Pavlovitch about this strange business the next day, “or he may hear of it at an unlucky moment, get angry, and take back his favor.”

The forester scratched himself, went back to his room without a word, and Mitya sat down on the bench to “catch the favorable moment,” as he put it. A deep gloom hung over his soul like a heavy fog. A profound, bitter gloom! He sat and thought, but could come to no conclusion. The candle burned low, a cricket chirped, and the hot room grew more and more stifling. All at once he pictured the garden, the path behind the garden, the door of his father’s house mysteriously opening and Grushenka running in. He jumped up from the bench.

“It’s a tragedy!” he said, grinding his teeth. Mechanically he walked over to the sleeping man and looked into his face. He was a lean, middle-aged peasant with a very long face, flaxen curls, and a long, thin, reddish beard. He wore a blue cotton shirt and a black waistcoat, and the chain of a silver watch showed from its pocket. Mitya looked into that face with fierce hatred, and for some reason he could not name, the curly hair annoyed him most of all.

What was so unbearably humiliating was this. He had left matters of great importance and made great sacrifices, and now here he was, Mitya, utterly exhausted, with business of such urgency, standing over this blockhead on whom his whole fate hung. And the blockhead snored away as if nothing were wrong, as if he had dropped from another planet.

“Oh, the irony of fate!” cried Mitya. Quite losing his head, he went back to shaking the tipsy peasant awake. He did it with a kind of fury. He pulled at him, shoved him, even hit him. But after five minutes of wasted effort, he went back to his bench in helpless despair and sat down.

“Stupid! Stupid!” cried Mitya. “And how dishonorable all this is!” something made him add. His head began to ache horribly. “Should he throw it all up and leave for good?” he wondered. “No, wait till tomorrow now. I’ll stay on purpose. What else did I come for? Besides, I have no way to leave. How am I to get away from here now? Oh, the idiocy of it!”

But his head ached more and more. He sat without moving, and without meaning to he dozed off and fell asleep sitting there. He seemed to have slept two hours or more. What woke him was a headache so unbearable that he could have screamed. His temples were hammering and the top of his head throbbed. It was a long time before he was properly awake and understood what had happened to him.

At last he saw that the room was full of charcoal fumes from the stove, and that he might suffocate. And the drunken peasant lay there snoring still. The candle was guttering and about to go out. Mitya cried out and ran, staggering, across the passage into the forester’s room. The forester woke right away. But when he heard that the other room was full of fumes, he took it with strange unconcern, though he did go and see to it. This surprised and angered Mitya.
“But he’s dead, he’s dead! And ... what do I do then?” cried Mitya, frantic.

They threw open the doors and opened a window and the chimney. Mitya fetched a pail of water from the passage. First he soaked his own head. Then he found a rag, dipped it in the water, and laid it on Lyagavy’s head. The forester still treated the whole thing with contempt, and as he opened the window he said grumpily:
“It’ll be all right now.”

He went back to bed, leaving Mitya a lit lantern. Mitya fussed over the drunken peasant for half an hour, wetting his head, and solemnly vowed not to sleep all night. But he was so worn out that when he sat down for a moment to catch his breath, his eyes closed. Without meaning to, he stretched out full length on the bench and slept like the dead.

It was dreadfully late when he woke, somewhere around nine o’clock. The sun was shining brightly through the two small windows of the hut. The curly-headed peasant sat on the bench with his coat on. In front of him stood another samovar and another bottle. Yesterday’s bottle was finished, and the new one was more than half empty. Mitya jumped up and saw at once that the cursed peasant was drunk again, hopelessly and incurably. He stared at him for a moment, eyes wide. The peasant was watching him in silence, slyly, with insulting calm and even a kind of contemptuous condescension, or so Mitya thought. He rushed up to him.
“Excuse me, you see ... I ... the forester here has probably told you. I’m Lieutenant Dmitri Karamazov, son of the old Karamazov whose copse you’re buying.”
“That’s a lie!” said the peasant, calm and sure.
“A lie? You know Fyodor Pavlovitch?”
“I don’t know any of your Fyodor Pavlovitches,” said the peasant, thick-tongued.

“You’re haggling with him over the copse, the copse! Do wake up, pull yourself together. Father Pavel from Ilyinskoe brought me here. You wrote to Samsonov, and he sent me to you,” Mitya gasped, out of breath.
“You’re l-lying!” Lyagavy blurted out again. Mitya’s legs went cold.
“For mercy’s sake! This is no joke! Maybe you’re drunk. Yet you can talk and understand ... or else ... I understand nothing!”
“You’re a painter!”
“For mercy’s sake! I’m Karamazov, Dmitri Karamazov. I have an offer for you, a good offer ... a very good offer, about the copse!”
The peasant stroked his beard with great importance.
“No, you took on the job and turned out a scamp. You’re a scoundrel!”
“I tell you, you’re mistaken,” cried Mitya, wringing his hands in despair. The peasant went on stroking his beard, then suddenly narrowed his eyes slyly.
“No, you show me this: name me the law that allows roguery. D’you hear? You’re a scoundrel! Do you understand that?”

Mitya stepped back gloomily, and suddenly “something seemed to hit him on the head,” as he said afterwards. In an instant a light seemed to break in his mind, “a light was kindled and I grasped it all.” He stood there stunned. How could he, a man of intelligence after all, have fallen for such folly, been drawn into such an adventure, and kept it up for almost twenty-four hours, fussing around this Lyagavy and wetting his head?
“Why, the man’s drunk, dead drunk, and he’ll go on drinking for a week now. What’s the use of waiting here? And what if Samsonov sent me here on purpose? What if she—? Oh, God, what have I done?”

The peasant sat watching him and grinning. At another time Mitya might have killed the fool in a rage, but now he felt as weak as a child. He walked quietly to the bench, picked up his overcoat, put it on without a word, and left the hut. The forester was not in the next room. There was nobody there. He took fifty kopecks in small change from his pocket and left them on the table for his night’s lodging, the candle, and the trouble he had caused. Outside the hut he saw nothing but forest on every side. He walked at random, not knowing whether to turn right or left. Hurrying there the evening before with the priest, he had not noticed the road. In his heart he felt no wish for revenge on anyone, not even Samsonov. He strode along a narrow forest path, aimless and dazed, paying no attention to where he was going. A child could have knocked him down, he was so weak in body and soul. Somehow he got out of the forest, however, and a view of fields, bare after the harvest, opened out as far as the eye could see.
“What despair! What death all around!” he repeated, striding on and on.

He was saved by meeting an old merchant who was being driven across country in a hired trap. Mitya caught up with him and asked the way, and it turned out that the old merchant was also going to Volovya. After some talk Mitya climbed into the trap. Three hours later they arrived. At Volovya, Mitya immediately ordered posting-horses for the drive to town, and suddenly realized he was ravenously hungry. While the horses were being harnessed, they made him an omelette. He ate it all in a moment, ate a huge hunk of bread, ate a sausage, and drank three glasses of vodka. After eating, his spirits and his heart grew lighter. He flew toward town, urged the driver on, and suddenly came up with a new and “unalterable” plan to get that “accursed money” before evening. “And to think, only to think that a man’s life should be ruined for the sake of that paltry three thousand!” he cried, scornfully. “I’ll settle it today.” And if it had not been for the thought of Grushenka and of what might have happened to her, which never left him, he might have become quite cheerful again.... But the thought of her stabbed him to the heart every moment, like a sharp knife.
At last they arrived, and Mitya ran straight to Grushenka.

chapters.title: III. Gold-Mines
paragraphs: This was the visit that Grushenka had described to Rakitin with such horror. She was waiting just then for the “message,” and she was hugely relieved that Mitya had not turned up either that day or the day before. She had been hoping that “please God he won’t come till I’m gone,” and now here he was, bursting in on her. The rest we know already. To get rid of him, she proposed right away that he walk with her to Samsonov’s, where she said she simply had to go “to settle his accounts.” Mitya went along at once, and at the gate she said good-by, making him promise to come at twelve o’clock and take her home. Mitya was delighted with this arrangement too. If she was sitting at Samsonov’s, she could not be off to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, “if only she’s not lying,” he added immediately. Still, judging by what he had seen, he thought she was not lying.

He was the kind of jealous man who, while the woman he loves is out of sight, dreams up every sort of dreadful picture of what may be happening to her and how she may be betraying him. Then, shaken and heartbroken and certain of her faithlessness, he runs back to her. But one look at her face, that gay, laughing, affectionate face, and he comes back to life. He drops every suspicion and, with joyful shame, calls himself names for having been jealous.
Once he had left Grushenka at the gate, he hurried home. Oh, there was so much still to do that day! But at least a weight had been lifted from his heart.

“Now I only have to rush and find out from Smerdyakov whether anything happened over there last night, whether she, by any chance, went to Fyodor Pavlovitch; ugh!” the thought flashed through his mind.
He had not even reached his lodging before jealousy was boiling up again in his restless heart.

Jealousy! “Othello was not jealous, he was trustful,” said Pushkin. That one remark is enough to show how deeply our great poet saw. Othello’s soul was shattered and his whole view of the world went dark simply because _his ideal was destroyed_. But Othello did not go hiding, spying, peeping. Quite the opposite: he was trustful. It took enormous effort to lead him along, push him, and work him up before he would even consider the idea of deceit. The truly jealous man is not like that. No one can imagine the shame and moral degradation a jealous man will sink to without a twinge of conscience. And it is not as if all the jealous were vulgar, base souls. A man of lofty feelings, whose love is pure and full of self-sacrifice, may nevertheless hide under tables, bribe the vilest people, and become well acquainted with the lowest disgrace of spying and eavesdropping.

Othello could not bring himself to accept faithlessness. He was not unable to forgive it; he was unable to accept it, though his soul was as innocent and free of malice as a baby’s. The truly jealous man is different. It is hard to imagine what some jealous men can bring themselves to accept and overlook, and what they can forgive! The jealous are the quickest of all to forgive, and every woman knows it. A jealous man can forgive astonishingly fast (after a violent scene, naturally). He can forgive unfaithfulness that is all but proved, even the very kisses and embraces he has seen with his own eyes, so long as he can somehow be persuaded that it was all “for the last time,” and that his rival will disappear from that day on and go off to the ends of the earth, or that he himself will take her away to some place the dreaded rival can never get near. Of course the peace lasts only an hour. For even if the rival did vanish the next day, he would invent another and be jealous of him. And you might ask what kind of love it is that has to be watched so closely, and what a love is worth if it needs such hard guarding. But the jealous will never understand that. And yet there are men of noble heart among them. It is remarkable, too, that these very men of noble heart, standing hidden in some cupboard, listening and spying, never feel a sting of conscience at that moment, at any rate, though with their “noble hearts” they understand perfectly well what shameful depths they have chosen to sink to.

When Mitya saw Grushenka, his jealousy vanished. For a moment he became trustful and generous and actually despised himself for his evil thoughts. But that only proved that his love for her held something far higher than he himself suspected, that it was not merely sensual passion, not merely the “curve of her body” he had talked to Alyosha about. Yet the moment Grushenka was gone, Mitya started suspecting her of every low trick of faithlessness, and he felt no sting of conscience over that either.

So jealousy was boiling up in him again. In any case he had to hurry. The first thing was to get hold of some money, even a small loan, just for the time being. The nine roubles had nearly all been spent on his trip. And, as we all know, you can’t take a step without money. But on the cart he had worked out where he could get a loan. He owned a fine pair of dueling pistols in a case, which he had never pawned until now, because he valued them more than anything else he had.

Some time ago, at the “Metropolis” tavern, he had got to know a young official, and had learned that this extremely well-off bachelor was passionately fond of weapons. The man bought pistols, revolvers and daggers, hung them on his wall, and showed them off to his acquaintances. He was proud of the collection and was something of a specialist in how a revolver works. Mitya went straight to him without a second thought and offered to pawn his pistols for ten roubles. The official was delighted and began urging him to sell them outright. Mitya would not hear of it, so the young man handed over ten roubles, insisting that nothing would make him charge interest. They parted as friends.

Mitya was in a rush. He hurried toward Fyodor Pavlovitch’s by the back way, to the arbor, hoping to catch Smerdyakov as soon as he could. So it is on record that three or four hours before a certain event, which I will describe later, Mitya did not have a farthing and pawned a treasured possession for ten roubles, although three hours after that he held thousands in his hands.... But I am running ahead of my story. From Marya Kondratyevna (the woman who lived next to Fyodor Pavlovitch) he got the very disturbing news that Smerdyakov was ill. She told him the story of the fall in the cellar, the fit, the doctor’s visit, and Fyodor Pavlovitch’s worry. He also heard, with interest, that his brother Ivan had left that morning for Moscow.

“So he must have driven through Volovya ahead of me,” thought Dmitri, but he was terribly upset about Smerdyakov. “What now? Who’ll keep watch for me? Who’ll bring me word?” he thought. He started eagerly asking the women whether they had seen anything the evening before. They knew exactly what he was after, and they put his mind completely at rest. Nobody had been there. Ivan Fyodorovitch had been there that night, and everything had gone just as usual. Mitya fell to thinking. He would certainly have to stand watch today, but where? Here, or at Samsonov’s gate? He decided he had to keep a lookout in both places, and meanwhile ... meanwhile.... The trouble was that he had a new plan, worked out on the way back, that he had to carry out. He was sure it would work, but he could not put it off. Mitya decided to spend an hour on it: “In an hour I’ll know everything, I’ll have everything settled, and then, then, first of all to Samsonov’s. I’ll ask whether Grushenka’s there and come straight back here, wait till eleven, and then go to Samsonov’s again to bring her home.” That was what he decided.

He flew home, washed, combed his hair, brushed his clothes, changed, and set off for Madame Hohlakov’s. Alas! It was on her that he had pinned his hopes. He had made up his mind to borrow three thousand from that lady. And, what is more, he suddenly felt sure that she would not turn him down. One may well ask why, if he was so certain, he had not gone to her first, to someone of his own kind, so to speak, rather than to Samsonov, a man he did not know, who belonged to another class, and who was someone he hardly knew how to talk to.

The truth was that he had never really known Madame Hohlakov, that he had not seen her for a month, and that he knew she could not bear him. She had disliked him from the very beginning because he was engaged to Katerina Ivanovna, whereas she had suddenly, for no clear reason, set her heart on Katerina Ivanovna jilting him and marrying the “charming, chivalrously refined Ivan, who had such excellent manners.” Mitya’s manners she loathed. Mitya openly laughed at her, and had once remarked that she was as lively and at ease in company as she was uneducated. But that morning in the cart a brilliant idea had come to him: “If she’s so keen that I shouldn’t marry Katerina Ivanovna” (and he knew she was positively hysterical on the subject) “why would she refuse me that three thousand now, so that I can drop Katya and get away from her for good? These spoiled society ladies, once they’ve set their hearts on something, will spare no expense to indulge a whim. Besides, she’s so rich,” Mitya reasoned.

His “plan” was exactly the same as before: he would offer his rights to Tchermashnya. But this time it was not as a business proposition, as it had been with Samsonov, not luring the lady with a possible profit of six or seven thousand, but only as security for the loan. As he worked out this new idea, Mitya was thrilled with it, but that was how he always felt about all his undertakings and all his sudden decisions. He threw himself into every new idea with passionate enthusiasm. Yet as he climbed the steps of Madame Hohlakov’s house, a shiver of fear ran down his spine. In that moment he saw clearly, with the certainty of a mathematical proof, that this was his last hope, and that if it failed, there was nothing left for him in the world except to “rob and murder someone for the three thousand.” It was half-past seven when he rang the bell.

At first luck seemed to be on his side. The moment his name was announced, he was received with remarkable speed. “As if she’d been waiting for me,” thought Mitya, and no sooner had he been shown into the drawing-room than the lady of the house herself came running in and announced that she had been expecting him.

“I was expecting you! I was expecting you! I had no reason at all to think you would come to see me, as you must admit yourself. But I did expect you. You may well marvel at my instinct, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but all morning I was certain you would come.”

“That is certainly remarkable, madam,” said Mitya, sinking limply into a chair, “but I’ve come to you about something very important.... Something of the utmost importance for me, I mean, madam ... for me alone ... and I’m in a hurry to—”

“I know it’s most important business that brings you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. It isn’t a presentiment, it isn’t any reactionary throwback to the miraculous (have you heard about Father Zossima?). It’s a matter of mathematics: after everything that has passed with Katerina Ivanovna, you couldn’t help coming. You couldn’t, you couldn’t, it’s a mathematical certainty.”
“The realism of real life, madam, that’s what it is. But please let me explain—”
“Realism indeed, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I’m all for realism now. I’ve had my fill of miracles. Have you heard that Father Zossima is dead?”
“No, madam, this is the first I’ve heard of it.” Mitya was a little startled. Alyosha’s face came into his mind.
“Last night, and just imagine—”

“Madam,” said Mitya, “all I can imagine is that I’m in a desperate position, and that if you don’t help me, everything will fall apart, and I first of all. Forgive the commonplace expression, but I’m in a fever—”

“I know, I know you’re in a fever. How could you not be? And whatever you tell me, I know it in advance. I’ve been thinking about your destiny for a long time, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I’m watching over it and studying it.... Oh, believe me, I’m an experienced doctor of the soul, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

“Madam, if you’re an experienced doctor, then I’m certainly an experienced patient,” said Mitya, forcing himself to be polite, “and I feel that if you are watching over my fate like this, you will come to my aid in my ruin. So at least let me lay out for you the plan I’ve dared to bring to you ... and what I’m hoping you will do.... I’ve come, madam—”

“Don’t explain it. It’s of secondary importance. As for help, you’re not the first person I’ve helped, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You’ve most likely heard about my cousin, Madame Belmesov. Her husband was ruined, ‘had come to grief,’ as you so characteristically put it, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I advised him to go into horse-breeding, and now he’s doing well. Do you know anything about horse-breeding, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?”

“Not the faintest idea, madam. Ah, madam, not the faintest!” cried Mitya, so nervous and impatient that he half rose from his chair. “I’m begging you, madam, just listen to me. Give me two minutes to talk freely, so I can lay out everything, the whole plan I came with. Besides, I’m short of time. I’m in a terrible hurry,” Mitya cried hysterically. He could feel she was about to start talking again, and he hoped to head her off. “I’ve come in despair ... in the very last gasp of despair, to beg you for a loan of three thousand. A loan, but with safe security, madam, the safest, with the most trustworthy guarantees! Only let me explain—”

“You must tell me all that afterwards, afterwards!” Madame Hohlakov raised her hand and demanded silence in her turn. “And whatever you tell me, I know it all beforehand. I’ve said so already. You ask for a certain sum, three thousand, but I can give you more, immeasurably more. I will save you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but you must listen to me.”
Mitya shot up from his chair again.
“Madam, will you really be so kind!” he cried, deeply moved. “Good God, you’ve saved me! You’ve saved a man from a violent death, from a bullet.... My eternal gratitude—”
“I will give you more, infinitely more than three thousand!” cried Madame Hohlakov, smiling radiantly at Mitya’s delight.
“Infinitely? But I don’t need nearly that much. I only need that fatal three thousand. For that sum I can give security, and infinite gratitude with it, and I have a plan to propose which—”

“Enough, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, it’s as good as done.” Madame Hohlakov cut him off, with the modest triumph of a woman who does good. “I promised to save you, and I will. I’ll save you just as I saved Belmesov. Now, what do you think of the gold-mines, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?”
“Gold-mines, madam? I’ve never given them a thought.”

“Well, I have, on your behalf. Over and over. I’ve been watching you for a month now. A hundred times I’ve seen you go by, and each time I’ve said to myself: there goes a man of energy who belongs at the gold-mines. I’ve studied the way you walk and concluded that you’re a man who would find gold.”
“From the way I walk, madam?” said Mitya, smiling.

“Yes, from your walk. You surely don’t deny that you can read character from a person’s walk, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Science backs it up. I’m all for science and realism now. After all this business with Father Zossima, which has upset me so much, I’m a realist from today on, and I want to devote myself to something useful. I’m cured. ‘Enough!’ as Turgenev says.”
“But, madam, the three thousand you were so generous as to promise to lend me—”

“It’s yours, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Madame Hohlakov put in at once. “Consider the money in your pocket. Not three thousand, but three million, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, and in no time at all. The idea is my gift to you: you’ll find gold-mines, make millions, come back a leading man, and wake us all up and lead us to better things. Must we leave everything to the Jews? You’ll found institutions and enterprises of every kind. You’ll help the poor, and they’ll bless you. This is the age of the railway, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You’ll be famous, and the Department of Finance, which is in such a bad way just now, won’t be able to do without you. The falling rouble keeps me awake at night, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. People don’t know that side of me—”

“Madam, madam!” Dmitri broke in, with an uneasy foreboding. “I may well take your advice, your wise advice, madam.... I may go ... to the gold-mines.... I’ll come and talk to you about it again ... many times, in fact ... but now, that three thousand you were so generous ... oh, that would set me free, and if you could manage it today ... you see, I haven’t a minute, not one minute to lose today—”
“Enough, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, enough!” Madame Hohlakov broke in emphatically. “The question is whether you’ll go to the gold-mines or not. Is your mind completely made up? Answer yes or no.”
“I’ll go, madam, afterwards.... I’ll go wherever you want ... but now—”
“Wait!” cried Madame Hohlakov. She leaped up and ran to a handsome bureau full of little drawers, and began yanking them out one after another, hunting for something in desperate haste.

“The three thousand,” thought Mitya, his heart almost stopping, “and right on the spot ... no papers, no formalities ... that’s what I call behaving like a gentleman! She’s a splendid woman, if only she didn’t talk so much!”
“Here!” cried Madame Hohlakov, running joyfully back to Mitya. “Here’s what I was looking for!”
It was a tiny silver ikon on a cord, the kind that is sometimes worn under the clothes, next to the skin, along with a cross.
“This comes from Kiev, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” she went on reverently, “from the relics of the Holy Martyr Varvara. Let me put it on you myself, and with it dedicate you to a new life, a new career.”

And she really did put the cord over his head and start to arrange it. Mitya, in extreme embarrassment, bent down to help her, and at last he worked it under his necktie and collar and down inside his shirt to his chest.
“Now you may go,” Madame Hohlakov pronounced, sitting back down in her place with an air of triumph.

“Madam, I’m so touched. I really don’t know how to thank you ... for such kindness, but ... If you only knew how precious time is to me.... That money, which I’ll owe to your generosity.... Oh, madam, since you are so good to me, so touchingly generous,” Mitya exclaimed impulsively, “let me tell you ... though of course you’ve known it for a long time ... that I love someone here.... I’ve been unfaithful to Katya ... to Katerina Ivanovna, I should say.... Oh, I’ve treated her inhumanly, dishonorably, but I fell in love here with another woman ... a woman you, madam, may despise, since you know everything already, but one I can’t give up on any account, and so that three thousand now—”

“Give up everything, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Madame Hohlakov broke in, in the most decisive tone. “Give up everything, women above all. The gold-mines are your goal, and women have no place there. Later, when you come back rich and famous, you’ll find the girl of your heart in the best society. She’ll be a modern girl, educated, with advanced ideas. By then the woman question, which is only beginning to dawn, will have made progress, and the new woman will have arrived.”
“Madam, that’s not the point, not at all....” Mitya clasped his hands, pleading.

“It certainly is, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. It’s exactly what you need, the very thing you’re longing for, though you don’t know it yourself. I’m not in the least against the women’s movement of today, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. The development of women, and soon even their political emancipation, that’s my ideal. I have a daughter myself, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. People don’t know that side of me. I wrote to the author Shtchedrin about this very subject. He has taught me so much, so much about woman’s vocation. So last year I sent him an anonymous letter of two lines: ‘I kiss and embrace you, my teacher, for the modern woman. Persevere.’ And I signed it ‘A Mother.’ I thought of signing it ‘A contemporary Mother,’ and wavered, but I stayed with plain ‘Mother.’ There’s more moral beauty in that, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. Besides, the word ‘contemporary’ might have reminded him of ‘_The Contemporary_,’ which is a painful memory for him, because of the censorship.... Good heavens, what’s the matter!”
“Madam!” cried Mitya, leaping up at last and clasping his hands before her in helpless entreaty. “You’ll make me weep if you keep putting off what you so generously—”

“Oh, weep, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, do weep! That’s a noble feeling ... and what a road lies open before you! Tears will ease your heart, and later you’ll come back rejoicing. You’ll hurry to me from Siberia, just to share your joy with me—”
“But let me say something too!” Mitya cried suddenly. “For the last time I beg you, tell me: can I have the sum you promised me today? And if not, when can I come for it?”
“What sum, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?”
“The three thousand you promised me ... that you were so generous—”
“Three thousand? Roubles? Oh no, I haven’t got three thousand,” Madame Hohlakov announced, serenely surprised. Mitya was stunned.
“But you just said ... you said ... you said it was as good as in my hands—”

“Oh no, you misunderstood me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You misunderstood me there. I was talking about the gold-mines. It’s true I promised you more, infinitely more than three thousand, I remember it all now, but I meant the gold-mines.”
“But the money? The three thousand?” Mitya exclaimed, clumsily.

“Oh, if you mean money, I have none. Not a penny, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I’m in a quarrel with my steward over it, and I’ve just borrowed five hundred roubles from Miüsov myself. No, no, I have no money. And you know, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, even if I had, I wouldn’t give it to you. For one thing, I never lend money. Lending money means losing friends. And you, in particular, I wouldn’t give it to. I wouldn’t, because I like you and want to save you, since all you need is the gold-mines, the gold-mines, the gold-mines!”
“Oh, the devil take it!” roared Mitya, and he slammed his fist down on the table with all his strength.
“Aie! Aie!” cried Madame Hohlakov in alarm, and she fled to the far end of the drawing-room.

Mitya spat on the floor and strode quickly out of the room, out of the house, into the street, into the darkness! He walked like a man possessed, beating his breast at the very spot where he had struck himself two days earlier in front of Alyosha, the last time he had seen him, in the dark, on the road. What those blows on his breast meant, _on that spot_, and what he meant by them, was for the time being a secret. Nobody in the world knew it, and he had not told even Alyosha. But for him the secret meant more than disgrace. It meant ruin, suicide. That was what he had resolved on if he failed to get the three thousand to pay his debt to Katerina Ivanovna, and so wipe away from his breast, from _that spot on his breast_, the shame he carried there, which weighed on his conscience. All this will be explained to the reader fully later on. For now, with his last hope gone, this man, so strong to look at, burst into tears like a little child, only a few steps from the Hohlakovs’ house. He walked on, not knowing what he was doing, wiping his tears away with his fist. So he came out on the square, and all at once felt that he had stumbled into something. A piercing wail came from an old woman he had nearly knocked over.
“Good Lord, you’ve almost killed me! Why can’t you watch where you’re going, you good-for-nothing?”
“Why, it’s you!” cried Mitya, recognizing the old woman in the dark. It was Samsonov’s old servant, the one Mitya had noticed particularly the day before.
“And who might you be, my good sir?” said the old woman, in a quite different voice. “I can’t make you out in the dark.”
“You live at Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. You’re a servant there?”
“That’s right, sir. I was just running over to Prohoritch’s.... But I still don’t know who you are.”
“Tell me, good woman, is Agrafena Alexandrovna there now?” said Mitya, beside himself with suspense. “I brought her to the house myself a while ago.”
“She was there, sir. She stayed a little while, then she went off again.”
“What? She went away?” cried Mitya. “When did she go?”
“Why, right after she came. She stayed only a minute. She just told Kuzma Kuzmitch some story that made him laugh, and then she ran off.”
“You’re lying, damn you!” roared Mitya.
“Aie! Aie!” shrieked the old woman, but Mitya was already gone.
He ran as hard as he could to the house where Grushenka lived. By the time he got there, Grushenka was already on her way to Mokroe. She had left not even a quarter of an hour before.
Fenya was sitting in the kitchen with her grandmother, the old cook Matryona, when “the captain” burst in. At the sight of him Fenya gave a piercing shriek.
“So you scream?” roared Mitya. “Where is she?”
But before the terrified Fenya could get out a word, he dropped in a heap at her feet.
“Fenya, for Christ’s sake, tell me where she is!”
“I don’t know. Dmitri Fyodorovitch, my dear, I don’t know. Kill me if you like, I can’t tell you.” Fenya swore and protested. “You went out with her yourself not long ago—”
“She came back!”
“She did not, indeed. I swear to God she didn’t come back.”
“You’re lying!” shouted Mitya. “From your terror I know where she is.”

He rushed off. Fenya, in her fright, was glad to have got away so lightly. But she knew very well that he had only been in too much of a hurry, or she might not have fared so well. And as he ran, he startled both Fenya and old Matryona with something unexpected. On the table stood a brass mortar with a pestle in it, a small brass pestle, hardly more than six inches long. Mitya already had the door open with one hand when, with the other, he grabbed the pestle and shoved it into his side pocket.
“Oh, Lord! He’s going to murder someone!” cried Fenya, throwing up her hands.

chapters.title: IV. In The Dark
paragraphs: Where was he running? “Where else could she be but at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s? She must have gone straight to him from Samsonov’s. That was clear now. The whole intrigue, the whole deceit, was plain as day.” ... It all went whirling through his head. He did not run to Marya Kondratyevna’s. “No need to go there ... not the slightest need ... he must not raise an alarm ... they would run and tell on him right away.... Marya Kondratyevna was clearly in the plot, and Smerdyakov too, yes, he too, they had all been bought!”

He settled on a different plan. He went a long way around Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house, crossed the lane, ran down Dmitrovsky Street and over the little bridge, and came out at the deserted alley behind the house, which was empty and uninhabited. On one side was the wattle fence of a neighbor’s kitchen-garden. On the other was the tall, strong fence that ran all around Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden. Here he chose a spot, apparently the very one where, as the story went and he knew it, Lizaveta had once climbed over. “If she could climb over it,” the thought came to him, God knows why, “surely I can.” He jumped up and at once got a grip on the top of the fence. Then he hauled himself up with all his strength and sat astride it. The bath-house stood close by in the garden, but from the fence he could also see the lit windows of the house.

“Yes, the old man’s bedroom is lit up. She’s there!” And he leapt down from the fence into the garden. He knew Grigory was ill, and probably Smerdyakov too, and that nobody could hear him. Even so, he hid by instinct, stood stock-still and listened. But all around was dead silence, and, as if arranged on purpose, perfect stillness. Not the slightest breath of wind.

“And naught but the whispering silence,” a line of verse rose in his mind, he did not know why. “If only nobody heard me jump the fence! I don’t think they did.” He stood still for a minute. Then he walked softly across the grass of the garden, keeping clear of the trees and shrubs. He went slowly, creeping on tiptoe at every step, listening to the sound of his own feet. It took him five minutes to get to the lighted window. He remembered that directly under the window there were several thick, tall bushes of elder and whitebeam. The door from the house into the garden, on the left side, was shut. He had looked carefully to make sure of that as he passed. At last he reached the bushes and hid behind them. He held his breath. “Now I must wait,” he thought, “so they settle down, in case they heard my steps and are listening ... if only I don’t cough or sneeze.”

He waited two minutes. His heart was pounding, and at times he could barely breathe. “No, this thumping won’t stop,” he thought. “I can’t wait any longer.” He stood behind a bush, in its shadow. The window’s light lay across the front of the bush.

“How red the whitebeam berries are!” he murmured, not knowing why. Softly and silently, step by step, he came up to the window and rose on tiptoe. Fyodor Pavlovitch’s whole bedroom lay open to his eyes. It was a smallish room, split in two by a red screen, “Chinese,” as Fyodor Pavlovitch liked to call it. The word “Chinese” flashed through Mitya’s mind, “and behind the screen is Grushenka,” thought Mitya. He began to study Fyodor Pavlovitch, who had on a new striped-silk dressing-gown that Mitya had never seen, tied with a silk cord with tassels. Under the collar of the gown peeped a clean, dandyish shirt of fine linen with gold studs. On his head Fyodor Pavlovitch wore the same red bandage Alyosha had seen.
“So he’s dolled himself up,” thought Mitya.

His father stood near the window, seemingly lost in thought. All at once he jerked his head up and listened for a moment. Hearing nothing, he went over to the table and poured himself half a glass of brandy from a decanter, which he drank off. Then he gave a deep sigh and stood a moment more. He strolled to the looking-glass on the wall, lifted the red bandage a little from his forehead with his right hand, and started inspecting his bruises and scars, which had not yet healed.
“He’s alone,” thought Mitya. “Most likely he’s alone.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch stepped away from the looking-glass, turned abruptly toward the window and looked out. Mitya slid back into the shadow at once.

“She may be there behind the screen. Perhaps she’s asleep by now,” he thought, with a stab at his heart. Fyodor Pavlovitch left the window. “He was looking out for her, so she isn’t there. Why else would he peer into the dark? He’s wild with impatience.” ... Mitya crept forward again at once and went back to gazing in at the window. The old man had sat down at the table, looking disappointed. At last he rested his elbow on the table and leaned his right cheek on his hand. Mitya watched him greedily.
“He’s alone, he’s alone!” he said again. “If she were here, his face would be different.”

Oddly enough, a strange, senseless annoyance rose in him that she was not here. “It’s not that she isn’t here,” he explained to himself immediately, “it’s that I can’t tell for certain whether she is or not.” Mitya remembered afterward that his mind was unusually clear at that moment and that he took in everything, down to the least detail, and missed nothing. But a feeling of misery, the misery of uncertainty and indecision, was growing in his heart with every instant. “Is she here or not?” The angry doubt filled him, and suddenly, making up his mind, he reached out and knocked softly on the window frame. He knocked the signal the old man had agreed on with Smerdyakov: two slow knocks, then three quicker ones, the signal that meant “Grushenka is here!”
The old man gave a start, jerked up his head, sprang to his feet and ran to the window. Mitya slid away into the shadow. Fyodor Pavlovitch opened the window and stuck his whole head out.
“Grushenka, is that you? Is it you?” he said, in a kind of shaky half-whisper. “Where are you, my angel, where are you?” He was dreadfully excited and gasping for breath.
“He’s alone.” That settled it for Mitya.

“Where are you?” the old man cried again. He pushed his head out farther, right out to the shoulders, staring in every direction, left and right. “Come here, I’ve a little present for you. Come, I’ll show you....”
“He means the three thousand,” thought Mitya.
“But where are you? Are you at the door? I’ll open it this minute.”

And the old man all but climbed out of the window, peering to the right, where a door led into the garden, trying to see through the darkness. One second more and he would surely have run out to open the door, without waiting for Grushenka to answer.

Mitya watched him from the side without moving. He hated that profile so: the dangling Adam’s apple, the hooked nose, the lips smiling in greedy expectation. All of it stood out brightly in the slanting lamplight falling from the room on the left. A horrible fury of hatred suddenly swept through Mitya: “There he was, his rival, the man who had tormented him and wrecked his life!” It was a surge of that sudden, furious, vengeful rage which he had described to Alyosha, almost as if he had foreseen it, four days before in the arbor. Alyosha had asked him, “How can you say you’ll kill our father?” and he had answered, “I don’t know, I don’t know. Perhaps I shall not kill him, perhaps I shall. I’m afraid he’ll suddenly be so loathsome to me at that moment. I hate his double chin, his nose, his eyes, his shameless grin. I feel a personal repulsion. That’s what I’m afraid of, that’s what may be too much for me.” ... That personal repulsion was becoming unbearable. Mitya lost all control. Suddenly he pulled the brass pestle out of his pocket.

“God was watching over me then,” Mitya himself said later. At that very moment Grigory woke on his sickbed. Earlier that evening he had gone through the treatment Smerdyakov had described to Ivan. He had rubbed himself all over with vodka mixed with a secret, very strong brew, and had drunk what was left of it while his wife said a “certain prayer” over him. Then he had gone to bed. Marfa Ignatyevna had tasted the stuff too. Not being used to strong drink, she slept like the dead beside her husband.

But Grigory woke in the middle of the night, quite suddenly. He thought for a moment, and though a sharp pain shot through his back at once, he sat up in bed. Then he thought again, got up and dressed in a hurry. Perhaps his conscience pricked him at the idea of sleeping while the house stood unguarded “in such perilous times.” Smerdyakov, worn out by his fit, lay motionless in the next room. Marfa Ignatyevna did not stir. “The stuff’s been too much for the woman,” Grigory thought, glancing at her, and with a groan he went out onto the steps. He surely meant only to look around from the steps, for he could hardly walk. The pain in his back and in his right leg was unbearable. But all at once he remembered that he had not locked the little garden gate that evening. He was the most punctual and exact of men, a man who held to a fixed routine and to habits of many years. Limping and twisting with pain, he went down the steps and toward the garden. Yes, the gate was standing wide open. He stepped into the garden without thinking. Maybe he imagined something, maybe he heard a sound. He glanced to the left and saw his master’s window open. Nobody was looking out of it just then.

“Why is it open? It’s not summer,” thought Grigory. And at that very instant he glimpsed something extraordinary ahead of him in the garden. Forty paces off, a man seemed to be running through the dark. Some kind of shadow was moving very fast.

“Good Lord!” cried Grigory, beside himself. Forgetting the pain in his back, he hurried to cut off the running figure. He took a short cut, evidently knowing the garden better. The figure in flight made for the bath-house, ran around behind it and dashed to the garden fence. Grigory followed, never losing sight of him, and ran, forgetting everything. He reached the fence just as the man was climbing over. Grigory cried out in a frenzy, pounced on him and seized his leg in both hands.
Yes, his foreboding had not deceived him. He knew him. It was he, the “monster,” the “parricide.”
“Parricide!” the old man shouted so loudly that the whole neighborhood could have heard. But he had no time to shout more. He dropped at once, as if struck by lightning.

Mitya jumped back into the garden and bent over the fallen man. He had the brass pestle in his hand, and he flung it away mechanically into the grass. It landed two paces from Grigory, not in the grass but on the path, in a very conspicuous place. For some seconds he stared at the figure stretched out before him. The old man’s head was covered in blood. Mitya reached out and began to feel it. Afterward he remembered clearly how desperately anxious he had been to find out whether he had smashed the old man’s skull or only stunned him with the pestle. But the blood was pouring out horribly, and in a moment Mitya’s fingers were drenched in the hot stream. He remembered pulling out of his pocket the clean white handkerchief he had put there for his visit to Madame Hohlakov and pressing it to the old man’s head, senselessly trying to wipe the blood off his face and temples. But the handkerchief was soaked with blood in an instant.

“Good heavens! What am I doing this for?” thought Mitya, suddenly pulling himself together. “If I’ve smashed his skull, how can I find out now? And what difference does it make now?” he added, hopelessly. “If I’ve killed him, I’ve killed him.... You’ve come to grief, old man, so there you must lie!” he said aloud. And turning suddenly to the fence, he vaulted over it into the lane and ran—he clutched the blood-soaked handkerchief crushed in his right fist, and as he ran he shoved it into the back pocket of his coat. He ran headlong. The few people who passed him in the dark streets remembered afterward that they had met a man running that night. He flew back to the widow Morozov’s house.

As soon as he had left it that evening, Fenya had rushed to the head porter, Nazar Ivanovitch, and begged him, for Christ’s sake, “not to let the captain in again today or tomorrow.” Nazar Ivanovitch promised. But then his mistress suddenly sent for him, and he went upstairs. On the way he met his nephew, a boy of twenty who had only lately come from the country, and told him to take his place, but forgot to mention “the captain.” Mitya ran up to the gate and knocked. The lad knew him at once, for Mitya had tipped him more than once. He opened the gate right away, let him in, and hurried to tell him, with a cheerful smile, that “Agrafena Alexandrovna isn’t at home now, you know.”
“Where is she, then, Prohor?” asked Mitya, stopping short.
“She set off this evening, about two hours ago, with Timofey, for Mokroe.”
“What for?” cried Mitya.
“That I can’t say. To see some officer. Somebody invited her, and they sent horses to fetch her.”
Mitya left him and ran like a madman to Fenya.

chapters.title: V. A Sudden Resolution
paragraphs: Fenya was sitting in the kitchen with her grandmother. The two of them were just about to go to bed. They trusted Nazar Ivanovitch to keep watch, so they hadn’t locked the door. Mitya burst in, pounced on Fenya and grabbed her by the throat.
“Tell me, now! Where is she? Who’s she with now, at Mokroe?” he roared furiously.
Both women screamed.
“Aie! I’ll tell you! Aie! Dmitri Fyodorovitch, darling, I’ll tell you everything this minute, I won’t hide a thing,” Fenya gabbled, frightened to death. “She’s gone to Mokroe, to her officer.”
“What officer?” Mitya roared.
“Her officer! The same one she knew before, the one who threw her over five years ago,” Fenya cackled, as fast as the words would come.

Mitya let go of her throat. He stood facing her, deathly pale and unable to speak, but his eyes showed that he had taken it all in, all of it, from the very first word, and had guessed the whole situation. Poor Fenya was in no state to notice whether he understood or not. She sat on the trunk exactly as she had been when he rushed in, shaking all over and holding her hands out in front of her as if to ward off a blow. She seemed to have frozen in that position. Her eyes were wide with fright and fixed on him without a flicker. To make matters worse, both his hands were smeared with blood. He must have touched his forehead with them as he ran, wiping away the sweat, because there were bloody patches on his forehead and on his right cheek. Fenya was close to hysterics. The old cook had leaped up and was staring at him like a madwoman, nearly out of her mind with terror.

Mitya stood for a moment, then dropped mechanically onto a chair beside Fenya. He sat there without thinking, stunned and numb with terror. And yet it was all as clear as day. That officer: he knew about him, he knew all about him. He had heard it from Grushenka herself, and he had known that a letter from the man had arrived a month ago. So for a whole month this had been going on behind his back, right up to the arrival of this new man, and he had never once thought of him! But how could he, how could he have failed to think of him? Why had he forgotten this officer, simply forgotten him the moment he heard of him? That was the question that rose up before him like some monstrous thing. And he stared at this monstrous thing in horror, going cold with horror.

But suddenly, as gently and mildly as an affectionate child, he began talking to Fenya, as if he had completely forgotten how he had just frightened and hurt her. He started to question her with a thoroughness that was astonishing in his state. The girl kept staring wildly at his bloodstained hands, yet she too answered every question with wonderful readiness and speed, as if she were eager to give him the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Little by little, even with a kind of enjoyment, she began to explain every detail. She had no wish to torment him. She seemed eager to be as useful to him as she possibly could.
