She told him about the whole of that day, down to the smallest thing: the visit from Rakitin and Alyosha, how she, Fenya, had kept watch, how her mistress had set off, and how she had called out of the window to Alyosha, asking him to give Mitya her greetings and tell him “to remember for ever how she had loved him for an hour.”
At the news of this message, Mitya suddenly smiled, and color rose in his pale cheeks. Just then Fenya said to him, not the least bit afraid now of being nosy:
“Look at your hands, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. They’re all over blood!”
“Yes,” Mitya answered mechanically. He gave his hands a careless glance and at once forgot both them and Fenya’s question.

He fell silent again. Twenty minutes had gone by since he ran in. The first shock had passed, but it was plain that some new, fixed resolve had taken hold of him. He suddenly stood up, smiling dreamily.
“What’s happened to you, sir?” said Fenya, pointing at his hands again. She spoke with pity, as though she now felt very close to him in his grief. Mitya looked at his hands once more.

“That’s blood, Fenya,” he said, looking at her oddly. “That’s human blood, and, good God, why was it shed? But ... Fenya ... there’s a fence here” (he looked at her as if he were setting her a riddle), “a high fence, terrible to look at. But tomorrow at dawn, when the sun comes up, Mitya will jump over that fence.... You don’t understand what fence, Fenya, and never mind.... You’ll hear tomorrow and then you’ll understand ... and now, goodbye. I won’t stand in her way. I’ll step aside, I know how to step aside. Live, my joy.... You loved me for an hour, so remember Mityenka Karamazov for ever.... She always called me Mityenka, do you remember?”
And with those words he abruptly left the kitchen. This sudden exit frightened Fenya almost more than his rushing in and attacking her had.

Exactly ten minutes later Dmitri arrived at the house of Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, the young official he had pawned his pistols to. It was already half-past eight. Pyotr Ilyitch had finished his evening tea and had just put his coat back on, meaning to go to the “Metropolis” for a game of billiards. Mitya caught him on his way out.
At the sight of his face smeared with blood, the young man cried out in astonishment.
“Good heavens! What on earth has happened?”
“I’ve come for my pistols,” said Mitya, “and I’ve brought the money. Thanks very much. I’m in a hurry, Pyotr Ilyitch, so be quick, please.”

Pyotr Ilyitch was growing more and more astonished. He suddenly noticed a wad of banknotes in Mitya’s hand. Besides, Mitya had come in holding the notes in a way no one ever holds money: in his right hand, stretched out in front of him, as though to display them. Perhotin’s servant boy met Mitya in the passage, and said afterwards that he had walked into the passage in the same way, with the money stretched out in his hand, so he must have carried it like that even in the street. They were all hundred-rouble notes of the rainbow-colored kind, and the fingers that held them were covered with blood.

Later, when Pyotr Ilyitch was asked how much money it was, he said it was hard to tell at a glance, but it might have been two thousand, or maybe three. It was a big, “fat” bundle. “Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” he testified afterwards, “didn’t seem himself either. He wasn’t drunk, but he seemed, as it were, carried away, lost to everything around him, and at the same time absorbed, as though he were turning something over and searching for something and couldn’t decide. He was in a great hurry, he answered abruptly and very oddly, and at moments he seemed not at all gloomy but quite cheerful.”
“But what _is_ the matter with you? What’s wrong?” cried Pyotr Ilyitch, staring wildly at his visitor. “How did you get covered in blood? Did you fall? Look at yourself!”
He took him by the elbow and led him over to the mirror.
At the sight of his bloodstained face, Mitya gave a start and scowled furiously.

“Damn it! That’s the last straw,” he muttered angrily. He quickly shifted the notes from his right hand to his left and jerked the handkerchief out of his pocket on impulse. But the handkerchief turned out to be soaked with blood too (it was the one he had used to wipe Grigory’s face). There was hardly a white spot left on it. It hadn’t just begun to dry, either, but had stiffened into a crumpled ball that couldn’t be pulled apart. Mitya flung it angrily on the floor.
“Oh, damn it!” he said. “Haven’t you got some kind of rag ... to wipe my face?”
“So you’re just stained, not wounded? Then you’d better wash,” said Pyotr Ilyitch. “There’s the washstand. I’ll pour you some water.”
“A washstand? Fine ... but what am I to do with this?”
In the strangest bewilderment he pointed to his wad of hundred-rouble notes, looking at Pyotr Ilyitch as though it were for him to decide what Mitya should do with his own money.
“Put it in your pocket, or on the table here. It won’t go missing.”

“In my pocket? Yes, in my pocket. All right.... But, I say, all this is nonsense,” he cried, as if suddenly waking from his trance. “Look, let’s deal with the business of the pistols first. Give them back to me. Here’s your money ... because I need them badly ... and I haven’t a minute, not one minute to spare.”
And taking the top note off the wad, he held it out to Pyotr Ilyitch.
“But I won’t have enough change for that. Haven’t you got a smaller one?”
“No,” said Mitya, looking at the wad again, and as if he didn’t trust his own words, he flipped over two or three of the top notes.
“No, they’re all the same,” he added, and again looked at Pyotr Ilyitch as if asking him.
“How did you get so rich?” the other asked. “Wait, I’ll send my boy to Plotnikov’s. They stay open late. He’ll see if they can change it. Here, Misha!” he called into the passage.

“To Plotnikov’s shop, splendid!” cried Mitya, as though an idea had struck him. “Misha,” he said to the boy as he came in, “listen, run over to Plotnikov’s and tell them Dmitri Fyodorovitch sends his greetings and will be there in a moment.... But listen, listen, tell them to have champagne ready before I come, three dozen bottles, packed the way it was when it went to Mokroe. I took four dozen with me that time,” he added (suddenly addressing Pyotr Ilyitch). “They know all about it, don’t you worry, Misha,” he said, turning to the boy again. “Wait, listen. Tell them to put in cheese, Strasburg pies, smoked fish, ham, caviare, and everything, everything they have, up to a hundred roubles, or a hundred and twenty like last time.... But wait, don’t let them forget dessert: sweets, pears, watermelons, two or three or four—no, one melon will do—and chocolate, candy, toffee, fondants. In fact, everything I took to Mokroe before, three hundred roubles’ worth with the champagne ... let it be exactly the same again. And remember, Misha, if that is your name—His name is Misha, isn’t it?” He turned to Pyotr Ilyitch again.
“Hold on a minute,” Pyotr Ilyitch cut in, listening and watching him uneasily. “You’d better go and tell them yourself. He’ll get it wrong.”

“He will, I can see he will! Eh, Misha! Why, I was ready to kiss you for running this errand.... If you don’t get it wrong, there are ten roubles for you. Run along, hurry up.... Champagne’s the main thing, make them bring plenty of champagne. And brandy too, and red and white wine, and everything I had then.... They know what I had then.”

“But listen!” Pyotr Ilyitch interrupted, a little impatiently. “Let him just run and get the money changed and tell them not to close, and you go and give the order yourself.... Give him your note. Off you go, Misha! Look lively!”

Pyotr Ilyitch seemed to be hurrying Misha out on purpose. The boy was standing there with his mouth and eyes wide open, plainly understanding very little of Mitya’s orders, and gazing in amazement and terror at his bloodstained face and at the shaking, bloodstained fingers that held the notes.
“Now come and wash,” said Pyotr Ilyitch sternly. “Put the money on the table, or else in your pocket.... That’s it, come along. But take off your coat.”
And as he started helping him out of his coat, he cried out again:
“Look, your coat’s covered in blood too!”

“That ... that’s not the coat. Just a little on the sleeve here.... And that’s only here, where the handkerchief was. It must have soaked through. I must have sat on the handkerchief at Fenya’s, and the blood came through,” Mitya explained at once, with an astounding, childlike lack of awareness. Pyotr Ilyitch listened with a frown.
“Well, you must have been up to something. You must have been fighting with somebody,” he muttered.

They began to wash. Pyotr Ilyitch held the jug and poured the water. Mitya, in desperate haste, hardly soaped his hands (they were shaking, and Pyotr Ilyitch remembered that afterwards). But the young official insisted that he soap them properly and scrub them harder. As time went on he seemed to gain more and more authority over Mitya. It may be mentioned in passing that he was a young man of firm character.

“Look, your nails aren’t clean. Now rub your face, here, on your temples, by your ear.... Are you going out in that shirt? Where are you going? Look, the whole cuff of your right sleeve is covered in blood.”
“Yes, it’s all bloody,” Mitya remarked, looking at his shirt cuff.
“Then change your shirt.”

“I haven’t time. You see, I’ll ...” Mitya went on with the same trusting simplicity, drying his face and hands on the towel and putting on his coat. “I’ll turn it up at the wrist. It won’t show under the coat.... See?”

“Now tell me, what have you been up to? Fighting with somebody? In the tavern again, like last time? Have you been beating that captain again?” Pyotr Ilyitch asked him reproachfully. “Who have you been beating this time ... or killing, perhaps?”
“Nonsense!” said Mitya.
“What do you mean, ‘nonsense’?”
“Don’t worry,” said Mitya, and suddenly laughed. “I just smashed an old woman in the market-place.”
“Smashed? An old woman?”
“An old man!” cried Mitya, looking Pyotr Ilyitch straight in the face, laughing and shouting at him as if he were deaf.
“Confound it! An old woman, an old man.... Have you killed somebody?”

“We made it up. We had a row, and we made it up. At a place I know. We parted friends. A fool.... He’s forgiven me.... He must have forgiven me by now ... if he’d got up, he wouldn’t have forgiven me”—Mitya suddenly winked—“only damn him, you know, I say, Pyotr Ilyitch, damn him! Don’t worry about him! I don’t want to, right now!” Mitya snapped, firmly.

“Why on earth do you have to go picking fights with everybody? ... Like you did with that captain, over some trifle.... You’ve been brawling, and now you’re off on a spree. That’s you all over! Three dozen bottles of champagne, what do you want with all that?”

“Bravo! Now give me the pistols. Honestly, I haven’t a moment now. I’d love to have a talk with you, my dear fellow, but I’ve no time. And there’s no need, it’s too late for talking. Where’s my money? Where did I put it?” he cried, thrusting his hands into his pockets.

“You put it on the table ... yourself.... Here it is. Forgot already? Money’s like dirt or water to you, it seems. Here are your pistols. Strange, isn’t it? At six o’clock you pawned them for ten roubles, and now you’ve got thousands. Two or three, I’d say.”
“Three, you bet,” laughed Mitya, stuffing the notes into the side pocket of his trousers.
“You’ll lose it like that. Have you struck a gold mine?”

“Mines? Gold mines?” Mitya shouted at the top of his voice and burst into a roar of laughter. “Would you like to go to the mines, Perhotin? There’s a lady here who’ll hand over three thousand for you if you’ll only go. She did it for me, she’s so terribly fond of gold mines. Do you know Madame Hohlakov?”
“I don’t know her, but I’ve heard of her and I’ve seen her. Did she really give you three thousand? Really?” said Pyotr Ilyitch, eyeing him doubtfully.

“As soon as the sun rises tomorrow, as soon as Phœbus, ever young, flies upward, praising and glorifying God, you go to her, this Madame Hohlakov, and ask her whether she handed over that three thousand or not. Try and find out.”

“I don’t know what footing you’re on with her ... but since you say it so positively, I suppose she did give it to you. You’ve got the money in your hand, and instead of going to Siberia you’re spending it all.... Where are you really off to now, eh?”
“To Mokroe.”
“To Mokroe? But it’s night!”
“Once the lad had all, now the lad has naught,” Mitya cried suddenly.
“How, ‘naught’? You say that with all those thousands!”
“I’m not talking about thousands. Damn thousands! I’m talking about the female character.
Fickle is the heart of woman, Treacherous and full of vice;
I agree with Ulysses. That’s what he says.”
“I don’t understand you!”
“Am I drunk?”
“Not drunk, but worse.”
“I’m drunk in spirit, Pyotr Ilyitch, drunk in spirit! But that’s enough!”
“What are you doing, loading the pistol?”
“I’m loading the pistol.”

Mitya unfastened the pistol case, actually opened the powder horn, and carefully poured in the powder and rammed down the charge. Then he took the bullet and, before putting it in, held it up between two fingers in front of the candle.
“Why are you staring at the bullet?” asked Pyotr Ilyitch, watching him with uneasy curiosity.
“Oh, just a whim. Tell me, if you meant to put that bullet in your brain, would you look at it first or not?”
“Why look at it?”

“It’s going into my brain, so it’s interesting to look and see what it’s like. But that’s foolishness, a moment’s foolishness. There, that’s done,” he added, putting in the bullet and driving it home with the ramrod. “Pyotr Ilyitch, my dear fellow, that’s nonsense, all nonsense, and if only you knew what nonsense! Now give me a little piece of paper.”
“Here’s some paper.”
“No, a clean new sheet, writing paper. That’s right.”

And taking a pen from the table, Mitya swiftly wrote two lines, folded the paper in four and pushed it into his waistcoat pocket. He put the pistols in their case, locked it and kept it in his hand. Then he looked at Pyotr Ilyitch with a slow, thoughtful smile.
“Now, let’s go.”
“Where are we going? No, wait a minute.... Are you thinking of putting that bullet in your brain, perhaps?” Pyotr Ilyitch asked uneasily.
“I was fooling about the bullet! I want to live. I love life! You can be sure of that. I love golden-haired Phœbus and his warm light.... Dear Pyotr Ilyitch, do you know how to step aside?”
“What do you mean, ‘stepping aside’?”

“Making way. Making way for someone dear, and for someone I hate. And letting the one I hate become dear to me. That’s what making way means! And saying to them: God bless you, go your way, move on, while I—”
“While you—?”
“Enough, let’s go.”
“On my word, I’ll tell someone to stop you from going there,” said Pyotr Ilyitch, looking at him. “What are you going to Mokroe for, anyway?”
“There’s a woman there, a woman. That’s all you need to know. Shut up.”
“Listen, you’re a savage, but I’ve always liked you.... I’m worried.”
“Thanks, old fellow. A savage, you say. Savages, savages! That’s just what I keep saying. Savages! Why, here’s Misha! I’d forgotten him.”

Misha came running in, in a great hurry, with a handful of notes in change. He reported that everyone at the Plotnikovs’ was in a bustle. “They’re carrying out the bottles, and the fish, and the tea. It’ll all be ready in a minute.” Mitya grabbed ten roubles and handed them to Pyotr Ilyitch, then tossed another ten-rouble note to Misha.

“Don’t you dare do that!” cried Pyotr Ilyitch. “I won’t have it in my house. It’s a bad habit, it spoils people. Put your money away. Here, put it here. Why waste it? You’ll be glad of it tomorrow, and I’d bet you’ll be coming to borrow ten roubles from me again. Why do you keep stuffing the notes in your side pocket? Ah, you’ll lose them!”
“Listen, my dear fellow, let’s go to Mokroe together.”
“What would I go for?”
“Listen, let’s open a bottle right now and drink to life! I want a drink, and I especially want to drink with you. I’ve never drunk with you, have I?”
“All right, we can go to the ‘Metropolis.’ I was just on my way there.”
“No time for that. Let’s drink at the Plotnikovs’, in the back room. Want me to ask you a riddle?”
“Go ahead.”
Mitya took the piece of paper out of his waistcoat pocket, unfolded it and showed it. In a large, clear hand it said: “I punish myself for my whole life, my whole life I punish!”
“I’m definitely going to tell someone, I’ll go right now,” said Pyotr Ilyitch, after reading the paper.
“You won’t have time, my dear boy. Come and have a drink. March!”

Plotnikov’s shop was at the corner of the street, two doors down from Pyotr Ilyitch’s. It was the largest grocery shop in our town, and by no means a bad one. It belonged to some rich merchants. They kept everything you could get in a Petersburg shop: groceries of every sort, wines “bottled by the brothers Eliseyev,” fruit, cigars, tea, coffee, sugar, and so on. They always employed three shop assistants and two errand boys. Our part of the country had grown poorer, the landowners had gone away and trade had got worse. Even so, the grocery stores flourished as before, more prosperous every year, because there were plenty of buyers for their goods.

They were waiting for Mitya impatiently in the shop. They remembered vividly how, three or four weeks ago, he had bought wine and goods of every kind to the value of several hundred roubles, paid for in cash. (They would never have let him have anything on credit, of course.) They remembered that then, as now, he had held a bundle of hundred-rouble notes in his hand and scattered them at random. He hadn’t bargained or stopped to think, or cared to think, what use so much wine and food would be to him. The story went all over the town that, when he drove off to Mokroe with Grushenka that time, he had “spent three thousand in one night and the following day, and come back from the spree without a penny.” He had picked up a whole troop of gypsies (camped in our neighborhood at the time), who for two days took money off him without limit while he was drunk, and drank expensive wine without limit. People used to tell, laughing at Mitya, how he had given champagne to peasants with grimy hands, and treated the village women and girls to sweets and Strasburg pies. It was rather risky to laugh at Mitya to his face, but there was a lot of laughter behind his back, especially in the tavern. They laughed at his own artless, public admission that all he had got out of Grushenka by this “escapade” was “permission to kiss her foot, and that was the most she had allowed him.”

By the time Mitya and Pyotr Ilyitch reached the shop, they found a cart with three horses harnessed abreast, with bells, and Andrey the driver waiting for Mitya at the entrance. Inside the shop they had almost finished packing one box of provisions. They were only waiting for Mitya to arrive so they could nail it shut and put it in the cart. Pyotr Ilyitch was astounded.
“Where did this cart come from so quickly?” he asked Mitya.

“I met Andrey as I ran to your place, and told him to drive straight here to the shop. There’s no time to lose. Last time I went with Timofey, but now Timofey has gone on ahead of me with the witch. Will we be very late, Andrey?”

“They’ll only get there an hour before us, at most, maybe not even that. I got Timofey ready to start. I know how he’ll go. Their pace won’t be ours, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. How could it be? They won’t get there an hour earlier!” Andrey replied warmly. He was a lanky, red-haired driver of middle age, wearing a full-skirted coat, with a kaftan over his arm.
“Fifty roubles for vodka if we’re only an hour behind them.”
“I guarantee the time, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. Ech, they won’t be half an hour ahead of us, let alone an hour.”

Mitya bustled about seeing to things, but he gave his orders oddly, in a scattered, jumbled way. He would begin a sentence and forget the end of it. Pyotr Ilyitch found himself having to step in and help.
“Four hundred roubles’ worth, not less than four hundred roubles’ worth, just like last time,” Mitya ordered. “Four dozen champagne, not a bottle less.”
“What do you want with so much? What’s it for? Wait!” cried Pyotr Ilyitch. “What’s this box? What’s in it? Surely there isn’t four hundred roubles’ worth here?”

The eager shopmen began explaining, with oily politeness, that the first box held only half a dozen bottles of champagne and only “the most essential articles,” such as savories, sweets, toffee and so on. But the main part of the goods ordered would be packed and sent off, as on the previous occasion, in a special cart, also with three horses, traveling at full speed. It would arrive no more than an hour after Dmitri Fyodorovitch himself.
“No more than an hour! No more than an hour! And put in more toffee and fondants. The girls there are so fond of them,” Mitya insisted hotly.

“The fondants are all right. But what do you want with four dozen champagne? One would be enough,” said Pyotr Ilyitch, almost angry. He began haggling and asking for an itemized bill, and wouldn’t be satisfied. But he only managed to save a hundred roubles. In the end it was agreed that only three hundred roubles’ worth should be sent.
“Oh, go to the devil!” cried Pyotr Ilyitch, thinking better of it. “What’s it to me? Throw your money away, since it cost you nothing.”

“This way, my economist, this way, don’t be angry.” Mitya drew him into a room at the back of the shop. “They’ll bring us a bottle here in a minute. We’ll taste it. Ech, Pyotr Ilyitch, come along with me, you’re a nice fellow, the sort I like.”

Mitya sat down on a wicker chair in front of a little table covered with a dirty napkin. Pyotr Ilyitch sat down opposite. The champagne soon appeared, and oysters were suggested to the gentlemen. “First-class oysters, the last lot in.”
“Oh, hang the oysters. I don’t eat them. And we don’t need a thing,” cried Pyotr Ilyitch, almost angrily.
“There’s no time for oysters,” said Mitya. “And I’m not hungry. Do you know, friend,” he said suddenly, with feeling, “I’ve never liked all this disorder.”
“Who does like it? Three dozen champagne for peasants, On my word, that’s enough to make anyone angry!”

“That’s not what I mean. I’m talking about a higher order. There’s no order in me, no higher order. But ... that’s all over. There’s no need to grieve about it. It’s too late, damn it! My whole life has been disorder, and now it has to be set in order. Is that a pun, eh?”
“You’re raving, not punning!”
“Glory be to God in Heaven, Glory be to God in me....
“That verse came from my heart once. It’s not a verse, it’s a tear.... I made it myself ... though not while I was pulling the captain’s beard....”
“Why do you bring him up all of a sudden?”
“Why do I bring him up? Foolery! Everything comes to an end; everything is made equal. That’s the long and short of it.”
“You know, I keep thinking about your pistols.”

“That’s all foolery too! Drink, and don’t get fanciful. I love life. I’ve loved life too much, shamefully much. Enough! Let’s drink to life, dear boy, I propose the toast. Why am I pleased with myself? I’m a scoundrel, but I’m satisfied with myself. And yet I’m tortured by the thought that I’m a scoundrel and satisfied with myself. I bless creation. I’m ready to bless God and His creation this minute, but ... I must kill one noxious insect, for fear it crawls about and spoils life for others.... Let us drink to life, dear brother. What can be more precious than life? Nothing! To life, and to one queen of queens!”
“Let’s drink to life, and to your queen too, if you like.”
They drank a glass each. Mitya was excited and expansive, but he was melancholy too. It was as if some heavy, crushing anxiety were weighing on him.
“Misha ... here’s your Misha come! Misha, come here, my boy, drink this glass to Phœbus, the golden-haired, of tomorrow morning....”
“What are you giving it to him for?” cried Pyotr Ilyitch irritably.
“Yes, yes, yes, let me! I want to!”
“E—ech!”
Misha emptied the glass, bowed, and ran out.

“He’ll remember that later,” Mitya remarked. “Woman, I love woman! And what is woman? The queen of creation! My heart is sad, my heart is sad, Pyotr Ilyitch. Do you remember Hamlet? ‘I am very sorry, good Horatio! Alas, poor Yorick!’ Maybe that’s me, Yorick? Yes, I’m Yorick now, and a skull later.”
Pyotr Ilyitch listened in silence. Mitya was silent for a while too.
“What dog is that you’ve got here?” he asked the shopman casually. He had noticed a pretty little lap dog with dark eyes sitting in the corner.
“It belongs to Varvara Alexyevna, the mistress,” answered the clerk. “She brought it and forgot it here. It has to be taken back to her.”

“I saw one like it ... in the regiment ...” murmured Mitya dreamily, “only that one had a broken hind leg.... By the way, Pyotr Ilyitch, I wanted to ask you: have you ever stolen anything in your life?”
“What a question!”
“Oh, I didn’t mean anything. From someone’s pocket, you know. I don’t mean government money, everyone steals that, and no doubt you do too....”
“Go to the devil.”
“I’m talking about other people’s money. Stealing straight out of a pocket? Out of a purse, eh?”
“I stole twenty kopecks from my mother when I was nine years old. I took it off the table on the sly, and held it tight in my hand.”
“Well, and what happened?”
“Nothing much. I kept it for three days, then I was ashamed, owned up, and gave it back.”
“And then?”
“Naturally I was whipped. But why do you ask? Have you stolen something?”
“I have,” said Mitya, winking slyly.
“What did you steal?” asked Pyotr Ilyitch, curious.
“I stole twenty kopecks from my mother when I was nine years old, and gave it back three days later.”
As he said this, Mitya suddenly got up.
“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, are you coming now?” called Andrey from the door of the shop.

“Are you ready? We’re coming!” Mitya started. “A few last words and—Andrey, a glass of vodka for the start. Give him some brandy as well! That box” (the one with the pistols) “put under my seat. Good-by, Pyotr Ilyitch, don’t hold anything against me.”
“But you’re coming back tomorrow?”
“Of course.”
“Will you settle the little bill now?” cried the clerk, springing forward.
“Oh, yes, the bill. Of course.”

He pulled the bundle of notes out of his pocket again, picked out three hundred roubles, threw them on the counter, and hurried out of the shop. Everyone followed him out, bowing and wishing him good luck. Andrey jumped up on the box, coughing from the brandy he had just swallowed. But Mitya was only just taking his seat when, to his surprise, he saw Fenya in front of him. She ran up panting, clasped her hands before him with a cry, and dropped down at his feet.

“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, dear good Dmitri Fyodorovitch, don’t hurt my mistress. And it was me who told you everything.... And don’t murder him, he was there first, he’s hers! He’s going to marry Agrafena Alexandrovna now. That’s why he’s come back from Siberia. Dmitri Fyodorovitch, dear, don’t take another human being’s life!”

“Tut—tut—tut! That’s it, is it? So you’re off there to make trouble!” muttered Pyotr Ilyitch. “Now it’s all clear, clear as daylight. Dmitri Fyodorovitch, give me your pistols right now, if you mean to behave like a man,” he shouted to Mitya. “Do you hear, Dmitri?”

“The pistols? Wait a bit, brother, I’ll throw them into the pool on the road,” answered Mitya. “Fenya, get up, don’t kneel to me. Mitya won’t hurt anyone, the silly fool won’t ever hurt anyone again. But listen, Fenya,” he shouted, after taking his seat. “I hurt you just now, so forgive me and have pity on me, forgive a scoundrel.... But it doesn’t matter if you don’t. It’s all the same now. Now then, Andrey, look alive, fly along at full speed!”
Andrey whipped up the horses, and the bells began ringing.
“Good-by, Pyotr Ilyitch! My last tear is for you!...”

“He’s not drunk, but he keeps babbling like a lunatic,” Pyotr Ilyitch thought as he watched him go. He had half a mind to stay and watch the cart being packed with the remaining wines and provisions. He knew they would cheat and defraud Mitya. But suddenly he felt annoyed with himself, turned away with a curse and went to the tavern to play billiards.

“He’s a fool, but he’s a good fellow,” he muttered as he went. “I’ve heard about that officer, Grushenka’s old flame. Well, if he has turned up.... Ech, those pistols! Damn it all! I’m not his nurse! Let them do as they please! Besides, it’ll all come to nothing. They’re brawlers, that’s all. They’ll drink and fight, fight and make up again. They’re not men who do anything real. What does he mean by ‘I’m stepping aside, I’m punishing myself’? It’ll come to nothing! He’s shouted phrases like that a thousand times, drunk, in the taverns. But now he’s not drunk. ‘Drunk in spirit’—they’re fond of fine phrases, the villains. Am I his nurse? He must have been fighting, his face was covered in blood. Who with? I’ll find out at the ‘Metropolis.’ And his handkerchief was soaked in blood.... It’s still lying on my floor.... Hang it!”

He reached the tavern in a bad mood and at once got up a game. The game cheered him. He played a second game, and suddenly began telling one of his partners that Dmitri Karamazov had come into cash again, something like three thousand roubles, and had gone to Mokroe again to spend it with Grushenka.... This news roused strange interest in his listeners. They all talked about it, not laughing, but with odd seriousness. They stopped playing.
“Three thousand? But where could he have got three thousand?”
Questions were asked. The story of Madame Hohlakov’s gift was received with skepticism.
“Hasn’t he robbed his old father?—that’s the question.”
“Three thousand! There’s something odd about it.”
“He boasted aloud that he would kill his father. We all heard him, right here. And it was three thousand he talked about ...”
Pyotr Ilyitch listened. All at once his answers became short and dry. He said not a word about the blood on Mitya’s face and hands, though he had meant to mention it at first.

They began a third game, and little by little the talk about Mitya died away. But by the end of the third game Pyotr Ilyitch had no more desire for billiards. He laid down the cue and, without having supper as he had intended, walked out of the tavern. When he reached the market place he stood still in bewilderment, wondering at himself. He realized that what he wanted was to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s and find out whether anything had happened there. “Over some stupid nonsense—as it’s sure to turn out—am I going to wake up the household and make a scandal? Fooh! Damn it, is it my business to look after them?”

In a very bad mood he went straight home, and suddenly remembered Fenya. “Damn it all! I should have questioned her just now,” he thought with annoyance. “I’d have heard everything.” And the wish to speak to her and find out became so pressing and insistent that, halfway home, he turned sharply and went toward the house where Grushenka lodged. Going up to the gate he knocked. The sound of the knock in the silence of the night sobered him and made him feel irritated. And no one answered him; everyone in the house was asleep.
“And I’ll be making a fuss!” he thought, feeling thoroughly uncomfortable. But instead of going away altogether, he started knocking again with all his might, filling the street with noise.
“Not coming? Well, I’ll wake them up, I will!” he muttered at each knock, fuming at himself. But at the same time he knocked even harder on the gate.

chapters.title: VI. “I Am Coming, Too!”
paragraphs: But Dmitri Fyodorovitch was racing down the road. Mokroe was a little over twenty versts away, but Andrey’s three horses ran so fast that they could cover it in an hour and a quarter. The speed brought Mitya back to life. The air was cool and fresh, and large stars stood out in the sky. It was the very night, and maybe the very hour, when Alyosha threw himself down on the earth and swore in a rapture to love it forever and ever.

Everything in Mitya’s soul was in confusion, pure confusion. Many things were goading his heart. Yet at that moment his whole being longed for her, his queen, and he was flying to see her for the last time. One thing I can say for certain: his heart did not waver for a single instant. People may not believe me when I say this, but the jealous lover felt no jealousy at all toward the new rival who seemed to have sprung out of the ground. Any other man who turned up would have made him jealous at once, and he might well have stained his violent hands with blood again. But as he flew through the night, he felt no envy and not even any hostility toward the man who had been her first lover.... True, he had not yet laid eyes on him.

“Here there was no room for dispute: it was her right and his. This was her first love, and after five years she had not forgotten it. So for five whole years she had loved only him, and I—what am I to her? What right do I have? Step aside, Mitya, and make way! What am I now? Now it’s all over, apart from the officer—even if he had never turned up, it would all be over ...”

These words would roughly have put his feelings into speech, if he had been in any state to reason. But he was not. His plan of action had not been reasoned out. It had sprung from feeling the moment Fenya spoke, and he had taken it up in a flash, with everything that followed from it. And still, despite his resolve, his soul was in turmoil, an agonizing turmoil. The resolve gave him no peace. Too much lay behind him, and it tormented him. At times it struck him as strange that he had written his own death sentence with pen and paper—“I punish myself”—and that the paper was lying in his pocket, ready, and the pistol was loaded, and he had already settled how he would meet the first warm ray of “golden-haired Phœbus” next morning.

Still, he could not shake off the past, all that he had left behind and that tortured him. He felt this wretchedly, and the thought sank into his heart like despair. For one moment he had the urge to stop Andrey, jump out of the cart, pull out his loaded pistol and finish everything without waiting for dawn. But the moment passed like a spark. The horses galloped on, “devouring space.” As he got closer to his goal, the thought of her, only of her, filled his soul more and more and drove out the terrible pictures that had haunted it. Oh, how he longed to see her, if only for a moment, if only from far off!

“She’s with _him_ now,” he thought. “Now I’ll see what she looks like beside him, her first love, and that’s all I ask.” Never before had this woman, who had such a fateful hold on his life, roused such love in his breast. It was a new, unknown feeling, which surprised even him, a feeling so tender that it was almost worship, a wish to efface himself before her. “I will efface myself!” he said, in a surge of almost hysterical ecstasy.

They had been galloping for nearly an hour. Mitya said nothing. Andrey, who was usually a talkative peasant, had not spoken either. He seemed afraid to, and only kept whipping up his three lean but spirited bays. Then suddenly Mitya cried out in horrible anxiety:
“Andrey! What if they’re asleep?”
The idea hit him like a blow. It had never crossed his mind until now.
“They may well be in bed by now, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”
Mitya frowned as if in pain. Yes, of course ... here he was rushing there ... with such feelings ... and they were asleep ... she was asleep, perhaps, there too.... Anger rose in his heart.
“Drive on, Andrey! Whip them up! Look alive!” he cried, beside himself.
“But maybe they’re not in bed!” Andrey went on after a pause. “Timofey said there was a whole crowd of them there—”
“At the station?”
“Not the posting-station, but Plastunov’s, the inn, where they hire out horses, too.”
“I know the place. So there’s a crowd, you say? How is that? Who are they?” cried Mitya, badly shaken by this news.

“Well, Timofey said they’re all gentlefolk. Two are from our town—who, I can’t say—and two more are strangers, and maybe there are others. I didn’t ask in particular. They’ve started playing cards, so Timofey said.”
“Cards?”
“So they may not be in bed if they’re at cards. It’s probably not even eleven.”
“Faster, Andrey! Faster!” Mitya cried again, in a nervous voice.
“Can I ask you something, sir?” said Andrey after a pause. “Only I’m afraid you’ll be angry, sir.”
“What is it?”

“Well, Fenya threw herself at your feet a while ago and begged you not to hurt her mistress, or somebody else, either ... so you see, sir— I’m the one driving you there ... forgive me, sir, it’s my conscience ... maybe it’s foolish of me to bring it up—”
Mitya suddenly grabbed him by the shoulders from behind.
“Are you a driver?” he asked wildly.
“Yes, sir.”

“Then you know a man has to give way. What would you say of a driver who wouldn’t give way to anybody, who just drove on and crushed people? No, a driver mustn’t run people down. You can’t run down a human being. You can’t wreck people’s lives. And if you have wrecked a life—punish yourself.... If you’ve only wrecked, if you’ve only ruined somebody’s life—punish yourself and go away.”
The words burst out of Mitya in something close to hysteria. Andrey was astonished, but he kept the conversation going.

“That’s right, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, you’re quite right. A man mustn’t be crushed or tormented, nor any creature, because God made every one of them. Take a horse, say. Some folks, even among us drivers, drive any way they like. Nothing holds them back, they just push the horse on.”

“To hell?” Mitya broke in, and let out his short, abrupt laugh. “Andrey, simple soul,” and he grabbed him by the shoulders again, “tell me, what do you think, will Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov go to hell or not?”

“I can’t say, darling, it depends on you, because you are ... you see, sir, when the Son of God was nailed to the Cross and died, He went down to hell from the Cross and set free all the sinners who were suffering there. And the devil groaned, because he thought he’d get no more sinners in hell. And God said to him then, ‘Do not groan, for you shall have all the mighty of the earth, the rulers, the chief judges and the rich, and you shall be filled up as you have been in all the ages till I come again.’ Those were His very words ...”
“A peasant legend! Wonderful! Whip up the left horse, Andrey!”

“So you see, sir, who hell is meant for,” said Andrey, whipping up the left horse, “but you’re like a little child ... that’s how we think of you ... and you may be hot-tempered, sir, but God will forgive you for your kind heart.”
“And you, Andrey, do you forgive me?”
“What have I got to forgive you, sir? You’ve never done me any harm.”
“No, for everyone, for everyone, you alone here on the road—will you forgive me for everyone? Speak, simple peasant heart!”
“Oh, sir! I’m afraid of driving you, the way you talk is so strange.”
But Mitya did not hear him. He was praying wildly and muttering to himself.

“Lord, take me as I am, with all my lawlessness, and do not condemn me. Let me slip past Your judgment ... do not condemn me, for I have condemned myself. Do not condemn me, for I love You, O Lord. I am a wretch, but I love You. If You send me to hell, I shall love You there, and from there I shall cry out that I love You forever and ever.... But let me love to the end.... Here and now, for just five hours ... until the first light of Your day ... for I love the queen of my soul ... I love her and I cannot help loving her. You see my whole heart.... I shall gallop up, I shall fall down before her and say, ‘You are right to go your way and leave me. Farewell, and forget your victim ... never trouble yourself over me!’”
“Mokroe!” cried Andrey, pointing ahead with his whip.

Out of the pale darkness of the night rose a solid black mass of buildings, dropped, it seemed, onto the vast plain. Mokroe was a village of two thousand people, but at that hour all of them were asleep, and only a few scattered lights still twinkled.
“Drive on, Andrey, I’m coming!” Mitya exclaimed in a fever.
“They’re not asleep,” said Andrey again, pointing his whip at the Plastunovs’ inn at the edge of the village. All six of its windows on the street were blazing with light.
“They’re not asleep,” Mitya repeated with joy. “Faster, Andrey! Gallop! Come in with a dash! Make the bells ring! Let everybody know I’ve come. I’m coming! I’m coming, too!”
Andrey lashed his worn-out horses into a gallop, swept up with a dash, and pulled his steaming, panting team to a stop at the high front steps.
Mitya sprang from the cart just as the innkeeper, who was heading for bed, looked out from the steps to see who had arrived.
“Trifon Borissovitch, is that you?”
The innkeeper bent forward and peered, then ran down the steps and hurried up to his guest with cringing delight.
“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, your honor! Is it really you again?”

Trifon Borissovitch was a stocky, healthy peasant of middle height, with a rather fat face. His look was stern and hard, especially toward the peasants of Mokroe. But he could put on the most cringing face imaginable when he smelled some profit in it. He dressed in the Russian way, in a shirt that buttoned at the side and a coat with full skirts. He had put by a good sum, yet he was forever dreaming of rising in the world. More than half the peasants were in his clutches, and everyone in the district owed him money. He bought and leased land from the neighboring landowners, and the peasants worked it to pay off debts they could never be rid of. He was a widower with four grown daughters. One was already a widow and lived at the inn with her two children, his grandchildren, working for him like a charwoman. Another had married a petty official, and in one of the inn’s rooms, among the family photographs on the wall, hung a small photograph of this official in uniform and official epaulettes. The two younger daughters wore fashionable blue or green dresses, tight in the back and with trains a yard long, on Church holidays or when they paid calls. Yet the next morning they would be up at dawn as always, sweeping the rooms with a birch broom, emptying slops and cleaning up after the lodgers.

For all the thousands of roubles he had saved, Trifon Borissovitch dearly loved to empty a drunken guest’s pockets. He remembered that less than a month before, in just twenty-four hours, he had taken two or even three hundred roubles from Dmitri, when Dmitri came on his spree with Grushenka. So he gave him an eager welcome now, scenting his prey the instant Mitya drove up to the steps.
“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, dear sir, so we see you again!”
“Hold on, Trifon Borissovitch,” Mitya began, “first of all, where is she?”
“Agrafena Alexandrovna?” The innkeeper understood at once and gave Mitya’s face a sharp look. “She’s here, too ...”
“Who’s with her? Who?”

“Some strangers. One is an official, a gentleman, a Pole by the sound of him. He’s the one who sent the horses from here to fetch her. And there’s another with him, a friend of his or a traveling companion, who can tell. They’re in civilian clothes.”
“Well, are they feasting? Have they money?”
“A poor sort of feast! Nothing to brag about, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”
“Nothing to brag about? And who are the others?”

“Two gentlemen from the town.... They’ve come back from Tcherny and put up here. One is quite a young gentleman, a relation of Mr. Miüsov, it must be, but I’ve forgotten his name ... and I expect you know the other as well, a gentleman by the name of Maximov. He’s been on a pilgrimage, he says, to the monastery in the town. He’s traveling with this young relation of Mr. Miüsov.”
“Is that all?”
“Yes.”
“Listen, Trifon Borissovitch, hold on. Tell me the main thing: what about her? How is she?”
“Oh, she only just got here. She’s sitting with them.”
“Is she cheerful? Is she laughing?”
“No, I don’t think she’s laughing much. She’s sitting there rather bored. She’s combing the young gentleman’s hair.”
“The Pole—the officer?”
“He isn’t young, and he isn’t an officer, either. Not him, sir. I mean the young gentleman who’s Mr. Miüsov’s relation ... I’ve forgotten his name.”
“Kalganov.”
“That’s the one, Kalganov!”
“All right. I’ll see for myself. Are they playing cards?”
“They were, but they’ve given it up. They’ve had tea, and the official gentleman called for liqueurs.”
“Hold on, Trifon Borissovitch, hold on, my good soul, I’ll see for myself. Now answer me one more thing: are the gypsies here?”
“No gypsies for you now, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. The authorities drove them off. But there are Jews in the village who play the cymbals and the fiddle, and we could send for them. They’d come.”
“Send for them. Yes, send for them!” cried Mitya. “And get the girls together the way you did before, Marya above all, and Stepanida, and Arina, too. Two hundred roubles for a chorus!”

“Oh, for money like that I can rouse the whole village, even though they’re asleep by now. But are the peasants here worth such kindness, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, or the girls, either? Throwing away that much on such coarse, rude people! What’s the use of giving a peasant a cigar, the stinking ruffian! And the girls are all lousy. Besides, I’ll get my own daughters up for nothing, never mind that sum. They’ve only just gone to bed—I’ll give them a kick and make them sing for you. The other day you gave the peasants champagne to drink, e—ech!”

Whatever sympathy Trifon Borissovitch pretended to feel for Mitya, on that last visit he had hidden half a dozen bottles of champagne, and he had picked up a hundred-rouble note from under the table and kept it.
“Trifon Borissovitch, last time I was here I sent more than a thousand flying. Do you remember?”
“Flying it went. How could I forget? You must have left three thousand behind.”
“Well, I’ve come to do the same again, do you see?”
And he pulled out his roll of banknotes and held it up right in front of the innkeeper’s nose.

“Now listen and remember. In an hour the wine will get here, with savories, pies and sweets—bring it all up at once. And that box Andrey has is to come up at once as well. Open it and pour champagne right away. And the girls, we need the girls, Marya most of all.”
He turned to the cart and took out the box of pistols.
“Here, Andrey, let’s settle. Here are fifteen roubles for the drive, and fifty for vodka ... for your willingness, for your love.... Remember Karamazov!”
“I’m afraid, sir,” Andrey faltered. “Give me five roubles extra, but I won’t take more than that. Trifon Borissovitch, you’re my witness. Forgive my foolish words ...”

“What are you afraid of?” asked Mitya, looking him over. “Well, go to the devil, if that’s how it is!” he cried, flinging him five roubles. “Now, Trifon Borissovitch, take me up quietly and let me have a look at them first, so they won’t see me. Where are they? In the blue room?”

Trifon Borissovitch gave Mitya a wary look, but at once did as he was told. He took him into the passage and went by himself into the first big room, next to the one where the guests sat, and carried away the light. Then he led Mitya in on tiptoe and set him in a dark corner, where he could watch the company freely without being seen. But Mitya did not look for long. In fact he could not see them at all. He saw her. His heart pounded, and everything went dark before his eyes.

She sat sideways to the table in a low chair, and next to her on the sofa was the pretty youth, Kalganov. She was holding his hand and seemed to be laughing, while he, who looked annoyed and would not look at her, was saying something loudly to Maximov, who sat across the table facing Grushenka. Maximov was roaring with laughter at something. On the sofa sat _he_, and on a chair beside the sofa sat the other stranger. The man on the sofa was leaning back and smoking a pipe. Mitya got the impression of a stoutish, short little man with a broad face, who was plainly angry about something. His friend, the other stranger, struck Mitya as remarkably tall, but he could make out nothing more. He caught his breath. He could not stand it for a minute. He set the pistol-case down on a chest and, his heart pounding and a chill running through him, walked straight into the blue room to face them all.
“Aie!” shrieked Grushenka, who was the first to see him.

chapters.title: VII. The First And Rightful Lover
paragraphs: Mitya crossed the room in long, quick strides and went straight to the table.

“Gentlemen,” he said, loudly, almost shouting, yet stumbling over every word, “I ... I’m all right! Don’t be afraid!” he exclaimed. “I—nothing’s the matter,” he said, suddenly turning to Grushenka, who had shrunk back in her chair toward Kalganov and was gripping his hand. “I ... I’m coming, too. I’m here till morning. Gentlemen, may I stay with you till morning? Only till morning, one last time, in this very room?”
He put this last question to the fat little man with the pipe, who sat on the sofa. The man took the pipe from his lips with great dignity and said sternly:
“_Panie_, this is a private party. There are other rooms.”
“Why, it’s Dmitri Fyodorovitch! What’s the matter with you?” Kalganov broke in. “Sit down with us. How are you?”
“Delighted to see you, my dear ... my precious fellow. I always thought the world of you.” Mitya answered joyfully and eagerly, and held out his hand across the table at once.
“Ow! What a grip you have! You’ve nearly broken my fingers,” laughed Kalganov.

“He always grips like that, always,” Grushenka put in cheerfully, with a timid smile. One look at Mitya’s face had suddenly convinced her that he wasn’t going to make a scene. She watched him with keen curiosity, and with some worry still. Something in him struck her. In fact, the last thing she had expected was for him to walk in and talk like this at such a moment.
“Good evening,” Maximov said blandly from the left. Mitya rushed over to him, too.

“Good evening. You’re here, too! I’m so glad to find you here, too! Gentlemen, gentlemen, I—” (He turned again to the Polish gentleman with the pipe, plainly taking him for the most important person there.) “I flew here.... I wanted to spend my last day, my last hour in this room, in this very room ... where I, too, worshiped ... my queen.... Forgive me, _panie_,” he cried wildly, “I flew here and swore— Oh, don’t be afraid, it’s my last night! Let’s drink to a good understanding between us. They’ll bring the wine in a minute.... I brought this along.” (Something made him pull out his bundle of notes.) “Allow me, _panie_! I want music, singing, a revel, just as we had before. But the worm, the useless worm, will crawl away, and there’ll be nothing left of him. On my last night I’ll honor my day of joy.”

He was almost choking. He had so much, so much to say, and nothing came out of his mouth but odd exclamations. The Pole stared hard at him, then at the bundle of notes in his hand, then at Grushenka, and plainly didn’t know what to make of it.
“If my suverin lady is permitting—” he started.

“What’s ‘suverin’? ‘Sovereign,’ I suppose?” Grushenka cut in. “You talk so funny I can’t help laughing. Sit down, Mitya, what are you going on about? Please don’t scare us. You won’t scare us, will you? If you won’t, I’m glad to see you ...”
“Me, scare you?” cried Mitya, flinging up his hands. “Oh, pass me by, go your way, I won’t stand in your road!...”

And suddenly he startled them all, and no doubt himself too. He dropped onto a chair and burst into tears, turning his face to the far wall, his arms wrapped tight around the chair back as though he were hugging it.

“Oh, come now, what a man you are!” cried Grushenka reproachfully. “That’s how he always comes to see me—he starts talking, and I can’t make out what he means. He cried like this once before, and here he is crying again! It’s a disgrace! What are you crying for? _As though you had anything to cry for!_” she added mysteriously, stressing every word, a little irritably.
“I ... I’m not crying.... Well, good evening!” He swung round in his chair at once and laughed—not his abrupt, wooden laugh but a long, shaky, silent, nervous one.

“Well, you’re at it again.... Come on, cheer up, cheer up!” Grushenka coaxed him. “I’m very glad you came, very glad, Mitya, do you hear, I’m very glad! I want him to stay here with us,” she declared to the whole room, though her words were clearly aimed at the man on the sofa. “That’s what I want, that’s what I want! And if he goes, I’m going, too!” she added, her eyes flashing.
“Whatever my queen commands is law!” announced the Pole, kissing Grushenka’s hand with a gallant air. “Please, _panie_, join our company,” he added politely to Mitya.
Mitya sprang up, evidently meaning to launch into another tirade, but no words came.
“Let’s drink, _panie_,” was all he blurted out in place of a speech. Everyone laughed.

“Heavens! I thought he was going to start in again!” Grushenka said nervously. “Listen, Mitya,” she went on, pressing him, “stop prancing about. But it’s nice that you’ve brought champagne. I’d like some myself, and I can’t bear liqueurs. And best of all, you’re here yourself. We were dreadfully bored.... You’ve come on a spree again, I suppose? But put that money away. Where did you get so much?”

The whole time, Mitya had been holding the crumpled bundle of notes in his hand, and every eye in the room was on it, the Poles’ most of all. Embarrassed, he hastily shoved it into his pocket. He blushed. Just then the innkeeper came in with an uncorked bottle of champagne and glasses on a tray. Mitya grabbed the bottle, but he was so rattled that he had no idea what to do with it. Kalganov took it out of his hands and poured the champagne.

“Another! Bring another bottle!” Mitya shouted to the innkeeper. Forgetting to clink glasses with the Pole he had so solemnly asked to drink to their good understanding, he downed his glass without waiting for anyone else. His whole face changed at once. The solemn, tragic look he had walked in with was gone, and something childlike took its place. He seemed suddenly gentle and subdued. He looked around at everyone, shy and happy, with a constant little nervous laugh, and with the blissful look of a dog that has done wrong, been punished and been forgiven. He seemed to have forgotten everything, and he gazed around at them all with a childlike smile of delight. He looked at Grushenka, laughing the whole time, and pulled his chair right up beside hers. Gradually he had begun to form some idea of the two Poles, though he had no clear picture of them yet.

The Pole on the sofa impressed him with his dignified manner and his Polish accent, and most of all with his pipe. “Well, so what? It’s a good thing he smokes a pipe,” he thought. The Pole’s puffy, middle-aged face, with its tiny nose and its two very thin, pointed, dyed, cheeky-looking mustaches, hadn’t raised the slightest suspicion in Mitya so far. He wasn’t even particularly struck by the man’s ridiculous wig, made in Siberia, with love-locks combed foolishly forward over the temples. “It must be all right, since he wears a wig,” he went on, musing blissfully. The other Pole, the younger one, was staring at the company with insolent defiance and listening to the talk in silent contempt. He impressed Mitya only by his great height, which made a striking contrast with the Pole on the sofa. “If he stood up, he’d be six foot three.” The thought flitted through Mitya’s head. It also occurred to him that this man must be the other’s friend, a kind of “bodyguard,” and that the big Pole was no doubt at the service of the little Pole with the pipe. But all this seemed to Mitya perfectly proper and not to be questioned. In his doglike mood of submission, every feeling of rivalry had died out.

He completely failed to understand Grushenka’s mood, or the mysterious tone of some of her words. All he understood, with a thrill in his heart, was that she was being kind to him, that she had forgiven him and let him sit by her. He was beside himself with joy, watching her sip her champagne. The silence in the room seemed to strike him, though, and he looked around at everyone with expectant eyes.
“Why are we just sitting here, gentlemen? Why don’t you get something going?” his smiling eyes seemed to ask.
“He keeps talking nonsense, and we’ve all been laughing,” Kalganov said suddenly, as if he had read Mitya’s thought, and he pointed at Maximov.
Mitya promptly stared at Kalganov, then at Maximov.
“Talking nonsense, is he?” he laughed his short, wooden laugh, suddenly delighted about something—“ha ha!”
“Yes. Believe it or not, he swears that all our cavalry officers in the twenties married Polish women. Isn’t that awful rot?”
“Polish women?” Mitya repeated, in sheer ecstasy.

Kalganov knew very well how Mitya felt about Grushenka, and he had guessed about the Pole as well. But that interested him little, perhaps not at all. What interested him was Maximov. He had come here with Maximov by chance, and he was meeting the Poles at this inn for the first time in his life. He had known Grushenka before and had once visited her with someone, but she hadn’t warmed to him. Tonight, though, she looked at him very fondly. Before Mitya arrived she had been fussing over him, but somehow it didn’t move him. He was a boy, not yet twenty, dressed like a dandy, with a very charming fair-skinned face and splendid thick fair hair. Out of that fair face looked beautiful pale blue eyes, with an intelligent and at times even deep expression, beyond his years in fact, though the young man sometimes looked and talked just like a child, and wasn’t the least ashamed of it, even when he noticed it himself. As a rule he was very willful, even capricious, though always friendly. Now and then there was something fixed and stubborn in his look. He would look at you and listen, and all the while seem to be dreaming doggedly of something else. He was often listless and lazy; at other times he would get excited, sometimes, it seemed, over the most trivial things.

“Just think, I’ve been dragging him around with me for the last four days,” he went on, drawling lazily, quite naturally though, with no affectation at all. “Ever since your brother, remember, shoved him off the carriage and sent him flying. That’s when I took an interest in him, and I took him with me to the country. But he talks such rot that I’m ashamed to be seen with him. I’m taking him back.”
“The gentleman has not seen Polish ladies, and says what is not possible,” the Pole with the pipe told Maximov.
He spoke Russian reasonably well, better, at any rate, than he let on. Whenever he used a Russian word, he twisted it into a Polish shape.
“But I was married to a Polish lady myself,” Maximov tittered.
“But did you serve in the cavalry? You were talking about the cavalry. Were you a cavalry officer?” Kalganov chimed in immediately.
“A cavalry officer, is he? Ha ha!” cried Mitya, listening eagerly, his questioning eyes going from one speaker to the next, as if there were no telling what he might hear from any of them.

“No, you see,” Maximov said, turning to him. “What I mean is, those pretty Polish ladies ... when they danced the mazurka with our Uhlans ... when one of them dances the mazurka with a Uhlan, she jumps onto his knee like a kitten ... a little white one ... and the _pan_-father and _pan_-mother watch and let it happen.... They let it happen ... and the next day the Uhlan comes and proposes.... That’s how it is ... proposes, he he!” Maximov finished, tittering.

“The _pan_ is a _lajdak_!” the tall Pole on the chair suddenly growled, crossing one leg over the other. Mitya’s eye fell on his huge greased boot with its thick, dirty sole. Both Poles’ clothes looked rather greasy.
“Now what’s this, _lajdak_! What’s he scolding about?” said Grushenka, suddenly annoyed.
“_Pani_ Agrippina, the gentleman saw servant girls in Poland, not ladies of good family,” the Pole with the pipe told Grushenka.
“You can count on that,” the tall Pole snapped scornfully.
“What next! Let him talk! People talk, so why stop them? It livens things up,” Grushenka said crossly.
“I’m not stopping them, _pani_,” said the Pole in the wig. He gave Grushenka a long look, sank back into dignified silence, and went on sucking his pipe.

“No, no. The Polish gentleman told the truth.” Kalganov was worked up again, as though it were a question of enormous importance. “He’s never been to Poland, so how can he talk about it? I suppose you weren’t married in Poland, were you?”

“No, in the Province of Smolensk. But a Uhlan had already brought her to Russia before that, my future wife, together with her mamma, her aunt, and another woman relative who had a grown-up son. He brought her straight from Poland and handed her over to me. He was a lieutenant in our regiment, a very nice young man. At first he meant to marry her himself. In the end he didn’t, because she turned out to be lame.”
“So you married a lame woman?” cried Kalganov.
“Yes. The two of them deceived me a little at the time, and kept it hidden. I thought she was hopping; she kept hopping.... I thought it was for fun.”
“She was so happy to be marrying you!” yelled Kalganov in a ringing, childish voice.

“Yes, so happy. But it turned out to be for quite another reason. Later, once we were married, that very evening after the wedding, she confessed, and asked forgiveness in a very touching way. ‘As a child I jumped over a puddle once,’ she said, ‘and hurt my leg.’ He he!”
Kalganov burst into the most childish laughter and nearly fell onto the sofa. Grushenka laughed, too. Mitya was at the peak of happiness.

“You know, that’s the truth, he isn’t lying this time,” Kalganov exclaimed, turning to Mitya; “and you know, he’s been married twice; it’s his first wife he’s talking about. But his second wife, you know, ran away, and she’s alive now.”
“Is that possible?” said Mitya, turning quickly to Maximov, utterly astonished.

“Yes. She did run away. I’ve had that unpleasant experience,” Maximov agreed modestly, “with a _monsieur_. And what made it worse, she’d had all my little property made over to her beforehand. ‘You’re an educated man,’ she told me. ‘You can always make a living.’ With that she settled my affairs. A venerable bishop once said to me: ‘One of your wives was lame, but the other was too light-footed.’ He he!”

“Listen, listen!” cried Kalganov, bubbling over. “If he tells lies—and he often does—he only does it to amuse us all. There’s no harm in that, is there? You know, sometimes I like him. He’s dreadfully low, but it comes naturally to him, eh? Don’t you think so? Some people are low for gain, but he’s simply made that way. Just think, he claims (he argued about it all the way yesterday) that Gogol wrote _Dead Souls_ about him. Remember, there’s a landowner named Maximov in it, the one Nozdryov thrashed. He was charged, remember, ‘with inflicting bodily injury with rods on the landowner Maximov while drunk.’ Can you believe it, he claims he was that Maximov and that he was beaten! Now can that be true? Tchitchikov made his journey at the very latest at the beginning of the twenties, so the dates don’t fit. He couldn’t have been thrashed then, could he?”
It was hard to guess what Kalganov was so stirred up about, but his excitement was real. Mitya went along with him without protest.
“Well, so what if they did thrash him!” he cried, laughing.
“It isn’t that they thrashed me, exactly, but what I mean is—” Maximov put in.
“What do you mean? Either they thrashed you or they didn’t.”
“What o’clock is it, _panie_?” the Pole with the pipe asked his tall friend, looking bored. The other shrugged in answer. Neither of them had a watch.

“Why not talk? Let other people talk. Are other people not allowed to talk just because you’re bored?” Grushenka flew at him, obviously set on picking a quarrel. Something seemed to dawn on Mitya’s mind for the first time. This time the Pole answered with unmistakable irritation.
“_Pani_, I raised no objection. I said nothing.”
“Fine, then. Come, tell us your story,” Grushenka called to Maximov. “Why is everyone so quiet?”

“There’s nothing to tell, it’s all so silly,” Maximov answered at once, plainly pleased, with a little mincing air. “Besides, it’s all allegory in Gogol, because he gave every name a meaning. Nozdryov was really called Nosov, and Kuvshinikov had quite a different name, Shkvornev. Fenardi really was called Fenardi, only he wasn’t an Italian but a Russian. And Mamsel Fenardi was a pretty girl, with her pretty little legs in tights and a short little skirt with spangles, and she kept turning round and round, only not for four hours but for four minutes, and she bewitched everyone...”
“But what did they beat you for?” cried Kalganov.
“For Piron!” Maximov answered.
“What Piron?” cried Mitya.

“The famous French writer Piron. We were all drinking, a big party of us, in a tavern at that same fair. They had invited me, and first of all I started quoting epigrams. ‘Is that you, Boileau? What a funny outfit!’ and Boileau replies that he’s off to a masquerade, meaning the baths, he he! They took it as aimed at them, so I hurried to recite another, a very biting one, known to every educated person:
Yes, Sappho and Phaon are we! But one grief is weighing on me. You don’t know your way to the sea!

That offended them even more, and they began to abuse me in the most unseemly way. And as bad luck would have it, to smooth things over I started telling a very cultured anecdote about Piron, how he was refused entry to the French Academy and, to get his revenge, wrote his own epitaph:
Ci-gît Piron qui ne fut rien, Pas même académicien.
They grabbed me and thrashed me.”
“But what for? What for?”
“For my education. A man can be thrashed for anything,” Maximov concluded, briefly and sententiously.
“Oh, stop it! That’s all stupid, I don’t want to listen. I thought it would be fun,” Grushenka snapped at them suddenly.

Mitya flinched and stopped laughing at once. The tall Pole stood up. He looked bored and out of place, and with a haughty air he began pacing from corner to corner of the room, hands clasped behind his back.
“Ah, he can’t sit still,” said Grushenka, eyeing him with scorn. Mitya began to feel uneasy. He also noticed that the Pole on the sofa kept looking at him with irritation.
“_Panie!_” cried Mitya. “Come, let’s drink! You and the other _pan_, too! Let’s all drink.”
In a flash he had dragged three glasses over and filled them with champagne.
“To Poland, _panovie_! I drink to your Poland!” cried Mitya.
“With great pleasure, _panie_,” said the Pole on the sofa, with dignity and a friendly, lordly air, and he picked up his glass.
“And the other _pan_, what’s his name? Drink, most illustrious, take your glass!” Mitya urged.
“Pan Vrublevsky,” put in the Pole on the sofa.
Pan Vrublevsky came over to the table, rolling a little as he walked.
“To Poland, _panovie!_” cried Mitya, lifting his glass. “Hurrah!”
All three drank. Mitya grabbed the bottle and filled three glasses again.
“Now to Russia, _panovie_, and let’s be brothers!”
“Pour some for us,” said Grushenka. “I’ll drink to Russia, too!”
“So will I,” said Kalganov.
“And I will, too ... to Russia, the old grandmother!” tittered Maximov.
“Everybody! Everybody!” cried Mitya. “Trifon Borissovitch, bring more bottles!”
The other three bottles Mitya had brought with him were set on the table. Mitya filled the glasses.
“To Russia! Hurrah!” he shouted again. Everyone drank the toast except the Poles, and Grushenka downed her whole glass in one go. The Poles left theirs untouched.
“What’s this, _panovie_?” cried Mitya. “Won’t you drink?”
Pan Vrublevsky took his glass, raised it and said in a ringing voice:
“To Russia as she was before 1772.”
“Now that’s more like it!” cried the other Pole, and they both emptied their glasses at once.
“You’re fools, you _panovie_,” Mitya blurted out suddenly.
“_Panie!_” shouted both Poles in a threatening way, bristling at Mitya like a pair of fighting cocks. Pan Vrublevsky was the angrier of the two.
“Can a man help loving his own country?” he shouted.

“Quiet! No quarreling! I won’t have it!” cried Grushenka in a commanding voice, and she stamped her foot on the floor. Her face was flushed and her eyes were bright. The glass she had just drunk was clearly working on her. Mitya was badly frightened.
“_Panovie_, forgive me! It was my fault, I’m sorry. Vrublevsky, _panie_ Vrublevsky, I’m sorry.”
“You, anyway, shut your mouth! Sit down, you idiot!” Grushenka scolded, angry and annoyed.
They all sat down. Nobody spoke; they just looked at one another.
“Gentlemen, it was all my fault,” Mitya began again, unable to make sense of Grushenka’s words. “Well, why are we just sitting here? What can we do ... to have some fun again?”
“Ach, nothing here is fun at all!” Kalganov mumbled lazily.
“Let’s play faro again, like we did a while ago,” Maximov tittered suddenly.
“Faro? Splendid!” cried Mitya. “If only the _panovie_—”
“It’s lite, _panovie_,” the Pole on the sofa answered, as though reluctantly.
“True,” agreed Pan Vrublevsky.
“Lite? What’s that, ‘lite’?” asked Grushenka.
“Late, _pani_! I mean ‘a late hour,’” the Pole on the sofa explained.

“With them it’s always late. They can never do anything!” Grushenka almost shrieked in her anger. “They’re dull themselves, so they want everyone else dull, too. Before you came, Mitya, they sat here just as silent and kept turning up their noses at me.”
“My goddess!” cried the Pole on the sofa. “I see you’re not kindly toward me, and that is why I’m gloomy. I’m ready, _panie_,” he added, turning to Mitya.
“Go ahead, _panie_,” Mitya agreed. He pulled his notes out of his pocket and put two hundred-rouble notes on the table. “I want to lose a lot to you. Take your cards. Deal the bank.”
“We’ll take the cards from the landlord, _panie_,” said the little Pole, gravely and firmly.
“That’s much the best way,” chimed in Pan Vrublevsky.
“From the landlord? Fine, I see, we’ll get them from him. Cards!” Mitya shouted to the landlord.

The landlord brought a new pack, still sealed. He told Mitya that the girls were getting ready and the Jews with the cymbals would probably arrive soon, but the cart with the provisions had not come yet. Mitya jumped up from the table and ran into the next room to give instructions. Only three girls had turned up, though, and Marya wasn’t there yet. And he himself didn’t know what instructions to give, or why he had run out. All he did was tell them to unpack the presents for the girls from the box, the sweets, the toffee and the fondants. “And vodka for Andrey, vodka for Andrey!” he cried in a hurry. “I was rude to Andrey!”
Suddenly Maximov, who had followed him out, tapped him on the shoulder.
“Give me five roubles,” he whispered to Mitya. “I’ll put something on faro, too, he he!”
“Capital! Splendid! Take ten, here!”
Again he pulled all the notes out of his pocket and picked out a ten-rouble one. “And if you lose that, come back, come back.”

“Very good,” Maximov whispered joyfully, and scurried back. Mitya went back too, apologizing for keeping them waiting. The Poles had sat down and opened the pack. They looked far friendlier now, almost warm. The Pole on the sofa had lit another pipe and was getting ready to deal. He had a solemn look about him.
“Take your places, gentlemen,” cried Pan Vrublevsky.
“No, I won’t play any more,” said Kalganov. “I just lost fifty roubles to them.”
“The _pan_ had no luck. Maybe he’ll be lucky this time,” the Pole on the sofa said, turning to him.
“How much is in the bank? Enough to match me?” asked Mitya.
“It depends, _panie_. A hundred, maybe two hundred, as much as you care to stake.”
“A million!” laughed Mitya.
“Perhaps the Pan Captain has heard of Pan Podvysotsky?”
“What Podvysotsky?”

“In Warsaw there was a bank, and anyone at all could come and bet against it. Podvysotsky comes, sees a thousand gold pieces, bets against the bank. The banker says, ‘_Panie_ Podvysotsky, are you putting down the gold, or are we to trust your honor?’ ‘My honor, _panie_,’ says Podvysotsky. ‘So much the better.’ The banker throws the dice. Podvysotsky wins. ‘Take it, _panie_,’ says the banker, and he pulls out the drawer and gives him a million. ‘Take it, _panie_, this is what you won.’ There was a million in the bank. ‘I didn’t know that,’ says Podvysotsky. ‘_Panie_ Podvysotsky,’ said the banker, ‘you pledged your honor and we pledged ours.’ Podvysotsky took the million.”
“That’s not true,” said Kalganov.
“_Panie_ Kalganov, in gentlemen’s company one does not say such things.”

“As if a Polish gambler would hand over a million!” cried Mitya, but he checked himself at once. “Forgive me, _panie_, my fault again. He would, he would hand over a million, for honor, for Polish honor. See how well I speak Polish, ha ha! Here, I bet ten roubles, the knave leads.”

“And I put one rouble on the queen, the queen of hearts, the pretty little _panienotchka_, he he!” laughed Maximov. He drew out his queen and, as though trying to hide it from everybody, edged right up close and crossed himself quickly under the table. Mitya won. The rouble won, too.
“A corner!” cried Mitya.
“I’ll bet one more rouble, a ‘single’ stake,” Maximov muttered gleefully, enormously pleased at having won a rouble.
“Lost!” shouted Mitya. “A ‘double’ on the seven!”
The seven was beaten as well.
“Stop!” cried Kalganov suddenly.
“Double! Double!” Mitya doubled his stakes, and every time he doubled a card, the Poles beat it. The rouble stakes kept winning.
“Double again!” shouted Mitya furiously.
“You have lost two hundred, _panie_. Will you stake another hundred?” the Pole on the sofa asked.
“What? Two hundred gone already? Then two hundred more! All doubles!”
And pulling the money from his pocket, Mitya was about to throw two hundred roubles down on the queen, but Kalganov covered it with his hand.
“Enough!” he shouted in his ringing voice.
“What’s the matter with you?” Mitya stared at him.
“Enough! I don’t want you playing any more. Don’t!”
“Why?”
“Because I don’t want it. Blast it, come away. That’s why. I won’t let you keep playing.”
Mitya looked at him in amazement.
“Give it up, Mitya. Maybe he’s right. You’ve lost plenty already,” said Grushenka, with a curious note in her voice. Both Poles stood up, looking deeply offended.
“Are you joking, _panie_?” said the short man, giving Kalganov a stern look.
“How dare you!” Pan Vrublevsky growled at Kalganov, too.
“Don’t you dare shout like that,” cried Grushenka. “Ah, you turkey-cocks!”
Mitya looked from one to the other. But something in Grushenka’s face suddenly caught his attention, and in that same instant a new idea flashed into his head—a strange new idea!
“_Pani_ Agrippina,” the little Pole was starting, red with anger, when Mitya suddenly stepped up to him and clapped him on the shoulder.
“Most illustrious, a word with you.”
“What do you want?”
“In the next room. I have two words to tell you, something pleasant, very pleasant. You’ll be glad to hear it.”
The little _pan_ was startled and gave Mitya a wary look. Still, he agreed straight away, on condition that Pan Vrublevsky went with them.
“The bodyguard? Let him come, I want him, too. I must have him!” cried Mitya. “March, _panovie_!”
“Where are you going?” asked Grushenka, anxious.
“We’ll be back in a moment,” Mitya answered.
There was a kind of daring in his eyes, a sudden confidence. His face had looked very different when he came into the room an hour before.

He led the Poles not to the big room where the chorus of girls was gathering and the table was being laid, but to the bedroom on the right. The trunks and packages were kept there, and there were two large beds, each with a heap of cotton pillows piled up like a pyramid. A candle was burning on a small deal table in the corner. The little man and Mitya sat down at this table across from each other, while the huge Vrublevsky stood by them with his hands behind his back. The Poles looked stern but plainly wanted to know what was coming.
“What can I do for you, _panie_?” lisped the little Pole.
“Well, look here, _panie_, I won’t keep you long. Here’s money for you,” and he took out his notes. “Do you want three thousand? Take it and be on your way.”
The Pole stared at Mitya, wide-eyed, with a probing look.
“Three thousand, _panie_?” He exchanged a glance with Vrublevsky.

“Three, _panovie_, three! Listen, _panie_, I can see you’re a sensible man. Take the three thousand and go to the devil, and take Vrublevsky with you—do you hear? But at once, this very minute, and for good. You understand, _panie_, for good. There’s the door, go out through it. What have you got there, a greatcoat, a fur coat? I’ll bring it out to you. They’ll bring the horses round straight away, and then—good-by, _panie_!”
Mitya waited for an answer, sure of himself. He had no doubts at all. A look of extraordinary determination came over the Pole’s face.
“And the money, _panie_?”

“The money, _panie_? Five hundred roubles I’ll give you this very moment for the journey, as a first payment, and two thousand five hundred tomorrow in town—I swear on my honor, I’ll get it, I’ll get it at any price!” cried Mitya.
The Poles exchanged glances again. The short man’s face grew more forbidding.

“Seven hundred, seven hundred, not five hundred, right now, this minute, cash in hand!” Mitya added, sensing that something was wrong. “What’s the matter, _panie_? Don’t you trust me? I can’t hand over the whole three thousand all at once. If I did, you might come back to her tomorrow.... Besides, I haven’t got the three thousand on me. It’s at home in town,” faltered Mitya, his heart sinking with every word. “On my word, the money is there, hidden away.”
In an instant a remarkable sense of his own dignity appeared on the little man’s face.
“What next?” he asked sarcastically. “For shame!” and he spat on the floor. Pan Vrublevsky spat too.
“You’re doing that, _panie_,” said Mitya, seeing with despair that it was all over, “because you hope to get more out of Grushenka? You’re a pair of capons, that’s what you are!”

“This is a mortal insult!” The little Pole went red as a crab and walked out of the room briskly, as if he couldn’t bear to hear another word. Vrublevsky lumbered out after him, and Mitya followed, confused and crushed. He was afraid of Grushenka, afraid the _pan_ would start shouting right away. And so he did. The Pole came into the room and flung himself down before Grushenka in a theatrical pose.
“_Pani_ Agrippina, I have suffered a mortal insult!” he exclaimed. But Grushenka suddenly lost all patience, as though they had hurt her in her most tender spot.
“Speak Russian! Speak Russian!” she cried. “Not another word of Polish! You used to speak Russian. You can’t have forgotten it in five years.”
She was red with fury.
“_Pani_ Agrippina—”
“My name is Agrafena, Grushenka. Speak Russian or I won’t listen!”
The Pole gasped with offended dignity and quickly and pompously said in broken Russian:
“_Pani_ Agrafena, I came here to forget the past and forgive it, to forget all that happened up to today—”
“Forgive? You came here to forgive me?” Grushenka cut him off, leaping up from her seat.

“Exactly so, _pani_. I am not pusillanimous, I am magnanimous. But I was astounded when I saw your lovers. Pan Mitya offered me three thousand, in the other room, to go away. I spat in the _pan’s_ face.”
“What? He offered you money for me?” cried Grushenka, hysterical. “Is that true, Mitya? How dare you? Am I for sale?”
“_Panie, panie!_” yelled Mitya. “She’s pure and shining, and I have never been her lover! That’s a lie....”
