“How dare you stand up for me to him?” shrieked Grushenka. “It wasn’t virtue that kept me pure, and it wasn’t fear of Kuzma. I did it so I could hold my head up when I met him, and call him a scoundrel to his face. And did he really turn down the money?”
“He took it! He took it!” cried Mitya. “Only he wanted all three thousand at once, and I could give him just seven hundred on the spot.”
“I see: he heard I had money, and came here to marry me!”
“_Pani_ Agrippina!” cried the little Pole. “I am—a knight, I am—a nobleman, and not a _lajdak_. I came here to make you my wife, and I find you a different woman, perverse and shameless.”

“Oh, go back where you came from! I’ll tell them to throw you out, and out you’ll go,” cried Grushenka, furious. “What a fool I’ve been, a fool, to be so miserable these five years! And it wasn’t even for his sake, it was my own anger that made me miserable. And this isn’t he at all! Was he like this? This could be his father! Where did you get that wig? He was a falcon, and this is a gander. He used to laugh and sing for me.... And I’ve been crying for five years, damned fool that I was, wretched and shameless!”
She sank back into her low chair and hid her face in her hands. At that moment the Mokroe chorus began to sing in the room on the left—a rollicking dance song.
“A regular Sodom!” Vrublevsky roared suddenly. “Landlord, drive those shameless hussies out!”
The landlord had been peering curiously in at the door for some time. Now he heard the shouting and guessed that his guests were quarreling, and he came into the room at once.
“What are you yelling for? Do you want to burst your throat?” he said to Vrublevsky, with astonishing rudeness.
“Animal!” bellowed Pan Vrublevsky.

“Animal? And what kind of cards were you playing with just now? I gave you a pack and you hid it. You played with marked cards! I could send you to Siberia for playing with false cards, do you know that? It’s the same as forging banknotes....”
And going over to the sofa, he stuck his fingers between the back and the cushion and pulled out a sealed pack of cards.
“Here’s my pack, still sealed!”
He held it up and showed it to everyone in the room. “From where I stood I saw him slip my pack away and put his own in its place—you’re a cheat and no gentleman!”
“And I saw the _pan_ switch a card twice!” cried Kalganov.
“How shameful! How shameful!” exclaimed Grushenka, wringing her hands and blushing with real shame. “Good Lord, he’s sunk to this!”
“I thought so, too!” said Mitya. But before he had finished saying it, Vrublevsky, his face confused and furious, shook his fist at Grushenka and shouted:
“You low harlot!”
Mitya was on him at once. He seized him with both hands, lifted him off the floor, and in a moment had carried him into the room on the right, the one they had just left.
“I’ve put him down on the floor in there,” he announced, coming straight back, panting with excitement. “He’s struggling, the scoundrel! But he won’t come back, never fear!...”
He shut one half of the folding doors and, holding the other half open a crack, called out to the little Pole:
“Most illustrious, would you care to go out as well?”
“My dear Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” said Trifon Borissovitch, “make them give back the money you lost. It’s as good as stolen from you.”
“I don’t want my fifty roubles back,” Kalganov declared suddenly.
“And I don’t want my two hundred, either,” cried Mitya. “I wouldn’t take it for anything! Let him keep it as a consolation.”
“Bravo, Mitya! You’re a prince, Mitya!” cried Grushenka, and there was a note of fierce anger in her cry.
The little _pan_, red with fury but still careful of his dignity, was heading for the door. He stopped short, though, and said suddenly to Grushenka:
“_Pani_, if you want to come with me, come. If not, good-by.”

And swollen with indignation and self-importance, he went to the door. He was a man of character: he thought so highly of himself that even after all that had happened he still expected her to marry him. Mitya slammed the door behind him.
“Lock it,” said Kalganov. But the key clicked on the other side; they had locked it from inside.
“That’s perfect!” exclaimed Grushenka without mercy. “It serves them right!”

chapters.title: VIII. Delirium
paragraphs: What came next was close to an orgy, a feast where everyone was welcome. Grushenka was the first to ask for wine.
“I want a drink. I want to get properly drunk, the way we did before. Do you remember, Mitya? Do you remember how we made friends here last time?”
Mitya was nearly delirious himself. He felt his happiness was within reach. But Grushenka kept sending him away from her side.

“Go and enjoy yourself. Tell them to dance and have a good time, ‘let the stove and cottage dance,’ just as we had it last time,” she kept calling. She was tremendously excited, and Mitya hurried to do as she said. The chorus was waiting in the next room. The room where the two of them had been sitting was too small. Cotton curtains split it in two, and behind them stood a huge bed with a puffy feather mattress and a pile of cotton pillows stacked like a pyramid. The four guest rooms all had beds in them. Grushenka sat down right by the door, and Mitya set an easy chair for her. She had sat in that same spot “the time before” to watch the dancing and singing, when they had made merry there. All the girls who had come tonight had been there then. The Jewish band with fiddles and zithers had come too, and in the end the long-awaited cart had turned up with the wines and provisions.

Mitya rushed about. All sorts of people began drifting into the room to watch. They were peasants and their women, woken from sleep and drawn by the hope of another wonderful entertainment like the one they had enjoyed a month earlier. Mitya remembered their faces and greeted and hugged everyone he knew. He uncorked bottles and poured wine for whoever came up. Only the girls were really eager for the champagne. The men liked rum and brandy better, and hot punch best of all. Mitya had chocolate made for all the girls. He also ordered three samovars kept boiling all night, so that anyone could help himself to tea and punch.

What followed was an absurd, chaotic muddle, but Mitya was in his element, and the sillier it got, the higher his spirits climbed. If the peasants had asked him for money just then, he would have pulled out his notes and given them away by the handful. That was probably why the landlord, Trifon Borissovitch, kept hovering near Mitya to protect him. He seemed to have given up all thought of bed that night. Still, he drank very little, just one glass of punch, and in his own fashion he kept a sharp eye on Mitya’s interests. He stepped in at just the right moment and, civil and fawning, talked Mitya out of giving the peasants “cigars and Rhine wine,” and above all money, as he had done the time before. He was also very indignant to see the peasant girls drinking liqueur and eating sweets.
“They’re a lousy lot, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” he said. “I’d kick every last one of them, and they’d take it as an honor. That’s all they’re worth!”

Mitya thought of Andrey again and had punch sent out to him. “I was rude to him just now,” he said again, in a sinking, softened voice. Kalganov didn’t want to drink and at first didn’t care for the girls’ singing. But after a couple of glasses of champagne he turned extraordinarily lively. He strolled around the room, laughing, praising the music and the songs, admiring everybody and everything. Maximov, blissfully drunk, never left his side. Grushenka was starting to get drunk too. She pointed at Kalganov and said to Mitya:
“What a dear, charming boy he is!”

And Mitya, delighted, ran to kiss Kalganov and Maximov. Oh, his hopes were high! She still hadn’t said anything, and she seemed to be holding back on purpose. But now and then she looked at him with tender, passionate eyes. Finally she suddenly seized his hand and pulled him hard toward her. At that moment she was sitting in the low chair by the door.
“Why did you come in just now, eh? You simply walked in!... I was scared. So you wanted to hand me over to him, did you? Did you really want that?”
“I didn’t want to get in the way of your happiness!” Mitya stammered, blissful. But she didn’t need his answer.
“Well, go and have a good time ...” she sent him off again. “Don’t cry. I’ll call you back.”

So he ran off, and she listened to the singing and watched the dancing, though her eyes followed him wherever he went. A quarter of an hour later she would call him again, and once more he would come running.
“Come here, sit by me and tell me. How did you find out about me, and about my coming here yesterday? Who did you hear it from first?”
And Mitya started to tell her everything, in a disjointed, rambling, feverish way. He spoke oddly, frowning often and breaking off suddenly.
“What are you frowning about?” she asked.
“Nothing.... I left a man lying ill back there. I’d give ten years of my life to see him get better, to know he was all right!”

“Oh, forget him, if he’s ill. So you were going to shoot yourself tomorrow! What a silly boy! Why? I like reckless men like you,” she lisped, her tongue a little unsteady. “So you’d go to any lengths for me, would you? Were you really going to shoot yourself tomorrow, you fool? No, wait a bit. Tomorrow I might have something to tell you.... I won’t say it today, but tomorrow. You’d like it to be today? No, I don’t feel like it today. Now go on, go and amuse yourself.”
Once, though, she called him over, puzzled and anxious.

“Why are you sad? I can see you’re sad.... Yes, I can see it,” she added, looking hard into his eyes. “You keep kissing the peasants and shouting, but I can tell something’s wrong. No, be merry. I’m merry, so you be merry too.... There’s somebody here I love. Guess who. Ah, look, my boy has fallen asleep, the poor dear. He’s drunk.”

She meant Kalganov. He was indeed drunk and had dozed off for a moment, sitting on the sofa. But it wasn’t only the drink that made him sleepy. He had suddenly sunk into gloom, or, as he put it, “boredom.” The girls’ songs depressed him deeply, because as the drinking went on they gradually turned coarse and wilder. The dances were just as bad. Two girls were dressed up as bears. A lively girl named Stepanida, stick in hand, played their keeper and started to “show them off.”
“Look sharp, Marya, or you’ll get the stick!”
In the end the bears rolled on the ground in the most indecent way, to roars of laughter from the crowd of men and women packed around them.
“Well, let them! Let them!” said Grushenka gravely, a rapturous look on her face. “When they get a day to enjoy themselves, why shouldn’t folks be happy?”
Kalganov looked as if someone had thrown mud on him.
“It’s disgusting, all this peasant silliness,” he muttered, moving away. “It’s what they play at in summer, when it never gets dark.”
There was one “new” song, set to a jaunty dance tune, that he disliked in particular. It told of a gentleman who came to try his luck with the girls and see whether they would love him:
The master came to try the girls: Would they love him, or would they not?
But the girls could not love the master:
He would beat me cruelly, And such love is not for me.
Then a gypsy comes along and tries his luck as well:
The gypsy came to try the girls: Would they love him, or would they not?
But they couldn’t love the gypsy either:
He’d be a thief, I fear, And cause me many a tear.
And many more men come to try their luck, a soldier among them:
The soldier came to try the girls: Would they love him, or would they not?
But the soldier is turned down with scorn, in two indecent lines. They were sung with perfect frankness and set the audience roaring. The song ends with a merchant:
The merchant came to try the girls: Would they love him, or would they not?
And it seems he wins their love, because:
The merchant will make gold for me, And his queen I’ll gladly be.
Kalganov was truly indignant.

“That’s only a song from yesterday,” he said aloud. “Who writes this stuff for them? They might just as well have had a railwayman or a Jew come to try his luck with the girls. He’d have won them all.”

And, almost as if he had been personally insulted, he announced right there that he was bored. He sat down on the sofa and fell asleep at once. His pretty little face looked rather pale as his head fell back on the cushion.
“Look how pretty he is,” said Grushenka, leading Mitya over to him. “I was combing his hair a while ago. It’s like flax, and so thick....”
And, bending over him tenderly, she kissed his forehead. Kalganov opened his eyes at once and looked at her. Then he got up and asked, very anxiously, where Maximov was.
“So it’s him you’re after.” Grushenka laughed. “Stay here with me a minute. Mitya, go and find his Maximov for him.”

As it turned out, Maximov couldn’t tear himself away from the girls. He only ran off now and then to pour himself a glass of liqueur. He had drunk two cups of chocolate already. His face was red, his nose crimson, and his eyes moist and sickly sweet. He came running up and announced that he was going to dance the “sabotière.”
“They taught me all those well-bred, aristocratic dances when I was little....”
“Go with him, Mitya, go on. I’ll watch from here how he dances,” said Grushenka.

“No, no, I’ll come and watch too,” cried Kalganov, brushing aside, quite innocently, Grushenka’s offer to sit with him. They all went to watch. Maximov danced his dance. But nobody much admired it except Mitya. It was nothing but skipping and hopping, with kicks of the legs, and at every skip Maximov slapped the sole of his raised foot. Kalganov didn’t like it at all, but Mitya kissed the dancer.
“Thank you. Are you tired, maybe? What are you looking for? Want some sweets? Or a cigar?”
“A cigarette.”
“Wouldn’t you like a drink?”
“Just a liqueur.... Do you have any chocolates?”
“Yes, there’s a heap of them on the table over there. Pick one, my dear soul!”
“I like the vanilla kind ... for old people. Hee hee!”
“No, brother, we don’t have that special kind.”
“I say,” the old man leaned over to whisper in Mitya’s ear. “That girl there, little Marya, hee hee! What if you helped me get friendly with her?”
“So that’s what you’re after! No, brother, that won’t do!”
“I wouldn’t do anyone any harm,” Maximov muttered, crestfallen.
“Oh, fine, fine. But they only come here to dance and sing, you know, brother. Damn it all, just wait!... Meanwhile, eat, drink and enjoy yourself. Don’t you want some money?”
“Later, perhaps,” Maximov smiled.
“All right, all right....”

Mitya’s head was burning. He went out onto the wooden balcony that ran along the inner side of the whole building, above the courtyard. The fresh air revived him. He stood alone in a dark corner, and suddenly he clutched his head in both hands. His scattered thoughts came together. His feelings merged into one, and it threw a sudden light into his mind. A fearful, terrible light! “If I’m going to shoot myself, why not now?” The thought went through him. “Why not fetch the pistols, bring them here, and finish it here, in this dark, filthy corner?” For almost a minute he stood undecided. A few hours earlier, as he raced here, he had been pursued by disgrace, by the theft he had committed, and by that blood, that blood!... Even so, it had been easier for him then. Then everything was over. He had lost her and given her up. She was gone, as far as he was concerned. Oh, then his death sentence had been easier to bear. At least it had seemed necessary and unavoidable, for what was there to keep him on earth?

But now? Was it the same as then? Now at least one phantom, one terror, was over. That first, rightful lover, that fateful figure, had vanished without a trace. The terrible phantom had shrunk into something so small and so comic. It had been carried into the bedroom and locked in. It would never come back. She was ashamed, and from her eyes he could now tell who it was she loved. Now he had everything he needed to be happy in life ... and yet he could not go on living, he could not. Oh, damnation! “O God! Bring back to life the man I knocked down at the fence! Let this fearful cup pass from me! Lord, You have worked miracles for sinners like me! But what, what if the old man is alive? Oh, then I would wipe out the shame of the other disgrace. I would give back the stolen money. I’d return it, I’d find it somehow.... Not a trace of that shame will be left, except in my heart forever! But no, no. Oh, these are impossible, cowardly dreams! Oh, damnation!”

And yet a ray of light and hope shone in his darkness. He sprang up and ran back to the room, to her, to her, his queen forever! Was one moment of her love not worth all the rest of life, even with the agonies of disgrace? This wild question gripped his heart. “To her, to her alone, to see her, to hear her, to think of nothing, to forget everything, if only for tonight, for an hour, for a moment!” Just as he turned from the balcony into the passage, he ran into the landlord, Trifon Borissovitch. The man looked gloomy and worried, he thought, and he imagined he had come looking for him.
“What is it, Trifon Borissovitch? Are you looking for me?”
“No, sir.” The landlord seemed thrown off balance. “Why would I be looking for you? Where have you been?”
“Why are you so glum? You’re not angry, are you? Wait a bit, you’ll be in bed soon.... What time is it?”
“Three o’clock, I’d say. Past three, it must be.”
“We’ll stop soon. We’ll stop.”
“Please, don’t mention it, it makes no difference. Keep it up as long as you like....”

“What’s wrong with him?” Mitya wondered for a moment, and ran back to the room where the girls were dancing. But she wasn’t there. She wasn’t in the blue room either, where only Kalganov lay asleep on the sofa. Mitya looked behind the curtain, and there she was. She was sitting in the corner on a trunk, bent forward, her head and arms resting on the bed beside her. She was crying bitterly, trying with all her might to smother her sobs so that no one would hear. When she saw Mitya she beckoned to him, and as he ran to her she gripped his hand tight.

“Mitya, Mitya, I loved him, you know. How I’ve loved him all these five years, all that time! Did I love him, or only my own anger? No, him, him! It’s a lie that it was my anger I loved and not him. Mitya, I was only seventeen then. He was so kind to me, so cheerful. He used to sing to me.... Or that’s how it seemed to a silly girl like me.... And now, O Lord, he’s not the same man. Even his face isn’t the same. He’s completely different. I wouldn’t have known him. I drove here with Timofey, and all the way I kept wondering how I’d meet him, what I’d say to him, how we’d look at each other. My soul was faint, and then all at once it was as if he had thrown a bucket of dirty water over me. He talked to me like a schoolmaster, so grave and learned. He received me so solemnly that I was struck dumb. I couldn’t get a word in. At first I thought he was ashamed to talk in front of his great big Pole. I sat staring at him and wondering why I couldn’t say a word to him now. It must have been his wife who ruined him. You know he dropped me to get married. She must have changed him like that. Mitya, how shameful it is! Oh, Mitya, I’m ashamed, I’m ashamed for the rest of my life. Curse it, curse it, curse those five years!”
She started crying again, but she kept a tight grip on Mitya’s hand and wouldn’t let it go.

“Mitya, dear, stay here, don’t leave. There’s one thing I want to tell you,” she whispered, and all at once looked up into his face. “Listen. Tell me who it is I love. There’s one man here I love. Who is he? You’re the one who has to tell me.”
Her tear-swollen face lit up with a smile, and her eyes glittered in the dim light.

“In flew a falcon, and my heart dropped. ‘Fool, that’s the man you love!’ my heart whispered to me at once. Then you walked in and everything lit up. What’s he scared of? I wondered. You were frightened, you couldn’t say a word. It’s not those people he’s afraid of—could he be scared of anyone? It’s me he’s afraid of, I thought, only me. So Fenya told you, you silly, that I called out of the window to Alyosha that I’d loved Mityenka for one hour, and that now I was off to love ... somebody else. Mitya, Mitya, what a fool I was, to think I could love anybody after you! Will you forgive me, Mitya? Do you forgive me or don’t you? Do you love me? Do you love me?” She leaped up and took him by the shoulders with both hands. Mitya, struck dumb with rapture, looked into her eyes, her face, her smile, and then suddenly crushed her in his arms and kissed her passionately.

“Forgive me for making you suffer, won’t you? I made you all suffer out of spite. Out of spite I drove the old man out of his mind.... Remember the day you were drinking at my place and smashed the wine glass? I remembered that, and today I smashed a glass too and drank ‘to my vile heart.’ Mitya, my falcon, why won’t you kiss me? He kissed me once, and now he draws back, looking and listening. Why are you listening to me? Kiss me, kiss me hard, yes, like that. If you love, then love! I’ll be your slave now, your slave all my life. Slavery is sweet. Kiss me! Beat me, treat me badly, do what you want with me.... I deserve to suffer, I do. Wait, stop, later, I won’t have it....” and she shoved him away all at once. “Off with you, Mitya, I’ll come and have some wine, I want to be drunk, I’ll get drunk and dance; I have to, I have to!” She wrenched herself free and vanished behind the curtain. Mitya went after her like a drunken man.

“Yes, come what may, whatever happens now, for a single minute I’d give the whole world,” he thought. Grushenka really did gulp down a full glass of champagne in one swallow, and was at once very tipsy. She sat in the same chair as before, smiling blissfully. Her cheeks were aglow, her lips were burning, her shining eyes were wet; they were full of passionate appeal. Even Kalganov felt his heart stir, and he went over to her.

“Did you feel it, when I kissed you while you were asleep just now?” she said in a thick voice. “I’m drunk, that’s all it is.... And you, aren’t you drunk? And why isn’t Mitya drinking? Mitya, why don’t you drink? I’m drunk and you’re not drinking....”
“I’m drunk! I’m drunk anyway ... drunk on you ... and now I’ll get drunk on wine too.”

He emptied another glass, and—he found it strange himself—that one glass made him completely drunk. All at once he was drunk, though up to then he had been quite sober; he remembered that. From that moment the world spun around him, as in a fever. He walked about, laughed, talked to everyone, not knowing what he did. Only one burning sensation stayed with him all the time, “like a red-hot coal in his heart,” as he said later. He went to her, sat down next to her, looked at her, listened to her.... She grew very talkative and kept calling everyone over, beckoning to one girl after another from the chorus. When a girl came up, Grushenka would kiss her or make the sign of the cross over her. Another minute and she might have cried. The “little old man,” as she called Maximov, amused her enormously. He kept running up to kiss her hands, “every little finger,” and at last he danced another dance, to an old song he sang himself. He put special vigor into the refrain:

The little pig says—umph! umph! umph! The little calf says—moo, moo, moo, The little duck says—quack, quack, quack, The little goose says—ga, ga, ga. The hen goes strutting through the porch; Troo-roo-roo-roo-roo, she’ll say, Troo-roo-roo-roo-roo, she’ll say!

“Give him something, Mitya,” said Grushenka. “Give him a present, he’s poor, you know. Ah, the poor, the insulted!... You know what, Mitya, I’m going to enter a nunnery. I will, I mean it, someday. Alyosha told me something today that I’ll remember as long as I live.... Yes.... But today we dance. Nunnery tomorrow, dancing today. I want to have my fun today, good people, so what? God will forgive us. If I were God, I’d forgive everybody: ‘My dear sinners, from this day on you’re forgiven.’ And I’ll go and ask forgiveness myself: ‘Forgive me, good people, I’m a silly wench.’ I’m a beast, that’s what I am. But I want to pray. I gave away a little onion. Wicked as I’ve been, I want to pray. Mitya, let them dance, don’t stop them. Everybody in the world is good. Everybody—even the worst. It’s a nice world. We may be bad, but the world’s all right. We’re good and bad, good and bad.... Come on, tell me, there’s something I want to ask you: come here, all of you, and I’ll ask you: Why am I so good? You know I’m good. I’m very good.... Come on, why am I so good?”

Grushenka went on babbling like this, getting drunker and drunker. At last she declared that she would dance too. She rose from her chair, swaying. “Mitya, give me no more wine—even if I ask, don’t give it to me. Wine brings no peace. Everything’s spinning, the stove and everything. I want to dance. Let everybody see how I dance ... let them see how beautifully I dance....”

She meant it. She took a white cambric handkerchief from her pocket and held it by one corner in her right hand, ready to wave it in the dance. Mitya dashed about, the girls went quiet, ready to burst into a dancing song at the first signal. When Maximov heard that Grushenka wanted to dance, he squealed with delight and went skipping about in front of her, humming:
With legs so slim and sides so trim And its little tail curled tight.
But Grushenka waved her handkerchief at him and chased him away.
“Sh-h! Mitya, why aren’t they coming? Let them all come ... and watch. Call in the ones you locked up, too.... Why did you lock them in? Tell them I’m going to dance. Let them watch too....”
With a drunken swagger Mitya went to the locked door and began pounding on it with his fist, calling the Poles.
“Hey, you ... Podvysotskys! Come out, she’s going to dance. She’s asking for you.”
“_Lajdak!_” one of the Poles shouted in answer.
“You’re a _lajdak_ yourself! You’re a little scoundrel, that’s what you are.”
“Stop laughing at Poland,” Kalganov said sententiously. He was drunk as well.
“Hush, boy! If I call him a scoundrel, I haven’t called the whole of Poland that. One _lajdak_ doesn’t make a Poland. Hush, my pretty boy, and eat some candy.”

“Ach, what fellows! As if they weren’t human. Why won’t they be friends?” said Grushenka, and she went forward to dance. The chorus struck up “Ah, my porch, my new porch!” Grushenka tossed back her head, parted her lips a little, smiled, waved her handkerchief—and suddenly, lurching violently, she stopped in the middle of the room, bewildered.
“I’m weak....” she said, worn out. “Forgive me.... I’m weak, I can’t.... I’m sorry.”
She bowed to the chorus, and then started bowing to everyone, in every direction.
“I’m sorry.... Forgive me....”
“The lady’s been at the drink. The pretty lady’s been drinking,” voices said.
“The lady’s had a drop too much,” Maximov explained to the girls with a giggle.
“Mitya, take me away ... lead me off,” said Grushenka, helpless. Mitya pounced on her, scooped her up in his arms and carried his precious burden through the curtains.

“Well, time for me to go,” thought Kalganov, and he left the blue room, closing both halves of the door behind him. But the orgy in the big room went on, getting louder and louder. Mitya laid Grushenka on the bed and kissed her on the lips.

“Don’t touch me....” she begged faintly. “Don’t touch me until I’m yours.... I told you I’m yours, but don’t touch me ... spare me.... Not with them here, right next door. He’s here. It’s foul here....”
“I’ll do as you say! I won’t even think of it ... I worship you!” Mitya muttered. “Yes, it’s foul here, it’s disgusting.”
And still holding her, he dropped to his knees by the bed.

“I know you’re a brute, but you’re generous,” Grushenka brought out with difficulty. “It has to be honorable ... from now on it will be honorable ... and let’s be honest, let’s be good, not brutes, but good ... take me away, take me far away, do you hear? I don’t want it here, but far, far away....”
“Oh yes, yes, it has to be!” said Mitya, hugging her to him. “I’ll take you and we’ll fly away.... Oh, I’d give my whole life for one year only, to learn about that blood!”
“What blood?” asked Grushenka, confused.
“Nothing,” Mitya muttered between his teeth. “Grusha, you wanted to be honest, and I’m a thief. I’ve stolen money from Katya.... What a disgrace, what a disgrace!”

“From Katya, from that young lady? No, you didn’t steal it. Give it back, take it from me.... Why make such a fuss? All I have is yours now. What does money matter? We’ll squander it anyway.... People like us can’t help squandering money. Better that we go and work the land. I want to dig the earth with my own hands. We have to work, do you hear? Alyosha said so. I won’t be your mistress, I’ll be true to you, I’ll be your slave, I’ll work for you. The two of us will go to the young lady and bow down to her, so she’ll forgive us, and then we’ll leave. And if she doesn’t forgive us, we’ll go anyway. Take her the money and love me.... Don’t love her.... Don’t love her anymore. If you love her, I’ll strangle her.... I’ll poke both her eyes out with a needle....”
“I love you. You are the only one I love. I’ll love you in Siberia....”

“Why Siberia? Fine, Siberia, if you want. I don’t care ... we’ll work ... Siberia has snow.... I love riding in the snow ... and there must be bells.... Listen, is that a bell ringing? Where’s that bell coming from? People are coming.... It’s stopped now.”

She shut her eyes, worn out, and dropped off to sleep for a moment. A bell had certainly sounded in the distance, but it had stopped ringing. Mitya let his head fall on her breast. He didn’t notice that the bell had stopped, or that the singing had stopped too, and that in place of songs and drunken uproar there was a dead silence in the house. Grushenka opened her eyes.

“What is it? Did I sleep? Yes ... a bell ... I was asleep, and I dreamed I was riding over the snow with bells, and I dozed off. I was with someone I loved, with you. Far, far away. I was hugging you and kissing you, snuggling up to you. I was cold, and the snow was sparkling.... You know how snow sparkles at night when the moon is out. It was as if I wasn’t on earth. I woke up, and my darling is next to me. How sweet that is!...”

“Next to you,” murmured Mitya, kissing her dress, her bosom, her hands. And suddenly a strange notion struck him: she seemed to be staring straight ahead, not at him, not into his face, but above his head, with an intent, almost eerie fixity. A look of wonder, almost of alarm, suddenly came over her face.
“Mitya, who is that, watching us?” she whispered.
Mitya turned, and saw that someone had in fact pulled the curtains apart and seemed to be watching them. And it seemed to be more than one person.
He leaped up and strode quickly toward the intruder.
“Here, come over here, to us,” said a voice, not loud, but firm and peremptory.

Mitya went through to the other side of the curtain and froze. The room was full of people, but not the ones who’d been there before. A sudden chill ran down his spine, and he shuddered. He knew every one of them at once. The tall, stout old man in the overcoat and the forage cap with a cockade was the police captain, Mihail Makarovitch. And the “consumptive-looking” dandy, so neat, “who always has such polished boots,” was the deputy prosecutor. “He has a chronometer worth four hundred roubles; he showed it to me.” And the small young man in spectacles.... Mitya had forgotten his surname, though he knew him and had seen him: he was the “investigating lawyer,” from the “school of jurisprudence,” newly arrived in town. And this one was the inspector of police, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, a man he knew well. And those fellows wearing brass plates, what were they doing here? And those other two ... peasants.... And over there at the door, Kalganov with Trifon Borissovitch....
“Gentlemen! What’s the meaning of this, gentlemen?” Mitya began, but all at once, as if he were out of his mind, with no idea what he was doing, he shouted at the top of his voice:
“I un—der—stand!”
The young man in spectacles stepped briskly forward to Mitya and began, with dignity but hurriedly:
“We have to make ... in short, I must ask you to step this way, over to the sofa.... You absolutely must give an explanation.”
“The old man!” Mitya shouted wildly. “The old man and his blood!... I understand.”
And he sank, nearly collapsed, into a chair beside him, as though he had been mown down by a scythe.
“You understand? He understands! Monster, parricide! Your father’s blood cries out against you!” the old police captain bellowed suddenly, coming up to Mitya.
He was out of his mind with rage, red in the face and shaking all over.
“This is impossible!” cried the small young man. “Mihail Makarovitch, Mihail Makarovitch, this won’t do!... Allow me to speak, please. I’d never have expected such conduct from you....”

“This is delirium, gentlemen, raving delirium,” the police captain cried. “Look at him: drunk, at this hour of the night, with a disreputable woman, his father’s blood on his hands.... It’s delirium!...”
“Dear Mihail Makarovitch, I most earnestly ask you to control yourself,” the prosecutor said in a quick whisper to the old police captain, “or I’ll be forced to resort to—”
But the little lawyer wouldn’t let him finish. He turned to Mitya and said, in a loud, firm, dignified voice:
“Ex-Lieutenant Karamazov, I must inform you that you are charged with the murder of your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, committed tonight....”
He said something more, and the prosecutor put in a word as well, but Mitya, though he heard them, did not take it in. He stared at them all with wild eyes.

chapters.title: I. The Beginning Of Perhotin’s Official Career
paragraphs: Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, who we left hammering on the heavy locked gates of the widow Morozov’s house, did get himself heard in the end. Fenya was still shaken by the scare she had had two hours before, and was too “upset” to go to bed. The furious pounding at the gate almost threw her into hysterics. She had watched him drive away with her own eyes, yet she imagined it was Dmitri Fyodorovitch knocking again, because nobody else could knock so savagely. She ran to the house-porter, who had already woken and gone out to the gate, and begged him not to open it. But the porter questioned Pyotr Ilyitch and found out that he wanted to see Fenya about very “important business,” and finally he decided to open up. Pyotr Ilyitch was shown into Fenya’s kitchen, though the girl asked him to let the house-porter stay with them, “because of her misgivings.” He started questioning her, and right away he got the most vital fact. When Dmitri Fyodorovitch ran out to look for Grushenka, he had grabbed a pestle from the mortar. When he came back he no longer had it, and his hands were smeared with blood.

“And the blood was simply pouring off him, dripping, dripping!” Fenya kept crying. That gruesome detail was only her overheated imagination at work. But even if the blood was not “dripping,” Pyotr Ilyitch had seen those bloody hands himself, and had helped wash them. Besides, what he had to settle was not how fast the blood dried. He had to settle where Dmitri Fyodorovitch had run with the pestle, or rather, whether it really was to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, and how he could be sure of it. Pyotr Ilyitch kept pressing this point. He found out nothing conclusive, but he left convinced that Dmitri Fyodorovitch could have gone nowhere except his father’s house, and so something must have happened there.

“And when he came back,” Fenya went on eagerly, “I told him the whole story, and then I started asking him, ‘Why have you got blood on your hands, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?’ And he said it was human blood, and that he’d just killed someone. He admitted it all to me, and suddenly he ran off like a madman. I sat down and began thinking, where’s he running off to now, like a madman? He’ll go to Mokroe, I thought, and kill my mistress there. So I ran out to beg him not to kill her. I was running to his lodgings, but I looked toward Plotnikov’s shop and saw him just setting off, and there was no blood on his hands then.” (Fenya had noticed this and remembered it.) Fenya’s old grandmother backed up her story as best she could. Pyotr Ilyitch asked a few more questions and left the house more upset and uneasy than he had been when he came in.

The easiest and most obvious thing would have been to go straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s and find out whether anything had happened there and, if so, what. Only once he was sure of that would he go to the police captain, which Pyotr Ilyitch firmly meant to do. But the night was dark, Fyodor Pavlovitch’s gates were stout, and he would have to knock all over again. He barely knew Fyodor Pavlovitch. And what if they let him in after all that knocking and nothing had happened? Then Fyodor Pavlovitch, with his sneering way, would tell the story around town of how a stranger called Perhotin had burst in on him at midnight to ask if anyone had killed him. It would be a scandal. And Pyotr Ilyitch dreaded scandal more than anything in the world.

Still, the feeling that had hold of him was so strong that, though he stamped his foot angrily and cursed himself, he set off again, not to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s but to Madame Hohlakov’s. He decided that if she denied having just given Dmitri Fyodorovitch three thousand roubles, he would go straight to the police captain. If she said she had given him the money, he would go home and leave the matter until morning.

It is obvious, of course, that turning up at eleven at night at the house of a fashionable lady he had never met, perhaps dragging her out of bed to put an astonishing question to her, was an even better way to cause a scandal than going to Fyodor Pavlovitch. But that is how it goes at times, especially in cases like this one, with the decisions of the most exact and level-headed people. And at that moment Pyotr Ilyitch was anything but level-headed. For the rest of his life he remembered how a nagging uneasiness crept over him, growing more and more painful and pushing him on against his will. The whole way he kept cursing himself, naturally, for going to this lady. But “I’ll get to the bottom of it, I will!” he told himself for the tenth time, gritting his teeth, and he did what he had set out to do.

It was exactly eleven when he walked into Madame Hohlakov’s house. They let him into the yard fairly quickly, but when he asked if the lady was still up, the porter could say only that she usually went to bed by that hour.
“Ask at the top of the stairs. If the lady wants to see you, she’ll see you. If she doesn’t, she won’t.”

Pyotr Ilyitch went up, but it was not so easy here. The footman did not want to announce him, and at last he called a maid. Pyotr Ilyitch asked her politely but stubbornly to tell her mistress that an official who lived in the town, named Perhotin, had come on particular business, and that he would never have dared come if it were not of the greatest importance. “Tell her in those words, in just those words,” he told the girl.

She went off. He stayed waiting in the entry. Madame Hohlakov was already in her bedroom, though not yet asleep. She had felt upset ever since Mitya’s visit, and she had a feeling she would not get through the night without the sick headache that always came over her after such excitement. She was surprised by the maid’s report. She irritably refused to see him. All the same, the unexpected call at such an hour from an “official living in the town,” a complete stranger, aroused her feminine curiosity enormously. But this time Pyotr Ilyitch dug his heels in like a mule. He earnestly begged the maid to go back with another message, in these exact words:
“That he had come on business of the greatest importance, and that Madame Hohlakov might regret it later if she refused to see him now.”
“I jumped in headfirst,” he said afterward, describing it.

The maid gave him an astonished look and went to take his message again. Madame Hohlakov was impressed. She thought it over for a moment, asked what he looked like, and was told he was “very well dressed, young and so polite.” I should mention, by the way, that Pyotr Ilyitch was a rather good-looking young man, and knew it. Madame Hohlakov made up her mind to see him. She was in her dressing-gown and slippers, but she threw a black shawl over her shoulders. “The official” was shown into the drawing-room, the same room where Mitya had been received a little earlier. The lady came to meet her visitor with a stern, questioning face, and without asking him to sit down she began at once with the question:
“What do you want?”
“I’ve taken the liberty of troubling you, madam, about our mutual acquaintance, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov,” Perhotin began.
But he had barely spoken the name when the lady’s face showed sharp irritation. She nearly screamed, and broke in on him furiously:

“How much longer am I going to be plagued by that dreadful man?” she cried hysterically. “How dare you, sir, how could you presume to disturb a lady you don’t know, in her own house at such an hour!... And to force yourself on her to talk about a man who came here, into this very drawing-room, only three hours ago, to murder me, and went stamping out of the room, the way no one leaves a decent house. I’ll have you know, sir, that I shall file a complaint against you, and I will not let this pass. Kindly leave at once.... I am a mother.... I ... I—”
“Murder! So he tried to murder you, too?”
“Why, has he killed somebody else?” Madame Hohlakov asked impulsively.

“If you’ll listen for half a moment, madam, I’ll explain it all in a couple of words,” Perhotin answered firmly. “At five o’clock this afternoon Dmitri Fyodorovitch borrowed ten roubles from me, and I know for a fact that he had no money. Yet at nine o’clock he came to my place with a wad of hundred-rouble notes in his hand, two or three thousand roubles’ worth. His hands and face were smeared with blood, and he looked like a madman. I asked him where he’d got so much money, and he said he had just got it from you, that you had given him three thousand to go off to the gold-mines....”
Madame Hohlakov’s face took on a look of intense, painful excitement.
“Good God! He must have killed his old father!” she cried, wringing her hands. “I never gave him any money, never! Oh, run, run!... Not another word! Save the old man ... run to his father ... run!”
“Pardon me, madam, so you did not give him money? You remember for certain that you gave him no money at all?”

“No, I didn’t, I didn’t! I refused him, because he wouldn’t have known how to value it. He ran out in a fury, stamping. He flew at me, but I slipped away.... And let me tell you, since I want to hide nothing from you now, that he actually spat at me. Can you imagine! But why are we standing? Ah, sit down.”
“Pardon me, I....”
“Or better still, run, run, you must run and save the poor old man from a terrible death!”
“But what if he’s already killed him?”
“Ah, good heavens, yes! Then what are we to do? What do you think we should do now?”

By now she had made Pyotr Ilyitch sit down, and she sat facing him. Briefly, but quite clearly, Pyotr Ilyitch told her what had happened, or at least the part he had seen himself. He told her about his visit to Fenya, too, and about the pestle. All these details overwhelmed the distracted lady. She kept letting out shrieks and covering her face with her hands....

“Would you believe it, I saw all this coming! I have that special gift, whatever I picture comes true. And how many times I’ve looked at that dreadful man and thought, that man will end up murdering me. And now it’s happened ... that is, if he hasn’t murdered me but only his own father, it’s only because the finger of God kept me safe. And besides, he was ashamed to murder me because, right here, I put the holy ikon from the relics of the holy martyr Saint Varvara around his neck.... And to think how close I was to death at that moment, I went right up to him and he stretched out his neck to me!... Do you know, Pyotr Ilyitch (I think you said your name was Pyotr Ilyitch), I don’t believe in miracles, but that ikon and this unmistakable miracle with me now—it shakes me, and I’m ready to believe anything you like. Have you heard about Father Zossima?... But I don’t know what I’m saying ... and just think, with the ikon on his neck he spat at me.... He only spat, it’s true, he didn’t murder me and ... off he dashed! But what shall we do, what must we do now? What do you think?”
Pyotr Ilyitch stood up and announced that he was going straight to the police captain to tell him all about it, and would leave it to the captain to do whatever he saw fit.

“Oh, he’s an excellent man, excellent! Mihail Makarovitch, I know him. Of course, he’s just the person to go to. How practical you are, Pyotr Ilyitch! How well you’ve thought of everything! I’d never have thought of it, in your place!”

“Particularly since I know the police captain quite well myself,” said Pyotr Ilyitch. He was still on his feet, and plainly wanted to get away as fast as he could from this impulsive lady, who would not let him say goodbye and go.

“And be sure, be sure,” she chattered on, “to come back and tell me what you see there, and what you find out ... what comes to light ... how they’ll try him ... and what they sentence him to.... Tell me, we have no death penalty, do we? But be sure to come, even if it’s three in the morning, or four, or half-past four.... Tell them to wake me, to wake me, to shake me if I don’t get up.... But, good heavens, I won’t be able to sleep! Oh, but wait, shouldn’t I come with you?”
“N—no. But if you would write three lines in your own hand, saying that you did not give Dmitri Fyodorovitch any money, it might perhaps be of some use ... in case it’s needed....”

“Of course!” Madame Hohlakov skipped over to her bureau, delighted. “And you know, I’m simply struck, amazed at how resourceful you are, how sensible in these matters. Are you in the service here? I’m so pleased to think you’re in the service here!”
And, still talking, she scribbled these lines on half a sheet of notepaper:

I’ve never in my life lent three thousand roubles today to that unhappy man, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov (for, in spite of everything, he is unhappy). I’ve never given him money, never: That I swear by all that’s holy!
K. HOHLAKOV.
“Here’s the note!” she said, turning quickly to Pyotr Ilyitch. “Go, save him. It’s a noble thing you’re doing!”
And she crossed him three times. She ran out to walk him to the passage.

“How grateful I am to you! You can’t imagine how grateful I am that you came to me first. How is it that I’ve never met you before? I shall feel flattered to see you at my house from now on. How delightful that you live here!... Such precision! Such practical ability!... They must value you, they must understand you. If there’s anything I can do, believe me ... oh, I love young people! I’m in love with young people! The younger generation is the one support of our suffering country. Her one hope.... Oh, go, go!...”

But Pyotr Ilyitch had already run off, or she would not have let him go so soon. Still, Madame Hohlakov had made a rather pleasant impression on him, and it had softened somewhat his worry at being drawn into so unpleasant an affair. Tastes differ, as we all know. “She’s not so old at all,” he thought, pleased with himself. “Why, I would have taken her for her own daughter.”

As for Madame Hohlakov, she was simply charmed with the young man. “Such sense! Such exactness! In so young a man! In our day! And all with such manners and looks! They say the young people of today are good for nothing, but here’s the proof!” and so on. So she simply forgot the “dreadful affair,” and only when she was getting into bed, as she suddenly remembered “how near death she had been,” did she exclaim: “Ah, it is awful, awful!”
But she fell at once into a deep, sweet sleep.

I would not have lingered over such trifling and irrelevant details, though, if this odd meeting between the young official and the by no means elderly widow had not turned out afterward to be the foundation of that practical and precise young man’s whole career. His story is still remembered with amazement in our town, and perhaps I shall have something to say about it once I have finished my long history of the Brothers Karamazov.

chapters.title: II. The Alarm
paragraphs: Our police captain, Mihail Makarovitch Makarov, was a retired lieutenant-colonel and a widower, and a thoroughly good man. He had lived among us only three years, yet everyone thought well of him, chiefly because he “knew how to keep society together.” He always had visitors and couldn’t have lived without them. Someone was forever dining at his house, and he never sat down to a meal alone. He also gave regular dinners, on all sorts of occasions, some of them quite surprising. The food wasn’t _recherché_, but there was plenty of it. The fish pies were excellent, and the wine made up in quantity for what it lacked in quality.

Guests came first into a well-furnished billiard room. On its walls hung pictures of English racehorses in black frames, a decoration every bachelor’s billiard room must have, as we all know. Cards were played there every evening, if only at a single table. Often, though, the whole society of our town gathered at his house to dance, mammas and young ladies and all. Mihail Makarovitch was a widower, but he didn’t live alone. His widowed daughter lived with him, along with her two unmarried daughters. They were grown girls who had finished their schooling, pleasant-looking and lively. Everyone knew they would have no dowry, yet they still drew all the fashionable young men to their grandfather’s house.

Mihail Makarovitch was not very efficient at his work, though he did it no worse than many others. To put it plainly, he was a man of rather limited education. He could not always be trusted to know where his official powers ended. He didn’t exactly fail to understand certain reforms of the present reign. Rather, he made glaring blunders when he interpreted them. This wasn’t because he was especially dull. He was careless, and always too hurried to look into the matter properly.

“I have the heart of a soldier, not a civilian,” he used to say of himself. He had never formed a clear idea of the basic principles behind the reforms connected with the emancipation of the serfs. He simply picked them up from year to year, so to speak, and added to what he knew through practice, without ever meaning to. And he was a landowner himself, too. Pyotr Ilyitch knew for certain that he would find some of Mihail Makarovitch’s visitors there that evening, but he didn’t know which ones. As it happened, the prosecutor was at that moment playing whist at the captain’s with Varvinsky, our district doctor. Varvinsky was a young man who had just come to us from Petersburg, where he had taken a brilliant degree at the Academy of Medicine. Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor, was really only the deputy prosecutor, but we always called him the prosecutor. He was a rather peculiar man, about thirty-five, inclined to consumption, and married to a fat, childless wife. He was vain and irritable, though he had a good mind and even a kind heart. The trouble with him seemed to be only this: he thought himself abler than he was. That made him seem constantly ill at ease. He also had higher, even artistic, leanings, toward psychology for instance, toward a special study of the human heart and a special knowledge of the criminal and his crime. He felt wronged on this account. He believed he had been passed over in the service, and he was firmly convinced that in higher circles he was not properly valued and had enemies. In gloomy moments he even threatened to resign and take up criminal cases as a barrister. The unexpected Karamazov case stirred him deeply: “It was a case that might well be talked about all over Russia.” But I am running ahead.

The young investigating lawyer, Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov, had come from Petersburg only two months before. He was sitting in the next room with the young ladies. Afterwards people talked about it and wondered that all these gentlemen should have gathered, as if by design, at the house of the chief authority on the very evening of “the crime.” Yet the explanation was perfectly simple, and it all came about quite naturally.

Ippolit Kirillovitch’s wife had had toothache for two days, and he had gone out to get away from her groans. The doctor, being what he was, could not spend an evening anywhere but at cards. As for Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov, he had been meaning for three days to drop in at Mihail Makarovitch’s that evening, as if by chance. His plan was to give the eldest granddaughter, Olga Mihailovna, a sly surprise. He would show her that he knew her secret: that it was her birthday, and that she was purposely hiding it so she wouldn’t have to give a dance. He looked forward to a great deal of fun, with many playful jokes about her age and her fear of telling it, about how he knew her secret and would tell everybody, and so on. The charming young man was a past master at such teasing. The ladies had named him “the naughty man,” and he seemed delighted with the name. Still, he was extremely well-bred, of good family, education and feelings. Though he lived for pleasure, his jests were always innocent and in good taste. He was short and delicate-looking, and on his white, slender, small fingers he always wore several big, glittering rings. When he was busy with his official duties, he turned extraordinarily solemn, as if he understood his position and the sacredness of the obligations laid on him. He had a special gift for baffling murderers and other criminals of the peasant class when he questioned them. If he didn’t win their respect, he certainly managed to make them wonder.

Pyotr Ilyitch was simply dumbfounded when he walked into the police captain’s house. He saw at once that everyone knew. They had actually thrown down their cards and were all on their feet, talking. Even Nikolay Parfenovitch had left the young ladies and come running in, looking keyed up and ready for action. The news that met Pyotr Ilyitch was astounding: old Fyodor Pavlovitch really had been murdered that evening in his own house, murdered and robbed. The news had reached them only a moment before, and this is how it came.

Marfa Ignatyevna was the wife of old Grigory, the man who had been knocked senseless by the fence. She was sleeping soundly in her bed, and after the dose of medicine she had taken she might well have slept till morning. But suddenly she woke up. A fearful epileptic scream from Smerdyakov, who lay unconscious in the next room, had no doubt roused her. That scream always came before his fits, and it always frightened and upset Marfa Ignatyevna. She had never been able to get used to it. She jumped up and ran, half asleep, to Smerdyakov’s room. It was dark there, and she could only hear the sick man beginning to gasp and thrash about. Then Marfa Ignatyevna herself cried out and was about to call her husband. But she suddenly realized that he had not been in bed beside her when she got up. She ran back to the bed and groped about with her hands, and the bed was indeed empty. So he must have gone out—but where? She ran to the steps and called him timidly. Of course there was no answer, but far off in the garden, in the darkness, she heard groans. She listened. The groans came again, and it was plain they were coming from the garden.
“Good Lord! It’s just like what happened with Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya!” she thought in confusion. She went timidly down the steps and saw that the garden gate stood open.
“He must be out there, poor dear,” she thought. She went up to the gate, and all at once she heard Grigory clearly, calling her by name: “Marfa! Marfa!” His voice was weak, moaning and dreadful.

“Lord, protect us!” Marfa Ignatyevna murmured. She ran toward the voice, and that was how she found Grigory. But he was not by the fence where he had been struck down. He was about twenty paces away. It came out later that when he came to himself he had crawled off, and he had probably taken a long time to get so far, losing consciousness several times. She saw at once that he was covered in blood, and she screamed at the top of her voice. Grigory was muttering, barely making sense:
“He’s murdered ... his father murdered.... Why scream, silly ... run ... get somebody....”

But Marfa kept on screaming. She saw that her master’s window was open and a candle was alight in it, so she ran over and began calling Fyodor Pavlovitch. But when she looked in at the window, she saw a fearful sight. Her master lay on his back on the floor, not moving. His light-colored dressing gown and white shirt were soaked in blood. The candle on the table brightly lit up the blood and the still, dead face of Fyodor Pavlovitch. Terror-stricken, Marfa rushed from the window and out of the garden. She drew the bolt of the big gate and ran headlong, by the back way, to the neighbor, Marya Kondratyevna. Mother and daughter were both asleep, but Marfa’s desperate, unceasing screams and her knocking at the shutter woke them. Shrieking and screaming incoherently, Marfa still managed to tell them the main fact and beg for help. As it happened, Foma had come back from his wanderings and was spending the night with them. They got him up at once, and all three ran to the scene of the crime. On the way Marya Kondratyevna remembered that about eight o’clock she had heard a dreadful scream from the garden next door. That must have been Grigory’s scream of “Parricide!” uttered when he caught hold of Mitya’s leg.

“One person screamed out and then it went quiet,” Marya Kondratyevna explained as she ran. They ran to the spot where Grigory lay, and the two women, with Foma’s help, carried him to the lodge. They lit a candle and saw that Smerdyakov was no better. He was writhing in convulsions, his eyes fixed in a squint, with foam running from his lips. They wet Grigory’s forehead with water and vinegar, and the water brought him round at once. Right away he asked:
“Is the master murdered?”

Then Foma and both women ran to the house. This time they saw that not only the window but also the door into the garden was wide open. Yet for the last week Fyodor Pavlovitch had locked himself in every night and had not let even Grigory in, whatever the excuse. Seeing that door open, they were afraid to go in to Fyodor Pavlovitch, “for fear something might happen afterwards.” When they went back to Grigory, the old man told them to go straight to the police captain. Marya Kondratyevna ran there and gave the alarm to the whole company at the captain’s. She arrived only five minutes before Pyotr Ilyitch. So his story did not come as his own guess and theory. It came as direct confirmation, from a witness, of the theory everyone held about who the criminal was. (Deep in his heart he had refused to believe that theory until that moment.)

They resolved to act with energy. The deputy police inspector of the town was commissioned to take four witnesses, go into Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house, and open an inquiry on the spot, following the regular forms, which I will not go into here. The district doctor, a zealous man new to his work, almost insisted on going with the police captain, the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer.

I will say briefly that Fyodor Pavlovitch was found quite dead, his skull smashed in. But with what? Most probably with the same weapon that had struck Grigory. And the moment that weapon was found, Grigory, who was at once given all possible medical help, told in a weak, breaking voice how he had been knocked down. They searched with a lantern by the fence and found the brass pestle, dropped in a most conspicuous place on the garden path. In the room where Fyodor Pavlovitch lay, there was no sign of disorder. But by the bed, behind the screen, they picked up from the floor a big, thick envelope. On it was written: “A present of three thousand roubles for my angel Grushenka, if she is willing to come.” Below that Fyodor Pavlovitch had added, “For my little chicken.” The envelope bore three seals of red sealing wax, but it had been torn open and was empty: the money had been taken. On the floor they also found a piece of narrow pink ribbon, which had been tied around the envelope.

One part of Pyotr Ilyitch’s evidence made a great impression on the prosecutor and the investigating magistrate. This was his idea that Dmitri Fyodorovitch would shoot himself before daybreak. Dmitri had resolved to do it, he had told Ilyitch so, he had taken the pistols and loaded them in front of him, he had written a letter and put it in his pocket, and so on. Pyotr Ilyitch still couldn’t quite believe it, and he had threatened to tell someone to prevent the suicide. Mitya had answered, grinning: “You’ll be too late.” So they must hurry to Mokroe and find the criminal before he really did shoot himself.
“That’s clear, that’s clear!” the prosecutor said again and again, in great excitement. “That’s exactly how these madmen go on: ‘I’ll kill myself tomorrow, so I’ll make merry until I die!’”
The story of how Mitya had bought the wine and provisions excited the prosecutor more than ever.

“Remember the fellow who murdered the merchant Olsufyev, gentlemen? He stole fifteen hundred, went straight off to have his hair curled, and then, without even hiding the money, carrying it almost in his hand like that, he went off to the girls.”

But the inquiry, the search and the formalities in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house held them all up. It took time, and so they sent someone ahead to Mokroe two hours before they set out. This was the officer of the rural police, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch Schmertsov, who had come into town the morning before to collect his pay. His orders were not to raise the alarm when he reached Mokroe. He was to keep constant watch over the “criminal” until the proper authorities arrived, and to find witnesses for the arrest, police constables, and so on. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch did as he was told. He kept his identity secret and gave no one the slightest hint of his secret business, except his old acquaintance Trifon Borissovitch. He had spoken to him just before Mitya met the landlord on the balcony, looking for him in the dark, and he noticed at once a change in Trifon Borissovitch’s face and voice. So neither Mitya nor anyone else knew he was being watched. Trifon Borissovitch had carried off the box with the pistols and put it in a suitable place. Only after four o’clock, almost at sunrise, did all the officials arrive, the police captain, the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer, in two carriages each drawn by three horses. The doctor stayed behind at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, to carry out a post-mortem on the body next day. But he was especially interested in the condition of the servant, Smerdyakov.

“Epileptic fits as violent and long as these, coming one after another for twenty-four hours, are seldom seen, and they are of interest to science,” he declared enthusiastically to his companions. As they left, they laughingly congratulated him on his find. The prosecutor and the investigating lawyer clearly remembered the doctor saying that Smerdyakov could not live through the night.
After these long but, I think, necessary explanations, we will go back to the point in our tale where we broke off.

chapters.title: III. The Sufferings Of A Soul, The First Ordeal
paragraphs: And so Mitya sat there, staring wildly at the people around him and not taking in a word they said. Then he sprang up, threw his hands in the air and shouted:
“I’m not guilty! I’m not guilty of that blood! I’m not guilty of my father’s blood.... I meant to kill him, yes. But I’m not guilty. Not I.”
No sooner had he said it than Grushenka burst out from behind the curtain and threw herself at the police captain’s feet.

“It’s my fault! Mine! My wickedness!” she cried in a heartbreaking voice, streaming with tears and stretching her clasped hands out to them. “He did it because of me. I tortured him, I drove him to it. In my wickedness I tortured that poor old man who’s dead, too, and brought him to this! It’s my fault, mine first, mine most, mine!”

“Yes, it’s your fault! You’re the chief criminal! You fury! You harlot! You’re the one most to blame!” shouted the police captain, threatening her with his hand. But he was stopped at once, and firmly. The prosecutor simply grabbed him.
“This is totally out of order, Mihail Makarovitch!” he cried. “You’re plainly obstructing the inquiry.... You’re ruining the case....” He was almost choking.
“Keep to procedure! Keep to procedure!” cried Nikolay Parfenovitch, who was terribly worked up himself. “Otherwise it’s absolutely impossible!...”
“Judge us together!” Grushenka cried wildly, still on her knees. “Punish us together. I’ll go with him now, even to my death!”

“Grusha, my life, my blood, my holy one!” Mitya dropped to his knees beside her and clasped her tight. “Don’t believe her,” he cried. “She’s not guilty of anything, not of any blood, not of anything!”

Afterwards he remembered that several men pulled him away from her by force, that she was led out, and that the next thing he knew he was sitting at the table. The men with the metal plates stood beside him and behind him. Across the table sat the investigating lawyer, Nikolay Parfenovitch, who kept urging him to drink a little water from the glass in front of him.

“It will refresh you, it will calm you. Be calm, don’t be frightened,” the lawyer added, with great politeness. Mitya (he remembered this later) all at once became intensely interested in the lawyer’s big rings, one set with an amethyst, the other with a clear, brilliant yellow stone. Long afterwards he still wondered how those rings had held his attention through all those terrible hours of questioning. He had been quite unable to look away from them or write them off as having nothing to do with his plight. On Mitya’s left sat the prosecutor, in the seat Maximov had taken at the start of the evening. On his right, where Grushenka had been, sat a rosy-cheeked young man in a shabby sort of hunting jacket, with ink and paper before him. This was the lawyer’s secretary, whom he had brought along. The police captain was now standing at the window at the far end of the room, next to Kalganov, who was sitting there.
“Drink some water,” the investigating lawyer said softly, for the tenth time.
“I’ve drunk it, gentlemen, I have ... but ... come, gentlemen, crush me, punish me, decide my fate!” cried Mitya, staring at the lawyer with fixed, terribly wide eyes.
“So you firmly declare that you are not guilty of your father’s death, Fyodor Pavlovitch?” the lawyer asked, softly but insistently.

“I’m not guilty. I’m guilty of the blood of another old man, but not of my father’s. And I weep for it! I killed him, I killed the old man and knocked him down.... But it’s hard to answer for that crime with another one, a terrible murder I didn’t commit.... It’s a terrible accusation, gentlemen, a knockout blow. But who killed my father, who killed him? Who could have killed him, if not I? It’s astonishing, extraordinary, impossible.”
“Yes, who could have killed him?” the lawyer began, but Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor, glanced at him and addressed Mitya himself.

“You needn’t trouble yourself about the old servant, Grigory Vassilyevitch. He is alive and has recovered. By his own account and yours, you dealt him terrible blows. Yet there seems no doubt that he will live, at least according to the doctor.”

“Alive? He’s alive?” cried Mitya, throwing up his hands. His face lit up. “Lord, thank You for the miracle You’ve worked for me, a sinner and a wrongdoer. That’s the answer to my prayer. I’ve been praying all night.” And he crossed himself three times. He could hardly breathe.
“So we have received from this Grigory evidence about you that is very important, namely that—” The prosecutor was about to go on, but Mitya suddenly leapt out of his chair.
“One minute, gentlemen, for God’s sake, just one minute. I’ll run to her—”
“Excuse me, that is out of the question just now,” Nikolay Parfenovitch almost shrieked. He had jumped up too. The men with the metal plates grabbed Mitya, but he sat back down on his own....

“Gentlemen, what a pity! I only wanted to see her for a minute. I wanted to tell her that it’s washed away, it’s gone, that blood that lay on my heart all night, and that I’m not a murderer now! Gentlemen, she is my betrothed!” he said with rapture and reverence, looking around at them all. “Oh, thank you, gentlemen! In one minute you’ve given me a new life, a new heart!... That old man used to carry me in his arms, gentlemen. He used to bathe me in the tub when I was a three-year-old baby that everyone had abandoned. He was like a father to me!...”
“And so you—” the investigating lawyer began.

“Allow me, gentlemen, just one more minute,” Mitya cut in. He put his elbows on the table and hid his face in his hands. “Let me have a moment to think, let me catch my breath, gentlemen. All this is horribly upsetting, horribly. A man is not a drum, gentlemen!”
“Have a little more water,” murmured Nikolay Parfenovitch.

Mitya took his hands from his face and laughed. His eyes were full of confidence. In one moment he seemed an entirely different man. His whole manner had changed. Once more he was the equal of these men, all of whom he knew, as if they had met the day before at some social gathering, when nothing had happened. We may mention in passing that Mitya had been warmly received at the police captain’s when he first came to town. Later, and especially in the last month, he had hardly visited at all. When the police captain met him in the street, Mitya had noticed that the man frowned and bowed only out of politeness. He knew the prosecutor less well. He did sometimes pay polite calls on the prosecutor’s wife, a nervous and fanciful lady, though he hardly knew why. She always welcomed him kindly and, for some reason, had taken an interest in him to the very last. The investigating lawyer he had not had time to get to know, though he had met him and talked with him twice, each time about women.

“I see you’re a very skillful lawyer, Nikolay Parfenovitch,” cried Mitya, laughing merrily, “but now I can help you. Oh, gentlemen, I feel like a new man, and don’t take offense that I speak to you so plainly and directly. I’m a bit drunk, too, I’ll tell you that frankly. I do believe I’ve had the honor and pleasure of meeting you, Nikolay Parfenovitch, at my kinsman Miüsov’s. Gentlemen, gentlemen, I don’t pretend we’re on equal terms. I understand, of course, in what capacity I sit before you. Oh, of course there’s a horrible suspicion ... hanging over me ... if Grigory has given evidence.... A horrible suspicion! It’s awful, awful, I understand that! But to business, gentlemen. I’m ready, and we’ll be done in one moment. Because, listen, listen, gentlemen! Since I know I’m innocent, we can finish this in a minute. Can’t we? Can’t we?”
Mitya talked a great deal and very fast, nervously and gushingly, as if he truly took his listeners for his best friends.

“So, for now, we will put down that you absolutely deny the charge against you,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch impressively. He leaned toward the secretary and dictated to him in a low voice what to write.

“Write it down? You want to write that down? Well, write it. I agree, I fully agree, gentlemen, only ... you see?... Wait, wait, write this. Of disorderly conduct I am guilty, of violence against a poor old man I am guilty. And there’s something else deep in my heart that I’m guilty of, too—but that you needn’t write down” (he turned suddenly to the secretary). “That’s my private life, gentlemen, that’s no concern of yours, the bottom of my heart, I mean.... But I am not guilty of murdering my old father. That’s a wild idea. A completely wild idea!... I’ll prove it to you, and you’ll be convinced right away.... You’ll laugh, gentlemen. You’ll laugh at your own suspicion!...”

“Be calm, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” said the investigating lawyer, plainly trying to settle Mitya’s excitement with his own composure. “Before we go on, I would like you, if you are willing to answer, to confirm that you disliked your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, and that you were forever quarreling with him. Here, at any rate, a quarter of an hour ago, you cried out that you wanted to kill him. ‘I didn’t kill him,’ you said, ‘but I wanted to kill him.’”
“I shouted that? Ach, I may well have, gentlemen! Yes, I’m sorry to say I did want to kill him ... many times I wanted to ... sorry, so sorry!”
“You wanted to. Would you be willing to explain what exactly led you to hate your father so?”

“What is there to explain, gentlemen?” Mitya shrugged sullenly and looked down. “I’ve never hidden how I felt. The whole town knows it—everyone in the tavern knows. Just lately I declared it in Father Zossima’s cell.... And that same day, in the evening, I beat my father. I nearly killed him, and I swore before witnesses that I’d come back and kill him.... Oh, a thousand witnesses! I’ve been shouting it for the past month, anyone will tell you so!... The fact stares you in the face, it speaks for itself, it cries out. But feelings, gentlemen, feelings are another matter. You see, gentlemen”—Mitya frowned—“I think you have no right to question me about feelings. I know your office binds you, I quite understand that, but that’s my affair, my private, intimate affair. And yet ... since I haven’t hidden my feelings before ... in the tavern, for instance, I talked to everyone, so ... so I won’t make a secret of it now. You see, gentlemen, I understand there are terrible facts against me in this business. I told everyone I’d kill him, and now, suddenly, he’s been killed. So it must have been me! Ha ha! I can make allowances for you, gentlemen, I really can. I’m thunderstruck myself, because who could have murdered him, if not I? That’s how it comes out, isn’t it? If not I, who could it be, who? Gentlemen, I want to know, I insist on knowing!” he exclaimed suddenly. “Where was he murdered? How was he murdered? How, and with what? Tell me,” he asked quickly, looking at the two lawyers.
“We found him in his study, lying on his back on the floor, his head smashed in,” said the prosecutor.
“That’s horrible!” Mitya shuddered. He put his elbows on the table and hid his face in his right hand.
“Let us go on,” Nikolay Parfenovitch put in. “So what drove you to this hatred? I believe you have stated in public that it came from jealousy?”
“Well, yes, jealousy. And not only jealousy.”
“A quarrel over money?”
“Yes, over money, too.”
“There was a dispute over three thousand roubles, I believe, which you claimed as part of your inheritance?”

“Three thousand! More, more,” cried Mitya hotly. “More than six thousand, more than ten, maybe. I told everyone, I shouted it at them. But I made up my mind to settle for three thousand. I needed that three thousand desperately ... so that packet of notes for three thousand, which I knew he kept under his pillow, ready for Grushenka, I counted as simply stolen from me. Yes, gentlemen, I regarded it as mine, as my own property....”
The prosecutor gave the investigating lawyer a meaningful look and managed to wink at him on the sly.
“We will return to that later,” the lawyer said quickly. “You will let us make a note of that point and write it down: that you regarded that money as your own property?”

“Write it down, by all means. I know that’s one more fact against me, but I’m not afraid of facts, and I bring them up against myself. Do you hear? Do you know, gentlemen, you take me for a different sort of man from what I am,” he added, suddenly gloomy and downcast. “You have before you a man of honor, a man of the highest honor. Above all—don’t lose sight of this—a man who has done a lot of nasty things, but who has always been, and still is, honorable at bottom, deep inside. I don’t know how to put it. That’s exactly what’s made me miserable all my life: I longed to be honorable, I was, so to speak, a martyr to the sense of honor, hunting for it with a lantern, the lantern of Diogenes. And yet all my life I’ve done filthy things like all of us, gentlemen ... that is, like me alone. That was a mistake, like me alone, me alone!... Gentlemen, my head aches ...” His brows drew together with pain. “You see, gentlemen, I couldn’t stand the sight of him. There was something ignoble in him, something shameless, that trampled on everything sacred, something sneering and irreverent, loathsome, loathsome. But now that he’s dead, I feel differently.”
“What do you mean?”
“I don’t feel differently, but I wish I hadn’t hated him so.”
“Do you feel remorse?”
“No, not remorse, don’t write that. I’m no great prize myself, I’m not very beautiful, so I had no right to find him repulsive. That’s what I mean. Write that down, if you like.”
Saying this, Mitya became deeply mournful. He had grown gloomier and gloomier as the inquiry went on.

Just then another unexpected scene took place. Grushenka had been removed, but not taken far. She was only in the second room along from the blue room where the examination was being held. It was a small room with one window, just past the large room where they had danced and feasted so lavishly. She sat there with nobody beside her but Maximov, who was terribly dejected and terribly frightened and clung to her side as if for protection. One of the peasants, with a metal plate on his chest, stood at their door. Grushenka was crying. All at once her grief was more than she could bear. She leapt up, flung out her arms and, with a loud wail, ran out of the room to him, to her Mitya. It was so sudden that nobody had time to stop her. Mitya heard her cry, trembled, jumped up and, with a yell, dashed to meet her, not knowing what he was doing. But they were not allowed to come together, though they could see each other. Men seized him by the arms. He struggled and tried to break free. It took three or four of them to hold him. She was seized too, and he saw her reaching out her arms to him and crying aloud as they carried her off. When the scene was over, he came to himself again, sitting in the same place as before, across from the investigating lawyer, and calling out to them:
“What do you want with her? Why do you torment her? She’s done nothing, nothing!...”
The lawyers tried to calm him. About ten minutes passed like this. Finally Mihail Makarovitch, who had been out of the room, came in hurriedly and said to the prosecutor in a loud, agitated voice:
“She’s been taken away, she’s downstairs. Will you let me say one word to this unhappy man, gentlemen? In your presence, gentlemen, in your presence.”
“By all means, Mihail Makarovitch,” the investigating lawyer replied. “In this case we have no objection.”

“Listen, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, my dear fellow,” the police captain began, and on his flushed face was a look of warm, almost fatherly feeling for the unlucky prisoner. “I took your Agrafena Alexandrovna downstairs myself and handed her over to the landlord’s daughters. That old fellow Maximov is with her the whole time. And I comforted her, do you hear? I comforted her and calmed her down.
