I explained to her that you have to clear yourself, so she mustn’t hinder you or depress you, or you might lose your head and give the wrong evidence. In a word, I talked to her and she understood. She’s a sensible girl, my boy, a good-hearted girl. She wanted to kiss my old hands and beg me to help you. She sent me herself to tell you not to worry about her. And I have to go, my dear fellow, I have to go and tell her you’re calm and easy in your mind about her. So you must be calm, do you understand? I was unfair to her. She is a Christian soul, gentlemen, yes, I tell you, a gentle soul, and not to blame for anything. So what am I to tell her, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Will you sit quietly or not?”

The kindly police captain said a great deal that was out of order. But Grushenka’s suffering, the suffering of a fellow human being, had touched his good heart, and there were tears in his eyes. Mitya jumped up and rushed toward him.

“Forgive me, gentlemen, oh, allow me, allow me!” he cried. “You have the heart of an angel, an angel, Mihail Makarovitch. I thank you for her. I will, I will be calm, cheerful even. Tell her, out of the kindness of your heart, that I am cheerful, perfectly cheerful, that I’ll be laughing in a minute, knowing she has a guardian angel like you. I’ll have finished with all this very soon, and the moment I’m free I’ll be with her, she’ll see, let her wait. Gentlemen,” he said, turning to the two lawyers, “now I’ll open my whole soul to you. I’ll pour it all out. We’ll wrap this up quickly, wrap it up cheerfully. We’ll laugh about it in the end, won’t we? But, gentlemen, that woman is the queen of my heart. Oh, let me tell you that. That one thing I’ll tell you now.... I see I’m among honorable men. She is my light, she is my holy one, and if only you knew! Did you hear her cry, ‘I’ll go to my death with you’? And what have I done for her, a penniless beggar? Why does she love me so? How can a clumsy, ugly brute like me, with my ugly face, deserve a love like that, so that she’s ready to go into exile with me? And how she fell at your feet for my sake, just now!... and yet she’s proud and has done nothing! How can I help adoring her, how can I help crying out and rushing to her as I did just now? Gentlemen, forgive me! But now, now I’m comforted.”

And he sank back in his chair, hid his face in his hands and burst into tears. But they were happy tears. He pulled himself together at once. The old police captain looked very pleased, and so did the lawyers. They sensed that the examination was entering a new phase. When the police captain went out, Mitya was positively gay.

“Now, gentlemen, I’m at your disposal, entirely at your disposal. And if it weren’t for all these petty details, we’d understand each other in a minute. There I go again with the details. I’m at your disposal, gentlemen, but I tell you we must trust each other, you me and I you, or there’ll be no end to it. I’m saying this for your sake. To business, gentlemen, to business, and don’t rummage in my soul. Don’t pester me with trifles, but ask me only about facts and what matters, and I’ll satisfy you at once. And damn the details!”
So spoke Mitya. The interrogation began again.

chapters.title: IV. The Second Ordeal
paragraphs: “You can’t imagine how much you encourage us, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, by being so willing to answer,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch. He looked animated, and obvious satisfaction shone in his very prominent, short-sighted, light gray eyes, from which he had just taken off his spectacles. “And you made a very fair point about mutual trust. In cases this important, we sometimes simply can’t get anywhere without it, as long as the suspect truly hopes to defend himself and is able to. For our part, we will do everything we can, and you can see for yourself how we are handling the case. Do you agree, Ippolit Kirillovitch?” He turned to the prosecutor.
“Oh, certainly,” replied the prosecutor. Next to Nikolay Parfenovitch’s eagerness, he sounded rather cold.

Let me say right now, once and for all, that Nikolay Parfenovitch had only recently come to our town. From the start he had felt a marked respect for Ippolit Kirillovitch, our prosecutor, and had become almost his bosom friend. He was nearly the only person who trusted without reservation in Ippolit Kirillovitch’s extraordinary gifts as a psychologist and an orator, and in the justice of his grievance. He had heard of him back in Petersburg. In return, young Nikolay Parfenovitch was the only person in the world whom our “unappreciated” prosecutor really liked. On the road to Mokroe they had found time to agree on how to handle this case. Now, sitting at the table, the sharp-witted junior read every sign on his senior colleague’s face—half a word, a glance, a wink—and understood it at once.
“Gentlemen, just let me tell it my own way and don’t break in with petty questions, and I’ll tell you everything in a minute,” said Mitya excitedly.

“Excellent! Thank you. But before we listen to your account, may I ask about one more small matter that interests us a great deal? I mean the ten roubles you borrowed yesterday around five o’clock from your friend Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, with your pistols as security.”
“I pawned them, gentlemen. I pawned them for ten roubles. What else is there to say? That’s all of it. The moment I got back to town, I pawned them.”
“You got back to town? So you had been out of town?”
“Yes, I took a trip of forty versts out into the country. Didn’t you know?”
The prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch looked at each other.

“Well, why don’t you start your story with a proper step-by-step account of everything you did yesterday, from morning on? Let us ask, for instance, why you were away from town, exactly when you left and when you came back—all those facts.”

“You should have asked me that way from the start,” cried Mitya, laughing out loud. “And if you like, we won’t begin with yesterday but with the morning of the day before. Then you’ll see how, why and where I went. The day before yesterday, gentlemen, I went to a merchant here in town, a man called Samsonov, to borrow three thousand roubles from him on safe security. It was urgent, gentlemen. I suddenly needed the money badly.”
“Excuse me for interrupting,” the prosecutor put in politely. “Why did you need exactly that sum, three thousand, so urgently?”

“Oh, gentlemen, there’s no need to go into the details, how, when and why, and why exactly this much money and not that much, and all that rigmarole. Why, it would fill three volumes, and then you’d want an epilogue!”
Mitya said all this with the good-natured but impatient familiarity of a man who is eager to tell the whole truth and means well.

“Gentlemen!”—he corrected himself hurriedly—“don’t be cross with me for being so restless, I’m asking you again. Believe me, I have the greatest respect for you, and I understand how matters really stand. Don’t think I’m drunk. I’m perfectly sober now. And being drunk wouldn’t get in my way anyhow. With me, you know, it’s just like the saying: ‘When he is sober, he is a fool; when he is drunk, he is a wise man.’ Ha ha! But I can see, gentlemen, that it isn’t right to joke with you, not until we’ve had our explanation, that is. And I have my own dignity to keep up, too. I understand the difference for now, believe me. After all, I’m in the position of a criminal, so I’m far from your equal. And it’s your job to keep an eye on me. I can’t expect you to pat me on the head for what I did to Grigory, because nobody breaks an old man’s head and gets off free. I suppose you’ll lock me up for him for six months, or maybe a year, in a house of correction. I don’t know what the punishment is—but it will be without loss of the rights of my rank, without loss of my rank, won’t it? So you see, gentlemen, I understand the distinction between us.... But surely you see that questions like these would baffle God Himself. ‘How did you step? Where did you step? When did you step? And on what did you step?’ I’ll get all muddled if you go on like this, and you’ll write it all down against me. And where will that get us? Nowhere! And even if I’m talking nonsense now, let me finish, and you, gentlemen, being men of honor and refinement, will forgive me! I’ll finish by asking you, gentlemen, to drop that conventional way of questioning. I mean this: you start with some miserable trifle, how I got up, what I had for breakfast, how I spat and where I spat, and so you lull the criminal’s attention, and then you suddenly knock him flat with an overwhelming question: ‘Whom did you murder? Whom did you rob?’ Ha ha! That’s your regular method, that’s where all your cunning comes in. You can catch peasants off guard that way, but not me. I know the tricks. I’ve been in the service, too. Ha ha ha! You’re not angry, gentlemen? You forgive my impertinence?” he cried, looking at them with a good nature that was almost startling. “It’s only Mitya Karamazov, you know, so you can let it pass. In a sensible man it would be inexcusable, but in Mitya you can forgive it. Ha ha!”

Nikolay Parfenovitch listened, and laughed along. The prosecutor didn’t laugh. He kept his eyes fixed sharply on Mitya, as if afraid of missing a single syllable, the slightest movement, the least twitch in any feature of his face.

“That’s how we’ve treated you from the very beginning,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, still laughing. “We haven’t tried to throw you off by asking how you got out of bed in the morning or what you had for breakfast. In fact, we started with questions of the greatest importance.”

“I understand. I saw it, and I appreciated it. I appreciate even more the kindness you are showing me now, a kindness unheard of, and worthy of your noble hearts. The three of us here are gentlemen, so let everything stand on mutual trust between educated, well-bred men, joined by the common bond of noble birth and honor. In any case, let me regard you as my best friends at this moment of my life, when my honor is under attack. That’s no insult to you, gentlemen, is it?”
“On the contrary. You have put all that so well, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Nikolay Parfenovitch answered, with dignified approval.
“And enough of those petty questions, gentlemen, all those tricky questions!” cried Mitya enthusiastically. “Or there’s no telling where we’ll end up! Is there?”

“I will follow your sensible advice entirely,” the prosecutor interposed, addressing Mitya. “But I am not withdrawing my question. It is vitally important for us now to know exactly why you needed that sum, I mean precisely three thousand.”
“Why I needed it?... Oh, for one reason and another.... Well, it was to pay a debt.”
“A debt to whom?”

“That I flatly refuse to answer, gentlemen. Not because I can’t, or don’t dare, or because it would hurt me, since it’s all a paltry business and completely trivial, but—I won’t, because it’s a matter of principle: that’s my private life, and I won’t let anyone intrude on my private life. That’s my principle. Your question has nothing to do with the case, and whatever has nothing to do with the case is my own affair. I wanted to pay a debt. I wanted to pay a debt of honor, but to whom, I won’t say.”
“Let me make a note of that,” said the prosecutor.
“Go right ahead. Write down that I won’t say, that I won’t. Write that I’d think it dishonorable to say. Ech! Write it; you’ve got nothing else to do with your time.”

“Let me caution you, sir, and remind you once more, in case you don’t know,” the prosecutor began, with a peculiar and stern gravity, “that you have every right not to answer the questions put to you now. We, for our part, have no right to wring an answer out of you if you refuse to give one, for whatever reason. That is entirely up to you. But in cases like this one, it is our duty to explain to you and lay before you how much harm you will do yourself by refusing to give this or that piece of evidence. After that, I will ask you to continue.”
“Gentlemen, I’m not angry ... I ...” Mitya muttered, rather thrown off balance. “Well, gentlemen, you see, that Samsonov I went to then ...”

We will not, of course, repeat his account of what the reader already knows. Mitya was anxious, almost impatiently so, not to leave out the smallest detail. At the same time he was in a hurry to be done. But his evidence was being written down as he gave it, so they had to keep stopping him. Mitya disliked that, but he put up with it. He got angry, though still good-humoredly. From time to time, it is true, he cried out, “Gentlemen, that’s enough to wear out an angel’s patience!” Or, “Gentlemen, it’s no use getting me worked up.”

But even though he cried out, for a while he kept his genial, expansive mood. So he told them how Samsonov had made a fool of him two days earlier. (By now he fully understood that he had been fooled.) That he had sold his watch for six roubles to get money for the trip was news to the lawyers. They at once took a lively interest, and even thought it necessary, to Mitya’s intense indignation, to write the fact down as further proof that he had hardly a farthing in his pocket at the time. Little by little Mitya began to turn surly. Then he described his journey to see Lyagavy, the night in the stifling hut, and so on, and came to his return to town. Here, without much urging, he began to give a detailed account of the agonies of jealousy he had gone through over Grushenka.

They heard him in silent attention. They asked in particular about the lookout he had in Marya Kondratyevna’s house, at the back of Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden, from which he watched for Grushenka, and about Smerdyakov bringing him news. They put special weight on this and noted it down. He spoke of his jealousy warmly and at length. Inwardly he was ashamed to expose his most intimate feelings to “public ignominy,” so to speak, but he plainly overcame his shame in order to tell the truth. The cold severity with which the investigating lawyer, and even more the prosecutor, stared at him as he talked finally threw him off quite badly.

“That boy, Nikolay Parfenovitch, to whom I was talking nonsense about women only a few days ago, and that sickly prosecutor are not worth my telling this to,” he reflected mournfully. “It’s ignominious. ‘Be patient, humble, hold thy peace.’” He closed his reflections with that line. But he pulled himself together and went on. When he got to his visit to Madame Hohlakov, his spirits came back, and he even wanted to tell a little anecdote about that lady that had nothing to do with the case. The investigating lawyer cut him off, however, and politely suggested he move on to “more essential matters.” Finally he described his despair, and told how, when he left Madame Hohlakov’s, he had thought he’d “get three thousand if he had to murder someone for it.” Again they stopped him, and noted down that he had “meant to murder someone.” Mitya let them write it without protest. At last he reached the point where he learned that Grushenka had deceived him: she had come back from Samsonov’s as soon as he left her there, though she had said she would stay until midnight.

“If I didn’t kill Fenya then, gentlemen, it was only because I had no time,” burst from him suddenly at that point. That, too, was carefully written down. Mitya waited gloomily and was starting to tell how he ran into his father’s garden, when the investigating lawyer suddenly stopped him. He opened the big portfolio lying on the sofa beside him and pulled out the brass pestle.
“Do you recognize this?” he asked, showing it to Mitya.
“Oh, yes,” Mitya laughed gloomily. “Of course I recognize it. Let me take a look at it.... Oh, damn it, never mind!”
“You forgot to mention it,” observed the investigating lawyer.
“Hang it all, I wasn’t hiding it from you. Do you think I could have got by without it? It just slipped my mind.”
“Please tell us exactly how you came to arm yourself with it.”
“Certainly, gentlemen, I’ll gladly tell you.”
And Mitya described how he picked up the pestle and ran.
“But what did you intend by arming yourself with such a weapon?”
“Intend? Nothing. I just grabbed it and ran off.”
“Why, if you had no intention?”

Mitya’s anger flared. He stared hard at “the boy” and smiled, gloomily and spitefully. He was feeling more and more ashamed that he had told “such people” the story of his jealousy so sincerely and so openly.
“Forget the pestle!” burst from him suddenly.
“But still—”
“Oh, to keep off dogs.... Oh, because it was dark.... In case something happened.”
“But did you ever before take a weapon along when you went out, if you’re so afraid of the dark?”
“Ugh! Damn it all, gentlemen! There’s simply no talking to you!” cried Mitya, driven past all endurance. He turned to the secretary, crimson with rage, and said quickly, his voice shaking with fury:

“Write this down at once ... at once ... ‘that I snatched up the pestle to go and kill my father ... Fyodor Pavlovitch ... by hitting him on the head with it!’ Well, are you satisfied now, gentlemen? Do you feel better?” he said, glaring defiantly at the lawyers.

“We understand perfectly that you made that statement just now out of exasperation with us and with our questions, which you think trivial, though in fact they are essential,” the prosecutor remarked dryly in reply.

“Well, honestly, gentlemen! Yes, I took the pestle.... What does a man pick things up for at such moments? I don’t know what for. I snatched it up and ran—that’s all. Because for me, gentlemen, _passons_, or I swear I won’t tell you any more.”

He sat with his elbows on the table and his head in his hand, turned sideways to them, staring at the wall and fighting down a feeling of nausea. He truly had an awful urge to stand up and announce that he wouldn’t say another word, “not if you hang me for it.”

“You see, gentlemen,” he said at last, controlling himself with difficulty, “you see. I listen to you and I’m haunted by a dream.... It’s a dream I have sometimes, you know.... I often have it—it’s always the same ... that someone is hunting me, someone I’m terribly afraid of ... that he’s hunting me in the dark, at night ... tracking me, and I hide from him somewhere, behind a door or a cupboard, hide in a degrading way, and the worst of it is that he always knows where I am, but he pretends not to know on purpose, to draw out my agony, to enjoy my terror.... That’s exactly what you’re doing now. It’s just like that!”
“Is that the kind of thing you dream about?” asked the prosecutor.
“Yes, it is. Don’t you want to write it down?” said Mitya, with a twisted smile.
“No, there’s no need to write it down. But you do have strange dreams.”
“It’s not about dreams now, gentlemen—this is realism, this is real life! I’m a wolf and you’re the hunters. Well, go on, hunt him down!”
“You are wrong to make such comparisons ...” began Nikolay Parfenovitch, with extraordinary gentleness.

“No, I’m not wrong, not at all!” Mitya flared up again, though his burst of anger had plainly eased his heart. He grew more good-humored with every word. “You may not trust a criminal, or a man on trial tortured by your questions, but an honorable man, the honorable impulses of the heart (I say that boldly!)—no! That you must believe, you have no right indeed ... but—
Be silent, heart, Be patient, humble, hold thy peace.
Well, shall I go on?” he broke off gloomily.
“If you’d be so kind,” answered Nikolay Parfenovitch.

chapters.title: V. The Third Ordeal
paragraphs: Mitya spoke sullenly, but it was plain he was working harder than ever not to forget or skip a single detail. He told them how he had jumped the fence into his father’s garden and crept up to the window. He told them everything that happened under that window. Clearly and precisely, step by step, he described what he felt in the garden during those moments, when he was desperate to know whether Grushenka was with his father or not. But, strange to say, both lawyers now listened with a chilling kind of reserve. They watched him coldly and asked few questions. Mitya could read nothing in their faces.
“They’re angry and offended,” he thought. “Well, forget them!”

Then he told how he had finally made up his mind to give his father the “signal” that Grushenka had come, so that the old man would open the window. The lawyers took no notice of the word “signal.” They seemed not to grasp what it meant here, so plainly that Mitya noticed it. He came at last to the moment when he saw his father peering out of the window, felt his hatred flare up, and pulled the pestle from his pocket. There he suddenly stopped, as if on purpose. He sat staring at the wall, aware that their eyes were fixed on him.
“Well?” said the investigating lawyer. “You took out the weapon, and ... what happened next?”
“Next? Why, next I murdered him ... hit him on the head and cracked his skull.... That’s your version, I suppose. That’s it!”
His eyes flashed suddenly. All the anger he had been smothering burst up in his soul with extraordinary violence.
“Our version?” repeated Nikolay Parfenovitch. “Well, and what is yours?”
Mitya lowered his eyes and said nothing for a long time.

“My version, gentlemen? Well, it went like this,” he began softly. “Maybe it was somebody’s tears, or my mother praying to God, or a good angel kissing me just then. I don’t know. But the devil lost. I tore myself away from the window and ran for the fence. My father was frightened. He saw me then, for the first time, and cried out and leapt back from the window. I remember that very well. I ran across the garden to the fence ... and there Grigory grabbed me, while I was sitting on top of it.”
Only now did he raise his eyes and look at his listeners. They seemed to be staring back with perfectly calm attention. A kind of fit of outrage took hold of Mitya.
“Why, you’re laughing at me this very minute, gentlemen!” he broke off.
“What makes you think so?” said Nikolay Parfenovitch.

“You don’t believe a single word, that’s why! Of course I see I’ve reached the vital point. The old man is lying there with his skull broken, and I—after telling you so dramatically how I wanted to kill him and how I snatched up the pestle—I simply run away from the window. A romance! Poetry! As if anyone could take a fellow at his word. Ha ha! You’re scoffers, gentlemen!”
And he swung around on his chair so hard that it creaked.
“And did you notice,” the prosecutor asked suddenly, as though he had not seen Mitya’s agitation, “as you ran from the window, whether the door into the garden was open?”
“No, it wasn’t open.”
“Not open?”
“It was shut. Who could have opened it? Bah, the door! Wait a minute!” He seemed to remember something all at once, and almost with a start he went on:
“Why, did you find the door open?”
“We did. It was open.”
“But who could have opened it, if you didn’t open it yourselves?” cried Mitya, astonished.

“The door stood open. Your father’s murderer went in by that door without a doubt, and when he had done the deed he went out again by the same door,” said the prosecutor slowly, as though chiseling out each word. “That is perfectly clear. The murder was committed inside the room and _not through the window_. We are quite certain of that from our examination, from the position of the body and everything else. There can be no doubt about it.”
Mitya was struck utterly dumb.

“But that’s completely impossible!” he cried, totally at a loss. “I ... I didn’t go in.... I tell you plainly, definitely, that door was shut the whole time I was in the garden and when I ran out of it. I only stood at the window and saw him through the window. That’s all, that’s all.... I remember it down to the last minute. And even if I didn’t, it would make no difference. I know it, because nobody knew the signals except Smerdyakov, myself and the dead man. And he wouldn’t have opened that door to anyone in the world without the signals.”

“Signals? What signals?” asked the prosecutor, with greedy, almost hysterical curiosity. All his reserve and dignity vanished at once. He asked it with a kind of cringing timidity. He smelled an important fact he had known nothing about, and he was already afraid that Mitya might refuse to reveal it.

“So you didn’t know!” Mitya winked at him, with a spiteful, mocking smile. “And what if I won’t tell you? Who else could you learn it from? Nobody knew about the signals but my father, Smerdyakov and me. That’s all. Heaven knew too, but Heaven won’t tell you. Still, it’s an interesting fact. Who knows what you might build on it! Ha ha! Take heart, gentlemen, I’ll tell you. You’ve got some foolish notion in your heads. You don’t know the man you’re dealing with! You’re dealing with a prisoner who testifies against himself, to his own harm! Yes, because I’m a man of honor, and you—are not.”

The prosecutor swallowed this without a murmur. He was shaking with impatience to hear the new fact. Mitya told them everything about the signals Fyodor Pavlovitch had devised for Smerdyakov, in minute and rambling detail. He told them exactly what each tap on the window meant, and drummed the signals out on the table. When Nikolay Parfenovitch suggested that he must have tapped the signal “Grushenka has come” when he knocked for his father, Mitya answered, quite exactly, that yes, he had tapped that one, “Grushenka has come.”
“So now you can go and build your tower,” Mitya broke off, and again turned away from them in contempt.
“So nobody knew the signals except your dead father, you and the valet Smerdyakov? Nobody else?” Nikolay Parfenovitch asked once again.
“That’s right. The valet Smerdyakov, and Heaven. Put down Heaven. That may be useful. Besides, you’ll be needing God yourselves.”
And of course they had already begun to write it down. But as they wrote, the prosecutor said suddenly, as if seizing on a new idea:

“But if Smerdyakov also knew these signals, and you flatly deny any responsibility for your father’s death, might it not have been he who gave the agreed knock, got your father to open the door to him, and then ... committed the crime?”
Mitya turned on him a look of deep irony and fierce hatred. He stared in silence for so long that the prosecutor blinked.

“You’ve caught the fox again,” Mitya said at last. “You’ve got the beast by the tail. Ha ha! I can see through you, Mr. Prosecutor. You thought, of course, that I’d leap at that, grab at your hint, and shout at the top of my voice, ‘Aie! It’s Smerdyakov! He’s the murderer!’ Admit it, that’s what you thought. Admit it, and I’ll go on.”
But the prosecutor admitted nothing. He kept silent and waited.
“You’re wrong. I’m not going to shout, ‘It’s Smerdyakov,’” said Mitya.
“And you don’t even suspect him?”
“Why, do you?”
“He is under suspicion as well.”
Mitya stared at the floor.

“Joking aside,” he said gloomily. “Listen. From the very start, almost from the moment I ran out to you from behind the curtain, I’ve had Smerdyakov in my mind. I’ve been sitting here shouting that I’m innocent, and all the while I’ve been thinking, ‘Smerdyakov!’ I can’t get Smerdyakov out of my head. In fact, I thought of Smerdyakov just now too, but only for a second. Almost at once I thought, ‘No, it isn’t Smerdyakov.’ It’s not his doing, gentlemen.”
“Then is there anyone else you suspect?” Nikolay Parfenovitch asked carefully.
“I don’t know who it can be, whether it’s the hand of Heaven or of Satan, but ... not Smerdyakov,” Mitya jerked out, with finality.
“But what makes you so sure, and so emphatic, that it isn’t he?”

“It’s my conviction—my impression. Smerdyakov is a man of the most abject character, and a coward. He’s not just a coward, he’s all the cowardice in the world walking about on two legs. He has the heart of a chicken. When he talked to me, he was always trembling in case I killed him, though I never lifted a hand against him. He fell at my feet and blubbered. He has kissed these very boots, literally, begging me ‘not to frighten him.’ Do you hear that? ‘Not to frighten him.’ What a thing to say! Why, I offered him money. He’s a whimpering chicken—sickly, epileptic, feeble-minded—a child of eight could thrash him. He has no character worth mentioning. It’s not Smerdyakov, gentlemen. He doesn’t care for money; he wouldn’t take my gifts. Besides, what reason would he have to murder the old man? Why, he’s very likely his son, you know—his natural son. Did you know that?”
“We have heard that tale. But you are your father’s son too, you know, and yet you told everyone yourself that you meant to murder him.”

“That’s a stab! And a nasty, petty one! I’m not afraid! Oh, gentlemen, isn’t it too low of you to say that to my face? It’s low, because I told you that myself. I not only wanted to murder him, I might have done it. And what’s more, I went out of my way to tell you, of my own free will, that I nearly murdered him. But you see, I didn’t murder him. You see, my guardian angel saved me—that’s what you haven’t taken into account. And that’s why it’s so low of you. Because I didn’t kill him, I didn’t kill him! Do you hear me? I did not kill him.”
He was nearly choking. He had not been so shaken at any point in the whole interrogation.
“And what has he told you, gentlemen—Smerdyakov, I mean?” he added suddenly, after a pause. “Am I allowed to ask that?”

“You may ask any question,” the prosecutor answered with icy severity, “any question that concerns the facts of the case, and we are bound, I repeat, to answer every inquiry you make. We found the servant Smerdyakov, the man you ask about, lying unconscious in his bed, in an epileptic fit of extreme severity, which had come back perhaps ten times. The doctor who came with us examined him and told us he may not live through the night.”
“Well, if that’s so, then the devil must have killed him,” broke suddenly from Mitya, as though until that moment he had been asking himself, “Was it Smerdyakov or not?”
“We will return to this later,” Nikolay Parfenovitch decided. “Now, would you care to continue your statement?”

Mitya asked for a rest, and it was courteously granted. After resting, he went on with his story, but he was clearly low in spirits. He was worn out, humiliated and shaken in his very soul. And to make matters worse, the prosecutor seemed to be irritating him on purpose with tiresome interruptions about “trifling points.” Mitya had hardly described how, sitting on the wall, he struck Grigory on the head with the pestle while the old man clung to his left leg, and how he then jumped down to look at him, when the prosecutor stopped him and asked him to describe exactly how he had been sitting on the wall. Mitya was surprised.
“Oh, I was sitting like this, astride, with one leg on one side of the wall and one on the other.”
“And the pestle?”
“I had the pestle in my hand.”
“Not in your pocket? Do you remember that for certain? Was it a hard blow you gave him?”
“It must have been hard. But why do you ask?”
“Would you be so good as to sit on the chair the way you sat on the wall then, and show us how you moved your arm, and in which direction?”
“You’re making fun of me, aren’t you?” asked Mitya, looking at the speaker with haughty scorn. But the man did not flinch.
Mitya whirled around, sat astride his chair, and swung his arm.
“That’s how I hit him! That’s how I knocked him down! What more do you want?”
“Thank you. Might I trouble you now to explain why you jumped down, what your object was, and what you had in mind?”
“Oh, blast it!... I jumped down to get a look at the man I’d hurt ... I couldn’t tell you why!”
“Though you were worked up and running away?”
“Yes, worked up and running away, and I still jumped down.”
“You wanted to help him?”
“Help!... Yes, maybe I did want to help him.... I can’t remember.”
“You can’t remember? So you weren’t altogether aware of what you were doing?”
“Not at all. I remember everything—every detail. I jumped down to look at him, and I wiped his face with my handkerchief.”
“We’ve seen your handkerchief. Were you hoping to bring him round?”
“I don’t know if I hoped that. I only wanted to find out whether he was alive or dead.”
“Ah! You wanted to find out? Well, and what then?”
“I’m no doctor. I couldn’t tell. I ran off thinking I’d killed him. And now he’s recovered.”
“Excellent,” the prosecutor remarked. “Thank you. That’s all I wanted to hear. Please go on.”

Alas! It never crossed Mitya’s mind to tell them, though he remembered it well, that he had gone back out of pity, and that standing over the man lying there he had even spoken a few words of regret: “You’ve come to grief, old man—there’s no help for it. Well, there you must lie.”

The prosecutor could draw only one conclusion: the man had gone back “at such a moment, and in such agitation, simply to find out whether the _only_ witness of his crime was dead; and so he must be a man of great strength, coolness, resolve and foresight, even at such a moment,” ... and so on. The prosecutor was well pleased. “I’ve provoked this nervous fellow with ‘trifles,’ and he’s said more than he meant to.”
Mitya went on, struggling painfully. But this time Nikolay Parfenovitch cut in right away.
“How was it that you ran to the servant, Fedosya Markovna, with your hands so smeared with blood, and, it seems, your face as well?”
“Why, at the time I never noticed the blood at all,” Mitya answered.
“That’s quite likely. It happens sometimes.” The prosecutor exchanged a look with Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“I just didn’t notice. You’re quite right about that, prosecutor,” Mitya agreed all at once.

Next came the story of how Mitya had suddenly resolved to “step aside” and leave the way clear for their happiness. But he could not bring himself to open his heart to them the way he had before and tell them about “the queen of his soul.” He hated talking about her in front of these cold men “who were fastening on him like bugs.” So, in answer to their repeated questions, he spoke briefly and curtly:

“Well, I decided to kill myself. What did I have left to live for? That question stared me in the face. Her first, rightful lover had come back, the man who’d wronged her but had hurried back after five years to offer her his love and make amends by marrying her.... So I knew it was all over for me.... Behind me was disgrace, and that blood—Grigory’s.... What was there to live for? So I went to redeem the pistols I’d pawned, to load them and put a bullet through my head tomorrow.”
“And a grand feast the night before?”

“Yes, a grand feast the night before. Oh, damn it all, gentlemen! Do hurry up and get this over with. I meant to shoot myself not far from here, out beyond the village, and I’d planned to do it at five in the morning. I even had a note in my pocket by then. I wrote it at Perhotin’s while I was loading the pistols. Here’s the letter. Read it! I’m not saying this for your sake,” he added with contempt. He pulled it from his waistcoat pocket and threw it onto the table. The lawyers read it with interest and, as usual, filed it with the papers of the case.
“And it didn’t even occur to you to wash your hands at Perhotin’s? You weren’t afraid of drawing suspicion?”

“What suspicion? Suspicion or none, I’d have galloped straight here just the same and shot myself at five o’clock, and you’d have been too late to do anything. If it weren’t for what happened to my father, you’d have known nothing and wouldn’t have come here at all. Oh, it’s the devil’s doing. The devil murdered father, and it’s thanks to the devil that you found out so fast. How did you get here so quickly? It’s marvelous, it’s a dream!”

“Mr. Perhotin told us that when you came to him, you were holding ... in your bloodstained hands ... your money ... a lot of money ... a bundle of hundred-rouble notes, and that his servant-boy saw it too.”
“That’s true, gentlemen. I remember that’s how it was.”

“Now, there’s one small point that arises. Can you tell us,” Nikolay Parfenovitch began, very gently, “where you got so much money all of a sudden, when the facts and the timing show that you had not been home?”
The prosecutor’s brows drew together at the question being put so bluntly, but he did not interrupt Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“No, I didn’t go home,” Mitya replied, looking perfectly calm but keeping his eyes on the floor.

“Then let me ask again,” Nikolay Parfenovitch went on, as if creeping up on the subject. “Where could you possibly have found such a sum all at once, when, as you admit yourself, at five o’clock that same day you—”

“I needed ten roubles, so I pawned my pistols with Perhotin, and then I went to Madame Hohlakov to borrow three thousand, which she wouldn’t give me, and so on, and all the rest of it,” Mitya cut in sharply. “Yes, gentlemen, I needed money, and then suddenly there were thousands, eh? Do you know, gentlemen, what you’re both afraid of right now? ‘What if he won’t tell us where he got it?’ Well, that’s just how it is. I’m not going to tell you, gentlemen. You’ve guessed right. You’ll never know,” said Mitya, chipping out each word with extraordinary determination. The lawyers were silent for a moment.
“You must understand, Mr. Karamazov, that it’s vitally important for us to know,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, in a soft, smooth voice.
“I understand. But I still won’t tell you.”

The prosecutor stepped in too. He reminded the prisoner once more that he was free to decline to answer questions if he judged that to be in his interest, and so on. But given the harm he might do himself by his silence, especially in a case as grave as—

“And so on, gentlemen, and so on. Enough! I’ve heard that rigmarole before,” Mitya broke in again. “I can see for myself how important it is, and that this is the crucial point, and I still won’t say.”
“What does it matter to us? It’s not our affair, it’s yours. You’re hurting yourself,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch nervously.

“Look, gentlemen, joking aside”—Mitya raised his eyes and looked at them both steadily—“I had a feeling from the very beginning that we’d clash at this point. But at first, when I started giving my evidence, it was all still far off and hazy; it was all floating about, and I was so naive that I began by assuming we trusted each other. Now I can see for myself that there can be no such trust, because sooner or later we were bound to run into this cursed stumbling-block. And now we’ve run into it! It’s impossible, and that’s the end of it! But I don’t blame you. You can’t believe it all just because I say so. I understand that, of course.”
He sank back into gloomy silence.

“Could you not, while keeping your resolve to say nothing about the main point, at least give us some small hint of what kind of motives are strong enough to make you refuse to answer, at a moment so dangerous for you?”
Mitya gave a sad, almost dreamy smile.

“I’m a lot more good-natured than you think, gentlemen. I’ll tell you why, and I’ll give you that hint, though you don’t deserve it. I won’t speak of it, gentlemen, because it would stain my honor. The answer to the question of where I got the money would bring me far greater disgrace than murdering and robbing my father would, if I had murdered and robbed him. That’s why I can’t tell you. I can’t, for fear of the disgrace. What, gentlemen, are you going to write that down?”
“Yes, we’ll write it down,” lisped Nikolay Parfenovitch.

“You shouldn’t write that down, about ‘disgrace.’ I only told you out of the goodness of my heart. I didn’t have to tell you. I made you a present of it, so to speak, and you pounce on it right away. Oh, well, write—write whatever you like,” he finished, in scornful disgust. “I’m not afraid of you, and I can still look you in the eye.”
“And can you not tell us what sort of disgrace it is?” Nikolay Parfenovitch ventured.
The prosecutor scowled darkly.
“No, no, _c’est fini_, don’t bother. It isn’t worth dirtying one’s hands. I’ve dirtied myself enough on your account already. You’re not worth it—nobody is ... Enough, gentlemen. I’m not going on.”
He said this too firmly to be argued with. Nikolay Parfenovitch did not press him further, but from Ippolit Kirillovitch’s eyes he could see that the prosecutor had not given up hope.
“Could you at least tell us how much money you had in your hands when you walked into Mr. Perhotin’s—how many roubles, exactly?”
“That I can’t tell you.”
“You told Mr. Perhotin, I believe, that you had three thousand from Madame Hohlakov.”
“Maybe I did. Enough, gentlemen. I won’t say how much I had.”
“Then would you be good enough to tell us how you came here, and what you’ve done since you arrived?”
“Oh! You can ask the people here about that. But I’ll tell you, if you like.”

He proceeded to tell it, but we won’t repeat his story. He told it dryly and curtly. About the raptures of his love he said nothing; he only said that he had dropped his plan of shooting himself because of “new factors in the case.” He gave the story without going into reasons or details. And this time the lawyers did not badger him much. It was plain that nothing here was of any essential interest to them.

“We’ll check all that. We’ll return to it when we examine the witnesses, which will, naturally, be done in your presence,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch in conclusion. “And now let me ask you to put on the table everything you have on you, above all any money you still have.”

“My money, gentlemen? Certainly. I understand that’s needed. I’m actually surprised you didn’t ask about it sooner. It’s true I couldn’t have got away anywhere. I’m sitting here in plain sight. But here’s my money—count it—take it. That’s everything, I think.”

He turned out all his pockets; even the small change—two twenty-copeck pieces—he dug out of his waistcoat pocket. They counted the money. It came to eight hundred and thirty-six roubles and forty copecks.
“And is that all?” the investigating lawyer asked.
“Yes.”
“A moment ago you stated in your evidence that you spent three hundred roubles at Plotnikovs’. You gave Perhotin ten, your driver twenty, you lost two hundred here, then....”
Nikolay Parfenovitch went through all of it. Mitya helped him willingly. They recalled every last farthing and put it in the sum. Nikolay Parfenovitch quickly added up the total.
“With these eight hundred, you must have started with about fifteen hundred?”
“I suppose so,” Mitya snapped.
“Why does everyone claim there was much more?”
“Let them claim it.”
“But you claimed it yourself.”
“Yes, I did, too.”

“We’ll compare all this with the evidence of other people we haven’t yet questioned. Don’t worry about your money. It will be properly looked after and will be returned to you at the end of ... what is now beginning ... if it appears, or, so to speak, is proved, that you have an undisputed right to it. Well, and now....”
Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly stood up and told Mitya firmly that it was his duty and obligation to carry out a minute and thorough search “of your clothes and everything else....”
“By all means, gentlemen. I’ll turn out every pocket, if you like.”
And he really did begin to turn out his pockets.
“You’ll need to take off your clothes as well.”
“What! Undress? Ugh! Damn it! Won’t you search me as I am? Can’t you?”
“It’s quite out of the question, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You must take your clothes off.”
“Have it your way,” Mitya gave in gloomily; “only please, not here, but behind the curtains. Who’s going to search them?”
“Behind the curtains, naturally.”
Nikolay Parfenovitch nodded his assent. His small face had a look of peculiar solemnity.

chapters.title: VI. The Prosecutor Catches Mitya
paragraphs: What happened next was completely unexpected, and it astonished Mitya. A minute earlier he could never have pictured anyone treating him, Mitya Karamazov, this way. Worst of all, it was humiliating, and the other side seemed “supercilious and scornful” about it. Taking off his coat was nothing. But then he was told to strip further. Not asked, really, but “commanded”; he understood that perfectly. Out of pride and contempt he did it without a word. Some peasants had come in with the lawyers and stood on the same side of the curtain. “They’re here in case they need force,” thought Mitya, “and maybe for some other reason, too.”

“Well, do I have to take off my shirt, too?” he asked sharply. Nikolay Parfenovitch didn’t answer. He and the prosecutor were absorbed in going over the coat, the trousers, the waistcoat and the cap, and plainly both of them found it fascinating. “They make no bones about it,” thought Mitya. “They don’t even bother with the most basic politeness.”
“That’s the second time I’ve asked—do I need to take off my shirt or not?” he said, sharper and more irritable still.
“Don’t worry about it. We’ll tell you what to do,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch. His tone was downright domineering, or so Mitya thought.

Meanwhile the lawyers were conferring in low voices. The coat turned out to have a huge patch of blood on it, especially on the left side at the back, dried but still stiff. The trousers had bloodstains, too. On top of that, Nikolay Parfenovitch, with the peasant witnesses looking on, ran his fingers along the collar, the cuffs and every seam of the coat and trousers. He was clearly searching for something—money, of course. He didn’t even hide from Mitya that he suspected him of being able to sew money into his clothes.

“He treats me like a thief, not like an officer,” Mitya muttered to himself. The two of them traded thoughts with amazing openness. The secretary, for example, who was also behind the curtain, bustling around and listening in, pointed out the cap to Nikolay Parfenovitch, which they were also feeling over.

“Remember Gridyenko, the copying-clerk,” said the secretary. “Last summer he got the pay for the whole office, then claimed he’d lost it while drunk. And where did they find it? In piping just like this on his cap. The hundred-rouble notes were rolled up tight and sewn inside the piping.”
Both lawyers remembered Gridyenko’s case very well. They put Mitya’s cap aside and decided that all his clothes would need a closer inspection later.
“Wait,” Nikolay Parfenovitch cried suddenly. He had noticed that the right cuff of Mitya’s shirt was folded under and bloody. “Wait, what’s this—blood?”
“Yes,” Mitya snapped.
“Meaning what blood? ... And why is the cuff folded under?”
Mitya explained that he had got the sleeve bloody tending to Grigory, and had folded it under while washing his hands at Perhotin’s.
“You’ll have to take your shirt off, too. It’s very important as material evidence.”
Mitya went red and exploded with rage.
“What, am I to stay naked?” he shouted.
“Don’t get excited. We’ll sort something out. For now, take off your socks.”
“You’re joking, aren’t you? Is that really necessary?” Mitya’s eyes blazed.
“We’re not in the mood for jokes,” Nikolay Parfenovitch answered sternly.

“Well, if I must—” Mitya muttered. He sat down on the bed and took off his socks. He felt unbearably awkward. Everyone else was dressed and he was naked. Oddly, with his clothes off he somehow felt guilty in front of them. He was nearly ready to believe he really was beneath them, and that they now had every right to look down on him.

“When everybody’s undressed you don’t feel any shame. But when you’re the only one undressed and everyone is staring, it’s degrading,” he kept telling himself over and over. “It’s like a dream. I’ve sometimes dreamed of being in degrading spots like this.” Taking off the socks was torture. They were filthy, and so was his underwear, and now everyone could see. Worse, he disliked his own feet. All his life he had thought both his big toes were hideous. He especially hated the coarse, flat, crooked nail on the right one, and now they’d all see it. The unbearable shame made him deliberately rougher, right away. He yanked off his shirt himself.
“Would you like to search somewhere else, if you’re not too ashamed?”
“No, there’s no need, for now.”
“So am I to stay naked like this?” he added savagely.
“Yes, nothing can be done about that for the moment.... Kindly sit down here a while. You can wrap yourself in a quilt from the bed, and I ... I’ll deal with all this.”

The items were shown to the witnesses. The record of the search was written up. At last Nikolay Parfenovitch left, and the clothes were carried out behind him. Ippolit Kirillovitch left too. That put Mitya alone with the peasants, who stood silent and never took their eyes off him. He wrapped himself in the quilt. He was cold. His bare feet stuck out, and he couldn’t pull the quilt over far enough to cover them. Nikolay Parfenovitch seemed to be gone a long time, “an insufferable time.” “He thinks I’m a puppy,” thought Mitya, grinding his teeth. “And that rotten prosecutor has gone, too. Scorn, no doubt—he can’t stand the sight of me naked!”

Mitya had supposed, though, that they would examine his clothes and hand them back. So he was outraged when Nikolay Parfenovitch returned with entirely different clothes, which a peasant brought in after him.

“Here, clothes for you,” he said airily, looking quite pleased with how his errand had gone. “Mr. Kalganov has kindly supplied these for this unusual emergency, and a clean shirt as well. Fortunately he had them all in his trunk. You can keep your own socks and underwear.”
Mitya blew up.
“I won’t wear other people’s clothes!” he shouted threateningly. “Give me mine!”
“Impossible!”
“Give me mine. And damn Kalganov and his clothes, too!”

It took them a long while to talk him round. But somehow they got him to calm down. They pressed on him that his clothes were stained with blood and so had to be “included with the other material evidence.” They said they “didn’t even have the right to let him keep them now ... given the possible outcome of the case.” At last Mitya understood. He fell into a dark silence and dressed in a hurry. He only observed, as he pulled the things on, that they were a good deal better than his old ones, and that he hated “coming out ahead on the exchange.” And the coat, besides, was “ridiculously tight. Am I to be rigged out like a fool ... for your entertainment?”
They insisted again that he was exaggerating. Kalganov was only slightly taller, they said, so at most the trousers might be a little long. But the coat really was tight across the shoulders.
“Damn it! I can barely do it up,” Mitya grumbled. “Be so kind as to tell Mr. Kalganov from me that I never asked for his clothes, and it’s not my idea that I’ve been dressed up like a clown.”
“He knows that, and he’s sorry ... I mean he’s not sorry to lend you the clothes, he’s sorry about this whole business,” Nikolay Parfenovitch mumbled.
“Confound his sorrow! Well, where to now? Do I just go on sitting here?”

They asked him to go back to the “other room.” Mitya walked in scowling with rage, trying not to meet anyone’s eye. In another man’s clothes he felt disgraced, even in front of the peasants, and Trifon Borissovitch, whose face showed up in the doorway for some reason and vanished at once. “He’s come to see me in my costume,” thought Mitya. He sat down on the same chair as before. He had a ridiculous, nightmarish sense of having lost his mind.

“Well, what next? Are you going to flog me? That’s the only thing you haven’t done,” he said through clenched teeth, speaking to the prosecutor. He refused to turn to Nikolay Parfenovitch, as if he were too proud to speak to him.
“He studied my socks far too closely, and he turned them inside out on purpose, so everyone could see how dirty they were—the scoundrel!”
“Well, now we have to move on to questioning the witnesses,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, as if in answer to Mitya’s question.
“Yes,” said the prosecutor thoughtfully, as though he were pondering something.

“We’ve done everything we could to help you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Nikolay Parfenovitch continued. “But since you have given us such a flat refusal to say where the money found on you came from, we now find ourselves—”
“What kind of stone is in your ring?” Mitya broke in suddenly, as if waking from a daydream. He pointed at one of the three big rings on Nikolay Parfenovitch’s right hand.
“My ring?” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, surprised.
“Yes, that one ... on your middle finger, with the little veins in it. What stone is it?” Mitya insisted, like a fretful child.
“A smoky topaz,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, smiling. “Would you like to see it? I’ll take it off ...”

“No, don’t take it off,” Mitya cried furiously, suddenly coming to and angry at himself. “Don’t take it off ... there’s no need.... Damn it!... Gentlemen, you’ve fouled my heart! Do you think I’d hide it from you if I had really killed my father? That I’d wriggle and lie and cover my tracks? No, that’s not Dmitri Karamazov. He couldn’t do it. And if I were guilty, I swear I wouldn’t have sat waiting for you to come, or for sunrise as I first planned. I’d have killed myself before now, without waiting for dawn! I know that about myself now. I couldn’t have learned so much in twenty years as I’ve found out in this accursed night!... And would I be like this tonight, at this moment, sitting with you? Could I talk like this, could I move like this, could I look at you and at the world like this, if I really had murdered my father? When the mere thought that I might have killed Grigory by accident gave me no peace all night—and not from fear—oh, not just from fear of your punishment! The shame of it! And you expect me to be open with scoffers like you, who see nothing and believe in nothing, blind moles and scoffers, and to confess one more nasty thing I’ve done, one more disgrace, even if it would clear me of your accusation! No, Siberia is better! The man who opened the door to my father and walked through it, he killed him, he robbed him. Who was he? I’m racking my brains and I can’t think who. But I can tell you it was not Dmitri Karamazov, and that’s all I can tell you, and that’s enough, enough, leave me alone.... Exile me, punish me, but stop pestering me. I won’t say another word. Call your witnesses!”

Mitya delivered this sudden outburst as if he had resolved to stay completely silent from then on. The prosecutor had watched him throughout. Only when Mitya stopped did he speak, as if it were the most ordinary matter, in a perfectly cold and composed manner:

“Ah, about the open door you mentioned a moment ago. We may as well tell you now, in passing, about a most interesting piece of testimony, extremely important to you and to us alike, which Grigory has given us—the old man you wounded. When he recovered, he stated clearly and emphatically, in answer to our questions, that this is what happened. He came out onto the steps, heard a noise in the garden, and decided to go in by the little gate, which was standing open. Before he saw you running through the dark from the open window where you had seen your father, as you have already told us, Grigory glanced to his left. He noticed the open window, and at the same moment he saw, much closer to him, the door standing wide open—the door you have stated was shut the whole time you were in the garden. I won’t hide from you that Grigory himself firmly affirms and testifies that you must have run out of that door. Naturally he didn’t see you do it with his own eyes, since he first noticed you some distance off in the garden, running toward the fence.”
Mitya had jumped up from his chair halfway through this speech.
“Nonsense!” he yelled in a sudden frenzy. “It’s a barefaced lie. He can’t have seen the door open, because it was shut. He’s lying!”
“It is my duty to repeat that he stands firmly by his statement. He doesn’t waver. He holds to it. We have questioned him closely several times.”
“Exactly. I questioned him several times myself,” Nikolay Parfenovitch confirmed warmly.

“It’s false, false! Either somebody wants to slander me, or it’s a madman’s hallucination,” Mitya kept shouting. “He’s simply raving from loss of blood, from the wound. He must have imagined it when he came to.... He’s raving.”
“Yes, but he noticed the open door not when he came to after being injured, but earlier, as soon as he went into the garden from the lodge.”
“But it’s false, it’s false! It can’t be! He’s slandering me out of spite.... He can’t have seen it ... I didn’t come out of that door,” Mitya gasped.
The prosecutor turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and told him with emphasis:
“Confront him with it.”
“Do you recognize this object?”
Nikolay Parfenovitch put a large, thick official envelope on the table. Three seals were still unbroken on it. The envelope was empty and torn open at one end. Mitya stared at it, wide-eyed.

“It ... it must be my father’s envelope, the one with the three thousand roubles in it ... and if it’s written on it, let me see, ‘For my little chicken’ ... yes—three thousand!” he shouted. “Do you see, three thousand, do you see?”
“Naturally we see. But the money wasn’t in it. The envelope was empty, on the floor by the bed, behind the screen.”
For a few seconds Mitya stood there as if struck by lightning.
“Gentlemen, it’s Smerdyakov!” he suddenly shouted at the top of his lungs. “He murdered him! He robbed him! Nobody else knew where the old man hid the envelope. It’s Smerdyakov, that’s obvious now!”
“But you also knew about the envelope, and that it was under the pillow.”

“I never knew it. I never saw it. This is the first time I’ve looked at it. I’d only heard about it from Smerdyakov.... He was the only one who knew where the old man kept it hidden; I didn’t know ...” Mitya was completely out of breath.
“But you told us yourself that the envelope was under your late father’s pillow. You specifically said it was under the pillow, so you must have known.”
“It’s written down,” Nikolay Parfenovitch confirmed.

“Nonsense! It’s absurd! I had no idea it was under the pillow. Maybe it wasn’t under the pillow at all.... I just happened to guess it was under the pillow. What does Smerdyakov say? Did you ask him where it was? What does Smerdyakov say? That’s the main point.... And I went out of my way to lie against myself.... I said it was under the pillow without thinking, and now you— Oh, you know how a man says the wrong thing without meaning to. Nobody knew except Smerdyakov, only Smerdyakov, no one else.... He didn’t even tell me where it was! But it’s his doing, his doing; there’s no doubt about it. He murdered him, and that’s as plain as day now,” Mitya cried, more and more wildly, repeating himself without sense, more and more exasperated and worked up. “You must understand that, and arrest him at once.... He must have killed him while I was running away and Grigory was lying unconscious, that’s clear now.... He gave the signal and father opened up to him ... because nobody but he knew the signal, and without the signal father would never have opened the door....”

“But once again you’re overlooking something,” the prosecutor remarked, in the same restrained tone, though with a hint of triumph. “There was no need to give the signal if the door was already standing open when you were there, while you were in the garden....”
“The door, the door,” Mitya muttered, staring at the prosecutor, unable to speak. He sank back in his chair, helpless. Nobody said anything.
“Yes, the door!... It’s a nightmare! God is against me!” he cried, staring straight ahead, utterly stunned.

“Well, you see,” the prosecutor went on with dignity, “you can judge for yourself, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. On one side we have the testimony about the open door you ran out through, a fact that overwhelms you and us alike. On the other side there is your incomprehensible, stubborn and, so to speak, obstinate silence about where the money came from that suddenly appeared in your hands, when only three hours earlier, by your own account, you pawned your pistols for ten roubles! Given all these facts, judge for yourself. What are we to believe, and what can we rely on? And don’t charge us with being ‘frigid, cynical, scoffing people’ who can’t believe in the generous impulses of your heart.... Try to put yourself in our position ...”
Mitya was indescribably agitated. He went pale.
“All right!” he exclaimed suddenly. “I’ll tell you my secret. I’ll tell you where I got the money!... I’ll expose my shame, so I won’t have to blame myself or you afterward.”

“And believe me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Nikolay Parfenovitch put in, in a tone of almost touching delight, “every honest and full confession from you now may later carry enormous weight in your favor, and may even, furthermore—”
But the prosecutor gave him a slight nudge under the table, and he stopped himself in time. Mitya, true enough, hadn’t heard him.

chapters.title: VII. Mitya’s Great Secret. Received With Hisses
paragraphs: “Gentlemen,” he began, as agitated as before, “I want to confess everything. That money was _my own_.” The lawyers’ faces dropped. This was not at all what they had expected.
“What do you mean?” Nikolay Parfenovitch stammered. “Earlier that same day, at five o’clock, you yourself told us—”

“Damn five o’clock that day, and damn what I told you! That has nothing to do with it now! That money was mine, my own, that is, stolen by me ... not mine, I mean, but stolen by me, fifteen hundred roubles, and I had it on me the whole time, the whole time ...”
“But where did you get it?”

“I took it off my neck, gentlemen, off this very neck ... it was right here, hanging round my neck, sewn up in a rag. I’d worn it a long time, a month, since the day I hung it there ... to my shame and disgrace!”
“And who was it you ... appropriated it from?”
“You mean ‘stole it’? Say it straight, now. Yes, I as good as stole it. But if you like, I ‘appropriated’ it. In my own mind I stole it. And last night I finished stealing it.”
“Last night? But you just said it was a month ago that you ... got hold of it?...”

“Yes. But not from my father. Not from my father, don’t worry. I didn’t steal it from my father, I stole it from her. Let me tell you without breaking in. It’s hard enough, you know. A month ago Katerina Ivanovna sent for me, the lady who used to be my betrothed. Do you know her?”
“Yes, of course.”
“I know you do. She’s a noble creature, the noblest of the noble. But she’s hated me for ever so long, oh, for ever so long ... and she had every reason to hate me, every reason!”
“Katerina Ivanovna!” Nikolay Parfenovitch cried out in astonishment. The prosecutor stared as well.

“Oh, don’t speak her name so lightly! I’m a scoundrel for dragging her in. Yes, I saw that she hated me ... for a long while.... Right from the start, even that evening at my lodging ... but enough, enough. You aren’t worthy even to hear about that. There’s no need for it at all.... All I need say is that a month ago she sent for me and gave me three thousand roubles to post to her sister and another relative in Moscow (as if she couldn’t have posted it herself!), and I ... it came just at the fatal moment of my life when I ... well, when I had just fallen in love with another woman, with her, with Grushenka, who’s sitting downstairs right now. I carried her off to Mokroe here, and in two days I blew half of that cursed three thousand, but the other half I kept on me. And I kept that half, that fifteen hundred, hung round my neck like a locket, until yesterday, when I undid it and spent it. What’s left of it, eight hundred roubles, is in your hands now, Nikolay Parfenovitch. That’s the change from the fifteen hundred I had yesterday.”
“One moment. How can that be? When you were here a month ago you spent three thousand, not fifteen hundred. Everybody knows it.”
“Who knows it? Who counted the money? Did I let anybody count it?”
“But you told everyone yourself that you’d spent exactly three thousand.”

“That’s true, I did. I said so to the whole town, and the whole town said so too. Even here in Mokroe everyone figured it was three thousand. But I didn’t spend three thousand. I spent fifteen hundred. The other fifteen hundred I sewed into a little bag. That’s how it was, gentlemen. That’s where yesterday’s money came from....”
“This is nearly miraculous,” Nikolay Parfenovitch murmured.
“Let me ask you something,” the prosecutor said at last. “Had you told anyone at all about this before, I mean that you had fifteen hundred left on you a month ago?”
“I told nobody.”
“That is odd. Do you mean literally nobody?”
“Literally nobody. Not a soul.”

“Why were you so reticent? Why did you make such a secret of it? To put it more exactly: you have now told us your secret, which you yourself call ‘disgraceful.’ Yet in reality—comparatively speaking, of course—this act, the taking of three thousand roubles belonging to someone else, and only for a time, naturally, is in my view merely extreme recklessness, and not so disgraceful, given your character.... Grant that it was highly discreditable. Still, discreditable is not ‘disgraceful.’... Many people have guessed during this last month that you spent Katerina Ivanovna’s three thousand, and I heard the tale myself, quite apart from your confession.... Mihail Makarovitch, for one, had heard it as well, so that it was hardly a tale any more, just the gossip of the whole town. There are also signs, if I am not mistaken, that you admitted this yourself to somebody, I mean that the money was Katerina Ivanovna’s. So I am greatly surprised that up to this moment you have made such an extraordinary secret of the fifteen hundred you say you set aside, and have, apparently, attached a feeling of positive horror to that secret.... It is hard to believe that confessing it could cost you such anguish.... Just now you cried out that Siberia would be better than confessing it ...”

The prosecutor broke off. He was irritated. He made no effort to hide his vexation, which was close to anger, and he poured out all his stored-up bile in a scattered, tangled way, without picking his words.
“The disgrace isn’t the fifteen hundred. It’s that I kept it apart from the rest of the three thousand,” Mitya said firmly.

“Why?” the prosecutor smiled sourly. “What is disgraceful, to your mind, in setting aside half of the three thousand you had taken discreditably, or ‘disgracefully’ if you prefer? That you took the three thousand matters more than what you did with it. And by the way, why did you do it—why did you put that half aside, for what purpose, with what aim? Can you explain that to us?”

“Oh, gentlemen, the purpose is the whole point!” Mitya cried. “I set it aside because I was vile, that is, because I was calculating, and calculating in such a case is vile ... and that vileness has lasted a whole month.”
“I can’t make sense of it.”

“You amaze me. But I’ll put it more clearly. Maybe it really is hard to follow. Now listen carefully. Say I take three thousand entrusted to my honor and blow it on a spree, say I blow all of it, and next morning I go to her and say, ‘Katya, I did wrong, I’ve squandered your three thousand.’ Well, is that right? No, it isn’t right. It’s dishonest and cowardly. I’m a beast, no better at holding myself back than a beast, that’s so, isn’t it? But I’m still not a thief, am I? Not an out-and-out thief, you’ll grant me that! I squandered it, I didn’t steal it. Now the second case, a little more favorable. Follow me closely, or I’ll get muddled again, my head’s going round. In the second case I spend only fifteen hundred of the three thousand here, only half. The next day I take that half to her and say, ‘Katya, take this fifteen hundred from me. I’m a low beast and a scoundrel you can’t trust, because I’ve wasted half the money, and I’ll waste this too, so save me from temptation!’ Well, what about that case? I’d be a beast and a scoundrel, whatever you like, but not a thief, not altogether a thief. If I were, I wouldn’t have brought back what was left, I’d have kept that too. She would see at once that since I’d brought back half, I would pay back what I’d spent, that I’d never stop trying, that I’d work for it and pay it back. So then I’d be a scoundrel, but not a thief, say what you please, not a thief!”
“I grant that there is a certain distinction,” the prosecutor said with a cold smile. “It is odd, though, that you see such a vital difference.”

“Yes, I see a vital difference! Any man can be a scoundrel, and perhaps every man is one, but not everyone can be a thief. For that you have to be an arch-scoundrel. Oh, of course, I don’t know how to draw these fine lines ... but a thief is lower than a scoundrel, that’s what I believe. Listen: I carry the money on me for a whole month. I might make up my mind tomorrow to give it back, and then I’m not a scoundrel anymore. But I can’t make up my mind, you see, though I decide every day, every day I push myself to do it, and still for a whole month I can’t bring myself to it. Is that right, do you think? Is that right?”

“Certainly it isn’t right. I understand that perfectly well, and I don’t dispute it,” the prosecutor answered stiffly. “Let us drop all discussion of these subtleties and distinctions and, if you would be so good, return to the point. And the point is this: you have still not told us—and we have asked—why in the first place you divided the money, squandering one half and hiding the other. What exactly was your purpose in hiding it? What did you intend to do with that fifteen hundred? I insist on that question, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

“Yes, of course!” Mitya cried, striking his forehead. “Forgive me, I’m tiring you out and not explaining the main thing, otherwise you’d understand at once, because it’s the motive itself that’s the disgrace! You see, it all had to do with the old man, my dead father. He was forever after Agrafena Alexandrovna, and I was jealous. In those days I thought she was wavering between him and me. So every day I kept thinking: what if she suddenly makes up her mind, what if she stops tormenting me and says, ‘I love you, not him. Take me to the other end of the world.’ And all I had was forty kopecks. How could I take her away, what could I do? I’d be done for. You see, I didn’t know her then, I didn’t understand her. I thought she wanted money, and that she wouldn’t forgive me for being poor. So, devil that I was, I counted out half of that three thousand and sewed it up, counting on it, sewed it up while I was still sober. And once it was sewn up, I went off to get drunk on the rest. Yes, that was base. Do you understand now?”
Both lawyers burst out laughing.
“I would have called it sensible and moral of you not to squander everything,” Nikolay Parfenovitch chuckled. “After all, what does it come to?”

“It comes to this, that I stole it! Oh, God, it horrifies me that you don’t understand! Every day I had that fifteen hundred sewn up round my neck, every day and every hour I told myself, ‘You’re a thief! You’re a thief!’ That’s why I’ve been so savage all this month. That’s why I fought in the tavern, that’s why I attacked my father: because I felt I was a thief. I couldn’t make up my mind. I didn’t dare even to tell Alyosha, my own brother, about that fifteen hundred. I felt like such a scoundrel and such a pickpocket. But you know, while I carried it I also told myself every hour, ‘No, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, you might still turn out not to be a thief.’ Why? Because next day I could go and pay that fifteen hundred back to Katya. And only yesterday I made up my mind to rip the amulet off my neck, on my way from Fenya’s to Perhotin’s. Until then I hadn’t been able to bring myself to do it. And the moment I tore it off, I became a downright thief, a thief and a dishonest man for the rest of my life. Why? Because with that I destroyed my dream, too, of going to Katya and saying, ‘I’m a scoundrel, but not a thief!’ Do you understand now? Do you understand?”
“What made you decide to do it yesterday?” Nikolay Parfenovitch broke in.

“Why? What a ridiculous question. Because I’d sentenced myself to die at five o’clock this morning, here, at dawn. I thought it made no difference whether I died a thief or an honorable man. But I see it isn’t so. It turns out it does make a difference. Believe me, gentlemen, what tortured me most this night wasn’t the thought that I’d killed the old servant, or that Siberia was hanging over me just when my love was being rewarded and Heaven was open to me again. Oh, that tortured me, but not like this. Not as much as the cursed knowledge that I’d finally torn that cursed money off my chest and spent it, and become a downright thief! Oh, gentlemen, I tell you again, with a bleeding heart, I’ve learned a great deal this night. I’ve learned that you can’t live as a scoundrel, and you can’t die as one either.... No, gentlemen, a man must die honest....”
Mitya was pale. For all his fierce excitement, his face looked haggard and worn out.

“I am beginning to understand you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor said slowly, in a soft and almost sympathetic tone. “But all of this, if you’ll forgive my saying so, is in my opinion a matter of nerves ... overwrought nerves, that is what it is. Why, for example, did you not spare yourself nearly a month of such misery by going and returning that fifteen hundred to the lady who had entrusted it to you? And why could you not have explained matters to her? Given your position, which you describe as so dreadful, why did you not turn to the remedy that would occur so naturally to anyone? After honestly confessing your mistakes to her, why did you not ask her to lend you the money you needed? With her generous heart she would surely not have refused you in your distress, particularly if you had offered some guarantee, or even the same security you offered the merchant Samsonov and Madame Hohlakov. I suppose you still consider that security to be worth something?”
Mitya suddenly went crimson.
“Surely you don’t take me for such an out-and-out scoundrel as that? You can’t be serious!” he said indignantly. He stared the prosecutor straight in the face, as if he couldn’t believe his ears.
“I assure you I am serious.... Why would you think I’m not?” Now it was the prosecutor’s turn to be surprised.

“Oh, how low that would have been! Gentlemen, do you know, you’re torturing me! All right, I’ll tell you everything. I’ll confess all my infernal wickedness, but only to put you to shame. You’ll be amazed yourselves at the depths of disgrace a jumble of human passions can sink to. You should know that I had that plan myself, the one you just mentioned, prosecutor! Yes, gentlemen, that thought has been in my head all this month too. I was on the point of deciding to go to Katya—I was mean enough for that. But to go to her, to tell her about my treachery, and for that very treachery, to carry it out, to pay for that treachery, to beg money from her, from Katya (to beg, do you hear, to beg), and go straight from her to run away with the other woman, her rival, who hated her and insulted her—to think of it! You must be mad, prosecutor!”

“I’m not mad, but I spoke in haste, without thinking ... about that feminine jealousy ... if there could be any jealousy in this case, as you claim ... yes, perhaps there is something of the kind,” said the prosecutor, smiling.

“But that would have been so infamous!” Mitya brought his fist down fiercely on the table. “It would have been filthier than anything! Do you know, she might have given me that money? Yes, she would have given it; she’d certainly have given it, out of revenge, to satisfy her vengeance, to show me her contempt. She has an infernal nature too, and she’s a woman of great wrath. I’d have taken it, oh yes, I’d have taken the money; I’d have taken it, and then for the rest of my life ... oh, God! Forgive me, gentlemen, I’m shouting like this because the thought has been in my mind so recently, only the day before yesterday, that night when I was having all that trouble with Lyagavy, and then all day yesterday, I remember, right up until that happened ...”
“Until what happened?” put in Nikolay Parfenovitch curiously, but Mitya did not hear.

“I’ve made you a terrible confession,” Mitya concluded gloomily. “You must appreciate it, and what’s more, you must respect it. If you don’t, if it leaves your souls untouched, then you simply have no respect for me, gentlemen, I tell you that. I’ll die of shame at having confessed it to men like you! Oh, I’ll shoot myself! Yes, I see, I can see already that you don’t believe me. What, you want to write that down too?” he cried in dismay.

“Yes, what you just said,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, looking at him in surprise. “That is, that right up to the last hour you were still thinking of going to Katerina Ivanovna to beg that sum from her.... I assure you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, that is a very important piece of evidence for us, for the whole case, I mean ... and especially for you, especially important for you.”

“Have mercy, gentlemen!” Mitya threw up his hands. “At least don’t write that down; have some shame. I’ve torn my heart in two in front of you, and you seize the chance to poke at the wounds in both halves.... Oh, my God!”
In despair he buried his face in his hands.

“Don’t upset yourself so, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor said. “Everything we write down will be read back to you afterwards, and whatever you don’t agree with we’ll change as you wish. But now I’ll ask you one small question for the second time. Did no one, absolutely no one, ever hear from you about that money you sewed up? I must tell you, that is almost impossible to believe.”
“No one, no one! I told you so already, or else you haven’t understood a thing! Leave me alone!”

“Very well. This matter is bound to be cleared up, and there’s plenty of time for that. But meanwhile, consider this. We have perhaps a dozen witnesses that you spread it around yourself, even shouted it almost everywhere, that you’d spent three thousand here. Three thousand, not fifteen hundred. And just now too, when you got hold of the money you had yesterday, you let many people understand that you’d brought three thousand with you.”
“You don’t have dozens of witnesses, you have hundreds! Two hundred witnesses, two hundred people heard it, thousands heard it!” cried Mitya.
“Well, you see, they all bear witness to it. And that word _all_ means something.”
“It means nothing. I talked rot, and everyone started repeating it.”
“But why did you need to ‘talk rot,’ as you put it?”

“The devil knows. Out of bravado, perhaps ... at having wasted so much money.... Or to try to forget the money I’d sewn up, perhaps ... yes, that was why ... damn it ... how many times are you going to ask me that? Well, I told a fib, and that was that. Once I’d said it, I couldn’t be bothered to take it back. Why does a man tell lies sometimes?”

“That’s very hard to say, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, why a man tells lies,” the prosecutor observed impressively. “Tell me, though, was that ‘amulet’ you wore around your neck, as you call it, a big thing?”
“No, not big.”
“How big, for instance?”
“Fold a hundred-rouble note in half, and that’s about the size.”
“You’d better show us what’s left of it. You must have it somewhere.”
“Damnation, what nonsense! I don’t know where it is.”
“But excuse me, where and when did you take it off your neck? By your own account you never went home.”
“I tore it off my neck on the way from Fenya’s to Perhotin’s, and took out the money.”
“In the dark?”
“What would I want a light for? I did it with my fingers in a minute.”
“Without scissors, in the street?”
“In the market-place, I think it was. Why scissors? It was an old rag. It tore in a minute.”
“And where did you put it afterwards?”
“I dropped it there.”
“Where, exactly?”
“In the market-place, in the market-place! The devil knows where. What do you want to know for?”
