“It’s extremely important, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. It would be material evidence in your favor. How is it you can’t see that? Who helped you sew it up a month ago?”
“No one helped me. I did it myself.”
“Can you sew?”
“A soldier has to know how to sew. It took no skill at all.”
“And where did you get the material, that is, the rag you sewed the money into?”
“Are you laughing at me?”
“Not at all. And we’re in no mood for laughing, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”
“I don’t know where I got the rag from—somewhere, I suppose.”
“I would have thought you couldn’t possibly have forgotten that?”
“Honestly, I don’t remember. I may have torn a piece off my linen.”
“That’s very interesting. Tomorrow we might find, at your lodgings, the shirt or whatever it is that you tore the rag from. What sort of rag was it, cloth or linen?”
“Goodness only knows what it was. Wait a bit.... I don’t think I tore it off anything. It was a bit of calico.... I think I sewed it up in a cap of my landlady’s.”
“In your landlady’s cap?”
“Yes. I took it from her.”
“How did you come by it?”

“Well, I remember once picking up a cap to use as a rag, maybe to wipe my pen on. I took it without asking, since it was a worthless rag. I tore it up, then took the notes and sewed them into it. I think it was in that very rag that I sewed them. An old piece of calico, washed a thousand times.”
“And you remember that for certain now?”
“I don’t know about for certain. I think it was the cap. But, hang it, what does it matter?”
“In that case your landlady will remember that her cap went missing?”
“No, she won’t. She never missed it. It was an old rag, I tell you, an old rag not worth a farthing.”
“And where did you get the needle and thread?”
“That’s it, I’m stopping. I won’t say another word. Enough of this!” said Mitya, losing his temper at last.
“It’s odd that you should have forgotten so completely where you threw the pieces in the market-place.”

“Have the market-place swept tomorrow, and perhaps you’ll find it,” Mitya sneered. “Enough, gentlemen, enough!” he decided in an exhausted voice. “I see you don’t believe me! Not for a moment! The fault is mine, not yours. I shouldn’t have been so quick to talk. Why, why did I lower myself by confessing my secret to you? It’s a joke to you. I can see it in your eyes. You led me into it, prosecutor! Go on, sing your hymn of triumph if you can.... Damn you, you torturers!”

He bowed his head and hid his face in his hands. The lawyers said nothing. A minute later he looked up at them with an almost vacant stare. His face now showed complete, hopeless despair. He sat mute and passive, hardly aware of what was going on. Meanwhile the others had to finish their business. They had to begin examining the witnesses at once. It was already eight o’clock in the morning. The lamps had been put out long before. Mihail Makarovitch and Kalganov, who had been in and out of the room all through the interrogation, had both left again. The lawyers too looked very tired. It was a wretched morning. The whole sky was overcast, and the rain came down in buckets. Mitya gazed blankly out of the window.
“Can I look out of the window?” he suddenly asked Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“Oh, look as much as you like,” the latter replied.

Mitya got up and went to the window.... The rain lashed at its little greenish panes. Just below the house he could see the muddy road, and farther off, through rain and mist, a row of poor, black, dismal huts that looked even blacker and poorer in the wet. Mitya thought of “Phœbus the golden-haired,” and how he had meant to shoot himself at his first ray. “Maybe it would be even better on a morning like this,” he thought with a smile. Then he suddenly swung his arm down and turned to his “torturers.”

“Gentlemen,” he cried, “I see I’m lost! But what about her? Tell me about her, I beg you. Surely she doesn’t have to be ruined along with me? She’s innocent, you know. She was out of her mind when she cried last night, ‘It’s all my fault!’ She’s done nothing, nothing! I’ve been grieving over her all night, sitting here with you.... Can’t you tell me, won’t you tell me, what you’re going to do with her now?”

“On that score you can set your mind completely at rest, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor answered at once, with obvious eagerness. “So far we have no grounds for troubling the lady you take such an interest in. I trust it will stay that way as the case develops.... On the contrary, we’ll do everything in our power on that point. Set your mind entirely at rest.”
“Gentlemen, thank you. I knew you were honest, straightforward men, in spite of everything. You’ve lifted a weight from my heart.... Well, what do we do now? I’m ready.”
“Well, we ought to hurry. We have to go on to the witnesses without delay. That must be done in your presence, and therefore—”
“Shouldn’t we have some tea first?” Nikolay Parfenovitch put in. “I think we’ve earned it!”

They agreed that if tea was ready downstairs (Mihail Makarovitch had no doubt gone down to fetch some), they would have a glass and then “go on and on,” leaving their proper breakfast for a better time. Tea really was ready below, and was soon brought up. At first Mitya turned down the glass that Nikolay Parfenovitch politely offered him, but then he asked for it himself and drank it greedily. He looked astonishingly worn out. With his Herculean strength, you might have thought that one night of carousing, even with the most violent emotions thrown in, would have done him little harm. But he felt he could hardly hold his head up, and from time to time everything around him seemed to heave and dance before his eyes. “A little more and I’ll start raving,” he said to himself.

chapters.title: VIII. The Evidence Of The Witnesses. The Babe
paragraphs: Now the questioning of the witnesses began. But we will not tell it in as much detail as we did before. We will skip how Nikolay Parfenovitch urged each witness to speak truthfully and according to his conscience, and told him he would later have to repeat his statement under oath. We will skip how each witness had to sign the protocol of what he had said, and the rest of the formalities. We will only say that the questioning kept returning to one point above all: the three thousand roubles. Had Mitya spent three thousand here at Mokroe the first time, a month earlier, or only fifteen hundred? And had he spent three thousand yesterday, or fifteen hundred? Alas, every witness’s testimony went against Mitya. Not one spoke for him, and some even offered new facts, almost crushing ones, that flatly contradicted Mitya’s own account.

Trifon Borissovitch was the first witness. He was not the least bit abashed in front of the lawyers. If anything, he looked sternly and severely indignant at the accused, and this made him seem honest and dignified. He said little and kept himself in reserve. He waited to be asked, and then answered precisely and without hurrying. He stated firmly and without any hesitation that the sum spent a month ago could not have been less than three thousand. All the peasants round here, he said, would swear they had heard Dmitri Fyodorovitch himself speak of three thousand. “And what a lot of money he threw away on the gypsy girls alone! A thousand went on them alone, I’d say.”
“I don’t think I gave them even five hundred,” Mitya muttered gloomily. “Pity I didn’t count the money at the time, but I was drunk....”
Mitya sat sideways, with his back to the curtains. He listened with a dark, tired, wretched look, as if to say:
“Oh, say whatever you like. It doesn’t matter now.”

“More than a thousand went on them, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” said Trifon Borissovitch firmly. “You scattered it around any old how, and they scooped it up. A thieving, rascally bunch they were, horse-stealers. They’ve been chased out of here, or maybe they’d tell you themselves how much they got from you. I saw that money in your hands with my own eyes—count it I didn’t, you wouldn’t let me, that’s true—but going by the look of it, I’d say it was far more than fifteen hundred ... fifteen hundred, ha! We’ve seen money too. We know how to judge a sum....”
About the money spent yesterday, he said that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had told him the moment he arrived that he had brought three thousand with him.
“Come now, Trifon Borissovitch, is that really so?” Mitya answered. “I can’t have said so definitely that I’d brought three thousand?”

“You said it, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You said it with Andrey there. Andrey’s still here himself. Send for him. And out in the hall, when you were treating the chorus, you shouted for everyone to hear that you’d leave your sixth thousand here—meaning, we have to understand, together with what you spent before. Stepan and Semyon heard it, and Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov was standing next to you then, too. Maybe he’ll remember it....”

This evidence about the “sixth” thousand made an extraordinary impression on both lawyers. They were delighted with the new way of counting. Three thousand and three thousand made six. Three then and three now, six in all. It was plain.

They questioned all the peasants Trifon Borissovitch had named: Stepan and Semyon, the driver Andrey, and Kalganov. The peasants and the driver backed up Trifon Borissovitch’s story without a moment’s doubt. They wrote down with special care Andrey’s report of what Mitya had said to him on the road: “‘Where am I going,’ he says, ‘Dmitri Fyodorovitch, to heaven or to hell? And shall I be forgiven in the next world or not?’”
Ippolit Kirillovitch, the psychologist, listened with a subtle smile. He finished by recommending that these remarks about where Dmitri Fyodorovitch was going be “included in the case.”

When Kalganov was called, he came in unwillingly, scowling and in a foul mood. He talked to the lawyers as if he had never set eyes on them, though they were acquaintances he had met every day for a long time. He began by saying that “he knew nothing about it and didn’t want to.” But it turned out he had heard of the “sixth” thousand, and he admitted he had been standing close by when it was said. As far as he could tell, he “didn’t know” how much money Mitya had in his hands. He stated that the Poles had cheated at cards. Pressed again and again, he said that once the Poles had been thrown out, Mitya’s standing with Agrafena Alexandrovna had certainly got better, and that she had said she loved him. He spoke of Agrafena Alexandrovna with reserve and respect, as if she were a lady of the best society, and not once did he let himself call her Grushenka. The young man plainly loathed giving evidence, yet Ippolit Kirillovitch questioned him at great length, and it was from him alone that he learned every detail of Mitya’s “romance,” so to speak, that night. Mitya never once interrupted Kalganov. At last they let the young man go, and he walked out of the room in undisguised indignation.

The Poles were questioned as well. They had gone to bed in their room, but they had lain awake all night. When the police officers arrived, they dressed hurriedly and were ready, knowing they would surely be sent for. They gave their testimony with dignity, though not without some nervousness. The little Pole turned out to be a retired official of the twelfth class who had served in Siberia as a veterinary surgeon. His name was Mussyalovitch. Pan Vrublevsky turned out to be a dentist without a certificate. Nikolay Parfenovitch put the questions to them as they came in, but both addressed their answers to Mihail Makarovitch, who stood off to one side. In their ignorance they took him for the most important man there, the one in command, and at every word they called him “Pan Colonel.” Only after Mihail Makarovitch himself corrected them several times did they understand that their answers were to go to Nikolay Parfenovitch alone. It turned out that they spoke perfectly correct Russian, except for an accent on certain words. When Pan Mussyalovitch spoke of his relations with Grushenka, past and present, he did it proudly and warmly. Mitya flared up on the spot and declared that he would not let that “scoundrel” talk like that in his presence! Pan Mussyalovitch at once pointed out the word “scoundrel” and asked that it be entered in the protocol. Mitya was boiling with rage.
“He’s a scoundrel! A scoundrel! Put that down. And put down, too, that whatever the protocol says, I still call him a scoundrel!” he shouted.

Nikolay Parfenovitch did enter this in the protocol, but he showed the most commendable tact and skill. He sternly reprimanded Mitya, then cut short every further question about the romantic side of the case and hurried on to what mattered. One part of the Poles’ evidence stirred the lawyers’ special interest. In that very room Mitya had tried to buy off Pan Mussyalovitch. He had offered him three thousand roubles to give up his claims: seven hundred roubles at once, and the other two thousand three hundred “to be paid next day in the town.” At the time he had sworn he did not have the whole sum with him at Mokroe, but that his money was in the town. Mitya said hotly that he had not said he would surely pay the rest next day in the town. But Pan Vrublevsky confirmed it. Mitya thought a moment, then admitted with a frown that it must have been as the Poles said, that he had been worked up at the time and might well have said it.

The prosecutor seized on this piece of evidence. It seemed to establish for the prosecution (and in fact they did draw this conclusion from it) that half of the three thousand that had come into Mitya’s hands, or at least part of it, might truly have been left hidden somewhere in the town, or even somewhere here in Mokroe. That would explain what had puzzled the prosecution so much: why only eight hundred roubles were found on Mitya. Small as it was, this fact had been the one piece of evidence that had so far counted somewhat in Mitya’s favor. Now it had fallen apart. The prosecutor asked where he would have found the remaining two thousand three hundred roubles, given that he himself denied having more than fifteen hundred. Mitya answered confidently that he had meant to offer the “little chap” no money at all, but a formal deed transferring his rights to the village of Tchermashnya, the same rights he had already offered to Samsonov and Madame Hohlakov. The prosecutor actually smiled at “the innocence of this dodge.”
“And you imagine he would have taken such a deed in place of two thousand three hundred roubles cash?”

“He would certainly have taken it,” Mitya said warmly. “Why, look, he could have grabbed not two thousand but four or six for it. He’d have set his lawyers on the job, Poles and Jews, and he might have got not three thousand but the whole estate out of the old man.”

Pan Mussyalovitch’s evidence was, of course, entered in the protocol in the fullest detail. Then the Poles were let go. The business of the cheating at cards was barely touched. Nikolay Parfenovitch was far too pleased with them already, and he did not want to trouble them over trifles. Besides, it was only a stupid, drunken quarrel over cards. There had been plenty of drinking and disorder that night.... So the two hundred roubles stayed in the Poles’ pockets.

Next old Maximov was called in. He came in timidly, with little steps, looking very rumpled and low in spirits. All this while he had been sheltering downstairs with Grushenka, sitting dumbly beside her. “Now and then he’d start blubbering over her and wiping his eyes with a blue check handkerchief,” as Mihail Makarovitch told it afterwards. So in the end she had been trying to soothe and comfort him herself. The old man admitted at once that he had done wrong. He had borrowed “ten roubles in my poverty” from Dmitri Fyodorovitch, he said, and he was ready to pay it back. Nikolay Parfenovitch asked him point-blank whether he had noticed how much money Dmitri Fyodorovitch had in his hand, since he must have seen the amount better than anyone when he took the note from him. Maximov declared in the most positive manner that there was twenty thousand.
“Have you ever seen as much as twenty thousand before, then?” Nikolay Parfenovitch asked with a smile.

“Of course I have. Not twenty, but seven, when my wife mortgaged my little property. She’d only let me look at it from a distance, and she boasted about it to me. It was a very thick bundle, all rainbow-colored notes. And Dmitri Fyodorovitch’s were all rainbow-colored....”

They did not keep him long. At last Grushenka’s turn came. Nikolay Parfenovitch was plainly nervous about what her appearance might do to Mitya, and he muttered a few words of caution to him. But Mitya only bowed his head in silence, letting him understand “that he would not make a scene.” Mihail Makarovitch himself brought Grushenka in. She came in with a stern, gloomy face that looked almost calm, and sat quietly in the chair Nikolay Parfenovitch offered her. She was very pale and seemed to be cold, and she drew her magnificent black shawl tightly around her. She had a slight feverish chill—the first sign of the long illness that followed that night. Her serious air, her direct, earnest look and her quiet manner made a very favorable impression on everyone. Nikolay Parfenovitch was even a little “fascinated.” Talking about it afterwards, he admitted that only then had he seen “how handsome the woman was.” He had seen her several times before, but he had always thought of her as something of a “provincial hetaira.” “She has the manners of the best society,” he said with enthusiasm, gossiping about her in a circle of ladies. But the ladies took this with real indignation and promptly called him a “naughty man,” to his great delight.

Coming into the room, Grushenka gave Mitya just one quick glance. He looked back at her anxiously, but her face calmed him at once. After the usual first questions and cautions, Nikolay Parfenovitch asked her, a little hesitantly but with perfect courtesy, how she stood with the retired lieutenant Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov. Grushenka answered firmly and quietly:

“He was an acquaintance. He visited me as an acquaintance this past month.” To further prying questions she gave plain, completely frank answers. She said that “at times” she had found him attractive, but that she had never loved him. She had won his heart, and his old father’s as well, “out of my own nasty spite.” She had noticed that Mitya was terribly jealous of Fyodor Pavlovitch and of everyone else, but that had only amused her. She had never meant to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch; she had only been laughing at him. “I had no thoughts for either of them this whole month. I was waiting for another man, one who had wronged me. But I think,” she finished, “you needn’t ask about that, and I needn’t answer, because it’s my own business.”

Nikolay Parfenovitch took the hint immediately. Once more he put the “romantic” side of the case aside and turned to the serious matter, the one that counted most, the three thousand roubles. Grushenka agreed that three thousand roubles had certainly been spent at the first carousal at Mokroe. She had not counted the money herself, but she had heard it was three thousand from Dmitri Fyodorovitch’s own mouth.
“Did he tell you so only when you were alone, or in front of somebody else? Or did you merely hear him say it to other people while you were present?” the prosecutor put in at once.
Grushenka answered that she had heard him say it in front of other people, and had also heard him say it when they were alone.
“Did he tell you so just once when you were alone, or several times?” asked the prosecutor, and found out that he had told Grushenka so several times.
Ippolit Kirillovitch was very pleased with this evidence. More questions brought out that Grushenka also knew where the money had come from: Dmitri Fyodorovitch had got it from Katerina Ivanovna.
“And have you never once heard that the money spent a month ago was not three thousand but less, and that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had set half of that sum aside for himself?”
“No, I never heard that,” Grushenka replied.
It was made clear, further, that Mitya had often told her the opposite: that he hadn’t a penny.
“He was always hoping to get some from his father,” Grushenka added at the end.
“Did he ever say in your hearing ... in passing, or in a fit of temper,” Nikolay Parfenovitch broke in suddenly, “that he meant to make an attempt on his father’s life?”
“Ach, yes, he said that,” Grushenka sighed.
“Once, or more than once?”
“More than once. Always when he was angry.”
“And did you believe he would do it?”
“No, I never believed it,” she said firmly. “I trusted his noble heart.”
“Gentlemen, permit me,” Mitya cried suddenly, “permit me to say a single word to Agrafena Alexandrovna, with you here.”
“Go ahead and speak,” Nikolay Parfenovitch allowed.
“Agrafena Alexandrovna!” Mitya rose from his chair. “Believe in God and believe in me. I am not guilty of my father’s murder!”

After saying this, Mitya sat back down. Grushenka stood up and crossed herself devoutly before the icon. “Thank You, O Lord,” she said, her voice trembling with feeling. Still standing, she turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and added:

“Believe him, now that he’s said it like that! I know him. He’ll say anything for a joke or out of stubbornness, but he’ll never lie to you against his conscience. He’s telling you the whole truth. You can believe it.”
“Thank you, Agrafena Alexandrovna. You’ve given me new courage,” Mitya answered in a shaking voice.

About the money spent the day before, she said she did not know how much it was, but she had heard him tell several people he had three thousand on him. Asked where he got the money, she said he had told her he “stole” it from Katerina Ivanovna. She had told him in reply that he hadn’t stolen it, and that he must pay it back the next day. The prosecutor pressed her hard: was the money he said he had stolen from Katerina Ivanovna what he spent yesterday, or what he squandered here a month ago? She declared that he meant the money spent a month ago, and that this was how she had understood him.

At last Grushenka was free to go. On a sudden impulse, Nikolay Parfenovitch told her she could go back to town at once, and that if he could help her in any way, with horses for instance, or if she wanted an escort, he ... would be—

“I thank you sincerely,” said Grushenka with a bow. “I’m going with this old gentleman. I’m taking him back to town with me. In the meantime, if you’ll let me, I’ll wait downstairs to hear what you decide about Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

She left. Mitya was calm and even looked more cheerful, but only for a moment. A strange bodily weakness was weighing on him more and more. His eyes were closing from exhaustion. The questioning of the witnesses was at last over. They began the final review of the protocol. Mitya stood up, went from his chair to the corner by the curtain, lay down on a big chest covered with a rug, and fell fast asleep at once.
He had a strange dream, one that had nothing to do with the place or the hour.

He was riding somewhere in the steppes where he had once been stationed, and a peasant was driving him in a cart with a pair of horses, through snow and sleet. He was cold. It was early November, and the snow came down in big wet flakes that melted the moment they hit the ground. The peasant drove him at a smart pace. He had a long fair beard. He was not old, perhaps fifty, and wore a gray peasant smock. A village lay not far ahead. He could see the black huts, and half of them had burned down, with only charred beams left standing. As they drove in, peasant women were lined up along the road, a great many of them, a whole row, all thin and wan, their faces a kind of brownish color. The one at the end was the worst, a tall, bony woman who looked forty but could have been only twenty, with a long, thin face. In her arms a small baby was crying. Her breasts looked so dried up that there could not be a drop of milk in them. The child cried and cried and stretched out its little bare arms, with fists blue from the cold.
“Why are they crying? Why are they crying?” Mitya asked as they dashed cheerfully past.
“It’s the babe,” the driver answered. “The babe is weeping.”
Mitya was struck by the way he said “the babe,” in his peasant fashion, and he liked that the peasant called it a “babe.” It seemed to hold more pity.
“But why is it weeping?” Mitya kept asking stupidly. “Why are its little arms bare? Why don’t they wrap it up?”
“The babe is cold. Its little clothes are frozen through and give no warmth.”
“But why? Why is it so?” foolish Mitya went on.
“Well, they’re poor folk, burnt out. They’ve no bread. They’re begging because they were burnt out.”

“No, no,” said Mitya, still seeming not to understand. “Tell me why those poor mothers are standing there. Why are people poor? Why is the babe poor? Why is the steppe bare? Why don’t they hug and kiss each other? Why don’t they sing joyful songs? Why are they so dark from black misery? Why don’t they feed the babe?”

He knew that his questions made no sense and were foolish, and yet he wanted to ask exactly these, and he had to ask them exactly this way. He felt a passion of pity rising in his heart, such as he had never known. He wanted to weep. He wanted to do something for all of them, so that the babe would cry no more, so that the dark-faced, dried-up mother would cry no more, so that from that moment no one would shed another tear. And he wanted to do it at once, right now, whatever stood in his way, with all the recklessness of the Karamazovs.

“And I’ll go with you. I won’t leave you ever again, not for the rest of my life. I’m coming with you,” he heard Grushenka’s tender voice beside him, trembling with feeling. And his heart glowed, and he pushed forward toward the light, and he longed to live, to live, to go on and on toward the new, beckoning light, and to hurry, hurry, now, at once!

“What! Where?” he exclaimed, opening his eyes and sitting up on the chest, smiling brightly, as if he had come to after a faint. Nikolay Parfenovitch was standing over him, proposing that he hear the protocol read aloud and sign it. Mitya figured he had slept an hour or more, but he did not hear a word Nikolay Parfenovitch said. All at once he was struck by a pillow under his head. It had not been there when he lay back, worn out, on the chest.
“Who put that pillow under my head? Who was so kind?” he cried, in a kind of rapturous gratitude, with tears in his voice, as though someone had done him a great kindness.

He never learned who the kind person was. Maybe one of the peasant witnesses, or Nikolay Parfenovitch’s little secretary, had felt sorry for him and thought to slip a pillow under his head. But his whole soul trembled with tears. He walked to the table and said he would sign whatever they wanted.
“I’ve had a good dream, gentlemen,” he said in a strange voice, with a new light in his face, as of joy.

chapters.title: IX. They Carry Mitya Away
paragraphs: When the protocol had been signed, Nikolay Parfenovitch turned solemnly to the prisoner and read him the “Committal.” It set out that in such a year, on such a day, in such a place, the investigating lawyer of such-and-such a district court had examined so-and-so (namely, Mitya), accused of this and of that (all the charges were carefully written out). It noted that the accused did not plead guilty to the charges against him and had offered nothing in his defense, while the witnesses, so-and-so and so-and-so, and the circumstances, such-and-such, spoke against him. Acting under such-and-such articles of the Statute Book, and so on, the lawyer had ruled that, to prevent so-and-so (Mitya) from any means of evading pursuit and judgment, he be held in such-and-such a prison. He hereby notified the accused of this and sent a copy of the same “Committal” to the deputy prosecutor, and so on, and so on.

In short, Mitya was told that from that moment he was a prisoner, that he would be driven into town at once, and that he would be shut up there in a very unpleasant place. Mitya listened closely and only shrugged his shoulders.
“All right, gentlemen, I don’t hold it against you. I’m ready.... I see you have no other choice.”
Nikolay Parfenovitch told him gently that the rural police officer, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, who happened to be on the spot, would escort him at once....
“Stay,” Mitya broke in suddenly. A feeling he could not hold back swept him along, and he spoke to everyone in the room:

“Gentlemen, we’re all cruel, we’re all monsters, we all make men weep, and mothers, and babes at the breast. But let it be settled here, now: of all of us, I am the lowest reptile! I swore to reform, and every day I’ve gone on doing the same filthy things. I understand now that men like me need a blow, a blow of destiny to catch them like a noose and bind them by a force from outside. Never, never would I have risen by myself! But the thunderbolt has fallen. I accept the torture of the accusation and my public shame. I want to suffer, and by suffering I will be purified. Perhaps I will be purified, gentlemen? But listen, for the last time: I am not guilty of my father’s blood. I accept my punishment, not because I killed him, but because I meant to kill him, and perhaps I really might have killed him. Still, I mean to fight it out with you. I warn you of that. I’ll fight it out with you to the end, and then God will decide. Good-by, gentlemen. Don’t be angry with me for shouting at you during the examination. Oh, I was such a fool then.... In another minute I’ll be a prisoner, but now, for the last time, as a free man, Dmitri Karamazov offers you his hand. In saying good-by to you, I say it to all men.”

His voice shook and he held out his hand. But Nikolay Parfenovitch, who happened to be standing nearest to him, made a sudden, almost nervous movement and hid his hands behind his back. Mitya noticed it instantly and started. He let his outstretched hand drop at once.

“The preliminary inquiry isn’t over yet,” Nikolay Parfenovitch faltered, rather embarrassed. “We’ll continue it in town, and I, for my part, of course, am ready to wish you every success ... in your defense.... The fact is, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, I’ve always been inclined to see you, so to speak, as more unfortunate than guilty. All of us here, if I may be so bold as to speak for all, are ready to acknowledge that you are, at bottom, a young man of honor, but, alas, one who has been carried away by certain passions a little too far....”

By the time he had finished, Nikolay Parfenovitch’s little figure looked positively majestic. Mitya had the thought that in another minute this “boy” would take him by the arm, lead him off to another corner and start up their talk about “girls” again. But all sorts of irrelevant, out-of-place thoughts will come into a man’s head, even a prisoner’s, as he is being led out to execution.
“Gentlemen, you’re kind, you’re humane. Could I see _her_ and say ‘good-by’ one last time?” asked Mitya.
“Of course, but given that ... the truth is, now it can’t be done except in the presence of—”
“Oh, well, if it must be so, it must!”
Grushenka was brought in, but the farewell was brief, said in few words, and did not satisfy Nikolay Parfenovitch at all. Grushenka bowed low to Mitya.
“I told you I am yours, and I will be yours. I will follow you forever, wherever they send you. Farewell. You are innocent, though you’ve been your own ruin.”
Her lips quivered, and tears flowed from her eyes.
“Forgive me, Grusha, for my love, for ruining you, too, with my love.”

Mitya would have said more, but he broke off and went out. Men who kept constant watch on him at once surrounded him. At the foot of the steps, where he had driven up so dashingly the day before with Andrey’s three horses, two carts stood ready. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, a sturdy, thick-set man with a wrinkled face, was annoyed about something, some sudden mix-up. He was shouting angrily. He told Mitya to get into the cart, with rather excessive surliness.

“The man had a very different face when I was standing him drinks at the tavern,” thought Mitya as he climbed in. A crowd had gathered at the gates: peasants, women, drivers. Trifon Borissovitch came down the steps as well. Everyone stared at Mitya.
“Forgive me at parting, good people!” Mitya suddenly shouted from the cart.
“Forgive us too!” he heard two or three voices say.
“Good-by to you, too, Trifon Borissovitch!”

But Trifon Borissovitch did not even turn around. Perhaps he was too busy. He, too, was shouting and fussing about something. It turned out that the second cart, in which two constables were to go along with Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, was not yet ready. The peasant who had been ordered to drive it was pulling on his smock, stubbornly insisting that it was not his turn to go but Akim’s. But Akim was nowhere to be seen. They ran to look for him. The peasant dug in his heels and begged them to wait.

“See what our peasants are like, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch? No shame at all!” exclaimed Trifon Borissovitch. “Akim paid you twenty-five copecks the day before yesterday. You drank it all, and now you start yelling. I’m simply astonished at how good-natured you are, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, with our low peasants. That’s all I can say.”
“But why do we need a second cart?” Mitya put in. “Let’s just set off in this one, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch. I won’t make trouble, I won’t run away from you, old fellow. What’s the escort for?”

“I’ll trouble you, sir, to learn how to speak to me, if nobody’s ever taught you. I’m not ‘old fellow’ to you, and you can keep your advice for another time!” Mavriky Mavrikyevitch snapped savagely, as though glad to vent his anger.

Mitya fell silent. He flushed all over. A moment later he suddenly felt very cold. The rain had stopped, but the dull sky was still covered with clouds, and a keen wind was blowing straight in his face.
“I’ve caught a chill,” thought Mitya, twitching his shoulders.

At last Mavriky Mavrikyevitch got into the cart too, sat down heavily, and, as though without noticing, squeezed Mitya into the corner. True, he was in a foul mood and greatly disliked the job that had been given him.
“Good-by, Trifon Borissovitch!” Mitya shouted again, and he felt himself that this time he had not called out from good nature, but involuntarily, from resentment.
But Trifon Borissovitch only stood there with an air of pride, both hands clasped behind him. He stared straight at Mitya, his face stern and angry, and gave no answer.
“Good-by, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, good-by!” Suddenly he heard Kalganov’s voice. Kalganov had dashed out and run up to the cart, and he held out his hand to Mitya. He had no cap on.
Mitya had time to seize and press his hand.
“Good-by, dear fellow! I won’t forget your generosity,” he cried warmly.
Then the cart lurched forward and their hands came apart. A bell began to ring, and Mitya was driven away.

Kalganov ran back, sat down in a corner, bent his head, hid his face in his hands and burst out crying. He sat like that for a long while, crying like a little boy instead of a young man of twenty. Oh, he believed almost without a doubt in Mitya’s guilt.
“What kind of people are these? What can men be after this?” he cried out incoherently, in bitter despondency, close to despair. At that moment he did not want to live.
“Is it worth it? Is it worth it?” cried the boy in his grief.
PART IV

chapters.title: I. Kolya Krassotkin
paragraphs: It was early November. A hard frost had set in, eleven degrees Réaumur, but there was no snow. A little dry snow had fallen on the frozen ground during the night, though, and a sharp, dry wind was picking it up and driving it along the dreary streets of our town, especially around the market-place. The morning was dull, but the snow had stopped.

Not far from the market-place, close to Plotnikov’s shop, there was a small house, very clean inside and out. It belonged to Madame Krassotkin, widow of a former provincial secretary, who had died fourteen years earlier. She was still a nice-looking woman of thirty-two, and she lived in her neat little house on her private means. Her life was one of respectable seclusion, and her nature was soft but fairly cheerful. She had been about eighteen when her husband died. They had been married only a year, and she had just borne him a son. Since the day he died she had given herself heart and soul to raising her precious treasure, her boy Kolya. For those fourteen years she had loved him passionately, yet he had brought her far more pain than happiness. Nearly every day she shook and almost fainted with fear that he would fall ill, catch cold, do something naughty, or climb on a chair and fall off it, and so on and so on. Once Kolya started school, his mother took up all the sciences herself so as to study them with him and help him with his lessons. She made a point of getting to know the teachers and their wives. She even made up to Kolya’s schoolfellows and fawned on them, hoping that this would keep Kolya from being teased, laughed at or beaten. She carried it so far that the boys began to mock him because of her, taunting him as a “mother’s darling.”

But the boy could stand up for himself. He was a resolute boy, “tremendously strong,” as the rumor went in his class, and he soon showed that it was true. He was agile, strong-willed, bold and enterprising. He did well at lessons, and word went around the school that he could beat the teacher, Dardanelov, at arithmetic and universal history. He looked down on everybody, yet he was a good comrade and never lofty about it. He took his schoolfellows’ respect as only his due, but he stayed friendly with them. Above all, he knew where to draw the line. When he had to, he could hold himself back, and with the teachers he never crossed that last mystic boundary beyond which a prank turns into an unpardonable breach of discipline. Still, on every possible occasion he loved mischief as much as the smallest boy in the school. It was less the mischief itself he wanted than the sensation: to think up something effective, something that people would notice. He was extremely vain. He even knew how to make his mother give way to him, and he ruled her almost like a despot. She gave way—oh, she had been giving way for years. The one thought she could not endure was that her boy did not love her much. She was forever fancying that Kolya was “unfeeling” toward her. At times she would dissolve in hysterical tears and reproach him with his coldness. The boy disliked this, and the more he was asked to show feeling, the more he seemed to dodge it on purpose. But it was not on purpose; it was instinct. It was simply his character. His mother was wrong: he was very fond of her. He just disliked “sheepish sentimentality,” as he called it in his schoolboy language.

The house had a bookcase holding a few books that had been his father’s. Kolya liked reading, and he had read several of them on his own. His mother did not mind. Sometimes she merely wondered at the sight of the boy standing for hours at the bookcase, absorbed in a book, instead of running off to play. That was how Kolya came to read some things not suitable for his age.

As a rule the boy knew where to draw the line in his mischief. Lately, though, he had begun to play pranks that gave his mother real alarm. There was nothing vicious in them, it is true, but they showed a wild, mad recklessness.

That July, during the summer holidays, mother and son traveled to another district, forty-five miles away, to spend a week with a distant relation. The relation’s husband was an official at the railway station (the very station, nearest to our town, from which a month later Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov left for Moscow). Kolya began by studying every detail of the railways with great care, since he knew he could impress his schoolfellows with his new knowledge when he got home. But other boys happened to be about, and he soon made friends with them. Some lived at the station and others in the neighborhood. There were six or seven of them, all between twelve and fifteen, and two came from our town. The boys played together, and on the fourth or fifth day of Kolya’s stay, the foolish lads made a mad bet. Kolya was nearly the youngest of them, and the others rather looked down on him for it. Out of vanity, or reckless bravado, he bet them two roubles that he would lie down between the rails at night, when the eleven o’clock train was due, and stay there without moving while it rolled over him at full speed. They did look into it first, it is true, and found that a person could lie so flat between the rails that a train would pass right over without touching him. But actually lying there was no joke! Kolya stoutly insisted that he would do it. They laughed at him at first and called him a little liar and a braggart, but that only egged him on. What stung him most was that these fifteen-year-olds turned up their noses at him so haughtily. At first they had been inclined to treat him as “a small boy,” unfit to keep their company, and that was an insult he could not bear.

So they decided to go that evening, half a mile from the station, so that the train would have time to reach full speed after leaving it. The boys gathered. The night was pitch-dark, without a moon. At the agreed time Kolya lay down between the rails. The other five, who had taken the bet, waited in the bushes below the embankment. Their hearts pounded with suspense, which gave way to alarm and remorse. At last they heard the train rumbling in the distance as it left the station. Two red lights gleamed out of the darkness, and the monster roared as it came on.

“Run, run away from the rails,” the boys cried to Kolya from the bushes, breathless with terror. But it was too late. The train rushed up and flew past. The boys ran to Kolya. He lay there without moving. They started tugging at him and lifting him up. Suddenly he got to his feet and walked off without a word. Later he explained that he had lain there as if unconscious in order to scare them. The truth, as he admitted to his mother long afterward, was that he had really lost consciousness. So his reputation as “a desperate character” was fixed forever. He went back to the station as white as a sheet. The next day he had a slight attack of nervous fever, but he was in high spirits and very pleased with himself. The incident did not come out at once. When they returned to town, however, it reached the school and even the ears of the masters. Then Kolya’s mother hurried to beg the masters to be lenient with her boy, and in the end Dardanelov, a respected and influential teacher, put in a word for him, and the matter was let drop.

Dardanelov was a middle-aged bachelor who had been passionately in love with Madame Krassotkin for many years. Some time before, about a year earlier, he had once ventured, trembling with fear and delicacy of feeling, to offer her his hand most respectfully. She had flatly refused him, feeling that accepting would betray her son. Yet certain mysterious signs gave Dardanelov reason to believe that the charming but all too chaste and tender-hearted widow did not find him repulsive. Kolya’s mad prank seemed to have broken the ice. Dardanelov was rewarded for pleading for the boy with a hint of hope. The hint was a faint one, it is true, but Dardanelov was such a paragon of purity and delicacy that for the time being it was enough to make him perfectly happy. He was fond of the boy, though he thought it beneath him to try to win him over, and in class he was severe and strict with him. Kolya, for his part, kept him at a respectful distance. He knew his lessons perfectly, ranked second in his class, and was reserved with Dardanelov. The whole class firmly believed that Kolya was so good at universal history that he could “beat” even Dardanelov. Indeed, Kolya had once asked him, “Who founded Troy?” Dardanelov gave a very vague reply, speaking of the movements and migrations of peoples, of how remote the period was, of the mythical legends. But who had founded Troy, meaning which individuals, he could not say, and for some reason he even considered the question idle and frivolous. The boys, however, stayed convinced that Dardanelov did not know who founded Troy. Kolya had read about the founders of Troy in Smaragdov, whose history was among the books in his father’s bookcase. In the end all the boys grew curious about who had founded Troy, but Krassotkin would not give up his secret, and his reputation for learning stood unshaken.

After the railway incident, Kolya’s manner toward his mother changed somewhat. When Anna Fyodorovna (Madame Krassotkin) heard of her son’s exploit, she nearly went out of her mind with horror. Her hysterics were so terrible, and went on with only short breaks for several days, that Kolya was seriously alarmed at last and gave his word of honor that such pranks would never happen again. At Madame Krassotkin’s insistence he swore it on his knees before the holy image, and swore it by his father’s memory. The “manly” Kolya burst into tears like a boy of six. All that day mother and son kept rushing into each other’s arms, sobbing. The next day Kolya woke up as “unfeeling” as ever, but he had grown quieter, more modest, sterner and more thoughtful.

Six weeks later he did get into another scrape, it is true, one that even brought his name to the attention of our Justice of the Peace. But it was a scrape of an entirely different kind, amusing and foolish, and as it turned out he was not the leader in it, only caught up in it. More of that later. His mother still fretted and trembled, and the more uneasy she grew, the higher Dardanelov’s hopes rose. It should be noted that Kolya understood and guessed what was in Dardanelov’s heart, and of course he despised him profoundly for his “feelings.” Before, he had been tactless enough to show this contempt in front of his mother, hinting vaguely that he knew what Dardanelov was after. After the railway incident, though, his behavior in this respect changed too. He allowed himself not the slightest allusion to the subject, and in front of his mother he began to speak of Dardanelov with more respect. The sensitive woman noticed it at once and was boundlessly grateful. But if a visitor merely mentioned Dardanelov in Kolya’s presence, she would blush as pink as a rose. At such moments Kolya would either stare out of the window with a scowl, or look over the state of his boots, or shout angrily for “Perezvon.” Perezvon was the big, shaggy, mangy dog he had picked up a month earlier and brought home. For some reason he kept it hidden indoors and showed it to none of his schoolfellows. He bullied the dog dreadfully and taught it all sorts of tricks. The poor creature howled for him whenever he was away at school, and when he came in it whined with delight, raced about as if it had gone crazy, begged, and lay on the ground playing dead, and so on. In fact it performed every trick it had been taught, not because it was ordered to, but from the sheer zeal of its excited, grateful heart.

I forgot, by the way, to mention that Kolya Krassotkin was the boy who had been stabbed with a penknife by the one the reader already knows as Captain Snegiryov’s son. Ilusha had been defending his father when the schoolboys jeered at him and shouted the nickname “wisp of tow.”

chapters.title: II. Children
paragraphs: So on that frosty, snowy, windy Sunday in November, Kolya Krassotkin sat at home. There was no school. It had just struck eleven, and he badly wanted to go out “on very urgent business.” But he had been left alone in charge of the house, since every one of the grown-ups was away because of a sudden and unusual event. Madame Krassotkin rented two small rooms, cut off from the rest of the house by a passage, to a doctor’s wife and her two small children. This lady was the same age as Anna Fyodorovna and a great friend of hers. Her husband, the doctor, had gone away twelve months before, first to Orenburg and then to Tashkend, and for the past six months she had heard nothing from him. Without her friendship with Madame Krassotkin, which was some comfort to the abandoned wife, she would surely have dissolved completely in tears. And now, on top of her troubles, her only servant, Katerina, had announced the evening before, to her mistress’s amazement, that she planned to have a baby before morning. It seemed almost miraculous to everyone that nobody had seen this coming. The astounded doctor’s wife decided to move Katerina, while there was still time, to a house in town kept by a midwife for just such emergencies. She thought a great deal of her servant, so she did this at once and stayed there to look after her. By morning, Madame Krassotkin’s friendly sympathy and energy were all needed, to help out and to find someone to turn to in the matter.

So both ladies were out of the house, the Krassotkins’ servant, Agafya, had gone to the market, and Kolya had been left for a while to guard and look after “the kids,” the doctor’s wife’s son and daughter, who were alone there. Kolya wasn’t afraid to mind the house. Besides, he had Perezvon, who had been told to lie flat under the bench in the hall and not move. Each time Kolya, pacing through the rooms, came into the hall, the dog shook his head and thumped the floor twice with his tail, loudly and with a hint. But alas! The whistle that would let him go never came. Kolya gave the luckless dog a stern look, and the dog sank back into obedient stiffness. The one thing that troubled Kolya was “the kids.” He regarded Katerina’s unexpected adventure, of course, with the utmost scorn, but he was very fond of the bereaved “kiddies,” and he had already brought them a picture-book. Nastya, the elder, was eight and could read, and Kostya, the boy, was seven and loved being read to by her. Krassotkin could, of course, have found more entertaining things to do with them. He could have made them stand side by side and played soldiers, or sent them hiding all over the house. He had done it more than once, and he wasn’t above doing it. In fact, a story once went around school that Krassotkin played horses with the little lodgers at home, prancing with his head to one side like a trace-horse. But Krassotkin haughtily parried the jab. To play horses with boys his own age, boys of thirteen, he said, would certainly be disgraceful “at this date.” But he did it for “the kids,” because he liked them, and nobody had a right to call him to account for his feelings. The two “kids” adored him.

This time, though, he was in no mood for games. He had very important business of his own ahead, something almost mysterious. Meanwhile time was passing, and Agafya, the one he could have left the children with, still hadn’t come back from the market. Several times already he had crossed the passage, opened the door of the lodgers’ room and looked in anxiously at “the kids,” who were sitting over the book, as he had told them to. Every time he opened the door they grinned at him, hoping he would come in and do something delightful and amusing. But Kolya was worried, and he didn’t go in.

Finally it struck eleven, and he decided, once and for all, that if that “damned” Agafya wasn’t back in ten minutes, he would go out without her. Of course he would first make “the kids” promise to be brave while he was gone, not to be naughty, and not to cry from fright. With that in mind he put on his wadded winter overcoat with the catskin collar and slung his satchel over his shoulder. His mother was always begging him to wear galoshes in such cold weather. He ignored her pleas; he gave the galoshes a scornful glance as he crossed the hall and went out in his boots alone. Perezvon, seeing him in his outdoor clothes, started drumming nervously but hard on the floor with his tail. He twitched all over and even let out a plaintive whine. But Kolya, seeing the dog’s passionate excitement, decided that this was a breach of discipline. He kept him under the bench for one more minute, and only after opening the door into the passage did he whistle for him. The dog sprang up like a madman and rushed bounding ahead of him, wild with joy.

Kolya opened the door to peep in at “the kids.” They were both sitting at the table as before, not reading now but arguing warmly about something. The children often argued together about the exciting problems of life, and Nastya, being older, always won. If Kostya didn’t agree with her, he nearly always appealed to Kolya Krassotkin, and both of them took his verdict as final. This time the “kids’” debate interested Krassotkin rather a lot, and he stopped in the passage to listen. The children saw that he was listening, and that made them argue with even more energy.

“I’ll never, never believe,” Nastya prattled, “that old women find babies in the cabbage patch. It’s winter now and there aren’t any cabbages, so the old woman couldn’t have brought Katerina a daughter.”
Kolya whistled softly to himself.
“Or maybe they do bring babies from somewhere, but only to people who are married.”
Kostya stared at Nastya and listened, thinking it over very deeply.
“Oh, Nastya, you’re so silly!” he said at last, firmly and calmly. “How can Katerina have a baby if she isn’t married?”
Nastya was exasperated.
“You know nothing about it,” she snapped irritably. “Maybe she has a husband, only he’s in prison, and so now she’s got a baby.”
“But is her husband in prison?” asked the matter-of-fact Kostya, gravely.

“Or, I’ll tell you what,” Nastya broke in impulsively, completely throwing out and forgetting her first guess. “She hasn’t got a husband, you’re right about that, but she wants to be married, and so she’s been thinking about getting married, and thinking and thinking about it, till now she’s got it, that is, not a husband but a baby.”
“Well, maybe,” Kostya agreed, totally beaten. “But you didn’t say that before. How was I supposed to know?”
“Come on, kiddies,” said Kolya, stepping into the room. “You’re terrible people, I can see.”
“And Perezvon’s with you!” Kostya grinned, and he started snapping his fingers and calling Perezvon.
“I’ve got a problem, kids,” Krassotkin began solemnly, “and you have to help me. Agafya must have broken her leg, since she still hasn’t turned up. That’s certain. I have to go out. Will you let me?”
The children looked anxiously at each other. Their smiling faces grew uneasy, but they didn’t yet quite understand what was wanted of them.
“You won’t be naughty while I’m gone? You won’t climb on the cupboard and break your legs? You won’t get scared by yourselves and cry?”
A look of deep gloom came over the children’s faces.
“And I could show you something as a reward, a little copper cannon that you can fire with real gunpowder.”
The children’s faces lit up at once. “Show us the cannon,” said Kostya, beaming all over.
Krassotkin reached into his satchel, took out a little bronze cannon and stood it on the table.
“Ah, I knew you’d ask! Look, it’s on wheels.” He rolled the toy along the table. “And you can fire it, too. You load it with shot and fire it off.”
“And it could kill somebody?”

“It could kill anybody; you just have to aim at him,” and Krassotkin showed them where the powder went in and where the shot was rolled in. He pointed out a tiny hole like a touch-hole, and told them it kicked back when fired.
The children listened with great interest. What fired their imagination most was that the cannon kicked.
“And have you got powder?” Nastya asked.
“I have.”
“Show us the powder, too,” she drawled, smiling to coax him.

Krassotkin dived into his satchel again and brought out a small flask with a little real gunpowder in it. He had some shot, too, in a twist of paper. He even uncorked the flask and shook a little powder into the palm of his hand.
“You have to make sure there’s no fire anywhere near, or it will blow up and kill us all,” Krassotkin warned them, making the most of it.
The children stared at the powder with an awestruck fear that only added to their enjoyment. But Kostya liked the shot better.
“Does shot burn?” he asked.
“No, it doesn’t.”
“Give me a bit of shot,” he begged, in a pleading voice.
“I’ll give you a bit of shot; here, take it. But don’t show it to your mother till I’m back, or she’ll be sure to think it’s gunpowder, and she’ll die of fright and give you a thrashing.”
“Mother never whips us,” Nastya said right away.
“I know, I only said that to round off the sentence. And never deceive your mother, except this one time, till I get back. So, kiddies, can I go out? You won’t be frightened and cry when I’m gone?”
“We sha—all cry,” Kostya drawled, already close to tears.
“We’ll cry, we’re sure to cry,” Nastya chimed in, hurriedly and timidly.
“Oh, children, children, how full of peril your years are! It can’t be helped, chickens, I’ll have to stay with you, goodness knows how long. And time is passing, time is passing, oogh!”
“Tell Perezvon to play dead!” Kostya begged.
“It can’t be helped, we’ll have to turn to Perezvon. _Ici_, Perezvon.” And Kolya started giving the dog orders, and the dog went through all his tricks.

He was a rough-haired dog, of middle size, with a coat of a sort of lilac-gray color. He was blind in his right eye, and his left ear was torn. He whined and jumped, stood and walked on his hind legs, and lay on his back with his paws in the air, stiff as if he were dead. In the middle of this last trick the door opened, and in the doorway appeared Agafya, Madame Krassotkin’s servant, a stout woman of forty with a pockmarked face. She was back from the market with a bag full of groceries in her hand. She held the bag up in her left hand and stood there watching the dog. Kolya had been so impatient for her return, but he didn’t cut the show short. He kept Perezvon dead for the usual time, and only then did he whistle to him. The dog leapt up and began bounding about, happy to have done his duty.
“Fancy that, a dog!” Agafya remarked, in her pompous way.
“Why are you late, female?” Krassotkin asked sternly.
“Female, indeed! Go on with you, you brat.”
“Brat?”

“Yes, a brat. What business is it of yours if I’m late? If I’m late, you can be sure I had good reason,” muttered Agafya, bustling around the stove, without a trace of anger or annoyance in her voice. She seemed quite pleased, in fact, to have a bit of a squabble with her cheerful young master.

“Listen, you frivolous young person,” Krassotkin began, getting up from the sofa, “can you swear by everything you hold sacred in the world, and something more besides, that you’ll keep a careful eye on the kids while I’m out? I’m going out.”
“And what would I swear for?” Agafya laughed. “I’ll look after them without that.”
“No, you have to swear on your eternal salvation. Or else I’m not going.”
“Well, don’t, then. What do I care? It’s cold out; stay home.”

“Kids,” Kolya said, turning to the children, “this woman will stay with you till I’m back or till your mother comes, since she should have been home long ago. She’ll give you lunch, too. You’ll give them something, Agafya, won’t you?”
“That much I can do.”

“Goodbye, chickens, I’m leaving with an easy mind. And you, granny,” he added gravely, in an undertone, as he passed Agafya, “I hope you’ll have pity on their tender years and not fill their heads with any of your old wives’ nonsense about Katerina. _Ici_, Perezvon!”
“Get out with you!” retorted Agafya, really angry this time. “What a ridiculous boy! You need a whipping for saying such things, that’s what you need!”

chapters.title: III. The Schoolboy
paragraphs: But Kolya did not hear her. At last he was free to go. Out at the gate he glanced around, hunched his shoulders, and said, “It’s freezing.” Then he walked straight down the street and turned right toward the market square. He stopped at the gate of the last house but one before the square, took a whistle from his pocket, and blew it with all his strength, as if giving a signal. He waited barely a minute. Then a rosy-cheeked boy of about eleven came darting out to meet him, in a warm, neat, even stylish coat. This was Smurov, a boy in the preparatory class (two classes below Kolya Krassotkin) and the son of a well-to-do official. His parents seemed to have forbidden him to keep company with Krassotkin, who was known to be a hopelessly naughty boy. So Smurov had plainly slipped out on the sly. He was—if the reader has not forgotten—one of the group of boys who had thrown stones at Ilusha two months before. He was the one who had told Alyosha Karamazov about Ilusha.
“I’ve been waiting for you for a whole hour, Krassotkin,” said Smurov flatly, and the two boys set off toward the market square.
“I’m late,” answered Krassotkin. “Circumstances held me up. You won’t be thrashed for coming with me, will you?”
“Oh, come on, I’m never thrashed! Have you brought Perezvon?”
“Yes.”
“You’re taking him along too?”
“Yes.”
“Ah, if only it were Zhutchka!”
“Impossible. Zhutchka doesn’t exist. Zhutchka has vanished into the mists of obscurity.”

“Ah, couldn’t we try something?” Smurov suddenly stopped. “Ilusha says Zhutchka was a shaggy, grayish, smoky-looking dog, just like Perezvon. Couldn’t you tell him this is Zhutchka? He might believe you.”
“Boy, steer clear of lies. That’s one thing. And even a lie told for a good purpose is another matter. Above all, I hope you haven’t told them I’m coming.”

“Heaven forbid! I know what I’m about. But Perezvon won’t comfort him,” said Smurov with a sigh. “You know his father, the captain, ‘the wisp of tow,’ told us he’d bring Ilusha a real mastiff pup today, with a black nose. He thinks that will cheer Ilusha up. I doubt it.”
“And how is Ilusha?”

“Ah, he’s bad, very bad! I think it’s consumption. He’s fully conscious, but his breathing! It’s gone all wrong. The other day he asked for his boots so someone could walk him around the room. He tried to walk and couldn’t even stand. ‘Ah, father,’ he said, ‘I told you before those boots were no good. I could never walk properly in them.’ He thought the boots were making him stagger, but it was only weakness, really. He won’t last another week. Herzenstube is treating him. And now they’re rich again—they’ve got heaps of money.”
“They’re rogues.”
“Who is?”

“Doctors. The whole gang of quacks, collectively and, of course, one by one. I don’t believe in medicine. It’s a useless institution. I intend to look into all of it. But what’s this sentimental business you’ve got going up there? The whole class seems to go every day.”
“Not the whole class. Only ten of us go and see him every day. That’s nothing special.”

“What I can’t make out in all this is the part Alexey Karamazov is playing. His brother is to be tried tomorrow or the day after for such a crime, and he still finds so much time for sentimentality with schoolboys.”
“It isn’t sentimentality. You’re on your way there yourself to make it up with Ilusha.”
“Make it up with him? What a ridiculous way to put it! And I don’t permit anyone to analyze my actions.”
“And Ilusha will be so happy to see you! He has no idea you’re coming. Why wouldn’t you come all this time, why?” Smurov cried with sudden warmth.

“My dear boy, that’s my business and not yours. I’m going of my own free will, because I choose to. The rest of you were all dragged there by Alexey Karamazov—there’s a difference, you know. And how do you know what I’m up to? Maybe I’m not going to make it up at all. It’s a stupid phrase.”

“It isn’t Karamazov at all. It’s not his doing. Our fellows started going there on their own. Of course, at first they went with Karamazov. But there was never any of that sort of thing—no silliness. One went, then another. His father was awfully glad to see us. You know, he’ll simply lose his mind if Ilusha dies. He can see Ilusha is dying. And he seems so glad we’ve made peace with Ilusha. Ilusha asked about you, that’s all. He only asks, and says nothing more. His father will go mad or hang himself. He acted like a madman before. You know, he’s a thoroughly decent man. We made a mistake back then. The whole fault lies with that murderer who beat him.”
“Karamazov is still a riddle to me. I could have got to know him long ago, but in some cases I like to keep a proper pride. Besides, I have a theory about him, and I have to work it out and test it.”

Kolya sank into a dignified silence. Smurov was silent too. Smurov, of course, worshiped Krassotkin and never dreamed of setting himself level with him. Now he was tremendously curious about Kolya’s saying he was “going of himself” to see Ilusha. He sensed there was some mystery behind Kolya’s suddenly deciding to visit him that day. They crossed the market square. At that hour it was full of loaded wagons from the country and a great number of live fowls. The market women sat in their booths selling rolls, cottons, threads and the like. These Sunday markets were naïvely called “fairs” in the town, and there were many such fairs in the year.

Perezvon ran about in the wildest spirits, sniffing first to one side, then to the other. Whenever he met other dogs, they went over each other eagerly with their noses, following the rules of canine etiquette.
“I like to watch such realistic scenes, Smurov,” Kolya said suddenly. “Have you noticed how dogs sniff each other when they meet? It seems to be a law of their nature.”
“Yes. It’s a funny habit.”

“No, it isn’t funny. You’re mistaken. There’s nothing funny in nature, however funny it may look to man with all his prejudices. If dogs could reason and criticize us, they’d certainly find just as much to laugh at in the social relations of men, their masters—more, in fact. Yes, I repeat it, because I’m convinced there’s far more foolishness among us than among them. That’s Rakitin’s idea, and a remarkable one. I’m a Socialist, Smurov.”
“And what’s a Socialist?” asked Smurov.

“It’s when everyone is equal and everyone owns everything together, there’s no marriage, and everyone has whatever religion and laws he likes best, and so on. You’re too young to understand that yet. It’s cold, though.”
“Yes, twelve degrees of frost. Father just looked at the thermometer.”

“Have you noticed, Smurov, that in the depth of winter, with fifteen or eighteen degrees of frost, we don’t feel as cold as we do now, at the start of winter, when a sudden frost of twelve degrees hits us, especially with so little snow? That’s because people aren’t used to it. With men, everything is habit—everything, even their social and political relations. Habit is the great driving force. What a funny-looking peasant!”

Kolya pointed to a tall, good-natured-looking peasant in a long sheepskin coat. He was standing by his wagon, clapping his hands together in their shapeless leather gloves to warm them. His long fair beard was white all over with frost.
“That peasant’s beard is frozen!” Kolya cried in a loud, provoking voice as he went by.
“Plenty of beards are frozen,” the peasant answered calmly and gravely.
“Don’t provoke him,” said Smurov.
“It’s all right. He won’t get angry. He’s a good fellow. Good-by, Matvey.”
“Good-by.”
“Is your name Matvey?”
“Yes. Didn’t you know?”
“No. It was a guess.”
“Well, I never! You’re a schoolboy, I take it?”
“Yes.”
“They whip you, I expect?”
“Nothing much—now and then.”
“Does it hurt?”
“Well, yes, it does.”
“Ech, what a life!” The peasant sighed from the bottom of his heart.
“Good-by, Matvey.”
“Good-by. You’re a fine lad, that you are.”
The boys walked on.
“Now there’s a good peasant,” Kolya said to Smurov. “I like talking to the peasants, and I’m always glad to do them justice.”
“Why did you lie and pretend we get thrashed?” asked Smurov.
“I had to, to please him.”
“How do you mean?”

“You know, Smurov, I don’t like being asked the same thing twice. I like people to catch on at the first word. Some things can’t be explained. In a peasant’s view, schoolboys get whipped, and have to be whipped. What kind of schoolboy wouldn’t be? And if I told him we aren’t, he’d be let down. But you don’t understand that. You have to know how to talk to the peasants.”
“Just don’t tease them, please, or you’ll land in trouble again, like with that goose.”
“So you’re scared?”
“Don’t laugh, Kolya. Of course I’m scared. My father would be furious. I’m strictly forbidden to go out with you.”
“Don’t worry, nothing will happen this time. Hello, Natasha!” he shouted to a woman in one of the market booths.
“Natasha, indeed! What next! My name is Marya,” the middle-aged woman shouted back at him.
“I’m so glad it’s Marya. Good-by!”
“Oh, you young rascal! A brat like you, carrying on like that!”
“I’m in a hurry, I can’t stay now. You can tell me next Sunday.” Kolya waved at her as if she had attacked him instead of the other way around.
“I’ve got nothing to tell you next Sunday. You started in on me, you cheeky young monkey. I never said a word,” bawled Marya. “What you want is a whipping, that’s what, you saucy jackanapes!”

The other market women around her roared with laughter. Suddenly a man darted out from the arcade of shops nearby, in a furious rage. He was young and not from the town, with dark curly hair and a long, pale, pockmarked face. He wore a long blue coat and a peaked cap and looked like a merchant’s clerk. He was stupidly worked up, and he shook his fist at Kolya.
“I know you!” he cried angrily. “I know you!”
Kolya stared at him. He couldn’t recall when he might have had a row with this man. But he’d been in so many street rows that he could hardly remember them all.
“Do you?” he asked sarcastically.
“I know you! I know you!” the man repeated idiotically.
“All the better for you. Well, I must be going. Good-by!”
“Up to your saucy tricks again?” cried the man. “Up to your saucy tricks again? I know it, you’re at it again!”
“It’s no business of yours, brother, whether I’m up to my tricks again,” said Kolya. He stopped and looked him up and down.
“No business of mine?”
“No. No business of yours.”
“Whose, then? Whose, then? Whose, then?”
“It’s Trifon Nikititch’s business, not yours.”
“What Trifon Nikititch?” asked the young man, gaping at Kolya with boorish amazement, but just as angry as before.
Kolya studied him gravely.
“Have you been to the Church of the Ascension?” he suddenly asked, with stern emphasis.
“What Church of the Ascension? What for? No, I haven’t,” said the young man, a little thrown.
“Do you know Sabaneyev?” Kolya went on, still more emphatically and still more sternly.
“What Sabaneyev? No, I don’t know him.”

“Then you can go to the devil,” said Kolya, ending the conversation. He turned sharply right and strode off, as if he would not lower himself to talk any longer with a dolt who didn’t even know Sabaneyev.
“Hold on, hey! What Sabaneyev?” The young man shook off his moment of stupefaction and was as worked up as before. “What did he say?” He turned to the market women with a foolish stare.
The women laughed.
“You never know what he’s getting at,” said one of them.
“What Sabaneyev is he talking about?” the young man repeated, still furious, swinging his right arm.
“Must be the Sabaneyev who worked for the Kuzmitchovs, that’s who it must be,” one of the women suggested.
The young man gave her a wild look.
“For the Kuzmitchovs?” another woman echoed. “But his name wasn’t Trifon. It’s Kuzma, not Trifon. And the boy said Trifon Nikititch, so it can’t be the same man.”

“It’s not Trifon and it’s not Sabaneyev, it’s Tchizhov,” a third woman put in suddenly. She had said nothing till then, and had been listening gravely. “Alexey Ivanitch is his name. Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch.”
“No doubt about it, it’s Tchizhov,” a fourth woman agreed firmly.
The bewildered young man looked from one to the other.
“But what was he asking, what was he asking, good people?” he cried, almost in despair. “‘Do you know Sabaneyev?’ he says. And who the devil would know who Sabaneyev is?”
“You’re a fool. I tell you it’s not Sabaneyev, it’s Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch Tchizhov, that’s who!” one of the women shouted at him, very earnestly.
“Which Tchizhov? Who is he? Tell me, if you know.”
“The tall one with the runny nose, who used to sit in the market in summer.”
“And what’s your Tchizhov to me, good people, eh?”

“How should I know what he is to you?” put in another. “You ought to know yourself what you want with him, if you’re making such a noise about him. He spoke to you, not to us, you fool. Don’t you really know him?”
“Know who?”
“Tchizhov.”
“The devil take Tchizhov, and you along with him. I’ll give him a hiding, that I will. He was laughing at me!”
“Give Tchizhov a hiding! More likely he’ll give you one. You’re a fool, that’s what you are!”
“Not Tchizhov, not Tchizhov, you spiteful, mischief-making woman. I’ll give that boy a hiding. Catch him, catch him, he was laughing at me!”

The woman guffawed. But Kolya was by now far away, marching on with a look of triumph. Smurov walked beside him, glancing back at the shouting group in the distance. He was in high spirits too, though he was still afraid of getting into some scrape in Kolya’s company.
“Which Sabaneyev did you mean?” he asked Kolya, already guessing the answer.

“How should I know? Now there’ll be an uproar among them all day. I like to stir up fools in every class of society. Look, there’s another blockhead, that peasant over there. You know the saying, ‘there’s no one stupider than a stupid Frenchman,’ but a stupid Russian shows it in his face just the same. Can’t you see it written all over his face that he’s a fool, that peasant, eh?”
“Leave him alone, Kolya. Let’s go.”
“Nothing could stop me now that I’ve started. Hey, good morning, peasant!”
A sturdy peasant with a round, simple face and a grizzled beard was walking past. He raised his head and looked at the boy. He seemed a bit drunk.
“Good morning, if you’re not making fun of me,” he answered slowly.
“And if I am?” laughed Kolya.
“Well, a joke’s a joke. Go on and laugh. I don’t mind. A joke does no harm.”
“Sorry, brother, it was a joke.”
“Well, God forgive you!”
“Do you forgive me, too?”
“I forgive you entirely. Go on your way.”
“I say, you seem like a clever peasant.”
“Cleverer than you,” the peasant answered unexpectedly, with the same gravity.
“I doubt it,” said Kolya, a little taken aback.
“It’s true, though.”
“Maybe it is.”
“It is, brother.”
“Good-by, peasant!”
“Good-by!”
“There are all kinds of peasants,” Kolya remarked to Smurov after a short silence. “How was I to know I’d picked a clever one? I’m always ready to acknowledge intelligence among the peasantry.”

In the distance the cathedral clock struck half-past eleven. The boys quickened their pace. They covered the long distance to Captain Snegiryov’s lodging fast and almost without a word. Twenty paces from the house Kolya stopped and told Smurov to go ahead and ask Karamazov to come out to him.
“First you have to sniff around a bit,” he told Smurov.
“Why ask him to come out?” Smurov objected. “Just go in. They’ll be awfully glad to see you. What’s the sense of making friends out here in the frost?”
“I know why I want to see him out here in the frost,” Kolya cut him short, in the despotic tone he liked to take with “small boys.” And Smurov ran off to do as he was told.

chapters.title: IV. The Lost Dog
paragraphs: Kolya leaned against the fence, trying to look dignified, and waited for Alyosha to appear. Yes, he had wanted to meet him for a long time. The boys had told him a great deal about Alyosha. Until now he had always put on a show of scornful indifference whenever Alyosha was mentioned, and he had even “criticized” what he heard. But secretly he longed to get to know him. Everything he was told about Alyosha was appealing and likable. So this moment mattered. To begin with, he had to show himself at his best and show his independence. “Or he’ll think I’m thirteen and take me for a boy, like the rest of them. And what are these boys to him? I’ll ask him once I know him better. It’s a pity I’m so short, though. Tuzikov is younger than I am, yet he’s half a head taller. But I have a clever face. I’m not good-looking. I know I’m hideous, but I’ve a clever face. I mustn’t talk too freely. If I throw myself into his arms all at once, he may think—Tfoo! How horrible if he should think—!”

These were the thoughts that stirred Kolya up while he did his utmost to look as independent as he could. What distressed him most was being so short. He did not mind his “hideous” face so much as his height. In a corner at home the year before, he had made a pencil mark on the wall to show how tall he was, and every two months since then he had anxiously measured himself against it to see how much he had gained. But alas, he grew very slowly, and this sometimes brought him almost to despair. His face was in fact by no means “hideous.” On the contrary, it was rather attractive, with fair, pale, freckled skin. His small, lively gray eyes had a fearless look and often glowed with feeling. He had rather high cheekbones and small, very red lips that were not very thick. His nose was small and unmistakably turned up. “I’ve a regular pug nose, a regular pug nose,” Kolya would mutter to himself when he looked in the mirror, and he always walked away from it indignant. “But perhaps I haven’t got a clever face?” he sometimes thought, doubting even that. But you must not suppose that his mind was taken up with his face and his height. On the contrary, however bitter the moments in front of the mirror were, he quickly forgot them, and forgot them for a long time, “abandoning himself entirely to ideas and to real life,” as he put it to himself.

Alyosha came out quickly and hurried over to Kolya. Before he reached him, Kolya could see that he looked delighted. “Can he really be so glad to see me?” Kolya wondered, feeling pleased. A word in passing: Alyosha’s appearance had changed completely since we last saw him. He had given up his cassock and now wore a well-cut coat and a soft round hat, and his hair was cropped short. All this suited him very well, and he looked quite handsome. His charming face always had a good-humored expression, but there was a gentleness and calm in his good humor. To Kolya’s surprise, Alyosha came out to him just as he was, without an overcoat. He had obviously come in a hurry. He held out his hand to Kolya at once.
“Here you are at last! We’ve been so eager to see you!”

“There were reasons, which you’ll hear in a moment. Anyway, I’m glad to meet you. I’ve been hoping for a chance for a long time, and I’ve heard a great deal about you,” Kolya muttered, a little breathless.
“We would have met anyway. I’ve heard a lot about you, too, but you’ve been a long time coming here.”
“Tell me, how are things going?”
“Ilusha is very ill. He’s certainly dying.”
“How awful! You have to admit that medicine is a fraud, Karamazov,” cried Kolya hotly.

“Ilusha has talked about you often, very often, even in his sleep, when he’s delirious, you know. You can tell you used to be very, very dear to him ... before the incident ... with the knife.... And there’s another reason.... Tell me, is that your dog?”
“Yes, Perezvon.”
“Not Zhutchka?” Alyosha looked at Kolya with eyes full of pity. “Is she gone for good?”

“I know you’d all like it to be Zhutchka. I’ve heard the whole story.” Kolya smiled mysteriously. “Listen, Karamazov, I’ll tell it to you myself. That’s what I came for. That’s why I asked you to come out here: to explain the whole episode before we go in,” he began with animation. “You see, Karamazov, Ilusha joined the preparatory class last spring.
