Well, you know what our preparatory class is—a crowd of small boys. They started teasing him right away. I’m two classes higher up, so of course I only watched them from a distance. I saw that the boy was small and weak, but he wouldn’t give in to them. He fought back. I saw he was proud, and his eyes were full of fire. I like children like that. And they teased him all the more. The worst of it was that he was dressed horribly then. His breeches were too small, and his boots had holes in them. They hounded him about it and jeered at him. That I can’t stand. I stood up for him at once and gave it to them hot. I beat them up, but they adore me, you know, Karamazov?” Kolya boasted impulsively. “Anyway, I’m always fond of children. I’ve got two chicks to look after at home right now—that’s what held me up today. So they stopped beating Ilusha, and I took him under my wing. I saw he was proud. I tell you, the boy was proud. But in the end he became slavishly devoted to me. He did whatever I asked, obeyed me as if I were God, tried to copy me. Between classes he’d run straight to me, and I’d walk around with him. On Sundays, too. People always laugh when an older boy makes friends with a younger one like that, but that’s a prejudice. If it suits me, that’s enough. I’m teaching him, developing him. Why shouldn’t I develop him if I like him? Look at you, Karamazov, taking up with all these nestlings. I can see you want to influence the younger generation—to develop them, to be useful to them. And I assure you, I’d heard about this trait of yours, and it attracted me more than anything else. But let’s get to the point. I noticed a sort of softness and sentimentality coming over the boy. And you know, I positively hate this sheepish sentimentality. I’ve hated it since I was a baby. There were contradictions in him, too. He was proud, but he was slavishly devoted to me, and yet all at once his eyes would flash and he’d refuse to agree with me. He’d argue and fly into a rage. Sometimes I’d put forward certain ideas, and I could see it wasn’t so much that he disagreed with them. He was simply rebelling against me, because I was cool toward his affection. And so, to train him properly, the tenderer he was, the colder I became. I did it on purpose. That was my idea. My aim was to form his character, to knock him into shape, to make a man of him ... and besides ... no doubt you understand me at a word. Then one day I noticed that for three days running he was downcast and dejected. It wasn’t because of my coldness. It was something else, something more important. I wondered what the tragedy was. I pumped him and found out that he’d somehow got to know Smerdyakov, who was footman to your late father—this was before his death, of course. Smerdyakov had taught the little fool a silly trick—that is, a brutal, nasty trick. He told him to take a piece of bread, stick a pin in it, and throw it to one of those hungry dogs that snap up anything without chewing, and then to watch what would happen. So they prepared a piece of bread like that and threw it to Zhutchka, that shaggy dog there’s been such a fuss about. The people of the house it belonged to never fed it at all, though it barked all day. (Do you like that stupid barking, Karamazov? I can’t stand it.) So it rushed at the bread, swallowed it, and began to squeal. It spun round and round, then ran off, squealing, until it was out of sight. That was Ilusha’s own account. He confessed it to me and cried bitterly. He hugged me, shaking all over. He kept repeating, ‘He ran away squealing.’ The sight haunted him. He was tormented by remorse, I could see that. I took it seriously. I decided to teach him a lesson for other things as well. So I have to admit I wasn’t quite straightforward, and I pretended to be more indignant than I perhaps was. ‘You’ve done a nasty thing,’ I said. ‘You’re a scoundrel. Of course I won’t tell on you, but I’m going to have nothing to do with you for a while. I’ll think it over and let you know through Smurov’—that’s the boy who just came with me, he’s always ready to do anything for me—‘whether I’ll have anything to do with you in the future or give you up for good as a scoundrel.’ He was tremendously upset. I have to own I felt I’d gone too far as I spoke, but there was no help for it. I did what I thought best at the time. A day or two later I sent Smurov to tell him I would not speak to him again. That’s what we call it when two schoolfellows break off all dealings with each other. Secretly I only meant to send him to Coventry for a few days and then, if I saw signs of repentance, to hold out my hand to him again. That was my intention. But what do you think happened? He heard Smurov’s message, and his eyes flashed. ‘Tell Krassotkin from me,’ he cried, ‘that I’ll throw bread with pins to all the dogs—all—all of them!’ ‘So he’s going in for a bit of temper. We’ll have to smoke it out of him.’ And I began to treat him with contempt. Whenever I met him I turned away or smiled sarcastically. And just then that affair with his father happened. You remember? You have to realize he was already fearfully worked up by what had gone before. The boys, seeing I’d given him up, set on him and taunted him, shouting, ‘Wisp of tow, wisp of tow!’ Soon he was having regular skirmishes with them, which I’m very sorry about. They seem to have given him one very bad beating. One day he flew at them all as they came out of school. I stood a few yards off, looking on. And I swear, I don’t remember laughing. It was quite the other way. I felt awfully sorry for him, and in another minute I’d have run over to take his side. But he suddenly met my eyes. I don’t know what he imagined, but he pulled out a penknife, rushed at me, and stabbed at my thigh, here in my right leg. I didn’t move. I don’t mind owning I can be plucky sometimes, Karamazov. I simply looked at him with contempt, as if to say, ‘This is how you repay all my kindness! Do it again, if you like, I’m at your service.’ But he didn’t stab me again. He broke down. He was frightened at what he’d done. He threw away the knife, burst out crying, and ran off. I didn’t sneak on him, of course, and I made them all keep quiet so it wouldn’t reach the masters. I didn’t even tell my mother till it had healed. And the wound was a mere scratch. And then I heard that the same day he’d been throwing stones and had bitten your finger—but you understand now what a state he was in! Well, it can’t be helped. It was stupid of me not to come and forgive him—that is, to make it up with him—when he fell ill. I’m sorry for it now. But I had a special reason. So now I’ve told you everything ... but I’m afraid it was stupid of me.”

“Oh, what a pity,” exclaimed Alyosha with feeling, “that I didn’t know earlier how things stood between you and him! I’d have come to you long ago to beg you to go to him with me. Would you believe it, when he was feverish he talked about you in his delirium. I didn’t know how much you meant to him! And you really haven’t managed to find that dog? His father and the boys have been searching all over town for it. Would you believe it, since he’s been ill I’ve heard him three times say, in tears, ‘It’s because I killed Zhutchka, father, that I’m ill now. God is punishing me for it.’ He can’t get that idea out of his head. And if the dog were found and proved to be alive, you could almost imagine the joy would cure him. We’ve all rested our hopes on you.”
“Tell me, what made you hope I’d be the one to find him?” Kolya asked, with great curiosity. “Why did you count on me and not on someone else?”

“There was a rumor that you were looking for the dog and would bring it once you’d found it. Smurov said something like that. We’ve all been trying to persuade Ilusha that the dog is alive and has been seen. The boys brought him a live hare. He just looked at it with a faint smile and asked them to let it go in the fields. And so we did. His father has just this moment come back, bringing him a mastiff pup, hoping to comfort him with it. But I think that only makes things worse.”
“Tell me, Karamazov, what kind of man is the father? I know him, but what do you make of him—a mountebank, a buffoon?”

“Oh, no. Some people have deep feelings and have somehow been crushed. In them, buffoonery is a form of resentful irony toward the people they don’t dare tell the truth to, because for years those people have humiliated and cowed them. Believe me, Krassotkin, that kind of buffoonery can be tragic in the extreme. His whole life now is centered on Ilusha. If Ilusha dies, he will either go mad with grief or kill himself. I’m almost sure of it when I look at him now.”
“I understand you, Karamazov. I see you understand human nature,” Kolya added warmly.
“And as soon as I saw you with a dog, I thought you were bringing Zhutchka.”

“Wait a bit, Karamazov, maybe we’ll find her yet. But this is Perezvon. I’ll let him go in now, and perhaps he’ll amuse Ilusha more than the mastiff pup. Wait a bit, Karamazov, you’ll see in a minute. But I say, I’m keeping you here!” Kolya cried suddenly. “You’ve no overcoat on in this bitter cold. You see what an egoist I am. Oh, we’re all egoists, Karamazov!”
“Don’t worry. It is cold, but I hardly ever catch cold. Let’s go in, though. And by the way, what’s your name? I know they call you Kolya, but what else?”
“Nikolay—Nikolay Ivanovitch Krassotkin, or, as they put it in official papers, ‘Krassotkin son.’” Kolya laughed for some reason, then added suddenly, “Of course I hate the name Nikolay.”
“Why is that?”
“It’s so trivial, so ordinary.”
“You’re thirteen?” asked Alyosha.

“No, fourteen—that is, I’ll be fourteen very soon, in two weeks. I’ll confess one weakness of mine, Karamazov, just to you, since it’s our first meeting, so you can understand my character right away. I hate being asked my age. More than that ... and in fact ... there’s a libelous story going around about me, that last week I played robbers with the preparatory boys. It’s a fact that I did play with them, but it’s a perfect libel to say I did it for my own amusement. I have reasons to think you’ve heard the story. But I wasn’t playing for my own amusement. It was for the children’s sake, because they couldn’t think of anything to do by themselves. But they always have some silly tale. This is an awful town for gossip, I can tell you.”
“But what if you had been playing for your own amusement? What’s the harm?”
“Come now, for my own amusement! You don’t play horses, do you?”

“But you have to look at it this way,” said Alyosha, smiling. “Grown-up people go to the theater, and there the adventures of all sorts of heroes are acted out—sometimes there are robbers and battles, too. Isn’t that just the same thing, in a different form, of course? And young people’s games of soldiers or robbers at playtime are also art in its first stage. You know, they spring from the growing artistic instincts of the young. And sometimes these games are much better than performances in the theater. The only difference is that people go there to look at the actors, while in these games the young people are the actors themselves. But that’s only natural.”

“You think so? Is that your idea?” Kolya looked at him intently. “Oh, you know, that’s rather an interesting view. When I get home, I’ll think it over. I’ll admit I thought I might learn something from you. I’ve come to learn from you, Karamazov,” Kolya concluded, in a voice full of spontaneous feeling.
“And I from you,” said Alyosha, smiling and pressing his hand.
Kolya was very pleased with Alyosha. What struck him most was that Alyosha treated him exactly as an equal and talked to him just as if he were “quite grown up.”
“I’ll show you something in a moment, Karamazov. It’s a theatrical performance, too,” he said, laughing nervously. “That’s why I’ve come.”
“Let’s go first to the people of the house, on the left. All the boys leave their coats in there, because the room is small and hot.”

“Oh, I’m only coming in for a minute. I’ll keep my overcoat on. Perezvon will stay here in the passage and be dead. _Ici_, Perezvon, lie down and be dead! You see how he’s dead. I’ll go in first and scout around, then I’ll whistle to him when I think the time is right, and you’ll see, he’ll dash in like mad. Only Smurov mustn’t forget to open the door at the right moment. I’ll arrange it all, and you’ll see something.”

chapters.title: V. By Ilusha’s Bedside
paragraphs: The reader already knows the room where retired captain Snegiryov’s family lived. At that moment it was stuffy and packed with visitors. Several boys were sitting with Ilusha. Like Smurov, all of them were ready to deny that Alyosha had brought them and reconciled them with Ilusha, but that was how it happened. His whole trick had been to bring them to Ilusha one by one, without any “sheepish sentimentality,” making it look casual and unplanned. It was a great comfort to Ilusha in his suffering. It touched him deeply to see the almost tender affection and sympathy of these boys, who had been his enemies. Only Krassotkin was missing, and his absence lay heavy on Ilusha’s heart. Of all his bitter memories, perhaps the bitterest was that he had stabbed Krassotkin, his one friend and protector. Clever little Smurov, who had been the first to make up with Ilusha, thought so too. But Smurov had hinted to Krassotkin that Alyosha wanted to come and see him about something, and Krassotkin cut him short. He told Smurov to tell “Karamazov” at once that he knew best what to do and wanted no one’s advice. If he went to see Ilusha, he said, he would pick his own time, because he had “his own reasons.”

That had been two weeks before this Sunday, and that was why Alyosha had not gone to see him, as he had meant to. He waited, though, and twice more he sent Smurov. Both times Krassotkin gave a curt, impatient no. He sent Alyosha word to stop bothering him, and said that if Alyosha came in person, he, Krassotkin, would not go to Ilusha at all. Smurov did not know until the very last day that Kolya meant to visit Ilusha that morning. Only the evening before, as they were parting, Kolya abruptly told him to wait at home next morning, because they would go to the Snegiryovs’ together. He warned him not to breathe a word about it, since he wanted to drop in casually. Smurov obeyed. Smurov’s notion that Kolya would bring back the lost dog came from something Kolya had let slip, that “they must be asses not to find the dog, if it was alive.” Smurov waited for a good moment and timidly hinted at his guess about the dog, and Krassotkin flew into a violent rage. “I’m not such an ass as to go hunting about the town for other people’s dogs when I’ve got a dog of my own! And how can you imagine a dog could be alive after swallowing a pin? Sheepish sentimentality, that’s what it is!”

For the past two weeks Ilusha had not left his little bed under the icons in the corner. He had not gone to school since the day he met Alyosha and bit his finger. He had fallen ill that same day, though for another month he could sometimes get up and walk around the room and the passage. Lately he had grown so weak that he could not move without his father’s help. His father was terribly anxious about him. He had even stopped drinking and was almost crazy with fear that his boy would die. Often, especially after walking Ilusha round the room on his arm and settling him back in bed, he would run off to a dark corner of the passage. There he would lean his head against the wall and burst into violent weeping, choking back his sobs so that Ilusha would not hear.

Back in the room, he would usually set about amusing and comforting his precious boy. He would tell him stories and funny anecdotes, or imitate comical people he had run into, or even howl and cry like animals. But Ilusha could not stand to watch his father clowning and playing the buffoon. The boy tried not to show how much he hated it, but with an aching heart he saw that his father was an object of contempt. The memory of the “wisp of tow” and that “terrible day” haunted him constantly.

Nina, Ilusha’s gentle, crippled sister, did not like her father’s buffoonery either (Varvara had left some time before to study at the university in Petersburg). The half-witted mother, however, was hugely entertained, and laughed heartily whenever her husband started capering about or acting something out. It was the only thing that could amuse her. The rest of the time she grumbled and complained that everyone had forgotten her now, that nobody showed her any respect, that she was slighted, and so on. In the last few days, though, she had changed completely. She kept looking over at Ilusha’s bed in the corner and seemed lost in thought. She had grown quieter and more silent, and when she cried, she cried softly so that no one would hear. The captain watched the change in her with sad bewilderment. At first the boys’ visits only made her angry, but gradually their cheerful shouting and stories began to divert her. In the end she liked them so much that, had the boys stopped coming, she would have felt miserable without them. When the children told a story or played a game, she laughed and clapped her hands. She called some of them over and kissed them. Smurov was her particular favorite.

As for the captain, the sight of the children in his room, come to cheer up Ilusha, filled his heart with rapturous joy from the start. He even hoped that Ilusha would now throw off his low spirits, and that this would speed his recovery. For all his fear for Ilusha, until lately he had not doubted for one minute that his boy would finally get well.

He greeted his little visitors with reverence and waited on them hand and foot. He was ready to be their horse, and even started letting them ride on his back, but Ilusha did not like the game, so it was dropped. He began buying small treats for them, gingerbread and nuts, and gave them tea and cut sandwiches. It should be said that all this time he had plenty of money. He had taken the two hundred roubles from Katerina Ivanovna, exactly as Alyosha had predicted. Afterwards Katerina Ivanovna heard more about their circumstances and about Ilusha’s illness, and came to see them herself. She got to know the family and managed to win over the half-witted mother. Since then she had given them generous help, and the captain, terrified that his boy might be dying, forgot his pride and accepted it humbly.

All this time Doctor Herzenstube, who had been called in by Katerina Ivanovna, came faithfully every other day. Little came of his visits, and he dosed the invalid mercilessly. But that Sunday morning a new doctor was expected, one who had come from Moscow, where he had a great reputation. Katerina Ivanovna had sent for him from Moscow at great expense. It was not especially for Ilusha but for another purpose, which will be explained in its place later. Since he was here, though, she had asked him to see Ilusha as well, and the captain had been told to expect him. He had not the slightest idea that Kolya Krassotkin was coming, although he had long wished for a visit from the boy Ilusha was pining for.

At the moment when Krassotkin opened the door and came in, the captain and all the boys were standing around Ilusha’s bed, looking at a tiny mastiff pup. It had been born only the day before, though the captain had ordered it a week earlier, to comfort and amuse Ilusha, who was still fretting over the lost and probably dead Zhutchka. Three days before, Ilusha had been told he would be given a puppy, and not just any puppy but a pedigree mastiff (a very important point, of course). Out of delicacy, he tried to pretend he was pleased. But his father and the boys could not help seeing that the puppy only reminded his little heart of the poor dog he had killed. The puppy lay beside him, moving feebly, and he stroked it with his thin, pale, wasted hand, smiling sadly. Plainly he liked the puppy, but ... it wasn’t Zhutchka. If he could have had Zhutchka and the puppy together, he would have been perfectly happy.
“Krassotkin!” one of the boys suddenly cried out. He was the first to see him come in.
Krassotkin’s entrance created a general commotion. The boys stepped back and stood on either side of the bed, so that he could see Ilusha fully. The captain ran eagerly to meet Kolya.
“Please come in ... you’re welcome!” he said hurriedly. “Ilusha, Mr. Krassotkin has come to see you!”

But Krassotkin shook hands with him quickly and at once showed how well he knew the manners of good society. First he turned to the captain’s wife, who sat in her armchair in a very bad temper just then, grumbling that the boys were standing between her and Ilusha’s bed and she could not see the new puppy. With the greatest courtesy he bowed to her, scraping his foot. Then he turned to Nina and, since she was the only other lady present, gave her the same bow. This politeness made an extremely good impression on the deranged lady.
“There, you can tell right away he’s a young man who’s been well brought up,” she said aloud, throwing up her hands. “But our other visitors, they come in one on top of another.”
“What do you mean, mamma, one on top of another? What’s that?” the captain muttered affectionately, though a little worried about her.
“That’s how they ride in. They climb on each other’s shoulders in the passage and prance in like that on a respectable family. Strange sort of visitors!”
“But who’s come in like that, mamma?”
“Why, that boy came in riding on that one’s back, and this one on that one’s.”

Kolya was already standing by Ilusha’s bed. The sick boy went visibly paler. He pushed himself up in bed and stared at Kolya. Kolya had not seen his little friend for two months, and the sight of him overwhelmed him. He had never imagined he would find such a wasted, yellow face, such enormous, feverishly bright eyes and such thin little hands. With grief and surprise he noticed Ilusha’s quick, labored breathing and dry lips. He stepped up close, held out his hand and, nearly overcome, said:

“Well, old man ... how are you?” But his voice failed him. He couldn’t put on an easy manner. His face suddenly twitched and the corners of his mouth shook. Ilusha gave a pitiful little smile, still unable to speak. Something made Kolya lift his hand and stroke Ilusha’s hair.
“Never mind!” he murmured softly, to cheer him up, or perhaps without knowing why he said it. For a minute they were silent again.
“Hey, so you’ve got a new puppy?” Kolya said suddenly, in a perfectly callous voice.
“Ye—es,” Ilusha answered in a long whisper, gasping for breath.

“A black nose, that means he’ll be fierce, a good watchdog,” Kolya remarked gravely and stolidly, as if all he cared about was the puppy and its black nose. In fact he was still straining every nerve not to burst out crying like a child, and whatever he did, he could not get it under control. “When he’s grown, you’ll have to keep him chained up, I’m sure.”
“He’ll be a huge dog!” one of the boys cried.
“Of course he will,” “a mastiff,” “big,” “like this,” “as big as a calf,” several voices shouted.

“As big as a calf, a real calf,” the captain chimed in. “I got one like that on purpose, from the fiercest breed, and his parents are huge and very fierce, they stand this high off the floor.... Sit down here, on Ilusha’s bed, or here on the bench. You’re welcome, we’ve been hoping to see you for a long time.... You were so kind as to come with Alexey Fyodorovitch?”
Krassotkin sat down on the edge of the bed, at Ilusha’s feet. On the way he had perhaps worked out a breezy way to start the conversation, but now he had lost the thread of it entirely.

“No ... I came with Perezvon. I’ve got a dog now, called Perezvon. It’s a Slavonic name. He’s outside ... if I whistle, he’ll run in. I’ve brought a dog too,” he said, suddenly turning to Ilusha. “Do you remember Zhutchka, old man?” he fired the question at him all at once.
Ilusha’s little face quivered. He looked at Kolya in agony. Alyosha, standing at the door, frowned and signaled to Kolya not to mention Zhutchka, but Kolya either did not notice or would not.
“Where ... is Zhutchka?” Ilusha asked, his voice breaking.
“Oh, well, my boy, Zhutchka’s gone. He’s done for!”
Ilusha said nothing, but he fixed his eyes on Kolya again, intently. Alyosha caught Kolya’s eye and made another vigorous sign to him, but Kolya looked away, pretending he hadn’t seen.

“He must have run off and died somewhere. He must have died after a meal like that,” Kolya said without pity, though he seemed a little out of breath. “But I’ve got a dog, Perezvon ... A Slavonic name.... I’ve brought him to show you.”
“I don’t want him!” Ilusha said suddenly.

“No, no, you’ve really got to see him ... it’ll cheer you up. I brought him specially.... He’s the same shaggy kind of dog.... Will you let me call my dog in, madam?” He turned suddenly to Madame Snegiryov, in a strangely excited manner.
“I don’t want him, I don’t want him!” cried Ilusha, with a sad catch in his voice. His eyes had a look of reproach.

“You’d better,” said the captain, getting up from the chest by the wall where he had just sat down, “you’d better ... some other time,” he muttered, but there was no holding Kolya back. He shouted hurriedly to Smurov, “Open the door!” and the moment it was open he blew his whistle. Perezvon came tearing into the room.

“Up, Perezvon, beg! Beg!” shouted Kolya, jumping to his feet, and the dog reared up on its hind legs beside Ilusha’s bed. What came next took everyone by surprise. Ilusha started, lurched hard forward, bent over Perezvon and stared at him, faint with suspense.
“It’s ... Zhutchka!” he cried suddenly, in a voice breaking with joy and pain.
“And who did you think it was?” Krassotkin shouted at the top of his voice, in a ringing, happy tone. He bent down, grabbed the dog and held him up to Ilusha.

“Look, old man, see, he’s blind in one eye and his left ear is torn, exactly the marks you described to me. That’s how I found him, right away. He didn’t belong to anyone!” he explained, turning quickly to the captain, then his wife, then Alyosha, then back to Ilusha. “He lived in the Fedotovs’ back yard. It was his home, but they never fed him. He was a stray that had run away from some village ... I found him.... Now listen, old man, he can’t have swallowed what you gave him. If he had, he’d have died, he’d have had to! So he must have spat it out, since he’s alive. You didn’t see him do it. But the pin pricked his tongue, and that’s why he squealed. He ran off squealing and you thought he’d swallowed it. No wonder he squealed, the skin inside a dog’s mouth is so tender ... tenderer than a man’s, much tenderer!” Kolya cried impetuously, his face glowing and radiant with delight. Ilusha could not speak. White as a sheet, he stared at Kolya with his mouth open and his great eyes almost starting out of his head. Krassotkin had no suspicion of it. If he had known what a disastrous and fatal effect such a moment might have on the sick child’s health, nothing would have made him play such a trick. But Alyosha was perhaps the only person in the room who realized it. As for the captain, he behaved like a small child.
“Zhutchka! It’s Zhutchka!” he cried in a blissful voice. “Ilusha, it’s Zhutchka, your Zhutchka! Mamma, it’s Zhutchka!” He was almost in tears.
“And I never guessed!” cried Smurov, sorry he had missed it. “Bravo, Krassotkin! I told you he’d find the dog, and he has!”
“He has found him!” another boy repeated gleefully.
“Krassotkin’s a star!” cried a third voice.
“He’s a star, he’s a star!” cried the other boys, and they began to clap.

“Wait, wait,” Krassotkin did his best to shout over all of them. “I’ll tell you how it happened, that’s the whole point. I found him, took him home and hid him at once. I kept him locked up there and didn’t show him to anyone until today. Only Smurov has known for the last two weeks, but I told him the dog’s name was Perezvon and he never guessed. Meanwhile I taught the dog all sorts of tricks. You should see everything he can do! I trained him so I could bring you a well-trained dog, in good shape, old man, so I could say to you, ‘See, old man, what a fine dog your Zhutchka is now!’ Haven’t you got a bit of meat? He’ll do a trick for you that’ll make you die laughing. A piece of meat, haven’t you got any?”

The captain ran across the passage to the landlady’s rooms, where their cooking was done. Kolya didn’t want to waste any of the precious time, so in desperate haste he shouted to Perezvon, “Dead!” The dog at once flipped over and lay on his back with all four paws in the air. The boys laughed. Ilusha watched with the same suffering smile, but the one who enjoyed the dog’s performance most was “mamma.” She laughed at him and began snapping her fingers and calling, “Perezvon, Perezvon!”

“Nothing will make him get up, nothing!” Kolya cried triumphantly, proud of his success. “He won’t budge if the whole world shouts at him, but if I call him, he’ll be up in a second. Ici, Perezvon!” The dog leapt up and bounded about, whining with delight. The captain came running back with a piece of cooked beef.

“Is it hot?” Kolya asked quickly, in a businesslike way, taking the meat. “Dogs don’t like hot food. No, it’s fine. Look, everybody, look, Ilusha, look, old man. Why aren’t you looking? I’ve brought him, and he isn’t even looking at him.”

The new trick was to make the dog stand perfectly still with his nose stretched out, and then to lay a tempting bit of meat right on his nose. The poor dog had to stand like that, with the meat on his nose and not moving, for as long as his master pleased, maybe half an hour. But Kolya kept Perezvon like that for only a moment.
“Paid for!” cried Kolya, and in a flash the meat flipped from the dog’s nose into his mouth. The audience, of course, showed delight and amazement.
“Did you really stay away all this time just to train the dog?” exclaimed Alyosha, with a note of reproach he couldn’t hold back.
“Just for that!” answered Kolya, in perfect simplicity. “I wanted to show him off at his best.”
“Perezvon! Perezvon,” Ilusha called suddenly, snapping his thin fingers and beckoning to the dog.

“What is it? Let him jump up on the bed! _Ici_, Perezvon!” Kolya slapped the bed, and Perezvon darted up next to Ilusha. The boy flung both arms around his head, and Perezvon licked his cheek at once. Ilusha snuggled against him, stretched out in the bed and hid his face in the dog’s shaggy coat.
“Dear, dear!” the captain kept saying. Kolya sat down again on the edge of the bed.

“Ilusha, I can show you something else. I’ve brought you a little cannon. You remember I told you about it before, and you said how much you’d like to see it. Well, here it is. I’ve brought it for you.”

And Kolya quickly pulled the little bronze cannon out of his satchel. He was in a hurry because he was so happy himself. At any other time he would have waited for the stir over Perezvon to die down. Now he rushed ahead without any thought for the right moment. “You’re all happy now,” he felt, “so here’s something to make you happier!” He was completely delighted himself.

“I’ve wanted this thing for ages. It’s for you, old man, it’s for you. It belonged to Morozov, he had no use for it, he got it from his brother. I swapped a book from father’s bookcase for it, _A Kinsman of Mahomet or Salutary Folly_, a scandalous book published in Moscow a hundred years ago, before they had any censorship. And Morozov likes that sort of thing. He was grateful to me, too....”

Kolya held up the cannon so everyone could see and admire it. Ilusha sat up and, with his right arm still around the dog, gazed at the toy, enchanted. The excitement grew when Kolya announced that he had gunpowder too, and that they could fire it off at once “if it won’t alarm the ladies.” “Mamma” asked straight away to look at the toy more closely, and she was allowed to. She was delighted with the little bronze cannon on wheels and began rolling it back and forth on her lap. She happily gave permission to fire it, with no idea what she had been asked. Kolya showed the powder and the shot. The captain, being a military man, took charge of loading it and put in a tiny amount of powder. He asked that the shot be kept for another time. They set the cannon on the floor, pointed at an empty part of the room, pushed three grains of powder into the touch-hole and put a match to it. There was a magnificent bang. Mamma was startled but at once laughed with delight. The boys stared in speechless triumph. But the captain, looking at Ilusha, was more enchanted than any of them. Kolya picked up the cannon and presented it to Ilusha at once, along with the powder and the shot.
“I got it for you, for you! I’ve been saving it for you for ages,” he said again, in his delight.

“Oh, give it to me! No, give me the cannon!” mamma began begging like a little child. Her face showed a pitiful fear that she wouldn’t get it. Kolya was thrown off balance. The captain fidgeted uneasily.

“Mamma, mamma,” he ran over to her, “the cannon’s yours, of course, but let Ilusha have it, since it’s a present to him. It’s just as good as yours, though. Ilusha will always let you play with it. It’ll belong to both of you, both of you.”
“No, I don’t want it to belong to both of us. I want it to be all mine, not Ilusha’s,” mamma insisted, on the verge of tears.

“Take it, mother, here, keep it!” Ilusha cried. “Krassotkin, may I give it to my mother?” He turned to Krassotkin with a pleading face, as if afraid Kolya would be hurt by his giving the present to someone else.
“Of course you may,” Krassotkin agreed warmly. He took the cannon from Ilusha and handed it to mamma himself, with a polite bow. She was so touched that she cried.
“Ilusha, darling, he’s the one who loves his mamma!” she said tenderly, and at once started wheeling the cannon back and forth on her lap again.
“Mamma, let me kiss your hand.” The captain darted over to her at once and did so.
“And I’ve never seen such a charming fellow as this nice boy,” said the grateful lady, pointing at Krassotkin.

“And I’ll bring you as much powder as you like, Ilusha. We make our own powder now. Borovikov found out how it’s done—twenty-four parts saltpeter, ten parts sulphur and six parts birchwood charcoal. You pound it all together, mix it to a paste with water and rub it through a fine cloth sieve—that’s the way.”
“Smurov told me about your powder, only father says it’s not real gunpowder,” said Ilusha.
“Not real?” Kolya flushed. “It burns. I don’t know, of course.”
“No, I didn’t mean that,” the captain put in, looking guilty. “I only said real powder isn’t made like that, but it doesn’t matter, it can be made that way.”

“I wouldn’t know, you know best. We lit some in a pomatum jar. It burned splendidly and was gone, with only a tiny bit of ash left. But that was only the paste, and if you rub it through ... but of course you know best, I don’t know.... And Bulkin’s father thrashed him over our powder, did you hear?” he said, turning to Ilusha.
“Yes,” answered Ilusha. He listened to Kolya with huge interest and enjoyment.

“We’d made a whole bottle of it and he kept it under his bed. His father found it. He said it might explode, and thrashed him on the spot. He was going to complain about me to the masters. He’s not allowed to go around with me now. Nobody is allowed to go around with me now. Smurov isn’t either. I’ve got a bad name with everyone. They say I’m a ‘desperate character,’” Kolya smiled scornfully. “It all started with that business on the railway.”

“Ah, we’ve heard about that exploit of yours, too,” cried the captain. “How could you lie still on the track? Is it possible you weren’t the least bit afraid, lying there under the train? Weren’t you frightened?”
The captain flattered Kolya abjectly, with no dignity at all.

“N—not particularly,” Kolya answered offhandedly. “What ruined my reputation here more than anything was that cursed goose,” he said, turning to Ilusha again. He put on an unconcerned air while he talked, but he still couldn’t keep himself in hand, and he kept missing the note he was trying to hold.
“Oh! I heard about the goose!” Ilusha laughed, beaming all over. “They told me, but I didn’t get it. Did they really haul you up before a court?”

“It was the stupidest, most trivial business. They made a mountain out of a molehill, the way they always do,” Kolya began carelessly. “One day I was walking across the market-place, just when they’d driven in the geese. I stopped to look at them. Suddenly a fellow who’s an errand-boy at Plotnikov’s now looked at me and said, ‘What are you staring at the geese for?’ I looked him over. He was a dull, moon-faced fellow of twenty. I’m always on the side of the peasants, you know. I like talking to them.... We’ve fallen behind the peasants—that’s an axiom. I think you’re laughing, Karamazov?”
“No, heaven forbid, I’m listening,” said Alyosha, looking perfectly good-natured, and the touchy Kolya was reassured at once.

“My theory, Karamazov, is clear and simple,” he hurried on again, looking pleased. “I believe in the people, and I’m always glad to give them their due, but I’m not for spoiling them. That’s a _sine qua non_ ... But I was telling you about the goose. So I turned to the fool and said, ‘I’m wondering what that goose is thinking about.’ He gave me a quite blank look. ‘And what is it thinking about?’ he asked. ‘See that cart full of oats?’ I said. ‘The oats are spilling out of the sack, and the goose has put its neck right under the wheel to gobble them up—see?’ ‘I see that fine,’ he said. ‘Well,’ I said, ‘if the cart rolled forward a bit, would it break the goose’s neck or not?’ ‘Sure to break it,’ he said, and grinned from ear to ear, delighted. ‘Come on, then,’ I said, ‘let’s try it.’ ‘Let’s,’ he said. It didn’t take long to set up. He slipped over to the horse’s bridle without being noticed, and I stood off to one side to steer the goose. The owner wasn’t watching, he was busy talking to somebody, so I hardly had to do a thing: the goose stuck its head in after the oats all by itself, under the cart, right under the wheel. I winked at the lad, he gave the bridle a tug, and crack! The goose’s neck was snapped in half. And, just my luck, every peasant there saw us at that very moment and started a row at once. ‘You did that on purpose!’ ‘No, not on purpose.’ ‘Yes, you did, on purpose!’ Then they shouted, ‘Take him to the justice of the peace!’ They dragged me along too. ‘You were in it too,’ they said, ‘you helped, the whole market knows you!’ And for some reason the whole market really does know me,” Kolya added conceitedly. “We all trooped off to the justice’s, and they brought the goose along as well. The fellow was in a great funk and crying, simply blubbering like a woman. And the farmer kept shouting that at this rate you could kill any number of geese. Well, of course, there were witnesses. The justice settled it in a minute: the farmer was to get a rouble for the goose, and the fellow could keep the goose. And he was warned not to try such pranks again. And the fellow went on blubbering like a woman. ‘It wasn’t me,’ he said, ‘he put me up to it,’ and he pointed at me. I replied with perfect calm that I hadn’t put him up to anything, I’d merely stated a general proposition, speaking hypothetically. The justice smiled, and immediately was annoyed with himself for smiling. ‘I’ll report you to your masters,’ he said, ‘so that in future you’ll stop wasting your time on general propositions and sit at your books learning your lessons instead.’ He didn’t report me to the masters, that was a joke, but the story got around and reached their ears. They’ve got long ears, you know! The classics master, Kolbasnikov, was especially scandalized, but Dardanelov got me off again. Kolbasnikov is savage with everybody now, like a green ass. Did you know, Ilusha, he’s just married, and got a dowry of a thousand roubles, and his bride is a regular fright of the first rank and the last degree. The third-class boys wrote an epigram about it:
Astounding news has reached the class, Kolbasnikov has been an ass.
And so on, awfully funny, I’ll bring it to you later. I’ve nothing against Dardanelov. He’s a learned man, no doubt about it. I respect men like that, and not because he stood up for me.”
“But you caught him out about the founders of Troy!” Smurov put in suddenly, plainly proud of Krassotkin at such a moment. The story of the goose had pleased him especially.
“Did you really catch him out?” the captain asked, flatteringly. “On who founded Troy? We heard about that. Ilusha told me at the time.”
“He knows everything, father, he knows more than any of us!” put in Ilusha. “He only acts like that, but really he’s top in every subject....”
Ilusha looked at Kolya with boundless happiness.

“Oh, all that about Troy is nonsense, a trifle. I consider it an unimportant question,” said Kolya, with haughty humility. By now he had fully regained his dignity, though he was still a little uneasy. He knew he was very worked up, and that he had told the story of the goose, for one thing, with too little restraint, while Alyosha had looked serious and hadn’t said a word the whole time. And little by little the vain boy began to be gnawed by the fear that Alyosha was silent because he despised him, and thought he was showing off. If he dared to think anything like that, Kolya would—
“I regard the question as quite trivial,” he snapped again, proudly.

“And I know who founded Troy,” said a boy who hadn’t spoken before, suddenly, to everyone’s surprise. He had sat silent and seemed shy. He was a pretty boy of about eleven, named Kartashov, and he was sitting near the door. Kolya looked at him with dignified amazement.

The fact was that who had founded Troy had become a secret for the whole school, a secret you could only find out by reading Smaragdov, and nobody had Smaragdov but Kolya. One day, when Kolya had his back turned, Kartashov had quickly opened the Smaragdov that lay among Kolya’s books, and at once hit on the passage about the founding of Troy. That was quite a while ago, but he felt uneasy about it and couldn’t bring himself to announce in public that he too knew who had founded Troy. He was afraid of what might happen, and of Krassotkin somehow shaming him over it. But now he couldn’t help saying it. For weeks he had been longing to.

“Well, who did found it?” asked Kolya, turning to him with haughty superiority. He saw from the boy’s face that he really did know, and he made up his mind at once how to take it. There was, so to speak, a jarring note in the general harmony.

“Troy was founded by Teucer, Dardanus, Ilius and Tros,” the boy rapped out at once, and in the same instant he blushed, blushed so deeply that it hurt to look at him. But the boys stared at him, stared at him for a whole minute, and then all the staring eyes swung round together and fixed on Kolya, who was still looking the bold boy over with scornful calm.
“In what sense did they found it?” he condescended to say at last. “And what does it mean, to found a city or a state? What do they do? Did each of them go and lay a brick, do you suppose?”
There was laughter. The guilty boy went from pink to crimson. He said nothing and was close to tears. Kolya kept him like that for a minute.

“Before you talk about a historical event like the founding of a nation, you must first understand what you mean by it,” he lectured him, in stern, cutting tones. “As for me, I attach no importance to these old wives’ tales, and I don’t think much of universal history in general,” he added carelessly, to the company at large.
“Universal history?” the captain asked, looking almost frightened.

“Yes, universal history! It’s a study of one folly of mankind after another, and nothing more. The only subjects I respect are mathematics and natural science,” said Kolya. He was showing off, and he stole a glance at Alyosha; his was the one opinion he feared there. But Alyosha was still silent and still serious. One word from Alyosha would have stopped him, but Alyosha said nothing, and “it might be the silence of contempt,” and that finally made Kolya angry.
“The classical languages too ... they’re plain madness, nothing else. You seem to disagree with me again, Karamazov?”
“I don’t agree,” said Alyosha, with a faint smile.

“The study of the classics, if you want my opinion, is just a police measure. That’s the only reason it was brought into our schools.” Gradually Kolya was growing breathless again. “They brought in Latin and Greek because they’re a bore and they numb the mind. School was dull already, so what could they do to make it duller? It was senseless enough already, so what could they do to make it more senseless? So they hit on Greek and Latin. That’s my opinion, and I hope I never change it,” Kolya finished abruptly. His cheeks were flushed.
“That’s true,” Smurov agreed suddenly, in a ringing voice of conviction. He had been listening closely.
“And yet he’s first in Latin himself,” one of the boys in the group called out suddenly.
“Yes, father, he says that, and still he’s first in Latin,” Ilusha echoed.

“What of it?” Kolya felt he had to defend himself, though the praise was very sweet to him. “I’m slogging away at Latin because I have to, because I promised my mother I’d pass my examination, and I think that whatever you do, it’s worth doing well. But deep down I have a profound contempt for the classics and all that fraud.... You don’t agree, Karamazov?”
“Why ‘fraud’?” Alyosha smiled again.

“Well, all the classical authors have been translated into every language, so it wasn’t to study the classics that they brought in Latin, but only as a police measure, to numb the intelligence. So what can you call it but a fraud?”
“Why, who taught you all this?” cried Alyosha, surprised at last.
“For one thing, I can think for myself without being taught. And besides, what I just said about the classics being translated, our teacher Kolbasnikov has said to the whole third class.”
“The doctor’s here!” cried Nina, who had said nothing until then.

A carriage belonging to Madame Hohlakov drove up to the gate. The captain, who had been waiting for the doctor all morning, rushed headlong out to meet him. “Mamma” pulled herself together and put on a dignified look. Alyosha went over to Ilusha and began straightening his pillows. From her invalid chair, Nina watched anxiously while he set the bed in order. The boys hurriedly said their goodbyes. Some promised to come back in the evening. Kolya called Perezvon, and the dog jumped down off the bed.
“I’m not going away, I’m not going away,” Kolya said hastily to Ilusha. “I’ll wait in the passage and come back when the doctor’s gone. I’ll come back with Perezvon.”

But by now the doctor had come in, an important-looking man with long dark whiskers and a shiny, clean-shaven chin, wearing a bearskin coat. On the threshold he stopped, taken aback; he probably thought he had come to the wrong place. “What is this? Where am I?” he muttered, taking off neither his coat nor his peaked sealskin cap. The crowd, the poverty of the room, the washing hung on a line in the corner, all puzzled him. The captain, bent double, was bowing low before him.
“It’s here, sir, here, sir,” he muttered, cringing. “It’s here, you’ve come to the right place, you were coming to us...”
“Sne-gi-ryov?” the doctor said loudly and pompously. “Mr. Snegiryov—is that you?”
“That’s me, sir!”
“Ah!”

Once more the doctor gave the room a squeamish look, and threw off his coat, displaying the grand decoration at his neck for all to see. The captain caught the fur coat in mid-air, and the doctor took off his cap.
“Where is the patient?” he asked emphatically.

chapters.title: VI. Precocity
paragraphs: “What do you think the doctor will say to him?” Kolya asked quickly. “What a repulsive face he has, though, don’t you think? I can’t stand medicine!”
“Ilusha is dying. I think that’s certain,” Alyosha answered sadly.
“They’re crooks! Medicine’s a fraud! I’m glad to have met you, though, Karamazov. I’ve wanted to know you for a long time. I’m only sorry we’re meeting in such sad circumstances.”
Kolya very much wanted to say something warmer and more heartfelt, but he felt awkward. Alyosha noticed this, smiled, and shook his hand.

“I learned long ago to respect you as a rare person,” Kolya muttered again, faltering and unsure. “I’ve heard you’re a mystic and that you were in the monastery. I know you’re a mystic, but ... that hasn’t put me off. Contact with real life will cure you.... It’s always like that with people like you.”
“What do you mean by mystic? Cure me of what?” Alyosha was rather astonished.
“Oh, God and all the rest of it.”
“What, you don’t believe in God?”

“Oh, I’ve nothing against God. Of course, God is only a hypothesis, but ... I admit He’s needed ... to keep the universe in order and all that ... and if there were no God, we’d have to invent Him,” added Kolya, beginning to blush. It suddenly struck him that Alyosha might think he was parading his knowledge and trying to prove he was “grown up.” “I don’t have the slightest wish to show off to him,” Kolya thought indignantly. And all at once he felt horribly annoyed.

“Honestly, I can’t stand getting into these discussions,” he said, as if closing the subject. “A person can love mankind without believing in God, don’t you think? Voltaire didn’t believe in God, and he loved mankind, didn’t he?” (“I’m at it again,” he thought to himself.)

“Voltaire believed in God, though not much, I think. And I don’t think he loved mankind much either,” said Alyosha, quietly, gently and quite naturally, as if he were talking to someone his own age, or even older. Kolya was particularly struck that Alyosha seemed so unsure of his own opinion of Voltaire. It was as though he were leaving the question for him, little Kolya, to decide.
“Have you read Voltaire?” Alyosha finished.
“No, not exactly read.... I read _Candide_, though, in Russian ... in a ridiculous, grotesque old translation ... (At it again! Again!)”
“And did you understand it?”

“Oh, yes, everything.... That is ... Why would you think I couldn’t understand it? There’s a lot of nastiness in it, of course.... Of course I can see it’s a philosophical novel, written to argue for an idea....” Kolya was getting muddled by now. “I’m a Socialist, Karamazov, I’m an incurable Socialist,” he announced suddenly, out of nowhere.
“A Socialist?” Alyosha laughed. “But when did you find time to become one? Why, I thought you were only thirteen.”
Kolya winced.

“First of all, I’m not thirteen but fourteen, fourteen in two weeks,” he said, flushing angrily, “and second, I can’t see what my age has to do with it. What matters is what I believe, not how old I am, isn’t it?”

“When you’re older, you’ll see for yourself how age affects what a person believes. I also thought these weren’t your own ideas,” Alyosha answered calmly and modestly, but Kolya interrupted him hotly:

“Oh, come on, you want obedience and mysticism. You have to admit that the Christian religion, for instance, has only ever served the rich and powerful, to keep the lower classes in slavery. That’s so, isn’t it?”
“Ah, I know where you read that, and I’m sure someone told you so!” cried Alyosha.

“Now, what makes you think I read it? And certainly no one told me. I can think for myself.... I’m not against Christ, if you like. He was a most humane person. If He were alive today, He’d be found in the ranks of the revolutionists, and might well play a prominent part.... There’s no doubt about that.”
“Where did you get that, where? What kind of fool have you been making friends with?” exclaimed Alyosha.
“Come on, the truth will out! It happens I’ve often talked to Mr. Rakitin, of course, but ... old Byelinsky said that too, so they say.”
“Byelinsky? I don’t remember that. He never wrote it anywhere.”
“Well, if he didn’t write it, they say he said it. I heard it from a ... but never mind.”
“And have you read Byelinsky?”
“Well, no ... not all of him, but ... I did read the passage about Tatyana, about why she didn’t run off with Onyegin.”
“Why she didn’t run off with Onyegin? Surely you can’t ... understand that already?”

“Why, you seem to take me for little Smurov,” said Kolya, with a grin of irritation. “But please don’t think I’m such a revolutionist. I often disagree with Mr. Rakitin. Just because I mention Tatyana doesn’t mean I’m for the emancipation of women. I accept that women are a subject race and must obey. _Les femmes tricottent_, as Napoleon said.” Kolya smiled, for some reason. “And on that question, at least, I’m completely of one mind with that pseudo-great man. I also think that leaving your own country and running off to America is contemptible, worse than contemptible—it’s silly. Why go to America when you can do great service to humanity here? Especially now. There’s a whole mass of fruitful activity open to us. That’s what I answered.”
“What do you mean? Answered whom? Has someone already suggested you go to America?”

“I’ll admit they’ve been at me to go, but I refused. That’s between us, of course, Karamazov; do you hear, not a word to anyone. I’m telling this only to you. I’m not at all keen to fall into the clutches of the secret police and take lessons at the Chain bridge.
Long will you remember The house at the Chain bridge.

Do you remember? It’s splendid. Why are you laughing? You don’t think I’m lying, do you?” (“What if he finds out that all I have is that one issue of _The Bell_ from father’s bookcase, and I haven’t read any more of it?” Kolya thought with a shudder.)

“Oh, no, I’m not laughing, and don’t imagine for a moment that you’re lying. No, really, I can’t imagine it, because all this, alas, is perfectly true. But tell me, have you read Pushkin—_Onyegin_, for instance?... You mentioned Tatyana just now.”
“No, I haven’t read it yet, but I want to. I have no prejudices, Karamazov; I want to hear both sides. Why do you ask?”
“Oh, no reason.”

“Tell me, Karamazov, do you have a terrible contempt for me?” Kolya rapped out suddenly, and drew himself up in front of Alyosha as if he were on parade. “Tell me, please, and don’t beat about the bush.”
“Contempt for you?” Alyosha looked at him in wonder. “Why would I? I’m only sad that a nature as charming as yours should be warped by all this crude nonsense before you’ve even started out in life.”
“Don’t worry about my nature,” Kolya broke in, not without self-satisfaction. “But it’s true that I’m stupidly sensitive, crudely sensitive. You smiled just now, and I thought you seemed to—”

“Oh, my smile meant something quite different. Here’s why I smiled. Not long ago I read what a German who had lived in Russia said about our students and schoolboys today. ‘Show a Russian schoolboy,’ he writes, ‘a map of the stars, which he knows nothing about, and he’ll hand it back to you the next day with corrections on it.’ No knowledge and unlimited conceit—that’s what the German meant to say about the Russian schoolboy.”

“Yes, he’s perfectly right,” Kolya laughed suddenly, “exactly so! Bravo for the German! But he missed the good side, don’t you think? Conceit, maybe, but that comes with youth, and it’ll be corrected if need be. On the other hand, there’s an independent spirit almost from childhood, a boldness of thought and conviction, and none of the spirit of those sausage makers, groveling before authority.... But the German was right all the same. Bravo for the German! Still, Germans need strangling. They may be good at science and learning, but they must be strangled.”
“Strangled, what for?” smiled Alyosha.

“Well, maybe I’m talking nonsense, I agree. I’m awfully childish sometimes, and when I’m pleased about something I can’t hold myself back and I’ll say any rubbish. But look, we’re chattering away here about nothing, and that doctor has been in there a long time. But maybe he’s examining the mamma and that poor crippled Nina. I liked that Nina, you know. As I was leaving she suddenly whispered to me, ‘Why didn’t you come before?’ And in such a voice, so reproachfully! I think she’s awfully nice and pitiful.”

“Yes, yes! Well, you’ll be coming often, and you’ll see what she’s like. It would do you a great deal of good to know people like that. You’d learn to value a great deal that you’ll find out by knowing them,” Alyosha said warmly. “That would have more effect on you than anything.”
“Oh, how I regret it, and blame myself for not coming sooner!” Kolya exclaimed, in bitter distress.
“Yes, it’s a great pity. You saw yourself how happy the poor child was to see you. And how he fretted, waiting for you to come!”

“Don’t tell me! You’re making it worse! But it serves me right. What kept me away was my conceit, my selfish vanity, and that beastly stubbornness I can never get rid of, though I’ve fought it all my life. I see that now. I’m a beast in lots of ways, Karamazov!”
“No, you have a charming nature, though it’s been twisted, and I quite understand why you’ve had such an influence on this generous, painfully sensitive boy,” Alyosha answered warmly.
“And you say that to me!” cried Kolya. “And would you believe it, I thought—I’ve thought several times since I got here—that you despised me! If only you knew how much I value your opinion!”
“But are you really so sensitive? At your age! Would you believe it, just now, while you were telling your story, I was watching you and thinking that you must be very sensitive!”

“You thought so? What an eye you’ve got, I must say! I bet it was when I was talking about the goose. That was just when I was imagining you had a great contempt for me for being in such a hurry to show off, and for a moment I quite hated you for it, and started talking like a fool. Then I imagined—just now, here—when I said that if there were no God we’d have to invent Him, that I was too eager to display my knowledge, especially since I’d got that phrase out of a book. But I swear I wasn’t showing off out of vanity, though I really don’t know why I did it. Because I was so pleased? Yes, I think it was because I was so pleased ... though it’s perfectly disgraceful to gush the moment you’re pleased, I know that. But I’m convinced now that you don’t despise me; it was all my imagination. Oh, Karamazov, I’m profoundly unhappy. Sometimes I imagine all sorts of things, that everyone is laughing at me, the whole world, and then I feel ready to overturn the whole order of things.”
“And you worry everyone around you,” smiled Alyosha.
“Yes, I worry everyone around me, especially my mother. Karamazov, tell me, am I very ridiculous now?”

“Don’t think about that, don’t think of it at all!” cried Alyosha. “And what does ridiculous mean? Doesn’t everyone constantly end up being, or seeming, ridiculous? Besides, nearly all clever people now are terribly afraid of being ridiculous, and that makes them unhappy. What surprises me is only that you feel it so early. I’ve been noticing it for some time, though, and not only in you. Nowadays even children have begun to suffer from it. It’s almost a kind of madness. The devil has taken the form of that vanity and gone into a whole generation; it’s simply the devil,” added Alyosha, without a trace of the smile that Kolya, staring at him, expected to see. “You’re like everyone else,” Alyosha concluded, “that is, like very many others. Only you mustn’t be like everybody else, that’s all.”
“Even if everyone is like that?”

“Yes, even if everyone is. You be the only one who isn’t. You really aren’t like everyone else: just now you weren’t ashamed to own up to something bad, even ridiculous. And who admits that much these days? No one. People have even lost the urge to look critically at themselves. Don’t be like everyone else, even if you’re the only one.”

“Splendid! I wasn’t wrong about you. You know how to comfort a person. Oh, how I’ve longed to know you, Karamazov! I’ve been eager for this meeting for ages. Can you really have thought about me, too? You said just now that you thought of me, too?”
“Yes, I’d heard about you and I had thought of you, too ... and if you’re asking partly out of vanity, that doesn’t matter.”
“Do you know, Karamazov, our talk has been like a declaration of love,” said Kolya, in a bashful, melting voice. “That’s not ridiculous, is it?”
“Not ridiculous at all. And if it were, it wouldn’t matter, since it’s been a good thing.” Alyosha smiled brightly.
“But you know, Karamazov, you have to admit you’re a little ashamed yourself now.... I can see it in your eyes.” Kolya smiled with a sort of sly happiness.
“Why ashamed?”
“Well, why are you blushing?”
“You’re the one who made me blush,” laughed Alyosha, and he really did blush. “Oh, well, I am a little, goodness knows why, I don’t know...” he muttered, almost embarrassed.
“Oh, how I love you and admire you at this moment, just because you’re a little ashamed! Because you’re just like me,” cried Kolya, in sheer ecstasy. His cheeks glowed, his eyes shone.
“You know, Kolya, you’re going to be very unhappy in your life,” Alyosha said suddenly, as if something made him say it.
“I know, I know. How you know it all beforehand!” Kolya agreed at once.
“But you will bless life on the whole, all the same.”

“Exactly, hurrah! You’re a prophet. Oh, we’ll get on together, Karamazov! Do you know what delights me most? That you treat me quite as an equal. But we’re not equals, no, we’re not, you’re better! But we’ll get on. You know, this whole last month I’ve been telling myself, ‘Either we’ll be friends at once, forever, or we’ll part enemies to the grave!’”
“And saying that, of course, you loved me,” Alyosha laughed gaily.
“I did. I loved you terribly. I’ve been loving you and dreaming about you. And how do you know it all beforehand? Ah, here’s the doctor. Goodness! What will he tell us? Look at his face!”

chapters.title: VII. Ilusha
paragraphs: The doctor stepped out of the room again, wrapped in his fur coat, his cap already on. He looked almost angry and disgusted, as if he feared catching some dirt. He threw a quick look around the passage and eyed Alyosha and Kolya sternly. Alyosha waved to the coachman from the doorway, and the carriage that had brought the doctor rolled up. The captain rushed out behind the doctor and, bowing and apologizing, caught him for one last word. The poor man looked totally crushed. His eyes were frightened.

“Your Excellency, your Excellency ... is it possible?” he began, but he couldn’t go on and wrung his hands in despair. Still he kept his eyes fixed on the doctor, pleading, as if a single word from him could yet change the poor boy’s fate.
“I can’t help it. I’m not God!” the doctor answered casually, though in his usual pompous manner.
“Doctor ... your Excellency ... will it be soon? Soon?”
“You must be ready for anything,” said the doctor, stressing each word and cutting it off short. He dropped his eyes and was about to step out to the carriage.
“Your Excellency, for Christ’s sake!” the captain, panic-stricken, held him back once more. “Your Excellency! Is there really nothing, nothing at all, that can save him now?”

“It’s no longer in my hands,” said the doctor impatiently, “but, h’m!...” He broke off suddenly. “If you could, say ... send ... your patient ... right away, without delay” (and the words “right away, without delay” came out with such angry sternness that the captain flinched) “to Syracuse, the change to the new, be-ne-ficial climate might perhaps bring about—”
“To Syracuse!” cried the captain, who could not make sense of it.
“Syracuse is in Sicily,” Kolya blurted out, by way of explanation. The doctor turned to look at him.
“Sicily! Your Excellency,” the captain stammered, “but you’ve seen”—he spread out his hands at his surroundings—“mamma and my family?”

“N—no, Sicily is no place for the family. The family ought to go to the Caucasus in early spring ... your daughter must go to the Caucasus, and your wife ... once she has taken the waters there for her rheumatism ... has to be sent straight on to Paris, to the mental specialist Lepelletier. I can give you a note for him, and then ... there may be a change—”
“Doctor, doctor! But look!” Again the captain threw out his hands in despair, pointing at the bare wooden walls of the passage.
“Well, that’s no concern of mine,” the doctor grinned. “You asked what treatment was possible, and I’ve told you what medical science says. As for the rest, I’m sorry to say—”

“Don’t be afraid, apothecary, my dog won’t bite you,” Kolya snapped loudly. He had noticed the doctor’s nervous glance at Perezvon, who stood in the doorway. Kolya’s voice was full of anger. He used the word apothecary instead of doctor on purpose and later explained that he used it “to insult him.”
“What was that?” The doctor jerked his head up and stared at Kolya in astonishment. “Who is this?” he asked Alyosha, as if demanding an explanation.
“I’m Perezvon’s master. Don’t mind me,” Kolya said sharply again.
“Perezvon?”[7] the doctor repeated, bewildered.
“He hears the bell, but where it is he cannot tell. Good-by, we’ll meet in Syracuse.”
“Who is this? Who is this?” The doctor went into a towering rage.

“He’s a schoolboy, doctor, a naughty boy. Pay no attention to him,” said Alyosha, frowning and talking fast. “Kolya, be quiet!” he cried to Krassotkin. “Pay no attention to him, doctor,” he said again, with some impatience.
“He wants a whipping, a good whipping!” The doctor stamped his foot, in a perfect fury.
“And you know, apothecary, Perezvon might bite!” said Kolya, pale now, his voice shaking and his eyes blazing. “_Ici_, Perezvon!”
“Kolya, one more word and I’m finished with you,” Alyosha cried in a tone that allowed no argument.
“Only one man in the world can give orders to Nikolay Krassotkin, and here he is”; Kolya pointed at Alyosha. “I obey him. Good-by!”

He strode forward, opened the door and went straight into the inner room, with Perezvon flying after him. The doctor stood rooted to the spot for five seconds, staring at Alyosha in amazement. Then, with a curse, he hurried out to the carriage, saying aloud over and over, “This is ... this is ... I don’t know what this is!” The captain rushed ahead to help him into the carriage. Alyosha went after Kolya into the room. Kolya was already beside Ilusha’s bed. The sick boy was holding his hand and calling for his father. A minute later the captain came back in too.

“Father, father, come ... we ...” Ilusha stammered in great agitation. He seemed unable to go on, so he threw his thin arms around his father and Kolya, pulled them together into one embrace and held them as hard as he could. The captain suddenly began to shake with silent sobs, and Kolya’s lips and chin trembled.
“Father, father! I feel so sorry for you!” Ilusha moaned bitterly.
“Ilusha ... darling ... the doctor said ... you’ll be all right ... we’ll be happy ... the doctor ...” the captain began.
“Ah, father! I know what the new doctor told you about me.... I saw it!” cried Ilusha, and once more he hugged them both with all his strength and hid his face against his father’s shoulder.
“Father, don’t cry. And when I die, find yourself a good boy, another one ... pick one out of all of them, a good one, call him Ilusha, and love him in my place....”
“Quiet, old man, you’ll get well,” Krassotkin burst out, in a voice that sounded cross.

“But don’t ever forget me, father,” Ilusha went on. “Come to my grave ... and, father, bury me by our big stone, where we used to walk, and come to me there in the evening, you and Krassotkin ... and Perezvon ... I’ll be waiting for you.... Father, father!”
His voice gave out. The three of them said nothing, still holding each other. Nina was crying softly in her chair, and finally, when she saw them all in tears, “mamma” started to weep too.
“Ilusha! Ilusha!” she cried.
Krassotkin suddenly freed himself from Ilusha’s arms.

“Good-by, old man, mother expects me home for dinner,” he said in a rush. “What a shame I didn’t tell her! She’ll be terribly worried.... But after dinner I’ll come straight back to you for the whole day, the whole evening, and I’ll tell you all sorts of things, all sorts of things. And I’ll bring Perezvon. I’ll take him with me now, though, because he’d start howling once I’m gone and would only trouble you. Good-by!”
He ran out into the passage. He hadn’t wanted to cry, but out there he burst into tears. Alyosha found him weeping.
“Kolya, you must be sure to keep your word and come back, or he’ll be terribly disappointed,” Alyosha told him firmly.
“I will! Oh, how I curse myself for not coming sooner!” Kolya muttered through his tears, not even ashamed of them any more.
Just then the captain flew out of the room and pulled the door shut behind him. He looked frantic, and his lips were shaking. He stood before the two of them and threw up his arms.

“I don’t want a good boy! I don’t want another boy!” he muttered in a wild whisper, grinding his teeth. “If I forget thee, Jerusalem, may my tongue—” His voice broke in a sob, and he dropped to his knees before the wooden bench. He pressed his fists to his head and began to sob with absurd, whimpering cries, struggling to keep them from being heard in the room.
Kolya ran out into the street.
“Good-by, Karamazov? Are you coming yourself?” he called out sharply and angrily to Alyosha.
“Yes, I’ll come this evening, for certain.”
“What was it he said about Jerusalem?... What did he mean?”
“It’s from the Bible. ‘If I forget thee, Jerusalem’ means, if I forget what is dearest to me, if I let anything take its place, then may—”
“I see, that’s enough! Be sure you come! _Ici_, Perezvon!” he shouted at the dog with real ferocity, and with long quick strides he set off for home.

chapters.title: I. At Grushenka’s
paragraphs: Alyosha was heading across the cathedral square to the widow Morozov’s house, to see Grushenka. She had sent Fenya to him early that morning with an urgent message asking him to come. Fenya told him, when he questioned her, that her mistress had been particularly upset since the day before. In the two months since Mitya’s arrest, Alyosha had often visited the widow Morozov’s house, partly because he wished to and partly to carry messages for Mitya. Three days after Mitya was arrested, Grushenka had fallen gravely ill, and she remained ill for almost five weeks. For one whole week she had lain unconscious. She had changed a great deal. She was thinner and a little sallow, although for the last fortnight she had been well enough to go out. Yet to Alyosha her face was more attractive than ever, and he liked meeting her eyes when he came in. Her face had taken on a look of firmness and intelligent purpose. There were signs in her of a spiritual transformation, and one could see a steadfast, fine, humble determination that nothing could shake. A small vertical line had appeared between her brows, and at first glance it gave her charming face a thoughtful, almost stern look. Hardly a trace remained of her old frivolity.

Alyosha found it strange, too, that the poor girl had not yet lost her youthful cheerfulness. A calamity had struck her: she was engaged to a man who was arrested for a terrible crime almost at the very moment of their engagement. She had been ill, and a sentence that seemed all but certain hung over Mitya. Even so, her cheerfulness had survived. Her once proud eyes now had a soft light in them, though now and then they blazed with the old vengeful fire, whenever one troubling thought gripped her harder than ever. What troubled her was the same as always: Katerina Ivanovna, whom Grushenka had even raved about in her delirium. Alyosha knew she was dreadfully jealous of her. And yet Katerina Ivanovna had not visited Mitya in prison even once, though she could have gone whenever she pleased. All this set Alyosha a hard problem, since he was the only person Grushenka confided in, and she kept asking him for advice. Sometimes he had nothing to tell her.

Anxious, he went into her rooms. She was at home. She had returned from visiting Mitya half an hour earlier, and the way she sprang up from her chair to meet him showed Alyosha she had been waiting for him with great impatience. On the table lay a pack of cards, dealt out for a game of “fools.” On the far side of the room a bed had been made up on the leather sofa, and Maximov lay on it, half sitting up. He wore a dressing-gown and a cotton nightcap. He was clearly ill and weak, but he was smiling happily. The homeless old man had come back from Mokroe with Grushenka two months earlier and had simply stayed, and he was still there. He had arrived with her in rain and sleet, sat down on the sofa soaked and frightened, and looked at her without a word, with a timid, imploring smile. Grushenka was in terrible grief and just coming down with fever. In everything she had to do in the first half-hour after she got home, she nearly forgot he was there. Then she happened to glance at him closely, and he gave a pitiful, helpless little laugh. She called Fenya and told her to give him something to eat. All that day he sat in the same spot, hardly moving. When it grew dark and the shutters were shut, Fenya asked her mistress:
“Is the gentleman staying the night, mistress?”
“Yes. Make up a bed for him on the sofa,” Grushenka answered.
She questioned him further and learned that he literally had nowhere to go. “Mr. Kalganov, my benefactor, told me flat out that he would not receive me again, and he gave me five roubles.”

“Well, God bless you, you’d better stay, then,” Grushenka decided, in her grief, and smiled at him with pity. Her smile wrung the old man’s heart, and his lips twitched with grateful tears. So the penniless wanderer had been with her ever since. He didn’t leave the house even while she was ill. Fenya and her grandmother, the cook, did not turn him out. They kept serving him his meals and making up his bed on the sofa. Grushenka had got used to him. When she came home from Mitya (she had started visiting him in prison before she was properly well), she would sit down and chat with “Maximushka” about small matters, so as not to think about her sorrow. The old man proved to be a good teller of stories now and then, and in the end she couldn’t do without him. Besides Alyosha, who did not come every day and never stayed long, Grushenka saw almost nobody. Her old merchant lay gravely ill at this time, “at his last gasp,” as people in town said, and in fact he died a week after Mitya’s trial. Three weeks before he died, sensing the end was near, he had at last made his sons, their wives and their children come upstairs to him, and he commanded them not to leave him again. From then on he gave his servants strict orders not to let Grushenka in, and to tell her, if she came, “The master wishes you long life and happiness and tells you to forget him.” Still, Grushenka sent almost every day to ask after him.

“You’ve come at last!” she cried, dropping the cards and welcoming Alyosha with delight. “Maximushka has been frightening me that you might not come. Ah, how much I need you! Sit down at the table. What will you have? Coffee?”
“Yes, please,” said Alyosha, taking his seat at the table. “I’m very hungry.”

“Good for you. Fenya, Fenya, coffee!” Grushenka cried. “It’s been ready for you for ages. And bring some little pies, and see they’re hot. Do you know, we had a storm over those pies today. I took them to the prison for him, and can you believe it, he threw them back at me. He wouldn’t eat them. He tossed one on the floor and stamped on it. So I told him, ‘I’m leaving them with the warder. If you haven’t eaten them by evening, your venomous spite must be all the food you need!’ And I walked out. Can you believe it, we quarreled again? Every time I go, we quarrel.”
Grushenka said all this in a single breath, upset as she was. Maximov grew nervous, smiled right away and looked down at the floor.
“What was the quarrel about this time?” Alyosha asked.

“I never saw it coming. Just think, he’s jealous of the Pole! ‘Why do you keep him?’ he said. ‘So now you’re keeping him.’ He’s jealous, jealous of me all the time, jealous when he’s eating, jealous when he’s asleep! Last week he even got it into his head to be jealous of Kuzma.”
“But he knew about the Pole already?”

“Yes, he did, but there you are. He has known about him from the very start, and today all at once he jumped up and began raging about him. I’m ashamed to repeat what he said. The silly fellow! Rakitin went in just as I was coming out. Maybe Rakitin is egging him on. What do you think?” she added, as if it hardly mattered.
“He loves you, that’s all it is. He loves you so much. And now he’s especially worried.”

“Well, he might be, with the trial tomorrow. And I went to him to say a word about tomorrow, because I’m afraid to think what will happen then. You say he’s worried, but how worried am I! And he goes on about the Pole! He’s too silly! At least he isn’t jealous of Maximushka yet.”
“My wife was terribly jealous over me, too,” Maximov put in a word.
“Jealous of you?” Grushenka couldn’t help laughing. “Who could she have been jealous of?”
“The servant girls.”

“Hush, Maximushka, I’m not in a laughing mood now. I’m angry. Stop eyeing the pies. You’re not getting any. They’re bad for you, and I won’t give you vodka either. I have to look after him as well, as if I were running an almshouse,” she laughed.
“I don’t deserve your kindness. I’m a worthless creature,” said Maximov, tears in his voice. “You’d do better to spend your kindness on people who are more use than I am.”

“Ech, everybody is of use, Maximushka, and who can say who’s most useful? If only that Pole didn’t exist, Alyosha. He’s gone and fallen ill today, too. I’ve been to see him as well. And I’ll send him some pies, too, on purpose. I hadn’t sent him any, but Mitya accused me of it, so now I will! Ah, here comes Fenya with a letter! Yes, it’s from the Poles—begging again!”

Pan Mussyalovitch had indeed sent a very long letter, eloquent in his usual way, begging her to lend him three roubles. A receipt for the sum was enclosed, with a promise to repay it within three months, signed by Pan Vrublevsky as well. Over the fortnight of her recovery Grushenka had received many such letters from her former lover, each with a receipt like this. She knew, though, that the two Poles had called to ask about her health while she was ill. The first letter they sent her was a long one, written on large notepaper and sealed with a big family crest. It was so obscure and high-flown that Grushenka put it down before she was halfway through, unable to make anything of it. She was in no state to deal with letters then. Next day a second letter followed the first, in which Pan Mussyalovitch asked her for a loan of two thousand roubles, for a very short time. Grushenka left that one unanswered too. Then came a whole series of letters, one a day, all just as pompous and rhetorical, but the sum they asked for kept shrinking. It fell to a hundred roubles, then twenty-five, then ten, and at last Grushenka got a letter in which both Poles begged for only one rouble and enclosed a receipt signed by the two of them.

Then Grushenka suddenly felt sorry for them, and at dusk she went to their lodging herself. She found the two Poles in great poverty, almost starving, with no food or firewood, without even cigarettes, and in debt to their landlady. The two hundred roubles they had carried off from Mitya at Mokroe had soon vanished. But Grushenka was surprised to be received with haughty dignity and self-importance, with the most elaborate manners and pompous speeches.
