Grushenka simply laughed and gave her old admirer ten roubles. Then she told Mitya about it, laughing, and he wasn’t in the least jealous. But from that day the Poles had fastened on Grushenka and bombarded her daily with demands for money, and she had always sent them small sums. And now, today of all days, Mitya had taken it into his head to be fearfully jealous.

“Like a fool, I stopped by to see him for just a minute on my way to Mitya’s, because he’s ill too, my Pole,” Grushenka began again, in a nervous rush. “I was laughing as I told Mitya about it. ‘Just think,’ I said, ‘my Pole had the happy idea of singing me his old songs, with a guitar. He thought I’d be touched and marry him!’ Mitya jumped up, swearing.... Well, there you are, I’ll send them the pies! Fenya, is it that little girl they’ve sent? Here, give her three roubles, wrap a dozen pies up in paper and tell her to take them. And you, Alyosha, be sure to tell Mitya that I did send them the pies.”
“I wouldn’t tell him that for anything,” said Alyosha with a smile.
“Ech! You think it hurts him? Not a bit. He’s jealous on purpose. He couldn’t care less,” Grushenka said bitterly.
“On purpose?” Alyosha asked.

“You’re silly, Alyosha, I tell you. For all your cleverness you understand nothing about this. It doesn’t offend me that he’s jealous of a girl like me. What would offend me is if he weren’t jealous. That’s the way I am. Jealousy doesn’t insult me. I have a fierce heart too, and I can be jealous myself. What does offend me is that he doesn’t love me at all. I tell you, he’s jealous now _on purpose_. Do you think I’m blind? Can’t I see? Just now he started on about that woman, about Katerina. She was this, she was that, she’d ordered a doctor from Moscow to try to save him, she’d ordered the best lawyer, the most learned one too. So he loves her, if he’ll sing her praises to my face. Shame on him! He’s treated me badly himself, so he went for me first, to make me the guilty one and put it all on me. ‘You were with your Pole before me, so I can’t be blamed over Katerina.’ That’s what it all comes to. He wants to dump the whole blame on me. He picked a quarrel on purpose, on purpose, I tell you, but I’ll—”
Grushenka never got to say what she would do. She hid her eyes in her handkerchief and broke into violent sobs.
“He doesn’t love Katerina Ivanovna,” Alyosha said firmly.

“Well, whether he loves her or not, I’ll find out soon enough,” said Grushenka, her voice turning threatening as she took the handkerchief from her eyes. Her face was twisted. Alyosha saw with sorrow that it had changed from mild and calm to sullen and spiteful.

“Enough of this nonsense,” she said suddenly. “That’s not what I sent for you about. Alyosha, darling, tomorrow—what is going to happen tomorrow? That’s what eats at me! And it eats at no one but me! I look around, and nobody is thinking about it. Nobody cares. Do you even think about it? Tomorrow he’s going on trial, you know. Tell me, how will they try him? You know it was the valet, the valet who killed him! Good heavens! Could they convict him in the valet’s place, with nobody to speak up for him? They haven’t bothered the valet at all, have they?”

“They questioned him hard,” Alyosha said thoughtfully, “but everyone came to the conclusion that it wasn’t him. He’s lying very sick now. He’s been ill ever since that fit. Really ill,” Alyosha added.
“Oh, dear! Couldn’t you go to that lawyer yourself and tell him the whole thing? They say he was brought down from Petersburg for three thousand roubles.”

“The three thousand came from the three of us together—Ivan, Katerina Ivanovna and me—but she paid the two thousand for the Moscow doctor herself. Fetyukovitch would have charged more, but the case is known all over Russia now. It’s discussed in every paper and journal. Fetyukovitch agreed to come mostly for the glory of it, since the case has become so notorious. I saw him yesterday.”
“Well? Did you speak to him?” Grushenka put in eagerly.
“He listened and said nothing. He told me he had already made up his mind. But he promised to give what I said some thought.”
“Some thought! Ah, they’re swindlers! They’ll be the ruin of him. And why did she send for the doctor?”
“As an expert witness. They want to prove that Mitya is insane and that he committed the murder without knowing what he was doing.” Alyosha smiled gently. “But Mitya won’t agree to that.”

“Yes, but it would be the truth, if he had killed him!” cried Grushenka. “He was mad then, completely mad, and that was my fault, wretch that I am! But of course he didn’t do it, he didn’t do it! And they’re all against him, the whole town. Even Fenya’s testimony went to show he’d done it. And the people at the shop, and that official, and at the tavern earlier, people heard him say it! They’re all, all against him, all shouting against him.”
“Yes, the evidence piles up terribly,” Alyosha remarked grimly.
“And Grigory—Grigory Vassilyevitch—sticks to his story that the door was open. He swears he saw it, and nothing will shake him. I went and talked to him myself. He was rude about it, too.”
“Yes, that may be the strongest evidence against him,” said Alyosha.

“And as for Mitya being mad, he certainly seems so now,” Grushenka began, looking oddly anxious and secretive. “Do you know, Alyosha, I’ve wanted to talk to you about this for ages. I go to see him every day and I’m just amazed by him. Tell me, what do you suppose he’s forever talking about? He goes on and on, and I can’t make anything of it. I thought it was something learned that I was too foolish to follow. Only then he suddenly started on about a babe—some child, that is. ‘Why is the babe poor?’ he said. ‘It’s for that babe that I’m going to Siberia now. I’m not a murderer, but I have to go to Siberia!’ What that meant, what babe, I couldn’t tell you for the life of me. I only cried when he said it, because he said it so sweetly. He cried himself, and I cried too. Then he suddenly kissed me and made the sign of the cross over me. What did it mean, Alyosha? Tell me. What is this babe?”
“It must be Rakitin, who’s been visiting him lately,” Alyosha said, smiling, “though ... this isn’t Rakitin’s doing. I didn’t see Mitya yesterday. I’ll see him today.”

“No, it isn’t Rakitin. It’s his brother, Ivan Fyodorovitch, who’s upsetting him. It’s his visits that do it, that’s what it is,” Grushenka began, and then stopped short. Alyosha stared at her in astonishment.
“Ivan visits him? Has he been there? Mitya told me himself that Ivan hasn’t come once.”

“There ... there! What a girl I am! Letting things slip!” cried Grushenka, flustered, blushing all at once. “Wait, Alyosha, hush! Since I’ve said this much, I’ll tell you the whole truth. He’s been to see him twice. The first time was the moment he arrived. He raced here from Moscow straight away, of course, before I got sick. The second time was a week ago. He told Mitya not to tell you about it, whatever happened, and not to tell anyone at all, really. He came in secret.”
Alyosha sat deep in thought, weighing something. The news had plainly made an impression on him.

“Ivan doesn’t talk to me about Mitya’s case,” he said slowly. “He’s hardly said a word to me these last two months. And every time I go to see him, he seems irritated that I’ve come, so I haven’t been near him for three weeks. H’m!... if he was there a week ago ... then there certainly has been a change in Mitya this week.”

“There has been a change,” Grushenka agreed quickly. “They’ve got a secret, they’ve got a secret! Mitya told me himself that there was a secret, and such a secret that Mitya can’t rest. Before that he was cheerful—and he is cheerful now, for that matter—but when he shakes his head like that, you know, and paces the room and keeps tugging at the hair on his right temple with his right hand, then I know something’s weighing on his mind.... I know! He was cheerful before, though, and he’s cheerful today, too.”
“But you just said he was worried.”

“Yes, he’s worried and cheerful both. One minute he’s irritable, then cheerful, then irritable again. And you know, Alyosha, I’m always amazed at him. With this terrible thing hanging over his head, he sometimes laughs at the most trifling things, like a baby himself.”
“And did he really tell you not to mention Ivan to me? Did he say, ‘Don’t tell him’?”

“Yes, he told me, ‘Don’t tell him.’ It’s you Mitya’s most afraid of. Because it’s a secret, and he said so himself. Alyosha, darling, go to him, find out what their secret is, and come and tell me,” Grushenka begged, suddenly eager. “Set my mind at rest, so I can know the worst that’s coming to me. That’s why I sent for you.”
“You think it concerns you? If it did, he wouldn’t have told you there was a secret.”
“I don’t know. Maybe he wants to tell me and doesn’t dare. He’s giving me a warning. There’s a secret, he says, but he won’t tell me what it is.”
“And what do you think?”

“What do I think? That it’s all over for me, that’s what. The three of them have been plotting to finish me, because Katerina’s part of it. It’s all Katerina, it all comes from her. She’s this and she’s that, which means I’m not. He tells me so in advance, to warn me. He plans to throw me over, that’s the whole secret. They’ve planned it together, the three of them—Mitya, Katerina and Ivan Fyodorovitch. Alyosha, I’ve wanted to ask you for ages. A week ago he suddenly told me that Ivan was in love with Katerina, because he goes to see her so often. Did he tell me the truth or not? Tell me, on your conscience, tell me the worst.”
“I won’t tell you a lie. I don’t think Ivan is in love with Katerina Ivanovna.”

“Oh, that’s what I thought! He’s lying to me, the shameless cheat, that’s all it is! And he was jealous of me just now so that he could put the blame on me afterward. He’s stupid, he can’t hide what he’s up to. He’s so open, you know.... But I’ll pay him back, I’ll pay him back! ‘You believe I did it,’ he said. He said that to me, to me. He threw that in my face! God forgive him! Just wait, I’ll make things hot for Katerina at the trial! I’ll say one little word then ... I’ll tell everything then!”
And she burst into bitter tears again.

“Here’s what I can tell you for certain, Grushenka,” said Alyosha, rising. “First, he loves you. He loves you more than anyone in the world, and you alone, believe me. I know. I do know. Second, I don’t want to pry his secret out of him. But if he tells me of his own accord today, I’ll say straight out that I’ve promised to tell you. Then I’ll come to you today and tell you. Only ... I think ... Katerina Ivanovna has nothing to do with it, and the secret is about something else. That’s certain. It doesn’t seem likely to me that it’s about Katerina Ivanovna. Goodbye for now.”

Alyosha shook her hand. Grushenka was still crying. He could see she put little faith in his comfort, but having had her cry and spoken of her trouble, she was the better for it. He was sorry to leave her in such a state, but he was pressed for time. He still had a great deal to do.

chapters.title: II. The Injured Foot
paragraphs: The first of these errands was at Madame Hohlakov’s house. He hurried over, wanting to get it done quickly so as not to be late for Mitya. Madame Hohlakov had been a little unwell for three weeks. For some reason her foot had swollen, and although she was not in bed, she lay all day half-reclining on the couch in her boudoir, in a fascinating but decorous _déshabillé_. Alyosha had noticed once, with innocent amusement, that despite her illness she had begun to take a good deal of trouble over her dress. Top-knots, ribbons and loose wrappers had appeared. He had an inkling why, though he pushed the thought away as frivolous. For the past two months the young official Perhotin had been calling at the house regularly.

Alyosha had not been there for four days, and he was in a hurry to go straight up to Lise, because she was the one he needed to talk to. Lise had sent a maid to him the day before with a special request that he come and see her “about something very important,” and for certain reasons that request interested Alyosha. But while the maid was gone to announce him to Lise, Madame Hohlakov heard from someone that he had arrived and at once sent a message begging him to come to her “for just one minute.” Alyosha decided it was best to give in to the mamma’s request, or else she would keep sending down to Lise’s room every minute he was there. Madame Hohlakov was lying on her couch. She was dressed with particular elegance and was obviously in a state of extreme nervous excitement. She greeted Alyosha with cries of rapture.

“It’s ages, ages, absolutely ages since I’ve seen you! A whole week—just think of it! Oh, but of course you were here only four days ago, on Wednesday. You’ve come for Lise. I’m sure you meant to creep up to her room on tiptoe so I wouldn’t hear you. My dear, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, if you only knew how worried I am about her! But we’ll come to that later, though it’s the most important thing, later. Dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, I trust my Lise to you completely. Since Father Zossima died—God rest his soul!” (she crossed herself)—“I’ve thought of you as a monk, even though you look so charming in your new suit. Wherever did you find a tailor like that in this town? No, no, that’s not the main thing—later. Forgive me for calling you Alyosha now and then; an old woman like me can take liberties,” she smiled coquettishly; “but that can wait as well. The important thing is that I don’t forget what’s important. Do remind me yourself. The minute my tongue runs away with me, you just say, ‘the important thing?’ Ach! How can I know now what matters most? Ever since Lise took back her promise—that childish promise, Alexey Fyodorovitch, to marry you—you’ve understood, of course, that it was only the playful whim of a sick child who’d been shut up in her chair for so long—thank God she can walk now!... And that new doctor Katya sent for from Moscow, for your unhappy brother, who tomorrow will—But why talk about tomorrow? The mere thought of tomorrow makes me ready to die. To die of curiosity.... That doctor was here yesterday and examined Lise.... I paid him fifty roubles for the visit. But that’s not the point, that’s not the point again. You see how I’m mixing everything up. I’m in such a rush. Why am I in a rush? I can’t make it out. It’s dreadful, the way I seem to be losing the power to understand anything. It all feels like one big tangle. I’m afraid you’re so bored that you’ll leap up and run off, and that will be the last I see of you. Goodness! Why are we sitting here without coffee? Yulia, Glafira, coffee!”
Alyosha hastened to thank her. He had only just had coffee, he said.
“Where?”
“At Agrafena Alexandrovna’s.”

“At ... at that woman’s? Oh, she’s the one who’s brought ruin on everybody. Not that I know anything about it. They say she’s turned into a saint, though it’s rather late in the day. She should have done it earlier. What good is it now? Hush, hush, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I have so much to tell you that I’m afraid I’ll end up telling you nothing. This awful trial ... I’m certainly going, I’m making arrangements. They’ll carry me there in my chair, and anyway I can sit up. I’ll have people with me. And, you know, I’m a witness. How am I to speak, how am I to speak? I don’t know what I’ll say. You have to swear an oath, don’t you?”
“Yes, but I don’t think you’ll be able to go.”

“I can sit up. Oh, you’ve muddled me! Oh, this trial, this savage deed, and then they’re all off to Siberia, some are getting married, and all of it so fast, so fast, everything changing, and in the end—nothing. Everybody grows old with death ahead of them. Well, so be it! I’m weary. This Katya, _cette charmante personne_, has let down all my hopes. Now she’s going to follow one of your brothers to Siberia, and your other brother is going to follow her and settle in the nearest town, and they’ll all torment one another. It drives me out of my mind. Worst of all is the publicity. The story has been told a million times in all the papers in Moscow and Petersburg. Oh, and would you believe it, one of them says I was ‘a dear friend’ of your brother’s ——, I can’t bring myself to say the horrid word. Just imagine, just imagine!”
“Impossible! Where did it appear? What did it say?”

“I’ll show you in a moment. I got the paper and read it yesterday. Here, in the Petersburg paper _Gossip_. It only started this year. I’m terribly fond of gossip, so I take it, and now it’s paying me back—so this is what gossip comes to! Here, this passage. Read it.”
And she handed Alyosha a sheet of newspaper that she had kept under her pillow.

She was not exactly upset so much as overwhelmed, and perhaps everything really was in a tangle in her head. The item was typical of its kind and must have been a great shock to her. But perhaps it was lucky that she could not hold her mind on any one subject just then. In a minute she might race off to something else and forget the newspaper altogether.

Alyosha knew very well that the story of the terrible case had spread over the whole of Russia. And, good heavens, what wild rumors about his brother, about the Karamazovs and about himself he had read during those two months, along with other equally credible news! One paper had gone so far as to say that he had entered a monastery and become a monk, out of horror at his brother’s crime. Another denied this and said that he and his elder, Father Zossima, had broken open the monastery chest and “made tracks from the monastery.” The piece in _Gossip_ carried the headline “The Karamazov Case at Skotoprigonyevsk.” (That, alas, was the name of our little town. Until now I had kept it secret.) It was short, and Madame Hohlakov was not named in it. In fact, no names appeared at all. It said merely that the criminal, whose coming trial was causing such a sensation—a retired army captain, an idle swaggerer and reactionary bully—was forever entangled in love affairs, and was a special favorite with certain ladies “who were pining in solitude.” One of these ladies, a pining widow who tried to look young although she had a grown-up daughter, was so infatuated with him that only two hours before the crime she had offered him three thousand roubles, if he would run away with her to the gold mines. But the criminal, counting on escaping punishment, had preferred to murder his father and take the three thousand rather than go off to Siberia with the middle-aged charms of his pining lady. This playful piece closed, naturally, with an outburst of generous indignation at the wickedness of parricide and at the recently abolished institution of serfdom. Alyosha read it with curiosity, then folded the paper and gave it back to Madame Hohlakov.

“Well, that’s me, of course,” she hurried on. “There’s no doubt I’m the one they mean. Not much more than an hour before it, I’d suggested gold mines to him, and now they say ‘middle-aged charms,’ as if that were my reason! He wrote that out of spite! May God Almighty forgive him for the middle-aged charms, as I forgive him! You know it’s— Do you know who it is? It’s your friend Rakitin.”
“Perhaps,” said Alyosha, “though I’ve heard nothing about it.”
“It’s him, it’s him! Don’t say ‘perhaps.’ You know I threw him out of my house.... You know the whole story, don’t you?”
“I know you asked him not to visit you anymore, but I haven’t heard why ... from you, at any rate.”
“Ah, so it was from him you heard it! He runs me down, I suppose, runs me down dreadfully?”
“Yes, he does; but then he abuses everybody. And I haven’t heard from him why you dropped him, either. I hardly ever see him now, in fact. We’re not friends.”

“Well, then, I’ll tell you everything. It can’t be helped, I’ll make a confession, since there is one point where I may have been at fault. Only a tiny, tiny point, so tiny that perhaps it doesn’t count. You see, my dear boy”—Madame Hohlakov suddenly turned arch, and a charming, enigmatic smile played on her lips—“you see, I suspect ... You must forgive me, Alyosha. I’m like a mother to you.... No, no, just the opposite. I’m speaking to you now as if you were my father—mother is quite out of place. Well, it’s as though I were confessing to Father Zossima, that’s exactly it. I called you a monk just now. So then, that poor young man, your friend Rakitin (Mercy on us! I can’t be angry with him. I’m cross, but not very), that frivolous young man, would you believe it, seems to have got it into his head that he’s in love with me. I only noticed later. At first, a month ago, he merely began coming to see me more often, nearly every day, though of course we knew each other before. I suspected nothing ... and then all at once it dawned on me, and I started noticing things, with astonishment. You know, two months ago that modest, charming, excellent young man, Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, who’s in the service here, became a regular visitor. You’ve met him here ever so many times yourself. And he’s such an excellent, serious young man, isn’t he? He comes once every three days, not daily (though I’d be glad to see him daily), and always so well dressed. In short, I love young people, Alyosha, talented and modest ones, like you. And he has nearly a statesman’s mind, he talks so charmingly, and I’ll certainly, certainly try to get him promoted. He’s a diplomat in the making. On that awful day he almost saved me from death by coming in the night. And your friend Rakitin turns up in such boots, and always stretches them out on the carpet.... Then he began to hint at his feelings, and one day as he was leaving he squeezed my hand terribly hard. My foot began to swell right after he’d pressed my hand like that. He’d met Pyotr Ilyitch here before, and would you believe it, he’s forever sneering at him, snarling at him, for no reason I can see. I simply watched the two of them together and laughed to myself. So I was sitting here alone—no, I was laid up then. Well, I was lying here alone when suddenly in comes Rakitin, and just imagine! He’d brought me some verses of his own writing—a little poem about my bad foot, that is, he’d described my foot in a poem. Wait a moment—how did it go?
A captivating little foot.

It began something like that. I can never remember poetry. I have it here. I’ll show it to you later. But it’s a charming piece—charming; and, you know, it isn’t only about the foot, it had a good moral too, a charming idea, only I’ve forgotten it; it was just right for an album, in fact. So of course I thanked him, and he was plainly flattered. I’d barely finished thanking him when in walks Pyotr Ilyitch, and Rakitin suddenly turned black as night. I could see Pyotr Ilyitch was in the way, since Rakitin obviously wanted to say something after handing me the verses. I had a presentiment of it; but there was Pyotr Ilyitch. I showed Pyotr Ilyitch the verses without saying who wrote them. But I’m convinced he guessed, though to this day he won’t admit it and swears he had no idea. He says that on purpose, though. Pyotr Ilyitch started laughing right away and began picking them apart. ‘Wretched doggerel,’ he called them, ‘some divinity student must have written them,’ and with such vehemence, such vehemence! Then, instead of laughing, your friend flew into a rage. ‘Good gracious!’ I thought, ‘they’ll go for each other.’ ‘I wrote them,’ he said. ‘I wrote them as a joke,’ he said, ‘because I think it’s degrading to write verses.... But they’re good poetry. They want to put up a monument to your Pushkin for writing about women’s feet, whereas I wrote mine with a moral purpose, and you,’ he said, ‘are a defender of serfdom. You have no humane ideas,’ he said. ‘You have no modern, enlightened feelings, progress hasn’t touched you, you’re a mere official,’ he said, ‘and you take bribes.’ Then I started screaming and pleading with them. And, you know, Pyotr Ilyitch is anything but a coward. He immediately put on the most gentlemanly tone, gave him a sarcastic look, heard him out, and apologized. ‘I had no idea,’ he said. ‘I wouldn’t have said it if I’d known. I’d have praised them. Poets are all so touchy,’ he said. In short, he mocked him under cover of that most gentlemanly tone. He explained to me afterwards that it was all sarcasm. I thought he meant it. Only, as I lay there, just as I’m lying before you now, I wondered, ‘Would it be the proper thing for me to throw Rakitin out for shouting so rudely at a visitor in my house, or would it not?’ And, would you believe it, I lay here with my eyes shut, wondering whether it would be proper or not. I worried and worried, my heart began to pound, and I couldn’t decide whether to raise an outcry or not. One voice seemed to tell me, ‘Speak,’ and the other, ‘No, don’t speak.’ And the moment the second voice had said that, I cried out, and fainted. Naturally, there was a commotion. I suddenly got up and said to Rakitin, ‘It pains me to say it, but I don’t wish to see you in my house again.’ So I threw him out. Ah! Alexey Fyodorovitch, I know very well I did wrong. I was putting it on. I wasn’t really angry with him at all; but I suddenly imagined—and that was what did it—what a fine scene it would make.... And yet, believe me, it came quite naturally, because I really did shed tears and cried for several days afterwards, and then one afternoon I suddenly forgot all about it. So it’s two weeks now since he’s been here, and I kept wondering whether he’d come back. I wondered even yesterday, and then last night this _Gossip_ arrived. I read it and gasped. Who could have written it? He must have. He went home, sat down, wrote it on the spot, sent it off, and they printed it. That was two weeks ago, you see. But, Alyosha, it’s dreadful how I go on talking and never say what I want to say. Ah! The words just come by themselves!”
“I really must get to my brother in time today,” Alyosha faltered.
“Of course, of course! You’ve just reminded me. Tell me, what is an aberration?”
“What aberration?” Alyosha asked, bewildered.
“In the legal sense. The kind of aberration that excuses everything. Whatever you do, they let you off at once.”
“What are you getting at?”

“I’ll tell you. This Katya ... Ah! She’s a charming, charming creature, but I can never make out who she’s in love with. She was here a while back and I couldn’t get a word out of her. All the more because now she only chats with me about trifles. It’s my health, my health, nothing else, and what a tone she takes with me! So I just said to myself, ‘Well, so be it. I don’t care’... Oh, yes. I was talking about aberration. The doctor has arrived. You know a doctor has arrived? Of course you do—the one who finds out who is mad. You sent for him. No, not you, it was Katya. It’s all Katya’s doing. Now, you see, a man can sit there perfectly sane and all at once have an aberration. He may be fully aware and know what he’s doing, and still be in a state of aberration. And there’s no doubt that Dmitri Fyodorovitch was suffering from aberration. People found out about aberration the moment the law courts were reformed. It’s all the fine result of the reformed courts. The doctor was here and asked me about that evening, about the gold mines. ‘How did he seem then?’ he asked. He must have been in a state of aberration. He burst in shouting, ‘Money, money, three thousand! Give me three thousand!’ and then he left and did the murder straight away. ‘I don’t want to murder him,’ he said, and suddenly he went and murdered him. That is why they will acquit him: he fought against it, and yet he murdered him.”
“But he didn’t murder him,” Alyosha cut in rather sharply. He was growing sicker and sicker with anxiety and impatience.
“Yes, yes, I know. It was that old man Grigory who murdered him.”
“Grigory?” Alyosha cried.
“Yes, yes, Grigory! He lay where Dmitri Fyodorovitch had knocked him down, then he got up, saw the door standing open, walked in and killed Fyodor Pavlovitch.”
“But why? Why?”

“From aberration. When he came round from the blow Dmitri Fyodorovitch gave him on the head, he was in a state of aberration, and he went and did the murder. As for his saying he didn’t, very likely he just doesn’t remember. Only, you know, it would be better, ever so much better, if it was Dmitri Fyodorovitch who murdered him. And that’s how it must have been, though I keep saying Grigory. It was certainly Dmitri Fyodorovitch, and that’s better, ever so much better! Oh! I don’t mean it’s better that a son should kill his father. I don’t defend that. Children should honor their parents. And yet it would be better if it were he, because then you’d have nothing to weep over, since he did it unconscious—or rather conscious, but without knowing what he was doing. Let them acquit him! That is so humane, and it would show what a blessing the reformed courts are. I knew nothing about all this, but they say the courts have been reformed for a long time. When I heard of it yesterday I was so struck that I wanted to send for you at once. And if he’s acquitted, make him come straight from the courtroom to dine with me. I’ll invite a party of friends and we’ll drink to the reformed courts. I don’t think he’d be dangerous. Besides, I’ll ask a great many friends, so that he could always be led out if he tried anything. And afterwards he could be made a justice of the peace or something in another town, since those who have been in trouble themselves make the best judges. And anyway, who isn’t suffering from aberration these days?—you, I, all of us are in a state of aberration, and there are plenty of examples. A man sits singing a song, something suddenly annoys him, he picks up a pistol and shoots the first person he sees, and nobody blames him. I read that recently, and all the doctors confirm it. The doctors are forever confirming; they’ll confirm anything. Why, my Lise is in a state of aberration. She made me cry again yesterday, and the day before, and today I suddenly saw that it’s all aberration. Oh, Lise grieves me so! I think she is completely mad. Why did she send for you? Did she send for you, or did you come of your own accord?”
“She sent for me, and I’m on my way to her now.” Alyosha rose, resolved.

“Oh, my dear, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, perhaps that’s the most important thing of all,” cried Madame Hohlakov, suddenly bursting into tears. “God knows I entrust Lise to you with all my heart, and I don’t mind that she sends for you on the sly, behind her mother’s back. But forgive me, I can’t so easily entrust my daughter to your brother Ivan Fyodorovitch, though I still take him for the most chivalrous young man. And just imagine, he’s been to see Lise, and I knew nothing about it!”
“What? How? When?” Alyosha was astonished. He had not sat down again but listened on his feet.

“I’ll tell you. Maybe that’s why I asked you here, though now I can’t think why I did. Well, Ivan Fyodorovitch has called on me twice since he came back from Moscow. The first time he came as a friend to pay a visit, and the second time Katya was here, and he came because he’d heard so. I never expected him to come often, of course, knowing how much he has on his hands already, _vous comprenez, cette affaire et la mort terrible de votre papa_. But then I suddenly learned he’d been here once more, not to see me but to see Lise. That was six days ago. He came, stayed five minutes and left. I only heard of it three days later, from Glafira, so it was a great shock. I sent for Lise at once. She laughed. ‘He thought you were asleep,’ she said, ‘and so he came in to ask me how you were.’ Of course, that must be how it was. But Lise, Lise, mercy on us, how she torments me! Would you believe it, one night four days ago, right after you had seen her for the last time and gone, she suddenly had a fit: screaming, shrieking, hysterics! Why do I never have hysterics? Then another fit the next day, and the same on the third, and yesterday too, and then yesterday that aberration. She suddenly yelled, ‘I hate Ivan Fyodorovitch. I insist that you never let him in the house again.’ These astonishing words struck me dumb, and I answered, ‘What grounds could I have for refusing to receive such an excellent young man, and so learned, and so unfortunate, too?’—for all this business is a misfortune, isn’t it? At my words she suddenly burst out laughing, so rudely, you know. Well, I was glad. I thought I’d amused her and the fits would stop, especially since I meant to refuse to receive Ivan Fyodorovitch in any case, because of his strange visits without my knowledge, and to ask him for an explanation. But early this morning Lise woke up and flew into a temper with Yulia and, would you believe it, slapped her face. It’s monstrous. I am always polite to my servants. And an hour later she was clasping Yulia’s feet and kissing them. She sent word that she wasn’t coming to me at all and would never come to see me again, and when I dragged myself down to her, she rushed to kiss me, weeping, and while she kissed me she pushed me out of the room, without a word, so that I couldn’t find out what was wrong. Now, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, all my hopes rest on you, and of course my whole life is in your hands. I simply beg you to go to Lise and learn everything from her, as only you can, and come back and tell me—me, her mother, for you understand it will be the death of me, simply the death of me, if this goes on, or else I shall run away. I can bear no more. I have patience, but I may lose it, and then ... then something terrible will happen. Ah, dear me! At last, Pyotr Ilyitch!” cried Madame Hohlakov, beaming all over as Perhotin came into the room. “You’re late, you’re late! Well, sit down, speak, relieve our suspense. What does the counsel say? Where are you going, Alexey Fyodorovitch?”
“To see Lise.”
“Oh, yes. You won’t forget, you won’t forget what I asked you, will you? It’s a matter of life and death!”
“Of course I won’t forget, if I can ... but I’m so late,” Alyosha muttered, hurrying off.
“No, you must, you must come back. Don’t say ‘If I can.’ I’ll die if you don’t,” Madame Hohlakov called after him, but Alyosha had already left the room.

chapters.title: III. A Little Demon
paragraphs: Going in to Lise, he found her half lying back in the invalid chair, the one she used to be wheeled around in when she couldn’t walk. She made no move to greet him. Her sharp, keen eyes simply stayed fastened on his face. There was a feverish look in them, and her face was pale and yellow. Alyosha was astonished at how she had changed in only three days. She had actually grown thinner. She did not offer him her hand. He touched her long, thin fingers where they lay motionless on her dress, and sat down opposite her without a word.
“I know you’re in a hurry to get to the prison,” Lise said shortly, “and Mamma has kept you there for hours, telling you about me and Yulia.”
“How do you know that?” asked Alyosha.
“I was listening. Why are you staring at me? I wanted to listen, so I did. What’s wrong with that? I won’t say sorry.”
“Has something upset you?”

“Quite the opposite, I’m very happy. For the thirtieth time I’ve just been thinking how lucky it is that I refused you and won’t be your wife. You’d make a hopeless husband. Say I married you, and then handed you a note for the man I loved after you. You’d take it, you’d certainly deliver it, and you’d bring his answer back, too. You could be forty and you’d still be running my love letters for me.”
Suddenly she laughed.
“You’re spiteful, and yet you’re open-hearted, too,” Alyosha said to her, smiling.

“The open-hearted part is that I’m not ashamed of myself in front of you. More than that, I don’t want to be ashamed in front of you, only you. Alyosha, why don’t I respect you? I’m very fond of you, but I don’t respect you. If I did, I couldn’t talk to you so shamelessly, could I?”
“No.”
“But do you believe I feel no shame with you?”
“No, I don’t believe that.”
Again Lise gave a nervous laugh, and she began to speak fast.
“I sent your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch some sweets in prison. You know, Alyosha, you’re rather pretty! I’m going to love you terribly for letting me stop loving you so quickly.”
“Why did you send for me today, Lise?”
“I wanted to tell you something I long for. I’d like somebody to torture me. To marry me and then torture me, to deceive me and leave. I don’t want to be happy.”
“You’re in love with chaos?”

“Yes, I want chaos. I keep wanting to burn the house down. I keep picturing how I’d creep up and set it alight on the sly. It has to be on the sly. They’d try to put it out, but it would keep burning. And I’d know, and say nothing. Ah, how silly! And how bored I am!”
She waved a hand, looking disgusted.
“It’s the soft life you lead,” Alyosha said gently.
“So being poor is better?”
“Yes, it is better.”

“That’s what your monk has taught you. It isn’t true. Let me be rich and everybody else poor. I’d eat sweets and drink cream and share with nobody. Ach, don’t talk, don’t say a word,” she shook her hand at him, though Alyosha hadn’t opened his mouth. “You’ve told me all this before. I know it by heart. It bores me. If I’m ever poor, I’ll murder someone, and if I’m rich, I might murder someone anyway, why just sit there? But do you know, I’d like to go reaping, to cut rye? I’ll marry you and you’ll turn into a peasant, a proper peasant. We’ll keep a colt, shall we? Do you know Kalganov?”
“Yes.”

“He’s forever drifting about, daydreaming. He says, ‘Why live in real life? Dreaming is better. You can dream up the loveliest things, but real life is a bore.’ And yet he’ll be married soon enough. He’s already been courting me. Can you spin a top?”
“Yes.”

“Well, he’s exactly like a top. He needs winding up and setting spinning, and then lashing, lashing, lashing with a whip. If I marry him, I’ll keep him spinning his whole life. You’re not ashamed to be with me?”
“No.”
“You’re terribly cross with me because I don’t talk about holy things. I don’t want to be holy. What do they do to you in the next world for the very worst sin? You ought to know all about that.”
“God will condemn you.” Alyosha watched her steadily.
“That’s just what I’d like. I’d walk up, they’d condemn me, and I’d burst out laughing in their faces. I’d dearly love to burn the house down, Alyosha, our house. You still don’t believe me?”
“Why wouldn’t I? There are children of twelve years old who long to set fire to something, and they really do set things on fire, too. It’s a kind of sickness.”
“That isn’t true, it isn’t! There may be children like that, but that’s not what I mean.”
“You mistake evil for good. It’s a crisis that will pass. Maybe it comes from your illness.”
“So you do despise me! It’s just that I don’t want to do good, I want to do evil. It has nothing to do with illness.”
“Why do evil?”

“So that everything would be destroyed. Ah, how lovely it would be if everything were destroyed! You know, Alyosha, sometimes I think of doing a terrible amount of harm, every bad thing there is. I’d keep doing it quietly for a long time, and then suddenly everybody would find out. They’d all stand around pointing at me, and I’d look back at them. That would be awfully nice. Why would it be so nice, Alyosha?”
“I don’t know. It’s a craving to wreck something good or, as you put it, to set something on fire. It happens at times.”
“I’m not only saying it, I’ll do it.”
“I believe you.”
“Ah, how I love you for saying you believe me. And you’re not lying even a little. But maybe you think I’m saying all this deliberately, to annoy you?”
“No, I don’t think so... although maybe there is a small wish to annoy me in it.”
“A small one, yes. I can never lie to you,” she declared, with a strange fire in her eyes.

What struck Alyosha most of all was how earnest she was. Not a trace of humor or teasing showed in her face now, though in the old days her fun and gaiety never left her, even at her most “earnest” moments.
“There are moments when people love crime,” Alyosha said thoughtfully.

“Yes, yes! You’ve put my own thought into words. They love crime, everybody loves crime, and always, not just at some ‘moments.’ It’s as if people had agreed together to lie about it, and have been lying ever since. They all say they hate evil, but in secret they all love it.”
“And are you still reading those nasty books?”
“Yes. Mamma reads them and hides them under her pillow, and I steal them.”
“Aren’t you ashamed, ruining yourself like that?”

“I want to ruin myself. There’s a boy here who lay down between the railway lines while a train went over. Lucky fellow! Listen, your brother is on trial now for killing his father, and everybody loves the fact that he killed his father.”
“Loves the fact that he killed his father?”
“Yes, loves it! Everybody does! They all say it’s so dreadful, but secretly they just love it. I, for one, love it.”
“There’s some truth in what you say about everybody,” Alyosha said softly.

“Oh, the ideas you have!” Lise shrieked with delight. “And you a monk! You can’t think how much I respect you, Alyosha, for never telling lies. Oh, I must tell you a funny dream I have. Sometimes I dream of devils. It’s night, I’m in my room with a candle, and suddenly devils are everywhere, in every corner, under the table. They open the doors, and a crowd of them stands behind the doors, wanting to come in and grab me. They’re just coming, just grabbing me. But suddenly I make the sign of the cross, and they all shrink back, though they don’t leave altogether. They wait at the doors and in the corners. Then a terrible longing comes over me to curse God out loud, and so I start, and they come crowding back, delighted, and grab me again. I cross myself again and they all shrink back. It’s awful fun. It takes your breath away.”
“I’ve had that same dream,” said Alyosha suddenly.
“Have you really?” cried Lise, surprised. “Listen, Alyosha, don’t laugh, this is terribly important. Can two different people have the same dream?”
“Apparently they can.”

“Alyosha, I’m telling you, it’s terribly important,” Lise went on, with truly excessive astonishment. “The dream isn’t what matters. What matters is that you had the same dream as me. You never lie to me, so don’t lie now. Is it true? You’re not laughing at me?”
“It’s true.”
Lise seemed extraordinarily struck, and for half a minute she said nothing.
“Alyosha, come and see me, come more often,” she said suddenly, in a begging voice.
“I’ll come to see you all my life,” Alyosha answered firmly.

“You’re the only person I can talk to, you know,” Lise began again. “I talk to nobody except myself and you. You alone in the whole world. And I talk to you more easily than to myself. And I’m not at all ashamed with you, not at all. Alyosha, why am I not ashamed with you, not at all? Alyosha, is it true that at Easter the Jews steal a child and kill it?”
“I don’t know.”

“There’s a book here where I read about the trial of a Jew. He took a child of four years old and cut the fingers off both hands. Then he crucified him on a wall, hammered nails into him and crucified him, and afterwards, at his trial, he said the child had died soon, within four hours. ‘Soon,’ he called that! He said the child moaned and went on moaning, and he stood there admiring it. That’s nice!”
“Nice?”
“Yes, nice. Sometimes I imagine I’m the one who crucified him. He hangs there moaning, and I sit across from him eating pineapple _compote_. I’m awfully fond of pineapple _compote_. Are you?”
Alyosha looked at her without speaking. Her pale, sallow face suddenly twisted, and her eyes burned.

“You know, after I read about that Jew, I sobbed and shook the whole night. I kept imagining how the poor little thing cried and moaned (a child of four understands, you know), and all the time I couldn’t get the pineapple _compote_ out of my head. In the morning I wrote a letter to a certain person, begging him _especially_ to come and see me. He came, and I suddenly told him everything about the child and the pineapple _compote_. _Everything_, _everything_, and I said it was nice. He laughed and said it really was nice. Then he got up and left. He was here only five minutes. Did he despise me? Did he despise me? Tell me, tell me, Alyosha, did he despise me or not?” She sat up on the couch, her eyes flashing.
“Tell me,” Alyosha asked anxiously, “was it you who sent for that person?”
“Yes, me.”
“You sent him a letter?”
“Yes.”
“Only to ask about that, about that child?”
“No, nothing to do with that. But as soon as he arrived, I asked him about it. He answered me, laughed, stood up and left.”
“That person behaved honorably,” Alyosha murmured.
“And did he despise me? Did he laugh at me?”
“No, because maybe he believes in the pineapple _compote_ himself. He’s very ill just now, too, Lise.”
“Yes, he does believe in it,” said Lise, her eyes flashing.
“He despises nobody,” Alyosha went on. “It’s only that he believes nobody. And if he doesn’t believe in people, then of course he does despise them.”
“So he despises me, me?”
“You, too.”
“Good,” said Lise, as if grinding her teeth. “When he walked out laughing, I felt that being despised was nice. The child with his fingers cut off is nice, and being despised is nice...”
And she laughed in Alyosha’s face, a feverish, spiteful laugh.

“Do you know, Alyosha, do you know, I’d like—Alyosha, save me!” She suddenly leaped from the couch, rushed at him and grabbed him with both hands. “Save me!” she almost groaned. “Is there anyone in the world I could tell what I’ve told you? I’ve told you the truth, the truth. I’m going to kill myself, because I loathe everything! I don’t want to live, because I loathe everything! I loathe everything, everything. Alyosha, why don’t you love me even a little?” she ended in a frenzy.
“But I do love you!” Alyosha answered warmly.
“And will you weep for me, will you?”
“Yes.”
“Not because I won’t be your wife, but just weep for me?”
“Yes.”

“Thank you! Your tears are all I want. Let everyone else punish me and trample me underfoot, everyone, everyone, _anyone_ at all. Because I don’t love anyone. Do you hear, not anyone! On the contrary, I hate him! Go, Alyosha. It’s time you went to your brother”; and she suddenly tore herself away from him.
“How can I leave you like this?” said Alyosha, almost alarmed.
“Go to your brother, the prison will close. Go, here’s your hat. Give Mitya my love, go, go!”

And she almost forced Alyosha out the door by pushing him. He looked at her in pained surprise, and then he noticed a letter in his right hand, a tiny letter folded tight and sealed. He glanced at it and read the address at once: “To Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov.” He looked quickly at Lise. Her face had turned almost threatening.
“Give it to him, you must give it to him!” she ordered, trembling and beside herself. “Today, right now, or I’ll poison myself! That’s why I sent for you.”

And she slammed the door at once. The bolt clicked. Alyosha put the note in his pocket and went straight downstairs without returning to Madame Hohlakov. In fact, he forgot her. As soon as he had gone, Lise unbolted the door, opened it a crack, stuck her finger in the gap and slammed the door with all her strength, crushing her finger. Ten seconds later she pulled her finger free, walked slowly and softly back to her chair, sat bolt upright in it, and stared hard at her blackened finger and at the blood seeping out from under the nail. Her lips were trembling, and she kept whispering rapidly to herself:
“I’m a wretch, wretch, wretch, wretch!”

chapters.title: IV. A Hymn And A Secret
paragraphs: It was quite late when Alyosha rang at the prison gate. Days are short in November, and dusk was already coming on. But Alyosha knew he would be let in without trouble. Our little town handled such things the way every town does. At first, once the preliminary inquiry was over, relatives and a few other people could see Mitya only after going through certain unavoidable formalities. Later the formalities stayed in place, but exceptions were made for some of Mitya’s visitors, at least. In fact, the meetings with the prisoner in the room set aside for them were sometimes practically _tête-à-tête_.

These exceptions were few, though. Only Grushenka, Alyosha and Rakitin were treated this way. The police captain, Mihail Mihailovitch, was very favorably inclined toward Grushenka. The way he had abused her at Mokroe lay heavy on the old man’s conscience, and when he learned the whole story he changed his opinion of her entirely. And strange to say, he was firmly convinced of Mitya’s guilt, yet once Mitya was in prison the old man judged him more and more mildly. “Perhaps he was a good-hearted man,” he thought, “who came to grief through drink and dissipation.” His first horror had turned into pity. As for Alyosha, the captain was very fond of him and had known him for a long time. Rakitin had recently begun visiting the prisoner very often. He was one of the closest acquaintances of “the police captain’s young ladies,” as the captain called them, and was always hanging about their house. He also gave lessons at the house of the prison superintendent. The superintendent was strict in carrying out his duties, but he was a kind old man. Alyosha had known him well for years, and the old man liked talking with him, usually about sacred subjects. He respected Ivan Fyodorovitch and stood in awe of his opinion, though he was a great philosopher himself, “self-taught,” of course. But Alyosha drew him irresistibly. This past year the old man had started studying the Apocryphal Gospels, and he was forever discussing his impressions with his young friend. He used to visit Alyosha at the monastery and talk for hours with him and with the monks. So even when Alyosha came late to the prison, he only had to go to the superintendent and everything was made easy. Besides, everyone in the prison, down to the lowliest warder, had grown used to Alyosha. And the sentry, naturally, gave him no trouble so long as the authorities were satisfied.

When Mitya was called from his cell, he always came down to the place set aside for interviews. As Alyosha entered the room, he found Rakitin just taking his leave of Mitya. Both were talking loudly. Mitya was laughing heartily as he saw Rakitin out, while Rakitin seemed to be grumbling. Rakitin did not like meeting Alyosha, especially lately. He hardly spoke to him and gave him a stiff bow. Seeing Alyosha come in, he frowned and looked away, as if he were completely taken up with buttoning his big, warm, fur-trimmed overcoat. Then he began hunting at once for his umbrella.
“I’d better be careful not to forget my things,” he muttered, just to say something.
“And be careful not to forget other people’s things,” said Mitya as a joke, and laughed right away at his own wit. Rakitin flared up at once.
“Save that advice for your own family, a slave-driving bunch if there ever was one, and don’t give it to Rakitin,” he cried, suddenly shaking with rage.

“What’s the matter? I was joking!” cried Mitya. “Damn it all! They’re all like that,” he said to Alyosha, nodding toward Rakitin’s fast-retreating back. “He sat here laughing and cheerful, and all at once he boils over like that. He didn’t even nod to you. Have you broken with him completely? And why are you so late? I haven’t just been waiting for you, I’ve been thirsting for you the whole morning. But never mind. We’ll make up for it now.”
“Why does he come here so often? You can’t be such great friends,” said Alyosha. He, too, nodded at the door where Rakitin had gone out.

“Great friends with Rakitin? No, not that much. Could I be, with a pig like that? He thinks I’m ... a blackguard. And they can’t take a joke, either. That’s the worst thing about people like him. They never understand a joke, and their souls are dry, dry and flat. They remind me of the prison walls the day I was first brought here. But he’s a clever fellow, very clever. Well, Alexey, it’s all over with me now.”
He sat down on the bench and made Alyosha sit beside him.
“Yes, the trial’s tomorrow. Are you so without hope, brother?” Alyosha said, uneasy at heart.

“What are you talking about?” said Mitya, giving him a rather uncertain look. “Oh, the trial, you mean! Damn it all! Up to now we’ve talked only about things that don’t matter, about this trial, and I haven’t said a word to you about the main thing. Yes, the trial is tomorrow. But it wasn’t the trial I meant when I said it was all over with me. Why are you looking at me so critically?”
“What do you mean, Mitya?”
“Ideas, ideas, nothing but ideas! Ethics! What is ethics?”
“Ethics?” Alyosha asked, puzzled.
“Yes. Is it a science?”
“Yes, there is such a science ... but ... to tell the truth, I can’t explain to you what kind of science it is.”

“Rakitin knows. Rakitin knows plenty, damn him! He’s not going to be a monk. He means to go to Petersburg. There he’ll take up criticism with an uplifting tendency. Who knows, he may be useful and make a career for himself, too. Ough! They’re first-rate at making careers, these people! Damn ethics, I’m done for, Alexey, I am, you man of God! I love you more than anyone. My heart aches just looking at you. Who was Karl Bernard?”
“Karl Bernard?” Alyosha was surprised again.
“No, not Karl. Wait, I got it wrong. Claude Bernard. What was he? A chemist, or what?”
“He must be a scholar,” Alyosha answered. “But I can’t tell you much about him either. I’ve heard of him as a scholar, but I don’t know what kind.”

“Well, the hell with him, then! I don’t know either,” swore Mitya. “A scoundrel of some sort, most likely. They’re all scoundrels. And Rakitin will make his way. Rakitin will get on anywhere; he’s another Bernard. Ugh, these Bernards! They’re everywhere.”
“But what’s wrong?” Alyosha pressed him.

“He wants to write an article about me, about my case, and start his literary career with it. That’s why he comes; he said so himself. He wants to prove some theory. He wants to say, ‘He couldn’t help murdering his father; he was corrupted by his environment,’ and so on. He explained it all to me. He’s going to add a tinge of Socialism, he says. But damn the fellow, he can add a tinge if he likes, I don’t care. He can’t bear Ivan, he hates him. He’s not fond of you, either. But I don’t throw him out, because he’s a clever fellow. Awfully conceited, though. I told him just now, ‘The Karamazovs aren’t blackguards but philosophers, because all true Russians are philosophers. And though you’ve studied, you’re no philosopher—you’re a low fellow.’ He laughed, so spitefully. And I said to him, ‘_De ideabus non est disputandum_.’ Not bad, eh? You see, I can pass myself off as a classicist!” Mitya suddenly laughed.
“Why is it all over with you? You said so a minute ago,” Alyosha put in.
“Why is it all over with me? H’m!... The thing is ... when you take it all together, I’m sorry to lose God. That’s why.”
“What do you mean, ‘sorry to lose God’?”

“Imagine this: inside, in the nerves, in the head—that is, these nerves are there in the brain ... (damn them!) there are sort of little tails, the little tails of those nerves, and the moment they start quivering ... that is, you see, I look at something with my eyes, and then they start quivering, those little tails ... and when they quiver, an image appears ... it doesn’t appear at once, but an instant goes by, a second ... and then something like a moment appears; that is, not a moment—devil take the moment!—but an image; that is, an object, or an action, damn it! That’s why I see and then think, because of those tails, and not at all because I have a soul, or because I’m some kind of image and likeness. All that is nonsense! Rakitin explained it all to me yesterday, brother, and it simply knocked me flat. It’s magnificent, Alyosha, this science! A new man is arising—that I understand.... And yet I’m sorry to lose God!”
“Well, that at least is a good thing,” said Alyosha.

“That I’m sorry to lose God? It’s chemistry, brother, chemistry! Nothing to be done about it, your reverence, you’ll have to move over and make room for chemistry. And Rakitin certainly dislikes God. Ough! Doesn’t he dislike Him! That’s the sore point with all of them. But they hide it. They lie. They pretend. ‘Will you preach this in your reviews?’ I asked him. ‘Oh, if I did it openly, they wouldn’t let it through,’ he said. He laughed. ‘But what will become of men then,’ I asked him, ‘without God and immortal life? All things are lawful then, they can do what they like?’ ‘Didn’t you know that?’ he said, laughing. ‘A clever man can do what he likes,’ he said. ‘A clever man knows his way around. But you put your foot in it by committing a murder, and now you’re rotting in prison.’ He says that to my face! A regular pig! I used to kick such people out, and now I listen to them. He talks a lot of sense, too. Writes well. Last week he started reading me an article of his. I copied out three lines of it. Wait a minute. Here it is.”
Mitya hurriedly pulled a scrap of paper from his pocket and read:
“‘To settle this question, it is above all essential to put one’s personality in contradiction with one’s reality.’ Do you understand that?”
“No, I don’t,” said Alyosha. He looked at Mitya and listened to him with curiosity.

“Neither do I. It’s murky and obscure, but intellectual. ‘Everybody writes like that now,’ he says, ‘it’s the effect of their environment.’ They’re afraid of the environment. He writes poetry, too, the rascal. He’s written some in honor of Madame Hohlakov’s foot. Ha ha ha!”
“I’ve heard about that,” said Alyosha.
“You have? And have you heard the poem?”
“No.”

“I’ve got it. Here it is. I’ll read it to you. You don’t know this—I haven’t told you—there’s quite a story behind it. He’s a rascal! Three weeks ago he started teasing me. ‘You’ve landed yourself in a mess, like a fool, over three thousand, but I’m going to grab a hundred and fifty thousand. I’m going to marry a widow and buy a house in Petersburg.’ And he told me he was courting Madame Hohlakov. She never had much brains, even in her youth, and now at forty she’s lost what she had. ‘But she’s awfully sentimental,’ he says. ‘That’s how I’ll get her. When I’ve married her, I’ll take her to Petersburg and start a newspaper there.’ And his mouth was simply watering, the beast, and not for the widow but for the hundred and fifty thousand. He made me believe it, too. He came to see me every day. ‘She’s coming round,’ he told me, beaming with delight. And then, all of a sudden, he was thrown out of the house. Perhotin’s carrying everything before him, bravo! I could kiss the silly old noodle for throwing him out. And Rakitin had already written this doggerel. ‘It’s the first time I’ve dirtied my hands writing poetry,’ he said. ‘It’s to win her heart, so it’s for a good cause. Once I’ve got hold of the silly woman’s fortune, I can be of great social use.’ They always have this social excuse for every nasty thing they do! ‘At any rate, it’s better than your Pushkin’s poetry,’ he said, ‘because I’ve managed to preach enlightenment even in that.’ I understand what he means about Pushkin, I quite see it, if Pushkin really was a man of talent and wrote only about women’s feet. But wasn’t Rakitin puffed up about his doggerel! The vanity of these fellows! ‘On the Recovery of the Swollen Foot of the Object of My Affections’—that’s the title he came up with. He’s a waggish fellow.
A captivating little foot, Though swollen and red and tender! The doctors come and plasters put, But still they cannot mend her.
Yet it’s not for her foot I dread— A theme for Pushkin’s muse more fit— It’s not her foot, it is her head: I tremble for her loss of wit!
For as her foot swells, strange to say, Her intellect is on the wane— Oh, for some remedy I pray That may restore both foot and brain!
He’s a pig, a regular pig, but he’s a sly one, the rascal! And he really has managed to slip in a progressive idea. And wasn’t he furious when she kicked him out! He ground his teeth!”
“He’s taken his revenge already,” said Alyosha. “He’s written a paragraph about Madame Hohlakov.”
And Alyosha told him briefly about the paragraph in _Gossip_.

“That’s his work, that’s his work!” Mitya agreed, frowning. “That’s him! These paragraphs ... I know them ... the insulting things that have been written about Grushenka, for instance.... And about Katya, too.... H’m!”
He crossed the room with a tormented air.

“Brother, I can’t stay long,” Alyosha said after a pause. “Tomorrow will be a great and terrible day for you. The judgment of God will be carried out ... and I’m amazed at you. You walk about here, talking about I don’t know what ...”

“No, don’t be amazed at me,” Mitya broke in warmly. “Am I supposed to talk about that stinking dog? About the murderer? We’ve talked enough about him. I don’t want to say another word about the stinking son of Stinking Lizaveta! God will kill him, you’ll see. Hush!”
He went up to Alyosha in excitement and kissed him. His eyes glowed.

“Rakitin wouldn’t understand this,” he began in a kind of exaltation. “But you, you’ll understand it all. That’s why I was thirsting for you. You see, there’s so much I’ve wanted to tell you for ever so long, here, inside these peeling walls. But I haven’t said a word about what matters most. The moment never seemed to come. Now I can’t wait any longer. I have to pour my heart out to you. Brother, in these last two months I’ve found a new man in myself. A new man has risen up in me. He was hidden inside me, and he would never have come to the surface if it hadn’t been for this blow from heaven. I’m afraid! And what do I care if I spend twenty years in the mines, breaking ore with a hammer? I’m not afraid of that at all. It’s something else I’m afraid of now: that the new man may leave me. Even there, in the mines, underground, I may find a human heart in another convict and murderer next to me, and I may make friends with him. Even there a man can live and love and suffer. You can thaw and revive a frozen heart in that convict, you can wait on him for years, and at last bring up from the dark depths a lofty soul, a feeling, suffering creature. You can bring forth an angel, create a hero! There are so many of them, hundreds of them, and we’re all to blame for them. Why did I dream of that ‘babe’ at such a moment? ‘Why is the babe so poor?’ That was a sign to me at that moment. It’s for the babe that I’m going. Because we’re all responsible for all. For all the ‘babes,’ because there are big children as well as little children. All are ‘babes.’ I go for all, because someone has to go for all. I didn’t kill father, but I have to go. I accept it. It all came to me here, here, inside these peeling walls. There are masses of them down there, hundreds of them underground, with hammers in their hands. Oh, yes, we’ll be in chains and there’ll be no freedom, but then, in our great sorrow, we’ll rise again to joy, without which man cannot live nor God exist, for God gives joy: it’s His privilege—a grand one. Ah, man should be dissolved in prayer! What would I be down there underground without God? Rakitin’s laughing! If they drive God from the earth, we’ll shelter Him underground. A man can’t exist in prison without God; it’s even more impossible than outside prison. And then we men underground will sing out of the bowels of the earth a glorious hymn to God, with Whom is joy. Hail to God and His joy! I love Him!”
Mitya was fighting for breath as this wild speech burst out of him. He had turned white, his lips shook, and tears ran down his face.

“Yes, life is full. There’s life even underground,” he started again. “You won’t believe it, Alexey, but how I want to live now! Inside these peeling walls a hunger for existence and awareness has come over me. Rakitin can’t grasp that. All he wants is to build a house and rent out apartments. But you, I’ve been longing for you. And what is suffering anyway? I’m not afraid of it, even if there were no end to it. I’m not afraid of it now. I was before. Do you know, maybe I won’t answer at the trial at all.... And I seem to have such strength in me now that I think I could bear anything, any pain at all, as long as I can say it to myself every moment: ‘I exist.’ In a thousand agonies—I exist. Stretched on the rack—I exist! Though I sit alone on top of a pillar—I exist! I see the sun, and if I can’t see the sun, I know it’s there. And a whole life lies in that, in knowing the sun is there. Alyosha, my angel, all these philosophies are the death of me. Damn them! Brother Ivan—”
“What about Ivan?” Alyosha broke in, but Mitya didn’t hear.

“You see, I never had any of these doubts before. They were buried in me. Maybe it was exactly because ideas I couldn’t understand were boiling up inside me that I drank and brawled and raged. I wanted to choke them down, quiet them, smother them. Ivan isn’t Rakitin. There’s an idea in him. Ivan is a sphinx, and he says nothing. He’s always silent. It’s God who worries me. Nothing else worries me but that. What if He doesn’t exist? What if Rakitin is right and God is only an idea men invented? Then, without Him, man is lord of the earth and of the whole universe. Magnificent! Only how is man going to be good without God? That’s the question. I keep coming back to it. Who will man love, then? Who will he thank? Who will he sing the hymn to? Rakitin laughs. Rakitin says you can love humanity without God. Well, only a sniveling idiot could say so. I can’t make sense of it. Life’s easy for Rakitin. ‘Better think about extending civil rights, or about holding down the price of meat. That’s a simpler, more direct way to show your love for humanity than philosophy.’ And I told him, ‘Well, you without a God are the very man who’d raise the price of meat, if it suited you, and squeeze a rouble out of every kopeck.’ He lost his temper. But after all, what is goodness? Answer me that, Alexey. Goodness is one thing to me and another to a Chinese man, so it’s relative. Or isn’t it? Isn’t it relative? A treacherous question! Don’t laugh when I tell you it’s kept me awake two nights. What amazes me now is that people can go on living and never give it a thought. Vanity! Ivan has no God. He has an idea. It’s beyond me. But he says nothing. I think he must be a Freemason. I asked him, and he said nothing. I wanted to drink from the springs of his soul—and he was silent. Only once did he let a word slip.”
“What did he say?” Alyosha asked at once.

“I said to him, ‘So everything is lawful, if that’s the case?’ He frowned. ‘Fyodor Pavlovitch, our papa,’ he said, ‘was a pig, but his ideas were sound enough.’ That’s what slipped out of him, and that’s all he said. That beats Rakitin by a mile.”
“Yes,” Alyosha agreed bitterly. “When was he here?”

“Later, I’ll tell you that later. Now I have to talk about something else. I haven’t told you anything about Ivan till now. I kept it for last. When all this is over here and the verdict is in, then I’ll tell you something. I’ll tell you everything. There’s something tremendous between us.... And you will be my judge in it. But don’t start on that now. Keep quiet. You talk about tomorrow, about the trial, but would you believe it, I know nothing about it.”
“Have you spoken with your lawyer?”

“What good is a lawyer? I told him the whole story. He’s a soft, city-bred rogue—a Bernard! And he doesn’t believe me, not a bit. Imagine, he thinks I did it. I can see it. ‘In that case,’ I asked him, ‘why did you come to defend me?’ Hang the lot of them! They’ve even brought in a doctor to prove I’m mad. I won’t stand for that! And Katerina Ivanovna means to do her ‘duty’ to the end, whatever it costs her!” Mitya smiled bitterly. “That cat! That hard-hearted creature! She knows I said at Mokroe that she was a woman of ‘great wrath.’ It was repeated to her. Yes, the facts against me now are as many as the sands of the sea. Grigory holds to his story. Grigory is honest, but a fool. Plenty of people are honest because they’re fools. That’s Rakitin’s notion. Grigory is my enemy. And some people are worth more as enemies than as friends. I mean Katerina Ivanovna. I’m afraid, oh, I’m afraid she’ll tell about how she bowed down to the ground over that four thousand. She’ll pay it back to the last farthing. I don’t want her sacrifice. They’ll shame me at the trial. I wonder how I’ll bear it. Go to her, Alyosha, and ask her not to bring that up in court. Can you do that? But the devil take it, it doesn’t matter! I’ll get through somehow. I don’t pity her. She’s done it to herself. She’s earned what she gets. I’ll have my own story to tell, Alexey.” He smiled bitterly again. “Only ... only Grusha, Grusha! Good Lord! Why must she suffer like this?” he cried out suddenly, in tears. “Grusha is killing me. Just thinking of her is killing me, killing me. She was with me a little while ago....”
“She told me you hurt her badly today.”
“I know. Damn my temper! It was jealousy. I was sorry. I kissed her when she left. But I didn’t ask her to forgive me.”
“Why didn’t you?” Alyosha cried.
All at once Mitya laughed, almost cheerfully.

“May God spare you, my dear boy, from ever asking pardon for some fault from a woman you love. Above all from a woman you love, however badly you were in the wrong. Because a woman—who the devil can make out a woman? I know a little about them, at least. But just try owning up to a woman that you’re at fault. Say, ‘I’m sorry, forgive me,’ and the reproaches come down like rain! She won’t simply and plainly forgive you, not for anything. She’ll grind you into the dust, haul out things that never happened, call up everything, forget nothing, add some of her own, and only then forgive you. And even the best of them, the very best, do this. She’ll scrape together every last scrap and pile it on your head. They’d skin you alive, I tell you, every one of them, these angels we can’t live without! I say it plainly and openly, dear boy: every decent man ought to be under some woman’s thumb. That’s my conviction—no, not conviction, my feeling. A man should be magnanimous, and there’s no disgrace in it for him! No disgrace for a hero, not even for a Cæsar! But all the same, never beg her pardon for anything. Remember that rule from your brother Mitya, who’s been ruined by women. No, I’d better make it up to Grusha some other way, without begging pardon. I worship her, Alexey, I worship her. Only she doesn’t see it. No, she still thinks I don’t love her enough. And she tortures me, tortures me with her love. The past was nothing! Back then it was only those infernal curves of hers that tortured me. But now I’ve taken her whole soul into mine, and through her I’ve become a man myself. Will they let us marry? If they don’t, I’ll die of jealousy. Every day I imagine something.... What did she say to you about me?”
Alyosha told him everything Grushenka had said to him that day. Mitya listened, made him go over certain things again, and seemed pleased.

“So she isn’t angry that I’m jealous?” he cried. “There’s a woman for you! ‘I’ve a fierce heart myself!’ Ah, I love such fierce hearts, though I can’t stand anyone being jealous of me. I can’t take it. We’ll fight. But I’ll love her, I’ll love her without end. Will they let us marry? Do they let convicts marry? That’s the question. And I can’t exist without her....”
Mitya crossed the room with a frown. It was nearly dark. All at once he seemed terribly uneasy.

“So there’s a secret, she says, a secret? We’ve hatched a plot against her, and Katya’s in it, she thinks. No, my good Grushenka, that’s not it. You’re far off the mark, with your silly woman’s ideas. Alyosha, darling, well, here goes! I’ll tell you our secret!”

He glanced around, stepped quickly up to Alyosha, who was standing in front of him, and whispered with an air of mystery, though in truth no one could hear them. The old warder was dozing in his corner, and not a word could reach the soldiers on guard.

“I’ll tell you our whole secret,” Mitya whispered in a rush. “I meant to tell you later. How could I decide anything without you? You’re everything to me. I say Ivan is above us, but you are my angel. Your decision will be the one that settles it. Maybe it’s you who are above us and not Ivan. You see, it’s a matter of conscience, of the higher conscience—the secret is so important I can’t settle it myself, and I’ve held it back until I could talk to you. Still, it’s too early to decide now, since we have to wait for the verdict. The moment the verdict comes, you’ll decide my fate. Don’t decide now. I’ll tell you now. You listen, but don’t decide. Stand there and keep still. I won’t tell you all of it. I’ll just give you the idea, no details, and you keep still. No questions, no moving. Agreed? But good heavens, what am I going to do about your eyes? I’m afraid your eyes will tell me your decision even if you say nothing. Oh! I’m afraid! Alyosha, listen! Ivan proposes that I _escape_. I won’t give you the details. It’s all been thought through, it can all be arranged. Hush, don’t decide. I’d go to America with Grusha. You know I can’t live without Grusha! What if they won’t let her follow me to Siberia? Do they let convicts get married? Ivan thinks not. And without Grusha, what would I do down there underground with a hammer? I’d only smash my own skull with the hammer! But then, on the other side, there’s my conscience. I’d have run away from suffering. A sign has come, and I’m refusing the sign. There’s a way of salvation open to me, and I’m turning my back on it. Ivan says that in America, ‘with the good will,’ I could do more good than underground. But what becomes of our hymn from underground? What is America? America is vanity again! And I expect there’s plenty of swindling in America too. I’d have run away from crucifixion! I’m telling you, Alexey, because you’re the only one who can understand this. There’s no one else. To everyone else it’s folly, madness, everything I’ve told you about the hymn. They’ll say I’ve lost my mind or I’m a fool. I haven’t lost my mind and I’m not a fool. Ivan understands about the hymn too. He understands, only he won’t answer—he won’t speak. He doesn’t believe in the hymn. Don’t speak, don’t speak. I can see how you look! You’ve decided already. Don’t decide, spare me! I can’t live without Grusha. Wait till after the trial!”
Mitya finished, beside himself. He gripped Alyosha’s shoulders with both hands, and his feverish, yearning eyes were fixed on his brother’s.
“They don’t let convicts marry, do they?” he asked a third time, in a begging voice.
Alyosha had listened in great astonishment, and he was deeply moved.
“Tell me one thing,” he said. “Is Ivan very set on this, and whose idea was it?”

“His, his, and he’s very set on it. At first he didn’t come to see me. Then suddenly he turned up a week ago and started in on it right away. He’s dead set on it. He doesn’t ask me, he orders me to escape. He has no doubt I’ll obey him, though I opened my whole heart to him as I have to you, and told him about the hymn too. He told me he’d arrange it. He’s found out everything. But more of that later. He’s just fixed on it. It all comes down to money: he’ll pay ten thousand for the escape and give me twenty thousand for America. And he says a magnificent escape can be arranged for ten thousand.”
“And he told you not to tell me, on any account?” Alyosha asked again.

“Not to tell anyone, and above all not you. Not to tell you on any account. No doubt he’s afraid you’ll stand in front of me as my conscience. Don’t tell him I told you. Don’t tell him, whatever happens.”
“You’re right,” said Alyosha. “It’s impossible to decide anything before the trial is over. After the trial you’ll decide for yourself. Then you’ll find that new man in you, and he will decide.”
“A new man, or a Bernard who’ll decide _à la_ Bernard, because I think I’m a contemptible Bernard myself,” said Mitya, with a bitter grin.
“But brother, do you have no hope at all of being acquitted?”

Mitya shrugged nervously and shook his head. “Alyosha, darling, it’s time you went,” he said, suddenly hurrying. “I hear the superintendent shouting in the yard. He’ll be in here any minute. We’re late, it’s against the rules. Embrace me quickly. Kiss me! Make the sign of the cross over me, darling, for the cross I have to carry tomorrow.”
They embraced and kissed.
“Ivan,” Mitya said suddenly, “proposes that I escape. But of course he believes I did it.”
A sorrowful smile crossed his lips.
“Did you ask him whether he believes it?” asked Alyosha.
“No, I didn’t. I wanted to, but I couldn’t. I hadn’t the nerve. But I saw it in his eyes. Well, good-by!”
They kissed again in a hurry, and Alyosha was already on his way out when Mitya suddenly called him back.

“Stand facing me! There, like that!” And once more he grabbed Alyosha, with both hands on his shoulders. His face went white all at once, so white that it showed dreadfully even in the failing light. His lips twitched, and his eyes bored into Alyosha.
“Alyosha, tell me the whole truth, as if you stood before God. Do you believe I did it? Do you, do you yourself, believe it? The whole truth, don’t lie!” he cried in desperation.
Everything seemed to heave and sway before Alyosha, and he felt something like a knife go into his heart.
“Hush! What are you saying?” he stammered helplessly.
“The whole truth, all of it, don’t lie!” Mitya repeated.
“Not for one moment have I believed you were the murderer!” The words came in a shaking voice from deep in Alyosha’s chest, and he raised his right hand into the air as though calling God to witness.
Mitya’s whole face shone with joy.

“Thank you!” he said slowly, like a man breathing out after a faint. “You’ve given me new life now. Would you believe it, until this moment I was afraid to ask you, you, even you. Well, go! You’ve given me strength for tomorrow. God bless you! Come on, go! Love Ivan!” Those were Mitya’s last words.

Alyosha left in tears. Mitya’s mistrust, his lack of faith even in him, in Alyosha—all of it suddenly opened up to Alyosha a depth of hopeless grief and despair in his unhappy brother’s soul that he had never suspected. Intense, endless pity swept over him at once. His torn heart ached sharply. “Love Ivan!”—he suddenly remembered Mitya’s words. And he was on his way to Ivan. He had badly wanted to see Ivan all day. He worried about Ivan as much as about Mitya, and now more than ever.

chapters.title: V. Not You, Not You!
paragraphs: On his way to Ivan’s, Alyosha had to walk past the house where Katerina Ivanovna lived. Lights were burning in the windows. He stopped short and decided to go in. He had not seen Katerina Ivanovna in over a week. Now it struck him that Ivan might be with her, especially with that terrible day so close. He rang, and started up the staircase, which was dimly lit by a Chinese lantern. A man was coming down. As they passed, he recognized his brother. So Ivan was just leaving Katerina Ivanovna’s.
“Oh, it’s only you,” said Ivan drily. “Well, goodbye. You’re going up to see her?”
“Yes.”
“I wouldn’t, if I were you. She’s upset, and you’ll only upset her more.”
Just then a door upstairs banged open, and a voice cried out:
“No, no! Alexey Fyodorovitch, are you coming from him?”
“Yes, I’ve been with him.”
“Has he sent me any message? Come up, Alyosha. And you, Ivan Fyodorovitch, you have to come back. You must. Do you hear?”
Katya’s voice was so peremptory that Ivan hesitated for a moment, then made up his mind to go back up with Alyosha.
“She was listening at the door,” he muttered to himself in anger, but Alyosha heard him.
