“Forgive me for keeping my greatcoat on,” said Ivan as he entered the drawing-room. “I won’t sit down. I’m not staying more than a minute.”

“Do sit down, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” said Katerina Ivanovna, although she herself remained standing. She had changed very little over those weeks, but there was an ominous glint in her dark eyes. Alyosha remembered later that she had struck him then as especially beautiful.
“What did he ask you to tell me?”

“Just one thing,” said Alyosha, looking her straight in the face. “He asks you to spare yourself, and at the trial not to speak about what” (he faltered a little) “... went on between you ... when you first met ... in that town.”

“Ha! The fact that I bowed to the ground before him for that money!” She gave a bitter laugh. “So which is he afraid for, me or himself? He asks me to spare—who? Him, or myself? Tell me, Alexey Fyodorovitch!”
Alyosha studied her intently, trying to understand.
“You and him both,” he answered quietly.
“Well, I’m glad to hear it,” she snapped spitefully, and all at once she flushed.
“You don’t know me yet, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she said, almost threatening. “I don’t know myself yet, either. After I’ve been examined tomorrow, you may want to trample me underfoot.”
“You’ll give your evidence honorably,” said Alyosha. “That’s all anyone asks.”

“Women are often dishonorable,” she snarled. “Only an hour ago I was thinking how I was afraid even to touch that monster ... as if he were some reptile ... and yet no, to me he’s still a human being! But did he do it? Is he the murderer?” she suddenly cried out, hysterical, wheeling round on Ivan. Alyosha saw at once that she had put this same question to Ivan before, perhaps only a moment before he walked in, and not for the first time but the hundredth, and that they had ended up quarreling.

“I went to see Smerdyakov.... You were the one, you persuaded me that he murdered his father. I believed no one but you!” she went on, still speaking to Ivan. He answered with a strained sort of smile. Her tone made Alyosha start. He had never guessed that they were on such familiar, intimate terms.
“Well, that’s enough of that,” Ivan said, cutting the talk short. “I’m going. I’ll be back tomorrow.” With that he turned on his heel, left the room and went straight down the stairs.
Katerina Ivanovna imperiously seized both of Alyosha’s hands.

“Go after him! Catch him! Don’t leave him alone, not for a minute!” she said in a quick whisper. “He’s mad! Don’t you know he’s mad? He has a fever, a nervous fever. The doctor told me. Go on, run after him....”
Alyosha jumped up and ran after Ivan, who was not yet fifty paces ahead.
“What do you want?” Ivan wheeled on him when he saw he was being chased. “She told you to catch me, because I’m mad. I know the whole speech by heart,” he added irritably.
“She’s wrong, of course. But she’s right that you’re ill,” said Alyosha. “I was watching your face just now. You look very ill, Ivan.”
Ivan kept walking and did not stop. Alyosha followed.
“Do you know, Alexey Fyodorovitch, how it happens that people lose their minds?” Ivan asked. His voice had suddenly gone quiet, with no trace of irritation, and sounded merely curious.
“No, I don’t. I suppose there are all sorts of ways.”
“And can a man notice for himself that he’s going mad?”
“I imagine he can’t see himself clearly at such a time,” Alyosha answered, surprised.
Ivan said nothing for half a minute.
“If you want to talk to me, change the subject,” he said abruptly.

“Oh, I almost forgot, I have a letter for you,” said Alyosha timidly. He took Lise’s note out of his pocket and held it out to Ivan. They were just under a street lamp. Ivan knew the handwriting at once.
“Ah, from that little demon!” he laughed maliciously. Without opening the envelope, he tore it to pieces and tossed them into the air. The wind blew the scraps away.
“Not even sixteen yet, I believe, and she’s already throwing herself at men,” he said with contempt, and strode on down the street.
“What do you mean, throwing herself?” Alyosha exclaimed.
“The way loose women do, naturally.”

“How can you say that, Ivan, how can you?” Alyosha cried hotly, in a grieved voice. “She’s a child! You’re insulting a child! She’s ill, she’s very ill. She may be close to madness herself.... I had hoped to hear something from you ... something that would save her.”
“You’ll hear nothing from me. If she’s a child, I’m not her nurse. Be quiet, Alexey. Don’t keep on about her. I’m not even thinking about it.”
For a moment they walked on in silence again.
“She’ll spend the whole night praying to the Mother of God to show her what to do tomorrow at the trial,” he said, again sharp and angry.
“You ... you mean Katerina Ivanovna?”

“Yes. Whether to save Mitya or destroy him. She’ll pray to be shown the way. She can’t make up her own mind, you see. She hasn’t had time to decide yet. She takes me for her nurse, too. She wants me to sing her to sleep.”
“Katerina Ivanovna loves you, brother,” said Alyosha sadly.
“Maybe so. I’m not very taken with her.”

“She’s suffering. So why do you ... sometimes say things to her that give her hope?” Alyosha went on, with timid reproach. “I know you have given her hope. Forgive me for talking to you like this,” he added.

“I can’t treat her as I should—break with her once and for all and tell her so to her face,” said Ivan irritably. “I have to wait until the murderer’s sentence has been passed. If I break with her now, she’ll get her revenge on me tomorrow by destroying that scoundrel at the trial. She hates him, and she knows she hates him. It’s all a lie—lie on top of lie! As long as I haven’t broken with her, she keeps hoping, and she won’t destroy that monster, because she knows how badly I want to get him off. If only that damned verdict would come!”
The words “murderer” and “monster” rang painfully in Alyosha’s heart.
“But how could she destroy Mitya?” he asked, turning Ivan’s words over in his mind. “What can she testify that would ruin Mitya?”
“You don’t know yet. She holds a document, written in Mitya’s own hand, that proves beyond question that he did murder Fyodor Pavlovitch.”
“That’s impossible!” cried Alyosha.
“Why impossible? I’ve read it myself.”
“There can’t be any such document!” Alyosha insisted hotly. “There can’t, because he is not the murderer. It was not he who killed father, not he!”
Ivan stopped abruptly.
“Then who is the murderer, according to you?” he asked, with an air of coldness. His voice even had a note of disdain.
“You know who,” said Alyosha, in a low voice that pierced.
“Who? You mean that fairy tale about the crazy idiot, the epileptic, Smerdyakov?”
Alyosha felt himself begin to shake from head to foot.
“You know who,” escaped him helplessly. He could hardly breathe.
“Who? Who?” Ivan cried, almost savagely. All his self-control was suddenly gone.
“I know only one thing,” Alyosha went on, still almost whispering, “_it wasn’t you_ who killed father.”
“‘Not you’! What do you mean, ‘not you’?” Ivan was stunned.
“It was not you who killed father. Not you!” Alyosha said again, firmly.
Neither spoke for half a minute.
“I know I didn’t. Are you out of your head?” said Ivan, with a pale, crooked smile. He stared fixedly at Alyosha. They were standing under a lamp-post again.
“No, Ivan. You have told yourself several times that you are the murderer.”
“When did I ever say that? I was in Moscow.... When did I say it?” Ivan stammered, helpless.

“You’ve said it to yourself many times, all alone, through these two dreadful months,” Alyosha went on, as softly and clearly as before. Yet he seemed to be speaking now not for himself, not of his own will, but under some irresistible command. “You have accused yourself. You have admitted to yourself that you are the murderer and no one else. But you didn’t do it. You are mistaken. You are not the murderer. Do you hear me? It was not you! God sent me to tell you so.”
Both were silent. The silence lasted a whole long minute. They stood motionless, looking into each other’s eyes. Both were pale. Then Ivan began shaking all over and gripped Alyosha by the shoulder.
“You’ve been in my room!” he whispered hoarsely. “You were there in the night, when he came.... Admit it ... have you seen him, have you seen him?”
“Who? Do you mean Mitya?” Alyosha asked, bewildered.
“Not him, damn the monster!” Ivan shouted, frantic. “Do you know that he comes to see me? How did you find out? Tell me!”
“Who is _he_? I don’t know who you mean,” Alyosha faltered, growing alarmed.
“Yes, you do know ... or how could you—? You can’t possibly not know.”
Then he seemed to stop himself. He stood still, apparently thinking. A strange grin twisted his mouth.

“Brother,” Alyosha began again, in a trembling voice, “I said this to you because I know you’ll believe what I say. I’m telling you once and for all: it’s not you. Do you hear, once and for all! God put it into my heart to tell you, even if it makes you hate me from this hour on.”
But by now Ivan had evidently pulled himself together.

“Alexey Fyodorovitch,” he said with a cold smile, “I can’t stand prophets and epileptics—messengers from God above all—and you know that only too well. From this moment I cut off all relations with you, and probably for good. Leave me at this turning, please. It’s the way to your lodgings as well. And take particular care not to come to me today! Do you hear?”
He turned and walked on with a steady step, without looking back.
“Brother,” Alyosha called after him, “if anything happens to you today, come to me before anyone else!”

But Ivan did not answer. Alyosha stood under the lamp-post at the crossroads until Ivan had disappeared into the dark. Then he turned and walked slowly home. Both Alyosha and Ivan lived in lodgings, since neither would live in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s empty house. Alyosha rented a furnished room from some working people. Ivan lived some distance off. He had taken a roomy, fairly comfortable lodge attached to a fine house, owned by a well-to-do lady, an official’s widow. His only servant was a deaf, rheumatic old crone who went to bed at six every evening and rose at six every morning. Ivan had lately become remarkably careless of comfort, and very fond of solitude. He did everything for himself in the single room he lived in, and he seldom set foot in any other room of the lodge.

He came to the gate of the house and already had his hand on the bell when he suddenly stopped. He realized he was shaking all over with rage. All at once he let go of the bell, turned back with a curse and hurried off in the opposite direction. He walked a mile and a half to a tiny, crooked wooden house, little better than a hut. Marya Kondratyevna was now lodging there. She was the neighbor who used to come to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s kitchen for soup, and Smerdyakov had once sung his songs to her and played the guitar. She had sold their little house and now lived here with her mother. Smerdyakov, who was ill—almost dying—had been with them ever since Fyodor Pavlovitch’s death. Ivan was going to see him now, driven by a sudden, irresistible impulse.

chapters.title: VI. The First Interview With Smerdyakov
paragraphs: Ivan had now gone to see Smerdyakov for the third time since coming back from Moscow. The first time was the day he arrived, when he saw him and talked with him. He went once more two weeks later, and then his visits stopped. By now more than a month had passed since he last saw him, and in that time he had heard next to nothing about him.

Ivan did not get back until five days after his father’s death, so he missed the funeral, which was held the day before he arrived. The delay was caused by Alyosha not knowing his Moscow address. He had to ask Katerina Ivanovna to telegraph Ivan, and she did not know it either, so she wired her sister and aunt, expecting Ivan to call on them the moment he reached Moscow. He did not go to them until four days after he arrived. When the telegram finally reached him, he naturally rushed to our town. Alyosha met him first. Ivan was very surprised to find that Alyosha, against the opinion of the whole town, would not suspect Mitya and spoke openly of Smerdyakov as the murderer. Later, after he had seen the police captain and the prosecutor and heard the details of the charge and the arrest, Alyosha surprised him still more. Ivan could explain his view only as exaggerated brotherly feeling and sympathy for Mitya, since Alyosha, as Ivan knew, was very fond of him.

Now, since we are on the subject, a word or two about how Ivan felt toward his brother Dmitri. He simply disliked him. At most he sometimes pitied him, and even that pity was mixed with strong contempt, almost disgust. Everything about Mitya, even his looks, put him off. Ivan watched Katerina Ivanovna’s love for his brother with indignation. Still, he went to see Mitya on the very day he arrived, and the visit, far from shaking his belief in Mitya’s guilt, made it stronger. He found his brother agitated and keyed up. Mitya talked a lot, but he was very absent-minded and could not keep to the point. His language was violent, he accused Smerdyakov, and he was terribly confused. Mostly he talked about the three thousand roubles, which he said his father had “stolen” from him.
“It was my money, mine,” Mitya kept saying. “Even if I’d stolen it, I’d have had a right to.”

He barely argued with the evidence against him, and when he did try to twist some fact in his favor, he did it absurdly and without any logic. He hardly seemed to care about defending himself, whether to Ivan or to anyone. On the contrary, he was angry and scornful, proud in his contempt for the charges, and kept flying into rages and abusing everybody. Grigory’s testimony about the open door only made him laugh with contempt, and he said that “the devil opened it.” But he could give no sensible explanation of the fact. He even managed to insult Ivan at that first meeting. He told him sharply that men who preached that “everything is lawful” had no business suspecting and cross-examining him. In short, he was anything but friendly to Ivan that day. Immediately after seeing Mitya, Ivan went to see Smerdyakov for the first time.

All the way from Moscow on the train he had kept thinking about Smerdyakov and about their last conversation, the evening before he left. Much of it struck him as puzzling and suspicious. Yet when he gave his statement to the investigating lawyer, he said nothing about that conversation, for the moment. He held it back until he had seen Smerdyakov, who was in the hospital at that time.

Doctor Herzenstube and Varvinsky, the doctor he met at the hospital, answered Ivan’s repeated questions with complete confidence: Smerdyakov’s epileptic attack was undoubtedly real. They were actually surprised that Ivan asked whether he might have been shamming on the day of the disaster. They explained that this attack had been exceptional. The fits had kept coming back, several of them, so that the patient’s life had truly been in danger, and only now, after treatment, could they say for certain that he would live. “Though it may well be,” added Doctor Herzenstube, “that his mind will be impaired for a long time, if not for good.” Ivan asked impatiently if that meant he was mad now. They said not yet, not in the full sense of the word, but that certain abnormalities could be noticed. Ivan made up his mind to find out for himself what they were.

At the hospital he was let in to see the patient straight away. Smerdyakov lay on a low narrow bed in a ward of his own. The room held just one other bed, and in it lay a tradesman from the town, swollen with dropsy and plainly close to death, so he would not get in the way of their talk. When Smerdyakov saw Ivan he grinned uncertainly and for a moment looked nervous, or so Ivan thought. It passed at once. For the rest of the visit it was Smerdyakov’s calm that struck Ivan. One look told him the man was very sick. He was weak and spoke slowly, as if his tongue were hard to move. He was much thinner and more yellow. Through the whole interview, which lasted twenty minutes, he complained of a headache and of aching in every limb. His thin, unmanly face seemed to have shrunk to nothing. His hair was untidy, and the crest of curls at the front stood up in a thin tuft. But the left eye, narrowed and seeming to hint at something, was the same as ever. “It’s always worth while speaking to a clever man.” Ivan remembered that at once. He sat down on the stool at the foot of the bed. Smerdyakov shifted in bed with painful effort, but he did not speak first. He stayed silent and did not even look very curious.
“Can you talk to me?” asked Ivan. “I won’t tire you much.”
“Of course I can,” mumbled Smerdyakov in a faint voice. “Have you been back long, your honor?” he added in a patronizing tone, as if to put a nervous visitor at ease.
“I got here today.... To see the mess you’re in.”
Smerdyakov sighed.
“Why the sigh? You knew all along,” Ivan blurted out.
For a while Smerdyakov said nothing, stolidly.
“How could I not know? It was plain beforehand. But how was I to tell it would come out like this?”
“What would come out? Don’t dodge! You predicted you’d have a fit, on your way down to the cellar, remember. You named the very place.”
“And have you said that at the examination yet?” Smerdyakov asked, quite composed.
Ivan felt a sudden flash of anger.
“No, not yet, but I will. You’ve a lot to explain to me, my man, and let me tell you, I won’t be played with!”
“Why would I play with you, when I trust you like God Almighty?” said Smerdyakov, in the same calm voice, closing his eyes just for a moment.

“First of all,” began Ivan, “I know you can’t predict epileptic fits. I’ve made inquiries, so don’t try to take me in. Nobody can foretell the day and the hour. Yet you told me the day and the hour in advance, and the cellar as well. How could you know you’d fall down the cellar stairs in a fit, unless you faked the fit on purpose?”

“The cellar was somewhere I had to go anyway, several times a day,” Smerdyakov drawled slowly. “A year ago I fell out of the garret in just the same way. It’s true enough that nobody can tell the day and the hour of a fit beforehand, but you can always have a foreboding.”
“But you did foretell the day and the hour!”
“As for my epilepsy, sir, you’d do much better to ask the doctors here. Ask them if it was a real fit or a fake. It’s no use my saying more about it.”
“And the cellar? How did you know about the cellar beforehand?”

“You just can’t let go of that cellar! Going down to it, I was in terrible fear and doubt. What frightened me most was losing you and being left with no defense in the whole world. So down I went into the cellar, thinking, ‘Here it comes, it’ll hit me any minute now, am I going to fall?’ And it was this fear that brought on the sudden spasm, the one that always comes ... and down I went flying. All of this, and everything I said to you at the gate the evening before, when I told you how frightened I was and spoke about the cellar, I told to Doctor Herzenstube and to Nikolay Parfenovitch, the investigating lawyer, and it’s all been put down in the record. And the doctor here, Mr. Varvinsky, told them all that the mere thought of it had brought it on, the dread that I might fall. And that was just when the fit got me. So they’ve written it down that this is how it must have happened, simply from my fear.”
With that Smerdyakov drew a deep breath, as though he were worn out.

“So you’ve said all this in your statement?” said Ivan, rather taken aback. He had meant to scare him with the threat of repeating their conversation, and now it seemed Smerdyakov had already reported all of it himself.
“What have I got to fear? Let them put down the whole truth,” Smerdyakov said firmly.
“And did you tell them every word of what we said at the gate?”
“No, not every word.”
“And did you tell them you can fake fits, as you boasted then?”
“No, I didn’t tell them that either.”
“Now tell me, why did you send me to Tchermashnya then?”
“I was afraid you’d go off to Moscow. Tchermashnya is closer, anyway.”
“You’re lying. You suggested my going away yourself. You told me to keep out of the trouble.”

“That was simply out of affection and sincere devotion to you. I saw trouble coming in the house and wanted to spare you. But I wanted to spare myself even more. That’s why I told you to keep out of harm’s way, so you’d understand there’d be trouble in the house and stay at home to protect your father.”
“Then why didn’t you say so straight out, you blockhead!” Ivan suddenly blazed up.

“How could I say it straight out then? It was only my fear that made me speak at all, and you might have been angry too. I could well have been afraid that Dmitri Fyodorovitch would make a scene and take that money, since he thought of it as practically his own. But who could have told it would end in a murder like this? I thought he’d only take the three thousand under the master’s mattress, in the envelope, and look, he has murdered him. How could you have guessed it either, sir?”
“You say yourself it couldn’t be guessed. So how was I supposed to guess it and stay at home? You’re contradicting yourself!” said Ivan, thinking hard.
“You might have guessed it from my sending you to Tchermashnya and not to Moscow.”
“How could I guess it from that?”
Smerdyakov seemed very worn out, and again he said nothing for a minute.

“You might have guessed it from the way I asked you to go to Tchermashnya and not Moscow. I wanted you nearer. Moscow is a long way off, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch, knowing you were not far away, wouldn’t be so bold. And if anything had happened, you could have come and protected me too, since I’d warned you about Grigory Vassilyevitch’s illness and that I was afraid of having a fit. And when I explained to you the knocks, the ones that let a person in to see the deceased, and that Dmitri Fyodorovitch knew them all through me, I thought you’d work out for yourself that he was sure to do something. So you wouldn’t even go to Tchermashnya, but stay.”
“He talks quite coherently,” thought Ivan, “mumbling aside. Where’s this impairment of his faculties that Herzenstube spoke of?”
“You’re being sly with me, damn you!” he exclaimed, growing angry.
“But at the time I thought you’d fully guessed,” Smerdyakov countered with a perfectly innocent air.
“Had I guessed, I’d have stayed,” cried Ivan.
“Well, I took it that you’d guessed, and that’s why you left in such a rush, just to get clear of the trouble, just to run away and save yourself in your fright.”
“You think everyone’s as big a coward as you are?”
“Forgive me, I thought you were the same as me.”

“Of course I should have guessed,” said Ivan, agitated, “and I did guess you were up to some mischief ... only you’re lying, you’re lying again,” he cried, remembering all at once. “Do you remember coming up to the carriage and saying to me, ‘It’s always worth while speaking to a clever man’? So you were glad I was leaving, since you complimented me?”
Smerdyakov kept sighing. A little color came into his face.

“If I was pleased,” he said, somewhat out of breath, “it was only because you’d agreed to go to Tchermashnya and not to Moscow. It was nearer, after all. But when I said those words, I didn’t mean them as praise but as a reproach. You didn’t understand.”
“What reproach?”
“That you saw such a calamity coming and still abandoned your own father, and wouldn’t protect us. I might have been arrested any day for stealing that three thousand.”
“Damn you!” Ivan swore again. “Wait a moment. Did you tell the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer about those knocks?”
“I told them everything exactly as it was.”
Once more Ivan marveled to himself.

“If I suspected anything then,” he began again, “it was only some wickedness on your part. Dmitri might kill him, but steal—I didn’t believe that then.... But I was ready for any wickedness from you. You told me yourself you could fake a fit. Why did you say that?”
“Out of plain simplicity. I’ve never faked a fit on purpose in my life. I only said it to boast to you. It was just foolish. I liked you so much then, and I was frank with you.”
“My brother flatly accuses you of the murder and the theft.”

“What else can he do?” said Smerdyakov with a bitter grin. “And who’ll believe him, with all the proofs against him? Grigory Vassilyevitch saw the door open. What can he say to that? But never mind him! He’s shaking with fear, trying to save himself.”
He trailed off slowly, then suddenly added, as if on second thought:

“And here’s something else. He wants to put it on me and make out I did it with my own hands—I’ve heard that already. But as for my being clever at faking a fit: would I have told you beforehand that I could fake one, if I really had planned something against your father? If I’d been planning such a murder, would I have been fool enough to give evidence against myself ahead of time? And to his own son! I swear! Is that likely? As if that could be—it’s never happened. Nobody hears this talk of ours now but Providence itself, and if you were to tell it to the prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch, you’d be defending me completely, because who would be such a criminal if he’s so open-hearted beforehand? Anyone can see that.”

“Well,” said Ivan, rising to cut the talk short, struck by Smerdyakov’s last argument, “I don’t suspect you in the least, and in fact I think it’s absurd to suspect you. On the contrary, I’m grateful to you for putting my mind at ease. Now I’m going, but I’ll come again. Meanwhile, good-by. Get well. Do you need anything?”
“I’m very grateful for everything. Marfa Ignatyevna doesn’t forget me, and out of her kindness she gets me anything I need. Good people visit me every day.”
“Good-by. But I won’t say anything about your being able to fake a fit, and I advise you not to either,” something made Ivan say suddenly.
“I quite understand. And if you say nothing about that, I’ll say nothing about our conversation at the gate.”

So Ivan left. He had gone a dozen steps along the corridor when he felt all at once that Smerdyakov’s last words had an insulting meaning. He nearly turned back, but the urge passed, and muttering “Nonsense!” he walked out of the hospital.

His main feeling was relief that the murderer was Mitya and not Smerdyakov, though you would have expected the reverse. He did not want to analyze why, and in fact felt a real repugnance at prying into his own feelings. He seemed to want to hurry up and forget something. Over the next few days he became convinced of Mitya’s guilt, as he learned how heavy the evidence against him was. Some of it came from unimportant people, Fenya and her mother for example, yet its effect was almost crushing. As for Perhotin, the people at the tavern and at Plotnikov’s shop, and the witnesses at Mokroe, their evidence looked conclusive. It was the details that did the damage. The secret of the knocks impressed the lawyers nearly as much as Grigory’s evidence about the open door. Grigory’s wife, Marfa, answering Ivan’s questions, declared that Smerdyakov had lain all night on the other side of the partition wall. “He was not three paces from our bed.” She was a sound sleeper, yet she had woken several times and heard him groaning. “He was groaning the whole time, groaning without a stop.”
Ivan told Herzenstube that in his opinion Smerdyakov was not mad, only rather weak, and drew nothing from the old man but a subtle smile.

“Do you know how he passes his time now?” he asked. “Memorizing lists of French words. He keeps an exercise book under his pillow, with the French words written out in Russian letters for him by someone, he he he!”

In the end Ivan put all his doubts aside. He could not think of Dmitri without disgust. One thing only was odd. Alyosha stuck to it that Dmitri was not the murderer and that “in all probability” Smerdyakov was. Ivan had always felt that Alyosha’s opinion counted for a great deal with him, and so he was astonished by it now. Another odd thing was that Alyosha never tried to talk to Ivan about Mitya, never raised the subject and only answered Ivan’s questions. This too struck Ivan in particular.

But at that time something quite different was taking up most of his mind. On his return from Moscow he had given himself up, hopelessly, to a mad and consuming passion for Katerina Ivanovna. This is not the place to begin on that new passion of Ivan’s, which left its mark on the whole rest of his life. It would make the subject of another novel, which I may never write. But I cannot leave out one thing here. When Ivan, as I’ve already related, left Katerina Ivanovna with Alyosha and told him, “I am not keen on her,” it was an absolute lie. He loved her madly, though at times he hated her so much that he could have murdered her. Many causes helped to produce this feeling. Shattered by what had happened with Mitya, on Ivan’s return she had rushed to meet him as her one salvation. She had been hurt, insulted and humiliated in her feelings. And now back to her had come the man who had loved her so ardently before (oh! she knew that very well), and whose heart and intellect she thought far superior to her own. But the sternly virtuous girl did not surrender altogether to the man she loved, in spite of the Karamazov violence of his passions and the great fascination he had for her. At the same time she was constantly tormented by remorse for having deserted Mitya, and in moments of discord and violent anger (and there were plenty) she told Ivan so plainly. This was what he had meant when he told Alyosha, “lies upon lies.” There was, of course, much that was false in it, and that angered Ivan more than anything.... But of all this later.

For a time he did, in fact, almost forget that Smerdyakov existed. And yet, two weeks after his first visit, the same strange thoughts as before began to haunt him. It is enough to say that he kept asking himself why, on that last night in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house, he had crept out onto the stairs like a thief and listened for what his father was doing below. Why had he remembered that afterwards with disgust? Why had he been suddenly so depressed on the journey next morning? Why, when he reached Moscow, had he said to himself, “I am a scoundrel”? And now he almost thought these tormenting thoughts would make him forget even Katerina Ivanovna, so completely had they taken hold of him again. It was just after thinking this that he met Alyosha in the street. He stopped him at once and put a question to him:

“Do you remember when Dmitri burst in after dinner and beat father, and afterwards, out in the yard, I told you I kept ‘the right to desire’?... Tell me, did you think then that I desired father’s death, or not?”
“Yes, I thought so,” Alyosha answered softly.

“And it was true. There was no guessing about it. But didn’t you also suppose that what I wanted was just ‘one reptile devouring another’; that is, that Dmitri should kill father, and as soon as possible ... and that I myself was even ready to help it along?”
Alyosha went rather pale and looked silently into his brother’s face.
“Speak!” cried Ivan. “More than anything I want to know what you thought then. I want the truth, the truth!”
He drew a deep breath and glared at Alyosha before the answer came.
“Forgive me, I thought that too, at the time,” Alyosha whispered, and he did not add a single softening word.

“Thanks,” snapped Ivan, and he left Alyosha and hurried on his way. From then on Alyosha noticed that Ivan clearly avoided him and even seemed to have taken a dislike to him, so much so that Alyosha stopped going to see him. Immediately after that meeting Ivan did not go home but went straight back to Smerdyakov.

chapters.title: VII. The Second Visit To Smerdyakov
paragraphs: By then Smerdyakov had been let out of the hospital. Ivan knew his new lodging: a run-down little wooden house, split in two by a passage. Marya Kondratyevna and her mother lived on one side, and Smerdyakov on the other. Nobody knew on what footing he lived with them, whether as a friend or as a lodger. It was assumed afterwards that he had moved in as Marya Kondratyevna’s fiancé and was staying for a while without paying for food or rent. Mother and daughter both respected him highly and thought him far above themselves.

Ivan knocked, and when the door was opened he walked straight into the passage. Marya Kondratyevna told him to go to the better room on the left, which was Smerdyakov’s. There was a tiled stove in the room, and it was extremely hot. The walls were cheerful with blue wallpaper, though it was badly worn, and under it, in the cracks, cockroaches swarmed in astonishing numbers, so there was a constant rustling. The furniture was very sparse: two benches along each wall and two chairs by the table. The plain wooden table was covered with a cloth with pink patterns. On each of the two little windows stood a pot of geranium. In the corner was a case of ikons. On the table stood a small copper samovar, much dented, and a tray with two cups. But Smerdyakov had finished his tea and the samovar had gone out. He was sitting on a bench at the table, looking at an exercise-book and slowly writing in it with a pen. Beside him were a bottle of ink and a flat iron candlestick, though with a composite candle in it. Ivan saw at once from Smerdyakov’s face that he had completely recovered from his illness. His face was fresher and fuller, and his hair stood up jauntily at the front and was plastered down at the sides. He was sitting in a parti-colored, wadded dressing-gown, rather dirty and frayed. He had spectacles on his nose, which Ivan had never seen him wear before. This trifling detail suddenly doubled Ivan’s anger. “A creature like that, and wearing spectacles!”

Smerdyakov slowly raised his head and studied his visitor through the spectacles. Then he slowly took them off and got up from the bench. He did it not at all respectfully, almost lazily, doing the bare minimum that common politeness required. Ivan noticed all this at once. He took it all in, and most of all the look in Smerdyakov’s eyes, which was positively malicious, surly and haughty. “What do you want, barging in?” it seemed to say. “We settled everything then. Why have you come again?” Ivan could hardly control himself.
“It’s hot in here,” he said, still standing, and unbuttoned his overcoat.
“Take off your coat,” Smerdyakov allowed.
Ivan took off his coat with trembling hands and threw it on a bench. He grabbed a chair, pulled it quickly up to the table and sat down. Smerdyakov got onto his bench before him.
“First of all, are we alone?” Ivan asked sternly and abruptly. “Can they hear us in there?”
“Nobody can hear anything. You’ve seen for yourself: there’s a passage.”

“Listen, my good fellow. What was that you babbled as I was leaving the hospital? That if I said nothing about your talent for faking fits, you wouldn’t tell the investigating lawyer our whole conversation at the gate? What do you mean by _all_? What could you possibly mean by it? Were you threatening me? Have I made some sort of deal with you? Do you think I’m afraid of you?”

Ivan said this in a perfect fury, plainly intending to show that he despised any evasion or hinting and meant to lay his cards on the table. Smerdyakov’s eyes gleamed with resentment, his left eye winked, and he answered at once, with his usual composure and deliberation. “You want everything out in the open; very well, you shall have it,” he seemed to say.

“This is what I meant then, and this is why I said it: that you knew beforehand about the murder of your own parent and left him to his fate. And that people shouldn’t afterwards draw any evil conclusions about your feelings, and perhaps about something else too—that is what I promised not to tell the authorities.”

Smerdyakov spoke without haste and plainly held himself in check, but there was something in his voice that was firm and emphatic, resentful and insolently defiant. He stared brazenly at Ivan. For the first moment a mist passed before Ivan’s eyes.
“What? What did you say? Are you out of your mind?”
“I’m in perfect possession of all my faculties.”
“Do you think I _knew_ about the murder?” Ivan cried at last, and brought his fist down hard on the table. “What do you mean by ‘something else too’? Speak, scoundrel!”
Smerdyakov said nothing and went on looking Ivan over with the same insolent stare.
“Speak, you stinking rogue! What is that ‘something else too’?”
“By ‘something else’ I meant that you, most likely, were very eager for your parent’s death as well.”

Ivan leaped up and hit him on the shoulder with all his strength, so that he fell back against the wall. In an instant his face was streaming with tears. Saying, “It’s a shame, sir, to strike a sick man,” he wiped his eyes with a very dirty blue check handkerchief and sank into quiet weeping. A minute went by.
“That’s enough! Stop it,” Ivan said sharply, sitting down again. “Don’t push me past all patience.”
Smerdyakov took the rag from his eyes. Every line of his puckered face showed the insult he had just received.
“So you thought then, you scoundrel, that I meant to kill my father together with Dmitri?”
“I didn’t know what thoughts were in your mind then,” said Smerdyakov resentfully. “And so I stopped you at the gate then to sound you out on that very point.”
“To sound out what? What?”
“Why, that very matter: whether you wanted your father murdered or not.”
What infuriated Ivan more than anything was the aggressive, insolent tone that Smerdyakov kept up all through.
“Was it you who murdered him?” he cried suddenly.
Smerdyakov smiled contemptuously.
“You know for a fact that it wasn’t me who murdered him. And I’d have thought a sensible man had no need to bring it up again.”
“But why, why did you suspect me at the time?”

“As you already know, it was simply from fear. I was in such a position, shaking with fear, that I suspected everyone. I decided to sound you out too, because I thought: if you wanted the same as your brother, then the business was as good as settled, and I would be crushed like a fly as well.”
“Wait, you didn’t say that two weeks ago.”
“I meant the same when I talked to you in the hospital. Only I thought you would understand without wasting words, and that, being such a sensible man, you wouldn’t care to talk of it openly.”
“What next! Come on, answer me, I insist: what was it ... what could I possibly have done to plant such a degrading suspicion in your mean soul?”
“As for the murder, you couldn’t have done that and didn’t want to. But as for wanting somebody else to do it, that was exactly what you did want.”
“And how coolly, how coolly he says it! But why should I have wanted it? What reason did I have for wanting it?”

“What reason did you have? What about the inheritance?” said Smerdyakov sarcastically, and somehow vengefully. “After your parent’s death there was at least forty thousand to come to each of you, and very likely more. But if Fyodor Pavlovitch had married that lady, Agrafena Alexandrovna, she would have had all his capital transferred to her right after the wedding, for she has plenty of sense. Your parent wouldn’t have left the three of you two roubles. And were they far from a wedding, either? Not by a hair’s breadth. That lady had only to lift her little finger and he would have run after her to church with his tongue hanging out.”
Ivan held himself back with painful effort.
“All right,” he said at last. “You see, I haven’t jumped up, I haven’t knocked you down, I haven’t killed you. Go on. So, in your account, I’d chosen Dmitri to do it. I was relying on him?”

“How could you help counting on him? If he killed him, he would lose all the rights of a nobleman, his rank and his property, and go off into exile. So his share of the inheritance would come to you and your brother Alexey Fyodorovitch in equal parts. You would each get not forty but sixty thousand. There’s no doubt at all that you counted on Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

“What I put up with from you! Listen, scoundrel, if I had counted on anyone then, it would have been on you, not on Dmitri. And I swear I did expect some wickedness from you ... at the time.... I remember my impression!”

“I thought for a minute, too, at the time, that you were counting on me as well,” said Smerdyakov with a sarcastic grin. “So that was exactly how, more than anything, you showed me what was in your mind. Because if you had a foreboding about me and went away all the same, you as good as said to me: ‘You can murder my parent, I won’t stop you!’”
“You scoundrel! So that’s how you understood it!”

“It was all that business of going to Tchermashnya. Why, you were meaning to go to Moscow, and you refused all your father’s pleading to go to Tchermashnya—and then at one foolish word from me you agreed at once! What reason did you have to agree to Tchermashnya? You went to Tchermashnya for no reason, simply on my word. That shows you must have expected something from me.”
“No, I swear I didn’t!” shouted Ivan, grinding his teeth.

“You didn’t? Then, as your father’s son, you should have had me hauled off to the lock-up and thrashed for what I said then ... or at the very least given me a punch in the face on the spot. But you weren’t the least bit angry, if you please. You at once acted, in the friendliest way, on my foolish word and went away. That was utterly absurd, for you ought to have stayed to save your parent’s life. How could I help drawing my conclusions?”
Ivan sat scowling, both fists pressed convulsively on his knees.

“Yes, I’m sorry I didn’t punch you in the face,” he said with a bitter smile. “I couldn’t have taken you to the lock-up just then. Who would have believed me, and what charge could I have brought against you? But the punch in the face ... oh, I’m sorry I didn’t think of it. Even though blows are forbidden, I would have pounded your ugly face to a jelly.”
Smerdyakov looked at him almost with relish.

“In the ordinary occasions of life,” he said, in the same smug, sententious tone in which he had taunted Grigory and argued with him about religion at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s table, “in the ordinary occasions of life, blows on the face are forbidden by law nowadays, and people have given them up. But in exceptional occasions of life people still fly to blows, not only among us but all over the world, even in the fullest Republic of France, just as in the time of Adam and Eve. And they never will leave off. But you, even in an exceptional case, did not dare.”
“Why are you learning French words?” Ivan nodded toward the exercise-book lying on the table.
“Why shouldn’t I learn them, to improve my education? I might happen to go some day to those happy parts of Europe myself.”

“Listen, monster.” Ivan’s eyes flashed and he shook all over. “Your accusations don’t scare me. Say what you like about me. If I’m not beating you to death, it’s only because I suspect you of this crime, and I’m going to drag you before a court. I’ll expose you.”

“To my mind, you’d do better to keep quiet. What can you accuse me of, when I’m perfectly innocent? And who would believe you? Only, if you start, I’ll tell everything too, because I have to defend myself.”
“Do you think I’m afraid of you now?”
“Even if the court doesn’t believe all I’ve just told you, the public will, and then you will be the one ashamed.”
“That’s as much as to say, ‘It’s always worth speaking to a sensible man,’ eh?” Ivan snarled.
“Exactly right. And you’d better be sensible.”

Ivan got up, shaking with indignation from head to foot. He put on his coat and, without another word to Smerdyakov, without even a glance at him, hurried out of the cottage. The cool evening air did him good. A bright moon hung in the sky. His mind was full of nightmare thoughts and feelings. “Should I go right now and denounce Smerdyakov? But what could I say? He’s not guilty, anyway. On the contrary, he’ll accuse me. And really, why did I go off to Tchermashnya then? What for? What for?” Ivan asked himself. “Yes, of course, I was expecting something, and he is right....” And for the hundredth time he remembered how, on his last night in his father’s house, he had listened on the stairs. But now the memory brought such anguish that he stopped dead where he stood, as if he had been stabbed. “Yes, I expected it then, that’s true! I wanted the murder, I did want the murder! Did I want the murder? Did I want it? I must kill Smerdyakov! If I don’t dare kill Smerdyakov now, life is not worth living!”

Ivan did not go home. He went straight to Katerina Ivanovna, and his appearance frightened her. He looked like a madman. He told her his whole conversation with Smerdyakov, every syllable of it. She tried hard to soothe him, but he would not calm down. He kept pacing the room, saying odd, disjointed things. At last he sat down, rested his elbows on the table, dropped his head into his hands and came out with this strange statement: “If it’s not Dmitri but Smerdyakov who’s the murderer, then I share his guilt, for I put him up to it. Whether I did, I don’t know yet. But if he is the murderer and not Dmitri, then of course I am the murderer too.”

When Katerina Ivanovna heard that, she rose without a word, went to her writing-table, opened a box on it, took out a sheet of paper and laid it in front of Ivan. This was the document Ivan later described to Alyosha as a “conclusive proof” that Dmitri had killed his father. It was the letter Mitya had written to Katerina Ivanovna while drunk, on the very evening he met Alyosha at the crossroads on the way to the monastery. That was after the scene at Katerina Ivanovna’s, when Grushenka had insulted her. After parting from Alyosha, Mitya had rushed off to Grushenka. I don’t know whether he saw her, but that evening he was at the “Metropolis,” where he got thoroughly drunk. Then he called for pen and paper and wrote a document that was to have weighty consequences for him. It was a wordy, rambling, frantic letter, a drunken letter in fact. It read like a drunk who gets home and starts telling his wife or someone in the house, with extraordinary heat, how he has just been insulted, what a rascal insulted him, what a fine fellow he himself is, by contrast, and how he will make that scoundrel pay. All of it at great length, with great excitement and no coherence, with drunken tears and thumps on the table. The letter was written on a dirty scrap of the cheapest ordinary paper. The tavern had provided it, and figures were scrawled on the back. Evidently there was not room enough for his drunken wordiness, because Mitya had not only filled the margins but written the last line right across the rest. The letter went like this:

FATAL KATYA: Tomorrow I will get the money and repay your three thousand and farewell, woman of great wrath, but farewell, too, my love! Let us make an end! Tomorrow I will try to get it from everyone, and if I can’t borrow it, I give you my word of honor I will go to my father and break his skull and take the money from under the pillow, if only Ivan has gone. If I have to go to Siberia for it, I’ll give you back your three thousand. And farewell. I bow down to the ground before you, for I’ve been a scoundrel to you. Forgive me! No, better not forgive me, you’ll be happier and so will I! Better Siberia than your love, for I love another woman and you got to know her too well today, so how can you forgive? I will murder the man who’s robbed me! I’ll leave you all and go to the East so as to see no one again. Not _her_ either, for you are not my only tormentress; she is too. Farewell! P.S.—I write my curse, but I adore you! I hear it in my heart. One string is left, and it vibrates. Better tear my heart in two! I will kill myself, but first of all that cur. I will tear three thousand from him and fling it to you. Though I’ve been a scoundrel to you, I am not a thief! You can expect three thousand. The cur keeps it under his mattress, in pink ribbon. I am not a thief, but I’ll murder my thief. Katya, don’t look disdainful. Dmitri is not a thief! but a murderer! He has murdered his father and ruined himself to hold his ground, rather than endure your pride. And he doesn’t love you. P.P.S.—I kiss your feet, farewell! P.P.P.S.—Katya, pray to God that someone will give me the money. Then I will not be steeped in gore, and if no one does—I will! Kill me!
Your slave and enemy, D. KARAMAZOV.

When Ivan read this “document,” he was convinced. So it was his brother, not Smerdyakov. And if not Smerdyakov, then not he, Ivan. To him the letter at once looked like a logical proof. There could be no more doubt at all of Mitya’s guilt. It never occurred to Ivan, by the way, that Mitya might have done the murder together with Smerdyakov. In fact such a theory did not fit the facts. Ivan was entirely reassured. The next morning he thought of Smerdyakov and his taunts with nothing but contempt. A few days later he actually marveled that he could have been so horribly distressed by his suspicions. He resolved to dismiss Smerdyakov with contempt and forget him. So a month went by. He made no further inquiry about Smerdyakov, but twice he happened to hear that the man was very ill and out of his mind.

“He’ll end in madness,” the young doctor Varvinsky said of him, and Ivan remembered this. In the last week of that month Ivan himself began to feel very ill. He went to see the Moscow doctor who had been sent for by Katerina Ivanovna just before the trial. And at that very time things between him and Katerina Ivanovna became painfully tense. They were like two enemies in love with each other. Katerina Ivanovna’s “returns” to Mitya, that is, her short but violent swings of feeling in his favor, drove Ivan into a perfect frenzy. Strange to say, until that last scene described above, when Alyosha came from Mitya to Katerina Ivanovna, Ivan had not once in that whole month heard her voice a doubt of Mitya’s guilt, in spite of those “returns” he hated so. It is remarkable, too, that although he felt he hated Mitya more every day, he understood that it was not because of Katya’s “returns” that he hated him, but simply _because he was the murderer of his father_. He knew this and admitted it fully to himself.

Even so, ten days before the trial he went to see Mitya and put a plan of escape to him—a plan he had clearly been turning over for a long time. Part of what drove him was a sore spot that Smerdyakov’s remark had left in his heart: that it was to his, Ivan’s, advantage for his brother to be convicted, since that would raise his inheritance and Alyosha’s from forty to sixty thousand roubles. He decided to give up thirty thousand to arrange Mitya’s escape. On the way back from seeing him he was very gloomy and downcast. He suddenly felt that he wanted Mitya to escape not only to heal that sore spot by sacrificing thirty thousand, but for another reason as well. “Is it because I am as much a murderer at heart?” he asked himself. Something very deep down seemed to be burning and festering in his soul. His pride above all suffered cruelly all that month. But of that later....

After his talk with Alyosha, Ivan stood with his hand on the bell of his lodging and suddenly decided to go to Smerdyakov. He was acting on a sudden, odd impulse of indignation. He had just remembered how Katerina Ivanovna had cried out to him in Alyosha’s presence: “It was you, you, who convinced me of his” (that is, Mitya’s) “guilt!” Recalling it, Ivan was thunderstruck. He had never once tried to convince her that Mitya was the murderer. On the contrary, he had suspected himself in front of her, that time when he came back from Smerdyakov. It was _she_, she, who had produced that “document” and proved his brother’s guilt. And now she had suddenly exclaimed: “I’ve been at Smerdyakov’s myself!” When had she been there? Ivan had known nothing about it. So she was not at all so sure of Mitya’s guilt! And what could Smerdyakov have told her? What, what had he said to her? His heart burned with violent anger. He could not understand how, half an hour before, he had let those words go by and not cried out on the spot. He let go of the bell and rushed off to Smerdyakov. “This time I may kill him,” he thought on the way.

chapters.title: VIII. The Third And Last Interview With Smerdyakov
paragraphs: Halfway there, the sharp dry wind that had blown early that morning picked up again, and a fine, dry snow came down thick and fast. It did not stay on the ground. The wind whirled it about, and before long it was a proper snowstorm. In that part of town, where Smerdyakov lived, there were hardly any street lamps. Ivan strode along alone in the dark. He paid no attention to the storm and found his way by instinct. His head ached, and his temples throbbed painfully. His hands, he noticed, were twitching convulsively. Close to Marya Kondratyevna’s cottage he ran into a lone drunken peasant, a small man in a coarse, patched coat. The man was zigzagging along, muttering and cursing to himself. Then, every so often, he would burst into song in a hoarse, drunken voice:
“Ach, Vanka’s gone to Petersburg; I won’t wait till he’s back.”

But every time he got as far as the second line he stopped and started cursing again, and then he began the same song from the top. Ivan hated him fiercely before he had even given him a thought. Then, all at once, he noticed the man and felt an irresistible urge to knock him down. At that moment they met. The peasant lurched violently and fell full tilt against Ivan, who shoved him back in a fury. The peasant flew backward and dropped like a log onto the frozen ground. He let out one pitiful “O—oh!” and then went quiet. Ivan stepped over to him. He lay on his back, not moving, quite unconscious. “He’ll freeze,” thought Ivan, and he went on to Smerdyakov’s.

In the passage, Marya Kondratyevna ran out with a candle in her hand to open the door. She whispered that Smerdyakov was very ill. “It’s not that he’s in bed, but he doesn’t seem himself. He even told us to take the tea away. He wouldn’t touch it.”
“What, does he make a row?” asked Ivan roughly.
“Oh, dear, no, it’s quite the opposite. He’s very quiet. Only please don’t talk to him for long,” Marya Kondratyevna begged him. Ivan opened the door and went into the room.

The room was as stuffy as before, but some things had changed. One of the benches along the wall had been taken out. In its place stood a big old mahogany sofa upholstered in leather, with a bed made up on it and fairly clean white pillows. Smerdyakov sat on the sofa in the same dressing-gown. The table had been pulled out in front of the sofa, so there was hardly any room to move. A thick book in a yellow cover lay on it, but Smerdyakov wasn’t reading. He seemed to be sitting there doing nothing at all. He met Ivan with a slow, silent look and didn’t appear surprised that he had come. His face had changed a great deal. He was much thinner and more sallow, his eyes were sunken, and there were blue shadows under them.
“Why, you really are ill?” Ivan stopped short. “I won’t keep you long. I won’t even take my coat off. Where can I sit?”
He went around to the far end of the table, pulled up a chair and sat down.
“Why are you staring at me and not saying anything? I’ve come with just one question, and I swear I’m not leaving without an answer. Has Katerina Ivanovna, the young lady, been to see you?”
Smerdyakov kept silent, looking quietly at Ivan as before. Then, with a wave of his hand, he suddenly turned his face away.
“What’s wrong with you?” cried Ivan.
“Nothing.”
“What do you mean, ‘nothing’?”
“Yes, she has. It’s none of your concern. Leave me alone.”
“No, I won’t leave you alone. Tell me, when was she here?”

“Why, I’d clean forgotten about her,” said Smerdyakov with a scornful smile. He turned his face back to Ivan and stared at him with a look of frenzied hatred, the same look he had given him at their last interview, a month before.
“You look very ill yourself, you know. Your face is sunken. You don’t look like yourself,” he said to Ivan.
“Never mind my health. Answer what I ask.”
“But why are your eyes so yellow? The whites are all yellow. Are you so worried?” He smiled with contempt and suddenly laughed out loud.
“Listen! I told you, I’m not going without an answer!” Ivan cried, hugely irritated.
“Why do you keep pestering me? Why do you torment me?” said Smerdyakov, looking pained.
“Damn it! I’ve nothing to do with you. Answer my question and I’ll be gone.”
“I’ve got no answer for you,” said Smerdyakov, looking down again.
“Don’t worry, I’ll make you answer!”

“Why are you so on edge?” Smerdyakov stared at him with more than contempt now. It was close to disgust. “Is it because the trial starts tomorrow? Nothing will happen to you. Can’t you believe that, at long last? Go home, go to bed and sleep in peace. Don’t be afraid of anything.”
“I don’t understand you.... What have I got to be afraid of tomorrow?” Ivan said in astonishment, and suddenly a cold breath of fear really did pass over his soul. Smerdyakov looked him over.
“You don’t understand?” he drawled, as if hurt. “Strange, that a man of sense would care to act out such a farce!”
Ivan stared at him, speechless. The man had once been his valet, and this astonishingly lofty tone was extraordinary in itself. He had not used such a tone even at their last interview.

“I tell you, you’ve nothing to be afraid of. I won’t say a word about you. There’s no proof against you. Look how your hands are shaking! Why are your fingers moving like that? Go home. It wasn’t _you_ who murdered him.”
Ivan started. He thought of Alyosha.
“I know it wasn’t me,” he faltered.
“Do you?” Smerdyakov pounced on him again.
Ivan leapt up and grabbed him by the shoulder.
“Tell me everything, you viper! Everything!”
Smerdyakov wasn’t the least bit scared. He simply fixed his eyes on Ivan with a mad hatred.
“Well, it was you who murdered him, if that’s how it is,” he whispered, furious.
Ivan dropped back onto his chair as if he were turning something over in his mind. He gave a nasty laugh.
“You mean my going away. What you were talking about last time?”
“Last time you stood right here in front of me, and you understood everything. You understand it now.”
“What I understand is that you’re mad.”

“Aren’t you sick of it? Here we are, face to face. What’s the use of keeping up this farce with each other? Are you still trying to pin it all on me, to my face? _You_ murdered him. You’re the real murderer. I was only your tool, your faithful servant, and I did it by your word.”
“_Did_ it? You mean you killed him?” Ivan went cold.
Something seemed to give way in his brain, and a cold shudder ran through him. Then Smerdyakov himself looked at him in wonder. Ivan’s horror was so real, it seems, that it struck him.
“You can’t mean you honestly didn’t know?” he faltered, distrustful, searching Ivan’s eyes with a forced smile. Ivan kept staring at him and seemed unable to speak.
Ach, Vanka’s gone to Petersburg; I won’t wait till he’s back,
rang out suddenly in his head.
“Do you know, I’m afraid you’re a dream, a ghost sitting here in front of me,” he muttered.
“There’s no ghost here. There’s just the two of us, and one more. He must be here, that third one, between us.”
“Who is he? Who’s here? What third person?” Ivan cried in alarm, looking about and hastily searching every corner with his eyes.
“That third one is God Himself—Providence. He’s the third beside us now. Only don’t look for Him. You won’t find Him.”
“It’s a lie that you killed him!” Ivan cried wildly. “You’re mad, or you’re teasing me again!”

Smerdyakov kept watching him with curiosity, as before, showing no fear. He still couldn’t quite shake off his disbelief. He still thought Ivan knew everything and was trying to “pin it all on him, to his face.”

“Wait a minute,” he said at last in a weak voice. He suddenly pulled his left leg out from under the table and began to roll up the trouser leg. He wore long white stockings and slippers. Slowly he undid his garter and groped down to the bottom of the stocking. Ivan watched, and suddenly he shuddered with a fit of terror.

“He’s mad!” he cried. He sprang up and backed away so fast that he knocked his back against the wall, and there he stood, pressed against it, stiff and straight. He stared in crazed terror at Smerdyakov. Smerdyakov paid no attention to his terror. He went on fumbling in his stocking, as if he were trying to catch hold of something with his fingers and draw it out. At last he got hold of it and started pulling it out. Ivan saw that it was a piece of paper, or maybe a roll of papers. Smerdyakov drew it out and laid it on the table.
“There,” he said quietly.
“What is it?” Ivan asked, trembling.
“Be so kind as to look at it,” Smerdyakov answered, still in the same low voice.
Ivan stepped up to the table, picked up the roll of paper and began to unfold it. Then he suddenly jerked his fingers away, as if he had touched some loathsome reptile.
“Your hands keep twitching,” Smerdyakov remarked, and he unfolded the bundle himself, unhurried. Inside the wrapper were three packets of hundred-rouble notes.
“It’s all there, the whole three thousand roubles. You needn’t count it. Take it,” Smerdyakov urged Ivan, with a nod at the notes. Ivan sank back into his chair. He was white as a handkerchief.
“You scared me ... with that stocking,” he said, with a strange grin.
“Can you really not have known till now?” Smerdyakov asked once more.
“No, I didn’t know. I kept thinking it was Dmitri. Brother, brother! Ach!” All at once he clutched his head in both hands.
“Listen. Did you kill him on your own? With my brother’s help, or without it?”
“Only with you, with your help, did I kill him, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch is perfectly innocent.”
“All right, all right. We’ll talk about me later. Why do I keep shaking? I can’t even talk straight.”

“You were bold enough then. You said ‘everything was lawful,’ and look how frightened you are now,” Smerdyakov muttered, surprised. “Won’t you take some lemonade? I’ll ask for some at once. It’s very refreshing. Only I must hide this first.”

And again he nodded at the notes. He was about to get up and call through the door to Marya Kondratyevna to make some lemonade and bring it in. But he wanted something to cover the notes, so she wouldn’t see them. He took out his handkerchief first, and when that turned out to be very dirty, he picked up the big yellow book that Ivan had noticed on the table when he came in, and laid it over the notes. The book was _The Sayings of the Holy Father Isaac the Syrian_. Ivan read the title without thinking.
“I don’t want any lemonade,” he said. “We’ll talk about me later. Sit down and tell me how you did it. Tell me all of it.”
“You’d better take your greatcoat off, or you’ll get too hot.” As if the thought had only just struck him, Ivan took off his coat and, without getting up, threw it onto the bench.
“Speak, go on, speak.”
He seemed calmer now. He waited, sure that Smerdyakov would tell him _all_ of it.
“How it was done?” sighed Smerdyakov. “It was done in the most natural way, just as you said.”

“Never mind what I said, we’ll come to that,” Ivan cut in again, seemingly quite in command of himself, choosing his words firmly and no longer shouting as before. “Only tell me exactly how you did it. All of it, as it happened. Don’t forget anything. Above all, the details. The details, I beg you.”
“You’d gone away, and then I fell into the cellar.”
“In a fit, or a faked one?”
“Faked, naturally. I faked it all. I went quietly down the steps to the very bottom and lay down quietly, and as I lay down I screamed and thrashed about, until they carried me out.”
“Wait! And did you keep faking it all through afterward, even in the hospital?”
“No, not at all. The next day, in the morning, before they took me to the hospital, I had a real attack, worse than any I’d had in years. For two days I was out cold.”
“All right, all right. Go on.”

“They laid me on the bed. I knew I’d be on the other side of the partition, because whenever I was ill Marfa Ignatyevna put me there, close to them. She’s always been very good to me, ever since I was born. At night I moaned, but quietly. All the while I was expecting Dmitri Fyodorovitch to come.”
“Expecting him? To come to you?”

“Not to me. I expected him to come into the house. I had no doubt he’d come that night. Without me there, and with no news, he was bound to come and climb over the fence, as he used to, and do something.”
“And if he hadn’t come?”
“Then nothing would have happened. I’d never have made up my mind to it without him.”
“All right, all right ... speak more clearly, don’t rush, and above all, don’t leave anything out!”

“I expected him to kill Fyodor Pavlovitch. I thought that was certain, since I had been preparing him for it ... these last few days.... He knew about the knocks. That was the main thing. Suspicious as he is, and with the fury that had been building in him all those days, he was bound to get into the house by means of those taps. It couldn’t be avoided, so I was waiting for him.”
“Wait,” Ivan interrupted. “If he’d killed him, he would have taken the money and gone off with it. You must have thought of that. What would you have gained by it afterward? I don’t see.”

“But he’d never have found the money. That was only what I told him, that the money was under the mattress. It wasn’t true. It had been lying in a box. And afterward I suggested to Fyodor Pavlovitch, since I was the only person he trusted, that he hide the envelope with the notes in the corner behind the ikons. Nobody would have guessed that place, especially if they came in a hurry. So that’s where the envelope lay, in the corner behind the ikons. It would have been absurd to keep it under the mattress. The box, at least, could be locked. But everybody believes it was under the mattress. A stupid thing to believe. So if Dmitri Fyodorovitch had committed the murder, he’d have found nothing. He would either have run off in a hurry, scared of every sound, as murderers always are, or he would have been arrested. Either way I could have climbed up to the ikons and taken the money away the next morning, or even that very night, and it would all have been put down to Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I could count on that.”
“But what if he didn’t kill him, but only knocked him down?”

“If he hadn’t killed him, of course, I wouldn’t have dared take the money, and nothing would have happened. But I reckoned he’d beat him senseless, and then I’d have time to take it. After that I’d make out to Fyodor Pavlovitch that nobody but Dmitri Fyodorovitch had taken the money, after beating him.”
“Stop ... I’m getting confused. So it was Dmitri after all who killed him, and you only took the money?”

“No, he didn’t kill him. Well, I might as well have told you now that he was the murderer.... But I don’t want to lie to you now, because ... because if you really haven’t understood until now, as I can see for myself, and you’re not pretending, just to pin your guilt on me to my face, then you’re still responsible for everything. You knew about the murder, you ordered me to do it, and you went away knowing all about it. So this evening I mean to prove to your face that you are the only real murderer in the whole affair. I’m not the real murderer, though I did kill him. You are the rightful murderer.”

“Why, why am I a murderer? Oh, God!” Ivan cried. At last he couldn’t hold himself back, and he forgot that he had put off discussing himself until the end of the conversation. “You still mean that Tchermashnya business? Wait, tell me, why did you want my consent, if you really took Tchermashnya for consent? How can you explain that now?”

“With your consent assured, I’d have known you wouldn’t raise a cry over losing those three thousand, even if suspicion had fallen on me instead of Dmitri Fyodorovitch, or on me as his accomplice. On the contrary, you’d have shielded me from others.... And once you had your inheritance, you’d have rewarded me whenever you could, for the rest of your life. For you’d have got your inheritance through me. If he had married Agrafena Alexandrovna, you wouldn’t have had a farthing.”
“Ah! So you meant to hold it over me for the rest of my life,” snarled Ivan. “And what if I hadn’t gone away then, but had informed on you?”

“What could you have informed on? That I talked you into going to Tchermashnya? That’s all nonsense. Besides, after our conversation you’d have either gone away or stayed. If you’d stayed, nothing would have happened. I’d have known you didn’t want it done, and I’d have tried nothing. Since you went away, it meant you were assuring me that you wouldn’t dare inform on me at the trial, and that you’d overlook my having the three thousand. And indeed you couldn’t have prosecuted me afterward, because then I’d have told everything in court. Not that I’d stolen the money or killed him, mind you, I wouldn’t have said that. I’d have said that you put me up to the theft and the murder, though I didn’t agree to it. That’s why I needed your consent, so you couldn’t have cornered me afterward. For what proof could you have had? I could always have cornered you, by exposing how eager you were for your father’s death. And I tell you, the public would have believed every word, and you’d have been ashamed for the rest of your life.”
“Was I so eager, then? Was I?” Ivan snarled again.

“Of course you were, and by your consent you silently approved of my doing it.” Smerdyakov looked firmly at Ivan. He was very weak and spoke slowly and wearily, but some hidden inner force drove him on. He evidently had some purpose. Ivan sensed it.
“Go on,” he said. “Tell me how that night went.”

“What is there left to tell? I was lying there, and I thought I heard the master shout. Just before that, Grigory Vassilyevitch had suddenly got up and gone out, and then he let out a scream, and after that it was all silent and dark. I lay there waiting, my heart thumping. I couldn’t stand it. In the end I got up and went out. The window on the left, the one facing the garden, was standing open. I stepped over to the left and listened for whether he was sitting in there alive, and I heard the master moving about and sighing. So I knew he was alive. ‘Ech!’ I thought. I went up to the window and called to him, ‘It’s me.’ And he called back, ‘He’s been here, he’s been here; he’s run off.’ He meant Dmitri Fyodorovitch had been. ‘He’s killed Grigory!’ ‘Where?’ I whispered. ‘There, in the corner,’ he said, and pointed. He was whispering too. ‘Wait a bit,’ I said. I went to the corner of the garden to look, and there was Grigory Vassilyevitch, lying by the wall, covered in blood and out cold. So it’s true, I thought, Dmitri Fyodorovitch really has been here. And on the spot I decided to put an end to it all. Grigory Vassilyevitch, even if he was alive, would never know what happened, lying there senseless like that. The one danger was that Marfa Ignatyevna might wake up. I felt that at the time. But the longing to get it done had come over me so badly that I could scarcely breathe. I went back to the window and told the master, ‘She’s here, she’s come; Agrafena Alexandrovna has come and wants to be let in.’ And he jumped like a baby. ‘Where is she?’ he gasped, but he couldn’t believe it. ‘She’s standing out there,’ I said. ‘Open up.’ He looked out of the window at me, half believing and half suspicious, and afraid to open. ‘Why, he’s afraid of me now,’ I thought. And it struck me as funny. So I thought of knocking on the window frame, right there before his eyes, with those taps we had agreed on as the sign that Grushenka had come. He didn’t seem to trust my word, but the moment he heard the taps, he ran to open the door. He opened it. I would have gone in, but he stood in the doorway so I couldn’t get past. ‘Where is she? Where is she?’ He stared at me, shaking all over. ‘Well,’ I thought, ‘if he’s that frightened of me, it looks bad!’ And my legs went weak with fear that he wouldn’t let me in, or would shout, or that Marfa Ignatyevna would come running, or that something else would go wrong. I can’t remember now, but I must have stood there pale, facing him. I whispered to him, ‘Why, she’s there, right under the window; how can you not see her?’ ‘Bring her, then, bring her.’ ‘She’s scared,’ I said; ‘the noise frightened her, she’s hiding in the bushes; go and call her yourself from the study.’ He ran to the window and put the candle on the sill. ‘Grushenka,’ he cried, ‘Grushenka, are you there?’ He cried it, but he wouldn’t lean out of the window, and he wouldn’t step away from me, because he was in a panic. He was so frightened he didn’t dare turn his back on me. ‘Why, there she is,’ I said. I went up to the window and leaned right out. ‘There she is; she’s in the bush, laughing at you, can’t you see her?’ All at once he believed it. He was shaking all over—he was terribly crazy about her—and he leaned right out of the window. I snatched up the iron paperweight from his table; you remember it, about three pounds in weight? I swung it and struck him on the top of the skull with the corner. He didn’t even cry out. He just sagged down, and I struck him again, and a third time. By the third blow I knew I had broken his skull. He suddenly rolled over on his back, face up, covered in blood. I looked round. There was no blood on me, not a spot. I wiped the paperweight and put it back. Then I went to the ikons, took the money out of the envelope, and flung the envelope on the floor with the pink ribbon beside it. I went out into the garden, shaking all over, straight to the apple tree with the hollow in it—you know the hollow. I’d marked it long before and left a rag and a scrap of paper ready inside. I wrapped all the notes in the rag and shoved it deep into the hole. And there it stayed for over two weeks. I took it out afterwards, when I came out of the hospital. I went back to my bed and lay down, thinking, ‘If Grigory Vassilyevitch has been killed outright, it may turn out badly for me. But if he’s not killed and he recovers, it’ll be first-rate, because then he’ll swear that Dmitri Fyodorovitch was here, and so Dmitri Fyodorovitch must have killed him and taken the money.’ Then I began to groan, from suspense and impatience, to wake Marfa Ignatyevna as soon as I could. At last she got up and ran to me, but when she saw that Grigory Vassilyevitch wasn’t there, she ran out, and I heard her scream in the garden. That set it all in motion, and it put my mind at rest.”

He stopped. Ivan had listened the whole time in dead silence, without moving or taking his eyes off him. While telling his story, Smerdyakov had looked at him now and then, but for the most part he kept his eyes turned aside. Now that he had finished, he was plainly agitated and breathing hard. Sweat stood out on his face. Whether he felt remorse, or something else, there was no way to tell.
“Hold on,” cried Ivan, thinking hard. “What about the door? If he opened the door only for you, how could Grigory have seen it open earlier? Grigory saw it open before you went in.”

It was remarkable that Ivan spoke quite amicably now, in a different tone, not angry as before. If anyone had opened the door at that moment and looked in, he would certainly have concluded that the two were talking peacefully about some ordinary, though interesting, subject.

“As for that door, and Grigory Vassilyevitch saying he saw it open, that’s only his imagination,” said Smerdyakov with a wry smile. “He’s no man, I assure you, he’s an obstinate mule. He didn’t see it. He only fancied he’d seen it, and nothing will shake him. It’s our luck that he took that notion into his head, because after it they can’t fail to convict Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

“Listen ...” said Ivan, who seemed bewildered again and was struggling to catch hold of something. “Listen. There are many questions I wanted to ask you, but I’ve forgotten them ... I keep forgetting, and I get muddled. Yes. Tell me this, at least. Why did you open the envelope and leave it lying on the floor? Why didn’t you just carry the envelope off?... When you were telling me, I thought you spoke of it as if it were the right thing to do ... but why, I can’t understand....”

“I had a good reason for doing it. Take a man who knew all about the matter, as I did, for instance. Say he’d seen those notes before, and maybe had put them in that envelope himself, and had watched with his own eyes while it was sealed and addressed. If a man like that did the murder, why would he rip the envelope open afterwards, and in such desperate haste, too, when he knew for certain the notes were inside? No, if the robber were someone like me, he’d simply put the envelope straight in his pocket and be off with it as fast as he could. With Dmitri Fyodorovitch it would be quite another thing. He knew about the envelope only by hearsay; he’d never seen it. If he’d found it under the mattress, say, he’d have torn it open as fast as he could, to make sure the notes were in it. And he’d have thrown the envelope down, with no time to think that it would count as evidence against him. For he was no regular thief and had never stolen anything outright before. He’s a gentleman born. And if he did bring himself to steal, it wouldn’t be real stealing, just taking what was his own, since he’d told the whole town beforehand that he would, and had even boasted aloud before everybody that he’d go and take his property from Fyodor Pavlovitch. I didn’t say any of this openly to the prosecutor when he questioned me. On the contrary, I steered him toward it with a hint, as if I didn’t see it myself, as if he’d thought of it on his own and I hadn’t put it in his head. And Mr. Prosecutor’s mouth positively watered at my suggestion.”
“But can you really have thought all that out on the spot?” cried Ivan, overwhelmed with astonishment. He looked at Smerdyakov again, with alarm.
“Mercy on us! Could anybody think all that out in such a desperate hurry? It was all worked out beforehand.”
“Well ... well, the devil must have helped you!” Ivan cried again. “No, you’re no fool, you’re a good deal cleverer than I thought....”

He rose, evidently meaning to pace the room. He was in terrible distress. But the table stood in his way, and there was scarcely room to squeeze between the table and the wall, so he only turned around where he stood and sat down again. Perhaps not being able to move irritated him, for he suddenly burst out, almost as furiously as before.

“Listen, you wretched, contemptible creature! Do you not understand that if I haven’t killed you, it’s only because I’m saving you to answer for this tomorrow at the trial? God sees,” Ivan raised his hand, “perhaps I too was guilty. Perhaps I really did have a secret wish for my father’s ... death. But I swear I wasn’t as guilty as you suppose, and perhaps I didn’t push you into it at all. No, no, I didn’t push you into it! But no matter. Tomorrow at the trial I will testify against myself. I’m resolved on it! I will tell everything, everything. But we’ll go there together. And whatever you say against me at the trial, whatever evidence you give, I’ll stand up to it; I’m not afraid of you. I’ll confirm all of it myself! But you must confess too! You must, you must; we’ll go together. That is how it will be!”
Ivan said this solemnly and with resolve, and his flashing eyes alone were enough to show that it would be so.
“You’re ill, I can see; you’re quite ill. Your eyes have gone yellow,” Smerdyakov observed, without the slightest irony, and with what seemed real sympathy.
