They thought he had some idea of his own in reserve, some hidden weapon of defense, which he would spring on us when the time came. Meanwhile, sure of his strength, he seemed to be amusing himself.

For example, when Grigory, Fyodor Pavlovitch’s old servant, gave evidence, the counsel for the defense simply pounced on him when his turn to ask questions came. Grigory was the one who had given the most damning testimony about the open door. It should be said that he walked into the hall calm and almost stately, not in the least put off by the majesty of the court or the huge audience listening to him. He gave his evidence as confidently as if he were chatting with his Marfa, only perhaps more respectfully. There was no making him contradict himself. The prosecutor questioned him first, at length, about the family life of the Karamazovs. The family portrait came out in lurid colors. You could see and hear that the witness was honest and fair. Despite his deep reverence for his dead master’s memory, he still testified that the old man had been unjust to Mitya and “hadn’t brought up his children as he should. He’d have been eaten alive by lice when he was little, if it hadn’t been for me,” he added, speaking of Mitya’s early childhood. “It wasn’t right either, a father cheating his son over his mother’s property, which was his by rights.”

The prosecutor asked what grounds he had for saying that Fyodor Pavlovitch had wronged his son in money matters. To everyone’s surprise, Grigory had no proof whatever to offer. Still, he insisted that the settlement with the son was “unfair” and that the father ought “to have paid him several thousand roubles more.” I should mention, by the way, that the prosecutor pressed this question, whether Fyodor Pavlovitch had really held back part of Mitya’s inheritance, on every witness who could be asked it, Alyosha and Ivan included. But he got no exact information from anyone. All said it was so, and none could produce any clear proof. Grigory’s account of the scene at the dinner table, when Dmitri burst in, beat his father and threatened to come back and kill him, left a sinister impression on the court. The old servant told it calmly, sparing his words, in his own odd way of speaking, and that was as effective as eloquence. He said he was not angry with Mitya for knocking him down and hitting him in the face. He had forgiven him long ago. Of the late Smerdyakov he said, crossing himself, that he was a gifted lad, but stupid and afflicted, and, worse still, a godless one, and that Fyodor Pavlovitch and his elder son had taught him to be so. But he defended Smerdyakov’s honesty almost warmly. He told how Smerdyakov had once found the master’s money in the yard and, instead of hiding it, had carried it to his master. The master had given him a “gold piece” for it and trusted him completely from then on. He insisted stubbornly that the garden door had been open. But he was asked so many questions that I can’t remember them all.

At last the counsel for the defense began his cross-examination. His first question concerned the envelope in which Fyodor Pavlovitch was supposed to have put three thousand roubles for “a certain person.” “Did you ever see it, you who attended your master so closely for so many years?” Grigory answered that he had not seen it, and had never heard of the money from anyone “till everybody was talking about it.” Fetyukovitch asked this question about the envelope of everyone who could conceivably have known of it, just as persistently as the prosecutor asked his about Dmitri’s inheritance, and he got the same answer from all: nobody had seen the envelope, though many had heard of it. From the beginning everyone noticed how Fetyukovitch kept coming back to this subject.

“Now, if you’ll allow me, I’ll ask you something,” Fetyukovitch said, suddenly and unexpectedly. “What was that balsam made of—or rather that decoction—which, as we learn from the preliminary inquiry, you rubbed on your lumbago that evening, hoping to cure it?”
Grigory stared blankly at him. After a short silence he muttered, “There was saffron in it.”
“Only saffron? You don’t remember anything else in it?”
“Milfoil, too.”
“And pepper, maybe?” Fetyukovitch asked.
“Yes, pepper too.”
“And so on. And all of it dissolved in vodka?”
“In spirit.”
A faint ripple of laughter ran through the court.
“You see, in spirit. And after rubbing your back, I believe, you drank what was left in the bottle, saying a certain pious prayer that only your wife knows?”
“I did.”
“Did you drink much? A glass or two, roughly?”
“Could have been a tumblerful.”
“A tumblerful, then. Maybe a tumbler and a half?”
Grigory didn’t answer. He seemed to see what was being aimed at.
“A glass and a half of neat spirit—not bad at all, is it? You could see the gates of heaven open, not just the door into the garden?”
Grigory kept silent. Again there was laughter in the court. The President shifted in his seat.
“And do you know for certain,” Fetyukovitch pressed on, “whether you were awake or not when you saw the open door?”
“I was standing up.”
“That doesn’t prove you were awake.” (Again there was laughter in the court.) “If someone had asked you a question at that moment, could you have answered it? What year it is, for instance?”
“I don’t know.”
“And what year is it, Anno Domini? Do you know?”
Grigory stood there bewildered, looking straight at his tormentor. Strange to say, he really did seem not to know the year.
“Then perhaps you can tell me how many fingers you have on your hands?”
“I am a servant,” Grigory said suddenly, in a loud, clear voice. “If my betters want to make sport of me, it is my duty to bear it.”

Fetyukovitch was slightly taken aback. The President stepped in and told him to keep his questions to the point. Fetyukovitch bowed with dignity and said he had nothing more to ask the witness. Of course, the public and the jury were left with a grain of doubt about a man who, while undergoing a certain cure, might have seen “the gates of heaven,” and who did not even know what year he lived in. But before Grigory left the stand, there was another episode. The President turned to the prisoner and asked if he wished to comment on the last witness’s evidence.

“All of it is true, except what he says about the door,” Mitya cried loudly. “I thank him for combing the lice off me, and I thank him for forgiving my blows. The old man has been honest all his life, and as faithful to my father as seven hundred poodles.”
“Prisoner, watch your language,” the President warned him.
“I am not a poodle,” Grigory muttered.
“Fine, I’m the poodle myself,” cried Mitya. “If it’s an insult, I’ll take it on myself, and I beg his pardon. I was a beast to him, and cruel. I was cruel to Æsop too.”
“What Æsop?” the President asked sternly again.
“Oh, Pierrot ... my father, Fyodor Pavlovitch.”
Again and again the President warned Mitya, very sternly and with great force, to watch his language.
“You are hurting yourself in the eyes of your judges.”

The counsel for the defense dealt just as cleverly with Rakitin’s evidence. I may say that Rakitin was one of the leading witnesses, and the prosecutor set great store by him. It turned out that he knew everything. His knowledge was amazing. He had been everywhere, seen everything, talked to everybody, and knew every detail of the lives of Fyodor Pavlovitch and all the Karamazovs. He had heard of the envelope, it is true, only from Mitya himself. But he described Mitya’s exploits at the “Metropolis” in minute detail, with all the compromising things he had done and said, and he told the story of Captain Snegiryov’s “wisp of tow.” Yet even Rakitin could say nothing definite about Mitya’s inheritance, and he kept to contemptuous generalities.

“Who could tell which of them was to blame, and which owed the other money, with their crazy Karamazov way of muddling things so that no one could make head or tail of it?” He put the tragic crime down to habits ingrained by ages of serfdom and to the sorry state of Russia, which he blamed on the lack of proper institutions. He was, in fact, allowed a good deal of freedom to speak. This was the first time Rakitin showed what he could do and drew notice. The prosecutor knew that the witness was preparing a magazine article on the case. Later, in his speech, as we shall see, he quoted some ideas from that article, which showed he had already seen it. The picture the witness painted was a gloomy, sinister one, and it greatly strengthened the case for the prosecution. Altogether, Rakitin’s talk fascinated the public by its independence and the remarkable nobility of its ideas. There were even two or three bursts of applause when he spoke of serfdom and the sorry state of Russia.

But Rakitin, in his youthful ardor, made a small blunder, and the counsel for the defense seized on it at once, with great skill. He was answering some questions about Grushenka. Carried away by the loftiness of his own feelings and by his success, of which he was of course aware, he went so far as to speak rather contemptuously of Agrafena Alexandrovna as “the kept mistress of Samsonov.” Later he would have paid a good deal to take those words back, for Fetyukovitch caught him out on them immediately. And it was all because Rakitin had not reckoned that the lawyer could have learned every detail so thoroughly in so short a time.

“Allow me to ask,” the counsel for the defense began, with the friendliest and even respectful smile, “you are, of course, the same Mr. Rakitin whose pamphlet, _The Life of the Deceased Elder, Father Zossima_, published by the diocesan authorities, full of deep and religious reflections and opening with an excellent, devout dedication to the bishop, I have just read with such pleasure?”
“I didn’t write it for publication ... it was published afterward,” muttered Rakitin, for some reason badly rattled and almost ashamed.

“Oh, excellent! A thinker like you can, and indeed ought to, take the widest view of every social question. Your most instructive pamphlet has circulated widely thanks to the bishop’s patronage, and has been of real use.... But here is the main thing I’d like to learn from you. You said just now that you were very well acquainted with Madame Svyetlov.” (It should be noted that Grushenka’s surname was Svyetlov. I heard it for the first time that day, during the trial.)
“I can’t answer for all my acquaintances.... I’m a young man ... and who can be responsible for everyone he meets?” cried Rakitin, turning red all over.

“I understand, I quite understand,” cried Fetyukovitch, as if he too were embarrassed and hurrying to make excuses. “You, like anyone, might well be interested in knowing a young and beautiful woman who would gladly receive the _élite_ of the young men of the neighborhood. But ... I only wanted to know ... It has come to my knowledge that a couple of months ago Madame Svyetlov was particularly eager to meet the younger Karamazov, Alexey Fyodorovitch, and promised you twenty-five roubles if you would bring him to her in his monastic dress. And that actually happened, on the evening of the very day when the terrible crime now under investigation was committed. You brought Alexey Karamazov to Madame Svyetlov, and did you receive the twenty-five roubles from her as a reward? That is what I wanted to hear from you.”
“It was a joke.... I don’t see how it could interest you.... I took it as a joke ... meaning to give it back later....”
“Then you did take— But you haven’t given it back yet ... or have you?”
“That doesn’t matter,” muttered Rakitin. “I refuse to answer such questions.... Of course I’ll give it back.”

The President stepped in, but Fetyukovitch declared he had no more questions for the witness. Mr. Rakitin left the witness box with his character not altogether free of stain. The effect of the lofty idealism of his speech was rather spoiled. Fetyukovitch’s expression, as he watched him go, seemed to say to the public, “Here is a sample of the high-minded people who accuse him.” I remember that this incident too did not pass without an outburst from Mitya. He was furious at the tone in which Rakitin had spoken of Grushenka, and he suddenly shouted “Bernard!” After Rakitin’s cross-examination, the President asked the prisoner whether he had anything to say, and Mitya cried out loudly:
“Since I’ve been arrested, he has borrowed money from me! He is a contemptible Bernard and an opportunist, and he doesn’t believe in God. He fooled the bishop!”

Mitya, of course, was called to order again for his wild language, but Rakitin was finished. Captain Snegiryov’s evidence was a failure too, though for quite a different reason. He turned up in ragged, dirty clothes and muddy boots, and despite the vigilance and trained eyes of the police officers, he proved to be hopelessly drunk. Asked about Mitya’s attack on him, he refused to answer.
“God bless him. Ilusha told me not to. God will make it up to me yonder.”
“Who told you not to tell? Who are you talking about?”
“Ilusha, my little son. ‘Father, father, how he insulted you!’ He said that by the stone. Now he is dying....”
The captain suddenly burst into sobs and dropped to his knees before the President. He was hustled out amid laughter from the public. The effect the prosecutor had prepared did not come off at all.

Fetyukovitch went on making the most of every chance, and amazed people more and more with his detailed knowledge of the case. Trifon Borissovitch, for example, made a great impression, of course, and a very damaging one for Mitya. He worked out almost on his fingers that on his first visit to Mokroe Mitya must have spent three thousand roubles, “or very little less. Just think what he squandered on those gypsy girls alone! And as for our lousy peasants, it wasn’t a matter of tossing half a rouble into the street. He gave them presents of twenty-five roubles each, at the least. He gave no less than that. And how much money was simply stolen from him! And if anyone did steal, he left no receipt. How could you catch the thief, when he was throwing his money away the whole time? Our peasants are robbers, you know. They have no thought for their souls. And the way he carried on with the girls, our village girls! They’re set up since then, I tell you. They used to be poor.” He recalled, in fact, every item of expense and added it all up. So the theory that only fifteen hundred had been spent, and the rest put away in a little bag, seemed impossible to believe.
“I saw three thousand in his hands, as plain as day. I saw it with my own eyes. I should think I know how to count money,” cried Trifon Borissovitch, doing his best to please “his betters.”

When Fetyukovitch came to cross-examine him, he hardly tried to refute his evidence. Instead he began asking him about an incident at the first carousal at Mokroe, a month before the arrest. Timofey and another peasant, Akim, had picked up from the floor of the passage a hundred roubles that Mitya had dropped while drunk. They had handed it to Trifon Borissovitch, and he had given each of them a rouble for it. “Well,” asked the lawyer, “did you give that hundred roubles back to Mr. Karamazov?” Trifon Borissovitch squirmed in vain.... Once the peasants had been examined, he had to admit that the hundred roubles had been found. He only added that he had scrupulously given all of it back to Dmitri Fyodorovitch “in perfect honesty, and it’s only because his honor was in liquor at the time that he wouldn’t remember it.” But he had denied the incident of the hundred roubles until the peasants were called to prove it, so his evidence about returning the money to Mitya was naturally viewed with great suspicion. And so one of the most dangerous witnesses brought forward by the prosecution was discredited once more.

The same thing happened with the Poles. They took a proud, independent stand. They shouted loudly that they had both served the Crown, that “Pan Mitya” had offered them three thousand “to buy their honor,” and that they had seen a large sum of money in his hands. Pan Mussyalovitch stuffed a terrible number of Polish words into his sentences. He saw that this only raised his standing with the President and the prosecutor, so he grew more and more pompous and ended by speaking Polish altogether. But Fetyukovitch caught them in his snares too. Trifon Borissovitch was called back and, despite his dodging, was forced to admit that Pan Vrublevsky had swapped in a different pack of cards for the one he had provided, and that Pan Mussyalovitch had cheated during the game. Kalganov confirmed this, and both Poles left the witness box with their reputations damaged, amid laughter from the public.

Then exactly the same thing happened with almost all the most dangerous witnesses. Fetyukovitch managed to put a stain on every one of them and send them off with a touch of mockery. The lawyers and experts were lost in admiration. They only could not see what good purpose it served, since everyone, I repeat, felt that the case for the prosecution could not be refuted, but was growing more and more tragically overwhelming. Yet from the confidence of the “great magician” they could see that he was serene, and they waited. They felt that “such a man” had not come from Petersburg for nothing, and that he was not a man to go home unsuccessful.

chapters.title: III. The Medical Experts And A Pound Of Nuts
paragraphs: The medical experts did the prisoner little good either. It came out later that Fetyukovitch had never counted on them much. He had taken up the medical line of defense only because Katerina Ivanovna insisted. She had sent to Moscow for a celebrated doctor for exactly this purpose. The defense could lose nothing by it, of course, and with luck might gain something. Still, the whole thing had a touch of comedy, because the doctors disagreed. The experts were the famous doctor from Moscow, our own Doctor Herzenstube, and the young Doctor Varvinsky. The last two were also witnesses for the prosecution.

Doctor Herzenstube was the first to be called as an expert. He was a gray, bald old man of seventy, of middle height and sturdy build. Everyone in town esteemed and respected him. He was a conscientious doctor and an excellent, pious man, a Hernguter or a Moravian brother, I am not sure which. He had lived among us for many years and carried himself with wonderful dignity. He was kind and humane. He treated the poor and the peasants for nothing, went to see them in their slums and huts, and left money behind for medicine. But he was as stubborn as a mule. Once an idea was in his head, nothing could shake it out. Almost everyone in town knew, by the way, that within two or three days of arriving, the famous doctor had made some extremely insulting remarks about Doctor Herzenstube’s qualifications. The Moscow doctor charged twenty-five roubles a visit. Even so, several people in town were glad of his arrival and rushed to consult him, whatever it cost. All of these had been Doctor Herzenstube’s patients, of course, and the celebrated doctor had criticized his treatment with extreme harshness. In the end, the moment he saw each patient he asked, “Well, who has been stuffing you with quack medicines? Herzenstube? He, he!” Doctor Herzenstube heard all this, naturally. And now all three doctors came forward one after another to be examined.

Doctor Herzenstube declared flatly that the prisoner’s mind was obviously abnormal. He gave his grounds for this opinion, which I leave out here, and added that the abnormality showed not only in many of the prisoner’s past actions but was plain even now, at this very moment. Asked to explain how it was plain at this very moment, the old doctor answered with simple-hearted directness. He said that the prisoner had come into court with “an extraordinary air, remarkable in the circumstances.” He had “marched in like a soldier, looking straight before him, though it would have been more natural for him to look to the left, where the ladies were sitting among the public. He was a great admirer of the fair sex, and he must be thinking a lot about what the ladies are saying of him now.” That is how the old man put it, in his peculiar language.

I must add that he spoke Russian fluently, but he built every sentence the German way. This never bothered him, because it was his weakness to believe he spoke Russian perfectly, better even than Russians do. He was also very fond of Russian proverbs, and always declared they were the best and most expressive sayings in the world. I may mention, too, that in conversation he often forgot the most ordinary words. Through absent-mindedness they would simply go out of his head, though he knew them perfectly well. The same thing happened when he spoke German. At such moments he always waved his hand in front of his face, as if trying to catch the lost word, and nobody could make him go on talking until he had found it. His remark that the prisoner ought to have looked at the ladies when he came in set off a whisper of amusement in the audience. All our ladies were very fond of the old doctor. They also knew that he had been a bachelor all his life, a religious man of exemplary conduct, who looked on women as lofty creatures. So his unexpected remark struck everyone as very odd.

Next the Moscow doctor was questioned. He repeated, firmly and emphatically, that he thought the prisoner’s mental condition abnormal in the highest degree. He spoke at length and learnedly about “aberration” and “mania.” From all the facts collected, he argued, the prisoner had certainly been in a state of aberration for several days before his arrest. If he had committed the crime, then even if he was aware of it, it must have been almost involuntary, since he had no power to control the morbid impulse that possessed him.

But besides temporary aberration, the doctor diagnosed mania, which, he said, promised to lead to complete insanity in the future. (I should note that I am giving this in my own words; the doctor used very learned, professional language.) “All his actions go against common sense and logic,” he continued. “I will not mention what I have not seen, that is, the crime itself and the whole catastrophe. But the day before yesterday, while he was talking to me, he had an unaccountably fixed look in his eye. He laughed suddenly when there was nothing to laugh at. He was constantly and inexplicably irritable, and used strange words, ‘Bernard!’ ‘Ethics!’ and others equally out of place.” But the doctor saw mania above all in the fact that the prisoner could not speak even of the three thousand roubles, which he considered himself cheated of, without extraordinary irritation. Yet he could talk fairly lightly about his other misfortunes and grievances. By all accounts, whenever the three thousand roubles came up in the past, he had flown into a perfect frenzy. And yet he was said to be a disinterested man, not a grasping one.

“As for the opinion of my learned colleague,” the Moscow doctor added ironically at the end, “that the prisoner would naturally have looked at the ladies when he came into court, and not straight ahead, I will say only this. Quite apart from the playfulness of the theory, it is radically unsound. I fully agree that the prisoner, entering the court where his fate will be decided, would not naturally stare straight ahead in that fixed way, and that this may really be a sign of his abnormal mental condition. But at the same time I maintain that he would naturally not look to the left at the ladies. He would look, on the contrary, to the right, to find his legal adviser, on whose help all his hopes rest and on whose defense his whole future depends.” The doctor gave his opinion positively and emphatically.

But then Doctor Varvinsky’s unexpected pronouncement put the last touch of comedy on the experts’ disagreement. In his opinion the prisoner was now, and had been all along, in a perfectly normal condition. Before his arrest he must certainly have been nervous and exceedingly excited, but there were several perfectly obvious causes for that: jealousy, anger, constant drunkenness, and so on. This nervous state, though, did not involve the mental aberration just mentioned. As for whether the prisoner should have looked to the left or to the right on entering the court, “in his modest opinion” the prisoner would naturally look straight ahead, as he had in fact done, because that was where the judges, who held his fate in their hands, were sitting. So it was exactly by looking straight ahead that he showed his perfectly normal state of mind at present. The young doctor finished his “modest” testimony rather heatedly.
“Bravo, doctor!” Mitya cried from his seat. “Just so!”

Mitya was reprimanded, of course. But the young doctor’s opinion had a decisive effect on the judges and the public, and, as it turned out later, everyone agreed with him. Doctor Herzenstube, though, was quite unexpectedly useful to Mitya when he was called as a witness. As an old resident of the town who had known the Karamazov family for years, he supplied some facts of great value to the prosecution. Then suddenly, as if remembering something, he added:

“But the poor young man might have had a very different life, for he had a good heart as a child and after childhood, that I know. But the Russian proverb says, ‘If a man has one head, it’s good, but if another clever man comes to visit him, it would be better still, for then there will be two heads and not only one.’”

“One head is good, but two are better,” the prosecutor put in impatiently. He knew the old man’s habit of talking slowly and deliberately, with no regard for the impression he was making or the delay he was causing. He also knew how highly the old man valued his flat, dull, always gleefully self-satisfied German wit. The old man loved to make jokes.

“Oh, yes, that’s what I say,” he went on obstinately. “One head is good, but two are much better, but he did not meet another head with wits, and his wits went. Where did they go? I’ve forgotten the word.” He passed his hand before his eyes and went on, “Oh, yes, _spazieren_.”
“Wandering?”

“Oh, yes, wandering, that’s what I say. Well, his wits went wandering and fell in a hole so deep that he lost himself. And yet he was a grateful and feeling boy. Oh, I remember him very well, a little chap so high, left neglected by his father in the back yard, running about with no boots on his feet and his little breeches hanging by one button.”
A note of feeling and tenderness suddenly came into the honest old man’s voice. Fetyukovitch gave a positive start, like a man who scents something, and caught at it at once.

“Oh, yes, I was a young man then.... I was ... well, I was forty-five then, and had only just come here. And I was so sorry for the boy then. I asked myself why shouldn’t I buy him a pound of ... a pound of what? I’ve forgotten what it’s called. A pound of what children are very fond of, what is it, what is it?” The doctor began waving his hands again. “It grows on a tree and is gathered and given to everybody....”
“Apples?”
“Oh, no, no. You have a dozen apples, not a pound.... No, there are a lot of them, and all little. You put them in the mouth and crack.”
“Nuts?”

“Quite so, nuts, I say so.” The doctor repeated it in the calmest way, as though he had never been at a loss for the word. “And I bought him a pound of nuts, for no one had ever bought the boy a pound of nuts before. And I lifted my finger and said to him, ‘Boy, _Gott der Vater_.’ He laughed and said, ‘_Gott der Vater_.’... ‘_Gott der Sohn_.’ He laughed again and lisped, ‘_Gott der Sohn_.’ ‘_Gott der heilige Geist_.’ Then he laughed and said as best he could, ‘_Gott der heilige Geist_.’ I went away, and two days after I happened to be passing, and he shouted to me of his own accord, ‘Uncle, _Gott der Vater, Gott der Sohn_,’ and he had only forgotten ‘_Gott der heilige Geist_.’ But I reminded him of it, and I felt very sorry for him again. But he was taken away, and I did not see him again. Twenty-three years passed. I am sitting one morning in my study, a white-haired old man, when there walks into the room a blooming young man I should never have known, but he held up his finger and said, laughing, ‘_Gott der Vater, Gott der Sohn_, and _Gott der heilige Geist_. I have just arrived and have come to thank you for that pound of nuts, for no one else ever bought me a pound of nuts; you are the only one that ever did.’ And then I remembered my happy youth and the poor child in the yard, with no boots on his feet, and my heart was touched and I said, ‘You are a grateful young man, for you have remembered all your life the pound of nuts I bought you in your childhood.’ And I embraced him and blessed him. And I shed tears. He laughed, but he shed tears, too ... for the Russian often laughs when he ought to be weeping. But he did weep; I saw it. And now, alas!...”
“And I am weeping now too, German, I am weeping now, you saintly man,” Mitya cried suddenly.

At any rate, the anecdote made a certain favorable impression on the public. But the chief sensation in Mitya’s favor was caused by Katerina Ivanovna’s evidence, which I will describe in a moment. In fact, once the witnesses _à décharge_, that is, those called by the defense, began to testify, fortune seemed all at once markedly kinder to Mitya. What was particularly striking was that this surprised even the counsel for the defense. But before Katerina Ivanovna was called, Alyosha was examined. He recalled a fact that seemed to furnish positive evidence against one important point made by the prosecution.

chapters.title: IV. Fortune Smiles On Mitya
paragraphs: Even Alyosha himself was taken by surprise at being called. He was not required to take the oath, and I remember that both sides questioned him very gently and kindly. Clearly his reputation for goodness had gone before him. Alyosha gave his evidence modestly and with restraint, but his warm sympathy for his unhappy brother could not be mistaken. Asked to describe his brother’s character, he said Mitya was perhaps hot-tempered and swept away by his passions, but also honorable, proud and generous, and capable of sacrificing himself if need be. He admitted, though, that his brother’s passion for Grushenka and his rivalry with their father had put him in an unbearable position lately. But he rejected with indignation the suggestion that his brother might have committed murder for money. He did recognize that the three thousand roubles had become almost an obsession with Mitya. Mitya saw it as part of the inheritance his father had cheated him of, and although he was normally indifferent to money, he could not even speak of that three thousand without fury. As for the rivalry between the two “ladies,” as the prosecutor put it, meaning Grushenka and Katya, he answered evasively, and on one or two questions he refused to answer at all.
“Did your brother tell you, at any rate, that he meant to kill your father?” asked the prosecutor. “You may decline to answer if you think it necessary,” he added.
“He didn’t tell me so directly,” answered Alyosha.
“What do you mean? Did he tell you indirectly?”
“He once spoke to me of his hatred for our father, and of his fear that at an extreme moment ... in a moment of fury, he might perhaps murder him.”
“And you believed him?”

“I’m afraid I did. But I never doubted that some higher feeling would save him at the fatal moment, and it did save him, because he did not kill my father,” Alyosha said firmly, in a loud voice that carried through the whole court.
The prosecutor started like a war-horse hearing a trumpet.

“Let me assure you that I fully believe your conviction is completely sincere. I do not put it down to your affection for your unhappy brother, nor confuse the two. Your peculiar view of this whole tragic affair is already known to us from the preliminary investigation. I won’t try to hide from you that it is highly individual and contradicts all the other evidence the prosecution has collected. So I think it essential to press you: what facts have led you to this conviction of your brother’s innocence, and of the guilt of another person, the one you named in your evidence at the preliminary inquiry?”
“I only answered the questions I was asked at the preliminary inquiry,” replied Alyosha, slowly and calmly. “I made no accusation against Smerdyakov on my own.”
“But you did give evidence against him?”

“I was led to it by my brother Dmitri’s words. I was told what happened at his arrest, and how he pointed to Smerdyakov, before I was questioned. I believe absolutely that my brother is innocent, and if he didn’t commit the murder, then—”
“Then Smerdyakov did? Why Smerdyakov? And why are you so completely convinced of your brother’s innocence?”
“I can’t help believing my brother. I know he wouldn’t lie to me. I could see from his face that he wasn’t lying.”
“Only from his face? Is that all the proof you have?”
“I have no other proof.”
“And you have no proof at all of Smerdyakov’s guilt, except your brother’s word and the look on his face?”
“No, I have no other proof.”

The prosecutor dropped his questions at that point. Alyosha’s evidence left the public bitterly disappointed. There had been talk about Smerdyakov before the trial. Someone had heard one thing, someone else had noticed another. People said that Alyosha had gathered some extraordinary proofs of his brother’s innocence and Smerdyakov’s guilt. And after all that there was nothing, no evidence at all except certain moral convictions, which are only natural in a brother.

But now Fetyukovitch began his cross-examination. He asked Alyosha when the prisoner had spoken to him of hating his father and possibly killing him, and whether Alyosha had heard it, say, at their last meeting before the catastrophe. Alyosha gave a start as he answered, as though he had just then remembered and understood something.
“I remember something now that I’d completely forgotten myself. It wasn’t clear to me at the time, but now—”

And, clearly struck by an idea for the first time only now, he eagerly told how at his last meeting with Mitya that evening, under the tree on the road to the monastery, Mitya had struck himself on the chest, “the upper part of the chest.” He had said several times that he had a way of recovering his honor, and that this way was here, here on his chest. “When he struck himself on the chest, I thought he meant it was in his heart,” Alyosha went on. “I thought he meant he might find strength in his heart to save himself from some awful disgrace that was waiting for him, and that he didn’t dare confess even to me. I must admit that at the time I did think he was talking about our father, and that the disgrace he was shuddering at was the thought of going to our father and doing him some violence. Yet just then he was pointing at something on his chest. I remember the thought struck me that the heart isn’t in that part of the chest but lower down, and that he was striking himself much too high, just below the neck, and kept pointing at that spot. My idea seemed silly to me then, but perhaps he was pointing to that little bag with the fifteen hundred roubles in it!”
“Just so,” Mitya cried from his place. “That’s right, Alyosha, it was the little bag I hit with my fist.”

Fetyukovitch hurried over to Mitya and begged him to keep quiet, and in the same moment he turned and pounced on Alyosha. Alyosha was carried along by his own memory, and he eagerly offered his theory that the disgrace was probably just that fifteen hundred roubles he carried. Mitya could have returned it to Katerina Ivanovna as half of what he owed her. But he had made up his mind not to repay her and to spend it on something else, namely on running away with Grushenka, if she would consent.

“That’s it, it must be!” exclaimed Alyosha, in sudden excitement. “My brother cried out several times that he could free himself at once from half of the disgrace, half of it (he said _half_ several times), but that he was so unhappy in his weakness of will that he wouldn’t do it ... that he knew beforehand he was incapable of doing it!”
“And you remember clearly and confidently that he struck himself on exactly this part of the chest?” Fetyukovitch asked eagerly.

“Clearly and confidently. I thought at the time, ‘Why is he striking himself up there when the heart is lower down?’ and the thought seemed stupid to me then ... I remember that it seemed stupid ... it flashed through my mind. That’s what brought it back to me just now. How could I have forgotten it until now? It was that little bag he meant when he said he had the means but wouldn’t give back the fifteen hundred. And when he was arrested at Mokroe he cried out—I know, I was told it—that he considered it the most disgraceful act of his life that he had the means of repaying Katerina Ivanovna half (half, note!) of what he owed her, and still couldn’t bring himself to repay it, and preferred to stay a thief in her eyes rather than part with the money. And what torture, what torture that debt has been to him!” Alyosha exclaimed in conclusion.

The prosecutor, of course, objected. He had Alyosha describe once more how it had all happened, and several times he pressed the question: “Had the prisoner seemed to point to anything? Or had he perhaps simply thumped himself on the chest with his fist?”
“But it wasn’t with his fist,” cried Alyosha. “He pointed with his fingers, and he pointed here, very high up.... How could I have forgotten it so completely until this moment?”

The President asked Mitya what he had to say about the last witness’s evidence. Mitya confirmed it. He said he had been pointing to the fifteen hundred roubles on his chest, just below the neck, and that this was of course the disgrace. “A disgrace I can’t deny, the most shameful act of my whole life,” cried Mitya. “I could have repaid it and I didn’t. I preferred to stay a thief in her eyes rather than give it back. And the most shameful part of it was that I knew beforehand I wouldn’t give it back! You’re right, Alyosha! Thank you, Alyosha!”

So Alyosha’s cross-examination came to an end. What mattered about it, and what struck everyone, was that at least one fact had come to light. It was only one tiny scrap, a mere hint of evidence, but it went some small way toward proving that the bag had really existed and had held fifteen hundred roubles, and that the prisoner had not been lying at the preliminary inquiry when he claimed at Mokroe that the fifteen hundred roubles were “his own.” Alyosha was glad. With a flushed face he went back to the seat set aside for him. He kept repeating to himself: “How was it I forgot? How could I have forgotten it? And what made it come back to me now?”

Katerina Ivanovna was called to the witness-box. As she came in, something extraordinary went through the court. The ladies seized their lorgnettes and opera-glasses. The men stirred, and some got to their feet for a better look. Afterwards everybody swore that Mitya had turned “white as a sheet” at the sight of her. She was dressed all in black, and she walked forward modestly, almost timidly. Her face gave no sign that she was agitated, but a resolute light shone in her dark and gloomy eyes. I may add that many people remarked how especially handsome she looked at that moment. She spoke softly but clearly, so that the whole court heard her. She kept her composure, or at least tried to seem composed. The President began his questions with tact and great respect, as though afraid of touching “certain chords,” and he was considerate of her great unhappiness. But in reply to one of the first questions, Katerina Ivanovna said firmly that she had once been engaged to the prisoner, “until he left me of his own accord...” she added quietly. When they asked her about the three thousand she had trusted Mitya to post to her relations, she said firmly, “I didn’t give him the money simply to send it off. I felt at the time that he was in great need of money.... I gave him the three thousand on the understanding that he should post it within the month if he cared to. There was no need for him to worry about that debt afterwards.”
I will not repeat every question put to her and every answer in detail. I will give only the substance of what she said.

“I was firmly convinced that he would send off that sum as soon as he got money from his father,” she went on. “I have never doubted his disinterestedness and his honesty ... his scrupulous honesty ... in money matters. He felt quite certain that he would receive the money from his father, and he spoke to me about it several times. I knew he had a feud with his father, and I have always believed that his father treated him unfairly. I don’t remember any threat he made against his father. He certainly never made any such threat in front of me. If he had come to me at that time, I would have set his mind at rest at once about that unlucky three thousand roubles. But he had stopped coming to see me ... and I myself was put in such a position ... that I couldn’t invite him.... And in fact I had no right to be demanding about that money,” she added suddenly, and there was a ring of resolution in her voice. “I once owed him more than three thousand for help he gave me in money, and I took it, although at that time I couldn’t foresee that I would ever be in a position to repay my debt.”
Her voice had a defiant ring. It was then that Fetyukovitch started his cross-examination.

“Did that happen not here, but at the beginning of your acquaintance?” Fetyukovitch put in cautiously, feeling his way, and at once scenting something in his favor. I must mention in parenthesis that Fetyukovitch had been brought from Petersburg partly at Katerina Ivanovna’s own wish, yet he knew nothing about the episode of the four thousand roubles Mitya had given her, or her “bowing to the ground to him.” She had hidden this from him and said nothing about it, which was strange. We can fairly safely assume that she herself did not know until the very last minute whether she would speak of that episode in court, and that she waited for the inspiration of the moment.

No, I can never forget those moments. She began telling her story. She told everything, the whole episode that Mitya had told Alyosha, her bowing to the ground, and her reason for it. She told about her father and how she went to Mitya. Not in one word, not in a single hint, did she let on that Mitya himself, through her sister, had suggested that they “send Katerina Ivanovna” to fetch the money. She generously kept that back, and she was not ashamed to make it seem that she had run to the young officer on her own impulse, counting on something ... to beg him for the money. It was something tremendous! I went cold and trembled as I listened. The court was hushed, straining to catch each word. It was something without precedent. Even from a girl as willful and scornfully proud as she was, such a frank confession, such sacrifice, such self-immolation, seemed unbelievable. And for what, and for whom? To save the man who had deceived and insulted her, and to help, however little, in saving him, by making a strong impression in his favor. And indeed, the figure of the young officer who, with a respectful bow to the innocent girl, handed her his last four thousand roubles, all he had in the world, was cast in a very sympathetic and attractive light. But ... I had a painful misgiving in my heart! I felt that slander might come of it later (and it did, in fact, it did). All over town afterwards it was repeated, with spiteful laughter, that the story was perhaps not quite complete, that is, in the statement that the officer had let the young lady leave “with nothing but a respectful bow.” People hinted that something had been left out here.

“And even if nothing had been left out, if that were the whole story,” the most respected of our ladies declared, “even then it’s very doubtful whether it was proper for a young girl to behave like that, even to save her father.”

And could Katerina Ivanovna, with all her intelligence and her morbid sensitiveness, have failed to see that people would talk like this? She must have seen it, and yet she decided to tell everything. Of course, all these nasty little doubts about whether her story was true came only later, and at first everyone was deeply moved. The judges and lawyers listened to Katerina Ivanovna in a respectful, almost shamefaced silence. The prosecutor did not dare to ask a single question on the subject. Fetyukovitch gave her a low bow. Oh, he was almost triumphant! A great deal of ground had been gained. A man gives his last four thousand on a generous impulse, and then that same man murders his father to rob him of three thousand. The idea seemed too incongruous. Fetyukovitch felt that the charge of theft, at least, was as good as disproved now. “The case” was thrown into quite a different light. A wave of sympathy for Mitya rose in the court. As for him.... I was told that once or twice while Katerina Ivanovna was giving her evidence, he jumped up from his seat, sank back again, and hid his face in his hands. But when she had finished, he suddenly cried out in a sobbing voice:
“Katya, why have you ruined me?” and his sobs were heard all over the court. But he checked himself at once, and cried out again:
“Now I am condemned!”

After that he sat stiff in his place, teeth clenched, arms crossed on his chest. Katerina Ivanovna stayed in the court and took her seat. She was pale and kept her eyes down. People sitting near her said she shook all over for a long time, as if she had a fever. Then Grushenka was called.

Now I come to the sudden catastrophe which was perhaps the final cause of Mitya’s ruin. I am convinced of this, and so is everyone, for all the lawyers said the same afterwards: if that episode had not happened, the prisoner would at least have been recommended for mercy. But more of that later. First, a few words about Grushenka.

She too was dressed all in black, with her magnificent black shawl over her shoulders. She walked to the witness-box with a smooth, soundless step and the slight sway of gait that is common in women of a full figure. She looked steadily at the President, glancing neither right nor left. To my mind she looked very handsome just then, and not at all pale, as the ladies said afterwards. They also insisted that her expression was tense and spiteful. I think she was simply irritated, and painfully aware of the scornful and prying eyes of our gossip-loving public. She was proud and could not stand being despised. She was one of those people who blaze up angrily and long to strike back at the mere suggestion of contempt. There was also a streak of timidity in her, of course, and an inward shame at being timid. So it is no wonder that her tone kept shifting. One moment it was angry, scornful and rough, and the next it had a sincere note of self-blame. Sometimes she spoke like someone taking a desperate plunge, as if she felt, “I don’t care what happens, I’ll say it....” On the subject of her acquaintance with Fyodor Pavlovitch, she remarked curtly, “That’s all nonsense, and was it my fault that he kept pestering me?” But a minute later she added, “It was all my fault. I was laughing at them both, at the old man and at him too, and I brought both of them to this. It all happened because of me.”

Somehow Samsonov’s name came up. “That’s nobody’s business,” she snapped at once, with a sort of insolent defiance. “He was my benefactor. He took me in when I hadn’t a shoe to my foot, when my family had thrown me out.” The President reminded her, though very politely, that she must answer the questions directly and not wander off into irrelevant details. Grushenka went crimson, and her eyes flashed.

She had not seen the envelope with the notes in it. She had only heard from “that wicked wretch” that Fyodor Pavlovitch had an envelope with three thousand in notes. “But that was all foolishness. I was only laughing. I wouldn’t have gone to him for anything.”
“Who do you mean by ‘that wicked wretch’?” inquired the prosecutor.
“The lackey Smerdyakov, who murdered his master and hanged himself last night.”
She was, of course, asked at once what grounds she had for so definite an accusation. But it turned out that she, too, had no grounds for it.

“Dmitri Fyodorovitch told me so himself. You can believe him. The woman who came between us has ruined him. She’s the cause of it all, let me tell you,” Grushenka added. She seemed to quiver with hatred, and there was a vengeful note in her voice.
They asked her again who she meant.
“The young lady there, Katerina Ivanovna. She sent for me, offered me chocolate, tried to charm me. There’s not much real shame in her, I can tell you that....”
Here the President stopped her sternly and begged her to moderate her language. But the jealous woman’s heart was on fire, and she did not care what she did.

“When the prisoner was arrested at Mokroe,” the prosecutor said, “everyone saw you run out of the next room and heard you cry: ‘It’s all my fault. We’ll go to Siberia together!’ So by then you believed he had murdered his father?”

“I don’t remember what I felt at the time,” answered Grushenka. “Everyone was crying out that he had killed his father, and I felt it was my fault, that he had murdered him on my account. But when he said he wasn’t guilty, I believed him at once. I believe him now and I always will. He’s not the man to tell a lie.”

Then Fetyukovitch started his cross-examination. I remember that, among other things, he asked about Rakitin and about the twenty-five roubles “you paid him for bringing Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov to see you.”

“There was nothing strange about his taking the money,” sneered Grushenka, with angry contempt. “He was always coming to me for money. He used to get thirty roubles a month out of me at least, mostly for luxuries. He had enough to live on without my help.”
“What made you so generous to Mr. Rakitin?” Fetyukovitch asked, in spite of an uneasy movement from the President.
“Why, he’s my cousin. His mother was my mother’s sister. But he’s always begged me not to tell anyone here, he’s so dreadfully ashamed of me.”

This came as a complete surprise to everyone. Nobody in the town or the monastery, not even Mitya, had known it. I was told that Rakitin went purple with shame where he sat. Somehow Grushenka had heard, before she came into court, that he had testified against Mitya, and that was why she was angry. This time the whole effect on the public of Rakitin’s speech, of his noble sentiments and his attacks on serfdom and on the political disorder of Russia, was finally ruined. Fetyukovitch was pleased: it was another godsend. Grushenka’s cross-examination was short, and of course her evidence could hold nothing especially new. She left a very unpleasant impression on the public. Hundreds of scornful eyes followed her as she finished her evidence and sat down again in the courtroom, a good way from Katerina Ivanovna. Mitya said nothing all through her evidence. He sat as though turned to stone, with his eyes on the floor.
Ivan was called to give evidence.

chapters.title: V. A Sudden Catastrophe
paragraphs: I should mention that Ivan had in fact been summoned before Alyosha. But the court usher had told the President that the witness couldn’t appear just then. He had been taken ill, or had some kind of fit, but he would give his evidence as soon as he was better. Nobody seemed to have heard this, and it only came out later.

For the first moment hardly anyone noticed him come in. The main witnesses, above all the two rival ladies, had already been questioned. For the time being curiosity was satisfied, and the public was almost worn out. Several more witnesses were still to be heard, and after all that had been said they probably had little to add. The time was passing. Ivan walked up with extraordinary slowness. He looked at no one, and he kept his head bowed, as if he were sunk in gloomy thought. His clothes were impeccable, but his face made a painful impression, on me at least. It looked earthy, like the face of a dying man. His eyes were dull. He lifted them and slowly looked around the court. Alyosha jumped up from his seat and moaned, “Ah!” I remember that, but hardly anyone noticed.

The President started by informing him that he was a witness not under oath. He could answer or refuse to answer, he said, but of course he must testify according to his conscience, and so on and so on. Ivan listened and stared back at him blankly. Little by little, though, his face relaxed into a smile. The President looked at him in astonishment, and the moment he finished, Ivan burst out laughing.
“Well, and what else?” he asked in a loud voice.
The court went quiet. Everyone felt that something strange was going on. The President began to look uneasy.
“You ... are perhaps still unwell?” he began, looking around for the usher.
“Don’t trouble yourself, your excellency, I’m well enough, and I can tell you something interesting,” Ivan answered with sudden calm and politeness.
“Do you have some special statement to make?” the President went on, still distrustful.
Ivan looked down and waited a few seconds. Then he raised his head and answered, almost stammering:
“No ... I don’t. I have nothing in particular.”

They began to question him. He seemed to answer unwillingly, in the fewest possible words, and with a disgust that grew more and more plain, though what he said was perfectly rational. To many questions he replied that he didn’t know. He knew nothing about his father’s money dealings with Dmitri. “I wasn’t interested in the subject,” he added. He had heard the prisoner threaten to murder his father. About the money in the envelope, he had heard from Smerdyakov.
“The same thing over and over again,” he interrupted suddenly, looking weary. “I have nothing in particular to tell the court.”
“I see that you are unwell, and I understand how you feel,” the President began.
He turned to the prosecutor and the defense counsel, to invite them to question the witness if they needed to. At that moment Ivan suddenly asked, in an exhausted voice:
“Let me go, your excellency, I feel very ill.”

And with those words, without waiting for permission, he turned and started to walk out of the court. After four steps, though, he stopped, as if he had made a decision. He smiled slowly and came back.

“I’m like that peasant girl, your excellency ... you know the story. How does it go? ‘I’ll stand up if I feel like it, and if I don’t, I won’t.’ They were trying to get her into her sarafan, to take her to church for her wedding, and she said, ‘I’ll stand up if I feel like it, and if I don’t, I won’t.’... It’s in some book about the peasantry.”
“What do you mean by that?” the President asked sternly.

“Why, this.” Ivan suddenly pulled out a roll of notes. “Here’s the money ... the notes that were in that envelope” (he nodded toward the table where the material evidence lay), “the money our father was murdered for. Where shall I put it? Mr. Superintendent, take it.”
The court usher took the whole roll and handed it to the President.
“How can this money have come into your hands, if it is the same money?” the President asked in wonder.

“I got it from Smerdyakov, from the murderer, yesterday.... I was with him just before he hanged himself. It was he who killed our father, not my brother. He murdered him, and I put him up to it ... Who doesn’t want his father dead?”
“Are you in your right mind?” broke involuntarily from the President.

“I should think I am in my right mind ... in the same nasty mind as all of you ... as all these ... ugly faces.” He turned suddenly to the audience. “My father has been murdered, and they act horrified,” he snarled, with furious contempt. “They keep up the pretense for each other. Liars! Every one of them wants his father dead. One reptile devours another.... If there hadn’t been a murder, they’d have been angry and gone home in a bad mood. It’s a spectacle they want! _Panem et circenses_. Though I’m one to talk! Have you got any water? Give me a drink, for Christ’s sake!” He suddenly clutched his head.

The usher went to him at once. Alyosha jumped up and cried, “He is ill. Don’t believe him: he has brain fever.” Katerina Ivanovna rose impulsively from her seat and stared at Ivan, rigid with horror. Mitya stood up and watched his brother hungrily, listening to him with a wild, strange smile.
“Don’t disturb yourselves. I’m not mad, I’m only a murderer,” Ivan began again. “You can’t expect eloquence from a murderer,” he added suddenly, for some reason, and gave a queer laugh.

The prosecutor leaned toward the President, plainly dismayed. The two other judges whispered to each other in agitation. Fetyukovitch pricked up his ears and listened closely. The whole hall was hushed, waiting. The President seemed suddenly to pull himself together.

“Witness, your words are incomprehensible and out of place here. Calm yourself, if you can, and tell your story ... if you really have something to tell. How can you back up your statement ... unless you are in fact delirious?”

“That’s just it, I have no proof. That cur Smerdyakov isn’t going to send you proofs from the other world ... in an envelope. All you people think about is envelopes—one is enough. I’ve got no witnesses ... except one, perhaps,” he said, smiling thoughtfully.
“Who is your witness?”

“He has a tail, your excellency, and that would be irregular! _Le diable n’existe point!_ Don’t pay any attention to him: he’s a paltry, pitiful devil,” he added suddenly. He stopped laughing and spoke almost confidentially. “He’s here somewhere, no doubt—under that table with the material evidence on it, perhaps. Where else would he sit? You see, listen to me. I told him I won’t keep quiet, and he started in about the geological cataclysm ... idiocy! Come on, let the monster out ... he’s been singing a hymn. That’s because his heart is light! It’s like a drunk in the street bawling about how ‘Vanka went to Petersburg,’ and I would give a quadrillion quadrillions for two seconds of joy. You don’t know me! Oh, how stupid all this business is! Come, take me instead of him! I didn’t come here for nothing.... Why, why is everything so stupid?...”
And he began slowly, as if lost in thought, looking around him again. But by now the whole court was in an uproar. Alyosha rushed toward him, but the usher had already taken Ivan by the arm.

“What are you doing?” he cried, staring into the man’s face. Then he grabbed him by the shoulders and threw him violently to the floor. But the police were right there, and they seized him. He screamed in fury. And all the way as they carried him out, he kept yelling and screaming something incoherent.

The whole court was thrown into confusion. I don’t remember everything in the order it happened. I was excited myself and couldn’t follow it all. I only know that later, when things had calmed down and everyone understood what had happened, the usher was reprimanded. He explained, quite reasonably, that the witness had seemed perfectly well. The doctor had seen him an hour before, when he had a slight attack of giddiness, and until he came into the court he had talked quite coherently, so nothing could have been foreseen. In fact, the usher said, Ivan had insisted on giving evidence. But before anyone had fully recovered from this scene, another followed it. Katerina Ivanovna had an attack of hysterics. She sobbed and shrieked loudly, but she would not leave the court. She struggled and begged them not to take her away. Suddenly she cried out to the President:

“I have more evidence to give, and I must give it now ... now! Here is a document, a letter ... take it, read it quickly, quickly! It’s a letter from that monster ... that man there, there!” She pointed at Mitya. “He is the one who killed his father, you’ll see that right away. He wrote to me that he would kill his father! But the other one is ill, he is ill, he is delirious!” she kept crying, beside herself.

The court usher took the document she was holding out to the President. She dropped into her chair and hid her face in her hands. Then she began to sob, convulsively and without a sound, shaking all over and stifling every noise for fear of being thrown out of the court. The document she had handed up was the letter Mitya had written at the “Metropolis” tavern, the one Ivan had called a “mathematical proof.” Alas! Its mathematical force was recognized. Without that letter Mitya might have escaped his doom, or at least the doom would have been less terrible. It was, I repeat, hard to take in every detail. What followed is still confused in my mind. The President must, I suppose, have passed the document straight to the judges, the jury, and the lawyers on both sides. I only remember that they then began examining the witness. The President gently asked whether she had recovered enough, and Katerina Ivanovna exclaimed impetuously:

“I’m ready, I’m ready! I’m quite able to answer you,” she added, evidently still afraid that something would somehow keep her from giving evidence. She was asked to explain in detail what this letter was and how she had come to receive it.

“I got it the day before the crime was committed, but he wrote it the day before that, at the tavern—that is, two days before he committed the crime. Look, it’s written on some kind of bill!” she cried breathlessly. “He hated me at that time, because he had behaved contemptibly and was running after that creature ... and because he owed me that three thousand.... Oh! That three thousand humiliated him, because of his own meanness! This is how it came about, that three thousand. I beg you, I implore you, listen to me. Three weeks before he murdered his father, he came to me one morning. I knew he needed money, and I knew what he wanted it for. Yes, yes—to win that creature and carry her off. I knew then that he had been false to me and meant to abandon me. And it was I, I, who gave him that money. I offered it to him on the pretext that he should send it to my sister in Moscow. And as I handed it over, I looked him in the face and said he could send it whenever he liked, ‘in a month’s time would do.’ How, how could he fail to understand that I was practically telling him to his face, ‘You want money to be false to me with your creature, so here is the money. I’m giving it to you myself. Take it, if you have so little honor as to take it!’ I wanted to prove what he was, and what happened? He took it, he took it, and squandered it with that creature in one night.... But he knew, he knew that I knew all about it. I assure you he understood, too, that I gave him that money to test him, to see whether he had lost every scrap of honor and would take it from me. I looked into his eyes and he looked into mine, and he understood it all, and he took it—he carried off my money!”

“That’s true, Katya,” Mitya roared suddenly. “I looked into your eyes and I knew you were dishonoring me, and I took your money anyway. Despise me as a scoundrel, all of you, despise me! I’ve earned it!”
“Prisoner,” cried the President, “one more word and I will have you removed.”

“That money tormented him,” Katya went on, in a rush. “He wanted to pay it back. He did want to, that’s true. But he needed money for that creature, too. So he murdered his father, and he never paid me back. He went off with her to that village where he was arrested. There he squandered the money he had stolen after killing his father. And the day before the murder he wrote me this letter. He was drunk when he wrote it. I saw that at once, at the time. He wrote it out of spite, and he was certain, absolutely certain, that I would never show it to anyone, even if he did kill him. Otherwise he wouldn’t have written it. He knew I wouldn’t want revenge and ruin him! But read it, read it carefully, more carefully, please, and you will see that he described everything in his letter, all in advance: how he would kill his father and where the money was kept. Look, please, don’t overlook this. There’s one phrase: ‘I shall kill him as soon as Ivan has gone away.’ So he thought out beforehand how he would kill him,” Katerina Ivanovna pointed out to the court, with venomous, spiteful triumph. Oh, it was clear she had studied every line of that letter and caught every meaning hidden under it. “If he hadn’t been drunk, he wouldn’t have written to me. But look, everything is written there in advance, exactly as he committed the murder afterwards. A complete program of it!” she exclaimed frantically.

She no longer cared about any consequences to herself, though no doubt she had foreseen them even a month ago. Even then, perhaps, shaking with anger, she had weighed whether to show the letter at the trial or not. Now she had taken the fatal plunge. I remember that the letter was read aloud by the clerk, right afterwards, I believe. It made an overwhelming impression. They asked Mitya whether he admitted writing it.

“It’s mine, mine!” cried Mitya. “I’d never have written it sober!... We’ve hated each other for plenty of reasons, Katya, but I swear, I swear, I loved you even while I hated you. And you didn’t love me!”

He sank back onto his seat, wringing his hands in despair. The prosecutor and the counsel for the defense began cross-examining her. Mostly they wanted to find out what had led her to hide such a document, and to give her evidence in such a different tone and spirit only a short while before.

“Yes, yes. I was lying just now. I lied against my honor and my conscience. But I wanted to save him, because he hates me so, and despises me!” Katya cried madly. “Oh, how horribly he despises me! He always has. Do you know, he has despised me from the very moment I bowed down to him for that money? I saw it.... I felt it right then, but for a long time I refused to believe it. How often I have read it in his eyes: ‘And yet you came of your own accord.’ Oh, he didn’t understand. He had no idea why I ran to him. He can imagine nothing but baseness. He measured me by himself. He thought everyone was like him!” Katya hissed furiously, in a perfect frenzy. “And he only wanted to marry me because I’d come into a fortune. Because of that, because of that! I always suspected it was because of that! Oh, he is a brute! He was always sure that I would tremble with shame in front of him all my life, because I had gone to him that time. He was sure he had the right to despise me forever for it, and so to stand above me. That’s why he wanted to marry me! That’s how it was, that’s all it was! I tried to win him with my love, a love without limits. I even tried to forgive him his unfaithfulness. But he understood nothing, nothing! How could he, really? He is a monster! I only received that letter the next evening. They brought it to me from the tavern. And that very morning, that very morning, I had wanted to forgive him everything, everything, even his treachery!”

The President and the prosecutor, of course, tried to calm her. I can’t help thinking they were ashamed to be taking advantage of her hysteria and listening to such confessions. I remember hearing them say to her, “We understand how hard this is for you; believe us, we can feel for you,” and so on, and so on. And yet they drew the evidence out of the raving, hysterical woman all the same. At last she described how Ivan had been almost driven out of his mind for the past two months, trying to save “the monster and murderer,” his brother. She spoke with that remarkable clearness which so often comes, if only for a moment, in such overwrought states.

“He tortured himself,” she exclaimed. “He was always trying to make his brother’s guilt smaller, and confessing to me that he, too, had never loved his father, and perhaps even wished for his death himself. Oh, he has a tender, too tender, conscience! He tormented himself with his conscience! He told me everything, everything! He came every day and talked to me as his only friend. I have the honor to be his only friend!” she cried suddenly, with a sort of defiance, and her eyes flashed. “He went to see Smerdyakov twice. One day he came to me and said, ‘If it wasn’t my brother but Smerdyakov who committed the murder’ (for the story was going around everywhere that Smerdyakov had done it), ‘perhaps I am guilty too, for Smerdyakov knew I didn’t like my father and perhaps believed I wanted my father dead.’ Then I brought out that letter and showed it to him. He was completely convinced that his brother had done it, and it overwhelmed him. He couldn’t bear the thought that his own brother was a parricide! Only a week ago I saw that it was making him ill. In the last few days he has talked incoherently in my presence. I saw his mind was giving way. He walked about raving. People saw him muttering in the streets. The doctor from Moscow examined him the day before yesterday, at my request, and told me he was on the eve of brain fever. And all on his account, on account of this monster! And last night he learned that Smerdyakov was dead! It was such a shock that it drove him out of his mind... and all because of this monster, all for the sake of saving the monster!”

Oh, of course, an outpouring like this, a confession like this, is possible only once in a lifetime. At the hour of death, say, on the way to the scaffold! But it was in Katya’s nature, and this was such a moment in her life. This was the same impetuous Katya who had once thrown herself on the mercy of a young profligate to save her father. This was the same Katya who, a little while before, in her pride and chastity, had sacrificed herself and her maidenly modesty in front of all these people. She had told of Mitya’s generous conduct, hoping to soften his fate a little. And now she sacrificed herself again, but this time for someone else. Perhaps only now, only at this moment, did she feel and know how dear that other man was to her! She had sacrificed herself out of terror for him. She had suddenly realized that he had ruined himself by confessing that he, not his brother, had committed the murder. She had sacrificed herself to save him, to save his good name, his reputation!

And yet a terrible doubt crossed one’s mind. Was she lying when she described her old relations with Mitya? That was the question. No, she had not meant to slander him when she cried that Mitya despised her for bowing down to him! She believed it herself. She had been firmly convinced, perhaps ever since that bow, that the simple-hearted Mitya, who even then worshipped her, was laughing at her and despising her. She had loved him with a hysterical, “lacerated” love, out of pride alone, wounded pride, and that love was less like love than like revenge. Oh, perhaps that lacerated love might have grown into real love. Perhaps Katya wanted nothing more than that. But Mitya’s unfaithfulness had wounded her to the depths of her heart, and her heart could not forgive him. The moment of revenge had come suddenly. All that had piled up so long and so painfully in the wronged woman’s breast burst out at once, without warning. She betrayed Mitya, but she betrayed herself as well. And as soon as she had given her feelings full expression, the strain was of course over, and shame overwhelmed her. The hysterics started again. She fell to the floor, sobbing and screaming. She was carried out. At that moment Grushenka, with a wail, rushed toward Mitya before anyone had time to stop her.

“Mitya,” she wailed, “that serpent of yours has destroyed you! See, she has shown you what she is!” she shouted to the judges, shaking with rage. At a signal from the President, men seized her and tried to take her out of the courtroom. She would not let them. She fought and struggled to get back to Mitya. Mitya let out a cry and strained toward her. They overpowered him.

Yes, I think the ladies who had come for the spectacle must have been satisfied. The show had certainly been varied. Next, I remember, the Moscow doctor came in. I believe the President had sent the court usher earlier to arrange medical help for Ivan. The doctor informed the court that the sick man had a dangerous attack of brain fever and had to be taken away at once. The prosecutor and the counsel for the defense questioned him. He said the patient had come to see him of his own accord the day before yesterday. He had warned him then that such an attack was coming, but the man had refused to be looked after. “He was certainly not in a normal state of mind. He told me himself that he saw visions while awake, that he met several dead people in the street, and that Satan visited him every evening,” the doctor finished. Having given his evidence, the celebrated doctor left. The letter produced by Katerina Ivanovna was added to the material evidence. After some deliberation, the judges decided to continue the trial and to enter both unexpected pieces of evidence (from Ivan and from Katerina Ivanovna) in the record.

But I will not set down the testimony of the other witnesses. They only repeated and confirmed what had been said already, each in his own characteristic way. I say again, it was all gathered up in the prosecutor’s speech, which I will quote shortly. Everyone was excited, everyone was electrified by the catastrophe we had just seen, and all of them waited with intense impatience for the speeches for the prosecution and the defense. Fetyukovitch was plainly shaken by Katerina Ivanovna’s evidence. The prosecutor, though, was triumphant. When all the evidence had been heard, the court adjourned for almost an hour. I believe it was exactly eight o’clock when the President took his seat again and our prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovitch, began his speech.

chapters.title: VI. The Prosecutor’s Speech. Sketches Of Character
paragraphs: Ippolit Kirillovitch began his speech trembling with nerves. Cold sweat stood on his forehead, and he felt hot and cold by turns all over his body. He described this himself afterwards. He regarded the speech as his _chef-d’œuvre_, the _chef-d’œuvre_ of his whole life, his swan song. He did die nine months later, of galloping consumption, so he really did have the right, as it turned out, to compare himself to a swan singing its last song. He had put his whole heart into that speech, and every bit of brain he had. And poor Ippolit Kirillovitch unexpectedly showed that he had some feeling, at least, for the public good and for “the eternal question” hidden away inside him. The real strength of his speech was its sincerity. He truly believed the prisoner was guilty. He was not accusing him merely as a duty of his office, and when he called for vengeance he trembled with a genuine passion “for the security of society.” Even the ladies in the audience, though they stayed hostile to Ippolit Kirillovitch, admitted that he made an extraordinary impression on them. He began in a voice that kept breaking, but it soon grew strong and filled the court until the end of his speech. As soon as he had finished, though, he nearly fainted.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” began the prosecutor, “this case has caused a stir all over Russia. But why should that surprise us? What is so especially horrifying in it for us? We are so used to such crimes! That is what is truly horrible: that such dark deeds no longer horrify us. What ought to horrify us is that we have grown so used to them, and not this or that single crime. What are the causes of our indifference, of our lukewarm attitude toward such deeds, toward such signs of the times, which are ominous for an unenviable future? Is it our cynicism? Is it the premature exhaustion of mind and imagination in a society that is sinking into decay in spite of its youth? Is it that our moral principles are shattered to their foundations, or perhaps that we have no such principles at all? I cannot answer such questions. Yet they are disturbing, and every citizen not only must, but ought to be troubled by them. Our newborn and still timid press has already done the public a good service, for without it we would never have heard of the horrors of unbridled violence and moral degradation that the press keeps bringing to the notice, not only of those who attend the new jury courts set up in the present reign, but of everyone. And what do we read almost every day? Of things beside which the present case grows pale and seems almost commonplace. But what matters most is that the majority of our national crimes of violence bear witness to a widespread evil, now so general among us that it is hard to fight against it.

“One day we see a brilliant young officer of high society, at the very start of his career, murder in a cowardly, underhand way, without a pang of conscience, an official who had once been his benefactor, and the servant girl as well, to steal back his own I.O.U. and whatever ready money he could find on the man. ‘It will come in handy for my pleasures in fashionable society and for my career in the future.’ After murdering them, he puts pillows under the head of each victim, and goes away. Next, a young hero ‘decorated for bravery’ kills the mother of his chief and benefactor, like a highwayman. To persuade his companions to join him he claims that ‘she loves him like a son, and so she will follow all his directions and take no precautions.’ Granted that he is a monster, yet I do not dare say, in these days, that he is the only one. Another man will not commit the murder, but will feel and think as he does, and is just as dishonorable in soul. In silence, alone with his conscience, he asks himself perhaps, ‘What is honor, and is the condemnation of bloodshed not a prejudice?’

“Perhaps people will cry out against me that I am morbid and hysterical, that this is a monstrous slander, that I am exaggerating. Let them say so—and heavens! I would be the first to rejoice if it were so! Oh, do not believe me. Think of me as morbid, but remember my words. Suppose only a tenth, only a twentieth part of what I say is true—even so, it is awful! Look at how our young people take their own lives. They never ask themselves Hamlet’s question, what lies beyond. There is no sign of such a question in them, as though everything that concerns the soul and what awaits us after the grave had long since been wiped from their minds and buried under the sands. Look at our vice, and at our profligates. Fyodor Pavlovitch, the unlucky victim in the present case, was almost an innocent babe compared with many of them. And yet we all knew him; ‘he lived among us!’...

“Yes, one day perhaps the leading minds of Russia and of Europe will study the psychology of Russian crime, for the subject deserves it. But that study will come later, at leisure, when the whole tragic topsy-turvydom of our present time lies farther behind us. Then it can be examined with more insight and more impartiality than I am able to bring to it. For now we are either horrified, or pretend to be, while in truth we gloat over the spectacle. We love strong and eccentric sensations that tickle our cynical, pampered idleness. Or else, like little children, we brush the dreadful ghosts away and hide our heads in the pillow, so as to go back to our games and merriment as soon as the ghosts have vanished. But one day we must begin life in sober earnest. We must look at ourselves as a society. It is time we tried to grasp something of our social position, or at least made a start in that direction.
