“A great writer[9] of the last generation compared Russia to a swift troika galloping toward an unknown goal. He exclaims, ‘Oh, troika, birdlike troika, who invented you!’ and adds, in proud ecstasy, that all the peoples of the world stand aside respectfully to let the recklessly galloping troika pass. That may be. They may stand aside, with respect or without it. But in my poor opinion, the great writer closed his book this way either out of childish, naïve optimism, or simply out of fear of the censors of his day. Suppose the troika were drawn by his own heroes, Sobakevitch, Nozdryov, Tchitchikov. It could reach no rational goal, whoever might be driving. And those heroes belonged to an older generation. Ours are worse specimens still....”

At this point Ippolit Kirillovitch’s speech was interrupted by applause. The liberal meaning of this comparison was appreciated. The applause did not last long, it is true, so the President did not think it necessary to warn the public, and only looked sternly in the direction of the offenders. But Ippolit Kirillovitch was encouraged. He had never been applauded before! All his life he had been unable to get a hearing, and now he suddenly had a chance to reach the ear of all Russia.

“What, after all, is this Karamazov family, which has gained such an unenviable notoriety throughout Russia?” he continued. “Perhaps I am exaggerating, but certain basic features of the educated class of today seem to me reflected in this family picture. Only in miniature, of course, ‘like the sun in a drop of water.’ Think of that unhappy, vicious, unbridled old man who has met such a sad end, the head of the family! He was born noble, but began life poor and dependent. An unexpected marriage brought him a small fortune. He was a petty knave, a toady and a buffoon, with fairly good though undeveloped intelligence, and above all he was a moneylender, who grew bolder as he grew richer. The abject, servile side of him fell away, and what remained was a malicious, sarcastic cynicism. Spiritually he was undeveloped, and his vitality was excessive. Life held nothing for him but sensual pleasure, and he raised his children to see it the same way. As a father he felt no duties at all. He mocked the very idea of them. He left his little children to the servants, was glad to be rid of them, and forgot them completely. The old man’s maxim was _Après moi le déluge_. He stood for everything that is opposed to civic duty, for the most complete and malignant individualism. ‘Let the world burn, for all I care, so long as I am all right.’ And he was all right. He was content, and he was eager to go on living the same way for another twenty or thirty years. He cheated his own son. He spent the money that came from the boy’s mother on trying to win his mistress away from him. No, I do not intend to leave the prisoner’s defense wholly to my talented colleague from Petersburg. I will speak the truth myself. I can well understand how much resentment the father had piled up in his son’s heart.

“But enough, enough of that unhappy old man. He has paid the penalty. Let us remember, though, that he was a father, and one of the typical fathers of our day. Am I being unjust when I say he is typical of many modern fathers? Alas! Many of them differ from him only in not professing such cynicism openly. They are better educated and more cultured, but their philosophy is at bottom the same as his. Perhaps I am a pessimist, but you have agreed to forgive me. Let us agree beforehand on this: you need not believe me, but you must let me speak. Let me say what I have to say, and keep some of my words in mind.
“Now for the children of this father, this head of a family. One of them is the prisoner before us, and the rest of my speech will concern him. The other two I will touch on only in passing.

“The elder is one of those modern young men with a brilliant education and a vigorous mind who have lost all faith in everything. Like his father, he has already denied and rejected a great deal. We have all heard him, for he was a welcome guest in local society. He never hid his opinions. Quite the contrary. That justifies me in speaking rather openly of him now, though not, of course, as an individual, but as a member of the Karamazov family. Another person closely tied to this case took his own life here last night. I mean an afflicted idiot, once the servant and possibly the illegitimate son of Fyodor Pavlovitch: Smerdyakov. At the preliminary inquiry he told me, in hysterical tears, how the young Ivan Karamazov had horrified him with his spiritual audacity. ‘According to him, everything in the world is lawful, and nothing must be forbidden in the future. That is what he always taught me.’ I believe that idiot was driven out of his mind by this theory, though the epileptic fits he suffered from, and this terrible catastrophe, no doubt helped to unhinge his faculties. But he let fall one very interesting remark, which would have done credit to a more intelligent observer. That is really why I have mentioned it. ‘If there is one of the sons who is like Fyodor Pavlovitch in character, it is Ivan Fyodorovitch.’

“With that remark I end my sketch of his character, since it would be indelicate to go further. Oh, I have no wish to draw any more conclusions and croak like a raven over the young man’s future. We saw today in this court that good impulses still live in his young heart. Family feeling has not been destroyed in him by lack of faith and by cynicism, which came to him more through inheritance than through any thinking of his own.

“Then the third son. Oh, he is a devout and modest youth, and he does not share his elder brother’s gloomy and destructive view of life. He has tried to hold on to the ‘ideas of the people,’ or to whatever goes by that name in certain circles of our intellectual classes. He held on to the monastery, and came within an ace of becoming a monk. It seems to me that, unconsciously and at so early an age, he has shown the timid despair that drives so many in our unhappy society. They dread cynicism and its corrupting influence, and they wrongly put all the mischief down to European enlightenment. So they go back to their ‘native soil,’ as they say, to the bosom, so to speak, of their mother earth. They are like frightened children, longing to fall asleep on the withered breast of their decrepit mother, and to sleep there forever, only to escape the horrors that terrify them.

“For my part, I wish this excellent and gifted young man every success. I hope that his youthful idealism, and his pull toward the ideas of the people, will never decay, as so often happens, into gloomy mysticism on the moral side and blind chauvinism on the political. These two are an even greater menace to Russia than the premature decay his elder brother suffers from, which comes of misunderstanding European ideas and taking them up for no good reason.”

Two or three people clapped when he spoke of chauvinism and mysticism. Ippolit Kirillovitch had indeed been carried away by his own eloquence. All this had little to do with the case, and it was somewhat vague as well. But the sickly, consumptive man was seized by a longing to say what he thought, just once in his life. People said afterwards that his criticism of Ivan came from unworthy motives. Ivan had once or twice beaten him in argument, they said, and Ippolit Kirillovitch, remembering it, was now trying to get his revenge. I do not know whether that was true. At any rate, all this was only an introduction, and the speech now turned to the case itself.

“But let us go back to the eldest son,” Ippolit Kirillovitch went on. “He is the prisoner before us. His life and his actions lie before us too. The fatal day has come, and everything has surfaced. His brothers seem to represent ‘Europeanism’ and ‘the principles of the people.’ He seems to represent Russia as she is. Oh, not all Russia, not all! God preserve us if he did! Yet here she is, our mother Russia, her very scent and sound. Oh, he is spontaneous. He is a marvelous mixture of good and evil. He loves culture and Schiller, and yet he brawls in taverns and tears out the beards of his drinking friends. Oh, he, too, can be good and noble, but only while all goes well for him. More than that, he can be swept off his feet, positively swept off his feet, by noble ideals, but only if they come to him of their own accord, if they drop from heaven into his lap, if he does not have to pay for them. He hates paying for anything and loves receiving, and he is like that in everything. Oh, give him every good thing in life (he could not be content with less), and put no obstacle in his path, and he will prove that he, too, can be noble. He is not greedy, no. But he must have money, a great deal of money. And you will see how generously, with what contempt for filthy lucre, he will throw it all away in a single night of reckless dissipation. But if he has no money, you will see what he is ready to do to get it, when he needs it badly. All that, however, comes later. Let us take events in the order in which they happened.

“First we see a poor abandoned child running about the back yard ‘without boots on his feet,’ in the words of that worthy and respected fellow citizen of ours, of foreign origin, alas, who spoke a little while ago. I repeat it: I yield to no one in defending the criminal. I am here to accuse him, but also to defend him. Yes, I, too, am human. I, too, can weigh what home and childhood do to a character. But the boy grows up and becomes an officer. After a duel and other reckless behavior, he is exiled to one of the far frontier towns of Russia. There, as an officer, he lived a wild life. And of course he needed money, money above everything. After long disputes he reached a settlement with his father, and the last six thousand was sent to him. A letter survives in which he practically gives up his claim to the rest, and ends his quarrel with his father over the inheritance in exchange for this six thousand.

“Then he met a young girl of lofty character and brilliant education. Oh, I do not venture to repeat the details; you have only just heard them. There was honor there, and self-sacrifice, and I will say no more. The young officer, frivolous and profligate, paying homage to true nobility and a lofty ideal, showed himself to us in a very sympathetic light. But the other side of the coin was turned toward us without warning right afterwards, in this very court. Again I will not venture to guess why it happened so, but there were reasons. The same lady, in tears of long-concealed indignation, stated that he, of all men, had despised her for her action. That action was rash, even reckless perhaps, but it was still prompted by lofty and generous motives. He, the girl’s betrothed, looked at her with that smile of mockery, which was harder to bear from him than from anyone. And knowing that he had already deceived her (he had deceived her, believing that she was bound to put up with anything from him, even betrayal), she purposely offered him three thousand roubles. She made it clear, too clear, that she was offering him the money so that he would deceive her. ‘Well, will you take it or not? Have you no shame left?’ was the silent question in her searching eyes. He looked at her and saw plainly what she was thinking (he has admitted before you that he understood it all). He took that three thousand without any conditions, and squandered it in two days with his new sweetheart.

“What are we to believe, then? The first legend, in which the young officer gives away his last farthing in a noble burst of generosity and bows before virtue? Or this second, revolting picture? Usually, when two extremes are in question, the truth lies somewhere between them. Here that is not so. In all likelihood he was truly noble the first time and just as truly base the second. And why? Because he had the wide Karamazov nature, which is exactly what I am leading up to, a nature that can hold the most incongruous contradictions at once and reach the greatest heights and the greatest depths. Remember the brilliant remark of a young man who has watched the Karamazov family at close quarters, Mr. Rakitin: ‘The sense of their own degradation is as essential to those reckless, unbridled natures as the sense of their lofty generosity.’ And it is true. They constantly need this unnatural mixture. They need two extremes at the same moment, or they are wretched and dissatisfied and their existence feels incomplete. They are wide, wide as mother Russia. They take in everything and put up with everything.

“By the way, gentlemen of the jury, we have just touched on that three thousand roubles, and I will venture to get a little ahead of my story. Can you imagine that such a man, having received that sum in such a way, at the price of such shame, such disgrace, such utter degradation, could that very day set aside half of it and sew it up in a little bag? And that he would have the strength of character to carry it about with him for a whole month afterwards, despite every temptation and his desperate need of it? Not in drunken debauchery in the taverns, and not when he was dashing about the countryside trying to get, from God knows whom, the money he so badly needed to remove the woman he loved from his father’s temptations, did he bring himself to touch that little bag! Surely, if only to avoid handing his mistress over to the rival he was so jealous of, he would have opened that bag and stayed at home to guard her. He would have waited for the moment when she finally said to him, ‘I am yours,’ and then fled with her, far from their fatal surroundings.

“But no. He did not touch his talisman, and what reason does he give? The chief reason, as I have just said, was that when she told him, ‘I am yours, take me where you will,’ he would have the means to take her. But that first reason, in the prisoner’s own account, counted for little beside the second. As long as I have that money on me, he said, I am a scoundrel, not a thief. For I can always go to my insulted betrothed, lay down half of the sum I took by fraud, and say to her, ‘You see, I have squandered half your money and shown myself a weak and immoral man, and, if you like, a scoundrel’ (I use the prisoner’s own expressions), ‘but though I am a scoundrel, I am not a thief. If I were a thief, I would not have brought you back this half of the money. I would have taken it as I took the other half!’ A marvelous explanation! This frantic but weak man, who could not resist taking the three thousand roubles at the price of such disgrace, suddenly displays the most stoical firmness. He carries a thousand roubles about with him and does not dare to touch it. Does that fit at all with the character we have analyzed? No. And I venture to tell you how the real Dmitri Karamazov would have acted in such circumstances, if he really had brought himself to put the money aside.

“At the first temptation, for example to entertain the woman with whom he had already squandered half of it, he would have unpicked his little bag and taken out a hundred roubles or so. Why, after all, should he have put back exactly half the money, fifteen hundred roubles? Why not fourteen hundred? He could just as well have said then that he was not a thief, since he was bringing back fourteen hundred roubles. Another time he would have unpicked it again and taken out another hundred, then a third, then a fourth. Before the month was out he would have taken out the last note but one, feeling that returning even a single hundred would serve, since a thief would have stolen the lot. And then he would have looked at that last note and told himself, ‘It is really not worth giving back one hundred. Let us spend that, too!’ That is how the real Dmitri Karamazov, as we know him, would have acted. One cannot imagine anything more at odds with the actual facts than this legend of the little bag. Nothing could be more unthinkable. But we shall come back to it later.”

Ippolit Kirillovitch went over what the trial had brought out about the money dealings between father and son. Again and again he argued that, from the facts known, it was utterly impossible to tell which of the two was in the wrong. Then he moved on to the medical experts’ testimony about Mitya’s fixed idea that he was owed three thousand.

chapters.title: VII. An Historical Survey
paragraphs: “The medical experts have tried hard to convince us that the prisoner is out of his mind, that he is in fact a maniac. I say he is sane. If he were not, he would have acted more cleverly. That he is a maniac I will grant on one point only, his fixed idea about the three thousand. Even there, I think, a far simpler cause can be found than any tendency to madness. I agree entirely with the young doctor who held that the prisoner’s mind has always been sound, and that he has merely been irritable and exasperated. What kept the prisoner in such constant and violent anger was not the sum itself. Something particular lay underneath it. That something is jealousy!”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch described at length the prisoner’s fatal passion for Grushenka. He began at the moment when the prisoner went to the “young person’s” lodgings “to beat her.” “Those are his own words,” the prosecutor explained. “But instead of beating her, he stayed on, at her feet. That is where the passion began. At the very same time, the prisoner’s father was captivated by the same young person. It was a strange and fatal coincidence. Both of them lost their hearts to her together, though each had known her before. In both she roused the most violent passion, a truly Karamazov passion. We have her own confession: ‘I was laughing at both of them.’ Yes, a sudden wish to make fun of them seized her, and she conquered them both at once. The old man, who worshiped money, immediately set aside three thousand roubles to pay for a single visit from her. Soon afterwards he would gladly have laid his fortune and his name at her feet, if only she would consent to be his lawful wife. We have good evidence of this. As for the prisoner, the tragedy of his fate is plain to see; it is before us. But that was the young person’s ‘game.’ The enchantress gave the unhappy young man no hope until the very last moment, when he knelt before her, holding out hands that were already stained with the blood of his father and his rival. He was arrested in that very posture. ‘Send me to Siberia with him! I brought him to this. I am the most to blame,’ the woman herself cried out, in real remorse, as he was arrested.

“Mr. Rakitin, the talented young man I mentioned earlier, summed up this heroine in a few striking words. ‘She was disillusioned early in life, deceived and ruined by a betrothed who seduced her and abandoned her. She was left in poverty and cursed by her respectable family. A rich old man took her under his protection, and she still regards him as her benefactor. There was perhaps much good in her young heart, but it was embittered too early. She grew prudent and saved her money. She grew sarcastic and resentful toward society.’ Given such a portrait, it is easy to see how she could laugh at the pair of them out of simple mischief, out of malice.

“For a month he loved without hope and sank morally lower. In that month he betrayed his betrothed and took money that had been entrusted to his honor. Constant jealousy drove the prisoner almost to frenzy, almost to madness. And jealous of whom? Of his own father! The worst of it was that the crazy old man was luring and tempting the woman the son loved with that very three thousand roubles. The son considered that money his own property, part of his inheritance from his mother, and he believed his father was cheating him out of it. Yes, I admit it was hard to bear! It could well drive a man mad. It was not the money that mattered, but the fact that it was being used, with such revolting cynicism, to ruin his happiness!”
Next the prosecutor described how the idea of murdering his father had first come into the prisoner’s head, and he supported his theory with facts.

“To begin with, he only talked of it in taverns, and he talked of it all through that month. Ah, he likes to have company around him all the time, and he likes to tell his companions everything, even his most diabolical and dangerous thoughts. He likes to share every idea with others. For some reason he expects those he confides in to meet him with perfect sympathy, to enter into all his troubles and worries, to take his side and never to oppose him in anything. If they do not, he flies into a rage and smashes up everything in the tavern. [Then followed the anecdote about Captain Snegiryov.] Those who heard the prisoner began to wonder at last whether he meant more than threats, and whether such a frenzy might turn threats into deeds.”

The prosecutor then recounted how the family had met at the monastery, what was said in the talks with Alyosha, and the horrible scene of violence when the prisoner burst into his father’s house straight after dinner.

“I cannot say for certain,” the prosecutor continued, “that the prisoner fully meant to murder his father before that incident. Yet the idea had come to him several times, and he had turned it over in his mind. For that we have facts, witnesses and his own words. I will admit to you, gentlemen of the jury,” he added, “that until today I was unsure whether to ascribe conscious premeditation to the prisoner. I was firmly convinced that he had pictured the fatal moment in advance, but that he had only pictured it, thinking of it as a possibility. When and how he might commit the crime, he had not yet decided.

“But I was unsure only until today, until that fatal document was laid before the court a moment ago. You heard for yourselves that young lady’s cry, ‘It is the plan, the program of the murder!’ That was her name for the unhappy prisoner’s wretched, drunken letter. And indeed that letter shows us that the whole murder was planned beforehand. It was written two days earlier. So we now know for a fact that, forty-eight hours before he carried out his terrible design, the prisoner swore that if he could not get money the next day, he would murder his father and take the envelope of notes from under his pillow, as soon as Ivan had gone. ‘As soon as Ivan had gone away.’ You hear that? He had thought everything through and weighed every circumstance, and he did it all exactly as he had written. The proof of premeditation is conclusive. The crime must have been committed for the money. That is stated plainly, written down and signed. The prisoner does not deny his signature.

“I shall be told that he was drunk when he wrote it. That takes nothing from the value of the letter, quite the contrary. Drunk, he wrote what he had planned sober. If he had not planned it sober, he would not have written it drunk. I shall be asked why, then, he talked about it in taverns. A man who premeditates such a crime keeps silent and says nothing to anyone. True, but he talked about it before he had a plan, when he had only the wish, only the impulse. Later he talked of it less. On the evening he wrote that letter at the ‘Metropolis’ tavern, he was silent, unlike his usual self, though he was drinking. He did not play billiards. He sat in a corner and spoke to no one. He did push a shopman out of his seat, but he did that almost without thinking, because he could never walk into a tavern without making a disturbance. It is true that once he had made his final decision, he must have feared that he had said too much about his plan in advance, and that it might lead to his arrest and prosecution afterwards. But there was nothing to be done. He could not take back his words. Yet his luck had served him before, and it would serve him again. He believed in his star, you know! And I must also admit that he did a great deal to avoid the fatal catastrophe. ‘Tomorrow I shall try to borrow the money from everyone,’ he writes, in his peculiar language, ‘and if they will not give it to me, there will be bloodshed.’”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch turned to a detailed account of all Mitya’s attempts to borrow the money. He described the visit to Samsonov and the journey to Lyagavy. “Harassed, jeered at, hungry, he had sold his watch to pay for the journey (though he tells us he had fifteen hundred roubles on him, a likely story). He was tortured by jealousy at having left the object of his affections behind in the town, and he suspected she would go to Fyodor Pavlovitch while he was away. At last he came back to the town, and to his joy found that she had not gone near his father. He took her himself to her protector. (Strange to say, he does not seem to have been jealous of Samsonov, which is psychologically interesting.) Then he hurries back to his ambush in the back gardens, and there he learns that Smerdyakov is in a fit and the other servant is ill. The coast is clear, and he knows the ‘signals.’ What a temptation! Still he resists it. He goes to see a lady who has lived in our town for some time and is highly respected among us, Madame Hohlakov. That lady had long followed his career with compassion. She gave him the most sensible advice: to give up his dissipated life, his unseemly love affair, and the waste of his youth and strength in pot-house debauchery, and to set off for the gold mines of Siberia. ‘That would be an outlet for your turbulent energy, your romantic character, your thirst for adventure.’”

Ippolit Kirillovitch then described what came of this conversation. He described the moment when the prisoner learned that Grushenka had not stayed at Samsonov’s, and the sudden frenzy of the luckless man, worn out with jealousy and nervous exhaustion, at the thought that she had deceived him and was now with his father. He ended by dwelling on the fatal part played by chance. “If the maid had told him that her mistress was at Mokroe with her former lover, nothing would have happened. But she lost her head. All she could do was swear and protest that she knew nothing. The prisoner did not kill her on the spot only because he rushed off in pursuit of his faithless mistress.

“But note this. Frantic as he was, he took a brass pestle with him. Why that? Why not some other weapon? The answer is that he had been contemplating his plan and preparing for it for a whole month, so he would seize on anything that looked like a weapon. For a month past he had understood that any object of that kind would do as a weapon. So he recognized at once, without hesitation, that it would serve his purpose. It was by no means unconsciously, by no means involuntarily, that he snatched up that fatal pestle. And then we find him in his father’s garden. The coast is clear, there are no witnesses, there is darkness and jealousy. The suspicion that she was there, with him, with his rival, in his arms, and perhaps laughing at him at that very moment, took his breath away. And it was not mere suspicion. The deception was open and obvious. She must be there, in that lighted room, she must be behind the screen. Yet the unhappy man would have us believe that he crept up to the window, peeped politely in, and tactfully withdrew, for fear that something terrible and immoral might happen. He tries to persuade us of that, us, who understand his character, who know his state of mind at that moment, and who know that he knew the signals by which he could go straight into the house.” At this point Ippolit Kirillovitch broke off to discuss at length the suspected connection of Smerdyakov with the murder. He went into great detail, and everyone realized that, although he claimed to despise that suspicion, he thought the subject very important.

chapters.title: VIII. A Treatise On Smerdyakov
paragraphs: “To begin with, where did this suspicion come from?” (Ippolit Kirillovitch began.) “The first person to cry out that Smerdyakov had committed the murder was the prisoner himself, at the moment of his arrest. Yet from that day to this he has not offered a single fact to support the charge, nor even the faintest hint of one. Only three people back it up: the prisoner’s two brothers and Madame Svyetlov. The elder brother voiced his suspicions only today, when he was undoubtedly in the grip of brain fever. We know, though, that for the last two months he fully shared our conviction of his brother’s guilt and made no attempt to argue against it. But more of that later. The younger brother has admitted that he has not the slightest fact to support his notion of Smerdyakov’s guilt. He was led to it only by the prisoner’s own words and the look on his face. Yes, that astounding piece of evidence he has offered twice today. Madame Svyetlov was more astounding still. ‘What the prisoner tells you, you must believe; he is not a man to tell a lie.’ That is all the evidence these three witnesses have produced against Smerdyakov, and all three are deeply concerned in the prisoner’s fate. And yet the theory of Smerdyakov’s guilt has been noised about, and is still maintained. Is that credible? Is it even conceivable?”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch thought it necessary to describe the character of Smerdyakov, “who had ended his life in a fit of insanity.” He portrayed him as a man of weak mind with a smattering of education. Philosophical ideas beyond his level had thrown him off balance, as had certain modern theories of duty. He had learned those theories in practice from the reckless life of his master, who was perhaps also his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch. In theory he had learned them from various strange philosophical conversations with his master’s elder son, Ivan Fyodorovitch, who readily indulged in this pastime, probably out of boredom or to amuse himself at the valet’s expense. “He spoke to me himself about his state of mind during his last few days in his father’s house,” Ippolit Kirillovitch explained. “But others have also borne witness to it: the prisoner himself, his brother, and the servant Grigory. That is, everyone who knew him well.

“Moreover, Smerdyakov’s health was shaken by his epileptic attacks, and he had not the courage of a chicken. ‘He fell at my feet and kissed them,’ the prisoner himself has told us, before he realized how damaging that statement was to himself. ‘He is an epileptic chicken,’ he said of him, in his own characteristic language. The prisoner chose him as his confidant (we have his own word for it) and frightened him until he finally agreed to act as a spy for him. In that role he betrayed his master. He told the prisoner that the envelope with the notes existed, and he told him the signals by which he could get into the house. And how could he have refused to tell him? ‘He would have killed me, I could see that he would have killed me,’ he said at the inquiry. He was trembling and shaking even in front of us, though his tormentor had by then been arrested and could do him no harm. ‘He suspected me every minute. In fear and trembling I hurried to tell him every secret to calm him, so that he would see I had not deceived him and let me off alive.’ Those are his own words. I wrote them down, and I remember them. ‘When he began shouting at me, I would fall on my knees.’

“He was naturally very honest, and he had enjoyed his master’s complete confidence ever since he returned some money his master had lost. So we may suppose that the poor fellow suffered pangs of remorse at having deceived a master he loved as his benefactor. People severely afflicted with epilepsy are, so the most skillful doctors tell us, always prone to continual, morbid self-reproach. They worry over their ‘wickedness.’ They are tormented by their consciences, often entirely without cause. They exaggerate, and often invent, all sorts of faults and crimes. And here we have a man of that type, who had really been driven to wrongdoing by terror and intimidation.

“Besides, he had a strong foreboding that something terrible would come of the situation developing before his eyes. Ivan Fyodorovitch was about to leave for Moscow, just before the catastrophe. Smerdyakov begged him to stay, but was too timid to say plainly what he feared. He only dropped hints, and nobody understood them.

“Note that he looked on Ivan Fyodorovitch as a protector. While Ivan was in the house, he felt, no harm could happen. Remember the phrase in Dmitri Karamazov’s drunken letter: ‘I shall kill the old man, if only Ivan goes away.’ So everyone took Ivan Fyodorovitch’s presence as a guarantee of peace and order in the house.

“But he left, and within an hour Smerdyakov, after his young master’s departure, was struck by an epileptic fit. That is perfectly understandable. I must mention here that Smerdyakov, weighed down by terror and a kind of despair, had sensed over those last few days that one of the fits he had suffered before at moments of strain might be coming on again. The day and hour of such an attack cannot, of course, be foreseen, but every epileptic can feel beforehand that one is likely. So the doctors tell us. And so, the moment Ivan Fyodorovitch had driven out of the yard, Smerdyakov, low-spirited at being left alone and unprotected, went to the cellar. Going down the stairs he asked himself whether a fit would come, and what if it came on him right then. And that very dread, that very asking, brought on the spasm in his throat that always comes before such attacks, and he fell unconscious into the cellar. And in this perfectly natural event people try to find grounds for suspicion, a hint that he was shamming the attack _on purpose_. But if it was on purpose, the question arises at once: what was his motive? What was he counting on? What was he aiming at? I say nothing about medicine. Science, I am told, may go astray, and the doctors could not tell the counterfeit from the real. That may be so, but answer me one question: what motive had he for such a counterfeit? If he had been plotting the murder, would he have wanted to draw the household’s attention by having a fit just beforehand?

“You see, gentlemen of the jury, on the night of the murder there were five people at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s. There was Fyodor Pavlovitch himself (but he did not kill himself, that is evident). Then there was his servant, Grigory, but he was almost killed himself. The third was Grigory’s wife, Marfa Ignatyevna, but it would be simply shameful to imagine her murdering her master. Two people are left: the prisoner and Smerdyakov. Now, if we are to believe the prisoner’s statement that he is not the murderer, then Smerdyakov must have been, for there is no other alternative, and no one else can be found. That is what accounts for the artful, astounding accusation against the unhappy idiot who committed suicide yesterday. Had a shadow of suspicion rested on anyone else, had there been any sixth person, I am convinced that even the prisoner would have been ashamed to accuse Smerdyakov. He would have accused that sixth person, for to charge Smerdyakov with this murder is perfectly absurd.

“Gentlemen, let us lay aside psychology, let us lay aside medicine, let us even lay aside logic. Let us turn only to the facts and see what the facts tell us. If Smerdyakov killed him, how did he do it? Alone, or with the prisoner’s help? Let us consider the first possibility, that he did it alone. If he killed him, it must have been for some purpose, for some advantage to himself. But he had not a shadow of the motives the prisoner had for the murder: hatred, jealousy, and so on. So Smerdyakov could only have murdered him for gain, to take the three thousand roubles he had seen his master put in the envelope. And yet he tells another person, and a person most closely interested, that is, the prisoner, everything about the money and the signals. He tells him where the envelope lay, what was written on it, what it was tied up with, and above all he tells him the signals by which he could enter the house. Did he do this simply to betray himself? Or to invite into the same enterprise a man who would be eager to get that envelope for himself? ‘Yes,’ I shall be told, ‘but he gave it away out of fear.’ But how do you explain this? A man who could conceive such an audacious, savage act, and carry it out, tells facts which no one else in the world knows, and which no one would ever have guessed if he had held his tongue!

“No. However cowardly he might be, if he had plotted such a crime, nothing would have made him tell anyone about the envelope and the signals, for that was as good as betraying himself beforehand. He would have invented something. If he had been forced to give information, he would have told some lie, but he would have kept silent about that. Consider the other course. Suppose he had said nothing about the money, but had committed the murder and taken it. Then nobody in the world could have accused him of murder for robbery, since he alone had seen the money and he alone knew it was in the house. Even if he had been accused of the murder, people could only have supposed some other motive. But no one had noticed any such motive in him beforehand. On the contrary, everyone saw that his master was fond of him and honored him with his confidence. So he would, of course, have been the last to be suspected. People would have suspected first the man who had a motive, a man who had himself declared he had such motives and had made no secret of it. They would, in fact, have suspected the murdered man’s son, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. Had Smerdyakov killed and robbed him, and the son been accused of it, that would, of course, have suited Smerdyakov. Yet are we to believe that, though he was plotting the murder, he told that son, Dmitri, about the money, the envelope and the signals? Is that logical? Is that clear?

“Now the day of the murder planned by Smerdyakov comes, and we have him tumbling downstairs in a _feigned_ fit. With what object? First, so that Grigory, who had been meaning to take his medicine, might put it off and stay on guard, seeing that there was no one else to watch the house. Second, I suppose, so that his master, seeing there was no one to guard him and in terror of a visit from his son, might redouble his vigilance and precautions. And most of all, I suppose, so that he, Smerdyakov, disabled by the fit, would be carried out of the kitchen, where he always slept apart from all the rest and could come and go as he liked, and put in Grigory’s room at the other end of the lodge. That was where he was always put, behind a screen three paces from their own bed. This was the old custom, set by his master and the kind-hearted Marfa Ignatyevna, whenever he had a fit. There, lying behind the screen, he would most likely, to keep up the sham, have begun groaning, and so kept them awake all night (as Grigory and his wife testified). And all this, we are to believe, so that he could more conveniently get up and murder his master!

“But I shall be told that he shammed illness on purpose, so that no one would suspect him, and that he told the prisoner about the money and the signals to tempt him into committing the murder. And then, when the prisoner had killed the old man and made off with the money, probably noisily enough to wake people, Smerdyakov got up—are we to believe this?—and went in. What for? To murder his master a second time and carry off money that was already stolen? Gentlemen, are you laughing? I am ashamed to put such suggestions to you. But incredible as it sounds, that is exactly what the prisoner alleges. He says that once he had left the house, knocked Grigory down and set off the alarm, Smerdyakov got up, went in, murdered his master and stole the money! I will not insist that Smerdyakov could hardly have counted on this in advance. He could hardly have foreseen that the furious, exasperated son, though he knew the signals, would merely peep in respectfully and then retreat, leaving Smerdyakov his booty. Gentlemen of the jury, I ask you in earnest: when could Smerdyakov have committed his crime? Name that moment, or you cannot accuse him.

“But perhaps the fit was real. The sick man suddenly came to himself, heard a shout, and went out. Well, and then? He looked around and said to himself, ‘Why not go and kill the master?’ And how would he have known what had happened, when he had lain unconscious until that moment? There is a limit to these flights of fancy.

“‘Very well,’ some shrewd people will say to me, ‘but suppose they were in agreement? Suppose they murdered him together and divided the money—what then?’ A weighty question, truly! And the facts behind it are astounding. One of them commits the murder and does all the work, while his accomplice lies to one side shamming a fit—evidently to rouse suspicion in everyone, and alarm in his master and in Grigory. I should like to know what motives could have led the two accomplices to hatch so insane a plan.

“Or perhaps Smerdyakov was no active accomplice, only a passive one. Perhaps he was cowed into agreeing not to prevent the murder. Foreseeing that he would be blamed for letting his master be killed without crying out or resisting, he may have obtained leave from Dmitri Karamazov to get out of the way by shamming a fit—‘you may murder him as you please; it is nothing to me.’ But this attack of Smerdyakov’s was bound to throw the whole household into confusion, so Dmitri Karamazov could never have agreed to such a plan. I will waive that point, however. Suppose he did agree. It would still follow that Dmitri Karamazov is the murderer and the instigator, and that Smerdyakov is only a passive accomplice—not even an accomplice, but a man who gave in against his will, out of terror.

“Yet what do we actually see? The moment he is arrested, the prisoner throws all the blame on Smerdyakov. He does not accuse him of being an accomplice; he accuses him of being the murderer himself. ‘He did it alone,’ he says. ‘He murdered and robbed him. It was the work of his hands.’ What odd accomplices, who start accusing each other at once! And think what a risk Karamazov ran. He commits the murder while his accomplice lies in bed, and then he puts the blame on the invalid. The invalid might well have resented that, and to save himself might well have confessed the truth. He might well have seen that the court would soon judge how far he was responsible, and might well have reckoned that his own punishment would be much lighter than the real murderer’s. In that case he would certainly have confessed. He has not. Smerdyakov never hinted at any complicity, though the actual murderer kept accusing him and insisting that he had done it alone.

“Moreover, Smerdyakov volunteered at the inquiry that it was _he_ who had told the prisoner about the envelope of notes and the signals, and that without him the prisoner would have known nothing of them. Had he really been a guilty accomplice, would he have admitted this so readily at the inquiry? Quite the opposite: he would have tried to hide it, to twist the facts or make little of them. But he did nothing of the kind. Only an innocent man, with no fear of being charged as an accomplice, could have behaved as he did. And then yesterday, in a fit of melancholy brought on by his illness and by this catastrophe, he hanged himself. He left a note in his peculiar language: ‘I destroy myself of my own will and inclination so as to throw no blame on any one.’ What would it have cost him to add: ‘I am the murderer, not Karamazov’? That he did not add. Are we to think that his conscience drove him to suicide but not to confessing his guilt?

“And what came next? Notes for three thousand roubles were brought into the court a short while ago. We were told that they were the same notes that lay in the envelope now on the table before us, and that the witness had received them from Smerdyakov the day before. I need not go back over that painful scene, but I will offer one or two comments, picking ones so small that they might escape notice at first glance and so be overlooked. First, Smerdyakov must have returned the money and hanged himself yesterday out of remorse. And only yesterday, as Ivan Karamazov tells us, he confessed his guilt to him. If that were not so, why would Ivan Fyodorovitch have stayed silent until now? And if Smerdyakov did confess, then I ask again: why did he not state the whole truth in the last letter he left behind, knowing that the innocent prisoner would face this terrible ordeal the next day?

“The money alone proves nothing. A week ago, quite by chance, I and two other persons in this court learned that Ivan Fyodorovitch had sent two five per cent. coupons, of five thousand each—ten thousand in all—to the chief town of the province to be exchanged. I mention it only to show that anyone may have money, and that there is no proving these notes to be the same ones that were in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s envelope.

“Yesterday Ivan Karamazov received a communication of the utmost importance from the real murderer, and did not stir. Why did he not report it at once? Why put it all off until the morning? I believe I have a right to guess why. His health had been failing for a week. He had admitted to a doctor and to his closest friends that he suffered from hallucinations and saw phantoms of the dead. He was on the eve of the brain fever that has laid him low today. In that state he suddenly heard that Smerdyakov was dead, and at once thought, ‘The man is dead; I can put the blame on him and save my brother. I have money. I will take a roll of notes and say that Smerdyakov gave them to me before he died.’ You will say that this was dishonorable: it is dishonorable to slander even the dead, even to save a brother. True. But what if he slandered him without knowing it? What if, finally unhinged by the sudden news of the valet’s death, he imagined it really was so? You saw the scene just now. You have seen the state the witness was in. He stood there and spoke, but where was his mind?

“Then came the document: the prisoner’s letter, written two days before the crime, which lays out a complete program of the murder. Why, then, should we look for any other program? The crime was carried out exactly according to this one, and by none other than the man who wrote it. Yes, gentlemen of the jury, it went off without a hitch! He did not run away humbly and timidly from his father’s window, although he was firmly convinced that the object of his affections was in there with the old man. No, that is absurd and improbable! He went in and murdered him. Most likely he killed him in a rage, burning with resentment, the moment he laid eyes on his hated rival. But having killed him, probably with a single blow of the brass pestle, and having searched carefully and made sure that she was not there, he still remembered to slide his hand under the pillow and take out the envelope. Its torn cover lies now on the table before us.

“I mention this so that you may notice one circumstance which seems to me very characteristic. Suppose he had been an experienced murderer, killing only for gain. Would he have left the torn envelope on the floor, where it was found, beside the corpse? Take Smerdyakov, for instance, murdering his master to rob him. He would simply have carried the envelope off. He would not have bothered to open it over his victim’s body, since he knew for certain that the notes were inside—they had been put in and sealed in his presence—and if he had taken the envelope with him, no one would ever have known there had been a robbery. I ask you, gentlemen, would Smerdyakov have acted in that way? Would he have left the envelope on the floor?

“No. This was the act of a frantic murderer, a murderer who was no thief and had never stolen anything before that day. He snatched the notes from under the pillow, not like a thief taking them, but as if he were seizing his own property back from the thief who had stolen it. For that was the idea that had grown into an almost insane obsession in Dmitri Karamazov about that money. He pounced on the envelope, which he had never seen before, and tore it open to make sure the money was inside. Then he ran off with the money in his pocket, never stopping to consider that he had left an astounding piece of evidence against himself in that torn envelope on the floor. All because it was Karamazov and not Smerdyakov: he did not think, he did not reflect, and how could he? He ran; he heard the servant cry out behind him; the old man seized him, tried to stop him, and was struck down by the brass pestle.

“The prisoner, moved by pity, leapt down to look at him. Would you believe it, he tells us that he leapt down out of pity, out of compassion, to see whether he could do anything for the man. Was that a moment for compassion? No. He jumped down only to make certain whether the one witness of his crime was dead or alive. Any other feeling, any other motive, would be unnatural. Note that he took pains over Grigory: he wiped his head with his handkerchief, and, satisfied that Grigory was dead, ran to his mistress’s house, dazed and covered with blood. How did it never occur to him that he was covered with blood and would be caught at once? But the prisoner himself assures us that he did not even notice the blood. That may be believed; it is quite possible; it always happens to criminals at such moments. On one point they show diabolical cunning, while on another they miss everything. But at that moment he was thinking of one thing only—where was _she_? He wanted to find out at once where she was, so he ran to her lodging and learned an unexpected and astounding piece of news: she had gone off to Mokroe to meet her first lover.”

chapters.title: IX. The Galloping Troika. The End Of The Prosecutor’s Speech.
paragraphs: Ippolit Kirillovitch had picked the historical method of telling his story. Nervous speakers love it, because its fixed limits keep their own eager rhetoric in check. At this point he turned aside into a long discussion of Grushenka’s “first lover,” and put forward several interesting thoughts on the subject.

“Karamazov had been frantically jealous of everyone. Yet before this first lover he simply collapsed, so to speak, and effaced himself on the spot. That makes it stranger still, since he seems to have given this formidable rival hardly a thought. He saw him as a danger far away, and Karamazov always lives in the present. Perhaps he took him for a fiction. But his wounded heart saw at once that the woman had been hiding this new rival from him and deceiving him. The man was anything but a fiction to her. He was the one hope of her life. The moment Karamazov grasped this, he gave in.

“Gentlemen of the jury, I cannot help dwelling on this unexpected side of the prisoner’s character. Suddenly he shows an irresistible longing for justice, a respect for woman, an acknowledgment of her right to love. And this at the very moment when he had stained his hands with his father’s blood for her sake! True, the blood he had shed was already crying out for vengeance. He had ruined his soul and his life in this world, and in that same instant he had to ask himself what he was now, and what he could be, to her, the being dearer to him than his own soul. He had to measure himself against that former lover, who had come back repentant, with a new love, to the woman he once betrayed, with honorable offers and the promise of a reformed and happy life. And what could he, the luckless man, give her now? What could he offer her?

“Karamazov felt all this. He knew that his crime had closed every road to him, and that he was a criminal under sentence, not a man with a life ahead of him! The thought crushed him. So he flew at once to one frantic plan, which a man of Karamazov’s character must have seen as the only possible escape from his terrible position. That escape was suicide. He ran to get the pistols he had left in pledge with his friend Perhotin. And as he ran, he pulled out of his pocket the money he had stained his hands with his father’s gore to get. Oh, now he needed money more than ever. Karamazov would die, Karamazov would shoot himself, and people would remember it! He was a poet, after all, and he had burned the candle at both ends all his life. ‘To her, to her! And there, oh, there I will throw a feast for the whole world, the like of which was never seen, and people will remember it and talk of it for years! Amid shouts of wild merriment, reckless gypsy songs and dances, I will raise my glass and drink to the woman I adore and to her new happiness! And then and there, at her feet, I will blow my brains out before her and punish myself! She will think of Mitya Karamazov now and then. She will see how Mitya loved her. She will feel for Mitya!’

“Here we see, in excess, the love of effect, the romantic despair and sentimentality, and the wild recklessness of the Karamazovs. Yes, but there is something more, gentlemen of the jury, something that cries out in the soul, throbs without rest in the mind, and poisons the heart unto death. That _something_ is conscience, gentlemen of the jury, its verdict, its terrible torments! The pistol will settle everything, the pistol is the only way out! But _beyond_—I do not know whether Karamazov, at that moment, asked himself ‘What lies beyond?’ or whether a Karamazov could, like Hamlet, ask ‘What lies beyond?’ No, gentlemen of the jury, they have their Hamlets, but we still have our Karamazovs!”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch gave a minute account of Mitya’s preparations: the scene at Perhotin’s, at the shop, with the drivers. He cited many words and actions, all backed up by witnesses, and the picture made a terrible impression on the audience. Once the facts were set side by side, the guilt of this harassed, desperate man stood out clear and convincing.

“What need had he to be careful? Two or three times he came close to confessing. He hinted at it, he all but said it outright.” (Then came the witnesses’ evidence.) “He even shouted to the peasant who was driving him, ‘Do you know you are driving a murderer!’ But he could not speak out. He had to reach Mokroe and finish his romance there. And what was waiting for the luckless man? Almost from the first minute at Mokroe he saw that his unbeatable rival might not be so unbeatable after all, and that the toast to their new happiness was neither wanted nor welcome. But you know the facts, gentlemen of the jury, from the preliminary inquiry. Karamazov’s triumph over his rival was complete, and his soul entered a wholly new phase, perhaps the most terrible one it has passed through or ever will.

“One may say with certainty, gentlemen of the jury,” the prosecutor went on, “that outraged nature and the criminal heart exact their own vengeance more fully than any earthly justice. More than that: justice and punishment on earth actually lighten the punishment of nature. At such moments they are even necessary to the criminal’s soul, to save it from despair. For I cannot picture the horror and the moral agony of Karamazov when he learned that she loved him, that for his sake she had turned away her first lover, that she was calling him, Mitya, to a new life and promising him happiness. And when was this? When everything was finished for him and nothing was possible!

“Let me note in passing, in parentheses, a point of importance for the light it throws on the prisoner’s position at that moment. This woman, this love of his, had remained until the last moment, until the very instant of his arrest, a being out of reach, passionately desired by him yet out of reach. Why, then, did he not shoot himself at that time? Why did he drop his plan and even forget where his pistol was? It was exactly that passionate longing for love, and the hope of satisfying it, that held him back. Through all their revels he stayed close to his adored mistress, who sat with him at the banquet and who was more charming and fascinating to him than ever. He did not leave her side, abasing himself before her in his homage.

“His passion might well stifle, for a moment, not only the fear of arrest but even the torments of conscience. For a moment, oh, only for a moment! I can picture the state of mind of a criminal hopelessly enslaved by such influences. First, the influence of drink, of noise and excitement, of the thud of the dance and the scream of the song, and of her, flushed with wine, singing and dancing and laughing to him! Second, the hope, in the background, that the fatal end might still be far off, that at least until morning they would not come to take him. So he had a few hours, and that is much, very much! In a few hours a man can think of many things. I imagine he felt something like what criminals feel on the way to the scaffold. They have another long, long street ahead of them, to be traveled at a walking pace, past thousands of people. Then comes a turn into another street, and only at the end of that street, the dreaded place of execution! At the start of the journey, I imagine, the condemned man, sitting on his shameful cart, must feel that he still has infinite life before him. The houses fall behind, the cart rolls on. Oh, that is nothing, the turn into the second street is still far off, and he still looks boldly to right and left at those thousands of callously curious people with their eyes on him, and still imagines that he is just a man like them. But now the turn comes, into the next street. Oh, that is nothing, nothing, there is still a whole street before him, and however many houses have gone by, he will still think many are left. And so to the very end, to the very scaffold.

“This, I imagine, is how it was with Karamazov then. ‘They have not had time yet,’ he must have thought. ‘I may still find a way out. Oh, there is still time to work out some plan of defense, and now, now—she is so fascinating!’

“His soul was full of confusion and dread, yet he managed to set aside half his money and hide it somewhere. I can explain in no other way why fully half of the three thousand he had just taken from his father’s pillow has vanished. He had been in Mokroe more than once. He had already caroused there for two days running, and he knew the big old house with all its passages and outbuildings. I imagine that part of the money was hidden in that house, not long before the arrest, in some crevice, under some floorboard, in some corner, under the roof. For what purpose? I shall be asked. Why, the catastrophe might strike at any moment, of course. He had not yet thought how to meet it, he had no time, his head was throbbing and his heart was with _her_. But money, money was needed in any case! With money a man is always a man. Perhaps such foresight at such a moment strikes you as unnatural? But he tells us himself that a month earlier, at a critical and exciting moment, he had divided his money in half and sewn it into a little bag. That was not true, as we shall shortly prove. But it shows that the idea was a familiar one to Karamazov, that he had turned it over in his mind. And there is more. When he declared at the inquiry that he had put fifteen hundred roubles in a bag (which never existed), he may have invented that bag on the inspiration of the moment. For two hours earlier he had divided his money and hidden half of it at Mokroe until morning, against an emergency, simply to avoid carrying it on him. Two extremes, gentlemen of the jury. Remember that Karamazov can entertain two extremes, and both at once.

“We have searched the house, but we have not found the money. It may still be there. Or it may have vanished the next day and be in the prisoner’s hands now. In any case, he was at her side, on his knees before her. She was lying on the bed, he had his hands stretched out to her, and he had forgotten everything so completely that he did not even hear the men come to arrest him. He had no time to prepare a line of defense in his mind. He was taken by surprise and confronted with his judges, the arbiters of his fate.

“Gentlemen of the jury, there are moments in the discharge of our duties when it is terrible for us to face a man, terrible for his sake, too! I mean the moments of watching that animal fear, when the criminal sees that all is lost, yet still struggles, still means to struggle. Every instinct of self-preservation rises in him at once. He looks at you with questioning, suffering eyes. He studies you, your face, your thoughts, unsure on which side you will strike. His distracted mind forms thousands of plans in an instant, but he is still afraid to speak, afraid of giving himself away! This purgatory of the spirit, this animal thirst for self-preservation, these humiliating moments of the human soul are awful. Sometimes they stir horror and pity for the criminal even in the lawyer. And that is what we all witnessed then.

“At first he was thunderstruck, and in his terror he let fall some very damaging phrases. ‘Blood! I deserve it!’ But he quickly pulled himself together. He had not prepared what to say or what answer to give. He had nothing ready but a bare denial: ‘I am not guilty of my father’s death.’ That was his fence for the moment, and behind it he hoped to throw up some kind of barricade. He hurried to explain away his first damaging cries by declaring that he was responsible only for the death of the servant Grigory. ‘Of that bloodshed I am guilty, but who killed my father, gentlemen, who killed him? Who can have killed him, _if not I_?’ Do you hear? He asked us that, us, who had come to put that very question to him! Do you hear that phrase, blurted out in such premature haste—‘if not I’? The animal cunning of it, the naïveté, the Karamazov impatience! ‘I did not kill him, and you must not think I did! I wanted to kill him, gentlemen, I wanted to kill him,’ he hurries to admit (he was in a hurry, in a terrible hurry), ‘but still I am not guilty, it was not I who murdered him.’ He grants us that he wanted to murder him, as though to say: you see for yourselves how truthful I am, so you will believe all the sooner that I did not murder him. Oh, in such cases the criminal is often amazingly shallow and credulous.

“At that point one of the lawyers asked him, as if by chance, the simplest of questions: ‘Wasn’t it Smerdyakov who killed him?’ Then, just as we expected, he was horribly angry that we had got ahead of him and caught him off guard, before he had time to prepare the ground and pick the moment when it would be most natural to bring in Smerdyakov’s name. He rushed at once to the opposite extreme, as he always does, and began assuring us that Smerdyakov could not have killed him, was not capable of it. But do not believe him. That was only cunning. He did not really give up the idea of Smerdyakov. On the contrary, he meant to bring him forward again, for indeed he had no one else to bring forward. But he would do it later, because for the moment that line was spoiled for him. He would bring him forward perhaps the next day, or even a few days later, choosing his chance to cry out to us, ‘You know I doubted Smerdyakov’s guilt more than you did, you remember that yourselves, but now I am convinced. He killed him, he must have done!’ For now, meanwhile, he falls back on a gloomy, irritable denial. Impatience and anger drove him, however, into the most clumsy and incredible account of how he looked in at his father’s window and how he respectfully withdrew. The worst of it was that he did not know how matters stood, or what evidence Grigory had given.

“Next we searched him. The search made him angry, yet it also gave him courage, because the whole three thousand was not on him, only half. No doubt it was only in that moment of angry silence that the fiction of the little bag first came to him. He must have known himself how unlikely the story was. He struggled painfully to make it more believable, to work it into a romance that would pass as plausible. In cases like this, the first duty of the investigators, their chief task, is not to let the criminal get ready. They must pounce on him unexpectedly, so that he blurts out his cherished ideas in all their simplicity, improbability and inconsistency. A criminal can be made to speak only when some new fact is suddenly and, as it seems, casually mentioned to him, some circumstance of great importance to the case that he knew nothing about and could not have foreseen. We had such a fact in reserve. It was Grigory’s evidence that the door was open, the door through which the prisoner had run out. He had entirely forgotten that door. He had not even suspected that Grigory might have seen it.

“The effect was astonishing. He sprang up and shouted at us, ‘Then Smerdyakov murdered him, it was Smerdyakov!’ With that he gave away the whole basis of the defense he had been holding back, and gave it away in its most improbable form. For Smerdyakov could only have committed the murder after the prisoner had knocked Grigory down and run off. We told him that Grigory had seen the door open before he fell, and had heard Smerdyakov behind the screen as he came out of his bedroom. At that, Karamazov was simply crushed. My esteemed and witty colleague, Nikolay Parfenovitch, told me afterwards that the sight of him almost moved him to tears. And to make matters better for himself, the prisoner rushed to tell us about the much-talked-of little bag. Very well, you shall hear this romance!

“Gentlemen of the jury, I have already told you why I regard this romance as more than an absurdity: I regard it as the most improbable invention that could have been offered in the circumstances. Suppose someone tried, for a wager, to make up the most unlikely story he could. He would hardly find anything more incredible. The worst of such stories is this. The triumphant romancers can always be thrown into confusion and crushed by the very details in which real life is so rich, and which these unhappy, involuntary storytellers dismiss as insignificant trifles. Oh, they have no thought to spare for such details! Their minds are fixed on their grand invention as a whole. And only imagine, someone daring to stop them over a trifle! But that is exactly how they are caught. The prisoner was asked, ‘Where did you get the stuff for your little bag, and who made it for you?’ ‘I made it myself.’ ‘And where did you get the linen?’ The prisoner was positively offended. He thought it almost an insult to be asked so trivial a question, and would you believe it, his resentment was genuine! But they are all like that. ‘I tore it off my shirt.’ ‘Then tomorrow we shall find that shirt among your linen, with a piece torn off.’ Only think, gentlemen of the jury. If we had really found that torn shirt (and how could we have missed it in his chest of drawers or trunk?), that would have been a fact, a material fact, supporting his statement! But he could not think that far. ‘I don’t remember, it may not have been off my shirt, I sewed it up in one of my landlady’s caps.’ ‘What sort of cap?’ ‘It was an old cotton rag of hers lying about.’ ‘And do you remember that clearly?’ ‘No, I don’t.’ And he was angry, very angry, and yet imagine not remembering it! In the most terrible moments of a man’s life, when he is being led to execution, for instance, he remembers just such trifles. He will forget everything else, but a green roof that flashed past him on the road, or a jackdaw on a cross, he will remember. This man kept the making of that little bag secret from his household. He must have remembered his humiliating fear that someone would walk in and catch him with a needle in his hand, and how at the slightest sound he slipped behind the screen (there is a screen in his lodgings).

“But, gentlemen of the jury, why do I tell you all this, all these details, these trifles?” cried Ippolit Kirillovitch suddenly. “For this reason: the prisoner still clings to these absurdities, even now. Since that fatal night two months ago he has explained nothing. He has not added a single real, illuminating fact to his earlier fantastic statements. It is all trivialities. ‘You must believe it on my honor.’ Oh, we are glad to believe it, we are eager to believe it, even if only on his word of honor! Are we jackals thirsting for human blood? Show us one single fact in the prisoner’s favor, and we shall rejoice. But it must be a substantial, real fact. It must not be a conclusion his own brother has drawn from the prisoner’s expression, or the notion that when he struck himself on the breast he must have meant to point to the little bag, in the dark, besides. We shall rejoice at the new fact. We shall be the first to drop our charge; we shall hasten to drop it. But as things stand, justice cries out, and we hold our ground. We cannot give up anything.”

Ippolit Kirillovitch moved on to his final peroration. He seemed to be in a fever. He spoke of the blood that cried out for vengeance, the blood of a father murdered by his son for the base motive of robbery! He pointed to the tragic and glaring consistency of the facts.

“And whatever you may hear from the talented and celebrated counsel for the defense,” Ippolit Kirillovitch could not help adding, “whatever eloquent and touching appeals he may make to your feelings, remember that you are now in a temple of justice. Remember that you are the champions of our justice, the champions of our holy Russia, of her principles, her family, all that she holds sacred! Yes, at this moment you represent Russia. Your verdict will be heard not in this hall alone. It will echo through the whole of Russia, and all Russia will listen to you as her champions and her judges. She will be encouraged or disheartened by what you decide. Do not disappoint Russia and her hopes. Our fatal troika races on in headlong flight, perhaps toward destruction. And for a long time now, all over Russia, men have stretched out imploring hands and begged it to halt its furious, reckless course. If other nations stand aside from that troika, it may be not out of respect, as the poet would like to believe, but simply out of horror. Out of horror, perhaps out of disgust. And it is well that they stand aside. But perhaps one day they will stand aside no longer. They will form a firm wall in front of the rushing apparition and stop the frenzied course of our lawlessness, for the sake of their own safety, enlightenment and civilization. Already we have heard voices of alarm from Europe. They are beginning to sound. Do not tempt them! Do not add to their growing hatred by passing a sentence that justifies a son’s murder of his father!”

Though Ippolit Kirillovitch was genuinely moved, he closed his speech with this rhetorical appeal. The effect was extraordinary. When he had finished, he hurried out and, as I have mentioned before, nearly fainted in the next room. There was no applause in the court, but the serious people were pleased. The ladies were less satisfied, although even they were pleased with his eloquence, particularly since they felt no anxiety about how the trial would end and had full faith in Fetyukovitch. “He will speak at last, and of course he will sweep everything before him.”

Everyone looked at Mitya. Through the whole of the prosecutor’s speech he had sat silent, teeth clenched, hands clasped, head bowed. Now and then he lifted his head and listened, above all when Grushenka was mentioned. When the prosecutor spoke of Rakitin’s opinion of her, a smile of contempt and anger crossed his face, and he murmured, quite audibly, “The Bernards!” When Ippolit Kirillovitch described how he had questioned and tortured him at Mokroe, Mitya raised his head and listened with the keenest curiosity. At one point he looked ready to jump up and shout, but he held himself in and only shrugged his shoulders with scorn. Afterwards people talked about the end of the speech and about the prosecutor’s great achievement in examining the prisoner at Mokroe, and they made fun of Ippolit Kirillovitch. “The man just couldn’t help bragging about how clever he was,” they said.
The court was adjourned, but for a short interval only, fifteen or twenty minutes at the most. The audience buzzed with talk and exclamations. I remember some of them.
“A weighty speech,” one gentleman in a group remarked gravely.
“He brought in too much psychology,” said another voice.
“But it was all true, the absolute truth!”
“Yes, he’s first-rate at it.”
“He summed it all up.”
“Yes, and he summed us up, too,” another voice chimed in. “Remember how at the start of his speech he made out we were all like Fyodor Pavlovitch?”
“And at the end, too. But that was all rot.”
“And obscure, too.”
“He got a little too carried away.”
“It’s unjust, it’s unjust.”
“No, it was cleverly done, anyway. He’s waited a long time, but now he’s had his say, ha ha!”
“What will the counsel for the defense say?”
In another group I heard:
“He had no business taking a jab at the Petersburg man like that. ‘Appealing to your feelings’—do you remember?”
“Yes, that was clumsy of him.”
“He was in too much of a hurry.”
“He’s a nervous man.”
“We laugh, but what must the prisoner be feeling?”
“Yes, what must it be like for Mitya?”
In a third group:
“Who is that lady, the fat one with the lorgnette, sitting at the end?”
“She’s a general’s wife, divorced. I know her.”
“That’s why she has the lorgnette.”
“She’s not good for much.”
“Oh, no, she’s a piquante little woman.”
“Two places beyond her there’s a little fair woman. She’s prettier.”
“They caught him smartly at Mokroe, didn’t they, eh?”
“Oh, smart enough. We’ve heard it before. How often he’s told that story in people’s houses!”
“And he couldn’t resist doing it now. That’s vanity.”
“He’s a man with a grievance, he he!”
“Yes, and touchy with it. And there was too much rhetoric, such long-winded sentences.”
“Yes, he tries to frighten us, he kept trying to frighten us. Do you remember about the troika? Something like ‘They have Hamlets, but so far we have only Karamazovs!’ That was cleverly said!”
“That was to appease the liberals. He’s afraid of them.”
“Yes, and he’s afraid of the lawyer, too.”
“Yes, what will Fetyukovitch say?”
“Whatever he says, he won’t get around our peasants.”
“Don’t you think so?”
A fourth group:
“What he said about the troika was good, that part about the other nations.”
“And it was true, what he said about other nations not putting up with it.”
“What do you mean?”

“Why, last week in the English Parliament a Member stood up and, speaking about the Nihilists, asked the Ministry whether it wasn’t high time to step in and educate this barbarous people. Ippolit was thinking of him, I know he was. He was talking about it last week.”
“Not an easy job.”
“Not an easy job? Why not?”
“Simple, we’d close Kronstadt and not let any grain through to them. Where would they get it then?”
“In America. They get it from America now.”
“Nonsense!”
But the bell rang, and everyone hurried back to their seats. Fetyukovitch mounted the tribune.

chapters.title: X. The Speech For The Defense. An Argument That Cuts Both Ways
paragraphs: A hush fell as the first words of the famous orator rang out. The eyes of the whole audience were fixed on him. He began very simply and directly, with an air of conviction but not the slightest trace of conceit. He made no attempt at eloquence, at pathos or at emotional phrases. He was like a man talking in a circle of close and sympathetic friends. He had a fine voice, deep and sympathetic, and the very sound of it had something genuine and simple about it. Yet everyone realized at once that the speaker might suddenly rise to true pathos and “pierce the heart with untold power.” His language was perhaps less regular than Ippolit Kirillovitch’s. But he did not use long phrases, and in fact he spoke with more precision. One thing displeased the ladies. He kept bending forward, especially at the start. It was not quite bowing; it was as if he were about to dart at his listeners. He folded his long spine nearly in half, as though it had a spring in the middle that let him bend almost to a right angle.

At the start he spoke rather disconnectedly, without system, one might say, taking the facts one at a time, though in the end they added up to a whole. His speech could be divided into two parts. The first was criticism, a refutation of the charge, at times malicious and sarcastic. In the second half, however, he suddenly altered his tone and even his manner, and rose at once to pathos. The audience seemed to have been watching for this, and they quivered with enthusiasm.

He went straight to the point. He began by saying that although he practiced in Petersburg, he had more than once gone to provincial towns to defend prisoners whose innocence he was convinced of, or at least had formed an idea of beforehand. “That is what has happened to me in the present case,” he explained. “From the very first reports in the newspapers, something struck me that strongly disposed me in the prisoner’s favor. What interested me most was a fact that often occurs in legal practice, but rarely, I think, in so extreme and peculiar a form as here. I ought to name that peculiarity only at the end of my speech. But I will name it at the very beginning, for it is my weakness to set to work directly, without keeping my effects in reserve or husbanding my material. That may be imprudent of me, but at least it is sincere. What I have in mind is this. There is an overwhelming chain of evidence against the prisoner, and yet not one fact in it will stand up to criticism when examined on its own. As I followed the case more closely in the papers, this idea grew stronger and stronger. Then I suddenly received a request from the prisoner’s relatives to take up his defense. I hurried here at once, and here I became completely convinced. I undertook the case in order to break down this terrible chain of facts, and to show that each piece of evidence, taken separately, was unproved and fantastic.”
So Fetyukovitch began.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” he suddenly protested, “I am a stranger to this district. I come with no preconceived ideas. The prisoner, a man of turbulent and unbridled temper, has never insulted me. But he has insulted perhaps hundreds of people in this town, and so he has set many of them against him in advance. Of course I recognize that the moral feeling of local society has been justly roused against him. He is a man of violent, turbulent temper. Yet he was received in society here. He was even welcome in the family of my talented friend, the prosecutor.”

(N.B. At these words two or three people laughed in the audience, but they quickly stopped, and everyone noticed. All of us knew that the prosecutor received Mitya against his will, only because Mitya had somehow aroused his wife’s interest. She was a lady of the highest virtue and moral worth, but fanciful, capricious and fond of opposing her husband, especially in trifles. Mitya’s visits, however, had not been frequent.)

“Nevertheless I venture to suggest,” Fetyukovitch continued, “that, for all his independent mind and fair character, my opponent may have formed a mistaken prejudice against my unfortunate client. Oh, that is so natural! The unfortunate man has only too well earned such prejudice. Outraged morality, and still more outraged taste, is often relentless. In the talented prosecutor’s speech we have heard a stern analysis of the prisoner’s character and conduct, and his severe, critical attitude to the case was plain.
