What is more, he entered into psychological subtleties that he could not have entered if he had felt the slightest conscious and malicious prejudice against the prisoner. But in cases like this there are things even worse, even more fatal, than the most malicious and consciously unfair attitude. It is worse if we are carried away by the artistic instinct, by the desire to create, so to speak, a romance, especially if God has gifted us with psychological insight. Before I set out for this place, I was warned in Petersburg, and I knew myself, that here I should meet a talented opponent whose psychological insight and subtlety had in recent years won him a peculiar fame in legal circles. But profound as psychology is, it is a knife that cuts both ways.” (Laughter among the public.) “You will of course forgive me this comparison. I cannot boast of eloquence. But let me take as an example any point in the prosecutor’s speech.

“The prisoner, running away through the garden in the dark, climbed over the fence. The servant seized him, and he knocked the man down with a brass pestle. Then he jumped back into the garden and spent five minutes over the man, trying to find out whether he had killed him. And the prosecutor refuses to believe the prisoner’s statement that he ran to old Grigory out of pity. ‘No,’ he says, ‘such delicacy of feeling at such a moment is impossible, it is unnatural. He ran to find out whether the only witness of his crime was dead or alive, and so he showed that he had committed the murder, since he would have had no other reason to run back.’

“There you have psychology. But let us take the same method and apply it to the case the other way round, and our result will be no less probable. The murderer, we are told, leapt down to find out, as a precaution, whether the witness was alive. Yet in his murdered father’s study he had left behind, as the prosecutor himself argues, an amazing piece of evidence: a torn envelope with an inscription saying that three thousand roubles had been in it. ‘If he had carried that envelope away with him, no one in the world would have known about the envelope and the notes in it, or that the prisoner had stolen the money.’ Those are the prosecutor’s own words. So on one side you see a complete lack of precaution. Here is a man who has lost his head and fled in a panic, leaving that clue on the floor. Two minutes later, when he has killed another man, we are asked to assume in him the most heartless and calculating foresight. But even granting this, I suppose it is psychological subtlety that discovers that in some circumstances I become as bloodthirsty and sharp-eyed as a Caucasian eagle, while in the next I am as timid and blind as a mole. But if I am so bloodthirsty and so cruelly calculating that, having killed a man, I run back only to see whether he is alive to witness against me, why should I spend five minutes looking after my victim, at the risk of meeting other witnesses? Why soak my handkerchief wiping the blood from his head, so that it can be used as evidence against me later? If he were so cold-hearted and calculating, why not strike the servant again and again on the head with the same pestle, to kill him outright and be rid of all anxiety about the witness?

“Again, though he ran to see whether the witness was alive, he left another witness on the path. That witness was the brass pestle, which he had taken from the two women, and which they could always recognize afterwards as theirs, proving that he had taken it from them. And it is not as if he had forgotten it on the path, or dropped it in carelessness or haste. No, he threw his weapon away, for it was found fifteen paces from where Grigory lay. Why did he do that? Just because he was grieved at having killed a man, an old servant, and so he flung the pestle away with a curse, as a murderous weapon. That is how it must have been. What other reason could he have had for throwing it so far? And if he could feel grief and pity at having killed a man, that shows he was innocent of his father’s murder. Had he murdered his father, he would never have run to another victim out of pity. He would have felt differently. His thoughts would have been centered on saving himself. He would have had none left for pity, and that is beyond doubt. On the contrary, he would have smashed the man’s skull instead of spending five minutes looking after him. There was room for pity and good feeling precisely because his conscience had been clear until then. Here we have a different psychology. I have used this method on purpose, gentlemen of the jury, to show that you can prove anything with it. It all depends on who uses it. Psychology lures even the most serious people into romancing, and quite without their knowing it. I am speaking of the abuse of psychology, gentlemen.”
Sounds of approval and laughter at the prosecutor’s expense were heard again in the court. I will not give the speech in detail. I will quote only some passages from it, some of the leading points.

chapters.title: XI. There Was No Money. There Was No Robbery
paragraphs: One point in Fetyukovitch’s speech struck everyone. He flatly denied that the fatal three thousand roubles had ever existed, and so denied that anyone could have stolen them.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” he began. “Anyone who comes to this case fresh and without prejudice will notice one odd feature in it. We have a charge of robbery, and no way at all of proving that there was anything to rob. We are told that three thousand roubles were stolen. Whether those roubles ever existed, nobody knows. Think how we came to hear of the sum, and who has actually seen the notes. The only person who saw them, and who said they had been put in the envelope, was the servant Smerdyakov. Before the catastrophe he mentioned it to the prisoner and to the prisoner’s brother, Ivan Fyodorovitch. Madame Svyetlov was told of it as well. Yet not one of these three ever saw the notes. Smerdyakov alone saw them.

“So a question arises. Suppose the notes did exist and Smerdyakov did see them. When did he see them last? Perhaps his master took the notes from under his bed and put them back in his cash-box without a word to Smerdyakov. Note this too. By Smerdyakov’s account the notes lay under the mattress. The prisoner would have had to drag them out, and yet the bed was perfectly smooth. The protocol records this with care. How could the prisoner find the notes without disturbing the bed? And how could his bloodstained hands have avoided marking the fine, spotless linen that had been so carefully laid on it?

“But I will be asked about the envelope on the floor. Yes, that envelope deserves a word or two. A moment ago I was somewhat surprised to hear the highly talented prosecutor say of himself (of himself, mark you) that without that envelope, without its being left on the floor, nobody in the world would have known that the envelope existed, or the notes inside it, and so nobody would have known the prisoner had stolen them. So by the prosecutor’s own admission that torn scrap of paper is the one proof on which the charge of robbery rests. ‘Otherwise no one would have known of the robbery, or perhaps even of the money.’ But does a scrap of paper lying on the floor prove that there was money in it, and that the money was stolen? It will be objected that Smerdyakov saw the money in the envelope. But when did he see it last? I ask you that. I spoke to Smerdyakov, and he told me he saw the notes two days before the catastrophe. Why then not picture old Fyodor Pavlovitch, locked up alone, waiting in hysterical impatience for the woman he adored, and passing the time by tearing open the envelope and taking out the notes? ‘What good is the envelope?’ he may have asked himself. ‘She will not believe the notes are in it. But if I show her thirty rainbow-colored notes in one roll, that will impress her, you may be sure. It will make her mouth water.’ So he rips the envelope open, takes out the money, and throws the envelope on the floor. He knows the money is his, and he has no fear of leaving evidence behind.

“Consider, gentlemen: could anything be more likely than this account and this action? Why should it be out of the question? And if something of the kind could have happened, the charge of robbery collapses. Where there was no money, no money was stolen. The envelope on the floor is supposed to show there had been money in it. Why may I not say the opposite, that the envelope lay on the floor because its owner had taken the money out?

“But I will be asked where the money went, if Fyodor Pavlovitch took it out of the envelope, since the police did not find it when they searched the house. First, part of the money was found in the cash-box. Second, he may have taken it out that morning, or the evening before, for some other use. He may have meant to give it away or send it off. He may have changed his mind and his plan altogether, and not thought it necessary to tell Smerdyakov beforehand. If such an explanation has even the barest chance of being true, how can anyone say so positively that the prisoner killed for the sake of robbery, and really carried out that robbery? That is to wander into the realm of fiction. If you claim something was stolen, you must produce the thing, or at least prove beyond doubt that it existed. But nobody ever saw these notes.

“Not long ago in Petersburg, a young man of eighteen, hardly more than a boy, who kept a small business as a costermonger, walked into a moneychanger’s shop in broad daylight with an ax. With extraordinary, typical audacity, he killed the shop’s master and took off fifteen hundred roubles. Five hours later he was arrested. Except for fifteen roubles that he had already managed to spend, the entire sum was found on him. What is more, when the shopman came back to the shop after the murder, he gave the police not only the exact amount stolen but the very notes and gold coins that made it up, and those same notes and coins were found on the criminal. The murderer then made a full and genuine confession. That, gentlemen of the jury, is what I call evidence! There I know the money, I see it, I touch it, and I cannot deny that it exists. Is it so in the present case? And yet here it is a matter of life and death.

“Yes, I will be told, but he was carousing that night and squandering money. He was shown to have had fifteen hundred roubles. Where did he get it? But look at the fact itself. Only fifteen hundred could be found, and the other half of the sum was nowhere to be discovered. That shows this money was not the same money, and had never been in any envelope. The preliminary inquiry proved, by a strict calculation of time, that the prisoner ran from those women servants straight to Perhotin’s, without going home, and that he had been nowhere else. So he was in company the whole time. He could not have divided the three thousand in half and hidden half of it in the town. This is exactly what has led the prosecutor to suppose that the money is hidden in some crevice at Mokroe. Why not in the dungeons of the castle of Udolpho, gentlemen? Is this supposition not far too fantastic and too romantic? And observe that if it breaks down, the whole charge of robbery is blown away. For then what became of the other fifteen hundred roubles? By what miracle did they vanish, when it is proved that the prisoner went nowhere else? And we are ready to ruin a man’s life with such tales!

“I will be told that he could not explain where he got the fifteen hundred he had, and that everyone knew he was penniless before that night. Who knew it, I ask you? The prisoner has given a clear and steady account of where that money came from. If you will have it so, gentlemen of the jury, nothing could be more probable than that account, or fit better with the prisoner’s temper and spirit. The prosecutor is charmed with his own romance. A man of weak will, we are told, who brought himself to take the three thousand so insultingly offered by his betrothed, could never have set half of it aside and sewn it up. Even if he had, he would have unpicked it every two days, taken out a hundred, and spent the lot within a month. You will remember that all this was put forward in a tone that allowed no reply. But what if the thing happened quite differently? What if you have been spinning a romance, and about quite a different kind of man? That is exactly it. You have invented a different man altogether!

“Perhaps I will be told that witnesses say he spent the whole three thousand from his betrothed in a single day, a month before the catastrophe, and so could not have divided it in half. But who are these witnesses? The court has already seen what their evidence is worth. Besides, a crust always looks bigger in another man’s hand. None of these witnesses counted that money. They all judged by eye. And the witness Maximov testified that the prisoner had twenty thousand in his hand. You see, gentlemen of the jury, psychology cuts both ways. Let me turn the other edge now and see what comes of it.

“A month before the catastrophe, Katerina Ivanovna entrusted the prisoner with three thousand roubles to send off by post. But is it true that they were entrusted to him in such an insulting and degrading way as we heard proclaimed just now? The young lady’s first statement on this was different, quite different. In the second statement we heard only cries of resentment and revenge, cries of hatred long kept hidden. The fact that the witness gave her first evidence incorrectly gives us the right to conclude that her second may be incorrect too. The prosecutor will not touch that story, he dares not (his own words). So be it. I will not touch it either. I will only venture to say this. A lofty, high-principled person, such as that highly respected young lady undoubtedly is, suddenly contradicts her first statement in court, with the plain motive of ruining the prisoner. Then it is clear that her evidence has been given neither fairly nor calmly. May we not assume that a woman bent on revenge has exaggerated a great deal? Yes, she may well have exaggerated, above all the insult and humiliation in her offering him the money. No, it was offered in a way that made it possible to take it. That is especially so for a man as easy-going as the prisoner, and above all because he expected soon to receive from his father the three thousand roubles he reckoned were owing to him. It was thoughtless of him. But it was just that irresponsible thoughtlessness that made him so sure his father would give him the money, that he would get it, and that he could therefore always send off the money entrusted to him and pay the debt.

“But the prosecutor refuses to allow that on the same day he could have set aside half the money and sewn it into a little bag. That is not his character, we are told. He could not have had such feelings. Yet the prosecutor himself spoke of the broad Karamazov nature. He cried out about the two extremes a Karamazov can hold in view at once. Karamazov is precisely such a two-sided nature, swinging between two extremes. Even in the grip of the wildest craving for revelry, he can pull himself up short if something strikes him from the other side. And on the other side is love, that new love which had flared up in his heart. For that love he needed money, oh, far more than he needed it for carousing with his mistress. If she were to say to him, ‘I am yours, I will not have Fyodor Pavlovitch,’ then he had to have money to take her away. That mattered more than carousing. Could a Karamazov fail to see it? That very worry was what he suffered from. What is improbable in his putting that money aside and hiding it for an emergency?

“But time went by, and Fyodor Pavlovitch did not give the prisoner the three thousand he expected. On the contrary, the prisoner heard that his father meant to use that sum to seduce the woman he, the prisoner, loved. ‘If Fyodor Pavlovitch does not give me the money,’ he thought, ‘I shall look like a thief to Katerina Ivanovna.’ Then the idea came to him of going to Katerina Ivanovna, laying before her the fifteen hundred roubles he still wore round his neck, and saying, ‘I am a scoundrel, but I am not a thief.’ So here we already have two reasons why he should guard that sum like the apple of his eye. They are why he should not unpick the little bag and spend it a hundred at a time. Why should you deny the prisoner a sense of honor? He has one. Grant that it is misplaced, grant that it often leads him astray. Still it exists, it is a passion in him, and he has proved it.

“But now the affair grows more tangled still. His torments of jealousy reach their height, and the same two questions torture his fevered brain more and more: ‘If I pay back Katerina Ivanovna, where will I find the means to go off with Grushenka?’ He behaved wildly in the course of that month. He drank and made disturbances in the taverns. Perhaps this was because he was miserable and strained past what he could bear. The two questions grew so sharp that at last they drove him to despair. He sent his younger brother to beg, for the last time, for the three thousand roubles. Without waiting for an answer, he burst in himself and ended by beating the old man before witnesses. After that he had no hope of getting the money from anyone, since his father would not give it to him after such a beating.

“That same evening he struck himself on the breast, on the upper part of the chest where the little bag hung, and swore to his brother that he had the means of not being a scoundrel. But he said he would still remain a scoundrel, because he foresaw he would not use that means. He did not have the character for it, he said, he did not have the willpower. Why, why does the prosecutor refuse to believe the evidence of Alexey Karamazov, given so genuinely and sincerely, so spontaneously and convincingly? And why does he, on the contrary, force me to believe in money hidden in a crevice, in the dungeons of the castle of Udolpho?

“That same evening, after the talk with his brother, the prisoner wrote that fatal letter. And that letter, we are told, is the chief proof, the most stupendous proof, that the prisoner committed robbery! ‘I shall beg from everyone, and if I do not get it I shall murder my father and take the envelope with the pink ribbon from under his mattress as soon as Ivan has gone.’ A full program of the murder, they say, so it must have been he. ‘It has all been done as he wrote,’ cries the prosecutor.

“But in the first place, this is the letter of a drunken man, written in great irritation. In the second place, what he writes about the envelope comes, once again, from what Smerdyakov told him, for he had not seen the envelope himself. And in the third place, he did write it, but how can you prove he did what it says? Did the prisoner take the envelope from under the pillow? Did he find the money? Did that money really exist? And remember, was it to get money that the prisoner ran off? He ran off in headlong haste, not to steal, but to find out where she was, the woman who had crushed him. He was not running to carry out a program, to do what he had written, that is, to commit a premeditated robbery. He ran suddenly, spontaneously, in a jealous fury. Yes! I will be told that when he got there and murdered him, he seized the money as well. But did he murder him after all? The charge of robbery I reject with indignation. A man cannot be accused of robbery if it is impossible to say exactly what he stole. That is an axiom. But did he murder him without robbing him? Did he murder him at all? Has that been proved? Is that too not a romance?”

chapters.title: XII. And There Was No Murder Either
paragraphs: “Gentlemen of the jury, I ask you to remember that a man’s life is at stake, and that you must take care. We heard the prosecutor himself admit that until today he had doubts about charging the prisoner with full and deliberate planning of the crime. His doubts lasted until he saw that fatal drunken letter, which was read out in court today. ‘All was done as written.’ But I say again: he was running to her, to look for her, for one purpose only—to learn where she was. No one can dispute that. Had she been at home, he would not have run off. He would have stayed beside her, and so would never have done what he promised in the letter. He ran on a sudden impulse, by chance, and by then he very likely no longer remembered his drunken letter. ‘He snatched up the pestle,’ they say, and you will remember how a whole edifice of psychology was built on that pestle—why he was bound to see it as a weapon, why he was bound to grab it, and so on and so on. A very ordinary thought comes to me here. Suppose that pestle had not been in view. Suppose it had not been lying on the shelf where the prisoner snatched it up, but had been put away in a cupboard. It would not have caught his eye. He would have run out without a weapon, with empty hands, and then he would certainly have killed no one. How, then, can I treat the pestle as proof of premeditation?

“Yes, but he talked in the taverns of murdering his father. And two days earlier, on the evening he wrote the drunken letter, he was quiet and did no more than quarrel with a shopman in a tavern—because a Karamazov cannot help quarreling, we are told! My answer is this. If he were planning a murder such as the letter describes, he certainly would not have quarreled even with a shopman. He would probably not have gone into the tavern at all. A man plotting such a crime wants quiet and privacy. He wants to efface himself and avoid being seen or heard, and he wants it not out of calculation but out of instinct. Gentlemen of the jury, the psychological method cuts both ways, and we can use it too. As for all this shouting in taverns through the whole month, do we not often hear children, or drunkards stumbling out of taverns, cry, ‘I’ll kill you’? Yet they murder no one. And that fatal letter—is it not simply drunken ill temper as well? Is it not just the cry of a brawler outside a tavern, ‘I’ll kill you! I’ll kill the lot of you!’ Why not? Why could it not be that? What reason do we have to call that letter ‘fatal’ and not absurd? Because his father was found murdered. Because a witness saw the prisoner running out of the garden with a weapon in his hand, and was knocked down by him. So, we are told, everything happened as he had planned in writing, and the letter was not ‘absurd’ but ‘fatal.’

“Now, thank God, we have reached the real point: ‘Since he was in the garden, he must have murdered him.’ In those few words—‘since he _was_, then he _must_’—the whole case for the prosecution rests. He was there, so he must have done it. But what if there is no _must_ about it, even if he was there? Oh, I grant that the chain of evidence and the coincidences are truly suggestive. But take these facts one by one, leaving aside how they connect. Why, for instance, does the prosecution refuse to believe the prisoner when he says he ran away from his father’s window? Remember the sarcasm the prosecutor heaped on the respectful and ‘pious’ feelings that supposedly came over the murderer all of a sudden. But what if there was something of the kind—a feeling of religious awe, if not of respect for his father? ‘My mother must have been praying for me at that moment,’ the prisoner said at the preliminary inquiry. And so he ran away as soon as he was satisfied that Madame Svyetlov was not in his father’s house. ‘But he could not have satisfied himself by looking through the window,’ the prosecutor objects. Why could he not? Why? The window opened to the signals the prisoner gave. Fyodor Pavlovitch might have spoken a word, cried out something, that told the prisoner she was not there. Why must we suppose that everything happened as we picture it, as we have resolved to picture it? A thousand things can happen in real life that the subtlest imagination misses.

“‘Yes, but Grigory saw the door open, so the prisoner was certainly inside the house, and therefore he killed him.’ Now, about that door, gentlemen of the jury.... Notice that we have the word of only one witness about that door, and at the time he was in such a state that— But suppose the door was open. Suppose the prisoner lied when he denied it, out of the instinct of self-defense that is natural in his position. Suppose he did go into the house—well, what of it? How does it follow that, because he was there, he committed the murder? He might have dashed in and run through the rooms. He might have pushed his father aside. He might have struck him. But once he had made sure that Madame Svyetlov was not there, he may have run off, glad that she was not there and that he had not killed his father. And perhaps it was exactly because he had escaped the temptation to kill his father, because his conscience was clear and he was glad he had not killed him, that he was capable of a pure feeling, of pity and compassion. That is why, a minute later, he jumped down from the fence to help Grigory, the man he had knocked down in his agitation.

“With terrible eloquence the prosecutor painted for us the dreadful state of the prisoner’s mind at Mokroe, when love lay before him once more and called him to a new life. Love was impossible for him, said the prosecutor, because behind him lay his father’s bloodstained corpse, and beyond that corpse—retribution. And yet the prosecutor still granted him love, which he explained in his own manner, speaking of the prisoner’s drunkenness, of a criminal being led to execution while it is still far off, and so on and so on. But I ask again, Mr. Prosecutor, have you not invented a new personality? Is the prisoner so coarse and heartless that at such a moment he could think of love, and of tricks to escape punishment, if his hands were really stained with his father’s blood? No, no, no! The moment it became clear to him that she loved him and was calling him to her side, promising him new happiness, oh, then, I insist, the urge to kill himself must have doubled and trebled in him. If his father’s murder had been on his conscience, he must have killed himself. Oh, no! He would not have forgotten where his pistols lay! I know the prisoner. The savage, stony heartlessness the prosecutor gives him is at odds with his character. He would have killed himself—that is certain. He did not kill himself precisely because ‘his mother’s prayers had saved him,’ and because he was innocent of his father’s blood. That night at Mokroe he was troubled and grieving only over old Grigory. He was praying to God that the old man would get well, that his blow had not been deadly, and that he would not have to pay for it. Why not accept such an explanation of the facts? What reliable proof do we have that the prisoner is lying?

“But we shall be told right away, once more, ‘There lies his father’s corpse! If he ran away without murdering him, who did murder him?’ Here, I say again, is the whole logic of the prosecution. Who murdered him, if not he? There is no one to put in his place.

“Gentlemen of the jury, is that really so? Is it positively, actually true that there is no one else at all? We watched the prosecutor count off on his fingers every person who was in that house that night. There were five of them. Three, I agree, cannot be held responsible: the murdered man himself, old Grigory, and his wife. That leaves the prisoner and Smerdyakov. And the prosecutor cries out, with great effect, that the prisoner pointed at Smerdyakov only because he had no one else to pin it on. If there had been a sixth person, he says, even the ghost of a sixth person, the prisoner would at once have dropped the charge against Smerdyakov, ashamed, and accused that other. But, gentlemen of the jury, why may I not draw the exact opposite conclusion? There are two persons—the prisoner and Smerdyakov. Why can I not say that you accuse my client simply because you have no one else to accuse? And you have no one else only because you have made up your minds to keep Smerdyakov free from all suspicion.

“It is true that Smerdyakov is accused only by the prisoner, his two brothers, and Madame Svyetlov. But others accuse him as well. There are vague rumors of a question, of a suspicion, an obscure report, a sense of expectation. Finally, there is the evidence of a combination of facts that is very suggestive, though, I admit, not conclusive. First, there is the fit that struck precisely on the day of the catastrophe. For some reason the prosecutor felt he had to defend its genuineness carefully. Then there is Smerdyakov’s sudden suicide on the eve of the trial. Then there is the equally startling testimony given in court today by the elder of the prisoner’s brothers. He had believed in the prisoner’s guilt, yet today he brought out a bundle of notes and named Smerdyakov as the murderer. Oh, I fully share the conviction of the court and the prosecutor that Ivan Karamazov is suffering from brain fever. His statement may truly be a desperate attempt, hatched in delirium, to save his brother by putting the guilt on a dead man. But still, Smerdyakov’s name has been spoken, and once more there is a hint of mystery. Something is unexplained, unfinished. And perhaps one day it will be explained. But we will not go into that now. That is for later.

“The court has resolved to go on with the trial. Meanwhile, I would like to make a few remarks on the portrait of Smerdyakov that the prosecutor drew with such subtlety and talent. I admire his talent, but I cannot agree with him. I have visited Smerdyakov. I have seen him and talked with him, and he made quite a different impression on me. His health was weak, it is true. But in character, in spirit, he was far from the weak man the prosecutor has made of him. I found no sign of the timidity the prosecutor made so much of. Nor was he simple. On the contrary, I found an extreme distrust, hidden behind a mask of _naïveté_, and a mind of considerable reach. The prosecutor was too simple in taking him for feeble-minded. He made a very definite impression on me, and I came away convinced that he was a plainly spiteful creature, wildly ambitious, vengeful, and intensely envious. I made some inquiries. He resented his birth and was ashamed of it, and he would grind his teeth when he remembered that he was the son of ‘stinking Lizaveta.’ He was disrespectful to the servant Grigory and his wife, who had looked after him in his childhood. He cursed Russia and sneered at it. He dreamed of going to France and becoming a Frenchman. He often used to say that he had not the money for it. I believe he loved no one but himself, and he held a strangely high opinion of himself. His whole notion of culture came down to good clothes, clean shirt-fronts and polished boots. He believed himself to be Fyodor Pavlovitch’s illegitimate son (there is evidence of this), and he might well have resented his position beside his master’s legitimate sons. They had everything, and he had nothing. They had every right, they had the inheritance, while he was only the cook. He told me himself that he had helped Fyodor Pavlovitch put the notes into the envelope. The purpose of that sum—a sum that would have made his career—must have been hateful to him. Besides, he saw three thousand roubles in new rainbow-colored notes. (I asked him about that on purpose.) Oh, beware of showing an ambitious and envious man a great sum of money all at once! And it was the first time he had seen so much money in one man’s hands. The sight of those rainbow-colored notes may have left a morbid mark on his imagination, but with no immediate result.

“The talented prosecutor, with remarkable subtlety, set out for us all the arguments for and against the theory that Smerdyakov is guilty. In particular he asked what reason Smerdyakov could have had to fake a fit. But he may not have been faking at all. The fit may have come on quite naturally, and it may equally well have passed quite naturally. The sick man may have recovered—not fully, perhaps, but enough to regain consciousness, as happens with epileptics.

“The prosecutor asks at what moment Smerdyakov could have committed the murder. But it is very easy to name that moment. He might have woken out of a deep sleep (for he was only asleep—an epileptic fit is always followed by deep sleep) at the very moment when old Grigory shouted at the top of his voice, ‘Parricide!’ That shout in the dark and the silence may have woken Smerdyakov, whose sleep may by then have been lighter. He might quite naturally have woken up an hour earlier.

“Getting out of bed, he goes almost without knowing it, with no clear purpose, toward the sound, to see what is wrong. His head is still muddled from his attack, and his mind is half asleep. But once he is in the garden he goes to the lighted windows, and his master, who would of course be glad to see him, gives him terrible news. His mind starts working at once. He hears every detail from his frightened master, and little by little, in his disordered brain, an idea takes shape—a terrible one, but tempting and irresistibly logical. Kill the old man, take the three thousand, and put all the blame on his young master. A terrible greed for money, for plunder, may have gripped him as he saw that he was safe from discovery. Oh, such sudden and irresistible impulses come so often when the chance is favorable, above all to murderers who never thought of committing murder beforehand. And Smerdyakov may have gone in and carried out his plan. With what weapon? Why, with any stone picked up in the garden. But why? For what purpose? Why, for the three thousand, which means a career for him. Oh, I do not contradict myself—the money may have existed. And perhaps Smerdyakov alone knew where to find it, where his master kept it. And the wrapping that held the money—the torn envelope on the floor?

“A little while ago the prosecutor was explaining his subtle theory that only an inexperienced thief like Karamazov would have left the envelope on the floor, and that a man like Smerdyakov would have taken care not to leave evidence against himself. As I listened, I felt I was hearing something very familiar. And, would you believe it, I had heard that very argument, that very guess at how Karamazov would have behaved, from Smerdyakov himself, exactly two days before. What is more, it struck me even then. I thought there was an artificial simplicity about him. I thought he was in a hurry to plant this idea in my mind, so that I would take it for my own. He slipped it in, so to speak. Did he not slip the same idea in at the inquiry, and suggest it to the talented prosecutor?

“I shall be asked, ‘What about the old woman, Grigory’s wife? She heard the sick man groaning close by, all night long.’ Yes, she heard it, but that testimony is highly unreliable. I once knew a lady who complained bitterly that a dog in the yard had kept her awake all night. Yet it turned out that the poor creature had yelped only once or twice. And that is natural. A man who is asleep hears a groan and wakes up, annoyed at being woken, but he drops off again at once. Two hours later he hears a groan again, wakes, and drops off again. Another two hours, and the same thing—three times in all during the night. In the morning the sleeper wakes and complains that someone was groaning all night and kept him awake. And it must seem that way to him. He has no memory of the two-hour stretches of sleep in between. He remembers only the moments of waking, so he feels he was awake all night.

“But why, why, asks the prosecutor, did Smerdyakov not confess in his last letter? Why did his conscience urge him to one step and not to the other? But forgive me: conscience implies repentance, and the suicide may have felt no repentance, only despair. Despair and repentance are two very different things. Despair may be vengeful and unforgiving, and a man who lays hands on himself may well have felt his hatred double for those he had envied all his life.

“Gentlemen of the jury, beware of a miscarriage of justice! What is there in all I have just laid before you that is so improbable? Find the flaw in my reasoning. Find the impossibility, the absurdity. And if there is only a shade of possibility, only a shade of probability in what I propose, do not condemn him. And is it only a shade? I swear by everything sacred that I fully believe in the account of the murder that I have just given. What troubles me and makes me indignant is this: of the whole mass of facts the prosecution has piled up against the prisoner, there is not one that is certain and beyond refutation. And yet the unhappy man is to be ruined by the sheer weight of these facts. Yes, the effect of the pile is awful: the blood, the blood dripping from his fingers, the bloodstained shirt, the dark night ringing with the shout ‘Parricide!’, and the old man falling with a broken head. And then the mass of phrases, statements, gestures, shouts! Oh, this has so much influence, it can so sway the mind. But, gentlemen of the jury, can it sway your minds? Remember that you have been given absolute power to bind and to loose. But the greater the power, the more terrible the responsibility.

“I do not withdraw one iota of what I have just said. But suppose, for a single moment, that I agreed with the prosecution that my luckless client did stain his hands with his father’s blood. This is only a supposition, I repeat. I never doubt his innocence for one instant. But so be it: I assume that my client is guilty of parricide. Even so, hear what I have to say. I have it in my heart to say something more to you, for I feel that a great struggle must be going on in your hearts and minds.... Forgive me for speaking of your hearts and minds, gentlemen of the jury, but I want to be truthful and sincere to the end. Let us all be sincere!”

At this point the speech was broken by rather loud applause. The last words had been spoken in such a sincere tone that everyone felt he really might have something to say, and that what he was about to say would matter very much. But the President heard the applause and announced in a loud voice that he would have the court cleared if it happened again. Every sound died away, and Fetyukovitch began in a voice full of feeling, quite unlike the tone he had used until then.

chapters.title: XIII. A Corrupter Of Thought
paragraphs: “Gentlemen of the jury, the pile of facts is not the only thing that threatens my client with ruin,” he began. “What truly condemns him is a single fact: the dead body of his father. Suppose this were an ordinary murder. You would throw out the charge, because the evidence is trivial, incomplete and fantastic once you examine each piece on its own. Or at least you would hesitate before destroying a man’s life only on account of the prejudice against him, which he has, sadly, earned only too well. But this is no ordinary murder. It is parricide. That grips men’s minds so hard that the evidence, trivial and incomplete as it is, begins to look less trivial and less incomplete, even to a mind free of prejudice. How can such a prisoner be acquitted? What if he did commit the murder and walks away unpunished? That is the thought every person in this room feels in his heart, almost without willing it, by sheer instinct.

“Yes, it is a fearful thing to shed a father’s blood. He is the father who gave me life and loved me, who held nothing back for my sake, who grieved over my illnesses from my earliest years, who spent his whole life worrying about my happiness and who lived in my joys and my successes. To murder such a father is unthinkable. Gentlemen of the jury, what is a father—a true father? What does that great word mean? What great idea lies in that name? We have already said in part what a true father is and what he ought to be. In the case that so occupies us, and over which our hearts ache, the father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, did not fit the idea of a father that we have just described. That is the misfortune. And some fathers truly are a misfortune. Let us look at this misfortune a little more closely. Given the weight of the decision before you, we must shrink from nothing. It is our special duty not to shrink from any idea, like children or frightened women, as the talented prosecutor happily phrased it.

“But in his heated speech my esteemed opponent (and he was my opponent before I had said a word) cried out several times, ‘Oh, I will not give up the defense of the prisoner to the lawyer who has come down from Petersburg. I accuse, but I defend also!’ He cried that out several times, yet he forgot something. This terrible prisoner was grateful for twenty-three years for a mere pound of nuts, given to him by the only person who had been kind to him as a child in his father’s house. Might not such a man well have remembered for those twenty-three years how he ran around his father’s backyard ‘without boots on his feet and with his little trousers hanging by one button’—the words of the kind-hearted Doctor Herzenstube?

“Oh, gentlemen of the jury, why must we look at this misfortune any closer? Why repeat what we all know? What did my client find when he came here, to his father’s house? And why portray him as a heartless egoist and a monster? He is uncontrolled, wild and unruly. That is what we are trying him for. But who is to blame for the life he has led? Who is to blame that his upbringing was so improper, despite his excellent nature and his grateful, sensitive heart? Did anyone teach him to be reasonable? Did study ever enlighten him? Did anyone, even in his childhood, love him the least bit? My client was left to Providence like a beast of the field. Perhaps, after long years of separation, he longed to see his father. A thousand times, perhaps, as he thought back on his childhood, he drove off the loathsome phantoms that haunted his childish dreams, and with all his heart he longed to embrace his father and forgive him! And what met him? Cynical jeers, suspicions, and squabbling over money. Day after day over the brandy he heard nothing but revolting talk and vicious maxims. In the end he watched his father lure his mistress away from him, and with his own money too. Oh, gentlemen of the jury, how cruel and revolting that was! And all the while that old man complained about his son’s disrespect and cruelty. He slandered him in society, harmed him, blackened his name, and bought up his unpaid debts in order to get him thrown into prison.

“Gentlemen of the jury, men like my client look fierce, unruly and uncontrolled on the surface, yet they are often—indeed most often—exceedingly tender-hearted. They simply do not show it. Do not laugh, do not laugh at my idea! The talented prosecutor mocked my client without mercy just now for loving Schiller, for loving the sublime and the beautiful! In his place I would not have laughed at that. Yes, such natures—oh, let me speak in their defense, they are so often and so cruelly misunderstood—such natures often hunger for tenderness, goodness and justice, as a contrast to their own unruliness and ferocity, and they hunger for it without realizing. On the surface they are passionate and fierce, but they are painfully capable of loving a woman, for instance, with a spiritual and exalted love. Again I say, do not laugh at me. This is very often so with such natures. But they cannot hide their passions, some of them very coarse, and those show and are noticed, while the man within stays unseen. Their passions burn out fast. Yet beside a noble and lofty person, this seemingly coarse and rough man looks for a new life. He tries to mend himself, to be better, to become noble and honorable, ‘sublime and beautiful,’ however much people have ridiculed the phrase.

“I said a moment ago that I would not dare to touch on my client’s engagement. But I may say half a word. What we heard just now was not evidence. It was the scream of a frenzied woman bent on revenge. And it was not for her—oh, not for her!—to accuse him of treachery, because she is the one who betrayed him! Had she had a little time to think, she would never have given such testimony. Oh, do not believe her! No, my client is not the monster she called him!

“On the eve of His Crucifixion the Lover of Mankind said: ‘I am the Good Shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep, so that not one of them might be lost.’ Let no man’s soul be lost through us!

“A moment ago I asked what the word ‘father’ means, and I cried out that it is a great word and a precious name. But we must use words honestly, gentlemen, and I will dare to call things by their right names. A father like old Karamazov cannot be called a father, and he does not deserve the name. Filial love for an unworthy father is an absurdity, an impossibility. Love cannot be made from nothing. Only God can make something from nothing.

“‘Fathers, provoke not your children to wrath,’ the apostle writes, out of a heart glowing with love. I do not quote these sacred words for my client’s sake. I mention them for the sake of all fathers. Who has given me authority to preach to fathers? No one. But as a man and a citizen I make my appeal—_vivos voco!_ We are not long on this earth. We do many evil deeds and speak many evil words. So let us all take hold of a good moment, while we are together, to say a kind word to one another. That is what I am doing. Since I am standing here, I am using my chance. It is not for nothing that the highest authority has given us this tribune—all Russia hears us! I am not speaking only to the fathers who are present. I cry out to all fathers: ‘Fathers, provoke not your children to wrath.’ Yes, let us first carry out Christ’s command ourselves, and only then dare to expect it from our children. Otherwise we are not fathers but enemies to our children, and they are not our children but our enemies, and we ourselves have made them so. ‘What measure ye mete it shall be measured unto you again’—I am not the one saying this; it is the precept of the Gospel: measure out to others what they measure out to you. How can we blame children if they measure us by our own measure?

“Not long ago, in Finland, a servant girl was suspected of having secretly given birth to a child. She was kept under watch, and in the corner of the loft, behind some bricks, they found a box that nobody had known about. They opened it, and inside lay the body of a newborn baby, which she had killed. In the same box were the skeletons of two more babies. By her own confession she had killed them as soon as they were born.

“Gentlemen of the jury, was she a mother to her children? She bore them, true. But was she a mother to them? Would anyone dare to give her the sacred name of mother? Let us be bold, gentlemen. Let us even be audacious. At this moment it is our duty, and we must not be afraid of certain words and ideas, as the Moscow women in Ostrovsky’s play are, who take fright at the sound of certain words. No, let us show that the progress of recent years has reached even us, and let us say it plainly: a father is not merely the man who begets the child, but the man who begets it and does his duty by it.

“Oh, of course, there is another meaning, another reading of the word ‘father,’ which insists that any father, even a monster, even an enemy of his children, remains my father simply because he begot me. But this is, so to say, the mystical meaning. My intellect cannot grasp it. I can only accept it by faith, or better, _on faith_, as I accept many other things that I do not understand but which religion tells me to believe. In that case, let it stay outside the sphere of actual life. That sphere has its own rights, but it also lays great duties and obligations on us. In that sphere, if we want to be humane—Christian, in fact—we must, or ought to, act only on convictions that reason and experience can justify, convictions that have been through the crucible of analysis. In a word, we must act rationally, not as if in a dream or a delirium, so that we do no harm and do not mistreat and ruin a man. Then it will be real Christian work, not only mystical but rational and philanthropic....”

At this passage violent applause broke out in many parts of the court. Fetyukovitch waved his hands as though begging them to let him finish without interruption. At once the court fell silent, and the orator went on.

“Do you imagine, gentlemen, that our children, as they grow up and start to reason, can avoid such questions? No, they cannot, and we will not put an impossible restriction on them. The sight of an unworthy father stirs tormenting questions in a young mind, whether he wants them or not, especially when he compares that father with the excellent fathers of his friends. The conventional answer is: ‘He begot you, you are his flesh and blood, and so you are bound to love him.’ The young man cannot help thinking: ‘But did he love me when he begot me?’ He wonders more and more. ‘Did he beget me for my sake? At that moment, the moment of passion, perhaps inflamed by wine, he did not know me, not even whether I was a boy or a girl. All he has passed on to me is a tendency to drink. That is all he has done for me.... Why am I bound to love him just for begetting me, when he has cared nothing for me for the rest of my life?’

“Oh, perhaps these questions strike you as coarse and cruel. But do not expect a young mind to show impossible restraint. ‘Drive nature out of the door and it will fly in at the window.’ Above all, let us not be afraid of words. Let us settle the question by the dictates of reason and humanity, not by mystic ideas. How shall it be settled? Why, in this way. Let the son stand before his father and ask, ‘Father, tell me, why must I love you? Father, show me that I must love you.’ If that father is able to answer and give him good reason, then we have a real and normal relation between parent and child. It rests not on mystical prejudice but on a rational, responsible and strictly humanitarian foundation. But if the father cannot, the family tie is at an end. He is no father to that son, and the son has the right to regard him as a stranger, even as an enemy. Gentlemen of the jury, our tribune ought to be a school of true and sound ideas.”

(At this point the orator was cut off by irrepressible, almost frantic applause. It was not the whole audience, of course, but a good half of it. The fathers and mothers present applauded. Shrieks and cries rose from the gallery, where the ladies sat. Handkerchiefs were waving. The President rang his bell with all his might. He was plainly irritated by the audience’s conduct, yet he did not dare to clear the court, as he had threatened to do. Even persons of high standing, old men with stars on their breasts, seated in the places reserved behind the judges, applauded the orator and waved their handkerchiefs. So when the noise died down, the President did no more than repeat his stern threat to clear the court. Fetyukovitch, excited and triumphant, continued his speech.)

“Gentlemen of the jury, you remember that dreadful night, of which so much has been said today, when the son climbed over the fence and stood face to face with the enemy and persecutor who had begotten him. I insist, most emphatically, that he did not run to his father’s house for money. The charge of robbery is absurd, as I showed earlier. Nor did he force his way into the house to murder him, oh, no! Had that been his plan, he would at least have thought to arm himself beforehand. The brass pestle he seized by instinct, without knowing why he did it. Suppose he did deceive his father by tapping at the window, suppose he did get in—I have already said that I do not believe that story for a moment, but let it be so, let us assume it for the moment. Gentlemen, I swear to you by all that is holy: had it been an ordinary enemy and not his father, he would have run through the rooms, made sure the woman was not there, and bolted in great haste, without harming his rival. He might have struck him, or pushed him aside, nothing more, for he had no thought and no time to spare for that. What he wanted to know was where she was. But his father, his father! Just the sight of the father who had hated him since childhood, who had been his enemy and persecutor and was now his unnatural rival, was enough! A feeling of hatred seized him, against his will, irresistibly, and clouded his reason. It all rose up in a single moment! It was an impulse of madness and insanity. But it was also an impulse of nature, avenging, irresistibly and unconsciously (like everything in nature), the violation of its eternal laws.

“Even then, however, the prisoner did not murder him. I maintain that, I cry it out loud! No, he only brandished the pestle in a burst of indignant disgust. He did not mean to kill him and did not know that he would kill him. Had he not held that fatal pestle in his hand, he might only have knocked his father down, and not killed him. As he ran away, he did not know whether he had killed the old man. Such a murder is no murder. Such a murder is no parricide. No, the killing of such a father cannot be called parricide. Only prejudice can count such a murder as parricide.

“But I appeal to you again and again, from the depths of my soul: did this murder really take place? Gentlemen of the jury, if we convict and punish him, he will tell himself: ‘These people did nothing for my upbringing, nothing for my education, nothing to better my lot, nothing to make me a good man, nothing to make me a man at all. These people never gave me food or drink, never visited me in prison or in my nakedness, and now they have sent me to penal servitude. We are quits. I owe them nothing now, and I owe no one anything for ever. They are wicked, and I will be wicked. They are cruel, and I will be cruel.’ That is what he will say, gentlemen of the jury. And I swear to you, by finding him guilty you will only make things easier for him. You will set his conscience at ease. He will curse the blood he has shed, and he will not regret it. At the same time you will destroy in him any chance of becoming a new man, for he will stay in his wickedness and blindness all his life.

“But do you want to punish him fearfully, terribly, with the most awful punishment imaginable, and at the same time to save him and give his soul new birth? If so, overwhelm him with your mercy! You will see, you will hear, how he trembles and is struck with horror. ‘How can I bear this mercy? How can I bear so much love? Am I worthy of it?’ That is what he will cry out.

“Oh, I know, I know that heart, gentlemen of the jury, that wild but grateful heart! It will bow down before your mercy. It thirsts for a great and loving act. It will melt and rise up. There are souls that, in their narrowness, blame the whole world. But overcome such a soul with mercy, show it love, and it will curse its past, because there are many good impulses in it. Such a heart will open wide and see that God is merciful and that men are good and just. He will be struck with horror. He will be crushed by remorse and by the vast debt that now lies on him. And then he will not say, ‘We are quits.’ He will say, ‘I am guilty before all men, and more unworthy than any of them.’ In tears of penitence and sharp, tender anguish he will cry: ‘Others are better than I. They wanted to save me, not to destroy me!’ Oh, this act of mercy is so easy for you. Without anything like real evidence, it would be too awful for you to pronounce the words: ‘Yes, he is guilty.’

“Better to acquit ten guilty men than to punish one innocent man! Do you hear, do you hear that majestic voice from the last century of our glorious history? It is not for an insignificant person like me to remind you that the Russian court exists not only to punish but also to save the criminal! Let other nations think of retribution and the letter of the law. We will cling to the spirit and the meaning: the salvation and reformation of the lost. If that is true, if Russia and her justice are such, she can go forward with good cheer! Do not try to frighten us with your frenzied troikas, from which all the nations turn aside in disgust. Not a runaway troika, but the stately chariot of Russia will move calmly and majestically toward its goal. The fate of my client is in your hands. The fate of Russian justice is in your hands. You will defend it, you will save it, you will prove that there are men to watch over it, that it is in good hands!”

chapters.title: XIV. The Peasants Stand Firm
paragraphs: That was how Fetyukovitch finished, and the audience’s enthusiasm broke out like a storm nobody could hold back. Stopping it was out of the question. The women wept, and so did many of the men. Even two important personages had tears on their faces. The President gave way and did not even ring his bell for a while. To put down such enthusiasm, as the ladies cried afterwards, would have been to put down something sacred. The speaker himself was genuinely touched.

And it was just then that Ippolit Kirillovitch got to his feet to raise some objections. People stared at him with hatred. “What? What does this mean? He actually has the nerve to object!” the ladies babbled. But if every lady in the world, his own wife among them, had protested, nothing could have held him back at that moment. He was pale and trembling with emotion. His first phrases were not even understandable. He gasped for breath, could hardly speak plainly and lost his thread. Soon, though, he pulled himself together. Of this second speech I will quote only a few sentences.

“... I am accused of having spun a romance. But what is this defense if not one romance heaped on another? The only thing missing was poetry. Fyodor Pavlovitch, as he waits for his mistress, rips open the envelope and flings it on the floor. We are even told what he said as he did this odd thing. Is that not a flight of fancy? And what proof do we have that he had taken the money out? Who heard what he said? The feeble-minded idiot Smerdyakov, made over into a Byronic hero who takes revenge on society for his illegitimate birth—is that not a romance in the Byronic style? And the son who bursts into his father’s house and murders him without murdering him is not even a romance. He is a sphinx that sets us a riddle he cannot solve himself. If he murdered him, he murdered him. What is the meaning of murdering him without having murdered him? Who can make head or tail of that?

“Next we are lectured that our tribune is a tribune of true and sound ideas, and from this tribune of ‘sound ideas’ a solemn declaration is made that calling the murder of a father ‘parricide’ is nothing but a prejudice! But if parricide is a prejudice, and if every child is to ask his father why he should love him, what will become of us? What will become of the foundations of society? What will become of the family? Parricide, it seems, is only a bogy for Moscow merchants’ wives. The most precious and most sacred guarantees for the destiny and future of Russian justice are laid before us in a twisted and frivolous form, all to reach a single aim—to justify something that cannot be justified. ‘Oh, crush him with mercy,’ cries the counsel for the defense. But mercy is all the criminal wants, and tomorrow we will see how crushed he is. And is the counsel for the defense not too modest in asking only that the prisoner be acquitted? Why not found a charity in honor of the parricide, to keep his exploit in memory for generations to come? Religion and the Gospel are corrected—all that is mysticism, we are told, and ours is the only true Christianity, the one that has been put to the test of reason and common sense. And so a false image of Christ is set up before us! ‘With what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again,’ cried the counsel for the defense, and he instantly concludes that Christ teaches us to measure as it is measured to us—and this from the tribune of truth and sound sense! We look into the Gospel only on the eve of making speeches, to dazzle the audience with our acquaintance with a book that is, at any rate, a rather original composition, and may be useful for creating a certain effect—all to serve our purpose! But what Christ commands us is something very different. He bids us beware of doing this, because the wicked world does it. We ought to forgive and to turn the other cheek, and not to measure out to our persecutors what they measure out to us. This is what our God has taught us. He did not teach us that forbidding children to murder their fathers is a prejudice. And we will not, from the tribune of truth and good sense, correct the Gospel of our Lord, Whom the counsel for the defense condescends to call only ‘the crucified lover of humanity,’ in defiance of all orthodox Russia, which cries out to Him, ‘For You are our God!’”

At this the President broke in and reined in the over-eager speaker. He begged him not to exaggerate, not to go beyond the proper limits, and so on, the way presidents always do in such cases. The audience was uneasy too. The public was restless, and there were even shouts of indignation. Fetyukovitch did not so much as reply. He only stepped up to the tribune, laid his hand on his heart and, in an offended voice, spoke a few dignified words. Once more he touched lightly and ironically on “romancing” and “psychology,” and at a fitting moment he quoted, “Jupiter, you are angry, therefore you are wrong.” This drew a burst of approving laughter from the audience, since Ippolit Kirillovitch was nothing like Jupiter. Next, _à propos_ of the charge that he was teaching the young generation to murder their fathers, Fetyukovitch declared with great dignity that he would not even reply. As for the prosecutor’s accusation of unorthodox opinions, Fetyukovitch hinted that this was a personal insinuation. He had expected, he said, to be safe in this court from charges “damaging to my reputation as a citizen and a loyal subject.” At those words the President stopped him as well, and Fetyukovitch ended with a bow, to a murmur of approval through the courtroom. And Ippolit Kirillovitch was, in the view of our ladies, “crushed for good.”

After that, the prisoner was given leave to speak. Mitya rose, but he said very little. He was dreadfully worn out, in body and in spirit. The strong, independent look he had worn on coming in that morning was almost gone. He seemed to have lived through something that day which had taught him, for the rest of his life, a very important lesson he had never grasped before. His voice was feeble, and he no longer shouted. His words carried a new note of humility, defeat and surrender.

“What can I say, gentlemen of the jury? The hour of judgment has come for me. I feel God’s hand on me! This is the end of a man who has gone astray! But I tell you again, before God, I am innocent of my father’s blood! For the last time I say it: I did not kill him! I went astray, but I loved what is good. Every moment I tried to reform, and yet I lived like a wild beast. I thank the prosecutor. He told me a great deal about myself that I didn’t know. But it’s not true that I killed my father. The prosecutor is mistaken. I thank my counsel too. I cried while I listened to him. But it’s not true that I killed my father, and he needn’t have supposed it. And don’t believe the doctors. I am perfectly sane; it’s only that my heart is heavy. If you spare me, if you let me go, I will pray for you. I will be a better man. I give you my word before God, I will! And if you condemn me, I’ll break my sword over my own head myself and kiss the pieces. But spare me, don’t rob me of my God! I know myself, I will rebel! My heart is heavy, gentlemen ... spare me!”
He nearly dropped back into his seat. His voice cracked, and he could barely get out the last words. Then the judges moved on to the questions and began asking both sides to state their conclusions.

But I will not go into the details. At last the jury got up to withdraw and deliberate. The President was very tired, so his final instructions to the jury were rather weak. “Be impartial. Do not let the eloquence of the defense sway you, but weigh the arguments nonetheless. Remember that a heavy responsibility rests on you,” and so on and so forth.

The jury went out and the court adjourned. People could stand up, walk about, trade the impressions they had stored up, and get refreshments at the buffet. It was very late, nearly one in the morning, but nobody left. The tension was so great that nobody could think of rest. Everyone waited with a sinking heart—though perhaps that goes too far, since the ladies were merely hysterically impatient, and their hearts were quite calm. An acquittal, they felt, was bound to come. They were all preparing for a dramatic moment of general rejoicing. I must admit that many of the men, too, were sure of an acquittal. Some were glad, some frowned, and some were simply downcast because they did not want him acquitted. Fetyukovitch himself was sure of his triumph. People crowded around him, congratulating him and flattering him.

“There are,” he told one group, as I heard later, “there are invisible threads that tie the counsel for the defense to the jury. During a speech one can feel them forming. I felt them. They exist. Our case is won. You can put your minds at ease.”
“What will our peasants say to all this?” asked a stout, sour-looking, pock-marked gentleman, a local landowner, as he walked up to a group of gentlemen talking together.
“But they’re not all peasants. There are four government clerks among them.”
“Yes, there are clerks,” said a member of the district council, joining the group.
“And do you know that Nazaryev, the merchant with the medal, is a juryman?”
“What about him?”
“He’s a man with brains.”
“But he never speaks.”
“He’s no great talker, but that’s all the better. The man from Petersburg has nothing to teach him. He could teach the whole of Petersburg himself. He’s the father of twelve children. Think of that!”
“Surely you don’t imagine they won’t acquit him?” one of our young officials exclaimed in another group.
“They’ll acquit him for certain,” said a firm voice.

“It would be shameful, disgraceful, not to acquit him!” cried the official. “Say he did murder him—there are fathers and fathers! Besides, he was in such a frenzy.... He may really have done nothing more than swing the pestle through the air and knock the old man down. But it was a pity they dragged the valet in. That was just an absurd theory! If I’d been in Fetyukovitch’s place, I would have said it straight out: ‘He murdered him, but he isn’t guilty, hang it all!’”
“That’s just what he did, only without the ‘Hang it all!’”
“No, Mihail Semyonovitch, he very nearly said that, too,” put in a third voice.
“Why, gentlemen, in our town during Lent they acquitted an actress who had cut the throat of her lover’s lawful wife.”
“Oh, but she didn’t finish cutting it.”
“That makes no difference. She started cutting it.”
“What did you make of what he said about children? Splendid, wasn’t it?”
“Splendid!”
“And about mysticism, too!”
“Oh, enough about mysticism!” cried someone else. “Think of Ippolit and what lies ahead of him from today. His wife will scratch his eyes out tomorrow, for Mitya’s sake.”
“Is she here?”
“Whatever for? If she’d been here, she’d have scratched them out in court. She’s at home with a toothache. He he he!”
“He he he!”
In a third group:
“They’ll acquit Mitenka in the end, I expect.”
“I wouldn’t be surprised if he turns the ‘Metropolis’ upside down tomorrow. He’ll be drinking for ten days!”
“Oh, the devil!”
“The devil’s bound to have a hand in it. Where else would he be, if not here?”
“Well, gentlemen, I admit it was eloquent. But still, it’s not the thing to break your father’s head with a pestle! Or what are we coming to?”
“The chariot! Do you remember the chariot?”
“Yes, he turned a cart into a chariot!”
“And tomorrow he’ll turn a chariot into a cart, whichever suits him.”
“What cunning fellows there are these days! Is there any justice to be had in Russia?”

But then the bell rang. The jury had been out for exactly an hour, not a minute more or less. A deep silence fell over the court as soon as the public had sat down again. I remember the jurymen filing in. At last! I won’t give the questions in order; I have in fact forgotten them. I remember only the answer to the President’s first and main question: “Did the prisoner commit the murder for the sake of robbery and with premeditation?” (I don’t remember the exact words.) There was total quiet. The foreman of the jury, the youngest of the clerks, announced in a clear, loud voice, in the deathlike stillness of the court:
“Yes, guilty!”

And the same answer came back to every question: “Yes, guilty!” with not the slightest word softening it. Nobody had expected this. Almost everyone had counted on at least a recommendation to mercy. The deathlike silence in the court held—everyone seemed turned to stone, those who wanted him convicted as much as those who had longed for his acquittal. But that was only for the first instant, and then a terrible uproar broke out. Many of the men in the audience were pleased. Some rubbed their hands and made no attempt to hide their delight. Those who disagreed with the verdict looked crushed. They shrugged, they whispered, but they still seemed unable to take it in. But how am I to describe the state the ladies were in? I thought they would start a riot. At first they could hardly believe their ears. Then all at once the whole court rang with cries: “What does this mean? What next?” They jumped up from their seats. They seemed to imagine it might be reviewed and overturned on the spot. At that moment Mitya suddenly stood up and cried out in a heartbreaking voice, stretching out his hands in front of him:
“I swear by God and the dreadful Day of Judgment, I am not guilty of my father’s blood! Katya, I forgive you! Brothers, friends, take pity on the other woman!”

He could not go on. He burst into a terrible sobbing wail that was heard all over the court, in a strange, unnatural voice that was not his own. From the farthest corner at the back of the gallery came a piercing shriek—it was Grushenka. She had managed to beg her way into the court again before the lawyers began their speeches. Mitya was led away. The sentence was put off until the next day. The whole court was in an uproar, but I did not stay to hear it. I remember only a few remarks I caught on the steps as I went out.
“He’ll get a twenty-year trip to the mines!”
“Not less.”
“Well, our peasants stood firm.”
“And finished off our Mitya.”

chapters.title: I. Plans For Mitya’s Escape
paragraphs: Five days after the trial, very early, at nine in the morning, Alyosha went to see Katerina Ivanovna. He had a matter of great importance to both of them to discuss, and a message to deliver. She received him in the same room where she had once received Grushenka. In the next room Ivan Fyodorovitch lay unconscious, burning with fever. Right after the scene at the trial, Katerina Ivanovna had had the sick, unconscious man carried to her house. She knew the gossip and the general disapproval were bound to follow, and she took no notice. Two relatives lived with her. One had left for Moscow right after the scene in court; the other had stayed. But if both had gone, she would not have changed her mind. She would still have nursed him and sat by him day and night. Varvinsky and Herzenstube were treating him. The famous doctor had gone back to Moscow and had refused to say how the illness would end. The doctors tried to encourage Katerina Ivanovna and Alyosha, but it was clear they could not yet promise any real hope of recovery.

Alyosha visited his sick brother twice a day. This time, though, he had particularly urgent business. He could see how hard it would be to bring up, and yet he had no time to waste. He had another appointment that same morning that could not be put off, so he had to hurry.
They had been talking for a quarter of an hour. Katerina Ivanovna was pale and worn out, and at the same time in a state of hysterical excitement. She already suspected why Alyosha had come.

“Don’t worry about what he decides,” she told Alyosha, with firm emphasis. “One way or another, he will have to come to it. He must escape. That unhappy man, that hero of honor and principle—I don’t mean him, not Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but the man lying on the other side of that door, who gave himself up for his brother,” Katya added, her eyes flashing, “told me the whole plan of escape long ago. You know he has already begun negotiating.... I’ve told you some of it already.... You see, it will probably happen at the third _étape_ from here, while the prisoners are being marched to Siberia. Oh, that is a long way off yet. Ivan Fyodorovitch has already called on the superintendent of the third _étape_. But we don’t know yet who will command the party, and it’s impossible to find that out so far ahead. Tomorrow, perhaps, I’ll show you the whole plan in detail. Ivan Fyodorovitch left it with me on the eve of the trial, in case it was needed.... That was when—do you remember?—you found us quarreling. He had just gone down the stairs, but I saw you and made him come back. Do you remember? Do you know what we were quarreling about?”
“No, I don’t,” said Alyosha.

“Of course he didn’t tell you. It was that plan of escape. He had explained the main idea to me three days earlier, and we started quarreling over it at once, and we went on for three days. We quarreled because he said that if Dmitri Fyodorovitch were convicted, he would get him abroad together with that creature. I was furious at once. I can’t tell you why, I don’t know myself why.... Oh, of course I was furious about that creature, and that she should go abroad with Dmitri, too!” Katerina Ivanovna exclaimed suddenly, her lips quivering with anger. “The moment Ivan Fyodorovitch saw I was furious about that woman, he decided I was jealous of Dmitri and still loved him. That is how our first quarrel started. I wouldn’t explain, and I couldn’t ask his forgiveness. I couldn’t bear that such a man could suspect me of still loving that ... when I had told him myself, long before, that I did not love Dmitri, that I loved no one but him! It was only my resentment of that creature that made me angry with him. Three days later, on the evening you came, he handed me a sealed envelope, which I was to open at once if anything happened to him. Oh, he saw his illness coming! He said the envelope held the details of the escape, and if he died or fell dangerously ill, I was to save Mitya, and only Mitya. Then he left me money, nearly ten thousand. Those are the banknotes the prosecutor mentioned in his speech, when he had heard from someone that Ivan had sent them to be changed. It struck me tremendously that Ivan Fyodorovitch had not given up on saving his brother, and that he trusted me with the plan of escape, even though he was still jealous of me and still sure I loved Mitya. Oh, that was a sacrifice! No, you can’t understand how great such self-sacrifice is, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I wanted to fall at his feet in reverence. But then it came to me that he would take it only as joy at the thought of Mitya being saved (and he certainly would have thought so!). The mere possibility of such an unjust thought in his head made me so angry that I lost my temper again. Instead of kissing his feet, I flew into a rage again! Oh, I am unhappy! It’s my character, my awful, unhappy character! Oh, you’ll see, I will end by driving him away, too, for another woman he can get on with better, as Dmitri did. But ... no, I couldn’t bear it, I would kill myself. And when you came in then, and I called out to you and told him to come back, the look of contempt and hatred he gave me enraged me so much that—do you remember?—I cried out to you that it was he, he alone, who had convinced me his brother Dmitri was a murderer! I said that spiteful thing on purpose, to hurt him again. He had never, never convinced me that his brother was a murderer. On the contrary, it was I who convinced him! Oh, my vile temper caused everything! I paved the way for that hideous scene at the trial. He wanted to prove to me that he was an honorable man, and that even if I loved his brother, he would not destroy him out of revenge or jealousy. So he came to the court ... I am the cause of it all, I alone am to blame!”

Katya had never made such confessions to Alyosha before. He felt she had reached the point of unbearable suffering where even the proudest heart painfully crushes its own pride and collapses, beaten by grief. Oh, Alyosha knew of another terrible cause of her misery. She had been careful to hide it from him in the days since the trial. For some reason it would have hurt him too much to see her brought so low that she spoke of it now. She was suffering over her “treachery” at the trial. Alyosha felt that her conscience was driving her to confess it to him, to him, Alyosha, with tears and screams and hysterical writhing on the floor. He dreaded that moment and longed to spare her. It made his errand harder still. He spoke of Mitya again.

“It’s all right, it’s all right, don’t be anxious about him!” she started again, sharp and stubborn. “All of that is only for the moment. I know him, I know his heart only too well. You can be certain he will agree to escape. It won’t be right away, after all. He will have time to get used to the idea. Ivan Fyodorovitch will be well by then, and he’ll arrange it all himself, so I’ll have nothing to do with it. Don’t be anxious. He will agree to run away. He has agreed already. Do you think he would give up that creature? And they won’t let her visit him, so he has to escape. It’s you he’s most afraid of. He’s afraid you won’t approve of his escaping, on moral grounds. But you must generously _allow_ it, if your blessing matters so much,” Katya added spitefully. She paused and smiled.

“He talks about some hymn,” she went on, “some cross he has to carry, some duty. I remember Ivan Fyodorovitch told me a great deal about it, and if you knew how he talked!” Katya cried suddenly, with a feeling she could not hold back. “If you knew how much he loved that wretched man when he told me, and how much he hated him, perhaps, in that same moment. And I listened to his story and his tears with a sneer of contempt. Brute! Yes, I am a brute. His fever is my fault. But that man in prison can’t suffer,” Katya finished irritably. “Can a man like that suffer? Men like him never suffer!”

Her words carried hatred and a contemptuous revulsion. And yet she was the one who had betrayed him. “Perhaps she hates him at moments because she knows how she has wronged him,” Alyosha thought to himself. He hoped it was only “at moments.” In Katya’s last words he heard a challenge, but he did not take it up.

“I sent for you this morning so that you would promise to persuade him yourself. Or do you, too, think that escaping would be dishonorable, cowardly, or ... unchristian, maybe?” Katya added, still more defiantly.

“Oh, no. I’ll tell him everything,” Alyosha muttered. “He asks you to come and see him today,” he blurted out suddenly, looking her straight in the face. She started and moved back a little from him on the sofa.
“Me? Is that possible?” she faltered, turning pale.
