“It can be, and it ought to be!” Alyosha began forcefully, growing more animated. “He needs you very much just now. I wouldn’t have brought it up and upset you if it weren’t necessary. He is ill, he is beside himself, and he keeps asking for you. He doesn’t want you so that he can make peace with you. He only wants you to come and show yourself at his door. So much has happened to him since that day. He understands that he has wronged you beyond measure. He doesn’t ask your forgiveness—‘It’s impossible to forgive me,’ he says himself—he only asks that you appear in his doorway.”
“It’s so sudden....” Katya faltered. “All these days I’ve had a feeling you would come with this message. I knew he would ask me to come. It’s impossible!”

“Then let it be impossible, but do it. Think of it: for the first time he understands how he has hurt you, the first time in his whole life. He never grasped it so fully before. He said, ‘If she refuses to come, I will be unhappy for the rest of my life.’ Do you hear? He has been sentenced to twenty years of penal servitude, and he is still planning to be happy. Isn’t that pitiful? Think, and you must go to him. He is ruined, but he is innocent,” Alyosha said, and it broke from him like a challenge. “His hands are clean, there is no blood on them! For the sake of the endless suffering waiting for him, go to him now. Go and see him off on his way into the darkness—just stand at his door, that is all.... You ought to do it, you ought to!” Alyosha ended, putting enormous stress on the word “ought.”
“I ought to ... but I cannot....” Katya moaned. “He will look at me.... I can’t.”
“Your eyes ought to meet. How will you live the rest of your life, if you don’t make up your mind to do it now?”
“Better to suffer all my life.”
“You ought to go, you ought to go,” Alyosha said again, with merciless emphasis.
“But why today, why right now?... I can’t leave our patient—”
“You can, for a moment. It will be only a moment. If you don’t come, he will be raving by tonight. I wouldn’t lie to you. Have pity on him!”
“Have pity on _me!_” Katya said, bitterly reproachful, and she burst into tears.
“So you will come,” Alyosha said firmly, seeing her tears. “I’ll go and tell him you’re coming right away.”
“No, don’t tell him that, not for anything,” Katya cried in alarm. “I will come, but don’t tell him beforehand. Maybe I will go, and not go in.... I don’t know yet—”
Her voice failed her. She gasped for breath. Alyosha stood up to leave.
“And what if I meet someone?” she said suddenly, in a low voice, turning white again.
“That is exactly why you must go now, so you won’t meet anyone. There will be nobody there, I can tell you that for certain. We will be expecting you,” he concluded firmly, and left the room.

chapters.title: II. For A Moment The Lie Becomes Truth
paragraphs: He hurried to the hospital where Mitya was now lying. The day after his fate was decided, Mitya had come down with a nervous fever and been sent to the prison ward of the town hospital. But several people (Alyosha, Madame Hohlakov, Lise and others) had asked Doctor Varvinsky to help, and he had put Mitya in a separate little room instead of with the other prisoners. It was the room where Smerdyakov had lain. There was a sentry at the far end of the corridor and a grating over the window, so Varvinsky could feel easy about the favor he had shown, which was not strictly legal. But he was a kind-hearted, sympathetic young man. He knew how hard it would be for a man like Mitya to be thrown all at once among robbers and murderers, and that he had to get used to it by degrees. The doctor and the overseer, and even the police captain, allowed relatives and friends to visit without any formal permission. But only Alyosha and Grushenka had come to see Mitya. Rakitin had twice tried to force his way in, but Mitya kept begging Varvinsky not to let him in.

Alyosha found him sitting on his bed in a hospital dressing gown, somewhat feverish, with a towel soaked in vinegar and water on his head. When Alyosha came in, Mitya looked at him with a vague expression, but there was something like a shade of dread in it. Since the trial he had become terribly preoccupied. Sometimes he would be silent for half an hour at a time, seeming to ponder something heavily and painfully, oblivious of everything around him. When he roused himself from his brooding and started to talk, he always spoke abruptly and never about what he really wanted to say. Sometimes he looked at his brother with a suffering face. He seemed more at ease with Grushenka than with Alyosha. True, he hardly spoke to her at all, but the moment she came in, his whole face lit up with joy.

Alyosha sat down beside him on the bed without a word. This time Mitya was waiting for Alyosha in suspense, but he did not dare to ask him anything. He found it almost unthinkable that Katya would agree to come, and yet he felt that if she did not come, something inconceivable would happen. Alyosha understood how he felt.

“Trifon Borissovitch,” Mitya began nervously, “has pulled his whole inn to pieces, I’m told. He’s torn up the flooring, taken the planks apart, split up the whole gallery, so I hear. He’s hunting for treasure all the time—the fifteen hundred roubles the prosecutor said I’d hidden there. They say he started these tricks the minute he got home. Serves him right, the swindler! The guard here told me yesterday; he comes from there.”
“Listen,” Alyosha began. “She will come, but I don’t know when. Maybe today, maybe in a few days, I can’t say. But she will come, she will, that’s certain.”

Mitya started and was about to say something, but stayed silent. The news had a tremendous effect on him. Clearly he badly wanted to know what had been said, but again he was afraid to ask. Anything cruel or contemptuous from Katya would have cut him like a knife at that moment.
“Among other things she said this: I must be sure to set your conscience at rest about escaping. If Ivan isn’t well by then, she will see to everything herself.”
“You’ve told me that already,” Mitya remarked musingly.
“And you repeated it to Grusha,” said Alyosha.

“Yes,” Mitya admitted. “She won’t come this morning.” He looked timidly at his brother. “She won’t come till evening. When I told her yesterday that Katya was taking steps, she said nothing, but she set her mouth. She only whispered, ‘Let her!’ She understood it was important. I didn’t dare press her further. I think she understands now that Katya doesn’t care for me anymore, but loves Ivan.”
“Does she?” broke from Alyosha.

“Maybe she doesn’t. It’s just that she’s not coming this morning,” Mitya hurried to explain again. “I asked her to do something for me. You know, Ivan is better than all of us. He ought to live, not us. He will recover.”
“Would you believe it, though Katya is alarmed about him, she hardly doubts he’ll recover,” said Alyosha.
“That means she’s convinced he will die. It’s because she’s frightened that she’s so sure he’ll get well.”
“Ivan has a strong constitution, and I, too, believe there’s every hope he’ll get well,” Alyosha said anxiously.
“Yes, he’ll get well. But she’s convinced he’ll die. She has a great deal of sorrow to bear...” A silence followed. A deep anxiety was gnawing at Mitya.
“Alyosha, I love Grusha terribly,” he said suddenly, in a shaking voice full of tears.
“They won’t let her go out there to you,” Alyosha put in at once.

“And there’s something else I wanted to tell you,” Mitya went on, his voice suddenly ringing. “If they beat me on the way or out there, I won’t put up with it. I’ll kill someone and be shot for it. And this will go on for twenty years! They talk to me rudely even now. I’ve been lying here all night, judging myself. I’m not ready! I can’t resign myself. I wanted to sing a ‘hymn’; but if a guard speaks rudely to me, I haven’t the strength to bear it. For Grusha I’d bear anything ... anything except blows.... But she won’t be allowed to come there.”
Alyosha smiled gently.

“Listen, brother, once and for all,” he said. “This is what I think about it. And you know I wouldn’t lie to you. Listen: you’re not ready, and such a cross is not for you. What’s more, you don’t need a martyr’s cross when you’re not ready for it. If you had murdered our father, it would grieve me to see you reject your punishment. But you’re innocent, and such a cross is too much for you. You wanted to make yourself a different man through suffering. I say only this: remember that other man always, all your life and wherever you go, and that will be enough for you. By refusing that great cross, you’ll only feel an even greater duty all your life, and that constant feeling may do more to make you a new man than going there would. Because there you wouldn’t endure it. You’d complain, and maybe in the end you’d say, ‘I’m quits.’ The lawyer was right about that. Such heavy burdens are not for everyone. For some they’re impossible. Those are my thoughts, since you want them so much. If other men had to answer for your escape, officers or soldiers, then I wouldn’t have ‘allowed’ you,” Alyosha smiled. “But they say—the superintendent of that _étape_ told Ivan himself—that if it’s well handled there won’t be any serious inquiry, and they can get off easily. Of course, bribery is dishonest even in such a case, but I can’t take it on myself to judge, because if Ivan and Katya asked me to act for you, I know I’d go and give bribes. I have to tell you the truth. So I can’t judge what you do. But let me assure you that I will never condemn you. And it would be strange if I could judge you in this. Now I think I’ve said everything.”

“But I do condemn myself!” cried Mitya. “I’ll escape, that was settled without you; could Mitya Karamazov do anything but run away? But I’ll condemn myself, and I’ll pray for my sin forever. That’s how the Jesuits talk, isn’t it? Just like us?”
“Yes.” Alyosha smiled gently.

“I love you for always telling the whole truth and never hiding anything,” cried Mitya with a joyful laugh. “So I’ve caught my Alyosha being Jesuitical. I have to kiss you for that. Now listen to the rest; I’ll open the other side of my heart to you. This is what I planned and decided. If I run away, even with money and a passport, even to America, it will cheer me to think I’m not running away for pleasure or happiness, but into another exile, as bad as Siberia, maybe. It is as bad, Alyosha, it is! I hate that America already, damn it. Even though Grusha will be with me. Just look at her; is she an American? She’s Russian, Russian to the marrow of her bones. She’ll be homesick for the mother country, and I’ll see every hour that she’s suffering for my sake, that she’s taken up that cross for me. And what harm has she done? And how will I put up with the rabble out there, though every one of them may be better than I am? I hate that America already! They may all be wonderful at machinery, damn them, but they’re not of my soul. I love Russia, Alyosha, I love the Russian God, though I’m a scoundrel myself. I’ll choke there!” he exclaimed, his eyes suddenly flashing. His voice shook with tears. “So this is what I’ve decided, Alyosha, listen,” he began again, mastering his emotion. “As soon as I get there with Grusha, we’ll set to work on the land at once, in solitude, somewhere very remote, with wild bears. There must be remote places even there. I’m told there are still Redskins there, somewhere on the edge of the horizon. So off to the country of the _Last of the Mohicans_, and there we’ll tackle the grammar right away, Grusha and I. Work and grammar—that’s how we’ll spend three years. And by then we’ll speak English like any Englishman. And as soon as we’ve learned it—good-bye to America! We’ll run back here to Russia as American citizens. Don’t worry—we wouldn’t come to this little town. We’d hide somewhere far off, in the north or the south. I’ll be changed by then, and so will she, in America. The doctors will make me some kind of wart on my face—what’s the use of their being so mechanical!—or else I’ll put out one eye, let my beard grow a yard long, and go gray, pining for Russia. I bet they won’t recognize us. And if they do, let them send us to Siberia. I don’t care. It will show it’s our fate. We’ll work on the land here, too, somewhere in the wilds, and I’ll pass as an American all my life. But we’ll die on our own soil. That’s my plan, and it won’t be changed. Do you approve?”
“Yes,” said Alyosha, not wanting to contradict him. Mitya paused a minute and then said suddenly:
“And the way they stirred it all up at the trial! Didn’t they just stir it up!”
“If they hadn’t, you’d have been convicted just the same,” said Alyosha with a sigh.
“Yes, the people here are sick of me! God bless them, but it’s hard to take,” Mitya moaned miserably. Again there was silence for a minute.
“Alyosha, don’t keep me in agony!” he suddenly exclaimed. “Tell me, is she coming now or not? Tell me! What did she say? How did she say it?”
“She said she would come, but I don’t know whether she’ll come today. It’s hard for her, you know,” Alyosha said, looking timidly at his brother.

“I should think it is hard for her! Alyosha, it’ll drive me out of my mind. Grusha keeps looking at me. She understands. My God, calm my heart: what is it I want? I want Katya! Do I even understand what I want? It’s that headstrong, evil Karamazov spirit! No, I’m not fit for suffering. I’m a scoundrel, that’s all anyone can say.”
“Here she is!” cried Alyosha.

At that moment Katya appeared in the doorway. For an instant she stood still, gazing at Mitya with a dazed look. He leapt to his feet on impulse, and a scared look came over his face. He turned pale, but at once a timid, pleading smile appeared on his lips, and with an irresistible impulse he held out both hands to Katya. Seeing this, she flew to him. She seized him by the hands and almost by force made him sit down on the bed. She sat down beside him and, still holding his hands, pressed them violently. Several times they both tried to speak but stopped short, and again they gazed at each other in silence, with a strange smile, their eyes fixed on one another. Two minutes passed like that.
“Have you forgiven me?” Mitya faltered at last, and at the same moment, turning to Alyosha, his face working with joy, he cried, “Do you hear what I’m asking? Do you hear?”

“That’s why I loved you, because you’re generous at heart!” broke from Katya. “My forgiveness is no good to you, nor yours to me; whether you forgive me or not, you’ll always be a sore spot in my heart, and I in yours—that’s how it must be....” She stopped to catch her breath. “Why have I come?” she began again in nervous haste. “To embrace your feet, to press your hands like this until it hurts—you remember how I used to squeeze them in Moscow—to tell you again that you are my god, my joy, to tell you that I love you madly,” she moaned in anguish, and suddenly pressed his hand greedily to her lips. Tears streamed from her eyes. Alyosha stood speechless and bewildered; he had never expected to see this.

“Love is over, Mitya!” Katya began again, “but the past is painfully dear to me. Know that it always will be. But now, for one minute, let what might have been come true,” she faltered with a drawn smile, looking joyfully into his face again. “You love another woman, and I love another man, and yet I will love you forever, and you will love me; do you know that? Do you hear? Love me, love me all your life!” she cried, with a quiver almost of menace in her voice.

“I will love you, and ... do you know, Katya,” Mitya began, drawing a deep breath at each word, “do you know, five days ago, that same evening, I loved you.... When you fell down and were carried out ... All my life! So it will be, it will always be so—”
So they murmured frantic words to one another, almost meaningless, perhaps not even true, but at that moment it was all true, and they both believed what they said completely.
“Katya,” Mitya cried suddenly, “do you believe I murdered him? I know you don’t believe it now, but then ... when you gave your evidence.... Surely, surely you didn’t believe it!”

“I didn’t believe it even then. I never believed it. I hated you, and for a moment I talked myself into it. While I was giving my evidence I persuaded myself and believed it, but as soon as I’d finished speaking I stopped believing it. Don’t doubt that! I’d forgotten that I came here to punish myself,” she said, with a new note in her voice, quite unlike the loving tones of a moment before.
“Woman, you carry a heavy burden,” came, as it were, involuntarily from Mitya.
“Let me go,” she whispered. “I’ll come again. I can’t bear any more now.”

She was getting up from her seat when she suddenly let out a loud scream and staggered back. Grushenka had walked into the room suddenly and silently. No one had expected her. Katya moved quickly to the door, but when she reached Grushenka she stopped abruptly, turned white as chalk, and moaned softly, almost in a whisper:
“Forgive me!”
Grushenka stared at her and, pausing for an instant, answered in a vindictive, venomous voice:
“We’re full of hatred, my girl, you and I! We’re both full of hatred! As if we could forgive each other! Save him, and I’ll worship you all my life.”
“You won’t forgive her!” cried Mitya, with frantic reproach.
“Don’t worry, I’ll save him for you!” Katya whispered rapidly, and she ran out of the room.
“She begged you to forgive her herself, and you could still refuse?” Mitya exclaimed bitterly once more.
“Mitya, don’t you dare blame her; you have no right to!” Alyosha cried hotly.
“It was her proud lips that spoke, not her heart,” Grushenka said in disgust. “If she saves you I’ll forgive her everything—”
She broke off, as though holding something back. She could not yet pull herself together. She had come in, as emerged afterwards, by chance, with no idea of what she would find.
“Alyosha, go after her!” Mitya cried to his brother. “Tell her ... I don’t know what ... just don’t let her leave like this!”

“I’ll come to you again at nightfall,” said Alyosha, and he ran after Katya. He caught up with her outside the hospital grounds. She was walking fast, but as soon as Alyosha reached her she said quickly:

“No, in front of that woman I can’t punish myself! I asked her forgiveness because I wanted to punish myself to the bitter end. She wouldn’t forgive me.... I like her for that!” she added in an unnatural voice, and her eyes flashed with fierce resentment.
“My brother didn’t expect this at all,” muttered Alyosha. “He was sure she wouldn’t come—”

“No doubt. Let’s leave that,” she snapped. “Listen: I can’t go to the funeral with you now. I’ve sent them flowers. I think they still have some money. If they need anything, tell them I’ll never abandon them.... Now go, please, leave me. You’re late already—the bells are ringing for the service.... Please, leave me!”

chapters.title: III. Ilusha’s Funeral. The Speech At The Stone
paragraphs: He really was late. The others had waited for him, then decided to take the little flower-covered coffin to the church without him. It was poor little Ilusha’s coffin. The boy had died two days after Mitya was sentenced. At the gate of the house, Alyosha was met by shouting from Ilusha’s schoolmates. They had all been waiting impatiently, and they were glad he had finally come. About twelve of them stood there, each with a school-bag or satchel slung over his shoulder. “Father will cry, be with father,” Ilusha had told them as he lay dying, and the boys had not forgotten it. Kolya Krassotkin was at the head of them.

“I’m so glad you’ve come, Karamazov!” he cried, holding out his hand to Alyosha. “It’s awful in there. It’s really horrible to watch. Snegiryov isn’t drunk—we know for a fact he’s had nothing to drink today—but he acts as if he were ... I am always manly, but this is awful. Karamazov, if I’m not keeping you, may I ask one question before you go in?”
“What is it, Kolya?” said Alyosha.
“Is your brother innocent or guilty? Did he kill your father, or was it the valet? Whatever you say, I’ll take as the truth. I haven’t slept for four nights, thinking about it.”
“The valet killed him. My brother is innocent,” answered Alyosha.
“That’s what I said,” cried Smurov.
“So he will perish, an innocent victim!” exclaimed Kolya. “He is ruined, but he is happy! I could envy him!”
“What do you mean? How can you say that? Why?” cried Alyosha, surprised.
“Oh, if only I, too, could sacrifice myself for the truth some day!” said Kolya with enthusiasm.
“But not in such a cause, not with such disgrace and such horror!” said Alyosha.
“Of course ... I would like to die for all humanity. And as for disgrace, I don’t care about that—our names may perish. I respect your brother!”
“And so do I!” cried the boy who had once announced that he knew who founded Troy. It came suddenly and unexpectedly, and he turned red to the ears like a peony, just as he had that other time.

Alyosha went into the room. In a blue coffin edged with a white frill, Ilusha lay with his eyes closed and his hands folded. The thin little face had barely changed, and oddly, the body gave off no smell of decay. His expression was serious and, as it were, thoughtful. His hands, crossed on his chest, looked especially beautiful, as if they had been carved in marble. Flowers lay in them, and flowers covered the coffin inside and out. Lise Hohlakov had sent those early that morning. Katerina Ivanovna had sent some too, and as Alyosha opened the door, the captain was holding a bunch in his shaking hands and strewing them once more over his dear boy. He hardly glanced at Alyosha as he came in. He would look at no one, not even at his crazy, weeping wife, “mamma,” who kept trying to rise on her crippled legs to see her dead boy more closely. The boys had pushed Nina’s chair up beside the coffin. She sat with her head resting against it, and no doubt she was quietly weeping as well. Snegiryov’s face was eager, yet bewildered and exasperated. His gestures were wild, and so were the words that broke out of him. “Old man, dear old man!” he kept saying, gazing at Ilusha. While the boy was alive, he had always called him “old man,” out of affection.

“Father, give me a flower, too. Take that white one out of his hand and give it to me,” the crazy mother begged, whimpering. Maybe the little white rose in Ilusha’s hand had taken her fancy, or maybe she wanted one from his own hand as a keepsake. She fidgeted, reaching out for the flower.
“I won’t give it to anyone, I won’t give you anything,” Snegiryov cried heartlessly. “They’re his flowers, not yours! Everything is his, nothing is yours!”
“Father, give mother a flower!” said Nina, lifting her tear-wet face.

“I won’t give away anything, and to her least of all! She didn’t love Ilusha. She took his little cannon, and he gave it to her,” the captain said, and he broke into loud sobs, remembering how Ilusha had given up his cannon to his mother. The poor, crazy creature wept without a sound, hiding her face in her hands.
The father clearly would not leave the coffin, and it was time to take it out. So the boys stood close around it and began to lift.
“I won’t have him buried in the churchyard,” Snegiryov suddenly wailed. “I’ll bury him by the stone, our stone! Ilusha told me to. I won’t let them carry him out!”
For three days now he had been saying that he would bury the boy by the stone. But Alyosha, Krassotkin, the landlady, her sister and all the boys stepped in to stop him.

“What a notion, burying him by an unholy stone, as if he’d hanged himself!” the old landlady said sharply. “The ground in the churchyard has been blessed with the cross. He’ll be prayed for there. You can hear the singing in church, and the deacon reads so clearly, every word, that it’ll reach him each time as though it were read over his grave.”

At last the captain made a hopeless gesture, as if to say, “Take him where you want.” The boys lifted the coffin. As they passed the mother, though, they paused and lowered it so she could say good-by to Ilusha. For three days she had seen that precious little face only from far off. Now, seeing it close, she shook all over, and her gray head began to jerk wildly above the coffin.

“Mother, make the sign of the cross over him, bless him, kiss him,” Nina cried to her. But the head kept jerking like a machine’s. Her face twisted with bitter grief, and without a word she began beating her breast with her fist. They carried the coffin past her, and as it went by, Nina pressed her lips to her brother’s for the last time. On his way out of the house, Alyosha asked the landlady to look after the people left behind. She cut him off before he had finished.
“Of course I’ll stay with them. We’re Christians, too.” The old woman was crying as she said it.

The church was not far, no more than three hundred paces. The day was clear and still, with a light frost, and the church bells were still ringing. Snegiryov ran after the coffin, fussing and distraught, in his short old summer overcoat, bareheaded, his soft, battered, wide-brimmed hat in his hand. He seemed bewildered and anxious. At one moment he put out a hand to hold up the head of the coffin and only got in the bearers’ way. At the next he ran alongside, trying to find some place for himself. A flower dropped onto the snow, and he dashed to pick it up, as if everything in the world depended on that one lost flower.

“And the crust of bread, we forgot the crust!” he cried suddenly, in dismay. But the boys reminded him right away that he had already taken the crust and that it was in his pocket. He pulled it out at once and calmed down.

“Ilusha told me to, Ilusha did,” he explained quickly to Alyosha. “I was sitting by him one night when he suddenly said, ‘Father, when my grave is filled in, crumble a piece of bread on it, so the sparrows will come down. I’ll hear them, and it’ll cheer me up, not to be lying alone.’”
“That’s a good thing,” said Alyosha. “We should take some often.”
“Every day, every day!” said the captain quickly, seeming comforted by the thought.

At last they reached the church and set the coffin down in the middle. The boys formed a ring around it and stood reverently there through the whole service. It was an old church, rather poor, with many ikons that had lost their settings. But such churches are the best for praying in. During the mass Snegiryov became somewhat calmer, though now and then the same unconscious, and as it were incoherent, anxiety broke out again. Once he went up to the coffin to straighten the cover or the wreath. Another time a candle fell from its holder, and he rushed to put it back and spent a dreadfully long time fumbling with it. Then he sank back and stood quietly by the coffin, looking blankly uneasy and perplexed. After the Epistle he suddenly whispered to Alyosha, who stood beside him, that it had not been read properly, but he did not say what he meant. During the prayer “Like the Cherubim,” he joined in the singing but did not follow it to the end. He fell to his knees, pressed his forehead to the stone floor, and stayed that way a long time.

Then came the funeral service itself, and candles were handed round. The distracted father started fussing again, but the touching, solemn prayers for the dead moved him and woke his soul. He seemed suddenly to shrink into himself and burst into quick, short sobs. At first he tried to smother them, but in the end he sobbed out loud. When they began the farewells and went to close the coffin, he flung out his arms as if he would not let them cover Ilusha, and kissed his dead boy on the lips, greedily and again and again. They finally talked him into stepping back from the platform, but suddenly he put out his hand on impulse and snatched a few flowers from the coffin. He looked at them, and some new idea seemed to strike him, so that for a minute he apparently forgot his grief. Little by little he seemed to fall into a brooding state, and he did not resist when the coffin was lifted and taken to the grave. It was an expensive one, in the churchyard right next to the church; Katerina Ivanovna had paid for it. After the usual rites the grave-diggers lowered the coffin. Snegiryov, flowers in hand, leaned so far over the open grave that the boys seized his coat in alarm and pulled him back. He did not seem fully to understand what was going on. When they started to fill in the grave, he suddenly pointed in anxiety at the falling earth and tried to say something. No one could make out what he meant, and he broke off. Then someone reminded him that he must crumble the bread. He was terribly excited, grabbed the bread, and began tearing it up and throwing the pieces onto the grave.
“Come on, fly down, birds, fly down, sparrows!” he muttered anxiously.

One of the boys pointed out that it was awkward to crumble bread with flowers in his hands, and suggested he give them to someone to hold for a while. He refused. He seemed suddenly frightened for his flowers, as though people wanted to take them from him altogether. Then he looked at the grave and, as it were, made sure that everything had been done and the bread crumbled. Suddenly, to everyone’s surprise, he turned and started for home, even calmly. But his pace quickened more and more until he was almost running. The boys and Alyosha kept up with him.
“The flowers are for mamma, the flowers are for mamma! I was unkind to mamma,” he suddenly began crying out.

Someone shouted to him to put his hat on, since it was cold. He threw the hat into the snow, as if in anger, and kept saying, “I won’t have the hat, I won’t have the hat.” Smurov picked it up and carried it after him. All the boys were crying, Kolya and the boy who had found out about Troy most of all. Smurov, the captain’s hat in his hand, was crying bitterly too. Even so, as he ran, he managed to snatch up a piece of red brick that lay on the snowy path and hurl it at a flock of sparrows flying past. He missed them, of course, and ran on crying. Halfway home Snegiryov stopped short. He stood still for half a minute as if something had struck him, then turned back toward the church and ran for the deserted grave. But the boys caught up with him at once and grabbed him from every side. Then he dropped helplessly onto the snow as though he had been knocked down, and struggling, sobbing and wailing, he began to cry out, “Ilusha, old man, dear old man!” Alyosha and Kolya tried to get him to his feet, soothing and coaxing him.
“Captain, stop it. A brave man has to hold himself together,” Kolya muttered.
“You’ll ruin the flowers,” said Alyosha. “And Mamma is waiting for them. She’s sitting there crying because you wouldn’t give her any before. Ilusha’s little bed is still there—”

“Yes, yes, Mamma!” Snegiryov suddenly remembered. “They’ll take the bed away, they’ll take it away,” he added, as if afraid they really would. He jumped up and ran for home again. But it was not far, and they all got there together. Snegiryov opened the door in a rush and called out to his wife, the same woman he had quarreled with so cruelly only a little while earlier:

“Mamma, my poor crippled darling, Ilusha has sent you these flowers,” he cried, holding out a little bunch that had been frozen and broken while he struggled in the snow. But at that moment he saw Ilusha’s little boots in the corner by the bed, where the landlady had set them neatly side by side. At the sight of the old, patched, rusty-looking, stiff boots he threw up his hands and rushed to them. He fell on his knees, snatched up one boot, pressed his lips to it and began kissing it greedily, crying, “Ilusha, old man, dear old man, where are your little feet?”

“Where have you taken him? Where have you taken him?” the madwoman cried in a heartbreaking voice. Nina, too, burst into sobs. Kolya ran out of the room, and the boys followed him. At last Alyosha went out too.
“Let them cry,” he said to Kolya. “Trying to comfort them now won’t help. We’ll wait a minute and then go back in.”

“No, it’s no use, it’s awful,” Kolya agreed. “Do you know, Karamazov,” he lowered his voice so that no one could hear, “I feel terribly sad. If it were only possible to bring him back, I’d give anything in the world to do it.”
“Ah, so would I,” said Alyosha.
“What do you think, Karamazov? Should we come back here tonight? He’ll be drunk, you know.”

“Perhaps he will. Let’s come together, you and I. That will be enough, to spend an hour with them, with the mother and Nina. If we all come together, we’ll remind them of everything again,” Alyosha suggested.
“The landlady is laying the table for them now. There’ll be a funeral dinner or something, and the priest is coming. Shall we go back for it, Karamazov?”
“Of course,” said Alyosha.
“It’s all so strange, Karamazov. Such sorrow, and then pancakes after it. It all seems so unnatural in our religion.”
“They’re going to have salmon, too,” the boy who had found out about Troy said in a loud voice.

“I earnestly ask you, Kartashov, not to interrupt again with your idiotic remarks, especially when nobody is talking to you and nobody cares whether you exist or not!” Kolya snapped irritably. The boy turned crimson but did not dare to answer.
Meanwhile they were strolling slowly along the path, and suddenly Smurov exclaimed:
“There’s Ilusha’s stone, the one they wanted to bury him under.”

They all stopped by the big stone. Alyosha looked at it, and the whole picture of what Snegiryov had told him that day rose at once before his imagination: how Ilusha, weeping and hugging his father, had cried, “Father, father, how he insulted you!”
Something seemed to seize his soul all at once. Serious and earnest, he looked from one to another of the bright, pleasant faces of Ilusha’s schoolmates, and then said to them:
“Boys, I’d like to say a word to you, here in this place.”
The boys gathered round him and at once fixed attentive, expectant eyes on him.

“Boys, we shall soon part. For a while I’ll be with my two brothers. One is going to Siberia, and the other is lying at death’s door. But soon I’ll leave this town, perhaps for a long time, so we’ll part. Let’s make a pact here, at Ilusha’s stone, that we will never forget Ilusha, or one another. And whatever happens to us later in life, even if we don’t meet for twenty years, let’s always remember how we buried the poor boy we once threw stones at, do you remember, by the bridge? And afterwards we all grew so fond of him. He was a fine boy, kind-hearted and brave. He cared about his father’s honor, he was hurt by the cruel insult to it, and he stood up for him. So, first of all, boys, we will remember him all our lives. Even if we’re busy with the most important matters, even if we win great honor or fall into terrible misfortune, let’s still remember how good it was here once, when we were all together, joined by a good and kind feeling. For the time we loved that poor boy, it made us better, perhaps, than we really are. My little doves—let me call you that, because you look very like them, those pretty blue birds, at this moment as I look at your good dear faces. My dear children, perhaps you won’t understand what I’m saying to you, because I often speak very unclearly, but you’ll remember it all the same, and some day you’ll agree with my words. You must know that there is nothing higher or stronger or healthier or better for life in the future than some good memory, especially a memory of childhood, of home. People talk to you a great deal about your education. But some good, sacred memory, kept from childhood, is perhaps the best education there is. If a man takes many such memories with him into life, he is safe to the end of his days. And even if only one good memory is left in our hearts, it may save us someday. We may even grow wicked later on. We may be unable to hold back from a bad action, may laugh at men’s tears, and at people who say, as Kolya did just now, ‘I want to suffer for all men,’ and may even jeer spitefully at such people. But however bad we may become—which God forbid—when we remember how we buried Ilusha, how we loved him in his last days, and how we have been talking like friends all together at this stone, the cruelest and most mocking of us, if we do become so, will not dare to laugh inwardly at having been kind and good at this moment! What’s more, perhaps that one memory may keep him from great evil, and he will stop and say, ‘Yes, I was good and brave and honest then!’ Let him laugh to himself, that doesn’t matter. A man often laughs at what’s good and kind. That’s only from thoughtlessness. But I assure you, boys, that as he laughs he will say at once in his heart, ‘No, I’m wrong to laugh, because that’s not a thing to laugh at.’”
“That will be so, I understand you, Karamazov!” cried Kolya, his eyes flashing.
The boys were excited and wanted to say something too, but they held back, watching the speaker intently and with deep feeling.

“I say this in case we become bad,” Alyosha went on, “but there’s no reason why we should become bad, is there, boys? Let’s be, first and above all, kind, then honest, and then let’s never forget each other! I say that again. For my part I give you my word that I’ll never forget a single one of you. Every face looking at me now I’ll remember, even thirty years from now. Just now Kolya said to Kartashov that we didn’t care whether he exists or not. But I can’t forget that Kartashov exists, and that he isn’t blushing now as he did when he found out who founded Troy, but is looking at me with his jolly, kind, dear little eyes. Boys, my dear boys, let’s all be generous and brave like Ilusha, clever, brave and generous like Kolya (though he’ll be ever so much cleverer when he’s grown up), and let’s all be as modest, as clever and as sweet as Kartashov. But why am I talking about those two? You are all dear to me, boys, from this day on. I have a place in my heart for every one of you, and I ask you to keep a place in your hearts for me! Well, and who has united us in this kind, good feeling which we shall remember and mean to remember all our lives? Who, if not Ilusha, the good boy, the dear boy, precious to us for ever! Let’s never forget him. May his memory live for ever in our hearts from this time on!”
“Yes, yes, for ever, for ever!” the boys cried in their ringing voices, their faces softened.
“Let’s remember his face, his clothes, his poor little boots, his coffin, his unhappy, sinful father, and how boldly he stood up for him, alone against the whole school.”
“We’ll remember, we’ll remember,” cried the boys. “He was brave, he was good!”
“Ah, how I loved him!” exclaimed Kolya.
“Ah, children, ah, dear friends, don’t be afraid of life! Life is so good when you do something good and just!”
“Yes, yes,” the boys repeated eagerly.
“Karamazov, we love you!” a voice, probably Kartashov’s, cried out impulsively.
“We love you, we love you!” they all echoed. Many of them had tears in their eyes.
“Hurrah for Karamazov!” Kolya shouted in ecstasy.
“And may the dead boy’s memory live for ever!” Alyosha added again, with feeling.
“For ever!” the boys chimed in again.
“Karamazov,” cried Kolya, “can it be true, what they teach us in religion, that we shall all rise from the dead and live and see each other again, all of us, Ilusha too?”
“Of course we’ll all rise again. Of course we’ll see each other, and we’ll tell each other, with joy and gladness, everything that has happened!” Alyosha answered, half laughing, half carried away.
“Ah, how splendid it will be!” broke from Kolya.

“Well, now we’ll finish talking and go to his funeral dinner. Don’t be put off by our eating pancakes—it’s a very old custom, and there’s something nice in it!” laughed Alyosha. “Well, let’s go! And now we go hand in hand.”
“And always like this, all our lives, hand in hand! Hurrah for Karamazov!” Kolya cried once more, rapturously, and once more the boys took up his cry: “Hurrah for Karamazov!”
THE END
